Uniform Title: Pauṣkaravṛtti Author: Jñānaprakāśācārya (also known as Jñānaprakāśa)
Manuscript: IFP Transcript 110

Description: Transcribed from a manuscript belonging to the Tondaimandalam Jñānaprakāśasvāmigal Maṭha in Kāñcīpuram, Cuddalore District. This is a palm-leaf manuscript measuring 4 cm × 36 cm, containing an average of ten lines per page. The handwriting is quite legible. The manuscript comprises the Daśakāryam, Pauṣkarajñānapadaḥ, and Prāsādaṣaṭślokī. It consists of 1 to 219 folios, and the transcript covers 936 pages.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark Dyczkowski.
Revision 0: October 22, 2009.
Place of publication: Pondicherry.
Country of Publication: India (p.
1). Hariḥ Oṃ. Pauṣkaravṛttiḥ.
Having prostrated before Gaṇeśa, Śiva along with his younger brother and Ambā, Vāgīśvarī, and the gurus,
I shall now compose this commentary on the Pauṣkara, which is a portion of the Vidyā.

Then, for the sake of the liberation of those men whose impurity (mala) takes the form of an obstacle that conceals their own innate auspiciousness— the state of being Śiva— and who have not yet attained the state of being "beyond the bindu" (abindu), the illustrious Supreme Lord, whose body consists of the five mantras, for the purpose of bestowing grace, proclaimed the Tantra named Pārameśvara.

He taught this Vidyā, composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter and numbering ten million verses, to the supreme king of kings, Ananta. Subsequently, having condensed it to one hundred thousand verses, he taught it to the illustrious Śrīkaṇṭha. He, in turn, abridged it further for Pauṣkara.

From the Supreme Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, who was teaching that which is celebrated by the name *Pīgeeta*, the sages Sanaka and others, having studied the two sections known as Kriyā and Caryā, [said]: "Now, the section called Jñāna must indeed be thoroughly accomplished. [This refers to] that which consists of the definition of the categories (*padārtha*) beginning with the six *patayas*.
Desiring to hear the section on knowledge (*jñānapāda*), and considering that an address to the Guru in the form of praise is itself auspicious,
they directed their attention toward him and addressed him as follows:
"O Blessed One, O God, Lord of Gods, Leader of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra!"
With a crest of matted hair tinged with reddish-brown, he bears the crescent moon as his head-ornament.
O ocean of compassion, you who wear a tiger skin as an upper garment and are adorned with serpents, you are constantly attended by hosts of enemy deer.
O you who burned the three cities and the god of love with the seven-flamed fire from your forehead-eye;
O you whose neck was darkened by the poison produced during the churning of the ocean.

"Bhagavan"—*bhaga* is characterized by manifest, pure *vidyā* (knowledge), because it possesses within itself the intensely radiant subtle body that is the locus of all knowledge; *aiśvarya* (sovereignty) consists of omniscience and the power of being the creator of everything within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). He who possesses these is thus [called *Bhagavat*]. This is the address to one who is such.

There exists the unsurpassed and inconceivable [power] of *aṇimā* and the rest. Although the state of Śiva (*śivatva*) is manifest, it was disregarded by the venerable Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, even though it is praiseworthy. Furthermore: "Of complete sovereignty, heroism, fame, and fortune..."
And indeed, the Vedic revelation states that "bhaga" consists of knowledge, dispassion, and the [other] six qualities.

Since the word *bhaga* functions by denoting six meanings, this [address] may be an invocation of one or another of these [qualities] belonging to someone like us who is endowed with dispassion (*vairāgya*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). Therefore, it says "O Deva.
He is called *deva* because he has the nature of sporting (*devana*) by means of the splendor characterized by *śivatva*. Thus, it is an invocation of him who is such.

Furthermore, although the word *deva* has an unrestricted application and might refer to any one of those who dwell in their own respective worlds, it is therefore addressed here as "Lord of the Gods" (*deveśa*). He is so called because he is the Lord and the commander of the gods; this is an address to one who is such. Even though that [status] indeed exists...

This may be an address to any one among Svayambhū and the others. Therefore, the phrase "this is Brahmā" and so forth refers to the leader or guide of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra; it is an address to one who has become such [a leader].
Furthermore, although the gods of gods—Kubera and the other seven—are indivisible from Īśa, the Great Lord (Maheśvara).

That great Mount Meru is described as being such that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the illustrious Mṛgendra, as previously mentioned, reside upon their respective peaks as sovereign lords; for there, the application of the term "Bhagavat" is also possible,
since He is worthy of it by virtue of His divinity, and thus there may be two forms of address for Him who is of such a nature.
Therefore, this [is expressed] by the phrase "āpiṅgala" and so forth. *Āpiṅgalā* means that which has become yellowish on all sides;
it refers to the massing of matted locks (*jaṭā*), that is to say, a topknot (*cūḍā*) or a braid (*kabarda*). Upon that is placed half of the moon, an *ardhendu*;
that itself is the crest-ornament (*śekhara*), the decoration for the head. Furthermore, it is like a topknot of matted locks that is yellowish-brown.
He whose crests—meaning the peaks characterized by those [crests]—are thus, is addressed as such;

and he upon whom half of Mount Meru has been placed by contemporary poets for the sake of indicating its loftiness is "one upon whom half is placed" (āropitārdhaḥ); and that Meru whose crest—the head-ornament—is the moon, is likewise described.
And as for the phrase "the address of one who has become such": there would be two separate addresses by dividing that very Meru mentioned previously.

Therefore, this [phrase] beginning with *vyāghra* (tiger) means: he whose garment (*paridhāna*)—that is, his clothing—is the skin (*carma*) of a tiger (*vyāghra*), which is an antelope-skin (*ajina*); he is described as being "of such a nature," and this is the address of one who has become such.

Furthermore, considering that there is a suffix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*), [the compound] *vyāghrapuṇḍarīkāḥ* means "there are tigers and white lotuses here, which are incapable of being used for clothing";
thus, it would be an address to that very Meru previously mentioned, as it is such [a place]. Therefore, this [phrase] follows after that.

Regarding the term *vyālabandhana*: "above that" means above the garment of deerskin (*ajināmbara*); "binding of the serpent" (*vyālabandhana*) refers to the binding of a snake (*vyāla*). He who possesses such [a garment] is so described; this is an address to him who is thus situated.
Furthermore, "above that"—meaning above the aforementioned dwelling place of the ascetic—is *Tripura*.

The term "dahanārtha-dhanurbhūtīkartum-jyārūpīkṛta-vyālasya-bandhana-nibandhana" refers to that which has as its binding the tethering of a serpent transformed into the form of a bowstring for the purpose of burning [the enemy] with a bow; such is the address to Meru mentioned previously. Therefore, it says "this very one is eternal," and so forth. "Eternal" (nityam) means always by the enemies.
He who is served by elephants, by deer, by antelopes, and by hosts of those who have become animals;
and he who is a "treasure of generosity" (*dadyānidhi*) and likewise a "mine of compassion" (*karuṇākara*)—such is his address. Furthermore, even if [he were] constantly [regarded] as an enemy...

It is that place where the great sages—who are oceans of compassion and who are served by a multitude (*anīka*) of animals such as elephants and lions existing in the present, whose pride has vanished through the majesty of beholding the Great One (*Amitābha*)—are found;
this is an address to Meru itself, which was mentioned previously. Therefore, it is this very one.

"O you by whom Tripura and Manmatha were burnt by the seven-rayed fire arising from that eye on the forehead"—this is how he is addressed. In this context, "Tripura" is used as an illustration; furthermore, it implies that the forehead-eye and the seven-rayed fire consumed the bodiless one (Ananga).

Up to this point: he who possesses three cities (*tripura*) that have been brought under his own control—that is, the three worlds—and who, because of the beautiful regions of the five-arrowed god of love (*manmatha*), is the cause of sexual union (*surata*); such is the address to Meru as previously described. Therefore, [the phrase] "this ocean" (*tadimambhodhi*) and so forth follows.

That in which waters (*ambhāṃsi*) are always stored is called the ocean (*ambhodhi*). By way of indicating the genus, it is referred to here as the Milk Ocean (*kṣīrasamudra*). Then, by the poison (*viṣa*) or venom (*garala*) produced and arisen from the churning—that is, from the whirling of Mount Mandara—he whose neck (*kaṃdhara*) or throat (*śirodhara*) was darkened or turned blue is such [as described].

The word "O Blessed One" (*bhagavan*) is to be supplied [to the verse]. Nor should it be said that there is conceptualization (*vikalpatā*) here either; for there is no basis [for such a claim], as it would be fruitless. As it has been said: "Without a purpose, one does not abandon the primary meaning of a word.
Thus, by means of the qualifiers "the burner of the city" (*puradahana*) and so forth, [the Lord] is recited among the *vidyeśvaras* and *yogīśvaras*.

Having addressed the Guru named Śrīkaṇṭha—who is distinguished from the two [other] Śrīkaṇṭhas, who dwells in the world of Śiva situated beyond the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and within the city of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and who is the bestower of the state of Śiva—the [disciple] asked: "For what purpose have I addressed you? That must be told. Thus [he spoke] to all.

Having shown the manner of conventional usage by stating that even when wealth exists, it is characterized by its non-perception, the Blessed One addressed them again; they then joyfully revealed his own intention:
"In the past, we heard from you with favor regarding the practice of ritual action."
Now, my desire to hear about the section on knowledge (jñānapāda) is very great.
"O Lord, it behoves you to remove that from us.
In response to the inquiry, "O Lord, what should you do?", they say:
"Our desire—that is, our longing or mental inclination directed toward another—is active; it speaks out. It behoves you to remove it, that is, to turn it away."

That is to say, "to fulfill by means of the attainment of an object. Now, one might ask: since this desire possesses a pure object according to the doctrine of Darśana, why is it not revealed as such within the self—as a manifestation of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) that is the function of Śiva-śakti augmented by Śiva-rāga? True; [it is not so revealed] because, for the most part, [the two are] inseparable.

Because it is to be known solely through the Vidyāpāda, it appears to the great sages—who have not attained the vision beyond that—as a mere mental modification (*manovṛtti*). Thus, there is no fault in what has been said. To make it known that [the scripture] is to be fulfilled by the attainment of its object, they declare that it is not devoid of objects (*nirviṣayā*), nor is it characterized by censurable objects (*nigarhitaviṣayā*).

"To hear" means to listen to the "foot of knowledge. This means that when there exists an object characterized by such a scripture (śruti), the intellects, through the medium of their respective sense organs, exert themselves to determine both the word and its referent (padārtha).

Now, since here, along with the vision of Śiva, there must also be performed the discernment between the state of being Śiva and the state of being a bound soul (paśu), this desire— which has realized the meaning of the words and sentences heard, is sustained by Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā),
and presides over a mind in which the qualities of rajas and tamas have been destroyed— is manifested through the function of the power of Śiva.
It is as stated in the *Śrīmataṅga* and other scriptures that one is able to discern and perceive [the Self] through the function (*vṛtti*) of the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*).

Why has this not been demonstrated here? True. The sages, though their conscious vision is embraced by that Pure Knowledge (*śuddha-vidyā*) when impelled by Śiva, do not know the meaning of the words of that [scripture]. As for us, we [do not know] that Pure...

"Those who do not know the nature of consciousness embraced by knowledge (vidyā) [are the ones meant]; thus, there is no fault of omission. Even if the subject matter is blameless, it is not proper to teach that which is too meager; therefore, following the conclusion of the Lord’s statement, they demonstrate its greater weight beforehand. Although "garīyasī" means "heavier," it implies "more weighty."

"It is not proper to instruct those who have not been initiated. Recalling the Lord’s statement regarding the cessation of [their] departure, they announce His existence, saying: "Formerly" (*purā*), previously, by Your grace—that is, by the favor in the form of initiation which is the motivator for hearing [the teachings] and so forth—we [attained] the *Kriyā* and *Caryā* [sections]; that is, the *Kriyāpāda* and *Caryāpāda*. (p. 12)

In the word *śrute* (in the hearing), the particle *tu* (*srutau*) is used for emphasis; the meaning is that "now," at this present time, the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is the subject without distinction, so let no alternative view be entertained here. Then, [the phrase] *bhaviṣyat bhavata iti* ("it will be for you") indicates: "Why then do you not teach us [this]?"—thus pointing out that while [the scripture] concerns the means (*sādhana*), it also concerns the goal (*sādhya*). And [the phrase] *tadena naḥ kim iti* ("then what is that to us?"). By using the suffix *-natva*, he suggests that you are not a teacher [of this]. And [the phrase] *sādhanaviṣayā sati sādhya-viṣayaśca* ("being concerned with the means, it is also concerned with the goal").
They report:
"O Lord, we have been appointed by you to this office;
for the office is to be accomplished through knowledge, and liberation is its manifestation, O Sovereign."

"O Lord, *adhikāra* is that by which one is authorized (*adhikriyate*) and favored (*anugṛhyate*). Favor toward the bound souls (*paśu-anugraha*) occurs through the restraint of their fetters (*pāśa-nigraha*). In this regard, we have been appointed and impelled by Your Honor. Here, let it be—what is the use of this?"—with these words of the Blessed One intended to discourage [the gods], he addresses them again with the particle *hi* to state his own position.

Indicating what is well-known, they say: "O Lord, since authority (*adhikāra*) is to be accomplished through knowledge, that authority—which consists of the characteristics of the agent and the performance of initiation—is established by the fact that it would otherwise be impossible [otherwise]; thus, the categories such as the Lord (*pati*) and so forth are established through the hearing of the *Jñānapāda*."
When one’s own true nature (*svarūpa*) is fully known, that which is to be accomplished must arise; therefore, you ought to instruct me on that.

Because there is a single syntactical connection (*ekakriyānvaya*) up to this point, there is an *anuṣaṅga* (supplying of a word from a previous sentence). By means of knowledge, its state of being "to be accomplished" is brought to completion. To the question, "What is the nature of that [accomplishment]?", they say: "Liberation (*mukti*) and manifestation (*vyakti*)."

The liberation from the three bonds (*pāśatraya-vimocana*) means, in effect, the characteristic of bestowing the state of Śiva (*śivatva*). In the *Mataṅga-vṛtti*, the Vidyās say to the Vidyeśa: "Our office has been fulfilled by us through the cutting of the bonds and the manifestation of the state of Śiva for the bound souls (*paśu*), as this was commanded by the Lord; [we now abide] in the form of the Teacher (*ācārya-mūrtistha*)."

Because [the terms] "Śiva’s manifestation of liberation" and "the seeker of liberation’s manifestation of liberation" are established [as having the same meaning], it is like saying "Devadatta’s cooking" or "the cooking of rice. Some claim that it means "one's own liberation and manifestation," but since this is already established without needing to state each [term] individually, such an explanation is indeed improper. Furthermore, if one takes pleasure even in that [interpretation], it remains to be proven.

In this context, the ellipsis must be supplied as follows: "Thus, for us, such a systematic connection is not possible," and "this is what is to be established. Having considered that this much [explanation] would be difficult to comprehend, the Blessed One, for the sake of easy understanding, first began to teach by setting aside the knowledge concerning the categories of the Jñānapāda.
O best of the twice-born, that by which the six categories beginning with Pati are known is called the Jñānapāda, which is the means for those whose self is the Guru.

O best of the twice-born, the phrase "the most excellent among those initiated" should not be explained as meaning that they have been consecrated by the Smārta rites because their pure status as twice-born is evident specifically through initiation (*dīkṣā*) among the four castes;
for without *dīkṣā*, one lacks the qualification to hear the Śiva-āgamas. By means of this, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is manifested.

The primordial Lord, augmented by the portions of the Tantra through Śiva and Śakti, [is the source]; and at the end [of that process], the six categories—beginning with the Lord and headed by Śiva—are known and understood as the entities (*vastūni*).
Those whose nature (*ātman*) or essential being is that of the Teacher (*deśika*), the instructor, are called "those whose self is the Teacher" (*deśikātmānaḥ*).

The means (*sādhana*) and the knowledge (*jñāna*) of those who are the guides (*deśika-ātman*), as well as their feet—the "Feet of Knowledge" (*jñānapāda*)—are said to be "Awakening" (*bodhana*) and "Tranquility" (*śama*); this is the collective teaching in the *Āgamas*, the word being neuter due to Vedic usage.
For one who desires liberation, the scripture is primary for the commencement of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and exposition (*vyākhyāna*), while initiation is primary for the practitioner.

It was stated [in the previous verse] "for the sake of making known those whose nature is that of a teacher" (*deśikātmanām*); the meaning is that this is the means of realization (*sādhana*) even for practitioners (*sādhaka*) and others. Now, one might object: since it is Śiva’s power alone that manifests the consciousness-will (*cicchakti*), and because the reality of Śiva and so forth is luminous, it is that power which is denoted by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Why then is the scripture (*śāstra*) mentioned? It is because [the reality] is to be illuminated [by the scripture], and not [manifested] by itself.

Anticipating the objection that the entity beginning with Śiva, being of the nature of light, must itself be the illuminator [of knowledge], the Blessed One says: "The stainless power inherent in Śiva, which consists of knowledge—that alone is declared to be 'knowledge'; verbal testimony is merely its indicator."

That which is inherent in Śiva, related to him through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), is of the nature of knowledge; that whose essence (*ātman*) is knowledge—that is, awakening—is thus described. It is stainless, meaning that no impurity exists in it. That very power (*śakti*), whose strength is such, is declared to be knowledge itself. The neuter form (*klībokti*) is used because it is expressed as a collective whole (*samudita*) by means of the predicate and other grammatical elements.

The verbal [scripture], being of the nature of a treatise, is not a means of inference for that [Śiva] because it lacks the status of a [direct] instrument; thus, its own [nature] is unsurpassed. Nor is it otherwise impossible [to know Śiva] through the impossibility of its own manifestation [occurring] otherwise, nor through the impossibility of its revealing Śiva and so forth otherwise; and he will state that "the words... [will convey the knowledge of Śiva].

The sense is this: since [these means] lead to the inference of the knowledge of Śiva through a traditional lineage (*pāramparya*), and because it is easy for this [knowledge]—which is the illuminator of Śiva and so forth—to arise by means of that power (*śakti*) which is the agent of Śiva and the ground for the manifestation of the knowledge of Śiva, why is it not well-known as being designated by the term "verbal knowledge" (*śiva-jñāna-śabda*)? Or rather, it is verbal (*śābdam*).

That knowledge of Śiva, when ascended upon the word (*śabdārūḍha*), is the means of inference; being the manifester of the valid means of knowledge characterized by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), it is the subsequent means of knowledge (*anuvyavasāya-pramāṇa*) here. For instance, the power of Śiva, having ascended upon the word and supporting the power of consciousness, [reveals] its own self as Śiva and so forth.
He shows those who have been initiated together with the *vastu* (the objective reality). As it is said in the *Mokṣakārikās*:
"In the word consisting of mantra and tantra, Śiva is the manifestation (*vyakti*) and also in the *kalās*;
the eye of consciousness (*cic-chakṣus*) validates this, and therefore nothing is contradictory."

Is it not the case that because of the scripture stating "Śiva empowers," this scripture [establishes] one for whom Śiva is well-empowered? Is it not the case that the power is well-empowered? True. For there is the scripture stating, "An action cannot exist without an instrument," and "The power is never without Śiva.
This scripture may also establish one for whom the power is well-empowered, as it expresses both injunction and prohibition.
The command of the Lord, His power, and the word are eternal, while the scripture may be either eternal or non-eternal.
Indicating that the knowledge of the true nature of the categories (padārthas) becomes easily accessible once their enumeration, definition, and examination have been performed, [the author],
showing that "enumeration" (uddeśa) consists in the mere mention of names, thus mentions them.
He recites this first sūtra:
"The Lord, Kuṇḍalinī, Māyā, the bound soul (paśu), and the fetter (pāśa), as well as the agent—
these six categories have been briefly declared in the Śaiva Tantra."

At the commencement of each subsequent chapter (*paṭala*), the fivefold relationship (*pañcavidhasambandha*) is stated; for in each case, the subject matter (*vastu*) consists of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*). Among these, the "relationship of the subject matter" (*vastusambandha*) pertains to each individual category. The "contextual relationship" (*prākaraṇika*), however, pertains to the chapters (*pāda*) and consists of the Chapter on Knowledge (*vidyāpāda*). And that—

Up until the Vidyāpāda, [the text] remains of a single form. But what is the use of his words? As for the statements in the Sūtra, since they follow immediately after the first Sūtra of the Tantra and constitute the Patalas, it is impossible to speak of them [separately]. However, the meaning of the verses will become easy to understand through the statement of their characteristics. First, the enumeration (uddeśa).

Because He is the presiding lord of all, [the power of] *pratibhu* follows; because of the capacity for its appropriation (*parigraha*), [the powers of] *bindu* and *māyā* follow. Even there, first, by way of direct appropriation through its purity, there is *bindu*; then, together with *māyā*, there is the *paśu*, who possesses the relationship of being the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment; and after that, the *pāśa* (bond) arising from such a relationship. Then...

The distinction is that [the cause] is the agent who effects the manifestation of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) by severing its connection [to the object]. Making known that "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) is a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), he defines them in sequence; first, he defines [the *pradhāna*]:
it is characterized by the threefold activity consisting of dissolution (*laya*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and authority (*adhikāra*).
An entity that is capable and never falls from its own nature is designated as the Lord (pati).
That which is described in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures—beginning with "Now, the presiding presence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Lord consists of the rays of His own power;

in that [power], He whose nature is intensely radiant, possessing an unwavering and immovable form"—is characterized by these specific attributes. Following that, He is characterized by the threefold activity consisting of dissolution (*laya*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and authority (*adhikāra*). Dissolution...

The maintenance of one's own nature through the suspension of one's own power (śakti) and the capacity for action is *bhoga* (enjoyment), which is the preservation of the *bindu*. *Adhikāra* (sovereignty) is the manifestation of the essential form of that activity. He is characterized, marked, and distinguished by these three functions defined by such characteristics. Now, are those operations not of the nature of vibration (*spanda*)?

Marked by those [attributes], he becomes subject to transformation. True. That which is, by its very nature, motionless and not fallen away from its own inherent property (*svadharma*), has not degenerated. But surely, agency consists in the penetration of action; if that were the case, how could there be non-falling away for it? True. That which is capable and competent—this is the intended meaning. It does not fall. It is not fallen. It is not lost. It is not destroyed. It is not severed. It is not split. It is not divided. It is not differentiated. It is not manifold. It is not many. It is not various. It is not diverse. It is not distinct. It is not separate. It is not other. It is not different. It is not another. It is not a second. It is not a third. It is not a fourth. It is not a fifth. It is not a sixth. It is not a seventh. It is not an eighth. It is not a ninth. It is not a tenth. It is not a hundred. It is not a thousand. It is not a hundred thousand. It is not a *koṭi*. It is not a *madhya*. It is not a *madhyamadhyama*. It is not a *madhyottama*. It is not an *uttama*. It is not an *uttamottama*. It is not an *anuttama*. It is not an *anuttamottama*. It is not an *anuttamānuttama*. It is not a *parama*. It is not a *parāpara*. It is not a *parāparottama*. It is not a *parāparānuttama*. It is not a *parāparānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvottama*. It is not a *sarvottamottama*. It is not a *sarvottamānuttama*. It is not a *sarvaparāpara*. It is not a *sarvaparāparottama*. It is not a *sarvaparāparānuttama*. It is not a *sarvaparāparānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvasarva*. It is not a *sarvasarvottama*. It is not a *sarvasarvottamottama*. It is not a *sarvasarvottamānuttama*. It is not a *sarvasarvaparāpara*. It is not a *sarvasarvaparāparottama*. It is not a *sarvasarvaparāparānuttama*. It is not a *sarvasarvaparāparānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamottama*. It is not a *sarvānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamānuttamān

Because it is of the nature of vibration (*spandana*), there is no form of action (*kriyā*) here. The agency of the agent does not consist in the performance of an action, as that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress through the postulation of further actions. Rather, it is the capacity to produce the vibration of an insentient object. As it has been said regarding the vibration of an insentient thing: "That which is the power [to act] is the agency of consciousness; because of its pervasiveness, it is without vibration."

"By form, like a perfected lump of iron, [it exists] by itself. Thus, he who possesses the state of being an entity is designated as "Lord" (*pati*); that is, the name "Lord" has arisen for him, or he is so designated. He is one whose name has been established as "Lord. In the state of dissolution (*layāvasthā*), because Śiva is devoid of power (*aśaktitvāt*), those possessing the supreme form are included along with him. [This refers to] the state of enjoyment (*bhogāvasthā*).
Because they possess powers equal to Śiva’s, the presiding lords of the worlds such as Śāntyatītā and the rest are included with him;

because they possess powers equal to Śiva’s while in their state of office (*adhikārāvastha*), the Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and Mantramaheśvaras are included with him. And those characterized by his defining marks are designated as "Lord" (*pati*) because of their belonging to the same genus (*sajāti*).

They are not names; nevertheless, they are mantras and so forth. And in the investigations of other categories of objects (*padārtha*), certain other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are described in relation to them. It defines the second [category]:
"That in which there is the activity of dissolution and so forth, arising from the pure state."
She, indeed, is Kuṇḍalinī, whose form is the eternal object of Śambhu’s presiding presence.

The conclusion is that [the powers] undergo the conventional designation of "dissolution" (laya) and so forth because they are the causes for Śiva’s activity consisting of dissolution and the rest. Therefore, "wherein" means in which [power] there is the activity of dissolution and so forth. Dissolution is the withdrawal of effects;
that of which this is the beginning is "the activity of dissolution and the rest. In reality, this occurs by virtue of being the cause thereof. Since—
That in whom the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) or the pure way (*śuddhamārga*), consisting of mantras and so forth, is born from the night [of ignorance]—

by means of the *ciṇ* suffix in the sense of the agent in the phrase "born from a lamp" (*dīpajanyā*) and so on— she is the eternal one, devoid of beginning and end, the form to be presided over by Śambhu, the path of the possession of Śiva; she is indeed named Kuṇḍalinī, the third [power].
He defines it:
That which produces the body, the sense organs, and so forth for the sake of accomplishing the state of being an enjoyer and the objects of enjoyment,
is Māyā, which is conditioned by the actions (karma) of men.

For the sake of achieving the state of being the enjoyer of objects to be enjoyed, which would otherwise be impossible without an instrument of action, and for the sake of establishing the relationship between the two selves— the object of knowledge and the knower characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion— the Supreme Lord, pervaded by His infinite power, [projects] the body, the senses, and so forth; that is, the principles beginning with *kalā*, of which the body and senses are the first.

That which is so described as "born" produces—that is, generates—that [body] in that [state]; it arises when that body, senses, and so forth have dissolved into its own [source], because the intellect (*buddhi*) of other men has been withdrawn by their [respective] karmas. Since it would follow that the *puruṣa* would be subject to modification if it were a product of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), it is called by the name "the one who has resided" (*kharcitā*), meaning it is supported or dependent upon [the source]. It is thus designated as "that which is being gathered together" (*sāmāyamānā*).
He defines the fourth [category]:

"The bound soul (paśu) is one whose expansion of perception and action is always firmly rooted in the state of being a bound soul (paśutva). It exists in three ways according to the division of *kalās* and *akalās*, due to the power of bondage."

"Whose expansion of vision and action is always obstructed by the state of being a bound soul (paśutva)" means: he whose expansion of vision and action is completely obstructed—that is, thoroughly suppressed—by the impurity of *paśutva*, and whose primary objects [of experience] are such [suppressed states]. Furthermore, [he is so called] because of bondage through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the three impurities, two impurities, or one impurity.

He exists in three ways through the division of *sakala* (with parts) and *vikala* (without parts). He who is determined by the three types of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is given the name "bound soul" (*paśu*). By the word "always" (*sadā*), it is indicated that once he has been restrained by initiation (*dīkṣā*) and has fallen from his state of opposition [to the Lord], he is no longer a bound soul; thus, the reading should be understood as "not a bound soul."
He defines the fifth [category]: "The real aggregate, beginning with Time and ending with Earth,
which exists as a collection— this category, consisting of bonds (*pāśa*), is enumerated as the fifth."

That which begins with *kalā* and ends with *kṣiti* (earth) is "from *kalā* to *kṣiti*" (*kalādikṣitiparyantā*). Being thus situated and established, it is real (*tāttvikī*) because it arises from reality (*tatva*). This collection (*saṃhati*) is real; this entity, being a real aggregate, consists of bonds (*pāśātmaka*). It is given the name "bond" (*pāśa*).

The fifth [category] is recited. By means of the qualifying attribute "this," the masculine designation indicates the sixth; O best of sages, the sixth category is declared in the Tantra as the one called *dīkṣā*, which consists of ritual action and has as its fruit the manifestation of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).

That [rite] which has as its fruits the manifestation of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*), and whose fruits are those very manifestations of enjoyment and liberation, is so described because it is the means for achieving the unsurpassed supreme liberation (*paramukti*). It is called *dīkṣā*— the rite known by the name "Initiation"— which is superior to other rites and is the bestower of Śiva-nature.
This category, consisting of throwing and so forth, is designated as the sixth category in the *Śivāgama* tantra.

The meaning is that the sixth [category] in the sequence is designated by the name "kāraka" (the agent). Enjoyment (*bhukti*), however, is of a dual nature—both supreme and non-supreme—due to the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of residing in worlds within *māyā* and being an inhabitant of those worlds. Liberation (*mukti*) also...
The liberated souls (muktas) possess both higher and lower forms due to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of objects such as Śiva, Viṣaya, Ananta, and so forth.

"Manifestation" (*vyakti*) is the manifestation of the state of Śiva-ness (*śivatva*). And that [manifestation] is twofold: "by every means" and "not by every means," corresponding respectively to the completely liberated (*paramukta*) and those whose objects are the completely liberated. It is [further characterized by] one's own system falling away and the other system being transcended.

Those of fallen intellect, the Śaiva-ekadeśins, following certain Vedāntins who claim that liberation comes from knowledge alone, assert that liberation arises from knowledge only and not otherwise. That is indeed improper. For impurity (*mala*) cannot be removed by knowledge; because it obscures the nature of the Self, like cataracts (*timira*). Thus [it is said] regarding impurity.

Because accomplished karma must be exhausted, [liberation] is not granted immediately by those who have received initiation but whose bodies have not yet been discarded; furthermore, because it is non-conclusive even in the case of those who attained immediate liberation through initiation into Śiva performed by a Kevalin—since for them there is no opportunity for the practice of that [initiation]. Now, one might object:
In those who possess only the self, the very power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) of Śiva is called "initiation" (*adīkṣā*) because it is characterized by the conjunction of bestowing and destroying;
this is due to the oneness of power. Furthermore, since it does not abandon its own nature as knowledge (*jñāna-rūpatā*), that same power is also designated by the word "knowledge.
In that case, how can it take the form of throwing clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth? True; even here, the throwing of clarified butter and the like is merely indicative (*lakṣaṇa*).
That action, augmented by ritual performance, is indeed the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Since *saṃskāra* has the person as its object, it is not initiation (*adīkṣā*).

And initiation, which is designated by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), is ultimately established; thus, everything is consistent. Therefore, initiation is an action that is a cause of bondage, because it is an action (*karmatvāt*)—this is the argument advanced by the opponent (on page 28), whereas [in our view] it is rather [a cause of] liberation.

The refutation [of the objection] by pointing out defects—such as the removal of transgressions through rituals like *prāyaścitta* acting as a means of reversal—is not elaborated here, because [the objection] pertains to a semblance of a means of knowledge (*jñānopāya-ābhāsa*) characterized by ritual action that is subject to deviation; for [in our view], immediate liberation (*sadyo-nirvāṇa*) is merely an ancillary part of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) does exist.

Thus, let the secondary nature [of these] be understood. Regarding the doubt as to why there is no enumeration of other categories—since impurity (*mala*), karma, and the principles beginning with Śiva have not been explicitly mentioned because they were already indicated—he says this for the purpose of dispelling it:
"Among the six categories taught, that which begins with Śiva and ends with the earth is the last."
Since everything is contained within it, they are examined by this method.

Because within those six categories, Śiva is the first and the earth is the last; and since the entire collection of principles beginning with Sadāśiva has that [earth] as its final limit, everything from Śiva down to the earth is entirely included and contained therein. For there is no fault of failing to indicate or of being uncharacterized in that regard.

By means of this method and through inference, those six alone are examined and investigated. The sense is that when they have been examined, everything that was indicated, defined, and examined is essentially included therein. Previously, by the statement "arising from the pure path" (*śuddhādhvāvāyatojanī*), the principles of Śiva and so forth were [included] because they are their effects.

By the statement "contained within Kuṇḍalinī and inlaid with karmas," it is shown that karma is contained within Māyā; and by the statement "the bound soul (paśu) is constricted by the state of being a bound soul (paśutva)," since the application of the word *paśu* is impossible without *paśutva*, it follows that impurity (*mala*)— by means of its obstructive power (*rodha-śakti*)— is the factor that underlies the meaning of the term *paśu*.

It is included therein; likewise, everything else is also seen to be included in those respective places later on. Having raised the doubt—by saying "the potter is the creator of the jar, but the water-carrier is its destroyer"—as to whether there is a difference in the agent for the production and destruction of the effect, [the author] says "udaka" (water).

Having considered that the agency of the sun, consisting of emission, withdrawal, and so forth, is established as being of a single nature, [the author], pointing out that this is an unsound view because even a potter is seen to possess such distinct functions, proceeds to examine the meaning of each term in sequence: [p. 30] *sarjanopasaṃhārādiṣṭha bhānorekarūpaṃ kartṛtvaṃ siddhamityākalayya kulālasyāpi tadbhedakatva-darśanāt asādhudarśanamidamiti jñāpayan kramataḥ padārthaparīkṣāṃ vidhatte -* [Translation: Having understood that the agency of the sun—consisting of creation, withdrawal, and so on—is established as being of a single form, [the author], making it known that this is an incorrect observation because even a potter is seen to have those distinct [functions], undertakes an examination of the meaning of the words in order.
In Śiva, there is no real distinction between the states of dissolution, enjoyment, and authority;
however, those [distinctions] pertaining to the *bindu* and the individual souls (*aṇu*) are considered to be real indeed.

It has been indicated that the Lord’s power (*śakti*) alone is the agency (*kartṛtva*) in the prior production of the activity of the vibration of the insentient; because it is capable of accomplishing manifold functions, it assumes manifold designations. Therefore, the distinction between the causes of dissolution, enjoyment, and authority within Śiva is neither real nor inherent; rather, what then?

Among those, the distinctions of the individual souls (*aṇu*s)—namely, the distinctions of the withdrawal of the form of the *bindu*, the distinctions of manifestation, the distinctions of the nature of the performed action, the distinctions of the nature itself, and the distinctions of the worlds—are real; for, according to the principle to be explained, they consist of those who are dissolved [into the cause], those who enjoy, and those who are qualified. These distinctions are indeed inherent and real. (p. 31)

Showing that it does not perceive any modification (*vikṛti*) and indicating its capacity through the production of the activity of dull vibration (*jaḍaspanda-kriyā*), he demonstrates with an illustration how it resorts to figurative designations of difference:
"Just as the sun [is said to produce] the lotus constantly through [its functions of] awakening, drying, and so forth."
In this world, Śiva likewise receives designations such as "the Awakener" (Bodhaka) and so forth on account of his actions.

Just as the sun, never departing from its own nature of heat and light, acts as the awakener by its mere presence, daily effecting through its activities— the opening, drying, and so forth, as well as the blooming, fading, and shining— of the lotus flower;
so too does he [the Lord] act as the awakener.
It receives such designations as "the dryer" and so forth; likewise, in this present context, Śiva—
though in reality distinct from action and consciousness— is designated as "action" because he is the cause thereof,
yet without falling away from his own essential nature or that of others, being characterized by volition (*saṃkalpa*).

By means of its mere proximity— characterized by the relationship with the power qualified by action for the sake of action— it brings about the *bindu* through operations such as dissolution (*laya*) and so forth, thereby receiving the designations of "dissolution" and the rest. To the question, "Why are these designations of dissolution and so forth not simultaneous in Śiva?", he says:
When the *bindu* is established as the self whose functions have been withdrawn, that state is called *laya*; indeed, that itself is the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*).

"When" means at which time; "one whose nature as the effect has been withdrawn" refers to one for whom the effect—the body to be acted upon—is withdrawn, unmanifested, and devoid of causal efficiency; this is because the fourfold set beginning with tranquility (*śānti*) is obscured by its separation from manifestation within the *kalā* that transcends tranquility.

The undivided essence of the *kalās*, designated as the *śivatattva*, is established as the *bindu*. At that time, Kuṇḍalinī remains present. That which serves as the cause for the withdrawal [of the universe] at that moment is the *tattva*. Because its effects have been withdrawn (*upasaṃhṛta*), it possesses the concealment of what is to be done; this is called "dissolution" (*laya*), which is its designation.

The meaning is that it receives the name "laya" (dissolution) because of its suchness. But why is the reality (*tattva*) distinct from this? To this he says: "For that very [reality] is Śiva-reality (*śivatattva*). The word "for" (*hi*) indicates what is well-known. That which is characterized as the substratum is called Śiva-reality; the meaning is that it is precisely that which is the reality of dissolution (*layatattva*). This is the *baindava* (the bindu-nature) which is about to be described.
One might ask: "Does this [consciousness] possess characteristics such as transformation (*pariṇāma*), as do the *tattvas*? He says: "No;

unlike the *tattvas* beginning with *vidyā*, this does not have the characteristic of being 'existent' (*sat*) and so forth. Rather, it is imperishable, consisting of the rays of the powers of self-perception and action."

This [reality] is all-pervasive, eternal, immovable, facing in all directions, and sovereign; because its effects have been withdrawn, it has transcended [the manifest]. Indeed, that which is designated by terms such as Śiva-tattva—which consists of the manifest and its effects—is not [this reality], for the Śiva-tattva characterized as the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), devoid of the bindu and beginning with Vidyā, is not something created.

Like the *tattvas*, those beginning with *sattva* and characterized by the [three] qualities (*guṇas*) are, in reverse order, the starting point for those whose first is *vidyā*— namely, the *tattvas* beginning with *vidyā*, such as *Īśvara*, *Sadāśiva*, and *Śiva*.

Just like the *tattvas* beginning with *vidyā*, the group of five *tattvas* beginning with *Śiva* possesses the states of being "ending in *sattva*" and "having undergone transformation," and so forth.

That which has impermanence and so forth [as its nature] does not possess that characteristic of being a word ending in the suffix *sat* (sannanta), nor does it possess the characteristic of being a word ending in the suffix *sat*. This is merely an illustration; as will be examined immediately below, both [the subject and the predicate] are likewise not so. But what is the nature of that Śiva-tattva? It is self-perceiving (*svadṛk*).

The power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which consists of rays, is of the same nature as that of Śiva himself; it is indeed his ray, being light itself. It is imperishable, devoid of decay because it is not obscured by impurity; it is all-pervading, unconditioned by space, eternal, unconditioned by time, and immovable, yet free from the vibration of the insentient.

Devoid of the form of action, facing all directions, encompassing all objects, and belonging to the Lord— such is the nature of that which pertains to the Lord. Now, having begun to show the reason for designating Śiva as the "Lay" (the place of dissolution) specifically for the Lord, [the text] proceeds to describe the Power, like the Himalaya mountain to one desiring to go to the ocean.
Anticipating the objection that [the Self] is like a wandering entity, he says:
"In that [Self], Śiva resides as the clearly manifest pure consciousness, possessing attributes such as omnipresence; and because of the inherence of His power, He is non-different from it."

Having acquired the designation "Śiva, Śiva," even though he has fallen into that reality of Śiva—which was previously described as consisting of the nature of supreme consciousness and power—he remains clearly pure consciousness alone. Having become specifically and clearly his own self-consciousness (*svasaṃvit*), it shines forth; because it consists solely of the knowledge of itself, it is called "self-consciousness."

That pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), independent of anything else, is the solitary form of consciousness itself; such a form, possessing power, acts as the instrument through the medium of supreme awareness (*para-saṃvitti*). It is the knowledge that has turned away from all objects of knowledge other than itself—whether conscious or unconscious—and it is described as the "activity of manifestation" (*lakṣaṇa-kriyā*) capable of bringing forth the vibration (*spanda*) of the unconscious (*acit*). Thus it was said [previously]. (p. 36) Para.

He is so described because he possesses the characteristic of being an agent (*kartṛ*), having the nature of a knower (*jñātṛ*) due to his agency in both types of purposeful action: the action characterized by the instrument (*karaṇa*), which is defined as the power (*śakti*) whose form is consciousness (*saṃvitti*), and the action characterized by the goal (*svārtha*), which is the object to be accomplished.

Furthermore, he possesses qualities such as pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*); by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the previously mentioned qualities of imperishability (*avyaya*) and so forth are included. And he is non-dual (*ananya*).

Regarding that power, which has been described as having Śiva-tattva as its essence: that supreme consciousness (*para-saṃvedana*), which is non-different from that power and whose nature is power, is itself self-consciousness (*sva-saṃvedana*). Being established by self-consciousness, it is of the nature of Śiva; thus, because it is not established separately (*apṛthak-siddhatvāt*), it is "non-other" (*ananya*)—meaning that while being other, it does not exist as such in itself. And it is also "other" (*anya*).
In reality, even a single cognition possesses the nature of being both self-luminous and luminous to others;

thus, it is described as "Śiva" when intended solely in its aspect as self-luminous, and as "Śakti" when intended solely in its aspect as luminous to others, by virtue of these well-established characteristics. Being of such a nature...

Through inherence (*samavāya*), having become of that very nature by way of being related through identity (*tādātmya*), he remains; he has thus remained. Therefore, unlike the Naiyāyikas and others, there is no need for the conceptual construction of a relationship of locus and located (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*). Through the *bindu* [the power of consciousness], the *śakti* [is reached], and through the *śakti*, the Lord (*pati*); thus, the attainment of the two designations for Śiva—namely, as *laya* and as *Śiva*—is easily obtained.
Thus [it is said]. He states another designation:
"Since this [agent] is capable, and because the powers have withdrawn from activity such as exertion, they abide in Śiva alone; and he indeed remains partless (niṣkala)."

This Lord, having already obtained the two designations, now obtains the designation "the powerful one" (śakta) and further, "the exceedingly powerful one" (bhūyaḥ-śakta). He states the reason for this: because His own powers have diminished due to the constant generation of bodies and so forth from the *bindu*—such as the infinite mantras and the Great Lord of Mantras (Maheśvara)—His powers [have become limited].
The mother and others who are about to be mentioned, having fallen away from activities such as exertion (*udyoga*),

and having dissolved through their engagement with the authority over enjoyment (*bhoga*) and its objects, abide in their very own Self, which is Śiva and designated as "Śiva" within the reality of Śiva. At that time, by the rejection of what is to be done (*kartavya*), [the state] characterized by the emission of the *bindu* and so forth [is attained].

The meaning is that [the Bindu] does not partake in the causality of the emanation of effects (*kārya-prasṛti*). Thus, that which possesses the three designations of sound (*śabda-vyapadeśa-traya*) becomes intent upon the production of the Bindu; however, because it is no longer joined with the emanation of effects, it receives the designation "partless" (*niṣkala*). The particle *eva* and the word *tu* serve to exclude non-connection and to delimit [the specific state].
To the question "When does the designation 'enjoyment' occur?", he says: "But when the *bindu* is engaged in action, then it is called enjoyment;
that very same [bindu] when engaged is Śiva, and that is Sadāśiva."
That very reality is called Sādākhya; in essence, there is no difference from Śiva.
Enjoyment consists solely in its preservation, for superimposition (adhyāsa) is impossible therein.

When, at whatever time during an activity, the *bindu* is exerted and becomes oriented toward its own dissolution (*prasvābhimukhībhūta*), then at that time, we—the enjoyments (*bhogāḥ*)—are the Great Māyā consisting of one's own appropriation. Immediately upon obtaining this designation [of being the enjoyer] of both one’s own consciousness and power, Śiva obtains what is called enjoyment; he is the one who has obtained enjoyment.

He alone possesses designations because he is the power that serves as the cause for those efforts; thus, he receives two designations: "Sadāśiva" and "the Effortful" (*udyukta*). By the word "and" (*ca*), it is also implied that he is designated as both "with parts" (*sakala*) and "without parts" (*niṣkala*). Furthermore, if the principle named *sādākhya* is the instrumental cause of what has been stated, it is said to be that very same [power], because it is non-different from the possessor of power (*śaktimān*).

The meaning is that [Sadāśiva] exists in that state as having the characteristics of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and so forth, clearly manifest. Regarding Sadāśiva, who has been described as abiding in the *śivatattva* characterized by *śakti*, there is a partiality of differentiation in his effects arising from some degree of the state of office (*adhikārāvasthā*). Because this is equivalent to the deficiency of differentiation in the state of office, he remains unmanifest even during that state of office.
Since the characteristic of being the presiding lord of the *bindu* exists in both [the states of] *laya* and *śānti*,
even in the state of *laya*— characterized by the withdrawal of *śānti* and the rest— he remains characterized by the preservation of the portion of the *bindu*;
and furthermore, even in the state of *adhikāra*, he remains essentially the preservation of the *bindu*, characterized by the exertion toward intermediate tasks.

Because both experience (*bhoga*) and its cessation (*sthiti*), as well as their dissolution (*laya*), are always characterized by equanimity (*samatva*), there is no interval [of difference] as there is in the case of *adhikāra* (empowerment); thus, there is neither distinction nor non-distinction. The state of equilibrium (*samānīti*) belongs to both the two principles of Śiva characterized by *śakti* and Sādākhya;
it likewise belongs to the two principles of Śiva characterized by *bindu* and Sādākhya.

Just as there is no absolute difference from the principle of Īśvara, so too there is no difference in authority (*adhikāra*); however, we shall explain immediately below that while there is a difference conditioned by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the case-inflections, there is none in reality. Since a difference from Śiva and the others is possible for him, one might ask: "How can experience (*bhoga*) be of the nature of a phenomenal appearance (*vivarta*)? Anticipating this, he says: "Experience," and so forth; here, "experience" refers to that [which is described].

The *bindu* is essentially of the nature of preservation (*pālana*); its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is precisely this preservation. Furthermore, preservation consists in the power (*śaktitva*) to bring about the manifestation of the face of procreation (*prasava*) and the production of activity; therefore, it is not a superimposition (*adhyāsa*). It is not like that of those dwelling in *saṃsāra*, which takes the form of an attribution (*āropa*) characterized by objects caused by bondage, such as "I am with pleasure," "I am with pain," or "I am with delusion. (p. 41)

It does not become something created there, because that [creation] is impossible; for that which is not of such a nature cannot truly possess that nature. Even though it is one, being devoid of any other nature, the power of Śiva—like the rays of the sun in a different locus—undergoes manifold conventional usage because it is capable of accomplishing various activities. This is the meaning. *Adhikāra*.
To the question "When does this designation [of agency] occur?", he says:

"O lords of sages, when the activity of the *bindu* proceeds toward its effects, then there arises the authority (*adhikāra*) of Śiva, which is preceded by non-duality and characterized by distinction."

O lords of sages, when—at whatever time—the *bindu* becomes active in its function, the *kuṇḍalinī* becomes the agent of that arising; at that time, it receives the designation "the office of Śiva. Although there is a distinction in states due to the previously mentioned specific *bindu* having become active in its function, [it remains] from the former.

Since [Śiva] is non-distinct from that which has been described as existing as the *sādākhya-tattva* characterized by His own power (*sva-śakti*), and since He is devoid of any inherent differentiating attributes, there is no natural difference or distinction for this Śiva who is to be described as abiding in the *īśvara-tattva* characterized by His own power. He states another designation:
He alone shall be the Lord (Īśvara), and that reality is called by the name Īśvara;
it is said that "this has begun to function," and thus the powers (śaktis) are considered to have become active.

He alone, having obtained authority and possessing the designation, would be the Lord (*īśvara*). He receives the designation "Lord. That reality which is called by the name "Lord" and designated as *Īśvara*—that too is precisely that [very same reality], because it consists of the rays of power (*śakti*) and is the cause for the activity of the effects of the *bindu*.
The meaning is that [the Lord] exists in that state as having the characteristics of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and so forth, clearly manifest.

This one, who has obtained the designation of "Lord" (*īśvara*), is said to have "commenced" (*pravṛtta*); he receives the designation "commenced. Why? Because the powers (*śakti*) are considered to have commenced their activity toward the effect.

It should be supplied [to the text] that they are intended as having reached the directions of the preliminary practice (*prayoga*) and so forth, and that they also receive the designation "all" (*sakala*). Those names beginning with Śiva are to be understood as common to the three principles (*tattva*) designated by Śakti and Bindu. This is indicated by such [verses] as "The sages are by nature unswerving and empowered" (*ṛṣayaḥ svabhāvād acyutaśśaktaḥ*).
Fearing that they might not clearly understand the performance of an action because it is perceived as a modification (*vikṛti*),
you have explained the distinction of Śiva specifically through the state of the *bindu*.
Since the *bindu* is insentient, its activity does not proceed by itself.
If the agent were to undergo modification for the sake of that activity, then he would be non-Śiva; since such a contradiction has arisen, O Lord, please state the resolution.

O Lord! Regarding the "particular state of the *bindu* (*bindvavasthāviśeṣeṇa*)": the particularity (*viśeṣaḥ*) of that [state] is its differentiation (*bhedaḥ*), characterized by the fact that the effects have been withdrawn.

By means of that, there is a differentiation of Śiva, a differentiation of the Lord (*pati-bheda*). Śiva is said to be Sadāśiva and Īśvara, as stated by You. [Objection: Because the differentiating attribute resides in a different substratum, it is not real (*na vāstavaḥ*).

The *bhāva* (the manifesting principle), having withdrawn its form, does not proceed toward attaining the state characterized by its effects, such as a jar, because it lacks the superintendence of consciousness from its own side; indeed, there is no exertion.

Why? Because, being insentient, it possesses the nature of an inert object. [It cannot] attain the state characterized by its own effects, such as a jar, etc., after having withdrawn [its prior state].

If the agent who has entered into action for the sake of setting the chariot in motion and for its impulsion were the Lord himself—unpresided over by a driver such as Jalavāhaka—then Śiva would be subject to modification;
he would possess a transformation into another nature. Such being the case, this contradiction having arisen, [the consequence] is his own insentience.

"Since the absence of co-inherence between immutability and activity has arisen, state and provide a resolution or a solution. Having considered this, the Guru began to properly dispel their ignorance regarding that subject.
O Brahmins, agency is of two kinds: through volition and also through the instrument. For a pot is not produced by potters through volition alone.

O Brahmins, agency—the capacity for cause and effect—is twofold; this is the remainder of the statement. Why? Because one [type] arises from volition (*saṃkalpa*), such as thinking, "Let this become thus," and the other arises from the activity of instruments, such as the movement of the hands, which serves as the cause of transformation. Now, an objection may be raised: since volition is necessarily present in both cases...

Thinking that agency might be of a single uniform nature by relying on that [mind] alone, he says: "Not indeed," and so forth. For it is not the case that, setting aside instruments such as the activity of moving the hands and so on, a potter creates a jar by merely intending, "Let this be thus," through memory after having stirred the clay. But then...

Śiva also says "so be it," [but one might ask] why this conceptualization of differentiation? To this he replies: "By the mere will of Śiva, he is always the agitator of the *bindu*, not by means of a specific activity through which he would become subject to transformation."

That Śiva, at the time of every new creation, being the cause of the activity of the insentient (acid), brings about the agitation of the *bindu* by means of His mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), which is the power of His own non-differentiated instruments—this being what is expressed by the word "activity" (*vyāpāra*). The meaning is that, having agitated the *bindu*, He effects the construction of the worlds beginning with Śāntyatīta. Not [otherwise].

Not merely by a specific activity of a distinct instrument, nor by another activity involving a modification—that modification by which this Śiva might become altered, possessing a transformation into another form—is he changed. Indeed, Śiva does not undergo modification without regard for his own activity; whereas the potter, having regard for that [activity], becomes modified.

When it was said, "He exists," [the question arose] what further purpose is served by him? To this, he says: "O twice-born ones, because of being devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and because of being stainless, those who possess limiting adjuncts are subject to modification upon the production of effects."

Consequently, immutability is not contradicted by agency. O twice-born ones, we do not speak out of partiality; rather, because Śiva is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), his own attributes manifest within the Self that has come into existence.

The limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—the body, the senses, and so forth—are called "clinging" because [the Self] is devoid of them all; thus, there is an absence of the relationship between the object of experience and the experiencer. Now, one might object: since volition and the like are impossible for those who are isolated from such adjuncts, how can Śiva be said to be so?

To the objection that [the soul] causes the agitation of the *bindu*, [the author] replies: "And because of its stainlessness. It is not merely that its state of being produced from that [Supreme Principle] is obscured by impurity as it is for those [other principles];
rather, due to its power being unobstructed by impurity, it lacks dependence on others, mutability, and so forth.
[Objection: But surely there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that wherever there is agency, there is mutability. [Reply: True; however, those...

Some embodied beings (*dehin*) possess limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) at the time of producing an effect—that is, at the generation of what is to be done. They are indeed subject to modification (*vikṛta*), being changeful because their agency depends upon the operation of their own power. This is because even in the case of potters and others, modification is impossible by their very nature. This applies wherever there is co-occurrence with the state of being embodied.

In that context, being an agent implies being subject to modification; however, because the pervasion (vyāpti) is limited by this condition, the state of being unchanging is not contradicted by agency. Its coexistence within the same substratum (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is not negated. Where there is consciousness and yet no modification, there is agency—as is inferred in the case of the Self, which is the agent of the movement of its own body.
To the objection, "Is it not the case that agency is faulty only for embodied beings; how then can there be agency for one who is bodiless? he says:
"Because of being devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhis), how could agency not be accepted [for such a one]?"
Because agency is restricted by the limiting adjunct (upādhi), it ceases upon separation from that adjunct.
O lords of sages, agency would indeed [be attributed] for the sake of abundance.
O lords of sages, since it is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) due to the absence of the entire body, senses, and so forth, why and in what manner is agency not accepted?

Is it not accepted that being embodied is pervaded by agency, or that agency is pervaded by being embodied? Regarding this, the first [position] is not tenable. For the body and senses—which are the locus of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) pervaded by agency—act as an obstruction to the manifestation of that [agency], just as smoke pervaded by fire obstructs the perception of its substrate. As for agency...

Because it is an obstruction, it is opposed to the manifestation of that [knowledge]. The intention is that "obstruction" consists in being directed toward some limited object. Due to separation from that—namely, through the dissociation from one's own respective causes, such as the body, sense organs, and so forth—agency, on the contrary, is further opposed by what is desired; [it results in] the agency of a limited knower.

The sense is that, due to its distinct nature, and even because of the absence of [the usual] power and so forth, it would—like smoke or a lamp—be for the sake of abundance and for the sake of extreme manifestation; thus it would have all things as its object. As it has been said: "The second kind of agency is pervaded by embodiedness. In that regard, whatever effect [is produced], it is [produced] by one endowed with a body. (p. 50)

Demonstrating the inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) regarding the claim that "it must be produced by an agent," he establishes the agency of the bodiless one through an illustration: "Just as there is agency even for one who is bodiless in the impelling of his own body."
Just as the sun is the benefactor of all activities by its mere presence.

In the same way, Śiva accomplishes everything through mere proximity. Thus, the agency of Śiva is understood to exist even though he is bodiless, just as one's own gross body is moved toward the impelling of its own body by means of the vibration of one's own subtle body.

Because defects such as mutability would follow from conjunction, agency is attained merely through proximity— characterized by a connection with specific powers qualified by action— without actually touching the object whose purpose is defined by the activity of volition (*saṃkalpa*). Now,
it may be argued that agency by mere will is observed in the movement and so forth of one's own presided-over body, but not in external objects.

True. For this very reason, because He is the eternal presiding substratum, the universe is inferred to be like the body of the Lord (*īśvara*). It is for this reason that Śiva, through the vibration of the subtle body characterized by the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*), causes the gross body characterized by the Impure Path (*aśuddhādhvan*) to vibrate, just as it does for those such as ourselves.

Now, one might object: "Since His will is not manifested by a real body and mind due to being devoid of impurity (mala), Śiva is bodiless; yet He must be the agent of something because He possesses manifest consciousness, like the individual self (ātman). [To this we reply: Agency is certainly not pervaded by having a body, nor is an effect pervaded by an embodied agent; [the author] demonstrates this by showing another flawed example, beginning with "Just as... and so forth.

Just as the sun, though devoid of actual movement, becomes the cause of assistance through its mere presence for the daily activities of living beings— the pulsations and motions occurring day after day—
so too Śiva, by his mere presence, having recognized the opportune moment suitable for the diverse transformation of the *bindu*, [effects] this very [transformation].
By the mere act of volition (*saṃkalpa*), He brings about everything; that is, He makes all things exist. Now, one might object:

unlike the sun and other such entities, the Lord’s presence in the location of the effect at that time does not consist in having previously been non-existent and then coming to abide there; rather, because He is eternally omnipresent, His "presence" consists solely in the purposeful activity characterized by volition.

[The definition of an agent is] the state of being connected with a specific action characterized by the power of volition (*sva-raśakti*). Now, it may be argued that the form of a deity is never like the body of those such as ourselves; because of its purity, that bodiless [deity] lacks the capacity for agency.
Furthermore, we observe that embodied beings such as Viśvakarman possess the agency to perform their intended tasks through mental effort (*saṃkalpita*).
He states that the universe, which is perceived as an effect, is pervaded by an agent: "If agency is admitted for every being, even for one possessing a body,
then [the universe] is pervaded by another agent because it is an effect, even though it is bodiless."

The intention is that just as [the Lord] is bodiless, so too for the Blessed One who possesses a body, [liberation] must be established because He is preeminent among those who possess bodies; furthermore, the intention is that there is no fear whatsoever on the pure path, just as there is on the impure path. This applies whether agency is desired—that is, if it is accepted—[as stated on page...].

53) Is that body, in reality, limited or unlimited? If it were unlimited, then it would be our own view that the very power of the *bindu* (the seminal point) of Śiva is metaphorically designated as the "body. If, however, it is limited, then because it possesses constituent parts (*sāvayavatva*), it must be said that it is not uncreated (*akārya*). Wherever there is possession of constituent parts, [there is necessarily causality].

The claim that "being an effect" (kāryatva) is the reason for [the existence of a creator] is undermined because it would entail the fallacy of destroying the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the valid probans, "having parts" (*sāvayavatva*). Indeed, the pervasion must not be restricted by the qualification "other than the body of God," for just as one who possesses a body is an agent in the movement of his own body, so too is the establishment of agency possible for one who is bodiless; thus, there is no basis for such a restriction.
Because it is effective. Therefore, since that body is also an effect—just like our own bodies—it must be produced by another agent, a creator other than [the one you propose].

Wherever there is "being an effect," there is "having an agent"; let this concomitance, established by the rule of universal association, suffice. What objection could there be to this? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Since his body and so forth are likewise [unreal], there is no abiding anywhere;
for at the time of the first creation, he was devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
The Great Lord alone is accepted as the agent who has set forth with his entire power,

because agency is not admitted for one who is bodiless. Since even the bodies and so forth of that creator of the universe are pervaded by another agent in this manner, there would be an infinite regress of agents, and thus he [the Great Lord] could not exist anywhere at all.

It does not occur; rather, the meaning is that there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Now, one might object: "We avoid the infinite regress by accepting that a certain body of an agent was produced by itself. To this we reply:
no, because it is not accepted that a bodiless being can possess agency with respect to its own body, nor is it possible for that body to have been produced by itself prior to [having] embodiedness.

If it is argued that [the body] is established (*siddham*), then since that very body must also be self-created, its establishment would lead to an unavoidable infinite regress; and because that regress is unavoidable, [the argument fails]. Furthermore, at the time of the commencement of the first creation, the bodies and sense-faculties of the first beings were already existent along with their bodies.

The intention [of the author] is that this refers to the foremost of the creators, such as Ananta and others. Regarding creation (*sṛṣṭi*), which is the act of bringing forth, [the Lord is] devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), liberated from all bodies, senses, and so forth, and possessed of all active powers. "Active" means having the form of activity characterized by volition (*saṃkalpa*); "all" means without exception.

He is so described because he possesses all the powers (śaktis), beginning with Ajananī. Maheśa Śiva is intended as the agent of the desired creation; this is well-stated because Paraśiva is established as having five faces and fifteen eyes. Those who speak of his body—whether it be the actual one consisting of power (śākta), or that which begins with the bindu (baindava)—[affirm this].

The particles *eva* and *tu* serve to exclude non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and connection with something else (*anya-yoga-vyavaccheda*), respectively. [Objection: But since Śiva’s agency is not observed in relation to jars and such things, how can he possess universal agency? [Response: True; in that case, his agency consists in being the instigator (*prayojakatva*).
Thus, everything is faultless. Having thus refuted the notion of universal agency for one who possesses a body, [the author proceeds].
He concludes that the differentiation of Śiva is established through power:
"This differentiation, beginning with dissolution and so forth, is likewise situated through power;
for the agitation of the *bindu* proceeds from the power of Śambhu alone."

This previously mentioned differentiation, beginning with dissolution (laya) and so forth, consisting of Śiva and the rest, is established as residing in the Lord through the medium of His power (śakti). Therefore, for that reason— because from that cause— the agitation of the Bindu (bindukṣobha), which is the manifestation of the Bindu, proceeds from the will-nature characteristic of the power of Śambhu, that is, Śiva.

It arises as follows: for indeed, the powers (*śaktayaḥ*), remaining within their own self by setting aside what is to be done, illuminate a particular state designated as "dissolution" (*layatattva*); they then assume the status of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the application of terms such as "partless" (*niṣkala*). When, however, they are intent upon the accomplishment of an effect, that [is not the case].

When they have reached the stage of application (*prayogabhūmi*), because they are engaged in its preservation and the realization of enjoyment (*bhoga*), they manifest a particular state designated as "the reality of enjoyment" (*bhogatattva*); thus, they serve as the cause for the employment of terms such as "with parts" (*sakala*) and "without parts" (*niṣkala*). Furthermore, when... (p. 57)

When these powers reach the stage of practical application, they manifest another state consisting of the designation of their respective specific functions; thus, they become the cause for the employment of terms such as "sakala" (the whole) and so forth.
