Therefore, the distinction among these powers here is not ultimate, being merely a conceptual construction based on the difference in their modes of operation.
As they say:
"The agent is held to be threefold—capable, prepared, and engaged;
the distinction among them is merely figurative, based on the difference between capability and engagement."

Surely, the purpose for employing a metaphorical designation (*bhedopacāra*) must be stated; as they say: "The transgression of the primary meaning of a word is not accepted without a purpose. It is replied:

For one who has been joined to the principle of *adhikāra* (qualification) through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, and who has been joined to the principle called *bhoga* (experience), and from that [state] to the principle of *laya* (dissolution)...

To demonstrate that for the soul (*aṇu*) who has been joined [to Śiva], there is indeed a real distinction here due to the manifestation of the gross, subtle, and supreme powers (*śakti*), the metaphorical designation of "distinction" is applied to the *saṃskāra* (purification/transformation). Thus, it is not purposeless;
for the distinction between the dissolution and other states of non-differentiation regarding the operations of Śiva, Śiva’s power, and the activity of Śiva and Śiva’s power is indeed real.
The purport is as follows: in response to the inquiry as to what kind of power that is, he defines its nature as sound:
"Though consisting of knowledge and action, it is the eternally risen radiance;
it is turned toward the Supreme (Parā) and is entirely free from even a trace of bondage."
Because she is not different from the auspicious [Śiva], she is in reality the very form of the Lord (Īśvarī).

She too consists of power, knowledge, and action; she is described as such because knowledge and action are her *ātman*, that is, her essential nature. By the term "consisting of knowledge," the power of grasping (*parigraha-śakti*), Kuṇḍalinī, is included.
It distinguishes [the state] as being free from impermanence and destruction; by this, it distinguishes it from the knowledge of the Buddhists.

It is "devoid of even a trace of all bonds," meaning it is liberated, being devoid even of the slightest trace (*leśa*)—that is, the residual portion (*adhikāra-mala*)—of all impurities and the like that constitute bondage. Thus, by this, [it distinguishes it] from the Vidyeśvaras and others.
[The author] distinguished the power (*śakti*) from [Śiva] by means of [the attributes] "eternal" and so forth. It is a manifestation that has been manifest since beginningless time;
thus, by this, he distinguished it from the Śiva-power that has already been described. That [power] is oriented toward the other [Śiva] and oriented toward objects;
thus, by the phrase "consisting of action" (*kriyātmikā*), and by the fact that it is primarily knowledge (*jñāna-pradhāna*), it is self-luminous.

It distinguishes [consciousness] from the nature of Śiva; for, by virtue of being an object of cognition, it possesses its own function characterized by the experience of that [Śiva], whose power is a consciousness whose form is non-different from Śiva.

When the establishment of Śiva as one’s own conscious nature is realized, although He is distinct from anything other than Himself, He shines forth as self-awareness by virtue of being a consciousness that is unlike any object of knowledge—since there is a contradiction in the notion of action directed toward oneself. That very same consciousness which is the perception of another, in its form as Power (*śakti*), is itself self-perception; thus, it is established through self-consciousness.

Because she is not established as separate from the form of Śiva, she is "non-other" (*ananya*), meaning that while being other, she does not exist independently. Furthermore, although she is other, her nature is one of non-dual consciousness; thus, with the intention of expressing only her nature as dependent on herself, she is called "Śiva," and with the intention of expressing only her nature as dependent on another, she is called "Śakti. Therefore, they are distinct.

It has been described as being established; that very [form] is indeed characterized by these defining marks in reality and by its own nature. It is the sovereign form belonging to Śiva. For the form of the Self is twofold: moving and unmoving.
Among these, the moving consists of the body composed of the elements and their products (*tāttvika-bhaumana*); the unmoving consists of knowledge and action.
This form (*mūrti*) is also such. Indeed, since form is conventionally treated as being real only when it is distinct [from consciousness], it is here non-distinct. As it is said in this regard:
"Knowledge and action are declared by Śiva to be pure and supreme with respect to all objects. And that [form]—
When it has reached the state of dissolution (laya), it takes on the form of neutrality;
indeed, that very state of complete dissolution is itself the neutral state resulting from the cessation of all activity.

When, at that time, [the subject] has transcended the state of dissolution (*layāvasthā*) and reached the stage of the *bindu*, it then possesses the nature of an indifferent observer (*udāsīnarūpaṇī*). At that time, how could there be any activity characterized by the performance of duties? Because of the absence of objects to be acted upon, the portion of activity characterized as one's own duty remains fixed within itself; therefore, it is indeed indifferent at that very moment.
The state of equilibrium (*sāmyavasthā*) is a condition of similarity; the ellipsis is "because [the soul] has attained the state of being engaged. To the question "Why?", he says:
"Because there is an equality of cognition and action among those agents who are engaged."
For in the thought "therefore I shall do this," there is equality between these two regarding the activity.
Because, as has been stated, among agents—

such as potters and others who contemplate the means for the successful accomplishment of their respective tasks— the equality of cognition and action (jñāna-kriyā), that is, of the two powers of knowing and acting (vedana and kṛti) within the activity of "I am doing this," is clearly discerned; therefore, [this applies] to the agent who is thus engaged.
In Śiva, although he is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), there exists a conceptualization (*savikalpa*) characterized by the absence of mental constructs permeated by words,
which consists in the grasping of the mutual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) between the meanings of the two terms [Śiva and Śivā].
Thus, within these two powers of knowledge and action, there is the form of knowledge and action expressed as "I do this."
In the performance [of the ritual], equality must be maintained. The word "this" (*etad*) is an indication of the cognitive aspect; "I do" (*karomi*) is an indication of the active aspect.
To the question, "In what state does one perform? he says: "In the state of authority (*adhikāra*), the action is seen as such, because one is authorized over the tasks."
The task to be performed is indeed the recollection of the conceptualization of the qualities.

In the state of authority (*adhikāra*), that is, during the period of possessing authority, the power consisting of action (*kriyātmikā śakti*) is predominant—that is, it exists in abundance—within the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). Therefore, since the power of action is authorized and engaged in its tasks (*kāryeṣu*), one asks: what is that task? To this he says: "And the task is that which is to be performed," for according to scripture, "it performs the task immediately following [the arising of] desire."

The very power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) of the Blessed One, having performed another duty characterized by will— which consists of vision and action and is designated by the terms "volition" and "intention"— exists as the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) fashioned by that [action].
Furthermore, even in the case of people such as ourselves, the power of action, when manifested by a mind possessed of passion, exists as that which is not yet [fully] realized.

The teachers maintain that such a power of will (*icchā-śakti*) exists; therefore, the power of agency (*kartṛ-śakti*), characterized by that power of will, is directed toward the mere object to be accomplished. That [power], whose nature is will, engages with its own effects through a will directed toward each respective object. Thus, that which is to be done—consisting of the mental construction of qualities and recollection—is directed toward each object in this very manner.
"Let it be"—this is the recollection characterized by a desire directed toward the qualities of the objects to be accomplished; that is the knowledge characterized by such [recollection].
However, it is not an activity; thus it has been stated that for the Lord, there is no recollection of those objects.
Therefore, it is established that Sadāśiva is of the nature of both knowledge and the knower.

The recollection of the Lord Śiva as its object is a memory whose scope consists of the effects of the *bindu* and His manifold qualities; it is not an activity (*vyāpāra*), for activity has been defined as a state of inert vibration (*jaḍaspanda*) consisting of functional exertion (*kriyā*) based on modification (*vikṛti*).
That [recollection] is so called because it is the cause of that [activity]. As it is said in the *Mālinīvijaya*:
Making the entire world known, she is called the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti);
furthermore, when [she intends], "Let this object become thus," [she is the power of action].
"Right at the moment it arises, that object performs [an action]; here, this is called 'action' (kriyā).

He states the conclusion: "Therefore," etc. Therefore, since even action is characterized by knowledge, Śiva remains at all times—in every moment—in the form of the knower of knowledge. He is not merely of the nature of self-luminosity, nor of the nature of other-luminosity.

The meaning is that it is well-established that [the world] has the characteristic of being an inert vibration (*jaḍaspanda*) and activity; for those who do not fully understand this, it is an illusion.
Having described the even and uneven states of the powers of knowledge and action according to their respective objects and in accordance with their own effects, he concludes:
The cause of these two knowledges is consciousness (citi), which is non-differentiated in nature;
it is said to be power (śakti), conceptualization (vikalpā), the Great Form (mahatī mūrti), and the Sovereign (aiśvarī).

The cause, the reason, for these two known [entities]—namely, the cognition whose object is various effects and the activity characterized by the cognition whose form is the conceptualization of their qualities—is that which consists of non-distinction (*aviśeṣātmikā*). That is, it is so called because its essential nature (*ātmasvarūpa*) is non-difference (*abheda*); it is common to both.

The meaning is that she is embodied (*rūpiṇī*). For this very reason, she is non-conceptual (*avikalpā*), free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa-rahitā*). She is the Great One (*mahatī*), pervading all objects, the Sovereign (*aiśvarī*), the immobile form inherent in Śiva, as previously described. In consciousness (*cit*), she is said to be consciousness itself; she is called the power (*śakti*) and the strength (*bala*) of Śiva.

She is the bestower of grace upon both the conscious and the unconscious (*cid-acid-anugraha-kartrī*); she is the bestower of grace upon the true consciousness (*satya-cid-anugraha-kartrī*). She is the veiler of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti-tirodhāyikā*).

The power that effects grace for consciousness becomes the concealer of the stainless power of consciousness. Because the power, being inherent in Śiva, is devoid of the property of transformation (*pariṇāma*), that effect consisting of knowledge and action is merely a figurative expression of duality;
it should be understood as non-separately established and of a single nature. As it is said in the *Ratnatraya*:
Even while performing an action against its will, the immutable consciousness (*cit*) acts according to its own will;
likewise, knowledge appears in the form of ignorance, and activity likewise manifests as transformation.
Not understanding the distinction between words and wandering in their confusion regarding mere synonymous designations, the sages raise this doubt again:
"O Lord, it has been stated that the reality called Śiva is the object to be purified through initiation."
Furthermore, it contradicts the statement that [the level] beyond peace (śāntyatīta) is pervaded by the power (kalā).

O Blessed One, it was stated that in initiation (dīkṣā), that which is called Śiva—the reality designated as Śiva, which has transcended the Bindu—is declared to be the object of purification (śodhya). It has also been said that it is to be purified (śodhanīya). Furthermore, it was taught that it is attained by the Kalā beyond Peace (śāntyatīta) and is permeated by the Kalā beyond Peace. Now, at this point, this appears to be contradictory.
Having transcended the state of being a mere drop (*bindu*), the Blessed One employs the word "truth" (*satya*) and, demonstrating partial acceptance, offers this rebuttal:
"What has been urged is indeed true; I shall speak it, so remain concentrated."
Because it is primordial nature (prakṛti), this Bindu is agitated by the All-Self.
In that regard, his undisturbed experience is the *śāntyatīta-kalā*;
however, the transformation consisting of the worlds beginning with *śānti* is that which arises from the *bindu*.
That which is called Sādākhya here is said to be the Śivatattva;
however, in the Śivāgama, that which is the Bindu-world is stated to be the Sādākhya-tattva.
That which is below Īśvara is said to be Anīśvara (non-Īśvara),

because it is *prakṛti* (primordial matter), because it is the supreme cause, and because, if it were subject to agitation in its entirety, there would follow the undesirable consequence of impermanence and infinite regress. This *bindu*, which is enumerated among the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), is not [subject to agitation] in its entirety— that is, in its whole nature.

It is agitated, yet it is not transformed. There, between the agitated and unagitated portions, that part of the *syabindu* which is unagitated is to be known as the *śāntyatītakalā*, the "kalā beyond peace.
That which consists of the worlds beginning with *śānti*—the term "beginning with *śānti*" being used as an indicator to include [the levels] up to and including *śāntyatīta*—is [the object of this].

He whose very self and essential nature consists of the worlds is so described. The "Baindava" (pertaining to the Bindu) refers to the transformation produced from the Bindu; here, by accepting its pervasion of the *śāntyatīta-kalā* and its state as that which is to be purified (*śodhya*), the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) is expressed, and not the Bindu characterized as having its effects withdrawn. That is its substratum.

Alternatively, the sense is that it consists of the rays of Śiva’s power; furthermore, this word "here" (atra) also indicates that the Śiva-tattva has been described here in the *Pauṣkara* regarding the Supreme Lord. Elsewhere, however, the Śiva-tattva is said to be located at the summit of Śānti, pervaded by the Śāntyatīta-kalā, and consisting of the single world of Śāntyatīta which is to be purified. Again, [it begins] with Śānti...

The four kalās beginning with Śānti constitute the essence of the worlds; they are pervaded by the kalā Śāntyatītā, which is the Śakti-tattva. Herein, the tattvas Sādākhya and Īśvara are not of the nature of the rays of Śiva and Śakti, or rather, they consist of the Bindu whose activity is directed toward the sphere of practical application.
Or rather, he says it consists of the *bindu*. "That," and so forth, [is stated] in the Śiva-āgama.
That world known as *bindu*, which is called *sādākhya* and *asādākhya*, is indeed that very same reality (*tattva*) designated as *sādākhya* which has arisen as the object to be purified.
However, the intention is not that it is "that" [the *bindu* itself], because its existence is in the lower portion, below that [level].
That which belongs to Īśvara, that which is related to Īśvara, and likewise that which is designated as Īśvara—this very thing is called Īśvara;
this alone is declared to be the principle of Īśvara (īśvaratattva) as it arises as the object to be purified. It is not intended to mean that "it is something other than that.
Having thus resolved [the objection], he concludes:
These three principles exist on the path of the self as the reality of continuity;
however, these very ones previously mentioned are nowhere to be purified.

These are to be attained by all men who have been joined with initiation. Reality (*tattva*) itself is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the self; that path which exists within the midst of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), being a path whose essence is reality—that is the path of reality. The intention is that it is "pure. These are the three *baindava* [levels].

The *tattvas* exist. It should be understood that the *vidyātattva* is subsumed within the *īśvaratattva*, and the *śaktitattva* is subsumed within the *śivatattva*. These alone are the objects to be purified (*śodhya*). In some places they are not mentioned as previously stated, being described instead as consisting of the rays of power (*śakti-kiraṇa*), or as having the nature of the *bindu* (the point) withdrawn from its substrate (*adhiṣṭheya*). [Objection: But is it not the case that the qualification for experience (*bhoga-adhikāra*) is conditioned by the worlds (*bhuvana*)?
Since power (*śakti*), by virtue of its tenfold nature, consists of the form of mantra, how could it not be subject to purification? True;

it is to be purified as having the nature of mantra, but not as having the nature of the *tattvas*. Thus, there is nothing inconsistent. Those [powers] which are of the nature of the *bindu* are, through initiation, united with all souls who are free from limitation.

It has been stated that objects of enjoyment are not to be obtained by all [liberated souls], even those who have been joined to the principle of *ālayatattva*. To the question of whether this is so, he says:

"Those who are joined to the principle of *ālayatattva* are liberated in the other world; yet, while abiding in that principle, they possess the authority for enjoyment, their power being merely manifest consciousness. (p. 71)

Above the infinite worlds of the Vidyā-tattva, there exist seven successive realms characterized by Sadāśiva, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, Bindu, and Paramaśiva; these are increasingly exalted and constitute the stages of liberation. Among them, with the exception of the single realm characterized by Paramaśiva, all others [are surpassed].

The principle known as *bindu*, extending from the *bhoga-tattva* down to the end of the *śāntyatīta*, has not been extracted from below because it is still subject to impulsion; thus, it is not yet liberated. Therefore, through initiation (*dīkṣā*), having performed the severing of the bonds (*pāśaccheda*) above the *māyā-tattva* until the end of the destruction of impurity (*malaviccheda*), those [souls] contained within itself...
Having established the manifestation of the Śiva-tattva— which corresponds to the series of tattvas from the pure [tattvas] down to the Bhoga-tattvas, and which possesses both gross and subtle forms—
one first effects the authority for the severance of the crest-lock (śikhāccheda), characterized by the cessation of being impelled by the power of concealment (tirodhāna-śakti).

For the sake of manifesting the state of Śiva: therefore, those who have been joined to the station characterized by Paraśiva— namely, the *bindu* that transcends the principle of dissolution (*layatattva*) after being extracted from the principle of enjoyment (*bhogatattva*)— are liberated, having attained universal sovereignty through the manifestation of supreme qualities similar to His.

Those whose bonds are released become like Śiva. Indeed, according to the scripture: "In that which is inexpressible, supportless, ungraspable, devoid of mind, and beyond all categories—union with this is liberation; such is the certainty of the Śāstra. Thus, for the sake of attaining supreme liberation, union (*yojanam*) occurs within Śiva, who possesses specific characteristics and is untouched by designations such as *laya* (dissolution).

The effect is real. Here, as in the venerable *Mataṅga*, everything that has arisen as the object of purification (*śodhya*) is included within the principle of non-enjoyment (*abhoga-tattva*). Therefore, there is nothing inconsistent in the fact that those [principles] joined above it are joined everywhere. Furthermore, in the dissolution (*laya*) where the *bindu* is not transcended, there is the authority for enjoyment (*bhogādhikāra*) in two principles.

And those who have been joined to that goal are liberated; the sense is that because they go to worlds such as Śāntyatīta, they do not return due to being impelled [by that state]. If so, what is their nature? They abide in the *tattvas* that constitute the sphere of Śiva’s enjoyment (*bhogādhikāra*), namely, the aforementioned Śāntyatīta and the others, which serve as the locus for Śiva’s enjoyment.

Abiding in the worlds, these powers are essentially manifest pure consciousness (*vyaktacinmātra-śaktayaḥ*). Their power of perception (*saṃdṛk-śaktayaḥ*) has been made manifest by Śiva. The sense is that, through their power of agency (*kartṛ-śakti*), they gradually assume various states of being, each slightly diminished [from the original state]. Now, one might object: "Since power is partless (*niraṃśatvāt*), how can there be manifestation through a partial aspect? It cannot occur in the aspect of action. This is true.

The powers (*śaktayaḥ*) of the venerable Ananta and the others, manifested as both gross and subtle, reveal all objects permeated by sound; this is because they depend upon sound and the other [sensory domains]. Furthermore, even the manifestation of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is not total; thus, everything is faultless. It has been indicated that the worlds exist also by virtue of being presided over by their respective world-rulers (*bhuvana-adhiṣṭhātṛ*).
It clearly demonstrates a distinct designation:
"For this [reality] is differentiated by the *bindu* alone, whereas the devotee is differentiated even by the worlds (*bhuvana*s).
[These are] Śāntyatītā, Śānti, Vidyā, Sthiti, and Nivṛtti. (p. 74)

By means of the *bindu*, this Śiva—though indeed not different from the state of *bindu* itself—obtains a distinct designation; likewise, subsequently, being differentiated by the worlds (*bhuvana*s), he obtains distinct designations corresponding to his presiding over each individual world. And those worlds, following the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*),...

At the beginning of creation, the Lord— who, conditioned by the gradually dissolving *bindu*, had assumed the state of *yukta* (union), and who, having attained the state of *adhikāra* (sovereign authority) characterized by the stage of application for gradual action, was intent upon exercising the authority to fashion the manifold creation— first fashioned *nāda* within the *bindu* as the creation of sound.

The Śāntyatītā [level] is the world of Śāntyatītā, which has become one’s own interior (*svāntabhūta*), the world of the supreme *dhikkāra* situated above; because it consists of the nature of the power of the Supreme Bindu (*parabindu*) in the form of Śāntyatītā, it is again characterized by non-liberation (*apunar-mukti*).

Since it is "without arrangement" (*nissanniveśa*) and "devoid of form" (*nirmomi*), it lacks the status of being a support for worlds; therefore, it belongs to the state of the quiescence of effects (*kārya-śānti*). (p.)

75) For this very reason, although it is designated as the *layatattva*, it is also well known as the world of Īśāna (*īśānabhuvana*), which is included within the *bhogatattva* even while being designated as such. [These are] Śānti, Vidyā, Sthiti, and Nivṛtti; these are the four worlds beginning with Sthiti and Pratiṣṭhā.

The four kalās beginning with Śānti constitute the abode of Śiva’s enjoyment and are the Śakti-tattva; this is because they are well-known as such in other [traditions]. However, it should be understood that here the Śakti-tattva is presented as being included within the Śiva-tattva. In this regard, he demonstrates the different designations for Śiva:
Within these great worlds, Śiva obtains five designations in sequence:
Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jāta.
These are the five faces of Bhoga belonging to the state of Sadāśiva;
these are the names of the great worlds (*bhuvana*s), so called because they exist above the upper worlds.
Within these five, Śiva resides as their presiding deity, and his designations, beginning with Īśāna, correspond respectively to these faces. (p. 76)
One obtains five. These [five] are the forms beginning with Īśāna, whose characteristics are the activity of the power designated as such;

they are the states of Sadāśiva, which are the states of Śiva—who is the aggregate form of the forms beginning with Īśāna—abiding as the presiding authority over the principle (tattva) of Sādākhya, yet existing in the form of individual manifestations (vyaṣṭi). He alone is...

That which is designated as "enjoyment" (bhoga) should be meditated upon in the form of the Īśāna-mūrti and others by those desiring the attainment of the Śāntyatītā and other levels; it then bestows the fruit [of that attainment].
Therefore, these [levels] such as Śāntyatītā are the faces of Śiva, who abides in the worlds of Śāntyatītā and so forth, as the individualized form (vyaṣṭi-rūpa) of enjoyment.

The fivefold [group]. [He] describes [the deity], showing that even if one accepts that [the body] is pervaded by the agent, there exists the well-established power (*śakti*) and its resonance (*anura*), as one whose form is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi-rūpa*) of Sadāśiva, whose body is indeed the effect (*kārya*) joined with the physical body— white, consisting of the five forms, eternal, both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*).
The form of Sadāśiva is to be known as that which sets all activities in motion.

(p. 77) Consisting of five forms (*pañcamūrtimayī*), she takes the form of the five mantra-forms beginning with Īśāna. She is white, to be worshipped as having a pure white appearance; she is eternal, being devoid of ultimate destruction.

Because her form is fashioned (*klipta*), the withdrawal of her fashioned form (*mūrte kliptarūpopasaṃhṛti*) is described in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures. [The deities] below that are both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*).

Because he is intent upon his task (*kāryodyuktatvāt*). For this very reason, we shall explain that even Sadāśiva, who possesses the status of the collective totality (*samaṣṭirūpa-adhikāra*), is described here as "enjoyment" (*bhoga*). Such a form or body is to be known as "belonging to Sadāśiva"—that is, it should be understood as pertaining to the venerable Lord Sadāśiva, who is the presiding deity of that which is called "Eternity" (*sadākhya*). Furthermore, she (or he) is the initiator of all activities.
To clearly demonstrate that she possesses the nature of five forms for the sake of accomplishing all tasks while condensing them into one, [the text] says:
"She has Īśāna as her crest-jewel, a male face, and Ghorā at her heart."
Vāmaguhyā, Sadyāṅgī, Hāriṇī, and likewise Jananī.

Having fashioned the senses by means of the three powers—Rodha, Itrī, and Iti—the Mother, who assumes a gross body as her effect and is the Ātman of Īśāna and the others, [acts]. The justification of the summarized meaning will be performed later. By means of the three powers—Rodha, Itrī, and Iti—[the senses] are fashioned; these are mentioned as illustrative examples (*upalakṣaṇatayā*).

She whose senses are accompanied by intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties is the one possessed of imagined senses; she is endowed with an imagined subtle body of instruments (*sūkṣmakaraṇatanu*).

Because she is the very nature of the expansion of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) among the eight powers headed by Īśāna, she is the one celebrated as possessing the powers known as the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), the power of will (*icchāśakti*), the power of concealment (*tirodhānaśakti*), and the power of grace (*anugrahaśakti*).
The expansions of the nature of the pentad are characterized by the power of the Self (ātma-śakti), which possesses the consciousness of Sadāśiva;
this is because Śiva possesses infinite powers. One should not suspect that this is merely a descriptive enumeration of these [powers], as he says:

O twice-born ones, these eight glorious goddesses were the consorts of the trident-bearing lords beginning with Īśa; their valor and their distribution are now described according to their true nature.
O twice-born ones! These eight illustrious goddesses, beginning with Īśānā, belong to Śiva, the wielder of the trident;

they are renowned for their fame because they are capable of accomplishing all tasks. The intention is that each of them is described according to her specific nature (*tanmātra*). The "power" (*vīrya*) of these Śaktis refers to their capacity and the differentiation of their respective functions.

It is described by its own nature; it is spoken of according to its intrinsic being. He speaks in sequence: "The supreme limit of Īśānī is conceived as the crest-jewel, because it is the cause of filling the universe through the functions of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth."
By means of his mouth, which is without equal, he bestows a mouth upon man;
the world of transmigration, consisting of terrible impurities and the like, is the opposite of that, while the All-pervading Lord is its antidote.
This true being (sadbhāva), together with its characteristics, is renowned as Aghora; and since the heart is also the true being, it is indeed that very same thing.
But because it is secret and subtle, this Vāma is composed of both knowledge and action;
since it brings about the birth of the universe, of sons, and so forth, in all its effects, O wise ones, this Vāma is therefore accepted as "the Secret" in this scripture.
Because he assumes a form consisting of the expansion of his own power through the mere desire to create, he is therefore remembered as Sadyomūrti (the one whose form is instantaneous).
O Īśānī, you who bestow grace, in the supreme state characterized by Śiva, you unite the disciple who is to be graced.

Endowed with the highest elevation, she is conceived as the crest and the head because she stands above all, like the pinnacle that is unsurpassed and supreme. She whose self is Īśānī is the Guru of dance and truth.

Her form as Sadāśivī is that which is meditated upon here as having a dual manifestation, with Śekhara as her crest. She whose crest is Īśāna [is Sadāśivī], through the functions beginning with Bindu and Nāda. Here, "functions beginning with Nāda" refers to the functions such as Nāda and so forth, which will be described in the chapter on Origination (Utpatti-paṭala). These are the functions beginning with Nāda.

The expansion of the self through the words and sentences of the scriptures fills the entire universe—from the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) up to the Unmanifest (*anāśrita*)—by virtue of its identity with them. This power, named *Pūraṇī*, causes [the world] to be concealed.
The mantra, being of that nature, is called "the Person" (*pumān*) because it is the cause of filling the universe by means of those [powers]. Because of this meaning...

Regarding the elements (*dhātūnām*): the term *pum* refers to "wind" (*pavana*), yet the element *pu* also functions in the sense of "filling. Alternatively, it is called *pumān* because it purifies (*punāti*) the accumulation of ignorance in men (*puṃsām*). Because it is the cause of a man's speech, and because of its similarity to the mouth (*vaktra*)—that is, due to their equality—it is called "mouth" (*vaktram*); thus it is said to be the "mouth. [It is] *pumān*.

That whose characteristic is the cause of the speech from the mouth, being the cause of fulfillment, is the body of Sadāśiva, the "male-mouthed" (puṃvaktra). Aghora is the transmigratory existence consisting of impurity and so forth—the transmigratory existence consisting of passion, hatred, and so on, which are the causes of impurity.
Because it is opposed to that [Aghora], the All-pervasive One (Vibhu) exists as the "twice-seated" (dvidāsī); she is the one who effects withdrawal. She is the power named Hārdī.

The mantra characterized by height is renowned as Aghora. This is the characteristic of peace, its own specific characteristic, true existence (*sadbhāva*), the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and also the heart (*hṛdaya*). According to worldly convention, it is called true existence; the ultimate reality is thus described. For that reason, Aghora is indeed that very heart; Aghora is peaceful.

The *sādāśivīmūrti* is that whose essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the heart-center (*hṛtsthala*), characterized by ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). The *aghorahṛtsthala* consists of vision and action; it is the *vāmā* [energy] whose essence is the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), which will be described as performing the three functions (*trikṛtyakarī*). The power named *vāmā*, whose essence is the gross body (*sthūladeha*), performs only maintenance (*sthitimātrakarī*). She is defined by those characteristics.
By means of the expression of difference (*vilakṣaṇokti*) regarding the word "Vāma" in this *Vāmanāma-mantra*—

due to its being secret, hidden, subtle, and imperceptible, like a limb of a living being that has never been seen before and is thus distinct— he is the creator and progenitor of the universe, as evidenced by the observation of effects such as sons and so forth.

The meaning is that the universal characteristic of an effect is inferred from the observation of its specific parts, which are like the limbs of a living being never seen before. This is because, in the case of effects such as a son, the cause is well-known and designated by the word "janana" (that by which something is produced), which refers to a means consisting of the limbs of a living being; therefore, this [is so].

The Left (Vāma) is the means for accomplishing all activities. O wise ones, in this Śiva-darśana, it is correctly understood—that is, properly inferred—to be "Guhya," denoted by the word Guhya. Vāmaguhyā is the form of Sādāśivī, whose nature is the secret (guhya) characterized by the generation of the world, which is distinct (vilakṣaṇa).
Thinking, "We shall undertake creation by the mere desire to create," Śiva enters his office; [this refers to] his own power consisting of the expansion of his own energy.
His own creative form is the power named Nāma-śakti; its expansions are the *kalās* (aspects) such as Siddhi and the rest, which have that [form] as their object.

One should attain a form consisting of that [essence], whose nature is the presiding deity of the Sadāśiva-tattva, possessing five faces and fifteen eyes as its bodily limbs. One should obtain this; manifested from the Supreme, one becomes identical in form with those limbs. Then, accompanied by the mantra, it is known as the Sadyo-mūrti; Sadyaḥ is the Sadyo-mūrti.
That form of Sadāśiva whose limbs (aṅga) are its constituent parts (avayava) is the Sadyojāta-limbed [Sādāśivī Mūrti]. He concludes:
"Thus, these five mantras are indeed bound by them;
yet in reality they are not distinct, because they are none other than His own power."

Thus, these five mantras—whose bodies are composed of the [five faces] beginning with Īśāna—are Śiva’s pure body; the Sādāśiva-form is constructed and formed according to the manner described. These, designated by the word "mantra," are in reality and by their very nature as if residents of the Vidyā-tattva; therefore, they are non-different from Śiva, because:
Because, by virtue of their own power, they consist of that very expansion, others do not become anything else. Furthermore, he says that there are other mantras:
"Likewise, there are other internal mantras whose essence is Śiva."
The heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, and weapons by name.

Similarly, there are five external limbs, such as Īśāna and the rest; however, within those same locations, there are internal limbs. There are other mantras that possess a construction situated within the body of Sadāśiva, which are of the nature of Śiva and consist of the expansion of Śiva’s power. He has shown their names beginning with "the Heart" (*hṛt*). He explains the meaning of the words "Heart" and so forth.
His heart is goodness; his head is the highest accumulated virtue;
his mastery is independent of others; and she who is situated above is Chicā.
Though capable of concealing itself from others, it is naturally hidden;
that armor of splendor, which accords with dharma, is designated by its own name.
Because it is the seed of omniscience, you do not behold it;
that irresistible majesty of Śambhu is called the weapon.

Of that five-mantra body, the Heart of Śiva is its true being (*sadbhāva*); the Head is characterized by the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and all the qualities (*guṇas*) rest upon it. Its own nature (*svadharma*) consists of the universal transformation; its sovereignty over both the conscious and the unconscious (*cid-acit*) is the power of impulsion. For this very reason, its characteristic is absolute independence (*svātantrya*), which is not subject to anything else; this is its "Tuft" (*śikhā*).
It is of the nature of splendor (*tejas*) and is hidden; it is protected by its own being and majesty, which is free from dependence.

That splendor is not only capable of concealing itself, but is also able to conceal others characterized as conscious and unconscious; because of its similarity to armor (*varman*) due to its common properties, it is designated by that name.

It is called "armor" (kavaca). The seed-syllable (*bīja*) of omniscience—which is recited in the midst of the six qualities—is the radiance of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), denoted by the word "eye" (*netra*). For this reason, "beholding with that radiance" refers to the Blessed One’s vision of all objects. That which is...
I am irresistible; my majesty is invincible. That which is born of consciousness and unconsciousness is dependent upon the object of enjoyment.
It is called *pratāpa* because it is extended (*pratat*) by virtue of being pre-eminently incapable of being denied. That splendor (*tejas*) of Śambhu, of Śiva, is called a weapon (*heti*);
it is designated as a missile (*astra*). [This constitutes] the bearing of body, armor, and weapons.

If it is asked, "What is this sovereignty (aiśvarya) that has been observed? he says: Sovereignty is held to be one's own quality at its highest limit, because that highest limit is a quality consisting of supreme excellence.

His sovereignty is the supreme limit, the highest elevation, the unsurpassed limit of being; it is manifest, consisting of the nature of possession. Why is this so? It is said: "it is accepted as his own quality. The meaning is that it is not distinct from him. Why? Because that supreme limit consists of an absolute excellence.

The attribute (*guṇa*): the attribute consisting of the manifestation of Śiva-hood in the form of omniscience and omnipotence, which is unsurpassed in nature, is designated by the terms "Śiva-bliss" (*śivānanda*) and "Śiva-enjoyment" (*śivabhoga*). We shall explain later that this very same attribute belongs to the liberated Śiva (*muktaśiva*) as well. He states another meaning:
Sovereignty is the state of being the master over both the classes of the sentient and the insentient;
sovereignty here is mastery, for it is the fruit of the one who commands.
Alternatively, sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is the state of being the master (*svāmitā*) over both the two categories—the conscious and the unconscious.

It is the state of being a master, meaning "that which has its own [property]" (*sva-m-asti*), consisting of the conscious and the unconscious. Here, in the case of Śiva, sovereignty is not merely "mastery" (*vaśitā*);
it is not the "mastery" (*vaśitā*) mentioned in the middle of the list beginning with *aṇimā*. That mastery belongs to the one who rules; therefore, he is the possessor of mastery (*vaśitāvān*).
The fruit is the cause of one's own bliss; it is characterized by the fulfillment of both self and others, free from dependence.

Having thus described the nature of the mantra for the Lord—who is immersed in supreme bliss and possesses sovereignty over the categories of consciousness and non-consciousness—for the sake of bestowing grace upon the conscious and the unconscious, he concludes:
All these mantras are indeed the powers (śaktis) of Parameṣṭhin;
they are declared to be eternally established, and Śiva is capable [of action] through union with them.

All these mantras consist of the five Brahmans and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). They are the powers (*śakti*) of Parameṣṭhin Śiva, consisting of the powers beginning with Īśānī. And those powers are said to be eternally established;
the meaning is that they are not like those residing in the *vidyā-tattva*. Through connection with them, [the mantra becomes] the power beginning with Īśānī.
Due to this connection, Śiva becomes possessed of powers such as Īśāna and so forth; he is always established in the state of Śiva.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "When those [powers] are engaged in activity, they are called 'śaktis' (powers)."
Thus, the distinction between power and the possessor of power has been explained as a consequence of the context.
These mantras are not distinct from Śiva by way of the *āṇava* [impurity];
for when they are engaged in activity— that is, when they have reached the ground of practical application as Īśāna and the others—
they are called "powers" (*śakti*), being powers that effect differentiation within the Lord who possesses power.

They are thus described. When [the powers], having withdrawn their characteristic functions, return to their own inherent state, then these powers—Īśānī and the others—are said to be the internal body of the Lord, whose essence is Brahman; this is the intended meaning.
Because the distinction between power and the possessor of power was introduced, and because the mention of the Sādāśiva body followed as a natural consequence, it has been explained in this manner.

Due to the difference in their functions, there is a distinction among the powers (śaktis) such as Īśānī and the rest; through connection with those [powers], the distinction among the possessors of power (śaktimat), such as Īśāna and the rest, is declared in their aggregate. Those mantras which are "sātmakāḥ" by Śiva—meaning they exist together with Śiva as their own self (ātman) or essential nature (svarūpa)—the sense is that they are characterized by the relationship of identity (tādātmya). This refers to Śiva’s...

They are as if dwelling within the reality (tattva) of knowledge; nor are they distinct individual souls (aṇu), for the soul is said to be non-different from its own nature, and thus they are so described. Having explained the distribution of the potency of the effects—the body and its inherent powers—he now extends that explanation to those consisting of the instruments (karaṇa).
She is declared by Śiva to be the captivating one, possessing the power of all ornaments;
or else, having drawn forth the individual soul (pudgala), she leads it to the supreme state.
Therefore, this power is called "the captivator" by the wise;
she is the mother of the world's birth and the boundless limit of intrinsic nature.

Śiva’s *māyā*, which is described as "the captivator, the captivator" (*hāriṇī hāriṇī*) because it possesses the power to withdraw everything— that power by means of which there is the withdrawal or dissolution of all subtle bodies, their causes, consciousness, the self, enjoyments, and so forth, through its infinite powers— is thus designated.

Alternatively, when Māyā is manifested for the sake of the rite of initiation (dīkṣā) for a person whose impurities are fully ripened, she is present there as the "sakala" [state] residing within the maṇḍala; when she is unmanifested therein, she effects the withdrawal of the pure worlds for the "pralayākala" situated in its midst, or the "vijñānākala" situated above it.
Alternatively, Śuddhavidyā, acting as a weaver, takes up all those beginning with Ananta— whether they be some who are detached—
or having taken up the *paśus* (bound souls), she weaves the three impurities (*mala*) together with the powers (*śaktis*) and their possessors (*śaktimats*).
Above that, she is supported by the innermost [principles] such as Antaratama, which exist in a sequential order.

Having gradually extracted [the soul] from the gross, subtle, and latent impurities (*mala*), as well as from the objects of experience (*artha*) and the presiding authorities (*adhikāra*), by means of the withdrawal of the bonds (*pāśa*) appropriate to each stage,

and having caused it to ascend through the manifestation of its own inherent Śiva-nature characterized by respective adjuncts (*sopādhika*), until the manifestation of that Śiva-nature which is free from all unsuitable adjuncts is reached, one leads it to the supreme state (*parasaṃsthāna*).
One should lead [the soul] to the state characterized by the supreme Śiva-nature, which is the manifestation of unconditioned supreme Śiva-hood; that is, one should cause it to attain that.

Therefore, by the wise who possess the vision of the Śiva-scriptures, this [power] associated with Hara is called *Hāriṇī*. Furthermore, in another Āgama, this very same [power] is described according to the sequence of its functions as *Jyeṣṭhā*.

And she who is called Raudrī is designated by two names. Now, as for the activity of the Mother: at the commencement of creation, when Śiva is fulfilling his office of manifestation within the manifold creation, that power of his which is useful for that purpose—immeasurable, undivided, and luminous—is the consciousness (*cit*) of the world, which is the nature of birth and is fit for manifestation. (Page [p.])
93) Since it brings about the manifestation of the *cit* (consciousness) in its various forms as the effect of the *bindu*,

as well as the manifestation of the *cit* conditioned by those [forms], through the gateway of infinite powers— thereby manifesting both the *cit* that is of the nature of *māyā* and the *cit* conditioned by that— it is called the "Mother" (*jananī*) because of its connection to the progenitor.
Even in initiation (*dīkṣā*), this [power] is the foundation, the mother of both the conscious and the unconscious; thus she is beyond comprehension.

Now, as for the function of the Obstructress (*rodhayitrī*): the Obstructress is that which establishes the restriction of the multitude of individual souls (*aṇu*) during the dissolution (*pralaya*).
And it bestows upon him enjoyments from whatever source they may come.

The power belonging to Śiva, who is intent upon obstructing the multitude of individual souls (*aṇu*), manifests directly at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) for those whose nature is that of the *pralayakevala*. During the period of persistence, it remains within the womb of Māyā according to the ripening of their own accumulated karma, and through the gateway of infinite powers (*anantaśakti*), it likewise functions during the experience of enjoyments. (p. 94)

By means of the *stiti* [ritual], there is the re-establishment (*pratiṣṭhāna*) in its own place even during initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the *māyā-maṇḍala*; and furthermore, by the word "also," for the entire multitude of *sakala-aṇus*, as well as for the *vijñānakevalin*s directly until the end of the ripening of impurity (*mala-pāka*), there is re-establishment in its own place up to the end of *māyā* during initiation; and also for one who has been joined to the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*).
He establishes *niyama* (restriction), which is characterized by concealment (*tirobhāva*) and the fall from that state;

furthermore, at the time of re-establishment, through initiation (*dīkṣā*) via the gateway of infinite power (*ananta-śakti*) upon the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*), and directly upon the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), He effects the establishment of each respective locus as consisting of its own specific causal efficiency (*svasvārthakriyātmikā*). Thus, by implication, He brings about established existence.

Because she acts from that [state] and from that [state], she is designated as "the Obstructress" (*rodhayitrī*), belonging to the Obstructress (*rodhayitṛ*). These two powers—the Mother (*jananī*) and the Obstructress (*rodhayitrī*)—which possess the functions of the three [aspects of] emission, maintenance, and concealment, and which are of a single nature and true, are said in other scriptures to belong to the subtle Vāmadeva. He concludes:
O Brahmins, these three powers, which constitute the instruments within the body, are eternally established in the omnipresent Lord, just as [the power of heat is] in fire itself.
These three powers, numbering three, are designated as Hāriṇī, Jananī, and Rodhayitrī;

they reside in the body—the gross form consisting of Īśānī and the others—and are of the nature of instruments (karaṇa), while their subtle bodies constitute their essential nature. They are called *vapuḥ* because they nourish (*puṣṇāti*) with supreme human goals (*pumartha*), and because they extend (*tanoti*) and expand the entire universe.
O Brahmins, those powers (śaktis) are of the same nature as His subtle body (tanuḥ), and they are eternally established in the omnipresent Śiva.
Why is that? Because they are indeed His own portions, consisting of His very own capacity. Now, He shows their state of existence:
In reality, the abiding state of those powers is within the principle of Īśvara,
because He is the impeller of the powers and activity proceeds from them.

The abiding of those powers, from Īśānī to Rodhayitrī, exists in reality by their very nature within Śiva, who is designated as the principle of Īśvara; for this reason, Śiva, called Īśa, is the impeller who, entering the state of practical activity, acts for the sake of their manifestation.

It possesses a manifold arrangement of qualities (*vicitraguṇasaṃklipti*). It should not be said that it is "devoid of bone" (*asthika*); for from that [source], because activity (*pravṛtti*)—the contemplation of the manifold qualities which are the effects of the *bindu*—is not otherwise possible through the powers (*śakti*).
At the very moment they are impelled toward their effect, they truly attain their unfolding (*unmīlana*). In that regard, within Śiva, who is called the "possessor of authority" (*adhikāra*).

The sense is that [the powers] reveal their own self as being non-distinct from Him (the Lord) by virtue of being established inseparably from Him. As it is said in the *Mataṅga*: "Having attained full manifestation, these true powers, when appointed to their respective offices within this one called the Lord, reveal their own selves."

Now, an objection may be raised: since Śiva, known by the name Sadāśiva, is the presiding deity of the principle of Sadākhya, and all powers reside within Him in a collective form during the state of the application of His creative activity (*kāryaprayoga*), how can "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) be described as existing here? It is true that His status as an *adhikārī* (one possessing authority or office) is fully established in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures; however, this pertains to His own specific task...

When the Bindu presiding over its own activity is devoid of division (*kalā*)—even though it is partless (*niṣkala*)—it nevertheless possesses a manifest power suitable for union; this is because it presides over the fourfold *bindu* which is both "part-and-whole" (*sakala-niṣkala*) and intent upon the emergence of the poet (the Creator). At the time of the commencement of creation, Śiva is designated as "part-and-whole" (*sakala-niṣkala*).

The power of vision (*dṛk*), whose nature consists in the preservation of the *bindu*, brings about the departure from the state of enjoyment; entering the stage of authority over the creation of the manifold universe that has been fully manifested, it acquires the name "Īśvara. It effects the creation of the worlds beginning with Śāntyatīta within the five levels—Śānti and the others—which are enumerated among the *kalās* that are the effects of the *bindu*.
With reference to the four *kalās*, while presiding over them, one who has fashioned the lower womb (*adhoyoni*) abandons, in due order,

the states of effort and enjoyment (*udyoga-bhoga*) situated above each respective [level] in the sphere of the effects produced by that [womb], and enters into authority (*adhikāra*). This is because, even there, the state of being engaged in the activity of the level below is present for the sake of conjunction (*sammelana*), owing to the state of being both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*).

Although the Śāntyatīta world is characterized by dissolution (laya), it is nonetheless characterized by enjoyment (bhoga) because it resides at the summit of tranquility (śānti). Even though it is designated as "dissolution," within the five worlds beginning with Śāntyatīta, one experiences that which is called enjoyment;
therefore, those desiring to attain the worlds of Īśāna and the others should meditate upon [Śiva] in the form of the manifestations (mūrtis) of Īśāna and the rest.

Having bestowed the fruit [of grace], immediately thereafter, presiding over the manifestation of the world called Sadākhya, he who is designated as Sadāśiva—consisting of a body formed by the five forms in their collective aspect—is to be constantly meditated upon.

Because he is of a collective nature, he possesses the state of being "with parts" (sakala); yet, even while possessing that fully developed authority, he remains superior to those below him, namely Īśvara and the others.

Since it is impossible for him to have reached the state of engaging in activity characterized by the infinite impulsion of the real and the unreal emanations (*nirmāṇa*), his exertion toward that [activity] is not possible; therefore, he is described here as the very Lord Bhaṭṭāraka known as Sadāśiva, who is *bhoga* (enjoyment). — Mataṅga.

In the *Sarvajñānottara*, however, having subsumed all the lower effects within the principle of Sadāśiva, that [state] is described as "enjoyment" (*bhoga*); thus, there is nothing inconsistent. The sages—namely the Sāṃkhyas, Buddhists, Jaiminīyas, Jainas, Cārvākas, and others—have proclaimed the proof of the Lord (*īśvara*) through their respective established scriptures.

Others, such as the followers of the Pāñcarātra and other systems, hold that the attainment of anything other than Śiva is the goal taught by the Gītā; thus, seized by doubt, they address the Blessed One with their faces turned toward Him:
"Blessed One, the category designated as the Pati has been correctly explained."
For the virtuous are indeed to be addressed by means of valid cognitions and understood through reasoning.

(p. 100) O Blessed One, although the meaning of the path has been explained through descriptions of its essential nature, such as right absorption (*samyak-laya*) and so forth, it must nevertheless be stated by means of proofs known as inference (*anumāna*), and established through those explanations, in order to uproot the doubts and attachments produced by the various conflicting views of disputants; for [the truth] is indeed to be understood through reasoning (*yukti*).
For the meanings (*arthāḥ*) are indeed to be understood—that is, they are to be made known—by means of reasonings and inferences;

for these meanings are established as having real existence (*siddhasattākāḥ*). Alternatively, "the virtuous" (*sādhavaḥ*) refers to faithful listeners (*āstika-śrotāraḥ*), because all disputants except the Cārvākas accept inference as the means of establishing supersensuous realities.
Because it is not subject to denial, the Blessed One, relying upon this, employs an inferential statement (*anumānavākya*) there against the Sāṃkhya in order to establish that [point]:
"O Brahmins, the insentient world, without the impulsion of a sentient being..."
Whether in engagement or in withdrawal, it is not independent, like a chariot or similar objects.

O Brahmins, this insentient world— whether in its essential reality (*tattva*) or its collection of constituent principles (*tātvikajāta*)— is not independent, nor is it devoid of dependence upon the impulsion of a conscious being,

whether for the sake of engaging in activity to achieve its own purpose or for desisting from it when that purpose is attained; just as a chariot, like a chariot and so forth, does not exist for its purpose without the impulsion of a charioteer.
One who is capable of bringing about the cessation of that [bondage] by means of understanding the nature of action—then who is the instigator? To this he says:
"He who is here the capable instigator is proclaimed as the Lord (pati).
There is no inconclusiveness of the reason, just as milk is for the growth of the calf."

In this context, that which is capable and competent to impel a conscious agent toward the performance or non-performance of an action is traditionally defined as the "instigator" (*prayojaka*), the "mover," or the "master. The earth and other such elements do not perform their own purposeful activity—characterized by supporting and so forth—without the instigation of a conscious being, because they are insentient. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: "Just like a chariot and the like."

The Sāṃkhyas maintain that just as even insentient milk performs its own purposeful activity (svārthakriyā) consisting in the nourishment of its calf, so too does primordial nature (prakṛti) perform its own purposeful activity consisting in the bestowal of experience and liberation for the person (puruṣa). Here, the opponent has raised the argument: "Primordial nature proceeds spontaneously because it is insentient, like milk."

Demonstrating that in the example there is a concomitance established with the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*), and further pointing out the contradictory nature (*viruddhatva*) of that reason, he states "no" to explain that this very illustration of milk would apply to the reason he himself has employed; therefore, it is not an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason.

Regarding the reason "because of insentience" that you have employed, my child, its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) is shown by milk, which causes the growth and nourishment of the body of the calf. Why is this so? To this he says:
"Because it is set in motion by a sentient cow for the sake of the calf's growth."
If [the capacity] were to proceed from clay and so forth, then it would have proceeded spontaneously; [but] that is not the case.

Furthermore, it does not proceed because consciousness remains dependent [on a conscious agent]. For milk is set in motion by a conscious cow and, being endowed with its own purposeful activity, serves to nourish the calf. If milk were to proceed by itself, without being presided over by consciousness, and yet were endowed with purposeful activity, then [the same would apply] to that which is dead.

If activity were to proceed from a body devoid of life and lacking consciousness—such as that of a cow—it would indeed be active; however, since it does not so proceed, it is established and certain that for the sake of initiating and ceasing activity, there must be a dependence upon a conscious being.
This is a subverting argument (*bādhakatarka*). [Objection: But here, in the case of magnets, grass, and pieces of crystal, there is their own inherent power regarding iron and grass...

Because [the example] is seen to be the cause for activity such as wandering, your reason is contradictory; therefore, it is not the case that your reason is non-conclusive or non-existent. To this he says:
"Nor is the example of the magnet a proof for the activity of the insentient."
Even the magnet functions as an initiator only by depending upon a speaker.

In the case of the "magnet-example" (ayaskānta-dṛṣṭānta), which is employed as a means to establish spontaneous activity in that which is insentient (*acetana*), the example of the magnet is not a proof for that reason. It should not be accepted as a valid reason (*saddhetu*).
Why? Because even the magnet, like milk, [requires] a conscious agent (*cetana-ātman*) such as Devadatta or others to function.

Only by observing the instigator (*prayojaka*) does that [magnet] become an activator through its very nature of grasping; it becomes engaged in its own purposeful action through the attraction of iron, but not by itself even in the case of a blade of grass, a jewel-fragment, or similar objects. Thus, this example is possible within our reason (*hetu*), and therefore there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) on this account. Now, [an objection]:
The blowing of the wind and the burning of fire are seen to be natural; yet others claim that action possesses the capacity to grant its own fruit independently. To refute this, Jaimini says: (p.
105) "Furthermore, even that which is the subject under discussion is inert, and it is something else that impels it."
That which is insentient remains thus, depending on another for its own activity.

Furthermore, as previously stated, something other than an insentient entity functions; that [other] has been made the subject (*pakṣa*), being delimited by the exclusion of all counter-arguments. This is the intended meaning: if the blowing of the wind and the burning of fire were observed to be inherent, then there would be a contradiction of their own nature, characterized by immobility and extinction.

Why is it that the blowing of wind, burning, and so forth are observed only occasionally? Therefore, since these occur as a result of being impelled by something, there must be another cause; thus, God is inferred as the impeller. Furthermore, the Self is also inferred as the cause for the blowing and non-blowing of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other winds. [Likewise,] the fruit of action...

Even though [the gift] is productive, because that person lacks all such knowledge as "I shall give this to him again after this much time with this means," or "I shall give this fruitless thing now separately along with another fruit," it is like the work of agriculture and so forth.
Therefore, it is not logical for agency to be the primary [attribute], because agency follows from the object. It is not devoid of independence. As it was stated by the perfected Guru:
"The state of being independent is the non-subordination to others; [agency consists in] the state of employing instruments and so forth."
For this independence of the agent does not exist without dependence on the object and other factors.

For this reason, it is certain that the insentient [pradhāna], in its own activity, depends upon another—namely, consciousness. This is the position of the followers of Jaimini (the Mīmāṃsakas). Based on such scriptural authorities as "Puruṣa alone is this," they maintain that in Yoga, this very Puruṣa is to be known as the Self, which is bound by its own good and evil deeds. And it is not...

They say that no one other than Īśvara can bring about that liberation. Keeping this in mind, the sages raise an objection: "If there are such conscious persons who are universally acknowledged, let them alone be the agents; what need is there for another, O Lord? (p. 107)
He is the Lord. And if it is thus one [Lord]: if the insentient is set in motion in dependence upon a sentient being, then there exist sentient persons accepted and acknowledged by all disputants;
let their very agency—along with the impelling of the body and so forth—be the cause of its creation. Speak! Tell us your own view, and not that of another.
The Lord is not established by that which is called "the Lord," O best of the twice-born, because this self is ignorant and lacks mastery;
even He would be dependent for His own activity, just like a jar or similar objects.

How can he be accepted as the agent? Therefore, O Maheśvaras, O best of the twice-born, since the Self is in the state of pure consciousness (*vijñāna-kaivalya*), its power of vision and action (*dṛk-kriyā*) is unmanifest; because it is beyond the scope of objects, it is impossible for the unknown to impel them—this is the sense.

Furthermore, in the state of dissolution or isolation (*kaivalya*), the individual soul (*ajantu*) lacks the knowledge—due to its disjunction from the *kalās* and other principles—that "I was previously such-and-such, and now I am creating this [body]," nor does it possess the impulsion of yoga; thus, it is incapable of being born again through its own conscious manifestation (*cidvyakti*) conjoined with its body. However, in the state of manifestation (*sakala-daśā*), that same soul is not independent (*anīśa*).

The impelling of the body and so forth is not independent even if it were unreal; for by this [power], the separation from one's own body, the creation of another body, or the impelling of that [body] according to its own will are not performed. If such [independence] existed, then all persons would always possess non-material bodies and be happy. Furthermore, that person [who possesses such power] would also [be subject to] his own activity and his own enjoyment.

Because liberation, being the self, possesses causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*), it must be dependent upon something else for its attainment, just like a jar. For instance, a jar is dependent on Devadatta and others for the accomplishment of its function characterized by the fetching of water; likewise, [liberation] would necessarily be dependent on Īśvara. For indeed, all those who possess discernment...
When they engage in actions that accomplish what is beneficial, as seen in worldly activities, they appear to act according to their inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

However, they are sometimes observed engaging even in harmful acts such as gambling or the killing of a Brahmin; this reversal of their nature is not without a cause. That which is the cause of this is the Lord (*Īśvara*).

Thus they say: "Impelled by the Lord, one may go either to heaven or even into a pit. Now, if this is so, since they perform acts such as the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) or the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) by taking the fruits of other actions as their objective, being impelled by the Lord, how can they possess agency (*kartṛtva*), given the absence of independence (*svātantrya*) in those cases? True.

Since those who are impelled also possess agency, they are possessed by pride regarding fruits such as self-sovereignty (*svārājya*)—which arises from an exceedingly intense state of being—and by fear, attachment, and the like. As agents of horse-sacrifices, Brahmin-slaughter, and the seizure of another's property, they are indeed perceived as having that very nature of agency characterized by independence. Thus it is not [the case that they lack agency].

This is somewhat inconsistent. For it is stated in the *Śrīmataṅga*: "Whosoever, having subdued [the soul] through the state of destruction, is employed as the shadow of Śiva for the sake of enjoyment, then his karma becomes identical with that.
Therefore, Maheśvara is the agent; that person of the aforementioned characteristics is the agent, being the impeller of the insentient.
"How? In what manner is it said?"—the meaning is that it is not accepted in any way whatsoever because it lacks the characteristics previously described.
Anticipating the objection, "Let them be as you have stated, since they are non-conscious and impelled by another," he says:
"If it is your thought that these [beings], being liberated, would indeed become agents..."
O twice-born ones, is the agent one who was liberated without beginning, or rather, one who is not liberated from the beginning?

O twice-born ones, they are liberated, endowed with the manifestation of Śiva-hood through the release from the three bonds. The word "tu" (but/then) has the sense of excluding [the possibility of] non-yoga or other forms of yoga. If the reading is "tarhi," it means "tadā" (then). They would become agents (*kartāraḥ*), meaning conscious instigators. (p. 111) If the intellect (*buddhi*) is the notion of "I" (*asmi-mati*), then what is liberated? What is the point?
He would be the creator; or else, he would be a creator who has been liberated from eternity. Regarding this, he states the resulting conclusion:

"If the creator were one eternally liberated, then it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*). If, however, he is liberated at the beginning [of creation], then his status as the creator is established even prior to that liberation."
Otherwise, how could this [agent] be liberated? It would always remain bound.

If it were an agent liberated from beginningless time, then—since the agency of the world has already been established and determined—the proof [offered] would be a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already proven); that is the reality, and "it would be a *siddhasādhana*" is the syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*). At the outset...

Existence (*bhava*) is the first. If that [first one] is liberated and yet an agent, then for that one who is liberated from the beginning, the agent is established—indeed, established even prior to liberation, as the cause of liberation. Even in that case, if one accepts a succession of such [liberated agents], then for each of them, an agent would be established through their respective liberation; thus, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). To avoid this, it is established that [existence] is beginningless (*anādi*).

And it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "The world must have been created by one who is established by his own nature (*svabhāvasiddha*); otherwise, how or in what manner could this primordial liberated Siddha exist if he were established only subsequently (*arvāksiddha*) or were some causeless being? Otherwise, in a different manner, independent of a beginningless, established Creator, how could this first liberated Siddha come to be?

Considering that [the soul] has been liberated from the beginningless [bondage], since there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence [as bound], it would have to be eternally bound. Now, one might argue: "Let the agent be one who is himself liberated from the fetters. To this we reply: No, because even the class of bound souls (*paśu*) and so forth would follow as being exclusively [bound]; furthermore, this is because it has been refuted [by scripture] that "the living being was ignorant from before. This is held in the heart [of the opponent].
Having set it down, he said: "Men never attain liberation through their own power alone,
except by the grace of the god Śiva, the remover of misfortune."

By the splendor characterized by the divinity of the Lord—who is playful in nature and who removes the inauspicious—[he acts]. "Auspiciousness" (*śiva*) is the power consisting of omniscience and omnipotence; that which is contrary to it is "inauspiciousness" (*aśiva*), namely impurity (*mala*). Having perceived that this inauspiciousness has reached full maturity, he removes it through his own manifest capacity during the rite of initiation; thus, he is "the remover of the inauspicious" (*aśivahārin*).

[They are] those who take away [bondage] from Śiva. The grace of Śiva is the favor in the form of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Without that, having abandoned it, persons never attain liberation by their own capacity—that is, by their own power. For instance, bound souls (*paśus*) cannot [attain it] without a Lord (*īśvara*) who is established from beginningless time and endowed with superior knowledge and action, [just as they cannot perceive] the body and so forth [without Him].

The bonds, such as the body and so forth, do not act by themselves for the purpose of severing the bonds, nor for the purpose of union, nor for the purpose of attaining the experience of pleasure; nor do they cease by themselves due to the experiences of pain or delusion. Because they lack independence, like animals such as rams, these bonds—the body and so forth—are dependent upon other causal factors.
Animals do not engage in [actions] by themselves, nor do they desist from them by themselves,

because they are insentient— like sheep and other animals [which do not act] or like ropes and other [inanimate] bonds. To those Mīmāṃsakas and others who maintain that the world was never otherwise than it is now, he demonstrates another argument:
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, hear another inference:
the world, which is the subject of dispute, must have been preceded by an omniscient creator.
Just as an effect such as a jar is established for both of us by virtue of its being an effect,
so too this universe possesses the nature of an effect because it is composed of parts, like a jar.
Since even ether and the like possess that [quality], being endowed with qualities just as a jar is,
therefore the world, which is the subject of dispute, must be preceded by a creator.

O best of the twice-born! Furthermore, regarding the proof of Ātmeśvara, another inference distinct from the previous one is stated as having parts; listen, for it is worthy of being heard: this universe, which is the subject of dispute—whether it has a creator or is without a creator—is a great tree shaken by the vibration of conflicting arguments. (p. 115)

The world, consisting of mountains, clouds, oceans, rivers, fire, wind, and so forth, possesses diverse forms. At that time, because it has been rendered free from dispute—being suitable for the present inquiry and having its subject matter characterized by a doubtful agent—it is observed as an instance where the lack of observation of an agent does not constitute a valid example; thus, jars and the like, whose agents are doubtful, serve as the [proper] examples.

It does not enter within the limit of the opposing side, nor is it the case that it does not enter; thus, since there is no agent therein, one might object that this would entail the Lord’s lack of sovereignty in that regard. However, even in the case of objects such as a jar, Śiva’s agency—characterized by being the prompter—is established; therefore, he is the "Knower of All" (*viśvavit*), because he knows the universe to be preceded by an agent.

"He who creates the universe is the 'creator of the universe' (*viśvakartā*); he who is both the knower of the universe and the creator is the 'knower-creator of the universe' (*viśvavid-kartā*). That which has such a knower-creator as its antecedent by virtue of being its own efficient cause is thus described. From what [is this known]? This is the proposition (*pratijñā*). Because it is an effect—this is the reason (*hetu*). Whatever is an effect is preceded by a knower-creator."

Just as the effect, such as a jar and the like, is established and accepted by both of us disputants, that indeed serves as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Now, it may be argued: "The state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is not established for the world; for bodies and so forth are never seen being produced by anyone at any time, since even those things which are perishable are seen [as existing] without being made. To this, we reply: that is not so regarding bodies and the like.

Even though its state of being currently produced (*kriyamāṇatva*) is not [directly] perceived, how is it not "seen"? For, although it is not an object of sensory perception, it is inferred as an effect because it comes into being after having not existed before, or because it is subject to destruction once it has become manifest. Now, one might object that even though it is seen, the world—such as the body and so forth—is never seen to have been otherwise; thus, according to the method of the Jaiminīyas' statement regarding the earth and other elements, [it must be eternal].
Neither has it been observed that [earth and other elements] come into being after not having existed, nor have they been seen to perish. To this, the Blessed One replies: "It is true.

Although the coming into being after non-existence and the state of perishing are established by scripture for earth and the rest, their status as effects is observed—just like a jar or a pot—because they possess parts and consist of constituent portions. (p. 117)

The fourth [point]: Now, how is it established that subtle earth and the other elements possess parts (*sāṃśatva*)? Logicians (*nyāyavādin*) assert that space and so forth are partless (*niraṃśatva*). That is not so; even space and the like possess parts and are composed of constituent elements (*sāvayava*), because they possess qualities (*saguṇatvāt*). [Their] qualities are perceivable by the external sense organs of beings such as ourselves.

Because they are associated [with other qualities]. For example, a jar is established as possessing qualities because it has constituent parts (*sāvayavatvāt*). Space and so forth are established as distinct from each individual subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) because they flow in the opposite direction [to the body]. Time and the mind are non-conscious because they are multiple. Even an atom is material (*mūrta*) like dust; and since time and the rest are established as effects, [they must likewise possess qualities].

Like a jar and other such objects, this [world] also does not deviate from being an effect (*kāryatva*). Therefore, for the purpose of establishing a specific agent (*viśiṣṭakartṛ*) by virtue of this world being situated [as a locus], the reason (*hetu*) is "being an effect. The application (*upanaya*), characterized by the conceptualization of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) as defined by the world, is: "because of that state of being an effect."

"The elephant under dispute is preceded by an agent. (p. 118) "Preceded" (*purassara*) means that which goes before. That whose preceding existence is due to an agent acting as its own instrumental cause is described as such. This constitutes the conclusion (*nigamana*), characterized by the postulation of a specific agent, as it is included within the subject (*pakṣa*) defined by the nature of this world.

Now, is it not the case that because of the specific arrangement (*sanniveśa*) found in dry land, stones, trees, clouds, oceans, rivers, whales, the sun, fire, wind, and so forth, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) for those [latter] things?
