For even if "being an effect" were established in some way for something possessing such a specific arrangement, the particular instance of an effect characterized by the three worlds would never [be established].

It is established that the pervasion [of the world] by any specific individual who is its creator is difficult to perceive. This establishment pertains to the reason (*hetu*) "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) as it functions to prove a creator. That [reason] is common to others as well; for instance, even when the fact that smoke existing in a kitchen is an effect of fire is established, it remains [uncertain] in some way or other, by whatever specific [agent].

Because the smoke located on the mountain—characterized by being produced at a specific place and time, being more subtle, larger, and having the form of lines and so forth—is distinct from that [smoke] located in the kitchen; for how could this be the effect of fire, given its extreme dissimilarity to the [smoke] existing in the kitchen? Thus, its status as the effect of fire is not established.
Furthermore, by this statement, since it would follow that the apprehension of pervasion for all inferences must occur within a subject (*pakṣa*) whose property is yet to be proven,

the pervasion of any particular instance of smoke with any particular instance of fire existing on a mountain could never be apprehended; thus, even for a reason such as "smokiness" established by common consensus, there would be no possibility of its being valid.

This sublation (*bādhā*), which renders even what is established unestablished, results in the total destruction of all inference; it thus follows for all proponents of inference. One [who faces this] is not to be questioned. As it has been said: "Where a fault belongs to both parties, or where the remedy is equal for both..."
One should not be questioned regarding such a determination of meaning.

(p. 120) Therefore, in order to avoid that [objection], since a specific [cause] is not a [necessary] cause, one observes an invariable concomitance (*avyāpti*) between the mere effect in desired cases such as pots and the mere agent, and between mere smoke in kitchens and so forth and mere fire; thus, everything is consistent. Now, [one might ask: what is the agent of the forest, grass, and so forth?

Because [the reason] is seen to be non-existent in the subject (*pakṣa*), it follows that this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); that is not so, because everything whose agent is unperceived—even forests, grass, and the like—is included within the subject. But is this not rather contradictory (*viruddha*)? As they say:
"When the example is established [as lacking the probandum], the reason becomes contradictory."
Furthermore, it would follow that there is agency with respect to destruction and so forth, even for one who is not the Lord (anīśvara).

That is incorrect; for since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed pervaded by the opposite, the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*). Furthermore, this example is not established as being invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with a non-omniscient agent, because even in the case of a potter, omniscience and universal agency would be established in relation to his own specific effects.

For that alone is lordship; for if, while residing therein, the power of non-perception were to produce non-pervasiveness, confusion, or error even by a fraction, then at that time he would not create the jar,
but rather something else undesirable, such as a pot with deficient parts or one unsuitable for its intended purpose.

Furthermore, he would act like a potter; or, like a potter whose tools and so forth have been destroyed, he would not act. For there is no destruction for him, because the self is eternal and it is that very self which possesses agency. Just as, having seen a jar with all its parts complete, one perceives its functional features—the broad base, the belly, and the other portions—[so too should one perceive the agent].

Since agency is not established for that which pervades [the universe] as if from a mountain peak or similar source, the potter’s capacity to act as a creator is inferred through his own work, which possesses pervasive extension. For there is no lack of visual power, no lack of agency, no lack of pervasion, nor any delusion. Thus, the entire universe, with its matchless beauty and every limb, [is perceived].

122) Even having seen that the activity of Īśvara pervades the universe, his power as a creator is inferred through his intellect. But surely, because a potter lacks knowledge and agency elsewhere than in his own specific work, and because [such qualities] are not pervasive, he is not Īśvara; likewise, the Lord of the World (Jagadīśvara) would also not be Īśvara, since the world is a created effect produced by a non-Īśvara creator, just like a jar.

"The jar" is thus inferred as being non-omnipotent. True; if there were anything other than the universe—the means for the attainment of enjoyment and liberation—that is its effect, then it could be correctly inferred in that manner. But how is it known that nothing else exists? It is said: let that thing exist; what of it?

Is it a means for attaining enjoyment (bhoga) and liberation (mokṣa), or is it not a means at all? In that regard, if it is a means, then like the body and its organs, it must necessarily be an effect. If it is not a means, then there is no purpose in it;
nor can there be ignorance regarding it, as in the case of a hare's horn and the like, for it would merely be an ornament. As they have said:
That which makes known the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted— which is the goal to be attained—
is accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but not that which makes everything known.
Therefore, since agency in the form of being purposeful exists even in the case of jars and other such objects,

their status as effects does not deviate [from the rule]; for they possess the nature of an effect characterized by the world— which is incomparable and distinguished by features such as having a specific arrangement, being all-pervasive, and being continuous.

Since no other [cause] is possible apart from that body and its effects, and since non-omniscience would entail a lack of lordship, it cannot be established [that there is another cause]; therefore, the Lord of the World is inferred by virtue of being endowed with unsurpassed power of knowledge, action, and will, which pervade all objects. Indeed, there is no further example [required].

Existing in the subject (*dharmin*) and present in all instances of the subject to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*), [these properties] are fully applicable in that manner. For example, in the argument "Sound is eternal because it is produced, like a jar," properties such as being the product of a potter, redness, containing water, and sphericity—which exist in the jar—would also exist in sound. Why is this so?

If it were the case that [these properties] do not exist, then this conceptual construction (*klipti*) would result in the total annihilation of all inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, the probandum (*sādhya*) is well-established in accordance with the property of the means of proof (*sādhana-dharma*). To illustrate: just as smoke and other effects—whether situated in a mountain cave, within its interior, upon its peak, or elsewhere—are related to their causes in a specific manner, so too is the probandum established.

Or, by means of what is perceived as being in proximity—characterized by its own nature such as water, leaves, and so forth, possessing whatever magnitude it has, whether thin, broad, linear, or dense like a mass of clouds—one infers its cause, which is characterized as fire. Thus, it is inferred to be of such a kind. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:
The excellence of the body is not seen even in the maintenance of the world, due to the excellence [of its cause];
for whatever effect is of such a nature and to such an extent, its cause is likewise.

Otherwise, in this case [the following would follow]: "The fire here does not reside on the mountain, because it is smoke; wherever there is smoke, there is no fire residing on the mountain, as in a kitchen. Thus, in all cases, the fallacy of the non-deviating contradictory (*viruddhāvyabhicāritva*) would result.

Now, one might object: "This is a proof of the opposite—namely, that the nature of the subject, which is characterized by having a single agent, is contrary to being characterized by having multiple agents."

It is contradictory; for we observe that things such as palaces and the like are constructed from numerous parts fashioned by carpenters, which are themselves composed of infinite atoms that mutually assist one another. Thus they say:
"Although all things, such as structural arrangements and the like, [presuppose] an intelligent agent..."
How can it be established that there is a single cause for the arrangement [of the world] and so forth?

That is incorrect. Even though the components of a chariot and so forth are fashioned by many different carpenters, they cannot exist as a chariot without the cognition of a single [observer]. Since they arise only through a relationship of mutual assistance and assistance-giver, the chariot and such are the substrata that perform the purposeful action of moving.

It is indeed logically established by virtue of being the initiator of substance (*dravyārambhakatva*). In that regard, there is no lack of logical consistency even at times when [the world] appears as a single entity through the cognition of a sovereign (*sthapati*). Furthermore, in this context as well, Śiva—whose consciousness is empowered by *kalā*, whose sphere of experience is revealed by *vidyā*, and who is colored by *rāga*—[acts] through the gateways of Ananta and the other [deities], as established by the scriptures.

The parts of the world, such as *kalā* and the rest, which are accomplished solely by His will and arise through a mutual relationship of helper and helped in order to assume the form of the universe, possess the single attribute of being the agents of action for the means to enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) characterized by the world He has fashioned; thus, they are like the *viśeṣa* atoms and so forth.

Thus, agency alone is established; it is not multiple agency, and so there is no contradiction. Now, an objection: since action cannot exist without an instrument (*karaṇa*), it is not logical for the world to have a cause that lacks an instrument. True. However, just as in the case of a yogin, the power of action characterized by will (*icchā*) itself serves as the instrument. It has been proven that for one who is bodiless, the performance of an action occurs through will alone.
This is even more so in the case of the lions and other [beings] mentioned previously. It is not written here in detail for fear of prolixity.

Now, it might be argued: "The Lord is endowed with instruments such as the senses because he is an agent; whatever is an agent is endowed with instruments such as the senses, just like a potter. This is incorrect, because [the Lord] possesses the power characterized by volition and purposeful action.
Agency arises merely through the proximity of the one possessing the characteristic of height (the Lord), just as the movement of one's own body is attributed to the self;
this has already been established. Now, [an objection]: "But surely, the self does not possess agency with respect to the movement of its own body, which is not its effect. True.
For this very reason, the universe—consisting of the pure and impure, and the subtle and gross—is [manifested].

Previously, it was established that [the body] is treated as if it were the body of the Blessed One. Therefore, indeed, in order to dissolve the conglomeration of objective functions through a process of conformity (*anulomyena*), one should regard even the gross body— characterized by the pure universe and defined by infinite bodies and so forth— as being like the Self, by means of the vibration of its own subtle body which possesses the characteristics of those [infinite] bodies.

It causes vibration. Now, has it not been stated that this [Lord] is accessible through the means of knowledge called inference? Is there not, then, accessibility through other means as well? To this he says:
"This Lord is accessible solely through the knowledge of the Lord, and He is indeed the cause of that [knowledge]."
In that interval, those who have attained perfection are animals by virtue of their pervasive state of being.
Therefore, they are both to be purified and to be awakened, because of the established state of their condition as bound souls (paśu).

Furthermore, this Lord of the Universe is established through the direct perception of yogis; he is established again by inference; and he is known solely through the knowledge of the Lord (pati). In that context, the mention of "solely" (eka) is for the purpose of restriction, [specifying] that he is known only through the knowledge of the Lord.

It is to be understood and realized through the Śivāgama alone; the result of this restriction is that it is not within the scope of other "treatises for bound souls" (paśuśāstra). In that Śivāgama, the power of vision (dṛk-śakti) of Śiva, through its full manifestation, empowers the consciousness-power (cicchakti) of the practitioners, meaning that it perfectly reveals Śiva to them. (p.)

129) Because it manifests that power which is the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the Śiva-āgama is designated by the term "the locus of its manifestation. Therefore, even figuratively, the power of Paraśiva is called "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) even in the immediate sense. Now, one might object: if the Āgama was created by Śiva, the Lord of the universe, and Śiva is known through the Āgama, [then there is a circularity].

There would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*). Therefore, Śiva—the Lord of the Universe—is not the cause of that scripture; rather, the meaning is that He is indeed the cause of its [existence]. The intention is as follows: because Śiva and the scripture possess similar natures and functions, they stand in a relationship of mutual dependence; Śiva is the author of the scripture, while the scripture is the means of making known the reality of Śiva. Thus, regarding Śiva and the scripture:

The status of being a producer (*kārakatā*) and the status of being an indicator (*jñāpakatā*) are not identical in terms of their action, because they are defined by different types of activity. For example, in common worldly usage, someone might say, "I, Devadatta, have arrived. Another person, upon hearing that very sentence, understands: "Ah, this Devadatta has arrived! In this case, there is no mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*). This is so even when the subject matter pertains to the science of cattle (*paśuśāstra*).
To the question "Why?", he says: "In other tantras," and so forth.
In other tantras such as the Pāñcarātra and others, whatever perfected beings (*siddhas*) are propounded on account of their conceit of being the Lord of the World—why are they [not included here]?
Because of the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in those tantras and among those perfected beings, due to their limited scope within those respective systems.

First, because it does not mention all the entities established in the Śiva-tantras, there is an absence of pervasiveness regarding that Śiva-tantra; furthermore, it conveys a meaning that is inferior to it. The followers of the Sāṃkhya with a Lord (Seśvara-sāṃkhya) hold that the group of divine origins beginning with Brahmā is the agent;
the Pāñcarātrikas hold that Hari, joined with a body and so forth, is the dweller in the world of Prakṛti.

The Naiyāyikas maintain that Īśvara is one who possesses knowledge born from connection with a human body. The followers of the Sāṃkhya, the Viśeṣa, and the Pātañjala systems maintain that Īśvara is one who possesses knowledge born from connection with the intellect (*buddhi*). The Paurāṇikas maintain that he is Īśvara while possessing a body. The Vedāntins, who uphold the non-duality of the individual soul and Brahman, maintain that he is the Lord of the Universe (*jagadīśvara*). That...

Since those who have attained perfection—like ourselves and others—are possessed of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and since their scriptures exhibit a limited scope, it follows that there can exist beings who transcend these limits and are endowed with unsurpassed knowledge and action; thus, there is an absence of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*).
Consequently, because their knowledge and agency are incomplete, those who are established as authors therein [of the Vedas] are not truly omniscient.

The bound souls (*paśu*) are perfected (*siddha*). Thus, because of the non-completion of the cause of their state as bound souls—namely, impurity (*mala*)—they are established therein by virtue of that duality. Therefore, they are to be purified by Śiva, the author who has achieved perfection through the scriptures of Śiva; by means of his skill in the operation of initiation (*dīkṣā*), they are to be liberated from Māyā, Karma, and Mala, and elevated to Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).

Immediately after that, one should unite the [principles] above the principle of Śuddhavidyā with the manifestations of Śivatva characterized as gross, subtle, and supreme. This is because, in the initiation of *asadyonirvāṇa*, the manifestation of Śivatva is not effected in its entirety. Following that, preceded by the instruction of the Śiva-scriptures—

One should join [the mind] with that [reality] daily through the performance of duties, preceded by the destruction of bondage. Now, there is a verse for the purpose of concluding the subject matter examined in this section and for introducing the subject matter to be examined in another section:
O twice-born ones, since the Lord has thus been indicated by way of an illustration of the statement regarding the three principles, the category known as Kuṇḍalinī shall be described hereafter.

O twice-born ones! Because of the illustration of the statement of the three principles—that is, because of the illustration of the statement regarding the dissolution and so forth of the three principles—and because of their extraction;

[he is] the Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe. Having been thus properly pointed out and thoroughly examined according to the stated method, thereupon the category known as Kuṇḍalinī is described and examined.
The first chapter in the *Śrīmat-pauṣkara-jñānapāda-vṛtti*, composed by the teacher Jñānaprakāśācārya, resident of Śrī-Śālivāṭipura.

Now, in this chapter on the *Kuṇḍalinī*, this discernment of the *bindu* is described as it follows logically from what was previously stated regarding the divisions of dissolution (*laya*) and so forth that belong to Śiva through his limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
That *bindu* is to be known as the object of thought; it is considered to be *kuṇḍalinī*.

Now, following the examination of the category of the "Lord" (*pati*), the analysis (*viveka*) concerning that which is called *bindu*—which follows the sequence of enumeration and is logically established—is here described as the examination (*parīkṣā*). It is thus performed.

The connection with the *pāṭalika* (chapter) was indicated by the conclusion of the preceding chapter; the connection with the *tantravastu* (the subject matter of the tantra), however, consists of various types of statements concerning the category known as Kuṇḍalinī, as expressed by such passages as "Kuṇḍalinī... and so forth. Furthermore, the previously mentioned classification of Śiva’s dissolution (*laya*) and other states is [also addressed].

The designation (*vyapadeśa*) refers to that which functions as the proximate presiding principle (*upasamīpe’dhiṣṭhātṛtvena vartini*) over a certain category of reality (*padārtha*) for whose sake it serves as a means;
in that case, since there is no state of illusory manifestation (*vivartatva*), it merely establishes and brings about the designation of difference (*bhedavyapadeśamātra*).
This is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) or state; when that exists, it should be understood that the *bindu* comes into being.
It should be understood thus. Nor should it be said that, at the commencement of the examination of Kuṇḍalinī, the commencement of the examination of Bindu is inappropriate;
for that very [Bindu] is considered to be Kuṇḍalinī. As it has been said:
"The essence of sound, the unvoiced speech, is certainly Brahmakuṇḍalinī."
The power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti) is the supreme sound (nāda), called Mahāmāyā by the teachers.
"It is declared to be the Bindu, and also as Vyoman and Anāhata.

He states another argument: "Furthermore, that by which the waters of Rudra are bound, or wherein they abide, or from which they are liberated—that should be understood as the Bindu. Moreover, I shall state yet another argument.
Those for whom the individual soul (*aṇvātman*) is like Rudra and distinct from Śiva are the *rudrāṇavas*, such as Ananta and others;
by means of which [body] produced they are bound—that is, joined—with a body and so forth;
or in which [worlds] produced they remain enjoying unsurpassed pleasures within the worlds; or from which [source] produced, such as Nāda and Vāma, [they arise] at the time of dissolution.

They are liberated; let it be understood that this is the *bindu*. Furthermore, he says: "Moreover, since yoga consisting of *sāda* arises immediately, and wherein it abides and dissolves—let that be understood as the *bindu*."

Furthermore, "sadātmā" refers to one whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the pure reality (*san*); that which exists within such a reality is "sādātmika. By means of this subsequent term, it is indicated that [the initiate] has been consecrated; thus, the path of yoga consists of mantras and so forth. Alternatively, "yoga" refers to the body of Sadāśiva, which is the fruit of yoga, since it arises immediately from the material cause, which is solely the will of Śiva.

It becomes manifest (*vyakta*); wherever it abides, it remains engaged in purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Wherever it dissolves and disappears, that should be understood as the *bindu*. Alternatively, according to the etymology previously stated, Yoga—the Great Mantra of the Palace—having become the ground for the manifestation of the mantra created by Śiva—

That from which [the effect] arises—merely through the activity of the power of agency in the practitioner who is immediately presided over by the power of Śiva; that wherein it exists in the form of *kalā*; and that wherein it dissolves—that should be understood as the *bindu*. Regarding this, there is a verse concerning its practical application: "The multitude of principles beginning with Sadāśiva has as its eternal material cause..."

"Because it is subject to modification, just as a jar is; and this [subject] is likewise, therefore it is so. By those who maintain the doctrine of *samavāya* (inherence), the power of cognition (*jñāna-śakti*) itself is called the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). By those who do not accept *bindu*, the power of action itself—having become the material cause (*upādāna-rūpa*) of the pure path—is called *kuṇḍalinī*. To refute that, he says:
In this case, power (*śakti*) is not the material cause (*upādāna*), because its nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), just as Śiva’s is;
moreover, transformation (*pariṇāma*), which is appropriate for [insentient matter], is not tenable for that whose nature is consciousness.

In this regard, within the effect which consists of the pure path (*śuddhavartman*), power (*śakti*) is inherent in Śiva as his very nature of action (*kriyātmaka*). Because its essence is consciousness (*cidrūpatva*), it is just like Śiva himself. There is a scriptural authority stating: "The world is born from the Consciousness-Bliss (*cidānanda*) of Brahman. For those who maintain that Brahman possesses the quality of transformation (*pariṇati-dharma*) due to the delusions arising [within it], they recite [the truth] as Consciousness-Bliss.

For those who have realized the Vedānta, the Great Māyā and Māyā—which bring about the bliss of the light of consciousness, the Self denoted by the word *brahman*—are considered to be transformations (*pariṇāma*). For those who follow other doctrines, transformation is held to be something inferior because it is contradictory [to their views]. It has been stated that the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) belongs to non-conscious entities such as Māyā, while it belongs to that which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*).

It is not logical for Śiva and other such entities [to be the material cause]. Whatever is a material cause (*upādāna*) is insentient by nature, just as clay and so forth; therefore, because the power (*śakti*) is insentient, it cannot be the material cause of Brahman, which possesses that power. Thus, regarding this Māyā—designated by the word "Brahman" and characterized as both pure and impure—the Vedic scripture states: "The Supreme Brahman... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10). Therefore, [it is not Śiva].

138) Thus, because there is no pervasion by the contrary in the example, the [opponent's] objection that it is contradictory does not refute the fact that consciousness is a vivarta; for if it were as they say— that it is merely a vivarta of consciousness— then there would be an absence of causal efficacy (*kārya-śūnyatā*).
How can the world, which is a transformation of consciousness, be established by all means of valid cognition?

By some followers of Advaita-vāda, it is asserted that the pure consciousness (*cit*) is merely an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). If that were the case—that is, if its nature were one of illusory manifestation—there would be an absence of effects (*kārya-śūnyatā*), meaning there would be no existence of any produced entity; yet this is not an acceptable conclusion.

For the world, beginning with the articulated speech (*vaikharī-vāk*) and so forth, is established by means of perception and other valid cognitions (*pratyakṣādi-pramāṇa-saṃsiddha*) as an illusory manifestation of consciousness (*cid-vivarta*), [which is] Śiva.

"How could there be a reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa)? It would not exist in any way whatsoever"—this is the meaning. Now, [an objection is raised]: "But surely that [reflection] has Māyā as its material cause (upādāna). To this he says: "No; for Māyā, by its own power, is merely a deluder (mohaka) and thus cannot be the material cause here."
For it is not the cause of the instruments belonging to the body of the awakened person.
All those who abide on the pure path are awakened by the splendor of Śiva;
even though they possess bodies, senses, and so forth, they are not unawakened among them.
In this context, within the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), *māyā* exists without a material cause (*upādāna*), because it is delusive by its own nature and through its own effects;

because it generates ignorance (*ajñāna*) in the form of the conceit of selfhood (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding what is not the Self; and because it is that which intensely manifests the power of the subtle body (*aṇu*), the physical body, the senses, and so forth for the sake of the awakened individual soul (*puṃs*).

Therefore, it is not the cause of the instruments [of perception]. Now, one might object: having assumed a body and so forth that are of the nature of light—like those of Śrīmat, Śrīkarṇa, and others, which are based on the deafening bonds—she deludes those who bow before her.
That cannot be so; for neither those who abide on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) nor those who do not possess authority there are capable of such things without initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Due to the impossibility of prostration [before the Lord], by the power of Śiva’s splendor—known as initiation (*dīkṣā*)—which is the power of Śiva, they have had the attachment to the office within the womb of *māyā* shaken off; thus their powers are awakened and fully manifested. (p.
140) The pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) does not have *māyā* as its material cause. Furthermore, although they possess bodies, senses, and so forth, in those [senses] there...
He dwelt [there]. Not even some among them were unaware, for their powers were not unmanifest;

because they lacked the basis for the great intoxication consisting of the conceit of self (*ātma-abhimāna*) which is other than that [Reality], he who is indeed not based on the material cause (*upādāna*) of Māyā is not a locus for the vision of that [Reality]. Likewise, the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*) is liberated.
He says "no" even on account of [their] being objects of action:
furthermore, all individuals abide on the path of purity, free from karma;
how then could there be a state within the transformation of Māyā according to karma?
O twice-born ones, there would be the appropriation of those bodies, senses, and so forth;
therefore, for this pure path, its own resonance alone is the cause.
O best of the twice-born, let this [path] called Kuṇḍalinī be accepted as pure.

Furthermore, all individuals (*pudgala*) on the pure path—both the lords of the worlds and those dwelling therein—are freed from karma and liberated from action. How, then, could Māyā undergo transformation according to their karma?

The meaning is that there is no state of existence consisting of a body and so forth in any way whatsoever. One should not raise the objection as to how the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha and others can abide there even while being free from karma; for their [abiding] is due to their connection with the office of the Garbhādhikārin within Māyā. Indeed, for those who have transcended Māyā and reside in the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan), [there is no such thing].

"And karma is the cause. O twice-born ones, what is the basis for their persistence there? Since persistence cannot be conceived through the transformation of *māyā*, there must be a material cause (*upādāna*) for those elements, senses, and so forth, because they would otherwise be impossible. By which [cause]...

It must exist by means of some material cause (*upādāna*); therefore, its purity—which conforms to itself and imitates the pure path—is precisely its state of being self-conforming. This very cause, characterized as the material cause, is that which is called *Kuṇḍalinī*.
O best of the twice-born! Let this be accepted; let it be admitted. The *bindu* has been indicated.
He refutes the doctrine of inherence (samavāya):
"And that Kuṇḍalinī, the power of Śambhu, is pure yet insentient by nature;
she does not exist through identity (tādātmya), but rather exists in a state of being held."

And that Kuṇḍalinī is the pure, insentient power (śakti) of Śambhu, the Auspicious One. She does not abide there through identity (tādātmya) or inherence (samavāya); rather, on the contrary, she abides as the power of apprehension (parigraha-śakti), having become an object while engaged in the contemplation of the pure path as its material cause—this is the meaning. In that regard:
He demonstrates the reasoning:
"Because of identity with Śiva as the agent, this Kuṇḍalinī does not abide [as a separate entity]; for that reason, she is the material cause, just as clay is in relation to a potter."

The meaning of the verse is clear. Furthermore, he establishes the *bindu*: Moreover, the material cause (*upādāna*) consisting of *māyā* and so forth produces the bodies and sense organs of men; when it is agitated, its effects—the body, sense organs, and so on—become the agents (*kartṛ*).

That which is born from a material cause (*upādāna*) should be understood as the *bindu*. Furthermore, what else is its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)? It is *māyā* and so forth as the material cause. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), *kalā* and the rest are included. [This refers] to the body and senses of men, by way of indicating the body, senses, and so on.

That [Bindu], being agitated and transformed, becomes capable of action and endowed with its own causal efficiency (*svārthakriyā*). Without an agent (*kartṛ*), it cannot be established by itself; for at that time, the impure path has not yet arisen. Therefore, let it be understood and known that the Bindu is that from which the body, senses, and so forth—the instruments of that agent—are produced as material causes (*upādāna*). Now, one might object:

O Śivā, why should there be agitation [of the world] by means of another agent? True; the postulation of the unseen follows from what is seen. Just as a king, the lord of the earth, is observed to perform himself certain internal functions—such as those pertaining to his domestic priest and other ministers—while leaving external matters to his appointed ministers and so forth.

Thus, by means of instigation alone, there is no contradiction with scripture even in this case. As it has been stated in the *Kiraṇa*: "In the Pure Sound (śuddhadhvani), Śiva is the agent; in the Ananta and Asita [worlds], the Lord is said to be the master.

Now, one might argue that this is due to the parsimony of conceptualization (*kalpanālāghava*). Let that be so, provided he is one whose body has been cast off; however, that does not apply to an agent who is subject to being employed [by another].

Because the body and so forth are established [as effects] like a potter and others. But surely He is independent and the agent of agitation; that is incorrect, because it would entail the consequence of an infinite regress, as there would be another internal and external cause for that [agitation]. Furthermore, since Māyā is the object to be agitated by the agent who employs it, it is impure, and thus, being subject to transformation like clay and other such materials— [The text continues: ...being subject to transformation like clay and other such materials—... [is not the case]. Therefore, the Lord is not the agent of agitation. If one were to say that the Lord Himself is the agent of agitation, then He would be subject to transformation and would lose His independence. Moreover, if He were the agent of agitation, He would be dependent upon something else, and thus He would not be the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, if He were the agent of agitation, He would be subject to change, and thus He would not be eternal. Therefore, the Lord is not the agent of agitation. This has also been stated because [māyā] pervades the interior of the insentient: in the *Ratnatraya*— "Since māyā pervades the interior of the insentient, is subject to transformation, and brings about the production of the *kalās* and so forth, it is endowed with a body and the like. (p. 145)
"It leads the person who is dependent on another, without doubt,
just as a goldsmith [leads gold] for the purpose of producing a crown.
Therefore, just as a *galūci* creeper, even when severed at its root, [grows again] by resorting to a particular location, so too...

Likewise, [the impurity] such as fragmentation, dullness, and maturation proceeds forward because it constitutes a bond (*pāśa*). Although pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) is fragmented, the latent impression of impurity belonging to Ananta,
having taken recourse to a specific locus characterized by the station of the authority that brings about [bondage] and the authority that is the basis of impurity, [remains].

Furthermore, it undergoes rebirth through the body and so forth, just as one bitten by a snake at the fatal hour [revives]. Even when his karma is exhausted, he remains for a long time with his body sustained by the power of mantras; likewise, even when his karma is exhausted, he continues to perform infinite offices with his body sustained by the power of the Lord known as *adhikāra* (office). [He is] pure.

(p. 146) That body, which manifests the gross Śiva-nature inherent in the womb, becomes its opposite; or rather, let it be like a deluding serpent that does not harm the Blessed One—who is infinite and sky-like—just as one snake does not harm another snake residing within its own body, or as poison does not affect the end of a thread. And just as [the soul] whose two bonds of impurity (*mala*) and karma have been destroyed...
The body composed of His own māyā does not obstruct the [perception of] Śrīkaṇāda and others; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
To the question "From where is it perceived?", he says:
"Furthermore, the cognitions of men arise associated with words."
For sounds could never possibly exist without a cause.
O Brahmins, that which is their instrument is the *sabindu* [the nasalized vowel] along with its many functions.

Furthermore, how is it that the cognitions of men—such as the reflective awarenesses "jar" and so forth—arise as being pierced by words, inscribed by words? O Brahmins, those words consist of the arrangement of phonemes (*varṇa*) and so on.
Because it possesses defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), external causes might at some time arise.

That which is their cause is the *bindu*, which has many functions (*bahuvṛttika*) and manifests as immeasurable effects. By some, such as the Sāṃkhyas, it is held to be the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*), the material cause of the gross word, by means of its effects; by others—

Some hold that the material cause [of sound] extends as far as space, while others maintain that speech resides in the *puruṣa*; yet others say it is a state of the power of action belonging to that [puruṣa]. He refutes this:
"And here, the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*) is not the manifestor of those [sounds], because..."
That which is the manifestor is not the manifested; the distinction between these two is well-established.

In this context, regarding the function of sound characterized by phonemes (*varṇa*), the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*)—which is indicated as being merely characterized by resonance (*dhvani*)—is not the cause [of the phonemes], because it is the cause of sound in general. From sound, ether (*ākāśa*) and the other elements are grasped; why? Because, through their respective effects, that subtle element is the manifester (*vyañjaka*) of those sounds characterized by phonemes. (p.)

148) *Prakaṭakāraka* (The Manifesting Agent): It arises as the essence of gross phonemes and sounds, manifested by space, air, and so forth, and is perceivable by the listener. As it has been said: "Born from space and air, the sound (*nāda*) emerging from the body attains the sequence [of phonemes]."
When divided among different positions, that sound which undergoes the state of being a phoneme (varṇa) is called *śabda*.

Thus: that which is a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), such as a lamp or the like, is not itself manifested (*vyaṅgya*); it does not arise in the form of something manifested, because fire and so forth, which are to be manifested, arise through a relationship of identity with the fire-particles and so on residing within the grass and other fuel. Therefore, between those two—the manifestor and the manifested—...
The state of being divided by difference is well-established. Because the *puruṣa* or its power (*śakti*) are subject to modification (*vikāritva*), they cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*).

As it is said in the *Nādakārikās*: "The Self is declared here to be unchangeable, and its power likewise; therefore, those two are not capable of existing in manifold ways. Or rather, [they are not so] because, being devoid of consciousness, they are subject to modification. For this reason as well, he states that it is perceived:

Furthermore, O best of sages, when [the mind] has been cultivated in the higher states, how could conceptual constructions arise as conditions? How could there be a variety of drops (*bindu*) in the interim?

O best of sages! Even in the absence of the diversity of the *bindu*—that is, the diversity of effects such as the sovereignty of the *baindava* [state]—there would be conceptual constructions (*vikalpāḥ*) regarding the principles (*tattvāni*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, which are destined to arise; that is, how could the cognitions (*pratyayāḥ*), meaning determinate perceptions (*savikalpakabodhāḥ*), possibly come into being? In what manner could they exist?

The meaning is: "not in any way whatsoever. To the objection that "let there be cognition for that purpose," he says: "Cognition, which is established among all disputants, is determinative; there could be no determination even without the interpenetration of words."

The intellect (*buddhi*) is established as that which, among all things such as the Sāṃkhya principles and so forth, is characterized by determination (*adhyavasāyinī*), possesses the stages of conceptualization regarding objects of consumption, and manifests cognition. Even though, previously, there was a determination of objects such as form and taste by the intellect alone— without the interpenetration of words (*śabdānuvedhana*) or the verbal articulation (*śabdollekhana*)— [it was nonetheless established].

Furthermore, the investigation of the conceptualization (*parāmarśa*) that has become the ground of knowledge would not even be accepted by some as denoting an object, because it is mental. For instance, in the external world, when an object has already become the domain of the senses such as the eye, the conceptual construction (*buddhi-vikalpa*)— which is permitted as its own level of activity— is merely a manifestor [of what is already present], [not a producer] of the speaker’s [intention].

Only when an object has been made an objective referent (*viṣayībhūta*) can there be a reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*) of it, whether by oneself or another; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a reflective awareness of all objects at all times. Therefore, those objects such as form, taste, and smell are brought by someone to the state of being reflected upon by the speaker’s cognition.

Thus, here within, by means of the *paśyantī* which consists of internal discourse (*sañjalpa*), that [word] is established. From the sound residing in the mouth of the speaker, it produces the cognition of the meaning (*vācyabuddhi*) even in the sound residing in the mouth of the listener, once it has been manifested as a gross sound situated in the mouth of the listener. He concludes:
Sound is not produced from sound, because it exists even below that [level of] subtle element (*tanmātra*).
Therefore, even for those whose nature is Sāṃkhya, sound is held to be purely elemental (*bainda*).
Because it exists below that *tanmātra*, it consists of sound and color-form and originates from sound;

it is not produced from the *tanmātra* of sound. Now, one might object: since the *tanmātra* resides within the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), its existence is conceivable even in subsequent stages. That is incorrect, because it [the *tanmātra*] exists in the space of the subtle body.
Because [the self] is established as being merely the cause and the substratum of the senses;
therefore, those for whom the Sāṃkhyas alone are the primary instigators of the self—namely, the Pāñcarātras and others—they are "Sāṃkhya-selves" (sāṃkhyātmānaḥ). Of them...

Even for those whose self is Sāṃkhya, sound is held to be purely *baindava* (originating from the *bindu*). Because of the word "even" (*api*), this applies to the agents who employ it as well, since they possess the knowledge of established alternatives (*siddhavikalpa*). Furthermore, even for Ananta and others, that [sound] is established for the sake of their realization; for it is impossible for the intellect consisting of the subtle elements (*tanmātra-buddhi*) to proceed there [to the level of the *bindu*] otherwise. Thus, sound is not established from that [intellect], and therefore the *bindu* must be established for its sake.
It is understood. The operation of sound is demonstrated: "Words are fourfold, distinguished as *vaikharī* and so forth;
they are named *vaikharī*, *madhyamā*, *paśyantī*, and *sūkṣmā*."

Even those sounds which serve as the cause for conceptual cognition have not been mentioned here; rather, the fourfold division of speech, beginning with *vaikharī*, is proclaimed by name in the sense of the verse. He defines *vaikharī* according to the maxim of the "gross and the obstructed": [The verse: "Speech (*vāk*) is said to be fourfold, divided into four types such as *vaikharī*. Among these, *vaikharī* is that which is articulated through the organs of speech, consisting of phonemes, words, and sentences. [The commentary: By the logic of the "gross and the obstructed," he characterizes *vaikharī*: it is that which is manifested through the vocal organs, composed of phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*). It is called *vaikharī* because it is "clearly manifest" (*viśada*) and "articulated" (*khyāta*) to others. It is the fourth type of speech, arising from the transformation of the subtle sound (*nāda*) produced by the movement of the breath. It is the basis for all linguistic convention and the primary means for the communication of meaning. It is this *vaikharī* alone that is perceived by the external senses and serves as the material cause for the subsequent stages of conceptualization. Thus, the fourfold division of speech—*parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*—is established. Among these, *vaikharī* is the most accessible to ordinary perception.

Vaikharī speech is the object of the sense of hearing; it consists of the apprehension of gross phonemes and is beneficial to the speaker when the vital air is impelled against the points of articulation.

Vaikharī, also known by the name *sthūlanādā* (the gross resonance), is generally bound to the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*). When it manifests in locations such as the heart and so forth, it assumes the form of gross phonemes (*sthūlavarṇa*). Being an object of the ear, it becomes accessible to the sense of hearing for the listener; thus, it serves as the cause for cognition on the level of conceptual construction (*vikalpabhūmikabodha*).
It is beneficial to the speaker and the listener. Regarding the middle [speech], he says:
"That speech which, preceded by the synthesis of phonemes through the intellect, expresses the meaning and transcends the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa), is called 'middle' (madhyamā)."

Transcending the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and being established through the renunciation of the bond of the vital breath's activity; it proceeds by first following the sequence of phonemes and subsequently adhering to them, as directed by the intellect; not having reached the object for the sake of hearing, it is the verbal expression of the meaning, taking on a form that is distinct from the objects such as "cow" and so forth, when present in the speaker.
And for the respondent, it is their own conceptualization that manifests non-dual knowledge; this very speech is called the "Middle" (Madhyamā).
It is said that the Middle [speech] speaks to the Visionary (Paśyantī):
"Devoid of the internal connection with the forms of phonemes, it blazes intensely within."
Just as the fluid within a peacock's egg, it holds all objects without distinction.
This third speech, known as *paśyantī*, should be understood in the teaching of Śiva.

It is connected with the forms of the phonemes (*varṇa*); it consists of the forms of the phonemes, having the nature of differentiation. It is intensely radiant within and has the nature of internal discourse. Just as, for example, the fluid within a peacock’s egg.

Just as [the word] "cow" (go) denotes an object characterized by non-distinction—such as blue, yellow, and so forth, or wings, beak, and so forth—even while manifesting non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), it remains inseparable from that; likewise, the [word] "horse" (*khura-kaṃ*) and "strength" (*balādi*), though denoting objects characterized by non-distinction, possess a nature that arises through conceptualization (*savikalpa*) even while being non-conceptual in truth (*nirvikalpa-satyapi*). [The other...]
In the teaching of Śiva, that which is known by the name Vidya-parā is itself the third speech, to be understood as Paśyantī, named Paśyantī. He describes the subtle process of its arising:
"The subtle [speech] has non-consciousness as its sole refuge, with all its powers withdrawn."
Madhyamā is the cause of Vaikharī, and Paśyantī is the cause of Madhyamā.

The subtle cause for that which is perceiving is the one whose nature is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), which has withdrawn all other functions of its own power and consists of the form of resonance (*dhvani*). Having withdrawn all other internal functions, it is of the nature of non-conceptualization; having consciousness as its sole refuge, consciousness itself—indeed, the power of consciousness alone—is the single refuge and support.
That which is thus described is known as the subtle one, whose other name is Ādā; she should be understood as the one named Sūkṣmā.
That primordial Kuṇḍalinī, conjoined with the Moon, Fire, and Sun, is to be known as residing in the region of the heart, situated like the source of a sprout.
That which resides in the *mātraka* and other [vessels] is like a serpent coiled upon a Buddha-statue;
it is like a female elephant that, having coiled its trunk, stands at the entrance of its cave.

According to the scripture, "She enters into the *Sarvajñānottara*," Mahāmāyā— considering the material cause (*upādāna*) of objects as they truly are— is that which is to be purified (*śodhya*), designated as the principle of Śiva-tattva, during the initiation (*dīkṣā*) in which the form of the effect has been withdrawn. This was established in such a manner with respect to the portion of the sacrifice characterized by joy and the like.
In the initiation (*dīkṣā*), that which is beyond the *śānti* [tattva]—being by its own nature incapable of sustaining the world and consisting of the path of *kalās*—is not to be purified;

however, with respect to its own agitated portion, it remains as that which is to be purified in initiation as the *śivatattva*, whose essence is the world of *śāntyatīta* situated at the summit of *śānti*. Likewise, the referent of the word [is established].

Speech, which has withdrawn its own effects in relation to the *pādas* and is designated as *śakti* and so forth, having received its name accordingly in relation to the creative, sustaining, and destructive portions, and having become the *kalās* of *kṣama*, *śānti*, and *atītā* by itself while maintaining the *nāda*, is undivided for each individual, yet [emerges] from the *dvādaśānta*.

She is to be meditated upon as being blissful. Nevertheless, the *nāda*—which is her direct effect, distinct for each individual, designated by its own name "Nāda," consisting of the crest of its own sparks (*viṣphulliṅga*), merged within itself, and existing in a subtle state—is the fifth *kalā*, beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*), of the *praṇava*. It is the gross form [of the *praṇava*] consisting of the syllables *ka*, *ā*, and *ma*.

The *nivṛtti*, *pratiṣṭhā*, *vidyā*, and *śānti* kalās, characterized by the bindu that is the ornament of the head, exist in a subtle state through their own dissolution. This four-part bindu, denoted by the word "bindu," consists of the aggregate of the four powers (*catuḥ-śakti-samāṣṭi-maya*) within the lotus of power (*śakti-paṅkaja*), which is distinct for each individual person in the heart; such is its nature.

Abiding as the manifestation of the subtle five-fold power (*pañcakalā-śakti*) beginning with *nivṛtti*, it exists from the navel downwards. Then, through the process of the transformation of *sattva*, it exists as the nature of the syllable *ha*, known as *prasāda*. Thereafter, that Great Māyā, named Śiva, abides in the heart as the resonance (*nāda*) which is its own effect; she is to be meditated upon there. These are indeed the common [powers] of Śiva.

The states of being (*tvattva*) of those with pure currents (*śuddhasrotas*) consist of threefold bodies—subtle, gross, and intermediate—which possess both common and uncommon characteristics, as they are essentially one and the same. Each of these is distinct and appropriate to its respective level.

Among these, the uncommon [state] is that which manifests the qualities such as omniscience, which are inherent in the mantras and other [entities], when they are presided over by their own respective [deities].

These would consist of pure worlds characterized by the subtle body composed of thirty pure *kalās*, as well as the common gross body and the common worlds. This has been stated by the Teachers in the *Siddhāntārthasamuccaya*:
"Because of its purity, it is indeed of a single form," and also in the commentary on the *Mataṅga*: "Together with the phonemes and the worlds..."

It has been stated that because even the instruments of action and so forth are non-dual with that reality-principle whose nature is pure discernment, the single form of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) is established. However, for the *sakala* (embodied) beings, [the principles] such as Nāda and Bindu are limbs of the subtle body belonging to Māyā; thus, they consist of their own worlds designated as common to Śiva.

She is Mahāmāyā, possessing power; she is Śiva, the Bindu—thus it is said that for the purification of the subtle body, she is to be contemplated as merged within one's own self in her unagitated aspect. Therefore, even prior to the connection with the subtle body, [this] is the nature of the first expansion of the Bindu.
Bound by the resonance (nāda), thereafter bound to the subtle body— which is presided over by the pure principles (śuddhatattva) through the gateway of sound and so forth—

the person, having manifested as mere vision and action up to the limit of the subtle body according to the procedure for the departure of the subtle body, becomes settled like a bee within the lotus of the heart.
Thus it has been said: "The Puruṣa is merged like a fire within the lotus of the fourfold power.
Furthermore: "The body is declared to be threefold: the gross (sthūla), the subtle (liṅga), and the supreme (para).
The gross is the elemental body (bhūta-śarīra), and the subtle consists of the eightfold group (puryaṣṭaka).
Furthermore, it is well-proclaimed that [the reality] arising from the Bindu is threefold.
"O Mataṅga, this entire path, which extends from Aśiva down to the earth, is all to be known as consciousness (cit); one is not liberated by means of non-consciousness (aśivatva). Furthermore:
"The Nāda, which is the swan of the right vital breath (prāṇa) when it has waned, is nourished by the function of the downward breath (apāna)."

From below the navel, it goes into the *kuṇḍalinī*, the foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*). Strengthened by the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa-vṛtti*), the swan of the vital breath (*prāṇa-haṃsa*)— whose left and middle [channels] have been exhausted as it moves transversely and upwards— or else the *nāda* consisting of the digit of the *Prāsāda*,
beginning separately from the tip of the nose and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahma-randhra*) up to the limit of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*), [resides] in that which turns downwards.

It dissolves into Kuṇḍalinī. [The practitioner] has made Śivāsinī the presiding deity of that which is characterized by the lotus pervaded by the three-syllabled Praṇava of its own seat, descended from the four-syllabled Praṇava; which is characterized by the stalk, knots, petals, and pericarp of its own root-lotus;
and which contains within it the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Earth and ending with Sadāśiva.

Because it consists of the portion of the subtle body— composed of the four-fold *bindu-kalā* situated within the hollow of the pericarp of the lotus made of the inner essence of the created and uncreated, as established by the sacred teachings— it is truly the *indhikā* and so forth for the sake of accomplishing the body of Śiva, which is both gross and subtle through its divine and internal aspects.

The portion of Śiva in the form of the gross body, beginning with Vyāpinī and ending with Samānā; the subtle body in the form of the vital breaths beginning with Vyāpinī and ending with Unmanā; the supreme body consisting of Unmanā alone; the five kalās within the Praṇava beginning with Śānti; and the Niṣkala Mahāmāyā at the crest of the Nāda.

Having joined the self to the subtle body characterized by the *mātrās*, through the sequence of the initiation of specific liberation (*viśeṣanirvāṇadīkṣā*), and by means of the Śiva-kalās— those which conform to the *nāda*-kalās, those which have ascended [to their respective levels], and those Śiva-kalās similar to the [initiate's own] Śiva-kalās arising from the contemplation "I am Śiva"— and preceded by the act of making oneself Śiva, [one proceeds] for the sake of internal worship within Śiva.
Furthermore, one who has been initiated should be established again within the resonance of the *praṇava-śikhā*;

for, through the manifestation of his supreme Śiva-nature, he must become the Supreme Self, the primordial Śiva. Although he is now—as will be explained—the individual self (*bhūtātmā*) and the inner self (*antarātmā*), this is indeed due to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as sound (*nāda*) and so forth.
That which is designated as "consciousness" is to be thoroughly known; though it is one, it shines manifoldly like a crystal. As it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The self of the elements [is so called] due to conjunction with the elements; the self of the principles (*tattva*) is established in the principles;
the self of mantra is to be known as consisting of mantra; and the inner self is endowed with speech."

The enjoyer of pleasures and pains, abiding in primordial nature (prakṛti) and endowed with the qualities (guṇas), is the individual soul (jīva). At the end of its life, when liberated from these, it is indeed the Supreme.

Furthermore, even though the ego (ahaṃkāra) has already arisen, its transition to the state of sound (nāda)—just as [the transition] to the state of vital breath (prāṇa) is possible—occurs through its own inherent power of action, together with the movement and return of the vital breath. By means of the subtle internal contraction consisting of the thought "I am" (haṃsa), it utters the sound designated by the letters of the word *haṃsa*. That...
He who knows [this] while remaining in solitude becomes supremely liberated. Since the meaning of the stage of generation (*samutpattikrama*) is easy to understand, it is not written here.
He demonstrates the established order: "And these four modes of activity of the atoms consist of the [four] conditions."
Three are situated within, while the others are established outside.

In this context, by the word *vṛtti* (function), the effect (*kārya*) is meant. It is the cognition (*pratyaya*) of the subtle selves (*aṇu*). Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the self (*ātman*), the essential nature (*svarūpa*), whether directly or through its own effects; those [cognitions] which are clearly distinguished as having their own conceptual and non-conceptual forms (*svavikalpāvikalpa*) by virtue of being manifested by themselves are thus described. Among them, three are [as follows].

The *madhyamā* and other [levels of speech], while being uttered, remain internal; the other, *vaikharī*, is established externally. This is because that which consists of articulated phonemes (*varṇa*) perishes as soon as it is uttered—the meaning is that its duration is exhausted. He says that all of these are uttered together:
From cowherds, women, and children, down to the barbarians who speak vernacular tongues—
even the beings dwelling within the water constantly recite those [mantras].

The Gopālas and others are well known. They are called Gopālas because they protect *gāṃ*—that is, the speech of Sadāśiva in the form of scripture. The Aṅgas are Ananta and the others; the Vidyās are numbered at seventy million; the Bālas are Maṇḍalī and others; the Paramantraiśas are the Mlecchas; and the Bhuvaneśas are Sāñjana, Gahaneśa, and others.

Those who speak Prakrit, the yogins established in the principle of *guṇa*, the divine beings (*devayoni*) established in the principle of *buddhi*, those within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) beginning with Brahmā, those situated in water— namely,
those residing in the coverings of water and so forth— the five and eight Rudras, and all sentient beings dwelling in their respective worlds; these too [are included].

All those others who dwell in the pure worlds (śuddhabhuvana) speak and utter words that are entirely pure for themselves. Since the sūtra takes the form of a concise indication (sūcana), the expression of two meanings is not contradictory. Furthermore, there is no resonance (dhvani) of the impure within the pure, as there is of the pure within the impure.
Nor should it be excessively doubted that [the Lord] lacks progression (*apragatva*), for there is an inconclusive counter-example (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the Lord (*īśvara*).

For just as His progression is established here because otherwise the effects characterized by the enjoyment and liberation of each individual soul would be inexplicable, so too is it established for this [Prakṛti];
thus there is no contradiction. He says: "The internal state of Being... (*antaraṅgā sattā*).
There is no bondage greater than these, nor is there any liberation other than from them;
for without their cessation, the capacity for vision and action remains obstructed.

And from these four, there is a supreme liberation; the remainder is not bondage. (p. 165) From these comes supreme liberation, and no other; why is it supreme? Because without the cessation of those [four], the bondages such as *māyā* and the rest—which consist of the subtle veils over vision and action—would not cease. Without the cessation of those, they do not cease; nor do they cease through mere words.

Without liberation, one has become empty; and among those who have attained the dissolution of consciousness (*vijñānapralaya*) and the *akala* state, speech is "future" because it remains unemerged due to its fitness for bondage. This is because of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "where there is impurity (*mala*), there is speech. For it is not the case that wherever there is speech, there is impurity, as this would be contradicted by the existence of pure sound (*dhvani*) among the inhabitants of the [pure] abodes.

Because liberation of speech can occur for one who is liberated from impurity, [the author] says that liberation from impurity is not supreme liberation, as it is impossible to distinguish [them]: "They consider those [impurities] to be distinct from the person (pudgala), but [this distinction] does not exist anywhere."
The notion that "I am suffering" or "I am happy," when struck by sound, is merely a mental construction.

Individuals— men who are struck by the sound "I am suffering" or "I am happy," and delineated by such sounds— do not, through some internal reflection, understand their own respective mental cognitions as being distinct and separate from those words that terminate in the power of consciousness, meaning, and purposeful action.

The intention is that, due to their proximity within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it appears in their form. Those who know the distinct [nature of the Self] become partakers of supreme liberation;

for it is established that this occurs only for those whose impurities have been severed by initiation (*dīkṣā*) into the discernment between the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*) and the Person (*puruṣa*). Through the discernment of Nature (*prakṛti*) and the Person, one abides in the worlds situated above that. This is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) corresponding to that.

Through initiation (*dīkṣā*) assisted by the discrimination between *māyā* and the person (*puruṣa*), there arises the isolation of consciousness (*vijñānakaivalya*). Through initiation assisted by the discrimination between *mala* and the person, there is abiding on the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*). Through initiation assisted by the discrimination between *mahāmāyā* and the person, supreme liberation (*parāmukti*), which consists in identity with Śiva, becomes possible. [This is illustrated by the examples of] the cuckoo and the crow, etc.
He describes the gradation of sound among those residing in the three paths—the pure, the impure, and the mixed—just like the gradation of articulated sounds:
"The voices of the pure path are subtle; those situated on the mixed path are gross."
Or they may belong to the impure path, remaining always in an extremely gross state.

The meaning of the verse is easy to understand. Possessing the power of the worlds (*bhuvana-śakti*), having become the nature of the manifestation of its own world (*sva-bhuvana-vyakty-ātman*) above the world of Sadāśiva (*sādāśiva-bhuvana*), that power of the worlds— which, by its very self, pervades whatever is to be pervaded— is the sustainer of the paths (*adhvan*) that are pure, impure-pure, and impure.
There is no absolute difference between *vṛtti* (functioning) and *pariṇati* (transformation), because transformation is said to consist of the worlds beginning with Śānti;

thus, there are transformations characterized by the term *vṛtti*. These are the *kalās* whose nature is the object [of experience], just as the subtle [elements] and so forth previously mentioned have the nature of sound. A *kalā* consists of both of these.
Having spoken of the *bindu*, he further explains its enclosures:
"And other states of the *bindu* consist of the *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti*:
namely, *nivṛtti*, *pratiṣṭhā*, *vidyā*, and likewise *śānti*."
These five, beginning with Śāntyatītā, reside in the pure path as being essentially pure;
yet they are mixed in the impure path, existing as the support for the principles (tattvas) and so forth.
The aspects of the object are to be known as the *kalās*, while those of the form of sound were previously described.
This *bindu* consists of both sound and the object, and its nature is fear; it does not consist of either one alone.

This is easy to understand. Regarding the *mṛgendraratnakriyā*, the basis for reciting the *śānti* and other [rites] for the two types of ritual procedures (*kalpa*)—namely, those concerning the world-soul (*bhuvanātman*) and those concerning the support of the paths (*adhvādhāraka*)—should be understood from that very source; therefore, it is not written here.
Furthermore, he states that there are four types of effects consisting of the principles (*tattva*):
Its nature is that of Vṛtti-tattva, established as the fourth;
[the levels] are Śiva-tattva, Sadeśa, Aiśa, and likewise that called Vidyā.
These pure principles belong to the great-souled Rudra-atom-beings;
they are vast and inlaid with various garlands of cities.
They are filled with celestial women and most wonderful enjoyments free from suffering, and they are lofty, adorned with subtle bodies, sense organs, and other such features.

The Śiva-tattva, which is the state of having power inherent within itself, exists here above the worlds of Sadāśiva; it is indeed the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the five kalās consisting of the worlds of Nivṛtti and the others, and nothing else. These four pure tattvas [are as follows]: those souls who, like Rudras, are individual selves (*aṇu-ātman*) distinct from Śiva are called *rudrāṇavas*. Of them, [there is] Ananta and so forth.

They are inlaid and made dense by the mutual conjunctions of the Rudra-atomic particles, which consist of rows of worlds such as Śāntātīta and others of various forms, adorned with diverse garlands of cities; and because they take the form of those exceedingly lofty and vast worlds, they are both great and highly elevated. Therein—

Because they remain in an uninterrupted succession, bodies are experienced; thus, "enjoyments" (*bhoga*) refers to women and the like, while "senses" (*indriya*) refers to those that are primary among these factors such as time.
Therefore, by means of these—namely, the bodies, enjoyments, senses, and so forth, which consist of celestial women who are causes of happiness and are devoid of suffering—[the yogin experiences].

[The worlds] are inlaid and constructed with parts that are devoid of attachment to suffering, and which are therefore most wonderful and possess great excellence—namely, manifestations of consciousness attached solely to pleasure. Furthermore, Ananta and the others are not possessed of a real body; because they are omniscient, Ananta and the others are not [ordinary] omniscient beings like Śiva.

If someone were to employ the reason, "because it possesses a body, like Devadatta," that would be sublated by scripture (*āgama*). Furthermore, the argument "the conch is impure because it is a part of a living being, like a human skull" would be subject to the fallacy of *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed).
Moreover, even for yogis such as Śrī Kaṇāda and others, [the reason] would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since [the conch] is composed of pure elements.

Doubt is not pervaded by non-omniscience, because it lacks that nature; thus, it would not be established [as a valid reason]. Furthermore, in response to the question of for whom these [powers] are easily obtained, he says:
"The power over enjoyment and authority is manifested here through initiation."
Indeed, for the sake of their enjoyment, these were fashioned by Śiva.
In that same manner, the Tattva of Sadāśiva and the Tattva of Śiva are fashioned;
for their actual existence is established within the Tattva of Experience (bhoga-tattva).
The principle of Īśvara is the domain of the manifest powers for the sake of their enjoyment;
however, the principle called Vidyā is the domain of persons who possess gross faculties.
The term *vidyā* is traditionally recited as the cause for the realization of the sciences (*vidyā*).

Here, in this *māyā-maṇḍala*, by way of illustration, within *māyā*—that is, through initiation (*dīkṣā*) performed by Śiva, whether with or without external substrata, which serves to effect purification for those whose impurities (*mala*) have reached full maturity— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

On the path of purity (*śuddhādhvan*), the forms of Śiva beginning with Īśāna are recited as the lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*). Thus, regarding enjoyment (*bhoga*) and authority (*adhikāra*), the equal power (*samāśakti*) of Śiva and Śakti is manifested and rendered capable; that is, the equal power is manifested in the two activities characterized by enjoyment and authority.

For the sake of their enjoyment, and not for the sake of the manifestation of consciousness, the principle of Sadāśiva was fashioned and regulated by Śiva through his creative power (nirmāyā). Likewise, for that same purpose, the principle of Śiva was also fashioned. Since it was created as something to be regulated, why is there no separate regulation for the principle of Śiva? Is it because there is no distinction [between them]?

To this he replies: Because, although dissolution into Śivatva is spoken of from the perspective of *samanā*, it is heard in other [scriptures] that the fourfold group of powers (*kalā*) beginning with *śānti* constitutes the locus of enjoyment (*bhoga-sthāna*) therein; and because it is also heard that even the world (*bhuvana*) called *Śāntyatīta*, which belongs to the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), is situated upon the crown of *Śānti*. Therefore, [the state] here is Sadāśiva.

Because it is stated that the *tattva* of experience (*bhogatattva*) is included within [the higher] *tattvas*; and because of the statement in the *Mṛgendra*: "The *tattva* from Īśāna up to the end of Śāntātīta is known as Sadāśiva," [this is established] in reality by its very nature. Within those two—the *tattva* of Śiva and the *tattva* of Sadāśiva—there is the abiding of both in the *tattva* of experience. [This occurs] within the essential nature of their own collective totality (*svasamaṣṭi*), which consists of the *tattva* of experience.

The meaning should be established as follows: "the state [of being] in the two-fold nature of enjoyment (*bhoga-tattva*) is the abiding in the relationship between the signifier and the signified. Alternatively, the literal meaning is: "in the nature of enjoyment—that is, in Śiva, who is the presiding deity designated as 'the nature of enjoyment'—there is the abiding characterized by that which is to be presided over. Consequently, it is established that the pair of principles exists for the sake of that [enjoyment].

The state [of *bhāva*]: the state of those whose office (*adhikāra*) has become manifest—meaning those whose powers (*śakti*) are equal to Śiva—or rather, those whose powers have been established as capable of performing their office; for the sake of enjoyment (*bhoga*), the principle of Īśvara was fashioned by him as a regulator. Not only that, but also for the sake of the persons (*puṃs*) whose selves have been initiated (*dīkṣita*).

For those who possess gross authority, the principle called Vidyā is fashioned as a subordinate [element] for the sake of the enjoyment of those whose authority is manifest and whose powers are equal to Śiva’s, by means of a gross modality. Now, one might object: since Śiva possesses by his own nature that power of complete omnificence, how can their power of agency arise gradually?

It is improper to claim that [Śiva's] power is equal to Śiva's because it possesses a slight deficiency; for in the case of Śiva—who is designated as the "sovereign" (*adhikāra*) because he manifests all effects—it is impossible for there to be a "power of agency" capable of bringing about the production of the effect characterized by Śiva’s activity known as "enjoyment" (*bhoga*). This is because [in the state of sovereignty], enjoyment...

Furthermore, for the protector of the *bindu*, there is the state of authority mediated by another state of authority; it consists of the selves whose nature is Śiva, possessing the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the worlds beginning with Īśāna. Now, that which brings about the orientation toward the production of the effect of the breast—that is, the manifestation of that [power]—is the agent capable of performing the transformation.

Is it not established that the dissolution of that power of enjoyment is the indifferent state (*udāsīnatā*) of Śiva, and that his active power (*vṛttimat-śakti*) does not exist [as such]? Therefore, those who are joined to Śiva—who possesses complete creative power (*kartṛśakti*) and is not distinct from Him—do not possess incomplete creative power; thus, they do not manifest as individuals with incomplete creative power.
There is something inconsistent here. But surely this is true: it is the seed of metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) with respect to Śiva.

For the seed of metaphorical treatment consists in the idea that through meditation on Śiva—who possesses a body composed of the five faces and fifteen eyes—one becomes of the same nature as Him; and the same applies here as well. Thus, in the end, everything is faultless.

From the scripture stating that those who have attained liberation possess an undivided office (*adhikāra*) together with Śiva, it is understood that the four types of Śivas—the three states (*tri-avastha*) and the state beyond the three (*tri-avasthātīta*)—are established as having equal power (*samaśakti*). This is stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"In both the *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts), there is equality everywhere; that is declared to be *sāyujya* (union), while *sārūpya* (likeness in form)..."

Regarding "equality of form" (*mūrtitulyatā*): because the principles (*tattva*) of Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara can be easily established as being inherently related to Śiva and the others through their respective connections, [the author] explains the etymological derivation of the words for the *vidyās* and *mantras*. In the knowledge of these and in the perception of their objects, there is the nature of being "beyond this" (*taditadantatva*).

The cause of the world—the duality, unity, and singular form, as well as the effects and instruments—is that which exists by way of production; it is the cause. Because it is born from this, it is traditionally recited as "Vidyā" (Knowledge) through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the instrument (*karaṇa*). By this, those who recite the mantra "the deity is indeed mere sound" are refuted; for if that were the case, the fruit [of the practice] would also be mere sound. As it has been said:
In the Parākhyatantra it is said: "When the mantra abides as mere sound, then its fruit is merely sound;
for there is no word devoid of meaning that possesses the sequential order found in a pada or a sentence."
And the signified must be distinct from the signifier, like the word "Devadatta" and so forth. Thus [it is said].

And this is an elliptical indication; it applies even to those who have been initiated (*dīkṣitānām*). For, by means of His own power, Śiva—acting as the *ācārya*—purifies those whose bonds (*pāśa*), such as impurity (*mala*) and the rest, have been severed through initiation characterized by *dīkṣā*.
At that time, [the scripture] reveals the nature of reality (*tattva-dharma*) consisting of discernment (*viveka*) manifested by Śiva, beginning with the mere [essential] attributes.

For those endowed with pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) who remain within the *maṇḍala* of Māyā as *sakalas*, the fire of discernment between their residual state of bondage (*paśutva*) and their true nature as Śiva proceeds, caused by the experience of the fruits of past actions (*prārabdhabhoga*).
This is stated in the *Mataṅga*:
And when that fire descends, then it is capable of establishing the boundary between the state of Śiva and the state of a bound soul (paśu) for the practitioner.

Thus, this illusory knowledge (*māyīya-vidyā*) therein should be understood in detail from that very source. He says that there is no transition of this [impure] into the pure due to impurity: "This universe is not established as the path of purity for those of the nature of bound souls (*paśu*)."
Because it is filled with suffering, therefore reality is its basis.

Just as it is with me, so too is this bondage on the pure path; for the sake of experience, the universe—the world appearing in its manifold forms—is fashioned for those bound souls whose power of experiencing has not yet been manifested through initiation. It does not abide on the pure path.

It is not certain that [the world] resides on the path of purity, because it is filled with suffering—that is, because of the momentary cause of being filled with suffering. Now, by whom is this agreed upon? Or rather, let it be established that it exists there in the form of suffering. That is incorrect; therefore, the characteristic of the universe is not being filled with suffering.
