Because of its established nature: just as the principle of *māyā* is a "binding" (*nibandhana*) because it is intensely binding due to its own effects, so too this [path], being described as the emergence of the universe consisting of the self and the non-self, would be both the pure path and a "binding" (*nibandhana*) that is intensely binding. Who has said that it is not a binding?
To refute this objection, he establishes: "This pure path is not a bond for the enjoyer, because it follows his will;
whatever is of the nature of an object of enjoyment, even if unseen, is not a bond."
Just as for Śiva, that reality known as *bhoga* (enjoyment) is not a cause of bondage;

so too this pure path (*viśuddhādhvan*) is not bondage for the enjoyer, because it is an object of enjoyment according to his sovereign power (*īdṛk-cānusārataḥ*). Whatever is of such a nature is not a cause of bondage, just as in the case of Śiva.
The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: "Therefore, because it follows the will [of the Lord], the state of being unmanifested for the sake of enjoyment is not the cause of bondage.
And by this he says:
"Furthermore, because there is an absence of connection with karma, it is the binder of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*)."
O twice-born ones, it is there that existence follows from karma on the path of purity.
Because enjoyment follows from desire, and action follows from desire,
karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of eons unless it has been experienced.

Furthermore, for this reason as well, the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*) is the binder of those on the pure course, yet it is not itself bound. This is because there is an absence of connection with karma, and because its production by karma is impossible. O twice-born ones, regarding that which is said to be the Pure Path, why is there an absence of connection with karma? Do not have such a doubt.

The minor [point]. Here, regarding experience (*bhoga*) that occurs on the path of purity (*śuddhādhvan*), because it follows the will (*icchānusāritvāt*), that is, because it conforms to the will, there is an absence [of karma] due to following the will. How so? The destruction is the minor point. Experience born of action (*karma*) does not follow the will; the remainder is that "it is seen to have been experienced. But [one might object]: "Is it not according to the will?"

In some cases here, because one observes the attainment of enjoyments born of karma, such as divine garments and the like, marked by the mind, it might be argued that only that which possesses the same nature [as the karma] should be enjoyed there, and not that which lacks that nature; however, this is incorrect. For karma that has not been experienced is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of kalpas, nor does it perish. Therefore, for those who abide on the pure path...

The sense is that those entering into liberation at the time of the great dissolution do not [re-enter]. The sages raise this doubt: "How can there be an absence of connection with karma for those who abide in the pure self, when everything seen here is observed to be dependent upon karma? They ask: "How is it that there is no persistence of karma for those who dwell in the pure path?"
It is taught that on the pure path there is great enjoyment, and karma does not exist.

O Lord, how is there diverse enjoyment for those who abide therein? O Lord, it has been stated and praised that on the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan) there is great enjoyment, yet because of its being the cause of that [enjoyment], karma does not exist; [therefore, one asks] how there can be a connection with karma for those abiding on the Pure Path?
[The opponent says: "Let it be so; however, tell me this: how is it that those who abide therein experience such diverse enjoyments?
The Lord replied:
"In the pure path, diversity of karma is not the cause."
The ripening of impurity, which is manifold, is the cause therein.

In the pure path (*śuddhavartman*), the cause of the diversity of enjoyments is not karma; rather, it is the diverse ripening of impurity (*mala*) that is the cause here. But surely, since the powers of impurity have ripened in a manner restricted to each individual soul, and because of the absolute separation [of souls] effected by initiation (*dīkṣā*) through Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), how can there be such a ripening?

It is true that, having observed this diversity, there is the application of the non-diverse state of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) and so forth, which transcends it. In the cluster of the eyeballs connected to the eyes, they are contained within the layers (*paṭala*) being severed by the power of the initial diversity inherent in the eyes; these [layers] correspond to the varying degrees of the dullness of their maturation (*pāka*).

Just as there are latent impressions (*vāsanās*) that produce various effects, so too, within the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*) which pertains to the soul destined to become a *Vidyā*, an *Īśvara*, and so forth, [the soul's nature] is being severed by the power of the diversity in the ripening of its own [karmic] impressions, while it exists as a *Vidyā*, an *Īśvara*, and so on.

There is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that there exist latent impressions (*vāsanās*) which are gathered together by the impure powers (*mala-śaktis*) specific to each individual, which take the form of varying degrees of dullness in their maturation, which produce diverse effects, and which arise from the nature of the *adhikāra-mala*. As it has been stated in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
For the perpetual ascetic there is the attainment of the supreme state, and for the ritual practitioner especially;
through the purification of latent impressions, he attains the station of a Vidyeśvara.
"Through the ripening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and through initiation (*dīkṣā*), one attains the Supreme.
Now, it is indeed heard that on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) beginning with the Three Jewels (*ratnatraya*), there exists ritual action (*karman*) consisting of the service of Īśvara.
This is true; however, for those who have become bodiless (*videha*) or isolated through knowledge (*vijñānakevalin*), this applies prior to their arrival at the pure path following initiation.

Regarding the phrase "of those who perform pure actions," it means that for those performers—even those who have received the material initiation (*bhautikadīkṣā*)—it does not bestow worldly enjoyment regardless of the diversity in the ripening of their impurities (*malapāka*). Thus, it is not universal and is therefore secondary; there is no contradiction here. He shows the corresponding destination [for such practitioners]:

He whose *taptaka* is preeminent in the principle of enjoyment (*bhogatattva*) is the enjoyer of enjoyment; the other, however, is called *īśa-vidyā*, and between those two, one becomes the partaker of enjoyment.
(p. 184) "O best of Brahmins, what is the use of ritual action here, since enjoyment is desired wherever one wishes?
The meaning of the aphorism is easy to understand. The sages raise an objection, fearing that if this were so, there would be no need to cultivate ripening within the kalās of consciousness.
In this way, the ripening of this impurity would occur spontaneously;
however, its ripening occurs through experience, and that experience arises from karma.

The ripening of this impurity (*mala*) would have to occur spontaneously, independent of any other cause; if that were the case, it would be a cause in the manner of liberation. However, it cannot be said that it arises spontaneously, according to the principle that "that which is unmixed does not undergo transformation. Therefore, the ripening of this impurity occurs through experience (*bhoga*), and its experience occurs through *anāgama-karman*.

It is not produced without karma; the sense is that it does not exist there [without it]. The Lord says: "Through knowledge, yoga, renunciation, or through the exhaustion of karma by experience, when that karma is exhausted, the body and so forth perish, and with their destruction, the state of being an experiencer ceases. (p. 185)
O twice-born ones, this impurity also becomes ripe through the power of auxiliary factors.
O twice-born ones, by means of the yoga of discernment regarding the illusory person (māyāpuruṣa), the knowledge of characteristics such as form, renunciation (sannyāsa), and the exhaustion of karma—
which acts like a bird producing the fruit of that exhaustion— from such karma, when it has reached the state of fruition, [the impurity is cast off].

Due to the destruction of the body and so forth, which are dependent on karma, there is the destruction of its state as an enjoyer; thus, the enjoyment dependent upon it comes to an end. Just as a defect residing in a cloth is first mixed with [remedies] and then, immediately following its own cessation, that defect becomes "cooked" (neutralized) through the power of the entire process—characterized by the prior application of ashes, cow dung, and dissolution—so too does this occur.
Furthermore, this impurity (*mala*), having been previously intermingled with its own fruit through the gateway of the bodily portion immediately following [the dissolution of] its own *niyati*,

becomes matured by virtue of this very [process] characterized by the dissolution of the latent impressions (*vāsana*) and karma deposited within itself, due to the power of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). This has been explained in detail in the *Kiraṇavṛtti*, and it is stated elsewhere as follows:

Having placed its own latent impression (*vāsanā*) within the impurity (*mala*), which brings about the subtle and stainless ripening of the body starting from the *kalā*, it likewise proceeds toward dissolution;
just as the cow-dung and other substances in a cloth are removed when the cloth is dissolved. To the question, "What would Śiva do in a state of equality? he says:
When all of them have reached full maturity, Śaṅkara,
by his own will, appoints them to various offices.
O twice-born ones, in that diversity, His own will alone is the cause, not karma;
nor does any cruelty ever arise here on the part of Śambhu toward any of those who are fit to travel upon the pure path among the Vijñāna-kevalas.
The word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even a sound that has reached maturation might split a mountain with its peak" is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).

By His own will—that is, by the very power of His will characterized by His own laws—He may appoint [souls] to various offices and objects of enjoyment. O twice-born ones! In that diversity, it is His will alone.

Śambhu is never at any time merciless—meaning devoid of compassion—with respect to the diversity of enjoyments here, nor with respect to the matter of their distribution here. Why is this? To this he says:
"For one who would assign [beings] to sufferings would be merciless both in this world and in the next."
Thus, on the pure path, experience is extracted as being essentially bliss itself.

One who impels or urges [beings] toward sufferings without any other motive is called "merciless. It is not so when one impels them toward happiness; for in the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) alone, [the soul] is elevated in the manner of liberation.
Enjoyment is made to rise as consisting of bliss itself; its nature as suffering is not to be established.
He summarizes:
"The greatness of the Great Self, Maheśvara, cannot be transgressed by desire;
it operates independently of karma and other factors, in accordance with the ripening of impurity."

The consciousness of the Great Lord, Maheśa, bestows grace even upon others who are merely individual souls (*kevala*). Because the will of the Great Lord possesses an inviolable majesty and an unsurpassable power, it acts independently of karma and other such factors, according to the ripening of impurity (*malapāka*). [This is] the ripening of impurity.

Following this diversity, He bestows grace upon those who are *vijñānakevalas* as well as those who are *sakala-pralayakevalas*. He ordains the manifestation of both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). Having accepted this, the sages raise a doubt:
"This path has been designated as the object of experience (*bhogya*), yet enjoyment is established through passion (*rāga*) and other such factors."
In this regard, O Maheśvara, how can there be enjoyment in the absence of these?

This pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) has been taught as the object of experience (*bhogya*); the manifestation of consciousness (*cidvyakti*) is the enjoyment of that object. Consciousness is ignited by *vidyā*, its range of perception revealed by *vidyā*. According to the scripture stating "colored by *rāga*," and so forth, there is a state [of bondage] through *rāga* and the other *kañcukas*. It is certain that [the soul] is made manifest (*vyaṅga*) by *rāga* and the others. O Maheśvara! The agent is pure.
How, and in what manner, does experience—the manifestation of consciousness—occur through the absence of those [obstacles] such as attachment and the rest on the path? Īśvara:
In this case as well, there are principles (tattvas) headed by Time, each succeeding one being different from the preceding.
But these Baindava [seeds] here, O best of the twice-born, are pure.
Here too, even on the pure path (*śuddhavartman*), time is a cause by virtue of its delimiting experience (*bhoga-avacchedakatva*). As they say:
"Alas, you have been found after a long time; I know not what I shall do—shall I enter into your limbs, drink you, or swallow you?"
Those principles, such as *kalā* and the rest, of which *kāla* is the primary and foremost, exist as "those headed by *kāla*" (*kālamukhya*).

Just as they are established within the sphere of *māyā* because their respective effects cannot otherwise be accounted for, yet even though they exist here on the pure path (*śuddhavartman*), those principles belonging to the *bindu* are pure. Thus say the sages.
They raise the objection that because of the conjunction with *kalā* and the other categories, the individual soul (*aṇu*) possesses subjection to them:
"Due to the union with the principles beginning with *kalā*, the state of being 'with parts' (*sakala*) arises for the atom;
when those [principles] exist or do not exist, [the soul] is either 'with parts' or 'without parts' (*akalā*)."

Due to the conjunction with the principles beginning with *kalā*, there exists for the individual soul (*aṇu*)— who dwells on the impure path and possesses a nature distinct from both the enjoyerhood of the intellect and so forth (which is the enjoyer of the principles beginning with *kalā*), and the enjoyerhood of the object of enjoyment—
the state of being "possessed of all" (*sakala*) and subjection to *kalā*. This is established here as well for those [principles] beginning with *kalā*.

Even those who are devoid of parts (*niṣkala*) become possessed of parts (*sakala*) through the union with the *bindu*-kalā at the end of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) preceded by the [recognition of] existence, stability, and consciousness;
thus, the *kalās* come under their control. Īśvara says:
"Even when they possess the *kalās* and so forth, there is dependence for those who have acted with ingratitude."
Therefore, those who possess only consciousness are both *sakala* (with parts) and *akala* (without parts).
For those who abide on the path of purity (*śuddhādhvan*), even though they possess *kalā* and the other [categories], they have not established dependence or subjection to them.
This is because they are not subject to the *māyīya* *kalā* that is joined with *māyā* and presides over the womb [of manifestation]. The sense is that this is not an invariable rule.
As it has been said: "Even when joined with *kalā*, they are not subject to the *kalās*, unlike the multitude of bound souls (*paśu*). [Vijñāna...]

The *kevalas* (isolates) reside in the *parikve* (the surrounding enclosure). Due to the initiation (*dīkṣā*) bestowed by Śiva, there is the manifestation of the state of Śiva in both its gross and subtle forms;

thus, they possess the designations of "Paraśiva" and "Śiva. Furthermore, those known as *vijñānakevalas*, whose characteristic state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*)—which conceals absolute isolation (*kaivalya*)—has been removed, are also called *sakalas* (those with parts), even though they are endowed with pure *kalās*. Therefore, they remain subject to dependence caused by that [state].
Because of its existence. For the purpose of summarizing the objects already examined and for the purpose of introducing the objects yet to be examined, there is this verse:
"Thus, the *bindu*, together with its functions (*vṛtti*), has been explained in brief."
O best of Brahmins, listen also to that which is called Māyā, along with its logical proofs.
The meaning of the verse is clear. Thus ends the second chapter in the Pauṣkara-jñānapāda-vṛtti.
The Chapter on Māyā:
Now, Māyā, which follows in the sequence [of topics], is described in brief. Because the entire universe emerges from it, it is therefore designated as Māyā.

Now, following the examination of the categories (*padārtha*) concerning Kuṇḍalinī, Māyā—which follows in sequence and has arrived as the reality to be examined—is described in brief, that is, concisely.
The connection between the chapters (*pāṭala*), indicated at the end of the preceding chapter, is as follows: "It is examined. This is the meaning within the Tantra.

The connection between entities consists of the nature of illusory objects (*māyā-padārtha*). However, that which consists of sentences is *māyā* without [such] objects, and it is of many kinds, such as "here" (*atra*) and so forth. From this object, the universe—the world of manifold forms—*mayati*, meaning it undergoes transformation; for that reason, it is proclaimed as *māyā*. It is derived from the root *māy-* (to transform).

In some places it is called *māyā* because it transcends the nature of power (*śakti*), knowledge (*vidyā*), and the self (*ātman*). However, in the *Kāmika*, it is stated: "Because it is the cause of appearing otherwise, this is celebrated as *māyā*. Furthermore, the statement of the subsequent examination reveals its true nature:
[Māyā] is eternal, one, non-pervasive, an entity whose form is not composed of action, and is auspicious (*śivā*).
And it is common to all the lords of sages without exception.

Since sacrificial acts and the like perish at the very moment they are performed, they cannot be the cause of heaven; for if they were to serve as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person, it would entail the undesirable consequence of the person being subject to modification and insentience. Therefore, one must admit that action characterized by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) called *apūrva*, produced by those acts, resides in the intellect (*buddhi*). [Otherwise,] upon the dissolution of the intellect...

Furthermore, because it exists as the nature of the cause whose effects have been withdrawn, Māyā is the substratum of karma by way of being the locus and the located. For that reason—namely, because it is the substratum of karma consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion—it is inauspicious (*aśivā*) and impure (*aśuddhā*). [Objection: But surely, since it is of the nature of a non-entity (*avastu-rūpa*), it has been declared by the knowers of the Vedānta...
How can it be the substratum? That is incorrect; this [entity] is indeed of the nature of matter (*rūpa*), as will be established later.

As for the atoms (*paramāṇu*) declared by the logicians to be the cause of the world—that too is incorrect, because this [atom] is singular. Since it is insentient, manifold, and corporeal, it would be non-eternal and subject to various states.

By implication, atoms cannot be the ultimate cause, because they possess form (*mūrtatva*). One should not suspect that this reason is subject to the fallacy of being "unestablished" (*asiddha*) with respect to the dissolution of time (*kāla*), for in our own scripture, atoms are established as impermanent. Therefore, they are eternal (*nityā*) only in the sense of being devoid of destruction (*nāśarahita*), due to their oneness (*ekatva*).
Because causality is impossible if [the cause] does not pervade its own effect; therefore, being pervasive and pervading its own effect,
she is common and universal (*sāmānya*) to all *sakalas* despite being differentiated through the medium of their respective effects—
this he establishes once again:
At the time of dissolution, for the transmigrating atom whose body has dissolved into my mouth,
Māyā is the cause of the body and so forth, consisting of both subtle and gross forms.
From the stage of *kalā* up to *dīkṣā*, [the soul] is initially undivided;
yet, due to its state of differentiation, it is like the trunk, leaves, fruits, and so forth that emerge from a seed.
For one whose body has dissolved at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), initiation is impossible because [the body] has been purified through ritual action (*karman*).

For the *pralayakevalin* who possesses *karman*, at the time of the commencement of creation—either at the mouth of Ahan or immediately thereafter—the attainment of the state of possessing *kalās* (*sakalatva*) occurs; prior to that, there exists a previously non-existent body, both subtle and gross in nature.

Māyā is the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa), defined by the exclusion of non-connection and the exclusion of connection with something else. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), its commonality with all the worlds from Kapālīśa down to Kālāgni—both directly and through succession—is included. According to the view of those who maintain that the effect pre-exists in the cause (satkāryavāda), this is because Māyā exists in the state of dissolution as the unmanifested nature of the *kalās* and other principles.
"Prior to differentiation" means prior to the manifestation of the divisions such as the *kalās* (limited powers) and so forth;
"just as it occurs in creation" means just as the sequence from *kalā* down to the earth (*pṛthivī*) comes into being, because therein [the elements] are differentiated and transformed.
It is like the seed of a *nyagrodha* tree or similar plant, wherein the characteristics of the trunk, leaves, fruit, and so on are unmanifest.
The remainder [of the argument] is that because the aggregates, leaves, fruits, and so forth exist in such a manner, they are the cause [of that state].
In no way is there an example [for this], because [the world] has been transformed by Vāyu, just as the great ocean is transformed in one part;
for it has been transformed by Ananteśa through his nature as Kalā and the rest. If [this were not the case] in every respect...

In that case, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress due to impermanence, as stated in the *Mṛgendra*: "By the reason of being an effect produced by an agent and an instrument, its nature as the material cause (*upādāna*) has been established through various statements; therefore, it is to be understood [that the Self is the cause]. For this very reason, the Sāṅkhyas and others assert that primordial matter (*prakṛti*) alone is the material cause of the world. To show that this is incorrect, he says:
Nor is the material cause of the three qualities figurative, because of their distinctness;
for the qualities are of a distinct nature, whereas primordial matter (prakṛti) is not perceived as something other than them.
In our established doctrine, that [nature] is propounded as having the form of differentiation;
therefore, it has not been discussed here in the same way as it is viewed in other philosophical systems.

The collection of qualities (*guṇas*) in a state of equilibrium is the secondary reality of the *guṇas* (*gauṇa-guṇatattva*), which is called *prakṛti* by the Sāṃkhyas and others. Furthermore, it cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*) of the three *guṇas*, such as *sattva* and the rest, because— being insentient, manifold, and impermanent— it must have a prior cause, just like jars and other such objects.
The intended meaning is that it is the supreme cause. If it is argued, "In that case, let Prakṛti be of an undivided nature," that is incorrect.
For in other systems such as Sāṃkhya, Prakṛti is not presented as being of an undivided nature;
rather, in our established doctrine (siddhānta), that Prakṛti is presented as being of a divided nature consisting of the *guṇas*. Therefore, for that reason, [the Sāṃkhya...]

The established conclusion has its nature proven. It is not equal to, nor thought to be equal to, nor even considered equal to, that "nature" which is the view of other systems—that is, a view established in another scripture or philosophical system by virtue of being perceived as its own object; such is the established conclusion.

That primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is established as the supreme cause; it is beyond praise or suspicion, corresponding to each individual subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), and because it exists as something distinct from the flow [of ordinary experience] and in its gross form, it is where the state of being the supreme cause is confirmed.
He says: "That which possesses a subtle state and unsurpassed excellence is called 'I' by me. (p. 199)

The subtle elements (tanmātras) are the subtle forms of earth and the other [gross elements]; from these arises the ego (ahaṃkṛti). The intellect (buddhi) is subtler than that, and primordial nature (prakṛti) is even subtler than that.
The group beginning with Kalā belongs to that [Māyā], and Māyā is subtler than that;
where the ultimate limit of subtlety is reached, that is designated as Māyā.

The meaning of the *Sukara-sūtra* is as follows: Being urged by the sages (*ṛṣi*), in order to refute the proponents of illusion (*māyāvādin*) who are intent on describing that which has no real entity (*avastu-rūpa*), he reveals his thought for the sake of establishing the present subject—that within the doctrine of illusion (*māyā-siddhānta*), because it produces effects in the form of real entities, it is indeed of the nature of a real entity; for there is no perception of a real entity from that which is not a real entity. Thus he discloses his intention.
This is *māyā*, which indeed has the nature of a real entity (*vastu*), since it is the progenitor of *kalā* and the other categories.
For here, *kalā* and the rest have the nature of a real entity; indeed, that which is not a real entity does not give birth to what is a real entity.
The meaning of the verse is clear. Thus, the sages whose minds were awakened by him [perceived] that *māyā* as the means for accomplishing *kalā* and the rest.
They raise the objection that substantiality cannot exist within the manifold of effects (kāryarūpaprapañca):
"The manifold is not of the nature of a real entity, because of the absence of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
likewise because of the absence of objects of cognition (prameya), and also because of the absence of relations."
The meaning, however, will become easier to understand through what is said later. They demonstrate this very point by analyzing it:
"This phenomenal world (*prapañca*), consisting of the distinctions between the subject (*pramātṛ*) and so forth, is not an object of the senses;
because perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the establisher of objects, not their negator."
Without negation, difference never exists;
therefore, perception is not a proof for the existence of the manifold world (prapañca).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and the act of knowing (*pramiti*)—which are non-different from the knower (*pramātṛ*)—are implied. The sense is that this entire manifold (*prapañca*) does not exist as anything apart from these four.
It is not within the range of the senses; that is to say, it is not an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since [direct perception] pertains to [external] objects.

Regarding the definitions of the objects of cognition (*meyalakṣaṇa*): that which has the characteristic of the operation of grasping mere existence as "this is so," which is produced by the power of the object, is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*)—that is to say, it is not a negation. For [non-conceptual perception] does not have the characteristic of the operation of grasping mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), such as "this is not a jar" or "this is not a cloth," because that belongs to conceptualization (*savikalpaka*).

Because it depends on place, time, and other such factors, it is not produced by the objective capacity [of the object]; therefore, we do not accept it as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Even if that were the case, with respect to its specific mode—such as "this is a jar"—it is the positive cognition that brings about the presentation, whereas perception is the negator that apprehends mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*).
Because we do not accept [that] as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor should it be said, "Let it be so; what is the use of this?
For without a negation, there can be no apprehension of difference, since the apprehension of that mutual absence (*itaretarābhāva*) is impossible without it.
At any time, difference—residing in the cognizer and so forth—does not exist and cannot exist, because they are mutually...

Because it is incapable of apprehending difference through the medium of being incapable of apprehending existence, perception is neither a proof nor a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the actual existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). They also refute that it falls within the scope of inference or scripture;
since inference is preceded by the observation of a pervasion (*vyāpti*), inference too is not a valid means of knowledge.
Scripture does not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge regarding an object that contradicts perception and the other [means of knowledge].

Since inference (*anumāna*) depends upon the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and since that pervasion—which is the rule of the concomitance of the probandum (*sādhya*)—is grasped by perception (*pratyakṣa*) as being preceded by it, and since perception is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and thus does not have the distinction between the mark (*liṅga*) and so forth as its object, inference also is not a valid cognition (*pramā*), nor is it a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This also applies to the apprehension of the capacity of a word (*yācaka-śakti-graha*). (p. [number])

203) Because it is rooted in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the authority of the sequence of negation—such as "there is no jar on this ground" and so forth—regarding objects contradicted by perception and the like is established. Since [other means of knowledge] such as comparison (*upamāna*) and the rest are included within these three, they are not separately refuted. In this way, the manifold world (*prapañca*) is proven to be non-substantial.

Having established the non-existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they seek to prove the non-existence of its definition, its object (*prameya*), and the relationship between the two. Therefore, the non-existence of the object of cognition is also established by virtue of the non-existence of the means of valid cognition;
thus, inference and the object of inference, as well as the relationship between the two, are difficult to find.
Those who investigate the meaning of this manifest [text] do not find that the connection between cognition and the jar is characterized by identity (*tādātmya*);
for if it were so, the jar would become internal, since cognition is internal.
Even the self that takes up the water for washing the feet could not possibly exist in vain within a dream;
likewise, if the phenomenal world were unreal, how could there be the illusion of reality?

Since it is being established that the cognitive power (*cicchakti*) alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to both knowledge and the jar, the connection (*saṃbandha*) between the definition of the means of valid cognition and the object of valid cognition (*prameya*) is [the one under discussion]. First of all, it is not characterized by identity (*tādātmya*); the word "first" (*tāvat*) indicates a sequence. Nor is it characterized by inherence (*samavāya*).

Because cognition is internal, being established as an inwardly manifest experience, whereas a jar is established externally; thus, a jar or the like could only exist through the necessity of its inherence [in that cognition]. The intention is that even in the waking state, the cognition of objects past or future would be impossible [if they did not reside within cognition]. Such is the meaning of the verse beginning with "evam" (thus).

[The opponent] did not offer a response. Īśvara, considering that even conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is incapable of negating invalid knowledge (*apramiti*), offers this rebuttal: "There is an ancient means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)."
First of all, direct perception is a means of valid cognition regarding objects that has differentiation as its domain.

First of all, regarding the existence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the ancient primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*). There exists a means of valid cognition whose object is the differentiation of things; therein, he demonstrates by analyzing the operation of perception as a means of valid cognition that it functions toward determinate cognition (*savikalpapramiti*).
In the doubt, "Is this a post or a person?", it is indeed a post;
the cognition that "it is not a person" is perceived by the senses as having a nature of distinction.

"Unimpaired" means that from the direct means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*), when there is a doubt as to whether it is a post or a person, [the cognition] determines "it is indeed a post; it is not a person.
That which has differentiation as its essence—where "differentiation" (*bheda*) is dissimilarity and "essence" (*ātmā*) is the intrinsic nature whose object is itself—is so described;
the meaning is that the cognition (*pratyaya*) is preceded by the sphere of differentiation and takes the form of the fruit of the means of valid cognition.

Knowledge is seen—that is, it is experienced—as having the nature of apprehending mutual non-existence; it does not become a negator prior to the apprehension of mutual non-existence. Otherwise, one seeking water might even beg for fire. For [only] perception produced by the capacity of the object possesses the status of being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Indeed, it is not [otherwise].
He refutes the previously proposed view that [the cognition] has names, genus, and so forth as its objects, stating:
"This [cognition] is erroneous because it is conceptual; let it be regarded as being like [the cognition of] a rope.
For at all times, for everyone, a jar is perceived only as a jar."
A rope never actually becomes a snake for some people while becoming a garland for others; such is not the case with jars, cloths, and the like.

The cognition "this is a cloth" and so forth is erroneous, because it relies on an object that does not possess that [perceived] form, since it is conceptual, like [the cognition of] a rope. It is just like the appearance of a snake and so forth in relation to a rope and the like; thus, let it be investigated and understood in this manner. For a jar is always perceived as a jar alone by everyone at all times.
"This is a jar, this is a jar"—thus it is perceived. In this way, the rope is not properly examined;

for that reason, at times it "acts like a snake" (*sarpāyate*) to men, meaning it appears like a snake. To others, however, it "acts like a garland" (*mālāyate*) or moves as if it were a garland. When [the darkness] and other such factors have ceased, it appears in its true form as a rope.

It is not perceived as such because it is sublated. This appearance (p. 208) is produced by defects such as cataracts and is indeed erroneous, since no specific difference is observed even at other times or in other places. However, the appearance of a jar and so forth arising from the cognition "this is a jar" is not sublated; therefore, jars, cloths, and the like [are real]. It is not otherwise.

They are perceived. However, due to similarity, this ignorance—which consists of the non-discrimination and the determination [of the one as the other]—comes about. To the question of how consciousness can evolve in the form of that [universe], given that there is a commonality [between them] despite their contradictory natures, he says:
Furthermore, while an error may indeed be possible here through the analogy of a rope [mistaken for a snake],
what similarity is there when consciousness is perceived in the form of jars and other objects?

The meaning of the verse is easy to understand. Now, one might object: "Does not the Self, whose nature is consciousness, evolve (*vivartate*) in the form of pleasure and so forth? This is true. Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is indeed twofold: one kind is produced by the similarity to an object previously experienced, such as [the perception] "this is silver" in what is not silver; the second kind, however, is produced by material defects such as cataracts or jaundice, as in [the perception] "the conch is yellow."

Thus, even though consciousness (*saṃvit*) is uniform, its manifestation as pleasure, pain, and so forth—as "with pleasure" or "with pain"—is due to its association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as impurity that produce false non-dualistic ignorance; therefore, there is nothing inconsistent in this. Since conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is itself a conceptualization whose nature is difference, [it does not contradict the ultimate non-duality].

It was stated that [perception] possesses validity; however, showing that this is untenable due to its inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva), he refutes the opponent’s assertion arising from their own words—that there is no apprehension of difference in non-conceptual [perception]—by stating: "Even in the cognition of a non-conceptual object, a cognition whose nature is difference persists."
Any subsequent consciousness having ceased, it does not arise again.
For one who has not yet grasped the distinction of the object through its specific names and so forth,

even when there is a cognition of the object as indeterminate, and even in the knowledge of a general object arising from the power of consciousness which is the indeterminate means of valid perception (*nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), the nature of differentiation remains untouched by name, genus, and the like, due to the non-utterance of words.

By relying on the mere capacity for extremely subtle objects, the cognitive operation (*pratyaya*) has as its object the differentiation of the form of the referent— such as "Śiva" and so forth— as excluded from other referents;
it is the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) of a universal (*jāti*) characterized by the similarity of various parts and various qualities.

Established in the perception of objects as conceptual, non-conceptual, or non-conceptual, it is certain that otherwise, for a person who has not grasped the distinction of an object and who depends upon words and so forth,

there would be no specific designation such as a name for that object; therefore, by virtue of those specific designations such as names, the object is distinguished from others and [distinguished] by itself.

A subsequent conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*) whose object is that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its unique feature does not arise. Since the effect follows the qualities of the cause and because the existence of the effect in the cause (*satkāryavāda*) is accepted, [the objection] is raised that [conceptual cognition] lacks authority due to its being conceptual. To this, it is replied that from the perspective of the Samanaya school, there is no conceptualization of the distinction between entities.

Because even non-conceptual [cognition] would fall into the state of being invalid; since it is not sublated, the validity of both conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions must be accepted. As they say:
"There exists first a non-conceptual cognition of mere observation."
The cognition arising from a pure object is similar to that of infants, the mute, and others;
thereafter, however, the object is determined by the intellect through properties such as genus and so forth, and that [determination] is also accepted as being of the nature of perception.

He demonstrates the establishment of the manifold world through another method: "Furthermore, let it be considered whether that means of valid cognition by which the non-existence of the manifold is asserted is itself a means of valid cognition or not."
If the manifold world exists as a means of valid cognition, since it is contained within that [cognition],
then the world would all the more be of a positive nature.

Furthermore, for this reason as well, there is an absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Consider this: by whatever means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that [absence] is asserted, is that means of valid cognition itself real or unreal?
Reflect upon it in this way: if the means of valid cognition exists and is real, then conceptual proliferation exists.

Scripture and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) lack validity for establishing non-duality, because they are devoid of proof [for it], like a dream; thus, they are sublated along with their own constituent parts—words, sentences, and so forth—which possess the characteristics of being such [means]. This has been explained in detail in the *Ratnatraya*; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. If [the means] were not a valid cognition, or if they were unreal...

In that case, since there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing non-duality, the realization of the non-dual, true Brahman alone would be like a dream-vision; consequently, the world would all the more clearly exist as a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa*). And this has been stated in the *Mokṣakārikās*:
"When there is difference, the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is held to occur, and not otherwise.
Why, then, do the learned posit a non-difference that is devoid of any means of valid cognition?
[Objection: "But if the Veda and so forth appear as if they were unreal, let the Veda and so forth be [regarded as] real and non-dual."

[Objection: That is incorrect. For the manifestation of existing things (*sat*) by those who possess consciousness (*savidinām*) occurs when they are of the nature of existence (*sadrūpāyām*); this is because [manifestation] is not seen for non-existent things such as a hare's horn. [Reply: How then is the appearance of silver and so forth in mother-of-pearl and the like real? It is certainly not that form [of the silver]. It belongs to consciousness (*saṃvidaḥ*).
Because it is subject to modification, it is not unattached to its objective support (*ālambana*), for it has been stated that what is non-existent cannot appear as a manifestation.

Nor does it have a contrary object, because it is impossible for an object that is non-existent in a particular form to appear in that very form. Rather, it occurs through the influence of specific places and times that produce such an error.
In dreams, the appearance of silver and the like from mother-of-pearl and so forth occurs due to the connection with latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that have not yet reached their end.

Even though the object of cognition is unreal, because the intellect assumes the form of various real objects through the medium of memory, it is not the case that there is no appearance based on what has been experienced; nor is a connection difficult to find, for that [appearance] is its objective domain.
Having clearly explained the state of being an object, he establishes the eternity of *māyā*—both by its being the ultimate cause and because the persistence of karma would otherwise be impossible:
(p. 213) "The relationship between cognition and the jar is characterized as that of the signified and the signifier."
In this way, how could the universe, which consists of real entities, arise from that which is non-existent?
Therefore, Māyā, whose essence is reality, exists as the agent of the universe;
she is eternal because, otherwise, she could not be the cause of all effects without exception.
Just as a thread is not eternal, so too Māyā is imperishable;
if this were held to be non-eternal, where would there be a locus for the persistence of karmas?
The *bindu* is not the locus of karmas, for the *bindu* is superior to karma;
nor do they reside within the Self, because if they did, the Self would become insentient.

The meaning of the syllable *kṣa* is easy to understand. By this, those partial Śaivas who assert that Māyā is produced from Kuṇḍalinī are refuted; and likewise, certain Sāṃkhyas [are refuted] by this [statement]: "Karma is indeed a particular nature of Prakṛti consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of attachment, aversion, and so forth; it does not reside there in the intellect (*buddhi*) of the Puruṣa."

Because agency and so forth are not admitted [to belong to the self], they declare that action is characterized by refinement (*saṃskṛti*) produced by an agent other than primordial nature (*prakṛti*), having a virtuous person as its agent. Regarding this, other sages, being doubtful as to whether it is that or something else, inquire:
"What are those actions here? What is the purpose served by them in this world?
Some say they are merely worldly (prākṛta), while others say they are otherwise.
"O Īśāna, O Īśvara, tell us all of that; we have doubts.
[The categories are: the material elements (*prakṛtāni*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and the characteristics of inherent nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇāni*). The meaning here is clear:
'Īśvara' and 'that which is other than him'—thus he utters speech in the form of grace."
If the state of being an enjoyer were indeed indistinguishable, why is it that some enjoy themselves in heaven while others suffer in the Avīci hell and similar realms?
This could not be without a cause.
O best of sages, it should be understood that karma is the cause in that regard.

In the state of being an enjoyer, [the causes are] *kalā*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, and the impurity (*kaluṣita*) consisting of *prakṛti-avidyā* and so forth. Since the capacity for action (*kartṛtva*) is not distinct and is common to all beings, some also hold that the word "but" (*tu*) has the meaning of the word "also" (*api*).
Some enjoy pleasures consisting of happiness in the sovereignty of the divine realm, while others experience sufferings consisting of pain among humans, foremost of whom are those in the Avīci hell.
This [state] would not exist and could not arise if it were inverted, causeless, or without reason; therefore, that which is the cause for that inversion [must exist].

"Karma" is to be understood as that which is to be reflected upon. Having established its existence through the inversion regarding unperceived results, he establishes it further through the inversion regarding perceived results:
"Yet, when two people are equal in their farming, one obtains grain."
O twice-born ones, there is nothing else for him but karma as the cause.

The meaning of the verse is easily understood. [The author] refutes the claim that *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is the cause: "And here, *prakṛti* is not the cause, because of the contradiction with its being an object of enjoyment; for that which is enjoyed is not the enjoyer. Therefore, let karma be declared as the cause here regarding this variety of experience. It is not the cause, neither as the enjoyer nor as the instrumental cause of being an object of enjoyment."

Because of the contradiction with the nature of the experiencer, that is, due to their being mutually exclusive: since that which is an object of experience is not the experiencer, and that which is the experiencer is not the object of experience—just as sandalwood and the like [are objects, not subjects]—therefore, the *puruṣa* (Self), being distinct from the nature of the *karmaprakṛti* (the material nature of karma) and possessing dissimilar characteristics, exists as the agent; yet, it appears as a quality within the intellect (*buddhi*).
Let the state of being established in future time be accepted. As it is said in the Mataṅga:
"The agent is proclaimed there as the cause of action;
action is the cause of the object of experience; and experience is the cause of bondage."
Anticipating an objection, he refutes it:
"If the thought is that the transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti) which consists of the eight categories is of the nature of the intellect (buddhi),
while another [transformation] consisting of action is for the sake of the object of experience (bhogya)."
That too is insubstantial because things consist of conditions;
moreover, those various conditions are always observed within atoms.
O noble ones, there can be no equality there for any reason whatsoever;
nor are things themselves the causes for their own diversity, because that would lead to an infinite regress.

The Buddhist [consciousness] exists as the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*) of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). It consists of the eight states, characterized by dharma and so forth; it is a transformation consisting of action because its characteristic is action, according to the view of the supreme [Sāṃkhya], or by the supreme [Yoga], or directly according to the view of equality, [it exists] externally.

If it is your thought that dharma and so forth— characterized by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by one's own beneficial actions— are distinct from one's own qualities because they are transformations of the intellect (*buddhi*) and are the material cause (*upādāna*) of karma; whereas that which is to be enjoyed, such as garlands, sandalwood, and women, is different [from the agent]— even if such a notion exists, that contemplation is nonetheless essence-less and not meaningful.

Because things possess the nature of being conditioned (*pratyayātmatā*), one might therefore say that they exist in such a way; yet this cannot be asserted. For those conditions of things—which consist of their gross forms and their states of fortune—are seen to be entirely equal within the atoms at all times. However, they are seen to be diverse and of many different kinds.
These [causes] are infinite. In that regard, for an effect characterized by diversity, there must be some cause;

whatever [is proposed] ought to be the cause. But why do causes not remain as ninefold by their own diversity, without depending on another external cause? Because of the lack of finality (*anavasthā*): from a diverse [cause] comes a diverse [effect], from that [diverse effect] another diverse [cause], and from that again likewise [another effect], leading to an infinite regress.

For this reason as well, he says: Furthermore, how could these [categories], which are common to all, serve as the cause for the diverse manifestation of Māyā even for a person who is devoid of action?
Furthermore, let alone the eyes whose objects are their own various [forms], even for persons who are inactive, these cognitions—
because they arise at intervals between actions— are universal, common to all;
just as in the cases of "delight in the variety of illusion" or "the Vedas are the authority."
"How could there be a change in gender and number? The meaning is: not in any way whatsoever.
Anticipating another intention of the opponent, he refutes it: "If [the transformation] were from Prakṛti, yet it were variegated and inherent..."
Let there be a diverse transformation arising from the Pradhāna that is inherent by its very nature.
For this manifold transformation does not belong to that which is inherent [in itself].

If this manifold transformation were inherent to primordial matter (*prakṛti*), then in my view the manifold transformation would be produced directly from the *pradhāna*; however, in your view, let even the *guṇa*—which consists of the intellect (*buddhi*)—be inherent. Of that...

The intrinsic nature [of the intellect], which is diverse for each person and consists of the intellect (*buddhi*), is not indeed manifold; nor is it manifold in its transformation, for this [nature] is seen to consist of the conditions (*pratyaya*) and so forth. If that [intrinsic nature] were also not dependent on causes, then, due to its independence, the consequence of non-termination would follow. Even if one were to concede this [consequence]:
He says, "I shall act for the sake of others": how can there be cessation—that is, the performance of such an act—when its very nature is engagement?
For engagement and cessation are indeed contradictory in a single substratum.

If this *pradhāna* possesses the nature of activity (*pravṛtti*), then because it undergoes various transformations, its own operation would be self-established; in that case, cessation, characterized by its dissolution, would be impossible. How then could there be such action? For both activity and cessation are two opposites, characterized by a contradiction established in themselves; thus, they cannot coexist in a single substratum (*dharmin*). This is how it is.
He demonstrates this:
although fire has luminosity as its inherent nature, it is not luminous even by that [nature] alone;
likewise, both engagement and withdrawal do not arise from themselves, but rather from a cause.
Whatever is the cause here, that is karma; therefore, the world is not accidental.
That which is unmanifest has its end in manifestation; it is not produced by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), but rather produced by limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
This means it is not non-causal—that is, not independent of other causes. The rest [is as follows].

The meaning of the term is clear. Nevertheless, in response to the doubt that if activity (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*) do not exist at the same time, they cannot share a single substratum (*dharmin*), he says:
"Furthermore, whatever is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a property, that must always belong to it."
Just as fire, even while manifesting light, also causes burning;
Thus, in this way, the engagement and the withdrawal [of activity] would both arise from primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Furthermore, it has been said: even without [external] effort, whatever is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of a phenomenon must always belong to that substratum (*dharmin*). Just as fire, although manifesting as light, performs the act of burning even while being light itself.

Therefore, for that reason, in this manner, there would have to be two simultaneous activities—both proceeding from and ceasing from *prakṛti*. But this is not observed; therefore, the meaning is that a second factor must be depended upon. The sages raise an objection, asserting that it is possible for two contradictory states to reside in a single substratum:
The eight categories beginning with Dharma and so forth are mutually contradictory;
likewise, the qualities such as Sattva and the rest—how then could they have a single cause?
The meaning will become easier to understand through this refutation. Īśvara says:

"Dharma and the other categories are not contradictory, because they consist of cognition (*pratyaya*). Since they are manifestations of the state of consciousness, they are knowledge; otherwise, they would simply be non-knowledge."
The dharmas and so forth, which are expressed by the word "existence" (bhāva), are not mutually contradictory because of what will be said later;

he demonstrates this very point. For those existents are of the nature of cognition (pratyaya); when they have reached the state of being objects of enjoyment, they consist of accomplishments (siddhi) and the like, appearing as light, and they possess various analytical statements in the subsequent examination of the intellect (buddhiparīkṣā).
(p. 223) Then he says—connecting it with what precedes—he demonstrates the nature of its non-contradictory manifestation.

Among these [categories] such as *dharma* and so forth, "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is listed; it is not the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*), nor is it the Buddhist [view], nor is it the human state of ignorance (*ajñatva*) consisting of a lack of determination (*adhyavasāya*). Rather, it is simply a form of knowledge that is otherwise.

Since error cannot arise from the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) by itself, that quality of the intellect (*buddhi*) through which the experience of doubt and misconception occurs as a consequence is here called "ignorance" (*ajñāna*), born from the appropriation of the karma characterized as *tamas*. He states the conclusion:
Therefore, all those particular cognitions—such as the cognition of "dharma" and so forth—are established;
for particulars are never contradictory to the universal.

The particulars (*viśeṣas*), however, being endowed with distinctions such as changeability (*anyathātva*) and so forth, are never at any time contradictory to the universal (*sāmānya*), namely the commonality of "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*). The meaning of the preceding portion is clear. Having thus removed the contradiction regarding existence (*bhāva*), [the author now addresses] the contradiction regarding qualities (*guṇa*), stating that they are common to both the manifestor of consciousness (*cid-vyañjaka*) and the universal.

That ignorance which was previously described as the absence of knowledge and as having the nature of non-utility for conscious power (*cicchakti*), he now states does not arise from the effects produced by the quality of *tamas*: "For *sattva* and *tamas* are never contradictory."
That which makes [reality] known as it truly is is sattva; that which makes it known otherwise is tamas.
It has been argued that there is no contradiction because there is no difference in their being illuminators;
however, darkness is never the effect [of an illuminator], whereas ignorance is like a stain and so forth.

For this reason— because the spiritual ignorance (*pauruṣājñāna*) characterized by the incapacity of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) to perform its function, and through that [ignorance], the non-manifestation of the determination regarding the accomplishment of the effect consisting in the appropriation of existence to be accomplished—
is called "non-accomplishment" (*asiddhi*) or "non-determination" (*anadhyavasāya*), which is intellectual knowledge (*bauddhajñāna*) born from the cause of *tamas*.

It is not born from a non-existent cause. Therefore, there is no contradiction in its being produced from the material cause of karma characterized by darkness (*tamas*), which consists of ignorance (*ajñāna*) in the form of erroneous cognition (*viparyaya*) and doubt (*saṃśaya*).
The meaning of the other words is easy to understand. (p. 225) He concludes:
Therefore, there is no production of two effects that are contradictory by their own nature anywhere;
thus, their contradiction arises from a difference in their causes.
Furthermore, that very action is impelled by God as its cause;
therefore, it is established that this doctrine of inherent nature (svabhāvavāda) is rooted in delusion.

Therefore, for the reasons stated previously—where "somewhere" or "even in some case" is to be supplied as an ellipsis—two effects that are contradictory by their very nature cannot have a single cause. Consequently, as explained above, since it is impossible [for them] to arise from themselves, the contradiction characterized by the activity and cessation of *prakṛti* must arise from another cause. And that [cause] is...

The cause characterized by cooperation is indeed karma; this is the intended meaning. Because it exists in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), like *māyā*, it is devoid of diverse forms; yet, as the cause that produces those diverse expressions, it is the impeller (*bhojaka*) due to its reliance upon other karmas of the same nature. (p. 226) Apart from the inherent nature of *prakṛti*, [it functions] as a quality within the intellect (*buddhi*).

Through the medium of the effect—characterized as the *saṃskāra* (latent impression) produced by external sacrificial rites and other actions performed by the person (*puruṣa*)—there arises the appropriation of *karman* characterized as that which is to be experienced (*bhogya*). This [object] consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; because it has manifested as *sattva* and the other qualities for the sake of experience, it undergoes transformation into the nature of pleasure and so forth. Thus, it is directly the object of experience, consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

First, one should understand the suffix denoting abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*). That [state] arises from its connection with that [action], because it has that as its purpose and because it is the substratum of experience.

However, the world, the body, and so forth—which ultimately consist of objects of experience—arise from the material cause called *māyā*, with *karman* acting as the auxiliary cause. Thus, the definition of *karman* is that which is produced both directly and indirectly.

The proof that the aggregate of living beings (*janakandhāraka*) is internal and subject to experience is established by such statements as: "Because it originates from truth and untruth, it consists of the nature of *dharma* and *adharma*," and so forth, as analyzed in the *Mṛgendra-tantra* and other texts. Furthermore, that very *karman* proceeds only when impelled and set in motion by the Lord (*īśvara*). This is demonstrated in the section on the establishment of the Lord (*īśvara-siddhi*).
Since it has already been refuted that an insentient entity possesses spontaneous activity, [the argument] that sattva causes those who are characterized by sattva to experience pleasure—

which is its nature— and to maintain an attachment toward objects of enjoyment belonging to that same class, or conversely, that it does not cause such maintenance, or furthermore, that it causes those who are asattvic— namely the tāmasa and rājasa— to experience pain, which is their nature, and aversion; [is untenable].

Alternatively, *adharma* is that which causes one to experience objects of enjoyment belonging to a different class [from those previously experienced]. Action (*karman*), which consists of both these [dharma and adharma], is to be performed by each individual; because it is manifold, it is to be experienced through the nature of various causal conditions and is indeed infinite.

Furthermore, this [action] is not a separate ontological principle (*tattvāntara*) from dharma and so forth; rather, it is a specific differentiation within the eight categories of existence, consisting of its own transformations, primordial matter (*prakṛti*), and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Because it possesses form (*rūpatva*). For without that [form], it would be impossible for *prakṛti* to function as a bond in the present context. Therefore, for that reason, the doctrine of inherent nature (*svabhāvavāda*)—which claims that the world's diversity arises from the very nature of *prakṛti* itself—is established as being rooted in delusion. It is determined that [the cause] is the cause of erroneous cognition residing in the intellect (*buddhi*), and not a stain (*mala*) distinct from *māyā*.

Because the effect arises from the cause of appropriation (*upādāna*), those who formulate this as a logical reason (*hetu*) state that the activity of *māyā*—which will be described as the concealment of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) through its non-engagement with both the distinct and the non-distinct—is the cause of that [effect].
Thus, the word "eternal" (*nitya*) used as a reason is unestablished due to a difference in locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*), like the argument: "Because a crow is black."
Thus, failing to understand this, the Pāśupatas and others who assert that Māyā is impurity (mala) prattle on.
Consequently, he refutes their statement: "And Māyā is not impurity, because [the powers] manifest as effects."
That which is illuminating with respect to an effect, however, is not its producer by its own nature.
Just as both fire and a lamp are seen to be illuminators,
fire is never a cause of illumination that is itself non-illuminating.
Māyā is neither impurity (*mala*) nor characterized by the activity of impurity; it does not obscure the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

By virtue of this proposition, through its effects—namely, the *kalās* and so forth—it is the illuminator and the manifester of the power of consciousness. Therefore, because it is a manifester, this is the logical reason (*hetu*). As for the phrase "by virtue of its effects":

The illuminator is the manifestor; by its own nature, that is, in its essential form, it is neither a producer nor a non-manifestor for the concealer. The meaning of the verse beginning with "Just as" and ending with "illuminator" is clear; this is the illustration. Even though the state of being a concealer belongs to Māyā through its effects, [it does not exist in itself].

It is impossible for that which does not manifest the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) to produce an effect; if its capacity as a concealer were conceivable through the medium of an effect, then, while that [power] exists—even when all effects have been withdrawn at the time of dissolution—there would follow the undesirable consequence that everyone is omniscient. Now, one might object:

Because it conforms to another contradictory cause, it possesses both the engagement with and the withdrawal from contradictory characteristics. Likewise, because it conforms to another non-illuminating cause, let it be non-illuminating by its own nature.
That is not so, because in the absence of impurity (*mala*), there is no other non-illuminating cause. Even if such a thing were to exist, it would not [be so] by its own nature.
He says that it does arise:
"And [the power] does not exist as something that performs a function for men by way of its own illusory nature;
because it does not assist at all through its effects, whatever is thus [ineffective] is not [identical] with itself."
Just as a thread [is not the cause] by its own nature, but only through its own effect, namely the cloth;

because of its being an auxiliary to the atom—thus the meaning of the sentence, consisting of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), is clear. Whatever entity is thus an auxiliary to itself by means of its own effect, that is not [an auxiliary] by its own nature, that is, not by its own essence.

It is cooperative. For example, a thread performs its function—characterized by the act of covering—only through its own effect, which is the cloth; it does not do so by itself or by its own nature. This is the illustration. Therefore, just as when there is a weak digestive fire, milk becomes a cause of defects such as phlegm, so too [is it] when there is a distinct impurity. (p.)
231) When there is *māyā*, it becomes the cause of defects such as delusion (*moha*)—which consists of the conceit of self (*ātman*) in that which is non-self (*anātman*)—by way of its effects;

however, it does not exist directly [in the soul], as is seen in the case of those who are liberated at the time of dissolution (*pralayakevalins*). Turning back like a lion’s glance, he now defines the nature of *karma* once again:
When one action is being performed and another arises that is obstructive and more powerful, if there is no contradiction, there is a combination (samuccaya).
While one action is being experienced and another action is being experienced, yet another action being experienced presents itself and arrives;

if that [third] is more powerful, it would act as a sublater (*bādhaka*) in case of conflict. This should be explained as "susceptible to various doubts. However, the meaning is that it is experienced first. In the absence of conflict, there is a combination (*samuccaya*).

When that which is powerful and that which is weak are experienced simultaneously, there would be a *dvandva* [co-ordinate] compound. He clarifies this very point: "O best of the twice-born, when a canine birth occurs while human existence is being experienced, if the canine state is obstructive and powerful, it supersedes the human."

Now, if attainment occurs from what is not contradictory, then there is a combination [of effects]. At whatever time, while a human being is experiencing— that is, while it is fit to be experienced— the fruit of the action consisting of the nature of humanity, at that very time, while it is being experienced, the birth in a dog's womb, characterized as the fruit of its own [past] birth, would come to be.

O best of the twice-born, if at that time the human state were powerful and obstructive, it would first be the one to be experienced. However, if there is an attainment therein of characteristics such as humanity and Brahminhood that are not mutually contradictory, then there would be a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of those two, characterized by being experienced simultaneously—that is, a pair (*dvandva*). In some cases...
He states that it is also obstructive even for one who possesses equal strength:
"Even if it has begun, if the strength is equal, it remains uncommenced;
for the [karma] that has already begun must be experienced, because it is blocked by the obstructing [karman]. (p. 233)
The body of a god and so forth, characterized as the fruit of what has already begun (*ārabdha*),

and the body of a human being and so forth, characterized as the fruit of what has not yet begun (*anārabdha*)— if both of these, through the ripening of the latter with intense velocity, are equally obstructed by the power of Śiva’s energy known as *rodhayitrī*, which bears the same name [as the former].

When the commencement of bondage has begun by means of the impelled infinite power (*ananta-śakti*) and that commencement has been obstructed, then only that which was commenced remains to be experienced.

When that has been experienced, even that [commenced karma] may arise at another time. However, if even commenced karma becomes light, then it is forcibly obstructed by uncommenced karma that is contrary to it and possesses intense momentum, as in the case of Nahuṣa.

Because the body of Sukhadeva was cast aside, he attained the extremely painful body of a python; since it is impossible for enjoyments to arise simultaneously due to the conflict between two uncommenced actions of equal strength, Śiva and Śakti act as the cause of destruction therein— thus he says:
When two simultaneous actions that are mutually contradictory are undertaken with force, at that very moment their destruction occurs through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).

The meaning of the verse is easy to understand; it refutes the proponents of an unjust doctrine who claim that actions reside within the self. Furthermore, the subsistence of those actions within the self is not logically tenable.
Because, like agriculture and similar activities, it produces a refinement (saṃskāra) of the primary element (pradhāna).

O best of the twice-born, they are established in illusion alone and not in anything else. O best of the twice-born, for those whose characteristics have been described, an abiding in the self through action is not possible;
rather, it is in the primary cause (pradhāna), that is to say, in the intellect (buddhi) which is the effect of primordial nature (prakṛti), because [action] produces latent impressions (saṃskāra).

The meaning is that just as in the case of agriculture and the like—which are performed by human agents—the cultivation of fields and so forth produces a refinement [of the soil], and thus the agent, the person, remains [as the source]; so it is here. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the self being insentient; however, for us, this is not the case because the self is sentient. In that regard, [the self acts] by performing the functions of consciousness.

It should not be said that the arising of consciousness (*cid-utpatti*) is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*); for that consciousness, being of the very nature of the Self (*ātman*), is to be established later [within the Self], and because it is perishable once performed. Furthermore, since action exists as a mental quality (*buddhi-guṇa*) in the form of an impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by itself, it possesses the characteristics of a supreme cause.

At the time of dissolution, within Māyā itself—which is characterized by the *bindu* and consists of its own material cause—they remain together with their respective qualities (*guṇin*). However, during re-creation, for the sake of experience (*bhukti*), those *karmas* arise, taking as their instrumental cause the inherent power of Māyā; these arise separately for each individual soul (*pratipuruṣa*) as the *kalā* [and the subsequent categories] ending with *kṣiti*.
Again, having taken his own capacity as the cause and relying upon that corresponding nature arising therefrom,

and subsequently taking his own capacity as the cause and [acting] through the medium of the qualities (*guṇa*), he produced a corresponding intellect (*buddhi*) arising therefrom; thus, indicating that the creation of the worlds follows immediately after the creation of the principles (*tattva*), he [proceeds] from the previously mentioned Self...
Immediately after the bondage connected to the *paradeha*, there occurs the bondage of the reality of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) which manifests consciousness (*cid-vyañjaka*).

Following that, there occurs the gross bondage consisting of the body born of the world-soul (*bhuvana-ātmaja*). He says that even those existing therein, having attained the state of being *sakala* (possessing all), are to be graced by Śiva through the medium of the Guru: [The original Sanskrit text continues: *“tadvartinopi sakalatvaṃ prāptā gurvadhikaraṇena śivenānugrāhyāḥ” iti āha—* [Translation: "Even those residing therein, having attained the state of being *sakala*, are to be graced by Śiva through the agency of the Guru"—thus he says.
From Māyā, creation is twofold, consisting of both the gross and the subtle;
the subtle, which manifests the power of vision, abides within the Self by means of the essence of the principles (tattvas).
The gross [principles], existing in the form of the worlds and as the body and so forth, are coarse;
whereas the subtle ones, beginning with *kalā*, first become gross and then bind the individual souls (*aṇu*).
Men situated within the illusory maṇḍala are considered to be *sakala* (with parts);
they are to be graced by Śiva through the instrument of the *iṣṭa* (the chosen deity).
The meaning of the syllables is explicit. He speaks of those who are graced by Śiva, who is without substrate during the times of dissolution:
"the eight Vidyeśvaras, Maṇḍalins, Krodha and the others, and likewise Śrīkaṇṭha."
And the Supreme Lord assigned the Śatarudras and Vīreśa as well.
Having first bestowed grace upon him himself, he appointed him to his office;
thus, in brief, has Māyā, who consists of the entire universe, been described.
One should contemplate the eight Vidyāmaṇḍalins and the eight Garbhitakalārāgavidyāmaṇḍalins,

who, beginning from the lower portion of the principle of passion (rāga-tattva), reside within their own eight excellent maṇḍalas situated at the summit of the kalās, accompanied by a maṇḍala and a maṇḍaleśa for each respective maṇḍala, according to the sequence of eight times eight. As it has been stated in the Mṛgendra:
In the great sixty-four-petaled mandala, these are the lords of the mandalas;

they are the principal lords because, due to their subtle nature as primordial matter (*prakṛti*), they are unfit to serve as the support for the worlds. Furthermore, the abodes of the thirteen Rudras, such as Vāmadeva and others, who have attained the status of Gurus bestowed by the Krodhas and other deities, are also located there.

Likewise, one should likewise [visualize] the eight [deities] beginning with Krodha, who reside at the head of Bhūtaguṇa; as well as Guṇatvanilaya, Prakṛtyagranilaya, and Śrīgala. As it is stated in the Mataṅga:
"Having divided its own potency into two parts, it descends into Pradhāna."

In that world which is the foremost abode of the supreme leader of all Rudras, situated at the limit of the *guṇa-tattva* during the internal dissolution (*pralaya*), there reside the disciples of Śrīkaṇṭha who dwell in the abode of the *guṇas*— namely the hundred Rudras and others who are disciples of Śiva— as well as Ananta and the other disciples of Śrīkaṇṭha.
They shine forth. When even that [world] is withdrawn, they shine forth in the world of Śrīkaṇṭha, which is the reality-level of passion (*rāgatatva*).

As it is stated in the *Mataṅga*: "Having reached the world of Śrīkaṇṭha, they sport. And as for the hundred Rudras situated in the worlds born of the skull outside the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), they reside in the gateway-section of the cosmic egg.

At the intermediate dissolution (*madhyamapralaya*), Śiva himself— residing in *prakṛti*, possessing a portion [of his nature], and being intent upon [the world]— graces Vīrabhadra, the Lord of Heroes, who is the abode of the worlds, even without depending on the office of a Guru. At the commencement of the creation of *māyā*, by means of the liberation from bonds, he bestows upon him omniscience and, up to his own limit, universal agency.

Having rendered them auspicious by making their own sovereignty inseparable from his own characteristics, and having favored them with divine bodies endowed with infinite gateways, he appointed them to the office characterized by the creation and manifestation of the worlds.
Now, one might ask: is it not the case that the manifestation of manifest Śiva-hood occurs only after the threefold severance of karma, impurity (*mala*), and *māyā*?

The *pralayakevala* state is concealed by the names of the other two types of Śivas; because it bears the name *pralayakevala*, how can there be the status of being a presiding authority (*adhikāritva*) over *māyā* when it is devoid of *māyā* and *kalā*? True. Even though the bonds (*pāśas*) such as impurity (*mala*) are severed, because the ripening of their dullness is suspended for a period of time, the presiding authority over the objects of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the innate impurity remains within *māyā*.

Due to a specific state, for Ananta and the others, Māyā is as pure as the *kalā* itself; being independent of the karma that causes pride (*abhimāna*) in that very [state], it is pure. However, the *kalā* sprouts again under its control; thus, there is no contradiction. As it has been said regarding the application of *kalā*: "Even though they are not subject to the *kalās*..."

"Like a herd of cattle.
