Furthermore, other lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśas*), beginning with Kapālīśa and ending with Kālāgni—both those with *añjana* (taint) and those without *añjana*—are to be understood by their own names as mentioned in the *Śrīmataṅga-pāda*. Among them, within the pure worlds (*śuddha-bhuvana*), the stainless ones (*nirañjana*) who are disciples of Śiva are Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, and so forth; [Ananta is] infinite.

The disciples residing within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), such as Śrīkaṇṭha and others, attain liberation equal to Śiva when [the cycle] ceases at the time of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya). Those who do not cease their activity during that cessation remain in their respective offices; furthermore, they become successive office-holders (adhikārin) while residing within the cosmic egg, possessing the qualities [of their station].

The stainless (nirañjana) disciples of Śrīkaṇṭha belonging to the lineage of Nila reside in the first dissolution (pralaya) or, having ceased [their activity], they remain in the middle dissolution; they attain supreme liberation (paramukti). If they do not cease [their activity], until the end of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), they become partakers of both the supreme and the non-supreme enjoyment (parāparabhukti), though their desire for it remains. The disciples of Ananta, however, possess impurity (sāñjana).
O Abode of Virtues, beginning with Kapālīśa! O Lord of the five groups of eight, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others, and the heart of the center!

You have declared peace (śānti). Having remained until the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), when karma is exhausted upon that dissolution, there is the liberation of pure consciousness (vijñāna-kaivalya); when it is not exhausted during the dissolution, there is the liberation of dissolution (pralaya-kaivalya); and upon re-creation, there is the attainment of one's own world.

When the transformation of impurity (*mala*) occurs, those disciples of Śrīkaṇṭha who possess the *añjana* (the ointment of knowledge) attain either the world above or their own respective worlds; beheld by their own world-guru, they become partakers of the liberation that is both higher and lower, and do not descend further.
Having remained until the end of the intermediate dissolution (*madhyamapralaya*), Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others, whose abode is within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), [attain this].

O abode of virtues! Those who have been withdrawn by Śrīkaṇṭha are, at the time of re-creation, [reborn] in due order starting from the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*) as enjoyers of experience;
or, during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), they remain in that state until the exhaustion of their karma, attaining liberation through knowledge (*vijñānakaivalya*).
When that [karma] is not exhausted, they attain dissolution-liberation (*pralayakaivalya*) during the dissolution, and upon re-creation, they attain the enjoyment of their own desired objects.

When the transformation of impurity (*malapariṇati*) has occurred, those who are beheld by their own world-teacher attain either the liberation of the Supreme and the Non-Supreme (*parāparamukti*), or they go to the Lord (*nātha*). This is because only those whose karma is entirely exhausted possess the qualification for [attaining] the state of Brahmā and so forth within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). Now, Ananta is the disciple who remains steadfast until the end of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

Because his impure karma has been destroyed, like a sweat-born firefly, he possesses a body characterized by the birth of *māyā* as a basis for his office. Having reached the world of Śrīkaṇṭha, which is the abode of *prakṛti* during the intermediate dissolution (*madhyamapralaya*), he sports there;
yet how can that Śrīkaṇṭha, who resides within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), be the abode of the *guṇas*?

It is heard in the *Sarvajñānottara* that, having been appointed by Śrīkaṇṭha during the intermediate dissolution (*madhyamapralaya*), he exists as Kālāgnirudra for the purpose of withdrawing [the universe]. This is true. During the intermediate dissolution, there is a withdrawal of the mere form of Kālāgni, which is sustained by the power of sovereign will (*prākāmya-śakti*). Alternatively, it refers to someone else who is established in that [state].

And the withdrawal of one similar to Rudra is also understood. Now, it may be argued that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others are heard of in the scriptures as being favored by Śiva at the time of dissolution, and that there are traditions concerning Svāyaṃbhuva and others. True;
however, they are those who undergo dissolution every night for Śrīkaṇṭha.

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, who are innumerable and enter into their respective offices every day— among them, for some, immediately upon the appointment to office, after a certain period of time has passed and when their impurities have been purified, the state of being stainless (nirañjanatva) manifests through grace; thus, there is nothing inconsistent in this.

Thus, by way of various streams, Māyā is perceived as flowing against the current along with those presiding over the womb of Māyā, such as Śrīkaṇṭha and others who are the foremost leaders of all the Rudras. In each individual stream that is common to the worlds, there exists a subtle body produced by a single Māyā; [likewise], in the stream produced by multiple Māyās that are common [to many], [there exist subtle bodies]. (p. 244)

The channels exist. This is stated in the *Mataṅga*: "They have the form of honeycomb cells and are composed of accumulated atoms. The pure channels, which are produced from Mahāmāyā, are of a single common form; they are distinct from the subtle body-self and the common pure *kalās* and so forth.
They are distinct and appropriate [to their respective lineages], because it is impossible for those following the Great Māyā (mahāmāyā) to follow Śuddhavidyā.
There are many currents (*srotas*) consisting of worlds that follow the Great Māyā, just like those that follow Māyā. As it is said in the *Svacchanda-tantra*, in the *Lalita-bheda*:
This [universe], established upon the head of the Waters, has the form of Śakti; indeed, Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ have the form of Śakti.
Then that very [Śakti] fell down, and immediately thereafter the Āgneya [element], as well as the Vāyavya, the Nābhāsa, the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the sense organs.

And likewise, O Mistress of the Gods, there are the various [tattvas]: mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*) in due order, as well as the intellectual (*bauddha*), the secondary (*gauṇa*), the natural (*prākṛta*), and the personal (*pauruṣa*);
furthermore, destiny (*niyati*), time (*kāla*), attachment (*rāga*), knowledge (*vidyā*), and limited agency (*kalā*).
Then come the principles of Māyā, Vidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
The Bindu, the Ardhendu, the Nirodhī, the Nāda, and the Nādi follow this;
above that is the Brahmabilam, O Goddess, and beyond that is the Śakti-tattva.
Beyond that, it is endowed with the five causes and is all-pervasive;
then there are Samanā and Unmanā, and thereafter the cosmic eggs (*aṇḍas*) of the creative process (*prakriyā*).
And just as, O Goddess, souls are established in incalculable numbers,
even so there are indeed incalculable cosmic eggs by the millions according to this process.
O beloved, when one [element] is described, the entire temporal path is not thereby described;
for as it is with one, so it is with the whole, established as the egg of the cosmic process.
"When all the spheres of manifestation (*prakriyāṇḍa*) have been well-established in their own respective natures, Śiva—the pervasive and subtle one—abides both within and without them. (p.
246) Each individual sphere of manifestation should be understood as consisting of the aggregate of sixteen spheres.

The mantras beginning with Ananta, headed by Śrīkaṇṭha, and ending with Kālāgni—beginning with Brahmā and the others—are threefold: Āṇava, Śambhava, and Śākta. Among these, the Āṇava mantras possess a real body by virtue of being presided over [by a deity]; they are both stainless (nirañjana) and stained (sāñjana), and they fulfill their office in a real manner.

The Śāmbhavas enjoy even those pleasures desired by the mind through their own respective wives—such as Brāhmī and others—who possess beautiful forms and naturally sustain the world of sentient beings and so forth. For them, Śiva alone assumes the forms of Brahmā and the other deities, fashioned by his presiding presence (adhiṣṭhātṛtā). The Śāktas [enjoy these] through his being their basis (adhiṣṭhānatā), fashioned [by him].
The power of Śiva alone possesses the forms of Brahmā and the other deities. With the verse beginning with "evam" (thus), the examination of Māyā is concluded.
Thus [ends] the work composed by Ācārya Jñānaprakāśa, a resident of Śrī Śālivāṭipura.
The third chapter in the commentary on the Vidyāpāda of the Pauṣkara.
The "flock of cattle" consists of the bound soul (*paśu*); because of its conjunction with the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*), it is called a "bound soul" as long as it is not liberated.
For this reason, although it possesses its own limited vision and action (*dṛkkriyā*) and is devoid of *kalā*, it is not the Lord (*anīśvara*).
The pervasive, consciousness-natured, and subtle [Self] is established as being like Śiva.

Following the examination of Māyā, at the end of the chapter, by the words beginning with "having favored," it is indicated that the bound soul (paśu) has been grasped; thus, the category of the bound soul (paśupadārtha) is now examined—this is the connection between the chapters.

The connection (*saṃbandha*) concerning the *tantravastu* consists of the categories of the bound soul (*paśu*). It is manifold, consisting of sentences, subtle principles (*aṇu*), eternal [principles], and so forth. This connection is the conjunction with the impurity (*mala*) that constitutes the state of being a bound soul; it is characterized by the relationship between the veiled and the veiler. Indeed, this conjunction is not a mere physical fusion.

Thus it should be explained, because both [the soul and the Lord] are formless (*amūrta*). Therefore, due to its connection with the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*), the fourth category, the "bound soul" (*paśu*), is so called; when liberated from that state of being a bound soul, it is no longer called a "bound soul. It is not designated as a "bound soul" because [it is no longer so].
Being included within the category of *pratipadārtha*, it is established as being of the same nature as Śiva.
Why is it liberated? Because it is subtle (*sūkṣma*), being free from the bonds (*pāśa*) such as impurity (*mala*) and the like;
whereas [the individual soul] is rendered distant due to its grossness (*sthūlatva*). But surely, subtlety exists here even for atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth?

Indeed, there is certainly no similarity with Śiva. This is true; he is liberated and consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*). Now, although his subtlety and nature as consciousness are established according to the *Pāñcarātra* perspective like that of a liberated soul, if he were somehow to have his pervasiveness obstructed by some particular limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), then—again...

Whence [can there be] similarity with Śiva? True. One who is liberated according to the Siddhānta is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), not one whose pervasion is obstructed by some adventitious condition (*upādhi*) in any way whatsoever. Now, even if that threefold nature exists, because of the reason of being unmanifest due to non-existence, there is no manifestation of existing things such as mountains and the like.

Because no prior manifestation is observed; for there is a lack of evidence for that nature [of the effect] existing unmanifested beforehand. Furthermore, whether one follows the perspective of the theory of non-existent effects (*asatkāryavāda*) and holds that what was non-existent arises, or the perspective of the theory of existent effects (*satkāryavāda*) and holds that what exists is manifested, [the result] would be impermanent, just like jars and other such things.

And as a consequence: if liberation were merely the state of being free from the impurities of debate once the dispute has concluded—according to the view of those who consider themselves accomplished practitioners (*siddha*)—then how could there be any resemblance to Śiva in one whose nature as Śiva remains unmanifest? True; even one who is fully liberated, though devoid of the *kalās*, possesses the manifestation of consciousness that is utterly purified.

The subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), though possessing the signs (*nimitta*) and being endowed with the capacity for action (*kriyāśālī*), is characterized by the manifestation of its own vision and the perfection of its own activity;

it possesses the manifestation of non-Śiva-hood within itself. This is the intended meaning: because the bound soul (*paśu*) is observed to have limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*), while Śiva is heard in scripture to possess omniscience (*sarvajñatva*), [the soul] is indeed distinct from both of those.
By virtue of possessing the power of knowledge of reality, he becomes like a stone.

Since the arising of the non-existent is impossible and must be established later, the manifestation of the existent is easily accomplished. Now, one might object: is there not a lack of manifestation for existent things such as mountains?
"How can there be manifestation by causal factors (*kārakas*) of that which exists [but is unmanifest], since its prior manifestation is impossible?

This is incorrect. We shall establish later how the non-manifestation of the existent prior [to action] does not contradict the utility of causal factors, and how the manifestation of the existent occurs.
[Objection: But then, even according to your view, since the scripture states that what exists is manifested and thus undergoes production and destruction, how is this resolved? [Reply: True.
Manifestation is indeed twofold: one consists in the removal of another form that was obscuring it.

For objects such as a jar, which are obstructed by other impediments like darkness and thus do not undergo perception or obtain causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) despite possessing their own causes, there occurs— once those impediments have been merely dispelled by causal factors such as a lamp— their perception and the attainment of causal efficiency.

[The first] is one *yojana* in extent. But the other [is that] which, having clay as its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), is connected with another form [of its own], such as a jar or the like; it is a product whose specific form is not perceived, and which has failed to obtain the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) appropriate to its attainment. Furthermore, by means of the instruments such as the potter’s wheel and so forth—(p. [number])...
251) Through the exclusion of what is not the cause from what is the cause, there is the attainment of the form of the effect;

this consists in the application to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) characterized by possession. In this very context, within the specific states of *śākalya* and so forth, there is manifestation associated with transformation, while in the specific state of its non-manifestation, there is the term "origination" (*utpatti*).

And the word "destruction" (nāśa) is applied metaphorically to specific sounds such as those of the throat and so forth within Brahman; it does not refer to the aforementioned specific manifestation that is devoid of modification, such as a jar, nor to the specific non-manifestation thereof.
Nevertheless, according to the method to be explained, in some cases the Self, when associated with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body, is [designated as such].

The terms "origination" and "destruction" are applied metaphorically to the specific non-manifestation of the consciousness of the stained self— which is itself free from modification— due to its being delimited by limiting adjuncts such as the body; they do not, however, apply to the limiting adjuncts themselves, such as the body.

That which is deficient due to the impurity of self-consciousness—the state of transformation—is not manifest; rather, it is metaphorically designated as "manifestation" only insofar as it is distinguished by the complete manifestation that is free from the three types of limitation and other such deficiencies. Now, one might ask:
is the removal of the veil of impurity not simply like the removal of the obstruction of darkness for an object such as a jar? Indeed, what else could it be?

It is the manifestation of Śiva-nature. That [manifestation] occurs not through the mere removal of coverings such as cataracts by means of action, nor through the service of collyrium and other such auxiliary factors— which serve as the cause for manifestation by way of removing the latent impressions that obstruct the power of the eye— nor indeed through the eyes and so forth [themselves].

Because it is seen as the power of the grasper, [the argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, just as there is the removal of a cataract through the activity of a well-trained and highly skilled physician, which effects the absolute cessation of the film without the need for the removal of its own form;
following that, there is the practice of applying collyrium (*añjana*)—which is its own awakener and the remover of the cataract's residual impression.
Furthermore, when that [power] is cultivated, it becomes independent of those [external means], and the manifestation of the luster of the eyes is characterized by further dissolution and cessation.
Likewise, without the removal of one's own limited form, there occurs an activity augmented by the power of Śiva— known as the initiation of a well-ripened and well-trained teacher.

Having brought about the cessation of absolute impurity (*atyantika-mala*), it subsequently brings about the cessation of the impurity of office (*adhikāra-mala*) and the impurity of the seed (*bīja-mala*). Having cultivated specific auxiliary rites that awaken its own [innate] power,
it becomes independent of those [rites] and, characterized by the cessation of further dissolution, it initiates the transformation of the fluctuations (*vṛtti-pariṇati-vivarta*).

The manifestation of unsurpassed auspiciousness (*śivatva*) is free from disturbance; thereafter, that manifestation— like the manifestation of the form of a jar, which is devoid of the defects of change caused by the movement of the potter’s stick, wheel, and so forth, as well as the lamp and other instruments, and is free from the darkness of its own causal form— is [the state] of stainlessness.

Through the two [processes] of the manifestation of Śiva-nature and the subsequent manifestation of consciousness effected by initiation (*dīkṣā*) performed by *kalā*, the manifestation of "other-Śiva-nature" (*aparaśivatva*) is not sublated. Everything is faultless,
because manifestation is the very nature of the manifestor, and since there is no further object to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*) beyond the manifestor itself.

The manifestation of the nature of Śiva, though previously non-existent, has that manifestation as its very essence when auxiliary causes are present; just as the light of a lamp, though previously existing,
does not have that illumination as its essence until it is in proximity to an auxiliary cause such as the act of breaking open a jar.

Since [an object] is illuminated by another illumination, if it is designated as such on account of the power of its action (*karman*), then is manifestation (*abhivyakti*) itself non-existent? Or is it an effect? Furthermore, if it was previously non-existent and unmanifested, yet becomes manifested when existing, then there must also be a manifestation of that manifestation.

Nevertheless, the notion that "the conceptualization is likewise established" leads to an infinite regress (anavasthā) in various instances; thus, the deluded conceptualization of bad logicians is thoroughly cast aside.
A detailed refutation of this is not elaborated here by one who fears prolixity. Now, was it not previously stated that [the object] is subtle?

Although the four characteristics— consisting of being composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), and the possession of vision and action (*dṛkkriyā*)— are present in both the liberated Śiva and the bound soul,

because agency (*kartṛtva*) in the case of the liberated Śiva is established as being primordially dependent upon the impulsion of Īśvara, it is said that "the liberated are impelled by Śiva. From the perspective of one who knows this principle, since they are impelled by Śiva, how [could they be considered independent]?

[The opponent claims] similarity with Śiva. [The author replies: True. But one who is liberated is "non-lord" (anīśvara), meaning one for whom the impeller of the Lord (īśvara-preraka) no longer exists. This is the intended meaning: although lack of independence (*asvātantrya*) and so forth are established [in the case of the bound soul], they may at some point cease, because they have impurities (*mala*) and the like as their cause, just like *kalā* and other [categories].
Because that [impurity] has not ceased, he too—like a Vidyeśvara—is bound by the impurity of *nimitta-adhikāra* (office based on purpose);
thus, because his desires are not fully realized, he is indeed unliberated.
Since it has been stated that he is "not like Śiva," both his superiority over Śiva and his identity with him are easily established.

Since it has been stated that "action" refers to those things which are to be discarded, and since the attainment of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*) alone constitutes the supreme liberation (*niḥśreyasa*), and since agency (*kartṛtva*) is also part of that very nature;
therefore, for those who have not attained that [nature], their desires being incomplete, there remains only omniscience.

Others who recite [this] are also refuted in the *Paramokṣanirāsakārikā*, where the superiority of Śiva and the [existence of] the feet and so forth are rejected in detail; it is not written here for fear of prolixity.
Now, in order to examine [the matter], he analyzes [it] by stating its specific definition:
The bound souls (paśus) are to be known as threefold: the sakala, the pralayākala, and the vijñānākala. Listen now to their characteristics in due order.
The meaning is very clear. He characterizes the *sakala* [state] in its entirety according to the sequence:

"One whose power of vision is obstructed by impurity (*mala*), who possesses the *ekalā* and other [powers] through the expansion of that [impurity], and who is connected with karma for the sake of experience—such a one is designated as *sakala*."
"The power of vision is obstructed by impurity"—here, the word "vision" (*dṛk*) should be supplied [with the verb], meaning "vision devoid of action.

"Possessing *kalā* and so forth" means for the sake of its expansion, that is, for the purpose of manifesting that power. By the word *kalā*, the thirty principles (*tattva*) characterized as the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) are denoted. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the remaining categories are included].

The gross body and so forth are grasped. For the sake of experience—that is, for the perception of pleasure, pain, and delusion—there is a connection with karma; it is not unmixed, because of transformation. Thus, through mutual assistance, there arises a state [of being] that has reached maturity, based upon the karma of a similar kind that is to be experienced.

The entire connection with action—consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion—is recited as it arises through various conditions, both as that which has already arisen and as that which is yet to arise. [The text] defines the one who is liberated at the time of dissolution:
"With the power of vision restrained as before, he is freed from the impurities of karma."
He who is fit for the future kalā through his karma is the *pralayākala*.

As before, the power of vision is obstructed by impurity; because the matured *karman*s have been experienced through fruition, that which is not yet matured does not grant its fruit, and the state of being a limited creator (*nirmātṛtva*) is maintained by the sustaining power (*kalā*). For that purpose, due to the ripening of *karman*, when the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) has arrived—
"Abandoned by *kalā*" means abandoned—that is, released—by *kalā* in the form of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*).

He is thus described as one who, through his karma having matured up to that limit, is fit for the connection with the *kalā* to be experienced; he is worthy of association with the subtle body that arrives at the time of the commencement of creation. And of him...
The *pralayākala*. He defines the *vijñānakevalin*: "Because his powers are obstructed by impurity (*mala*), his own vision and action are as if void;
he is recited in the Tantra as the third, by the name *vijñānakevala*."
"Empty kalpa" means that which is like the non-existent; this is the easy meaning of the verse.
They are to be known as being bound by one, two, or three [syllables] in reverse order. Furthermore, the complete [type] is of two kinds:
that with a subtle body and that with a gross body. Moreover, the one with a subtle body is also of two kinds.

[The soul] is either one that has not yet attained an external body or one whose external body has perished. And the one whose external body has perished is of two kinds: one possessing a subtle body while still bound by impurity (*mala*), karma, and *māyīya* bondage, and one who possesses the three bondages (*tribandhī*) during the stages of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and so forth to be described hereafter.

By some means, having become subject to two types of karma through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), even though the gross body has been shaken off, one remains bound because of possessing a subtle body; thus, there are two types of bondage until the attainment of absolute liberation (*vijñānakaivalya*), namely those involving the connection with *mala* and *māyā*. Furthermore, the possessor of a gross body is of two kinds.

The threefold bondage consisting of impurity (*mala*), action (*karman*), and illusion (*māyīya*) is destroyed through knowledge, yoga, renunciation, or by the exhaustion of karma through experience; yet,
due to the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), the body continues to be sustained like the whirling of a potter's wheel, and thus that latent impression persists.

He is one who possesses mere sensation and enjoyment, being bound by the impurity of *māyā*, and thus doubly bound. This very person, while possessing a gross body, attains immediate liberation through pure consciousness (*vijñānakaivalya*) due to the complete exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); however, due to the persistence of residual impressions, he attains liberation through pure consciousness (*vijñānakaivalya*).
The limit of attainment has been declared; one who possesses the two-fold bondage becomes one who has attained the state of having destroyed the external body.
He demonstrates their threefold abiding:
"Their sequential arrangement is in Māyā and so forth, and finally within the womb."
And the persistence [of the self] is characterized by bondage, because of the atom's omnipresence.

In the state of bondage, it is characterized by the connection with the *kalās* which are the effects of *māyā* for all [souls]; in the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), by the connection with *karman* suitable for that connection for the *kevalins*; and in the state of pure consciousness (*vijñāna-kevalin*), by the connection with the stainless (*amala*) which is devoid of both [the previous two]. This is due to the seed of metaphorical designation (*upacāra-bīja*).
It is seen. The meaning of the other words is easy to understand. The sages raise a doubt, thinking that if this is so, the statement that *māyā* touches the *vijñānakevalins* is inappropriate:
"For the bondage of the *vijñānakevala* individual souls consists solely of *mala*."
Since impurity is all-pervasive, how could there be a state of existence at the end of Māyā?
"Depending on Māyā, [the world] is to be withdrawn. The meaning of this verse is easy to understand. Īśvara said:

"O auspicious ones, O highly wise brahmins! Regarding that Pure Path (śuddhādhvan) previously mentioned, it is [to be understood] by way of its being about to be enjoyed and the other [impure path] by way of its having been enjoyed."
By implication, those established in the middle state are said to be "isolated in consciousness" (*vijñānakevala*);
indeed, those very ones, O bull among sages, are directly the "isolated in consciousness."
"Subsequently, by the will of Śiva, they shall belong to the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*).

Regarding "of the other [path]," namely the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*), the meaning follows from what has been stated for the purpose [of the teaching]. The remaining matter is easily understood from one and a half verses. O best of sages! Now, as for "the state of being possessed of parts" (*sakalatva*) directly...

Those who possess the dual state of *pralayākala* (the state of dissolution) and, subsequently, the single state of *pariśivatva* (the nature of supreme Śiva), yet whose individual characteristics of isolated liberation (*kaivalya*) remain concealed,

are the *vijñānakevalas*, as established by scripture (*āgama*). Furthermore, these bound souls (*paśus*), whose nature consists of *karman* and *māyā*, cannot be refuted by anyone and are established through reasoning (*yukti*).

Even those who are bound can exist as being devoid of karma alone, because it is accepted that the bondage consists of impurity distinct from that [karma]. For when something is distinct from the bondage of certain things, that thing constitutes their bondage even in its absence, just like shackles and the like. (p. 262)

Subsequently, when the impurity has reached full maturity, by the will of Śiva and through initiation (dīkṣā) into Śiva— which is without substratum— one attains the state characterized by supreme Śiva-hood; this is one's own specific nature as the Supreme Śiva,

which consists of the isolation of pure consciousness (vijñānakaivalya) that is free from even a trace of impurity designated by its own name, yet which is characterized by the state of a bound soul (paśutva).

Those of the Śiva class, whose consciousness consists solely of their own specific characteristics and who possess their own names, will attain immediate supreme liberation due to the ripening of their impurities (*mala*). However, those remaining—due to the dullness of the ripening of their impurities—will belong to the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*). This is because those abiding therein are free from impurity.

The meaning is that the state characterized by the isolation (*kaivalya*) of consciousness is not the definition of another Śiva; rather, it is only the Lords (*patayaḥ*) who, without the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of Śiva, cannot enter the pure path (*śuddhavartman*).

However, those whose impurities (*mala*) are unripened do not [attain this], because they are far from the purification provided by initiation; due to their state of being impure, they consist of nothing but impurity (*malamātra*).

Since it has been stated that "the state of being endowed with yoga" is characterized by the isolation of consciousness (*vijñānakaivalya*), those who possess the isolation of consciousness remain above *māyā* until the end of the ripening of impurities, at which point they attain pure knowledge (*viśuddhavidyā*).
He restrains [them]: by virtue of being the restrainer of the atom, Māyā [restrains] those on the Pure Path;
it is not the *sakalas* who are restrained, but rather the *vijñānakevalas*.

Those who are free from the impurity of worldly authority (adhikāra-mala) and are always permitted by the will of Śiva attain liberation through dissolution (pralaya-kaivalya) by means of their individual selves (aṇu) via their respective functions;
whereas those who possess all the kalās, having been endowed with the pure kalā, [attain it] through the pure path (śuddha-vartman) by virtue of being governed [by the Lord], just like Māyā.

This [state] belongs to Paraśiva alone—endowed with the pure *kalā* obtained through prior initiation (*pūrvadīkṣā*) and resulting in the isolation of consciousness (*vijñānakaivalya*)—and not to anyone else; thus, by virtue of being the regulator (*niyāmaka*) and the agent of necessity (*niyatikāraka*), all those who abide therein are reckoned as *sakala*. This refers to those who have attained the isolation of dissolution (*pralayakaivalya*) as a preliminary stage.
The pure aspect (*śuddhakalā*) is attained; however, among those innumerable *vijñānakevalas* who abide in the lower station of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*),
those whose impurities have matured manifest their own state of Śiva through initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Those who bear the name of the Supreme Śiva (Svāparaśiva), who abide on the pure path endowed with their own pure *kalā*, whose state of bondage (*paśutva*)— characterized by the concealment of absolute liberation— is [overcome], and who possess the knowledge of their own specific nature (*svalakṣaṇavijñānakevala*),
are established below Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) while still being affected by their own impurity (*mala*). But not...

It should be explained that they remain there as pure consciousness alone (*vijñānakevala*). For those who follow the pure path, their specific characteristic is being joined with *mala* alone; however, because they have transcended *mala*, [the impurity] for those in the state of *adhikāra-mala* is the *māyīya-mala* which, conjoined with *mala*, causes delusion.

Due to the complete cessation of the impurity of Māyā and the other [impurities], which act as obstacles to perception and action— just as the nature of the self as a person is obscured by the lack of right practice— the state of authority (adhikāra) arises in the Great Māyā; this is characterized by attachment to the enjoyment of the creation and other manifestations produced from latent impressions free from impurity.

Devoid of impurities and completely liberated from dependence at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), they will attain supreme liberation; until that point, they are always and at all times authorized by the will of Śiva and do not transgress the system of Śiva’s power (*śivaśaktitantra*). If this is so, [what then of those] situated within the sphere of *māyā*?

Fearing that the application performed by the Guru for the sake of attaining the experience of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) through initiation might be futile for those like us whose impurities (*mala*) have already matured, [it is said that] immediately after the purification of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) through the purification up to the level of *kalā* and *tattva* by means of initiation, even for such persons as ourselves...

Considering that liberation through dissolution (*pralaya-kaivalya*) is established prior to the purification of karma, immediately following the purification of karma, one attains liberation through supreme knowledge (*vijñāna-kaivalya*). Immediately thereafter,
through a practice that effects the absolute destruction of the impurities associated with its limbs, the attainment of the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*) occurs without further transformation.
Indicating that through the removal of those two kinds of impurities there is the attainment of pure consciousness alone (*vijñānakaivalya*), he demonstrates its accomplishment: (p.
266) "The reasoning for the accomplishment of those who possess pure consciousness is stated here."
Whether by initiation that purifies up to the level of the *tattvas* and *kalās*, or even through knowledge, [one attains liberation].
When karma is exhausted either through yoga, through enjoyment, or through renunciation, and when Māyā, which is dependent upon that [karma], is likewise exhausted;

Impurity alone is the distinguishing factor; therefore, those who possess only consciousness [attain liberation] through initiation that purifies up to the *kalā-tattva*, or even through knowledge. Since the distinction between *māyā* and the *puruṣa* has for the most part already been accomplished by the separation of *kalā* and the *puruṣa*, it concerns the distinction between *māyā* and the *puruṣa*.

Or else, through knowledge; or through yoga, by means of the mastery of the mind aided by the limbs beginning with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*); or through the fruit of the discrimination between *māyā* and the *puruṣa*;

or through renunciation, by surrendering all this to the Lord—that is, through the renunciation of action characterized by dedication to the Lord; or finally, through experience, [of that which has been] offered to the Lord.

The exhaustion of karma occurs either through the experience of the fruits of action or through enjoyment; the word "of karma" is to be supplied [to both], while the remainder is easy to understand. May [liberation] come about through knowledge and so forth, produced by the practice of the views of the Vedāntins, Sāṃkhyas, Kṣapaṇakas, Saugatas, Pāñcarātrikas, and Pādārthikas.

Anticipating the thought in one's heart, "What is the point of this isolation of consciousness (*vijñānakaivalya*) if it is distinguished by these [qualities]?", he says that for one who possesses such knowledge, that state does not abandon its state of being "all-encompassing" (*sakalatva*), because attachment and the rest are not eliminated through the mere practice of that [knowledge], since they have not been fully understood. Thus he states:
Even liberation (kaivalya) is not accepted for those who have abandoned the views of the Buddhists and others,
because even above the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), there is no complete exhaustion of karmas.
Those should be known as mere parts (kalā), since the conjunction of parts (kalā-yoga) is established therein.
Let the statement regarding the Vedāntins and others be made easy for each individual, even if it involves many syllables. He now demonstrates the accomplishment of dissolution alone:
In this very way, those who have attained perfection through the yoga of the individual soul (*aṇava-yukti*) are *pralayakevalas*.
Upon the withdrawal of the principles (*tattva*), either due to cosmic dissolution or the exhaustion of their karma,
they abandon their subtle and gross physical bodies, yet remain bound by the causes for future experience.
"Let those parts (kalās) associated with unripened karmas be dissolved;
that is, when the withdrawal or dissolution of the principles (tattvas) in their gross and subtle forms has occurred—
or rather, by the expression 'or rather' (athavā), the sense is that they are accomplished one by one— since karma is the cause for the persistence of the principles."

The phrase "due to the dissolution" (pralayāt) refers to the destruction resulting from the experience of pleasure and other such qualities produced by one's own transformation; "due to the exhaustion" (kṣayāt) means its cessation following the enjoyment by its own agent—the connection with the word "abandoned" (tyaktā) is clear. The meaning of the remaining words is evident.
He demonstrates all the supernatural powers (siddhis):
Possessing all its parts through the conjunction with *kalā*, it is twofold—subtle and gross.
This principle (*tattva*), beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth (*avanī*), is determined for each individual soul (*puṃs*).
The Lord bestows grace even upon the atoms of dissolution by His own will alone. (p.

269) The subtle *akalās* are the principles (*tattvas*) consisting of specific bodies determined for each individual soul (*puṃs*), beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth (*avanipañcama*), starting from Kapālīśa and ending with Kālāgni.

That reality, consisting of the common worlds, is the gross *kalā*, because it is an object of enjoyment even for other selves. Herein are included the common and uncommon [entities] such as the worlds, bodies, and so forth, which are described as such. The meaning of the first half [of the verse] is clear.

At that time, since the existence of a presiding teacher (guru) is impossible, Śiva—by His own will, like the case of the individual souls of consciousness (vijñānāṇu)—grants grace to even the atoms of dissolution (pralayāṇu) without a presiding teacher, through His own power alone, resolving: "May there be for you both liberation from bonds (pāśavimukti) and the manifestation of Śiva-nature. The Sages said:
Now, if it is held that here the atom receives assistance when there is an equilibrium of karma,
then since this equilibrium of karma occurs through experience, how can these [atoms] receive assistance?

In this regard, for the individual soul (*aṇu*) within the entire domain [of transmigratory existence], when there is an equilibrium of karma, it must be brought about by "ripening" (*pāka*) through the granting of the time for experience. Since that [ripening] is impossible for these *pralayākalas*, how can their liberation (*anugraha*) be desired? [The opponent argues: "The cause of liberation is the equilibrium of karma, occurring without the ripening of impurity (*mala*)."
It was said by those who establish contradictory statements before and after: "Is it indeed proper for this to be spoken?

My statement, though appearing consistent in another context, should have its meaning made contrary to my intended sense once the contradiction is recognized"—thus did the Lord indicate while [the discourse] was closely engaged.
In this regard, there is no motive for favoring [a disciple] based on their past actions;
rather, the ripening of impurity itself is the cause of such favor.

The meaning of the verse is easily understood. He states that otherwise there would be a contradiction: "Furthermore, those for whom there exist causes for future enjoyments, even when they are under Śiva’s grace, these are not objects of Śiva's [direct] concern; rather, they have reached maturity through their own karma."
If the equality of all karmas is the cause of grace,
then how, according to you, can there be grace for those who are solitary consciousnesses (*vijñānakevalins*)?
Furthermore, since causality must be stated as being due to the state of having performed an act of assistance (*anugraha*),
there is thus causality through assistance in all cases.
If there exists an equilibrium of karma for those whose future experiences are yet to come, and whose karmas remain unripened, they are not *pralayākalas*.
Objects of experience are [the means] for Śiva’s grace; however, since those whose karma has ripened— meaning those with fully matured karma— are indeed *sakala* (embodied) beings,
how then can there be grace for the *vijñānakevalas*, who by definition no longer depend upon karma?

The meaning is that it could not possibly occur in any way whatsoever. It refers to the equilibrium of the subtle karmas— which are difficult to perceive— belonging to one who has become a Vijñānākala, characterized by the state of an Avijñānākala, and which constitute his own fruit and subtle body.

Some teachers say that there is a cause for the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). [Others ask: "How can there be grace even for those who are liberated through knowledge (*vijñānakevala*)? This is refuted by the statement regarding the projection of Śiva;
for indeed, with respect to each individual person, there is knowledge, yoga, renunciation, and experience.
Furthermore, for those whose sole purpose has been fulfilled by isolation (kaivalya), how could there be an equality of mutual conjunction through non-opposition among those who have met again?
The second [type of conjunction] is characterized by the discrimination between Māyā and Puruṣa.

How could there be equality of karma for one who is solitary in his conduct as a rival consciousness (*pratibhaṭavijñāna*), or for one who is a mere fragment of consciousness (*vijñānakalā*)? Or, is there a need for that [equality] regarding all objects? To this he says:
"And for the *sakalas* (those with all coverings), equality of karma is not the cause in every respect."
Because, even when there is equality of karma, this applies only to those other karmas.
The command of the Supreme Lord remains uncontradicted even when other [means] are present;
for this [liberation] occurs through action, whether that action is equalized, ripened, or otherwise.
The sovereign power of the Lord approaches that very [object] for its destruction;
therefore, O best of sages, that [power] is not desired as being common even in the case of grace.
It is heard in scripture that the equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*), which exists everywhere for all beings, is neither the cause [of liberation] nor the motive for grace.
Because it does not grant the ultimate goal, even when the word "equilibrium of karma" is mentioned in a specific context, it is [repeatedly] stated again [to emphasize its insufficiency].

The intention is that [the author] has relied upon the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit (*kākatālīya-dhanyāya*). For this very reason, since it is inappropriate for the word here to have a different meaning, the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha, in his commentary on this *Kiraṇatantra* verse— "When a similar action has occurred, due to the power of another time..."— has stated "due to the ripening of time" (*kālapākavaśāt*) rather than [interpreting it otherwise].
Having explained that [the term] "same" means "for the sake of the transformation of impurities," it is said:
"He who does not rejoice in a benefit nor become angry at an injury toward all beings everywhere—he is called one liberated while living. Thus [it is stated in] the *Śrutaprakāśikā*.

The action of assistance and injury characterized by the fruit of karma was explained immediately following the section on equality (*samatva*). In the *Mṛgendra* as well, the two manifestations of karma were explained in that same way in the passage beginning with "equal" (*sama*). He now demonstrates the reason for the statement that "the equality of karma is not the cause. Therefore:

For this reason, even when there is equality of karma—that is, even when some karmas are equal—yet while other karmas remain unripe, the supreme Lord’s command, the power of Śiva (*śiva-śakti*), does not descend as a bestower of grace. To the question "Does it not? he says: "Contrary," and so forth.

It stands as that which prevents liberation from the obstruction caused by contrary [karmas], bestows other [experiences], grants the full enjoyment of the essence of liberation, and furthermore, grants the isolation of dissolution (*pralayakaivalya*). Here, the singular number is used for the aforementioned *karman* due to its identity with the genus. When there is equality—that is, when the time for the granting of experience is equal—then even in the case of the other [karmas].

And when all karma has been ripened, that sovereign power of the Lord, which effects concealment and its own cessation, approaches— that is, arrives at and intends— the cutting off of that entire karma,
as well as the granting of liberation through pure knowledge (*vijñānakaivalya*). For it is not otherwise.

For the sake of liberation: O bulls among sages! Since it is not desired that the equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*) be the cause for [attaining] grace (*anugraha*), the author examines the nature of *māyā* in the *Māyā-paṭala* and now defines the remaining nature of karma (*karmasvarūpa*) in order to demonstrate that very point once again through detailed analysis.

In this regard, karma is seen to be threefold: that which is to be experienced in the present life, that which is to be experienced in a future life, and, in brief, that whose time of experience is indefinite.

The meaning is easily understood through the statement of its characteristics. In that regard, he demonstrates karma whose fruition is experienced in the present life: "That which is accomplished through the power of mantras—such as longevity, yoga, or the removal of diseases—and yields its fruit in that very birth, is called 'dṛṣṭabhogya' (experienced in the present life)."

The *āyuryoga* is the practice that increases longevity; it is accomplished through *galucī* and other herbs, and is cultivated by the power of medicines such as *amṛtavalī*. Because an insentient object lacks inherent activity, [the result] occurs through the power of the mantra, directed toward which the deity is recited and meditated upon.

By its very power at the time of birth, it causes that body to persist for as long as one desires, thereby transgressing the scriptural rule that "a man has a lifespan of a hundred years" and making him the agent of results even beyond that; such [karma] is called "experienced through direct perception. He now shows that which is "to be experienced through the unseen" (adṛṣṭa):

In the Śiva-darśana, it is stated that karma is that which, at the end of the body, results in the enjoyment of sovereignty or the Avīci hell according to merit and demerit, and which is unseen yet to be experienced.

At the end of the body, upon the fall of the physical frame, those two— which consist of the fruits of merit and demerit, and which are to be experienced as the sovereignty of heaven and the Avīci hell characterized by human existence— are related to that; such karma, consisting of merit and demerit, is not seen [as leading to liberation] in the Śiva-darśana, the scripture of Śiva, but is rather to be experienced [within the cycle of rebirth].
The object of enjoyment has been explained. Now he shows that the object of enjoyment is not fixed:
"The horse-sacrifice and the killing of a twice-born both grant enjoyment when the time is fulfilled;
however, due to their conjunction, one [of them] was previously more powerful."
Just as at the beginning, so too in the middle of time,
the Aśvamedha sacrifice performed by someone at a certain time, through its ripening, bestows enjoyment;
it is prepared to grant him the enjoyment characterized by the attainment of heaven, and by that [sacrifice], even the killing of twice-born brahmins [is accounted for].

At that time, Kāla (Time) was ready to grant the experience characterized by the attainment of hell; this is because of the conjunction (*samuccaya*) of those two [karmas], and not because of a conjunction in the granting of experiences at the same time. Among them, however, one was previously more powerful.

The first [karma], impelled by the power of the Controller (*niyantṛ-śakti*) even though it is extremely remote, yields its fruit. The other, which is different from that, yields its fruit among the others of the remaining karmas, provided it is more powerful; as long as it is more powerful, it yields its fruit earlier and earlier. Because its time is indefinite, it is non-existent [in the sense of being ineffective] until then.
He for whom the time for giving is fixed at the same time as the enjoyment [of the fruit] is described as such. To the question, "What follows from this equality of power?
he says:
provided that there is the possibility of two [acts] having equal fruits pertaining to this world.
Due to their impotence, the divine power fell there upon those whose very selves were impotent.
Having accumulated other karma, however, by the force of one [karma], that [other] becomes powerful enough to be experienced at that very time; the other will come to fruition at another time.

When there is a possibility of two actions occurring— both pertaining to results in this very world (*aihika*), both connected to the fruit of existence, possessing equal strength, having their own respective functions, characterized by weakness and non-weakness respectively, having the nature of being neuter and masculine respectively, and having contradictory effects— the production of the fruit does not occur through the ripening [of karma].

When the primary [state] exists, there the sovereign power (*aiśvarī śakti*) belonging to Śiva falls upon both [aspects], becoming thoroughly purified. Therein, for one of the two, another action of the same kind is difficult to overcome even by Brahmā himself due to its inherent force.
By combining, joining, and assisting through the purposeful activity characterized by its own volition,

it then renders that karma powerful and determinate; otherwise, it may become indeterminate, or its fruition as a neuter state may be experienced at a later time, provided there is equality between the offense and the fruit of attaining a higher world.

In cases such as being dragged by two men while in love, it is the very power of Śiva’s concealment (tirodhāna-śakti) that has descended there, like the cruel power of a king. Having destroyed that [previous karma], it renders another karma—characterized by opposition and distinguished by its ripeness—to be experienced; thus he says:
Likewise, when the horse-sacrifice and the killing of a Brahmin— which pertain respectively to this world and the next—
occur simultaneously, the capacity of both is neutralized.
She ordains for the person another object of enjoyment equal to his karma;
like a royal decree regarding a woman sought by two men,
she destroys two conflicting actions and, being ripened, bestows the fruit of other conflicting karmas.

When a person is drawn by two opposing actions, they fall like a woman of ill repute; yet destiny impels that person again, and having lifted them up, it restrains them to the fruit of another action—
even in the case of an equality of equally powerful actions, such as the horse-sacrifice and the killing of a Brahmin.

Since the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*) has fulfilled its purpose by resulting in its own destruction, how could its own activity—characterized by liberation—be equal to that? The term *āmuṣmikayoḥ* refers to those two [powers] pertaining to this world (*amuṣmin*) or the next world (*āmuṣmika*). The meaning of the verse is easily understood.
He shows that when two [karmas] bound by strong [obstacles] are equal and have fixed times, their own manifestation occurs;
whereas in the case of two [karmas] that are not fixed in time, are ripe,
and are mutually opposed, that power [of the stronger karma] brings about the destruction of the other through its own emergence.
The destruction of those two is "tannāśaḥ" (the destruction of that); by means of that destruction, others follow as consequences (*anuṣaṅga*).

This is the meaning of the verse regarding good conduct (*sucarita*). Furthermore, this is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*); for even when there is similarity in being of the same class, there is a difference between the respective fruits of heaven and the Brahma-world, and likewise between the respective fruits of Raurava and Avīci, despite their commonality.

Because they are contradictory, it is destructive, like the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). But how can that which is performed later be equal to that which was performed earlier?
That is incorrect; for in the case of agriculture and similar activities, such [later action] results from the rapid ripening [of the effects].

It is incorrect to argue that because the bestowal of equal fruits is observed, the power of the Lord does not fall [into contradiction] even when there is no [corresponding] effort; for just as even an archer such as Arjuna, though infinitely well-trained,
does not always strike down with his own arrows the collection of weapons like arrows discharged by his enemies, but rather only when—
That which results from the injury of one's own body occurs through opposition to the karma of longevity;

at that very moment, because of that very opposition, it cuts [the life-span]. Thus, when there is such opposition, the Blessed One employs his own power, thereby demonstrating the mastery over all karma.
When all other karma is completely destroyed,
then, through the destruction of karma, the absolute isolation (kaivalya) of consciousness shall belong to the person.

When all other actions have become equalized, the power of Śiva belonging to that one whose actions are equalized becomes the obstructer and destroyer of all action. Then, from that cause—the destruction of action—there would be for the person the isolation of pure consciousness (*vijñānakaivalya*), but not liberation (*mukti*). Thus.
He concludes by stating that the ripening of impurity (*mala*) is the cause for the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*), which brings about the equilibrium of karma:
"Upon the destruction of karma, [the ripening] of impurity also [occurs], with [karma] acting as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) in its maturation."
The power Unmīlinī, whose nature is that of grace, descends.

[Objection: But surely, for those who have transcended action (*vikarmin*)—the *vijñānakevalins*—there is no ripening of impurity (*mala*), according to the principle that [only] mixed [karma] undergoes transformation. [Response: True.
However, when karma is exhausted through the practice of knowledge (*vijñāna*), yoga, renunciation (*sannyāsa*), or through experience (*bhoga*), that [impurity] is dependent upon that karma.

"The state of being an enjoyer [belongs] to the body and so forth; with their destruction, that state of being an enjoyer perishes. O twice-born ones, even the impurity (mala) becomes ripened through the power of auxiliary factors (sahakārin). Thus it has been said. To the question, "What should be remembered regarding forgetfulness? he says: "That" (seti).
Even from the destruction of karma, by means of the subtle body which is the fruit of karma, [the impurity persists] through the influence of auxiliary factors.

"Having placed its own latent impression (*vāsanā*) within the impurity (*mala*), it goes to dissolution," according to the scripture. This means that prior to the destruction of its own [impurity] through the fruition of its own effects, even when the karma whose latent impressions have been destroyed by itself has reached maturation (*pāka*), there is the dissolution of the atoms (*pralayāṇu*).

O Paurṇāka, even though karma exists, it remains in its entirety throughout all states; yet, by the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by itself after the enjoyment has been experienced, and because it is mixed with the direct experience of the fruits of various karmas, it becomes manifest during the ripening characterized by degrees such as "more intense."

The power (*śakti*) of consciousness, which possesses the transformation of impurity (*malapariṇati*), bears the fruit of beholding the state of Śiva; or rather, it is averted from favoring the non-conscious (*acid*) and inclined toward favoring the conscious (*cit*). For this very reason, it consists of that [consciousness’s] grace.
This power possesses its own effect, characterized by the manifestation of liberation through that [grace]. [This occurs] through an intense degree of maturation (*tīvratara-pāka*) and so forth.
Because it conforms to the nature of impurity, it falls with a well-defined intensity and so forth;
[the author] intends that "may fear of saṃsāra and attachment to liberation arise in him," while some have explained that it falls due to the destruction of certain karmas.

Since the word "auxiliaries" (*sahakāriṇaḥ*) would otherwise be redundant— given that the power (*śakti*) which destroys all bonds does not fall for the sake of that [bond] alone— it flashes forth that this [position] is incorrect. In that regard, even for all [beings], due to the ripening of extremely intense impurity (*malaparipāka*) in some instances, [this occurs] with respect to the entirety of their karma.

When [the body] falls once it has ripened, by the mere act of falling, the persistence of the body continues by relying on the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of that karma which has been destroyed; thus, even in the case of *sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*, which consists in the destruction of all bonds, [this process occurs].
The body remains for some time due to the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), like the whirling of a potter’s wheel.

This has been explained in detail in the *Aśuddhavidyā-tattva-paṭala* of the *Mataṅga*. In some cases, one falls [into a lower state] even when karma is not yet fully ripened, due to the sluggishness of the ripening of impurity (*mala*). Now, as for that which is unripened...
How does its destruction occur? Truly, having reached maturity through the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the mantra, it perishes.
As it has been said: "But how can unripened karmas be experienced simultaneously? Unripened karmas [are experienced] by the power of the efficacy of the mantra. [At] the improper time...

By the principle of the production of flowers, [the soul] attains ripeness; through this body, it enjoys [fruits] simultaneously, being possessed of sovereign power (*prākāmya*). Also, in the *Kiraṇatantra*:
"The karma pertaining to many births is burnt by the atoms, like a seed."
"Even that which is yet to come is restrained by him through the enjoyment of the power of his teeth. Thus [it is said].
He demonstrates that for all [beings], this occurs immediately following the descent of the power: "As soon as she has descended, the regulating power of impurity ceases;
when that has ceased, [the state of] the Great Self [is attained]."
Detachment from the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra arises quickly,
and a desire to behold the lotus feet of Śambhu also arises.
"When shall I behold the Lord of Gods? When shall I be liberated from this bondage? Who indeed will show me Śambhu?"—such thoughts arise within him.
Thus, when the Lord bestows grace upon one who is terrified of *saṃsāra*,
as soon as that person has fallen into the power (*śakti*) of Śiva— which is conjoined with passion for Śiva and is not subject to a womb—
that [power] effects stability in *saṃsāra* and prevents its cessation; it does not, however, do so by means of an initiation that obscures the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

Because the impurity (*mala*) is yet to be described, the powerful impurity of *śakti-mala*—such a power of the Lord—is withdrawn. When that has ceased, the transmigratory existence remains as if non-existent, because even the passion that produces the power of *saṃsāra* exists only as if it were non-existent; this is the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) for the Great Soul.
The meaning of the passage ending with "the Lord [is] the purifier of that [person], through dispassion," etc., is easy to understand and thus easily accomplished.
To the question "How does He bestow grace? He says:
"In accordance with their fitness, by means of [His grace] which is pregnant with compassion."
Or whomsoever the Supreme Lord purifies by means of his authority.

The Supreme Lord Śiva, acting as the locus [of grace], beholds with a glance whose essence is compassion and which rests upon the sense of smell; having looked with that glance— which conforms to the fitness of the soul and is suited to qualities such as dispassion— and having subsequently fashioned [for them] an authority endowed with power.

It is not the case that initiation (*dīkṣā*), exposition (*vyākhyā*), consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), or the authority over the measures (*mātrā*) occurs together with the duty of service to the Guru or with living in his company; for this would contradict the statement to be made later, "whomsoever [it purifies]. Indeed, it purifies—that is, it cleanses—even one who is lowly by virtue of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*).
As it is stated in the Mataṅga:
"The Lord is declared to be the benefactor everywhere, unimpeded by obstacles,
for the entire multitude of beings from Brahmā down to the level of stationary objects."

"He acts without dependence, bestowing upon even the minute atom a strength equal to his own"—this is stated in the *Yomavyāptistava* as well. "The bliss of liberation, which grants fullness, is not joined with the restriction of birth; rather, salutations to Him who bestows happiness upon all beings. (p. 289)

Regarding the word "that": he says that this is known as *dīkṣā*—that power of the nature of grace which obstructs the movement of impurity (*mala*), by which the power of that impurity is destroyed; that is *dīkṣā*, the ritual action of Śambhu.

By that power, which consists of grace and takes the form of the vision of the Seer of Consciousness (*cid-ṛṣi*) and so forth, the threefold state of the self’s power of consciousness—which had previously encompassed all objects—is obstructed; thus it is called the "obstructress" (*nirodhikā*).
Among the powers of impurity (*mala*), which consist of the non-functioning of the infinite powers of the individual souls (*puruṣa*) and their capacities, and so forth—[it is this power among them].

The power belonging to that [individual soul], which is purified by the descent of Śiva’s power (*śaktipāta*) consisting of grace toward consciousness (*cidanugraha*), is diminished. Now, one might object: since the attribute of the impurity (*mala*), namely its nature as an obstructer, is innate—just as upward flaming is innate to fire—it follows that when that [attribute] ceases, the impurity itself must also perish.

[Objection: If one were liberated, it would follow that everyone is liberated. [Reply: That is not so, because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to cases such as *kālikā* [mold]. For instance, there is the power (*śakti*) residing in rice grains characterized by being covered by husks, which belongs to those [grains] that are still alive, and there is the absence of power (*aśakti*) belonging to the object [of ripening] when it is connected with *kālikā* [mold] or a conch-shell [acid]. Thus, [the reason] is inconclusive.

Through the destruction of [impurities] such as *nakālika*, the non-destruction [of the Self] occurs; by means of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) consisting of mantra, the destruction—characterized by cessation and a transformation of state—is brought about of the impurity (*mala*), which has the nature of being an obscuration of power (*śakti*), just as fire has the nature of burning. Consequently, at that time, there is a change of form.
The transformation will occur; thus, there is no existence in its own essential nature.

Although the nature of the power of impurity (*mala-śakti*)—characterized by obscuration—is transformed into another nature characterized by cessation, even when it has become the essential nature [of the Self], it is as if the Person were separated from disease.

Because of the obstruction of its power (*śakti*), although it is impossible to move [the Self] to another location due to its omnipresence (*vibhutva*) in both states, it is said that it is "separated from impurity" (*malaviśliṣṭa*). If this were so, then because the nature of the Person (*puruṣa*) is characterized by immutability (*anivṛtti-lakṣaṇa*)—that is, by cessation—there would be a transformation into a different nature; thus, [he would become] insentient (*jaḍatva*).

Otherwise, there would be a modification of the elements (*bhūta-vikāra*). However, no modification whatsoever is observed in the ether (*ākāśa*) due to the cessation of its temporal functions. Likewise, when the capacity of the object—which corresponds to the *puruṣa*—ceases, no destruction of its essential nature, such as color or form, is ever observed.
Just as the fruit of the *kataka* tree, such as *meghaja* and others,
even when merely cast into water while its natural impurities have not yet been consumed, is observed to effect the cessation of turbidity in the water; indeed,
is there not some nature in the water that is distinct from this other nature of the water?

Taking up its own nature, one should cast it elsewhere; by that, only the turbidity is destroyed. Just as the eye, through the removal of a cataract by means of collyrium and so forth, regains its power, so too does the capacity of that [consciousness] arise upon the cessation of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

What is called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is that which manifests as existing without being altered by its own power; no modification whatsoever is observed through the imposition of another intrinsic nature. Just so, since the state of being a noble one (*āryatva*) is not produced by the presence of impurity (*mala*), it lacks the status of being an adventitious intrinsic nature.

By means of their cessation, it brings about the manifestation of one's innate Śiva-nature, which consists of omniscience and is free from modification; thus, initiation is not a cause of transformation as will be explained hereafter. As it has been said in the *Bhogakārikās*:

And because it attains the manifestation of its own nature, it is neither a modification nor destroyed. Now, one might object: even with respect to impurity (*mala*), that state of being veiled—which is expressed by the terms "state of bondage" (*paśutva*) and "non-manifestation"—is not distinct from the ignorance (*ajñatva*) characterized by non-agency and non-knowerhood; therefore, how can there be an innate, extremely pure Śiva-nature apart from that impurity?

Existence as a single essence together with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not tenable because it is contradictory. And so, casting [this view] aside, the Blessed Matanga [says]: "The state of Śiva would be utterly pure; the state of the bound soul (*paśu*) would be utterly impure."
O Blessed One, how can oneness be understood from this contradiction?

Thus, because the innate nature (*sahaja-svabhāva*) cannot be revoked, ignorance does not exist by way of revoking Śiva-hood. If, on the other hand, Śiva were to exist together with ignorance, then impurity (*mala*) would be entirely ineffective therein; for [the nature of] impurity is Śiva-hood.

Nothing other than the disruption [of the soul's nature] is perceived as having any causal efficacy. If it is argued that impurity (*mala*) is efficacious by way of removing the state of being Śiva, that is incorrect;
for since it would involve the disruption of the innate nature, it would follow that the Self itself does not exist. To this, it is replied:
Just as water, though contrary to fire, possesses a natural characteristic of coolness and yet, when joined with fire, performs its own contrary effect characterized by burning;
so too does that Śiva-nature, when joined with the contrary impurity (mala).

Since an action characterized by cognition, which has an object as its domain, produces its own contrary effect by being established within itself, there can never be, in any way or for anyone, the existence here of an innate nature; otherwise, it would follow that the entity itself is non-existent. As it is said in the *Mataṅga*:
Water, though opposed to fire, burns when joined with it at that very moment;
O tiger among sages, because of its existence, such opposition is not tenable here.
And it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Just as the state of being gold exists latent within that very ore,
so too should the state of Śiva be known as latent within the individual soul (*pudgala*)."

Now, it might be argued that just as the nature of coldness, characterized by coolness, when conjoined with impurity, performs an effect contrary to itself—namely, the activity of agency characterized by knowledge and action due to its lack of awareness—is this not an inconsistent analogy? For it has been stated that [the soul] produces an effect that is opposed to its own nature. (p. 295) This is not an inconsistent example.

If it has been stated that [ignorance] is characterized by the cognition of burning, then when it is stated that there is likewise ignorance in the case of the subject of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*), one might object that this is inconsistent; therefore, it must be said that it performs its function as characterized by an obscuration. This is true. Just as...
Water, which is cold by nature, through contact with fire becomes the cause of an effect characterized by its own opposite,
namely heat; thus, figuratively speaking, it provides an opportunity for fire to produce its own effect— characterized by burning— upon objects such as the body.

It is said that [fire] performs an effect characterized by burning. Likewise, Śiva-hood—which has as its essential nature the performance of action characterized by the perception of all objects—becomes the performer of an effect characterized by limited knowledge and action (which are contrary to itself) due to its connection with impurity (mala); this occurs because the nature of impurity is characterized by being an obscuration.

Since it provides the opportunity for the effect characterized by its own obscuration to be produced within the entity, one may figuratively say that "it produces the effect characterized by obscuration" at that time; thus,
the example is not inconsistent with omniscience.

The state of Śiva, characterized by universal agency, exists inherently within one's own self; whereas the opposite of that, characterized by the absolute absence of Śiva-nature, is the state of non-agency caused by ignorance, which is conditioned by impure objects and exists only with respect to impure objects. Thus, because their respective domains are distinct, [the two] do not [contradict each other].

The contradiction between the state of being Śiva and the state of being a bound soul (paśutva) is characterized by their mutual non-coexistence. Even for you who rely on the shadow of Sāṃkhya, if the Puruṣa is pure, how can there be ignorance (avidyā) consisting of a contrary apprehension regarding him? Or, if purity resides in his own self while the contrary [apprehension] pertains to the object, [then...]

Regarding what you have stated— that there is no contradiction here because "practice" (*pratipatti*) and "ignorance" (*avidyā*) have different objects, since "everything is erroneous with respect to its objective support (*ālambana*), but not in any way with respect to itself"—
that is equal in the other case as well; the objection applies to both, for the fault exists in both instances.
Because the refutation is equal [to the objection], one should not be further questioned. Enough of this;
for fear of prolixity, let us follow the main subject, having moved beyond the digressions that have followed upon the primary topic. That action, which consists of the power of Śiva, is Śāmbhavī.

For the sake of bestowing grace upon all, initiation— divided into categories such as the Śāmbhavī and others— is designated as "initiation" (dīkṣā) because its nature consists of the giving and the destruction [of bonds]. Since grace cannot be accomplished without the relationship between teacher and disciple, that relationship, in turn, cannot exist without Śiva.
He says that it is indeed so:
"In the discipline of the one to be favored and likewise in the compassion of the one who favors, Śiva is the agent; the conjunction of these two is very difficult to obtain."

In that regard, the state of being Śiva which is to be manifested in the one to be favored—that is, the disciple—is "discipline" (*vinaya*) according to the specific method. The Guru, being essentially identical with that [Śiva], acts as the impeller toward that discipline and thereby establishes a relationship characterized by the one to be favored. This pertains to the one who favors (*anugrāhaka*).

The compassion of the Guru, who manifests that state of Śiva, is indeed *kāruṇya* (compassion); the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is applied here because the word begins with the group of four vowels (*caturvarṇādi*).

And through that compassion—even when there is a desire for grace expressed by the word [itself]—the Guru becomes a witness and, by means of that grace, effects the connection with the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) for the disciple.

Otherwise, without the impulsion of Śiva, their union—their relationship characterized by the recipient of grace (*anugrāhya*) and the bestower of grace (*anugrāhaka*)—is extremely difficult to attain; it is impossible to obtain even with great effort. He concludes:
The descent of power (śaktipāta) is to be inferred by these uninterrupted signs from those great souls;
this initiation is not [attained] by those who have not been purified by the descent of power.
Other Śiva-dharmas, established through scripture and other means by the teachers,
are to be examined within the Śiva-scripture for the sake of [determining] the descent of grace (śaktipāta) upon the disciples.
When these aforementioned signs of detachment (*vairāgya*) and so forth are uninterrupted and firmly established,
then— supplying the words "the power of fire at the end of the year"— the other constituent elements [of the ritual] are easily accomplished because they are simple to perform.

The phrase "for the sake of knowing the descent of power" (*śaktipātajñānārtham*) is to be supplied [as the purpose]. Since this is performed by Mataṅga, Bharadvāja, and others at a time close to the attainment of initiation (*dīkṣā*), it is beyond doubt that even those Śiva-dharmas established by the Vedas and other authorities must be examined. This [examination] is not restricted to a specific time.

The meaning is as follows: the ripening of impurity (*malaparipāka*) has enjoyment (*bhoga*) as its cause; inseparable from that is *śakti*; the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is inseparable from that; initiation (*dīkṣā*) is inseparable from that; and liberation (*mukti*) is inseparable from that. He states that initiation performed while the impurity remains unripened is futile:
"This [initiation] is for the purpose of destroying the lack of devotion, the state of being non-twice-born, cruelty, fearlessness, or the falling away from ritual action;
such is the command of the Supreme Lord."
Cruel means devoid of compassion; fearless means having no fear in performing what is prohibited by the Śiva scriptures.
Non-devoted means lacking faith in the Śiva Āgamas and their prescribed rites, and being devoid of devotion to the devotees of Śiva. And devotion is...
It is a specific kind of knowledge characterized by the penetration of fitness (*yogyatā*). As it has been said:
"Furthermore, even another [state] characterized by the penetration of fitness, which is established here as devotion (*bhakti*), is also a constituent part of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*)."
"Non-twice-born" (*advija*) refers to one who has not been granted the purity of the twice-born status through special initiation; such a person is devoid of the state of being twice-born.

Even a Brāhmaṇa who lacks this [initiation] is, in relation to a pure twice-born, a Śūdra, as stated in the *Kāmika-śruti*: "Even pure Brāhmaṇas and others would become Śūdras. Therefore, having initiated him [who was previously a Śūdra], the Guru—

"One should perform initiation for oneself once again," according to the *Kāmika-śruti*; furthermore, because it is heard there that even a Śūdra who is not [originally] pure attains the status of a purified twice-born (*dvija*) through that [initiation]. As it is stated in the *Skanda-kālottara*:
