"O Six-faced One, burn the two born of the Śūdra caste with fire; having established their true Śūdra status, perform the sixteen rites. Once they have attained the state of actual Brahmins, thereafter perform the initiation. Thus it is said.

"Devoid of ritual action": that which ought to be performed immediately thereafter has fallen away. Initiation, which is my command and takes the form of my power, when performed by preceptors out of greed or for the sake of knowledge and such, destroys [the disciple].

This means that, just as the initiation of Śūdras—such as the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*) and so forth—is fruitless because they lack the entitlement to recite [the Vedas], so too [initiation given for wrong reasons] becomes ineffective.

Thus, in this manner, the command-power (*ājñā-śakti*) belonging to the Supreme Lord, associated with Paramaśiva—sustained by the speech arising from His mouth and having issued forth [to] my Guru Anantāgra; such is the intended meaning. Now, having previously seen that which is distinct from this...

Having determined that a person has been purified by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and has received initiation, there should be no further concealment (*tirobhāva*) consisting of the transgression of rules (*samayollaṅghana*). Yet such concealment is observed; therefore, it is true that the descent of power is not the cause of grace (*anugraha*). That power, falling upon a soul whose impurities have ripened, [acts as grace].
Having performed the self-contemplation that effects the destruction of impurities, it ceases from its own activity like a flash of lightning;
for this matter is established by logic itself, as it is impossible to perform again what has already been done.
Even though [the cessation] is seen [to be momentary], the attainment of liberation is undoubtedly certain because of the transgression of the [limited] time [of the body]. To illustrate:

Even one who has been duly initiated may, at some time, by the force of fate or human agency, have his universal self concealed from the universal self; such a person attains liberation through expiation. That which results from the transgression of the rules of expiation is itself the characteristic of that expiation.
Transgression of the rules (samaya) in this very context is said to result in a hundred years of servitude, like the fruit of optional rites that acts as an obstacle to the fruit of initiation;
this being so for one who has been purified by penance in the manner described.

"Pure destiny is proclaimed" (p. 303): according to this scripture, for one who has been initiated, there occurs the manifestation of primordial Śiva-nature preceded by the cessation of bonds, arising from the purification of the locus of the intellect through the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as initiation and the previously mentioned scriptural injunctions.

Through the application of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) residing in the intellect— which is the cause of the purification of the substratum consisting of the person characterized by the [auspicious] marks, and which prevents the fall [of consciousness] through the recitation of mantras and meditation—
there occurs the initiation (*dīkṣā*) that effects the purification of the self into the state of "I am Śiva," as proclaimed in the stages of Śiva-yoga.
The purification (*saṃskāra*) that arises is characterized by the manifestation of the state of Śiva;

thus, unlike the purifications of Vedic Sāṃkhya and Yoga, it does not have the body, mind, and so forth as its locus. Rather, it has consciousness (*caitanya*) as its locus. Therefore, liberation, which is the fruit of initiation (*dīkṣā*), is [the realization] of that which has consciousness as its locus.

One who is hidden receives [initiation]; thereafter, initiation, accompanied by its own specific characteristics, does not fail to yield its own fruit—thus, there is nothing inconsistent. Nor should it be questioned why power (*śakti*) is not suspected of being a cause of transgression (*pratyavāya*), for it should be understood that this is merely a figurative designation of its dullness (*mandatva*).
Those learned in the Śiva scriptures maintain that the very power of grace proceeds toward that end by way of concealment;
this is not achieved through yoga alone as the Sāṃkhyas hold, nor through renunciation alone as the Vedāntins hold, nor through human effort alone as the followers of Jaimini hold.
Anticipating the doubt that liberation might be innate, he says:
"Initiation alone shall release one from bonds and bestow the state of Śiva upon the individual soul;
that which bestows [this] consists of knowledge and action, and is none other than His own power."
But there is never an arising [of the self] even from the assumption of another location.

The preceding matter is clear. Immediate initiation for liberation (*asadyo-nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*) consists in the manifestation of Śiva-nature through the severance of impurities (*mala*) and so forth by one who is not yet the universal Self (*asarvātman*). [This applies to] karma whose effects have already begun (*ārabdha-kārya-karma*).
The favor bestowed by the Blessed One through the restriction of enjoyments must likewise be made abundant by means of instruction; thereafter, in that which remains after initiation,
it should be practiced daily according to tradition as the cause for the severance of impurities and so forth.

And because even knowledge, for the sake of manifesting the state of Śiva, is invariably connected with action by way of contemplation (*anusandhāna*); the meaning is that the means such as knowledge and so forth are proclaimed as being distinguished by the teachings of the Śiva-āgamas, and not all [means] are so. This refers to the remaining [aspects of] knowledge.
Furthermore, [the author] will refute the status of being a cause; for once the Lord has bestowed His own state of Śiva-hood through initiation, He would no longer be Śiva Himself. As they say:
"If Sadāśiva were to bestow His own infinite powers upon Ananta..."
"May he then attain the auspicious and most effective power that bestows [all] things.

For this purpose, it is said "by means of this gift," and so forth; for "gift" (*dāna*) is merely a name (*nāma*), a verbal designation, which is essentially composed of knowledge and action, just like one's own power (*śakti*).

For those such as the *vijñānakevalas* and others, there occurs a gradual manifestation of their own inherent nature—characterized by omniscience and so forth—which consists in the cessation of all bonds through one, two, or three characteristics; this is figuratively called the "bestowal of Śiva-hood" by Śiva upon persons. [Objection: But surely... [without... *(Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a philosophical commentary on Kashmiri Śaivism, likely discussing the process of liberation for various classes of souls. The final portion of the sentence is incomplete, but the translation reflects the available text.)*

It is true that there is a transgression of the primary meaning of the words intended for a specific purpose. However, the inherent nature of the self is not always manifested by itself because it is obscured. Just as one who is temporarily covered does not remove the covering by himself, so too a person is not established as being able to remove his own ignorance merely by himself, like a blind man.
It is like the power of vision when covered by a cataract; rather, it is like an oculist who surpasses that [natural vision].
Here too, the Lord alone is the agent of liberation, and this has been elaborated upon in the *Patipatala*.
However, it is not as if he bestows another state at that very moment, as is the case for the followers of the Pāśupata and other systems. (p. 307)

For those who maintain that [the soul] arises from Śiva, even its arising does not bring about the exclusion of supreme liberation as it does for the proponents of origination (samutpattivādins). Now, if there is arising, then through that penetration (āveśa) there is eternality and sovereignty.
There is no existence of an example for proving the transference of qualities.

The detailed refutation of [theories such as] origination, transmigration, possession, and identity through such passages as these is to be understood from that very source. Some, falling under the shadow of Viśiṣṭādvaita accepted by certain Vedāntins and having ceased from the teachings of the Śiva Āgamas, [assert] identity with Śiva alone.

The statement that "liberation [is attained]" is indeed rendered fruitless; for, by way of such an indication, the non-metaphorical identity with Śiva—which is denoted by the term "identity with Śiva" (*śivatādātmya*)—is being refuted, since that very term "identity with Śiva" is not [the intended meaning here]. However, the term "identity with Śiva" [does not refer to that].
The claim that "union with Śiva" is what is signified [by the term] is incorrect; for it is stated even here in the *Paramokṣanirāsakārikā*—due to its formlessness:
"Regarding the transmigration of that which is formless, there are neither worlds nor investigators."
The transition of the insentient into the insentient is logical for one who maintains the doctrine of transformation.

Thus says the Śruti. Furthermore, in the *Mṛgendravṛtti*, it is explained that for two formless entities, conjunction does not mean physical contact (*saṃśleṣa*). Now, one might object: "The term 'identity with Śiva' (*śivatādātmya*) denotes inherence (*samavāya*) with Śiva.
That is incorrect; for [inherence] belongs to two categories of things related by inherence, as is the case for the Logicians (*Tārkikas*).

In the relationship of the locus (*ādhāra*) and the located (*ādheya*), there is no lack of identity with that nature; rather, it is precisely the state of being inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*) as that very nature.

Otherwise, it would be impossible to speak of it in any other way. The Lord will refute this in the "Examination of the Category of Bondage" (*pāśapadārthaparīkṣā*). If that is so, one might ask: "What follows from that?"—but this need not be said.

Because inherence (*samavāya*) is never perceived as having either that nature or its opposite, and because those two natures always exist [in their respective substrata]: Śiva is omniscient, while the bound soul (*paśu*) is limited in knowledge;
Śiva is not the experiencer of pleasure and pain, whereas the bound soul is the experiencer thereof—and so forth, [these are] mutually [distinct].
Pierced; established by direct revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*); all is divided. Now, [it may be argued:
"The identity with Śiva (*śiva-tādātmya*) is indeed the state of being the manifestor and the manifested (*vyañjaka-vyaṅgya-bhāva*) denoted by the word 'Śiva'.
That is incorrect, because it is being refuted in the section on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-paṭala*). Now, [it may be argued: "Identity with Śiva..."

The relationship of pervader and pervaded expressed by the word "Śiva" is untenable in the state of Sāra (the essence). According to the *Mataṅga-śruti*, consciousness (*saṃvit*) is to be placed within the body characterized by the head as the eternal attribute of the intellect (*citi*). Thus, the attribute of consciousness resides in a single part of the locus (*dharmiṇi*), which is the power of contemplation (*kalayā*).

If it is said that [the soul] is designated as an individual by virtue of being the seed of metaphorical usage, then in the absence of a restrictive principle, if that were asserted even in liberation, the postulation of another Śiva pervading that [liberated] Śiva would be logically consistent; thus, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is unavoidable. Now, one might object: "But is there not a co-extensiveness with Śiva, expressed by the term 'identity with Śiva' (*śivatādātmya*)?"

That is incorrect. Since that statement is poorly formulated—being merely smeared with dharma—the simultaneous reading of "equal status" (*sahapada*) does not hold together. [Rather,] it is the state of Supreme Śiva-ness (*paraśivatva*), which possesses equal pervasion with Śiva, is similar to Śiva-Śakti, consists of the supreme six qualities, and is proclaimed as the supreme, unsurpassed liberation.

Because of our descent into this philosophical system, [we hold that] the state of being in a single flavor (*samarasībhāva*) with Śiva, which is inseparable from the state of being in a single flavor with Śakti, is the manifestation in every way of one's own power (*svaśakti*). Having specifically designated that state there by the word "identity" (*tādātmya*), what [more remains]?

This is not a valid refutation, because it involves [the fallacy of] having a substratum (*sāspadatvāt*). Now, if you say that what is designated by the term "identity with Śiva" is actually a merging with Śiva (*śivasāṃkarya*), that is incorrect, because it would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all things are non-figuratively one;
furthermore, the Vedāntin would be victorious, as he maintains that the omniscient Lord is distinct from all [else].

And because of this analysis, the Blessed Rāmakaṇṭha, having exposed that very fault, has refuted such confusion. [An objection: "Is it not the case that what is designated by the term 'identity with Śiva' (śivatādātmya) is union with Śiva (śivasāyujya), characterized by a relationship consisting in making Śiva the object [of cognition]? That is incorrect."

Because it takes as its object only that which consists of all categories (*padārtha*), it is appropriately joined with all categories. And let this system of ours have Śiva alone as its counter-correlative (*vipakṣa*). Now, one might object:
"The state of being Śiva denoted by the term 'identity with Śiva' (*śivatādātmya*) is not inherent Śiva-hood [itself], because [it arises] from the manifestation of Śiva."
The claim that Śiva-hood arises from the manifestation of Śiva’s qualities within oneself due to some excellence is untenable; for if that were the case,

then the transfer of Śiva’s qualities, the possession by Śiva, or the presiding over one by Śiva would inevitably occur either during the state of another (the opponent's view) or during the state of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
Because Śiva is not something that must be made so, His state of being Śiva does not arise from Himself; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress.

It has been stated that the state of being Śiva, which is inherently latent within, is manifested through initiation (*dīkṣā*). As it says in the *Sarvajñānottara*: "Just as copper, once its essence is perfected, attains the state of gold."
In the same way, the self, through its connection with knowledge, attains the state of Śiva.
Thus, the reflection of Śiva and so forth are set aside as impossible, and we shall conclude here. Now, one might object:

since the scripture states that the "likeness to Śiva" denoted by the term "identity with Śiva" (*śivatādātmya*) is indeed the *jāti* (universal), it ultimately results in [the conclusion] that the *jāti* is Śiva himself. If this were so, then [the relationship between] Śiva and Śiva’s power (*śiva-śakti*), which is characterized by Śiva...

Our own philosophical system alone is entirely consistent with the fact that the state of Supreme Śiva— characterized by the six qualities, described as the supreme, unsurpassed, and unique self-definition— is the complete manifestation in every respect of one's own power (sva-śakti). This is so even in the case of the terms "union with Śiva" (śiva-yoga), "dissolution into Śiva" (śiva-laya), and "attainment of Śiva" (śiva-gati).
Because it has that as its purpose. As it is said in the *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra* (p.
313): "In both the Sakala and Niṣkala [states], it is everywhere the same;
that is declared to be sovereignty (*sārvajya*), which is similarity of form (*sārūpya*) and equality of embodiment (*mūrtitulyatā*)."
In the *Mṛgendra*: "Sovereignty is imperial rule; enjoyment is one's own bliss as well as that of another;
being beyond bonds, it is great and eternal; dissolution is the attainment of identity with That."
When one remains in a state of non-duality, having well-bestowed the *niśvāsakārikā* upon the excellent *paśu* and others, that is called its "going.

But how can there be going for the All-pervading? It is metaphorically said that one attains the state of *unmanā* and *śivatva*. Connection is what is called "going"; but how can there be going for the All-pervading?

Beginning from Śuddhavidyā, through the multiplication of the qualities (*guṇakāra*), there are ten [levels] starting from the first; thus, according to the *Mṛgendra-śruti*, "from the peak of Nāda it is called Unmanā," the state of Supreme Śiva is well-established. These [levels], which consist of the six qualities (*ṣaḍguṇamaya*), are the supreme [states] characterized by grosser, gross, and subtler limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and they rest upon the peak of Nāda as the cessation [of duality].
Those who do not know that the manifestation of the state of Paraśiva occurs immediately after the dissolution of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),

[mistake] the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*)— which is purified immediately thereafter— for another manifestation characterized by the impairment of its own nature and the capacity for the activity of knowing and acting upon all objects.

Not finding [any other goal], they [realize] that the manifestation of one's own and the supreme state of Śiva—characterized by the three qualities consisting of the differentiation of the power of knowledge (such as omniscience) and the differentiation of the power of action (such as sovereignty)—is indeed what must be accomplished.
Enjoyment is one's own innate bliss and that which is supreme; this is well-established in the scriptures such as the *Mṛgendra*.

Those who do not understand that this very [state] is the manifestation of Śiva-nature, described by such terms as the bliss of Śiva, the supreme happiness of the enjoyment of Śiva, the supreme delight, the supreme essence, the supreme prosperity, and the supreme, unsurpassed, absolute fulfillment, instead perceive it merely as omniscience, contentment, and beginningless awakening.

"Independence, eternally undiminished power, infinite power, and a stainless self— possessing a pure body, one attains the state of Śiva. This is well-established by the scriptural authority of the *Sarvajñānottara*, which consists of the eightfold qualities and comprises omniscience and omnipotence.

Thinking that "Śiva-ness does not go beyond [these]," they again hold that omniscience and omnipotence are Śiva-ness; then again, they think that the two—omniscience and omnipotence—are not Śiva-ness, while Śiva-ness exists and omniscience and omnipotence do not exist.
Thus, like those who speak of a barren woman's son, they wander and recite [these views] regarding supreme liberation.
Furthermore, because it possesses the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of non-conceptual knowledge and action which is unattached to all objects,

those who do not perceive the power (*śakti*) consisting of the six qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*)— which arises from the stability of the worlds below the limit of the sixty million [tattvas] and from supreme liberation (*paramukti*)— distort that very power within supreme liberation by subjecting it to transformation.

Those who say that one's own power of consciousness (*svacicchakti*)—in which the knowledge, action, and desire regarding all objects have dissolved—is submerged in Śiva, [claim] that one's own state of Śiva-hood does not exist *per se*. Because of this immersion in Śiva, one emerges from that state;
when one is established in oneself as consisting of Śiva, the experience of the bliss of Śiva is called "Śiva-enjoyment" (*śivabhoga*).
Some, entering into the very depths of the millions of sides of the state of possession (*āveśa*), declare:
"They do not tolerate being interrupted. [This] is disregarded and left aside. They further declare:
"The manifestation of the qualities (*guṇa*) is not any form of pleasure; therefore, it is not the purpose of the Spirit (*puruṣārtha*)."

When they ask us, while we are in the state of saṃsāra, "What is happiness?", what would they say? Even after traveling far, they would say that the truth is the manifestation of the quality of goodness (*sattva-guṇa*), which has become the ground for the manifestation of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) that was previously unmanifest. But what is the purpose of this for them?

Alas! It is accomplished, yet it is not accomplished; what indeed is accomplished? Whether in every way or not in every way, in both saṃsāra and liberation, there exists that which is conditioned and that which is innate, characterized by being non-universal or universal, having the nature of limited animalhood or Śiva-hood, and possessing purposeful activity through the convergence of all objects.

The manifestation of one's own qualities, characterized by the power of one's own consciousness, is declared to be the state of bliss (*sukhapada*); this is the *puruṣārtha* (the goal of human existence).

This has been stated in the *Bhogakārikās*: "When the seed of the universe, permeated by the will of the Lord, is cast off, enjoyment—which is colored by the fluctuations of the intellect—is accomplished through the means [of practice]. Thus it is said in the *Kiraṇa*.
"Just as Śiva is omniscient and devoid of even a trace of limited knowledge, and is fully manifest in his state of Śiva-hood, so too is the transmigrating soul; it is not otherwise than that."
"Indeed, the very ray bestows the bliss of supreme nectar; herein lies the manifestation of Śiva-nature according to the rule of the [spiritual] birth.
This is not merely the bliss of liberation, but it bestows fullness upon all beings—salutations to You, who are thus! For Your Veda declares: 'You are the Pervader of Space' (Vyomavyāpin)."

Fullness, which is designated by the word "bliss," has been explained. That very [fullness] is experienced as the manifestation of one's own Śiva-nature (*svaśivatva*), as the enjoyment of one's own Śiva (*svaśivabhoga*), and as the bliss of one's own Śiva (*svaśivānanda*).
As it is said in the *Kāmika*:
That by which one may plunge undisturbed into the great awakening of innate bliss—
that alone is liberation, that indeed is Nirvāṇa, and that is the supreme state.

Thus, upon the removal of the three impurities (mala), the nature of the Self—characterized by the state of being Śiva, manifest, consisting of consciousness and bliss—is called *sāyujya* (union). And elsewhere [it is said]: "Liberation is not the annihilation of the self, nor is it the identity of the bound soul (*paśu*) and Śiva; here, liberation is the absence of ignorance."

There is no reduction in food intake, nor the disappearance of qualities, nor even liberation from the body like a stone. Since the nature of the self is manifest upon the removal of the three impurities as consisting of consciousness and bliss, that state of union (sāyujya) cannot be described; it is the omnipresent one similar to Śiva, which is the final liberation according to the Śaiva Tantra. Now, [it may be asked]: [The text continues: "Indeed..."
It has been stated that the liberated possess powers of knowledge and action equal to those of Śiva. (p.

319) If the power of action were the performer of all effects, then the doctrine of multiple gods (anekaiśvaravāda) would follow as a consequence. If it is not the performer of all effects, then how is it true that this [power] is similar to Śiva’s? That much [remains to be addressed].
The state of being the agent of all is indeed manifest. As it is stated in the *Mokṣakārikās*:
"Through the manifestation of consciousness, the Siddhas possess universal agency just like Īśvara;
otherwise, even Īśvara would lack agency, just like the Siddhas."
Indeed, the manifestation of consciousness (cid-vyakti) is not conjoined with the power of agency in only one part. As it has been stated in that very same work:
"The manifestation of consciousness is not conjoined with the power of the agent in only one part;
nor is there an absence of agency, because [agency] is beginningless, and for that reason, this [consciousness] is such."
If even the Manifest (vyaktā), though she exists, is not the agent of action, then what is the distinction? As it is said in that very same [text]:
"If there is no difference between the liberated one and the Manifest, nor between her and the bound soul (paśu), then what distinction is there?
[The answer is: She would perform all actions, whereas the Siddha possesses universal agency. This refers to the object of knowledge and the task to be accomplished.

And manifestation (*vyakti*) consists in the capacity for the performance of one's own purposeful action (*svārthakriyā*) and the capacity for the cognition that has reached the stage of practical application. If the capacity for action regarding the effect were limited in its purposeful activity, then manifestation would not be fully effective in every respect. As it is said in that very same [text]:
"Activity occurs when everything is accomplished; manifestation is nothing other than that which pertains to it.
Knowledge, having set out for the illumination of all things, is called 'manifestation'.
Even so, when liberated, [the soul] is established in its own object, with the sole purpose of manifesting its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

They possess rest because the duty of performing auspicious acts for the sake of the highest goal has been fulfilled; they do not possess *prapatti* directed toward any further task to be performed. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:
"And they do not perform creation and so forth, since they are established in their own purpose."

Nevertheless, because the manifestation of one's own capacity for action— which consists in reaching the stage of application toward purposeful activity— is unavoidable, when Śiva, whose mind is intent on the creation of the world, thinks "let this be thus," your own volition is equal to that of those who have attained liberation.

Nevertheless, for those who practice that gift while abstaining from passion, hatred, and the like— yet who, prior to the auspicious mind, harbor a self-conception marked by the distinction between the rise and fall of the new and the old, thinking "this is new" or "this is old"— and who serve as the locus for the doctrine of many lords; [for them, this is not so].
They act thus. As it has been said:
"At that time, for them, there arises a collective resolve regarding creation and so forth;
indeed, there is no inequality of resolve among them, because of the absence of any such cause."

How, then, is it said? When Śiva forms the volition (*saṃkalpa*), "Let this become thus," then, because it is not subject to rejection, there arises from the volition of Śiva a primordial and immediate [will] whose form is the volition: "Let it become thus."

Indeed, those who practice [the path] as non-different from Śiva follow a mind that—by virtue of its elevation at the beginning and its lack of depression—is possessed of a realization of fruit not distinct from the fruit of the *śivasaṃkalpa*; a mind that does not conceive of "this is my own" and "that is another's" as being unmixed;
and which acts as non-different from Śiva. For this very reason, it is called the "Śiva-mata" (the doctrine of Śiva) and the "Sva-mata" (one's own doctrine).
Because they possess self-restraint and loftiness of mind, there are no separate creators of the world. As it is stated in the *Mokṣakārikās*:
"Those who are free from passion, hatred, and the like, whose intellects have all things as their object..."
These [principles] are established as consisting of the Unmanifest (Prakṛti) and the Selves (Puruṣas), yet they are endowed with those that possess differentiation.
"Those [powers] have been declared by the wise to be non-distinct in their office by Śiva;
therefore, the arising of all effects here is not contradicted."
And it has been said in the *Siddhāntadīpikā*: "The fivefold activity of the liberated ones is established as inseparable;
for Śiva alone, being established in his own purpose, acts for their welfare out of compassion."
"They are not the creators of the universe, for the Creator is indeed Śiva alone.
Therefore, whether in the manifest (sakala) or the unmanifest (niṣkala), those [powers] do not exist anywhere as something truly real.

Considering that "union" (*sāyujya*) is [attained] through the scripture known as the *Viśvasādākhya*, and that even qualities such as omniscience and so forth are established for the pearl-like soul in the *Niśvāsakārikā*— where it is maintained that [the soul] conforms [to the Lord] in a manner consistent with its meaning— it is not contradictory. This very point has been set forth by us in detail regarding our established doctrine concerning the nature of Śiva.

Therefore, this must be understood from that very source. Enough with this dispute concerning the mental distress of ascetics by those who have not served their gurus. Let us return to the subject at hand. Setting aside those who have attained equality with Paraśiva due to the intense ripening of their impurity (*mala*), [we shall consider] the ripening of the intensity and so forth of *vijñānakevala* [impurity].

He states that [Śiva], having regard for their relative gradation, unites them with the Śivatattva, the Sadāśivatattva, the Bhogatattva, the Īśvaratattva, and the Adhikāratattva consisting of the Vidyātattva—
by first bestowing grace through His will alone upon those who are *vijñānakevalas*: "Having first favored the *vijñānakevalas* by His mere will..."
Depending solely upon the digestion of impurities, some [beings] abide within the domain of the pure path.
Having made some [souls] preeminent through their vision and action, he appoints them to offices;
others he calls to experience (bhoga) in each respective principle (tattva), while still others he calls to the state called Īśvara.
I invoke other omniscient and powerful beings within the principle of Vidyā,
who are endowed with the qualities of Sadāśiva and have resorted to the principle called Bhoga.
Enjoying various pleasures desired by the mind,
they engaged in the duties and responsibilities of their husband according to his will.
Those who have attained the state of Īśāna, who are especially qualified for ritual action,
endowed with the qualities of their office, are great universal monarchs (cakravartins).
The eight [goddesses], beginning with Anantasūkṣmā, possess an increasing degree of qualities as listed before;
they are exceedingly beautiful and graceful, and their minds are forever undiminished.
Having attained the state known as Vidyā, these seven crores of beings were all free from defilement, great-souled, and possessed of immeasurable splendor.
At the beginning, at the time of the commencement of creation, by His will, through His own power which is without substratum,

[He creates beings] endowed with manifest powers and intensified by vision and action; here, the phrases "possessing qualities equal to Sadāśiva" and "possessing qualities equal to their respective offices" are to be supplied as ellipses for each of the duties and offices.

Like the *praṇava* and other [mantras], even Ananta and the others who enjoy the objects of desire wished for by the mind are engaged in the five activities of the Lord (*pati*) through the intervention of *māyā*, according to His will; for this very reason, they are superior in action, as the scripture states: "He whose form consists of infinite streams is like a honeycomb. (p. 326)
Because of his authority over the *māyā*-maṇḍala: from Ananta, who is subtler than Śivottama, comes Sūkṣma;
from Ekanetra, who is subtler than Śivottama, comes Ekanetra; from Ekarudra, [comes] Ekanetra; from Trimūrti, [comes] Ekarudra;
from Śrīkaṇṭha, [comes] Trimūrti; and from Śikhaṇḍin, [comes] Śrīkaṇṭha—such is the sequence of the *kalās* descending downward.
Because their agency is diminished. As before, they do not deviate from the first [state], yet they possess superior qualities;

they possess superior power of action; their minds are undiminished; their powers are unimpeded; [they possess] sciences and mantras. For this very reason, all are joined in a threefold manner; their impurities are stilled.
Those whose impurities have been exhausted by initiation preceded by the ripening [of karma] perceive other objects clearly.

For those great universal monarchs, there is an infinite supreme state; for the Śruti declares that "the supreme state is the cause consisting of all-agency. Their final liberation occurs after the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).
It exists even previously. To the question "What exists?", he says: (p.
327) "Of these [faculties], for that great-souled one in whom dispassion has arisen, why should these [defilements] exist, being obstacles to the highest good and devoid of authority?"
Thus, the Supreme Lord, having regard for the ripening of that impurity,
bestows grace by His own will in such a manner as to bring about the manifestation of liberation.
Then, for the sake of liberation, the Lord bestows grace upon one who is near to that state and appoints him to that position;
he also appoints another to that same position.

Among these, for those who have attained supreme liberation while abiding in the principle of authority (*adhikāra-tattva*), including the ten [deities] residing in the *Sadāśiva-tattva*— such as Śiva, Īśa, Sūkṣma, Kāla, and Daśa— who are illuminated by the *praṇava* during the state of the subtle time (*sūkṣma-kāla-daśā*), and together with others residing therein or above it; [this applies to them].

In the case of that Great Soul—be it Vasiṣṭha, Mantra, Ananta, or others—who stands amidst the peaceful mantras, and for whom [this] modification, being an adversary and obstacle to the manifestation of sovereignty in the form of the supreme purpose of his own welfare, is almost as futile as if directed toward him; or rather, "what [is there to fear]? means this.

Dispassion arises from the cessation of one's office. When that has emerged, the Supreme Lord does not forcibly restrain that great-souled one from his office—characterized by the fivefold acts or characterized by experience—but rather [restrains him] in consideration of the ripening of impurity (*mala*). Of that impurity...

Since the principles of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*) and the rest are utterly severed, having understood that the destruction of the impurity of *adhikāra* arising from their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is the primary [goal], one should— by one's own will and through one's own power alone, without further substratum—
for the sake of manifesting liberation, effect such a total release from bonds as results in the manifestation of the state of Supreme Śiva (*para-śivatva*).
By means of the fruit, through the observation of what must be done by his power, he bestows grace; he manifests such liberation immediately thereafter.
The meaning is that the Blessed One [places him] in that very station, in that office, as one who is near, immediate, and junior—meaning directly so. From that [state]... (p. 329)

For the sake of liberation, he establishes a connection by appointing [the disciple] as one possessing qualities similar to his own, through an act of grace based on that [disciple’s] status as the youngest; even in that state, he [establishes a link] with another who has attained supreme liberation, whether that person occupies a position of authority in the city of liberation or has already departed from such a position.

Having bypassed that which is separated [by rank], he favors the immediate junior who has reached the station of authority and appoints him; likewise in that position as well— thus proceeding by way of this ascending order,
the mantra is situated among the *praṇavas* and so forth, and among Ananta and the others.

Among others, or in the middle, or in the final and lowest position, having performed the naming of the qualities of the Lord within the atom for the sake of the uninterrupted continuity of the instruction of the scriptures, the authority over ritual duties, and the wheel of *māyā*, he appoints [the disciple].
If detachment arises in Śikhaṇḍin and others within the interval of an atom (*aṇvantara*), it is not because of the application of the shortest sequence; rather,
the Vidyās grant favor only upon beholding this creation of the *piṇḍa* performed by the Grandfather, which is utterly overwhelmed by sin.

Being dispassionate, they have determined that in this world, where creation is utterly afflicted, we are not capable of performing even the office of action— which consists of enjoyment and protection and is presided over by the Lord— nor are we able to do so; thus,
having resolved that the command of the Supreme Lord must necessarily be carried out, [they approach] another teacher.

In the case of those *vijnanakalas* who are to be graced immediately following their own grace, the impurity (*mala*) is [removed] in supreme liberation by Śiva’s impelling power, which is independent of any external instrument and devoid of a substratum; it occurs through His direct agency and instrumentality by means of His own potency.

And those *pralayākalas* who are fit for the state of a Lord of Mantras [attain it]; while for those *sakalas*— individual souls (*aṇus*) connected with gross bodies— this creation of Brahmā, consisting of impurity (*mala*) and karma, is brought about at that very moment through the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*).
Having rendered them auspicious by liberating them from both impurity and karma,
and having withdrawn from that activity, they wait upon the grace of the Lord in order to enter supreme liberation.
Impelled by the Supreme Lord, Ananta maintained them solely for the sake of [bestowing] authority;
then, by means of them, Ananteśa was questioned:
"O Blessed One, although this authority is utterly contemptible, it has been [granted] by us for the purpose of severing the bonds."

Because the Lord has ordained that even bound souls (*paśu*) are essentially characterized by the manifestation of their own Śiva-nature, Ananteśa replied: "Among you, those who have now set out to practice for liberation—why have we been detained?
[He continued: "Among you..."
Because they are possessed of the full maturation of their supreme impurities,

let those who have ceased from their office go to liberation by the command of the Supreme Lord alone; but those who, being the opposite of that, still desire their office, let them go to the Great Dissolution.

"Let them remain," he said. Then they [thought]: "How indeed does our Lord, who bestows happiness upon all beings, urge us toward an object that is not desired by people like us? Saying "No," they were satisfied; and having consulted one another as to which of them was entitled to which [object], those who held authority—

The beloved women have become instruments for Śiva through their connection with the Guru; they do not possess the capacity to bestow grace *independently* (*svataḥ*) as the first half [of the verse] might suggest. Half of the army, numbering seventy million, attained supreme liberation, while the remaining ones, by this statement, became free from objective substrates (*niradhikaraṇa*) even within the context of the *sakala* [deities].
It should be understood that there are those who are fit for the grace of Śiva. The Cārvākas hold that the self consists of the great elements;
the Saugatas [Buddhists] hold that it consists of a continuum of consciousness because of its momentary destruction;
and the Naiyyāyikas hold that it is eternal, all-pervading, conscious, and possesses nine qualities such as cognition and so forth.

The Sāṃkhyas [hold that the self] is by nature pure, devoid of qualities, and not an agent. The Digambaras [hold that it] possesses the eight qualities beginning with delusion (*moha*), which are the root of karma that obstructs its sovereignty, and is characterized by contraction and expansion. [Others hold that the self is] non-created, eternal, and all-pervading, like Brahmā or Īśvara.

The followers of Vedānta, having gradually attained maturity, as well as the Pāñcarātrikas, maintain that the Māyāvādins hold the view that the one and only Supreme Self is perceived as manifold due to the distinctions of various limiting adjuncts (upādhi) characterized by the diverse minds [of individual souls]. The Jaiminīyas, on the other hand, maintain that the ignorant [individual soul] is the agent; such are the assertions of these disputants.

The sages, burdened by doubts regarding the existence of that Dharma through arguments arising from both the even and the uneven, first challenge [the position] with the Cārvāka perspective: "If the Self were truly established, then everything previously stated would be proven."
Therefore, O Śambhu, let the means of valid cognition for its existence be stated.

O Śambhu, O Blessed One, since the root *āp* signifies "going continuously," that which is reached through continuity and known is called the *ātman*. As you have stated, it is eternal and all-pervasive, being unconditioned by space and time. When that *ātman* is thus established in its true nature, then that which was previously mentioned—

The entire application of the various terms such as "knowledge" (*vidyā*) and so forth would [then] exist. Therefore, let the proof for its existence be stated. First of all, its establishment is not through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because that which has the nature of being eternal and all-pervading is not perceived apart from the body.

Furthermore, because it does not extend even an atom's breadth beyond the body, it cannot be an object of inference; for if it were inferable, it would follow that it is "other" (para), like Devadatta and others. Whatever illuminates itself is the Self, and its illumination is not something other.
If the distinction between one's own self and another's self were established solely through their respective states of being self-luminous and being luminous to others,
then there would be a confusion and a lack of stability regarding the clearly manifest states of self and other as they appear in their distinctness. As it has been said:

"If the self were an object of cognition, its cognizer would be something other [than itself]. In that case, the self would be 'other,' being that which is measured by another. Therefore, who is its inferer?
If it is knowledge, then that very [knowledge] is the self by virtue of being the inferer; since it is not perceived as distinct from that, what is the use of anything else?

Nor can it be established by scripture, because such a scripture is unproven for us; the sense is that its operation is based on a meaning contradicted by perception and inference. [Objection: Then does God not exist? [Reply: Or how could the self exist? Because of the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is only doubt.
Therefore, even for the Cārvākas, who hold that perception alone is the means of valid cognition and not inference,

the consideration of what is a means of valid cognition and what is not, as well as the determination of the great elements and the Veda, necessarily involves inference; thus, [inference] is unavoidable within their own system.

Since the self is established by perception through the experience of one's own nature, and since the supreme self is inferred as being merely an object of inference—dissimilar to the object of knowledge (*meyavisadṛśa*)—and because it is accepted as an object of knowledge in other bodies according to the view of the Naiyāyikas and others, there is an inference regarding it. (p. 336)
It formulates an inference:
"The body and so forth, while functioning, are always presided over by a conscious being,
because they lack intrinsic activity due to their insentience, like a jar and other such objects."
That which is designated as the "self" (ātman) is the initiator;
that which is being initiated consists of the body and so forth, characterized by coming and going and performing purposeful action (svārthakriyā).
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the sense organs and the like are included, [all of which] are presided over by consciousness.
At the time of initiating activity, [the body] always proceeds impelled by consciousness. This is the proposition;

it is established by the reason of "insentience" (jaḍatva), because [an insentient thing] is naturally devoid of spontaneous activity. This reason—by supplying the word "just like" (yathā) as in "just like a jar and so forth"—is easily understood and should be formulated as a *śliṣṭa* (cohesive/connected) argument for the sake of clarity.
Its establishment is also possible through inference from the remainder (*śeṣavat-anumāna*); following that is the sequence of formal application (*prayoga*). In the *Mṛgendra* (p. 337):

"The earth and so forth are effects, and their agent is [the Lord]; for such an agent is not employed for his own sake, because he is insentient; nor is he without purpose, because it would entail the absurdity of a creator."
"By process of elimination, that [which is for another] is the supreme Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) beyond those two.
Thus, the seers demonstrate the unestablished nature of the reason— characterized by the absence of spontaneous activity— applied toward proving the existence of a self distinct from the body.
From the observation of consciousness in the body, it does not follow that the self possesses consciousness.
For when X is present, Y is observed, then X is the cause of Y.

Since consciousness is observed when the body is present, and if it were not observed when the body is absent, then [consciousness] would have its own specific property as its defining characteristic.

The person (*puruṣa*) is a body characterized by its own causal consciousness, because it possesses sentience; even that which acts spontaneously is [of this nature]. For he would not be one whose nature is the consciousness of the Self. That which has consciousness as its characteristic mark of the Self is described as such, by virtue of being the cause of its own activity.
The meaning is that there would be no consciousness characterized as a self distinct from itself.
They show an illustrative example: when heat and so forth are observed in something such as fire, that fire and so forth is indeed the cause of that heat; but is this not also the case for a jar?
Since it is composed of the elements (*bhūta*), why is it not the cause of consciousness? To this they say:
"In this case, the body is the establisher of consciousness because its causality is no different [from that of other causes].
This is like the production of the effects known as liquor and cakes from the combination of the body and a jar."
Even flour, sugar, and other ingredients are seen to be present in the cake;
yet, prior to the cake, the power of intoxication was not in them. Thus, it resides in itself [only when combined].
Therefore, since consciousness arises from the body itself which is composed of the elements,
what need is there for another self or a Lord to preside over that consciousness?
Even though the body is composed of the elements (*bhūta*), between the body and a jar,

consciousness can only arise from the body because it is the cause [of life]. It is certain that consciousness— which was non-existent in the elements and their effects such as the jar— arises from the body, being non-different from its essence.
They state the conclusion: "That," and so forth. O Lord, the presiding agent who causes the body's activity, consciousness has arisen as non-different from that body;
and because the notion of "I" is observed only with respect to the body—as in "I am fat"—therefore, it is "I."

Since the cognition "the embodied one" (śarīrī) is merely figurative—just like the expression "Rāhu’s head"—and since [the self] is established as acting spontaneously, your stated reason is unproven (*asiddha*). Therefore, what need is there for an unauthoritative, separate *ātman* that is distinct [from the body], which is equivalent to a horse's horn? Otherwise, how could the effect [of action] be accounted for?
The sense is that since [the self] is already established in some way, there is no further purpose in establishing it.

Therefore, because the observer also perishes upon the destruction of the body, and because there would be an absence of those who pass to the next world, it has been stated that the next world is not established; for as long as one lives, one may live like a god, yet there is none who is beyond the reach of death.

"How can there be a return for one who has been reduced to ashes and is extinguished? To this, the Lord refutes [the objection] from the perspective of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*): "By whom was it said that there is no variety among distinct effects produced by powers?"
An effect that is contradictory does not arise from a cause that is contradictory.
Furthermore, how could consciousness, which is diametrically opposed [to it], arise from the insentient body?

Even for effects that are distinct, a single cause may exist through its various powers; the diversity residing in the cause consists of the powers of the producer and the produced. Who has said that there is no diversity? By whom was this said? By whom? By this [very question]—it was said.

By stating that [the opponent] possesses such a claim, it is indicated—preceded by a demonstration of his error—that he is not a teacher of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). To the question, "Then what is said from your perspective? he says: "From a contradictory cause, such as water and so forth, a contradictory effect, such as heat and so forth, does not arise. (p.)

342) The intended meaning is that consciousness thus arises from what is insentient; however, just as heat cannot arise from water, how could consciousness arise from the body, which is its opposite—being insentient?
The sense is that it could not arise in any way whatsoever. Having set forth another argument, he refutes it:

Furthermore, O twice-born ones, when a property belongs to something, the destruction of that property results in the destruction of the substratum, because of the presence of a contradictory quality; otherwise, it would not be so.

O twice-born ones, even though the body exists, why is consciousness not admitted in one who is dead? Furthermore, for whatever thing—such as snow or fire—there is a specific property, such as coldness, burning, or illumination; [if that property were inherent in the body, it would likewise persist].
From the destruction of that [quality] and the exhaustion of its attributes, the destruction of the substratum follows without doubt; this is observed. [Objection:

But surely, even when qualities such as blackness and the like perish in copper and similar substances, their essential nature (*bhāva*) is not seen to perish. [Response: True; it is for this purpose [that the following is stated]. Or rather, even in the case of two contradictory qualities...
Because they do not attain their own nature through mutual destruction— just as, for example,

in the case of mold, conch shells, and so forth, there is no attainment of their own nature through the destruction of properties characterized by being an obscuration or the cessation thereof— so it is here.

When the qualities characterized by consciousness are suppressed within the body, it cannot be said that the quality characterized by consciousness attains its own nature; therefore, one should not ask "what is the loss?
because of the presence of a contrary quality, which results in the acquisition of a quality opposed to that characteristic of consciousness.

Otherwise, that substratum (dharmin) would become something else. It would possess a transformation into another form characterized by the cessation of its obscuring nature, like a black conch shell and so forth; or it would possess a transformation into another form characterized by consciousness (citi) in its entirety. Yet, it is never observed to be so. Now, as for the [change] of the property (dharma)...
He says that there is no harm for us in the destruction of the six categories; rather, there is indeed no harm.

When the body has died and reached the state of the five elements (*pañcatā*), even though the faculty of sight remains, why is consciousness not accepted as being like the coldness of snow? Why is it not admitted? And yet—

It cannot be said that consciousness (*caitanya*), being suppressed by the manifestation of the qualities characterized as non-conscious (*acit-lakṣaṇa*), is not perceived at that time; for those qualities characterized as non-conscious exist even during the state of the individual soul (*jīva*). [Objection: But what about in a dead body?
Because it is admitted that there is also fire in the form of heat within the wind whose nature consists of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth;

and because, as in the state of being alive, the elements that constitute the body are absent [in death], it cannot be argued that there is no sentience at that time, for this would lead to the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*). This is not so, for even those whose life-force has departed...
For indeed, some [elements] with moving joints and some possessing heat are perceived for a certain period of time;

yet, even when those exist, there is no existence of consciousness. Now, one might object: "Due to the particularity of transformation (*pariṇāma*), even in the state of Śiva, there is a most subtle self-awareness (*saṃvedana*). To that we reply: no, it is not bodily.

Because of the specific nature of transformation, it has been stated with supporting arguments immediately following that the consciousness's capacity to undergo such [transformation] is not tenable; as it was said: "When the body exists, consciousness is perceived, for it is not perceived when it does not exist. This, however, is incorrect, because it is unestablished for us. Now, this...

Just as a jar or similar object exists when light and other conditions are present, consciousness is established there previously by being manifested through that body; it is not a product [of those conditions]. For in this way, [consciousness] is indeed all-pervasive. Nor can it be imagined that the Self was previously non-existent in those various places, as is the case with light and so forth.
Its prior existence is already established, just as that of a jar and so forth; this will also be examined later on.

Now, one might ask: "Why is there no sensory non-perception of this [self], as there is of a jar? That is incorrect. For in the form in which it is established according to your own doctrine—namely, as the nature of self-awareness—the self is not [perceived] in that same form therein.

It is possible; however, it is not absolutely unestablished because, like the sense faculties themselves, its nature is such that the sense faculties are not perceived as its objective support. [Objection: But how was its equality previously ascertained?
It is merely a doubt. [Response: True; for ordinary people, this occurs without the recollection of what is beneficial or harmful.
Since [the body] must be inferred from future actions such as contraction and extension, the existence of the observer is established even prior to birth; therefore, on the contrary:
"That by whose presence or absence the body undergoes movement or lack of movement..."
And that is declared to be consciousness, which is indeed distinct from the body.
In the subtle body, through the presence or absence of which [gross] states,

and through the union or separation with the manifesting instruments characterized as the organs of action, there occurs within oneself the manifestation or non-manifestation of one's own power; thus, there is movement, effort, and contraction.
Stretching, revolving, going, coming, and so forth would belong to that which is characterized by their absence; [that consciousness] would carry them.

And since that consciousness is the self (*ātman*), because it is not dependent on other purposes, it is stated—by means of the exclusion of non-connection and the exclusion of connection with others—that it is distinct from and other than the body.

Just as heat, which conforms to the increase and decrease of the fire, appears as if it were the fire itself, so too consciousness— which conforms to the increase and decrease of the body resulting from causes such as the diet and fasting of a youth or an adult— is considered to be identical with the body, even in those of very small stature.
Furthermore, even when reading the *Mahāmatitva-darśana*, you who claim that it is Buddhist because it imitates that [work] have failed to realize that this is untenable; thus he says:
"Moreover, due to the distinctions between childhood, youth, and old age..."
And how is there a recollection of the body and of what was done in childhood?
"One remembers, 'This very woman was enjoyed by me previously';
therefore, the doctrine that the body is the self is refuted by direct perception."
Therefore, [the notion] "I am fat" and so forth is to be understood as being like the head of a snake;
moreover, the cognition "the body is mine" and so forth certainly exists in abundance.

Due to the distinction between the various states of the body, such as childhood and so forth— and specifically due to their difference— the knowledge that conforms to those [states] also possesses distinction; thus, there is a difference between what was done in childhood and [the memory thereof] at the stage of youth,
and between what was done in youth and [the memory thereof] from the word [at a later time].

The continuity observed in the state of old age [is explained as follows]: memory cannot belong to anyone other than the experiencer; how could what was experienced by Devadatta come to pass for his son, except through a single, identical Self? The meaning is that it could not happen in any way whatsoever [without such a Self].

He demonstrates the method of that recollection: because she has transcended her youthful stage, he gradually recollects—that is, he recognizes—how this very woman was previously enjoyed and embraced by him in the past. Therefore, this...

The doctrine that the body is the self is refuted by direct perception; this very [doctrine] is rejected by the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Therefore, because it is refuted by direct perception, the cognition "I am stout" and so forth should be understood as being like the expression "the head of Rāhu."

Just as there is a statement regarding the superimposition of Rāhu even though he is not perceived within the head, so too, although the "gross" (sthūla) self is not perceived within, that gross state— which resides in its own location and exists within a body distinct from itself—
is superimposed upon it. Furthermore, [this applies to] such expressions as "I am gross."

The meaning is: what need is there for deliberation here regarding the lack of discernment in such thoughts as "I am fat," which arise from non-discrimination, whereas the well-known, abundant cognition characterized by discrimination is expressed as "this is my body" and so forth, which is contrary to [the notion of] being a mere condition (*pratyaya*)? Thus, by this, [it is shown that] through the internal contact of being an object of enjoyment, [the body] takes on the nature of a thorn and the like.

And externally, through the investigation of the body— which is determined by the intellect according to its distinctions such as softness or hardness— there follows an investigation into the self, the investigator, by means of the manifestation of the cognition that takes the form of that body.

That which has the nature of a synthesizer (*anusandhātṛ*), whose synthesis is its own causal efficiency (*svārthakriyā*), and which is distinct from the body, is called the power of supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvitti-śakti*); for if it were an object of cognition, there would be a contradiction regarding activity within itself.
It manifests as appearing within the synthesizer, whose characteristic is self-experience and whose form is one's own immediate presence (*svapratyakṣa-rūpa*).

This is indeed established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvit-pratyakṣa*). For this very reason, inference was employed against the Lokāyatas in order to demonstrate the validity of inference, and not because the Self is directly perceived through self-awareness.

The fallacious argument—that because the self is established through inference, it follows that the self is an object external to itself—is cast far away as a mere product of bad logic and false conceptualization. As it has been said: "What correspondence can there be with what is perceived, by virtue of which that [perception] could have validity? Thus, since the body is established as an object of experience, [it cannot be the self], just as one cannot grasp oneself with the tip of one's own finger.

Just as the quality of touch is not established in the tip of a finger, the status of being an enjoyer is not established [in the intellect]; thus, he says that those following the systems of the Naiyāyikas and others should abandon the notion of a self even with respect to the intellect and so forth:
"The intellect and the rest do not possess the nature of the self, since it is from their effects that the self is established."
Since their establishment is based on their being the causes for effects other than that [object].
In this case as well, if those [faculties] were to serve as the cause, then the entire universe should be accepted as one.

Furthermore, consciousness and the rest do not possess the nature of the self; for the existence of the self is established from its specific effect—that is, from the effect characterized by the capacity to apprehend both itself and others.

Because they are the cause of effects other than that— namely, because those [factors] such as cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth are the cause of visible effects such as the determination of an object to be grasped, which is distinct from the effect characterized by the grasping of self and other— their existence is established and certain. In this case as well:

Even regarding the effect characterized by the grasping of self and other, since those [causes] function as causes, the postulation of a plurality [of causes] is not refuted by the difference in effects; thus, it is sufficient for a single [cause] to accomplish all effects. Consequently, because their respective diverse effects would otherwise be inexplicable, the entire universe is established as being of a diverse nature.
(p. 352) Let it be accepted that the entire world, from the *kalā* down to the earth (*kṣiti*), as will be described hereafter, is a single [entity].

Thus, since the agent and the action are established otherwise, the Cārvāka sub-sects—the Sensory-Consciousnessists (*indriyacaitanika*), the Mental-Consciousnessists (*manaścaitanika*), and the Epistemic-Consciousnessists (*pramāṇacaitanika*)—follow that very view.

The status of the six organs, beginning with the mirror and the scriptures, as instruments is established; since activity cannot occur without an agent, the independent activity of air—due to its insentience—has been refuted in this chapter. Furthermore, in this chapter, [the view that] the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is sentient is rejected on the grounds of other effects, such as the ego-grasping and the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*).
Since it will be stated that [the self] is established, the Buddhists who maintain that consciousness is mental (caitanyavādins) argue that because cognition reveals a self of stable form,
the existence of that self is established through the otherwise inexplicable nature of the recollection of prior experiences; however, the followers of the Pāda school (pādārthikas) [disagree].

The Vedāntins and Pāñcarātras maintain that, because he possesses qualities such as omniscience and so forth, the Self must be established hereafter as one who has conquered those qualities; whereas the Kṣapaṇakas maintain that the Self must be established hereafter as all-pervading.

The Sāṃkhyas, however, maintain that the self is both an enjoyer and a non-agent; the followers of Jaimini (Mīmāṃsakas) hold that the nature of the person (*puruṣatva*) is adventitious (*aupādhika*), as will be demonstrated later. Thus, these [views] are for the most part already refuted. The sages [say]: "Because of their fallacious reasoning, false conceptualizations, and erroneous views..."
They adhere to the doctrine of a single self (aikātmyavāda) in order to explain it.
Self-experience is what has been taught; by what means is plurality perceived? It is not accessible through direct perception, nor is it the object of inference.
Since difference is a property of the object of cognition (*meyadharma*), how could the cognizer (*mātṛ*) be the object of cognition?

Although you have stated that there are many selves due to the distinction between the "complete" (*sakala*) and "incomplete" (*akala*) [forms], even if the self's status as established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanapratyakṣa*) exists, by what means is that plurality [established]?

It is understood through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To that extent, it is not accessible to perception (*adhyakṣa*) because it is not within the range of direct perception; for self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is impossible with respect to itself. Therefore, since pervasion (*vyāpti*) is preceded by perception—

It is not an object of inference, nor indeed is it within the range of inference. Now, if that [object] were cognizable, then because the distinction between entities—which possess mutually dissimilar characteristics—is a property of the object of knowledge (*meyadharma*), the object as a distinct entity would be separate from both the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the knower (*mātṛ*); therefore, for the sake of establishing that distinction within the knower, [it must be admitted].

"It must undoubtedly be stated that [the Self] is an object of knowledge (*meyatva*). To this he replies: "How could that Knower (*mātā*) be an object of knowledge within itself? Due to the contradiction of an action operating upon itself, it could not be so in any way whatsoever. This is the intended meaning; furthermore, it would lead to the fallacies of confusion (*saṃkara*) and infinite regress (*anavasthā*). As it has been said: "Consciousness is one and shines forth."

But that which is other than this is manifested; and it must be something manifested. How can there be an object (*karman*) without an agent (*kartṛ*)? This has already been shown in the section on the Cārvāka doctrine. [Objection: But if this is so, not only is difference established in the case of the knower (*mātṛ*), but because difference is a property of the object of knowledge (*meyadharman*).

Even by your proposed reason, since the state of being distinct from the object of cognition (*meyavyatiriktatva*) is equal [in both cases], there would be a lack of the quality of difference (*bhedaguṇakatva-vaidhurye*); thus, that [distinction] would apply equally to the cognizer (*mātṛ*) and the means of cognition (*māna*). How could the means of cognition be established as distinct from the cognizer? Therefore, that means of cognition is not distinct from the cognizer.

They say that difference is established in the Self by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the means of knowledge (*sādhana*); that the difference [of the object] from the knower and the act of knowing is established from the examination of *māyā* in the chapter on *māyā*, and it will also be established later; yet they say that this is not so. No.

The state of being a probans for a qualified [subject] also establishes a difference in the self; that [state] exists because of the difference in the property of the qualified self, and thus it serves as a reason in another case that possesses a limiting condition (*upādhi*). Furthermore, the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the probans of the mind, given that it is distinct from the mother, also [establishes this].

It does not establish a real difference in the self (*ātman*). For if it were not so, the impossibility of that [difference] would remain; therefore, they say: "The property of the self is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); it is produced by those adjuncts, such as the body, which qualify the self."

The meaning is that since qualities such as pleasure exist in that very self when it is delimited by another body through the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the proof for the difference of selves based on those adjuncts is exhausted by that very fact. They cite an example of this:
Just as when the space within one jar is joined with dust, smoke, and so forth,
not all [spaces] are joined [with them], so too are the individual souls [joined] with pleasure and the like.
Therefore, let a remedy be prescribed for this state of being a single self;
just as when one space within a jar is joined with dust, smoke, and the like,
all other spaces within jars, ladles, pots, and huts remain untouched by it.
Just as space conditioned by various limiting adjuncts such as water is not affected by the dust or smoke residing therein,

so too, while the individual soul (*jīva*)— conditioned by the limiting adjunct of the body— is joined with pleasure and the like, it remains like space which, though appearing divided by its limiting adjuncts, is one.
The individual selves (*jīva*), conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the various bodies and the various states of pleasure and pain,

are not joined with the pleasure and other experiences residing therein; thus, there is a certain Supreme Self (*paramātman*) which, though appearing divided by the distinctions conditioned by the two kinds of mental adjuncts, conforms to no other inherent nature.

When understood as they truly are, these lead to spiritual elevation. However, the mind’s association with the worldly conditions of pleasure, pain, and so forth—though it is in fact non-different from them, like the sun appearing divided by the limiting adjuncts of reflections in water—manifests as if it were distinct; it is therein that bondage resides.

In reality, distinctions such as liberation and so forth are not said to exist; consequently, it is well-established that the appearance of duality is an illusion, just like the cognition of two moons.
Thus, the venerable Bhartṛhari has said therein:
Just as people afflicted by cataracts perceive the pure sky as if it were filled with various and diverse specks, so too do they falsely imagine it to be cluttered.
"Thus, this immortal Brahman, though changeless, appears to function in the form of differentiation, as if it had become defiled by ignorance.
Therefore, that very [Brahman] exists in this state of non-dual selfhood which is favored by the knowers of the Vedānta.

Let the refutation, which is free from all doubt, be stated regarding that whose essential nature is praised in numerous scriptures such as the *Paramānanda*, and which is established solely as the Supreme Self; let it be performed. He brings forth from his own mouth the statement concerning the form of the refutation residing in the Lord:
There are many selves, due to the distinctions of birth, death, and so forth;
for qualities such as birth and destruction are observed in distinct entities.

Therefore, birth, destruction, and so forth, which exist as the differentiators of the self, do not fail to produce the result intended by the use of the plural form for the self. Having established that these are the means (*sādhana*), they are said to be "many. This is the proposition (*pratijñā*): [the plurality] is due to the distinctions of birth, death, and so on.

By the word "etc. (ādi), pleasure, pain, desire, and so forth are included. The reason is that birth, destruction, and other such changes are observed among distinct entities. The statement of the example is made by supplying the phrase "just as in the case of the body, senses, and so forth. Then, having supplied the application (*upanaya*) "and so too these [consciousnesses, etc.]," and having appended "therefore" (*tataḥ*), [the conclusion follows].

Since the meaning of half a verse is easy to understand, its conclusion should be easily composed. Having raised the doubt that birth, destruction, and so forth are observed in the body, senses, and other such things— which have been used as examples— but not in anything else [such as the Self],
[the author] says the following to show that this is incorrect because of the observation of innate consciousness:
Birth and so forth do not belong to the body alone, nor do they belong to the selves together with the bodies and other such things;
for if birth and so forth belonged only to the body and its like, there would be no perception of consciousness.
(p. 360) On that day, O Jita, consciousness is admitted even in infants;
though endowed with consciousness, it arises in the form of the body and so forth.
Therefore, bodies, which possess distinctions such as birth and so forth, are the means for establishing the distinction of consciousness.
The meaning of the sūtra is easily understood. Anticipating the objection of another's intention, he refutes it:
"If the thought arises: 'How can there be birth for eternal consciousness here?'"
This is far too little; moreover, these bodies, senses, and so forth are impermanent.

The sense is that this reflection is too limited and pertains to gross objects. Therefore, the sense is that [the soul] is not eternal like the body, senses, and so forth, which undergo birth. The meaning of the verse is easy to understand.
Now, how is it that there is no eternality for those who undergo birth and death?

How could there be "always" for a sentient being, given that only the sentient being is eternal? Or how could such a state of always-existence belong to the body and so forth? In response to this doubt, and in order to establish that [point], the proponents of the theory of pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) present four positions; some [hold that] it is power (*śakti*).

They declare that the cause, which consists of a collection [of powers], is nothing other than the powers themselves when they have become manifest, and thus receive the designation of "effect. As it has been said:
"Because of the transformation of an entity that is a mere aggregate of powers..."
"Sometimes a certain power is manifested, and sometimes another is dissolved. Regarding this, others say that for entities, manifestation is not a transformation into a different form;
rather, it is simply the state of being perceived, and that alone is called "birth. Others, however, [disagree].

Others, however, maintain that the effect is merely a particular arrangement of the cause, just as bracelets, armlets, and other ornaments are [mere arrangements] of gold; for they argue that entities, possessing a nature characterized by successive variety,
undergo an infinite succession of distinct states such as birth and so forth.

They have accepted that [entities] partake of designations; thus, he demonstrates the application of this principle to all four positions: "The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being."
Therefore, this doctrine of a single self has been imagined by those of deluded intellect.

There is no non-existence of that which is non-existent, such as a rabbit’s horn. For it is said that if [the effect] were already existent, then—just as with a mountain—it would possess the state of being already produced (*kṛtatva*); and since there can be no production of what is already produced, the causal factors (*kāraka*) would be rendered useless due to their incapacity to effect anything. True. [This applies] to the four positions within the doctrine of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*).

First, in the case of the second and third positions, because a transformation into another form is observed in milk, curd, and so forth, [the example] is not analogous; for there is no such transformation into another form. Furthermore, in that case, because a change from sweetness to the taste of a creeper and so on is observed, it is not analogous.

"Arrangement" [is not the definition], because it is non-pervasive. In the *Mṛgendra*, by accepting the first position regarding the definition of a cause: "Then, during withdrawal, the effects exist as supports in the form of powers (*śakti*)."
In the transformation, the individual forms operate for the accomplishment of the purpose.

From scripture: it is precisely the potencies of the effect, which exist in the form of the cause, that become manifest and are designated by words denoting the effect. Furthermore, by accepting the fourth position, [it is stated] in the venerable *Mataṅga*:
"If that which belongs to us arises from our own selves through devotion, one should establish it."
O tiger among sages, for it is heard in scripture that "the locus also does not undergo deliberation": when milk and so forth in a vessel such as a basin have perished, they do not go elsewhere;
rather, curd and so forth arise from that very same state. Therefore, it is certainly not the case that something comes from somewhere else.

It is perceived through direct perception; however, because that very same entity possesses a nature characterized by a sequence of diverse states, it conforms to infinite specific conditions— both in its causal and its resultant aspects— and thus it is both cause and effect.

Or it is expressed by words: because the cause consists of a collection of potencies (*śakti*), and because it has the nature of the power of *māyā*, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if one were to postulate further potencies for that potency. Therefore, the effect itself possesses potency; thus, it is the "potency of the effect" (*kārya-śakti*).

Because it consists of a synthesis [of powers], *māyā* is understood to possess power; and because its own causal power is its own limb (*svāṅga*), it is understood to be subordinate to its own effect. Therefore, in the sense that "this is the cause of this," the cause is that which is characterized by a causal power whose effects are not yet manifested through its own delimiters (*svāvacchedaka*). In the case of the primary cause (*kāraṇa*), [it is so].

Because it is not distinct from that capacity, there is a connection with the cause; thus, the form of the effect— which is characterized by the manifestation of its own power through the form of the cause— is such that, although it exists in the nature of that power, its own-nature is manifested through the proximity of the causal factors (*kāraka*).
In the examination of the manifestation of Śiva-nature, it has been examined in some small measure; thus, by means of causal factors (*kārakas*)—
