which possess generative power (*janaka-śaktimat*), which are instrumental causes (*nimitta-kartṛ*), and which act as co-operative agents (*sahakartṛ*)— the form of the cause is set aside, and the effect is not produced in its own nature through the characteristics of the form of the effect.
Thus, because existence consists in manifestation, that very manifestation is what constitutes "production"; therefore, there is no futility of the causal factors (*kāraka*).

As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "That manifestation is called 'production' because it relies upon those causal factors. By means of the shuttle and other tools, the form residing in the threads—which was obstructed by the state of being a non-cloth—is removed, and thus the cloth [is produced]."

"The individual is manifested. By this statement, "the generative power (janya-śakti) is the regulator," it is shown that power (śakti) does not deviate from its possessor (śaktimat). Therefore, in the case of the Three Jewels and so forth, transformation (pariṇāma) indeed consists in the relinquishing of a previous state by entities.
For in that state, there is first only the milk, and from that, subsequently, the curd.

"Subsequently, there is buttermilk and likewise *māyā*, due to manifold transformations. According to this scripture (*śruti*), the very substance that takes the form of milk and so forth becomes established separately through its successive stages as curd, fresh butter, and various other individual natures; thus, the nature of the curd and so forth was previously unmanifest.

Milk. For indeed, it is evident that at the time of the effect, curds and so forth exist in the state of being unmanifest, while at the time of the cause, milk and so forth exist in the state of being their own nature as unmanifest potential; thus, through the persistence of its own attributes, it remains inherent.
In the view that the effect is [previously non-existent], the material cause would have to be designated by the term "inherent cause" (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*).

However, this is not the case in the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma-pakṣa*); for at the very moment the effect arises, the cause is not inherently connected (*samavāyin*) with the effect in the manner described by the Naiyāyikas and others, such as through the state of being inseparable (*ayuta-siddhatva*).

The following reasoning is established: manifestation and disappearance are designated by the term "birth" (janman). Therefore, [the terms] "arising" and "destruction" are used figuratively, because the effect is delimited by its cause. Otherwise, there would be a continuity even for a barren woman who is not so delimited.

First, there is the establishment of the effect's nature (*kāryatattvasiddhi*). Then, there is its manifestation through the removal of the obstructing causal form of the body and so forth, which constitutes a transformation (*anyathātva*).
Furthermore, there is a transformation consisting in the removal of the causal form by the effect's own form.

In the case of an instrument (*karaṇa*), there is no capacity for *lakṣaṇā* (indication); rather, it is described in sequence as "causing to fall" (*pātana*) and "destruction" (*nāśa*). Likewise, when the self is associated with the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), its characteristic of being an obscuration of its own consciousness—acting as a hindrance to itself—is present therein within the gross body (*sthūladeha*) by means of the *kalās* and other factors.
By the Lord, through the removal of impurity (*mala*), there occurs the cessation of the state of being an obscurer within the cause;
for [the soul] has the single nature characterized by that cessation of impurity.

Through the imposition of another form upon the impurity—which is characterized by its own cessation—there occurs a transformation (*pariṇati*) into that other form characterized by such cessation. And of that...
Because it resides within itself, which is established in the non-material *mala*, its manifestation is an unmodified state of its own consciousness;

furthermore, even when the gross body has fallen and the *kalās* and other components that constitute the subtle body exist as if they were non-existent, there remains the state of being unobstructed by anything that could act as a veil.

Because, by the Lord’s act of transforming [the soul] through the removal of the impurity characterized by cessation, [the soul] possesses the single nature of the cessation of its obscuring quality; whereas in the case of impurity,
[the Lord acts] by inducing a different essential nature characterized by its own state of obscuration.

Due to the transformation of its form into the characteristics of the "Tall" (tallakṣaṇa), and because that [transformation] resides within itself while being dependent on the impurities of others, there occurs a non-manifestation characterized by the lack of modification of one's own consciousness; this is described as birth and destruction in succession. For those endowed with the eye of knowledge, it is the very knowledge itself that constitutes the object of knowledge.

Because it pervades mere existence (*sattāmātra*). For there is no such thing as a manifold state characterized by the manifestation or non-manifestation of its own consciousness-power (*svacit-śakti*)— occurring when the effect exists at the time of the cause in the form of its own potentiality (*svaśakti*), and when the cause exists at the time of the effect in the form of the manifestation of that potentiality.

Furthermore, [the existence of the Lord] is not unestablished due to the non-perception of Him by the sensory perception of those such as ourselves, because His existence is established by means of divine vision. Moreover, Mahāmāyā, Māyā, and the rest are indeed the supreme and ultimate cause of their respective effects.

It consists of power (*śakti*). It is not, however, that Śiva and so forth are the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), nor that the *bindu*—which has impurity (*mala*) as its auxiliary (*sahakārin*) in relation to Śiva and so forth—is the auxiliary cause;
rather, it is that which possesses the power to generate Śiva, Śakti, and so forth, with Śiva acting as its auxiliary. Thus, the effect, the supreme *āmnāya*, is produced.

Because it is impossible for [the Lord] to abide in Śiva and others in the form of power alone; whereas in the case of bodies and so forth, He abides in the form of the manifestation of His power as modified by the concealment of His own nature. Thus, the term "non-eternal" is applied there figuratively; therefore, everything is consistent.

Therefore, because birth, death, and so forth are distinct, the existence of distinct selves is established; as stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other works: "The Puruṣas are repeatedly perceived as separate," and from the Śruti: "Therefore, there is no oneness"; and because their respective individual experiences are established as being repeatedly distinct.

This doctrine of a single self has been devised by those of deluded intellect and ignorance, such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others, and is thus falsely established. [Objection: But surely they too are omniscient; it is true that they do not know what is beyond their own limit, so there is no fault. [Reply: That is incorrect.
If the Sugata is omniscient and Kapila is not, what is the basis for this distinction? Or if both are indeed omniscient, how can there be a difference between them?

Thus, although the sages have dispelled the fallacious arguments of wicked logicians according to the method described, they, being under the influence of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of that [dualistic] scripture, urge him again: "Now, just as space [is present] within jars, pots, buckets, and so forth..."
Just as that [space] remains one and the same, so too the Self (ātman) is situated within bodies.
The meaning of the verse is clear: "The water-drawing vessel has a hole, and the nose [is like it]. The Lord says:
"And that space is of a single form, but consciousness is not held to be thus."
When one person has the desire to eat and another has the desire to go;
Thus, it is established that consciousness is of a different nature from this [body];
for if it were non-different, then everyone would simultaneously desire to experience [the same object].

(p. 371) Everywhere—in jars, water-jars, and so forth—that space, which is situated [within them], is inferred to be of a single nature by way of its effect, which is characterized solely by its own term "space.
In the same way, consciousness is not accepted as being of a single nature. Why? To this he says: "In order to experience," and so on. When...
At that time, at that moment, thus and in this manner, from this— due to the distinction of desire (icchā)— at one time, at one moment,
the other object is clearly perceived. The sages have not stated [this] because of the distinction of the attributes of the Self which possess limiting adjuncts (sopādhika).

[Objection: But we have already stated that this is due to the difference in the attributes (*dharma*) of the self (*ātman*) when it is possessed of limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*). This is the intended meaning: desire (*icchā*) is a modification of the mind (*manovṛtti*); therefore, the difference in those desires results ultimately in the proof of a difference in minds.
For it has been stated that the nature of the mind is the attribute of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāradharma*). [Reply: That is incorrect, because of desire...

Because its nature is consciousness (*cit*), it possesses an exertion established in itself characterized by the manifestation of objects; for it is impossible for that [consciousness] to be conjoined with insentience (*acetana*). Since it is certain that desire is a function (*vṛtti*) of the power of consciousness manifested by the mind, [desire] does not belong to the minds. Therefore, the scriptures [teach] that [the self] is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

Bondage and liberation must be admitted as belonging to the selves (*ātman*) alone through their involvement in phenomenal existence (*pravṛtti*). Otherwise, it would be like saying that the mother is barren; for if there were only one non-dual Brahman as the ultimate reality, then the claim that knowledge alone is the means to liberation would be like speaking to a barren woman. As it has been said:
In the *Mokṣakārikā*:
"The vision of oneness is the means for liberation; however, it is sublated by one's own self.
For one who establishes a distinction between the liberated, the liberator, and the agent of liberation, [liberation] would not come to pass. Thus it is said.

Thus, when liberation has been accepted, in order to avoid the consequence that the liberation of one would entail the liberation of all, a plurality of selves must be admitted. For the scripture states that "the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth is the characteristic of the person's enjoyment," and because a diversity in that [experience] is observed, it follows accordingly.

The proof of the difference between things inhering [in a common substrate] does not lead one to abandon the delusion that individual manifestations are identical when the universal is one. Furthermore, the reality of an object is established by its own self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), because it is not cognizable by anything other than itself. That which is not cognizable by anything other than itself is established by its own self-awareness and is real.

It is like Brahman. Nor should it be asked, "What follows from that? For each individual self appears in its own consciousness as distinct from other selves, precisely because it is merely a portion of the supreme Self.
If even that which is established by one's own experience were unreal, then if, on the other hand, one's own experience is real—
In that case, she [the Śruti] would be perceived as either dissolved or unreal, being an opponent to the non-duality of Brahman.

However, according to your view, since even the Śrutis are ultimately unreal, the fabrication of truth regarding them would be as baseless as the drawing of many rabbit-horns or the perception of two moons; for even Brahman— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument presented.]

If [the world] were identical to Brahman, it would be blind and non-existent; or else, if its non-difference from that [Brahman] were established in some way or another, then since "all this is indeed Brahman," who could do what to whom?
Thus, it is incoherent. Furthermore, if there were knowledge of Brahman as distinct [from the world],...

If Brahman is always and in every way the body [of all], then the state of being unconditioned by any body whatsoever arises; thus, the misconception will vanish. If, at any time and in any manner, it is not conditioned by anything whatsoever, then the abode of consciousness resides in one place among the body and so forth.

It is so. Indeed, for those reciting the *Bhāṣya* which has a single essence, a state of self free from delusion will never reach complete perfection. The Lord, having previously placed all this in his heart through the words uttered from his own mouth, said:
O noble ones, if the non-difference of the atom were established, then it should be stated accordingly;
however, when difference has been proven by reasonings, it is not auspicious to accept its non-establishment.
For this very reason, when the space within a jar is joined with dust, smoke, and so forth, not all [spaces] are joined in that same way; thus, this [objection] is no ornament [to our position].

(p. 375) These are the elder brothers. Since the non-difference of the atomic self (*aṇu-ātman*) has been established through reasons consisting of its innate qualities (*svābhāvikadharma*), one must speak of it as "this" along with its adventitious attributes (*sopādhikadharma*) in order to avoid the conventional usage of perceived difference. [This is done] by means of arguments that firmly establish the innate difference within the self.

When the difference [of the subject] is established by means of its characteristics, its own cognition, and its nature as a phenomenon (*dharma*), then the acceptance of non-establishment (*asiddhi*) therein is not auspicious. Thus, the meaning of the verse beginning with "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is clear; it demonstrates the prior non-establishment in the reason (*hetu*) employed for that purpose.
As for what was previously urged— that "difference is a property of the object of cognition"—
that reason is unestablished (asiddha) here, because it applies to both objects that are cognized and those that are not.
Even if difference were established as residing in both [the subject and the object], there would be no lack of knowability for the Mother;
nor would there be a loss of Śiva’s omniscience if the sentient selves were not objects of knowledge.

The knower is not merely the act of knowing (*jñapti-mātra*), because it is the grasper of the object. Here, regarding the establishment of non-difference, since difference is a property of the object of cognition (*meyadharma*),
that reason which was previously employed and by which [the opponent] suspected [the proof to fail]— that very reason is [refuted by the fact that] the object of cognition...

Being conjoined with both the means of knowledge (*meya*) and the object (*artha*), it is unestablished (*asiddha*). Merely because it resides in the subject (*pakṣa*) consisting of the form of the object of knowledge, it becomes unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*). To the question "Why is that?", he says: "Even difference (*bheda*)," meaning that when the distinction between the measure (*mātra*) and the object of measurement (*meya*) is being made, even difference [is established] through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for that [conjunction].
Even though they possess mutually dissimilar characteristics, [the two] would nonetheless reside in both by virtue of being the delimiting factors (*paricchedaka*).
Furthermore, why should the mother not also be the object of knowledge? For the sense is easily established by supplying the word "of Śiva" (*śivasya*).

This has been stated from the perspective of the Naiyāyikas. The underlying intention (*āśaya*) is as follows: regarding an object that is not an object of knowledge (*ameya*), [if one were to consider it] as an object of knowledge...
The "limit" (*amiti*) of even the omniscient Śiva is not a defect, but rather an ornament;

for as a cognizable object (*meyatayā*), it is merely the state of being limited by the objects of cognition, since [Śiva] pervades all that is measurable. Just as Śiva perceives his own self as distinct from the objects of cognition, he is the one who does not contemplate anything other than himself.

He perceives them directly as mere appearances. Thus, by his own power of consciousness (*svacicchakti*), he perceives them directly—because they manifest in some way as being dissimilar to the objects of knowledge (*meyavisadṛśatayā*), yet because their manifestation is based on a well-observed similarity to himself. Therefore, "consciousness" (*cit*) here is Brahman; it is not omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and so forth.

Their qualities are adventitious because they are dependent on limiting conditions (*upādhi*). This very point has been raised as a doubt regarding the Three Jewels: "Due to the influence of objective conditions (*kāryopādhi*), there may indeed be what is called 'power' (*śakti*) in consciousness; however, the power of the conscious subject does not actually exist in dependence upon anything else. As for the phrase "some [say]": from that, the impairment of its omniscience is not accepted.
Anticipating the objection of an opponent in his heart, he refutes it with the words beginning with "jñātā" (the knower).
This Śiva—the word "ca" (and) being used for the purpose of conjunction—is the Self;

and although he is by nature a knower characterized by self-consciousness (*svasaṃvit*), he is a "perceiver of all" (*parisaṃvettā*) because he possesses universal consciousness (*parasaṃvit*), and not merely a "knower" (*jñaptṛ*).

It is not merely that the nature of consciousness is devoid of the distinction between self and other objects; for it would be an inferior description to say it is "devoid of another's cognition" and "of the nature of one's own cognition. In the term *svasaṃvit* ("one's own cognition"), what is supported by the word *sva* ("one's own") is a cognition that is self-known (*svasaṃvedya*) yet dependent upon another. However, that which is supported by the word *saṃvit* ("cognition")...

Consciousness is said to be independent of others, dependent upon the consciousness of another established by its own locus, and characterized by the immediate nature of the consciousness of another established by its own locus. This applies even in the case of the term "self-cognizable" (*svasaṃvedya*).

Self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is said to be established by its own terms and independent of anything else. On the other hand, awareness of another (*parasaṃvitti*), which is an object of cognition, is established by words and dependent on another;
here, in the term "awareness of another," "another" refers to objects of consciousness other than oneself, such as the mind and mental factors.

Cognition supported by words is called "supreme cognition" (*parasaṃvitti*). In this way, through some [intermediate] means therein, another [cognition] is not established. Why? Because the knower is always observed to be one who grasps the object and knows the meaning of the word. As it has been said in the *Mṛgendra*:

"Because he is the creator of all, the Omniscient One knows everything along with the means, the constituent parts [of those means], and the fruits; whatever he knows, he creates that very thing—this is well-established. Thus [it was said]. The Sages said:
This very one is designated as having the nature of cognition; his state of being a knower is considered to belong to the Great One (Mahat).
In the Tantra as well, this Maheśvara is held to have the nature of the great determinative faculty (adhyavasāya).

O Maheśvara! This individual soul (jīva), designated by us as the Supreme Self (paramātman) and known as the non-dual Śiva, has been perceived by us as the nature of pure consciousness (jñaptyātman). As it is stated in the Sūtasaṃhitā:
"Due to its atomic nature, there is never any difference between the conscious [Self] and the Consciousness [itself]."

The state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is the state of being conscious of both self and other; this is intended as the definition of the Great Intellect (*mahatī mati*). And in this very system (*tantra*), it is heard—that is, the remainder of the statement is that "the Great One is intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature is determination (*adhyavasāya*), and whose form is the apprehension of the object"—thus [it is said]. The Lord—
In this world, all living beings are always seen to be knowers;
this quality of being a knower does not belong to the intellect (buddhi), because it is insentient.
All those who know the Vedas, from the liberated ones at the beginning up to the supreme self, are non-dualists;

and as for living beings like us, they are indeed knowers of non-duality in this world, perceiving their own consciousness and the consciousness of others. This is always observed. Now, one might object: let it be that there is no bondage simply because of such a conviction.

That [notion of] being a knower is not [the case]. This state of being a knower, which is experienced as the perception of various objects by another, is not Buddhist. It is not logical that it inheres in the intellect (*buddhi*), because that [intellect], being non-intelligent, is insentient (*jaḍa*). But how can there be an inherence of consciousness in an insentient self?

It is proclaimed by those who speak according to logic (*nyāya*). As it has been said: because the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) is to be established later as being non-different from its qualities (*guṇa*) due to having that very nature. He states another objection:
(p. 381) "Furthermore, cognition is always manifested here by [mental states] such as understanding (*buddhi*)."
Moreover, the self is indeed experienced as that which illuminates both itself and others.

Furthermore, since its nature as the illuminator of others is eternal, it is an eternal attribute; moreover, for this reason also, it is not established by pure consciousness alone, because in this body, knowledge arises from the state of being a knower through the intellect and other faculties by means of their own effects, such as illumination.

It is always manifested; therefore, one should not ask, "From where does it arise? For it has been examined in the *Bindupatala* that what is a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is not itself the manifested (*vyaṅgya*). Furthermore, the Self is indeed perceived as the illuminator of the Supreme Self, eternally undeluded, and consisting of the awareness of both self and other objects.

Alternatively, being self-luminous due to its independence from a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), Śiva—like the sun which illuminates itself and others—manifests a power similar to its own within another, namely fire characterized by the sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*), thereby illuminating both itself and the other. Just as the sun is the illuminator of both itself and others, so too is Śiva. (p.)

382) Because it is independent, having become self-luminous, it manifests its own power— which is similar to its own nature, which liberates others from their mere bonds, and which illuminates both itself and others— thereby becoming the light of both self and other. Thus, the impurity produced by the power of the liberated Śiva [is removed].

Immediately upon the complete manifestation of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*), which is the cessation [of limitation] at the very limit of power, there is no further recurring dependence as there is for the power of the bound soul (*paśu-śakti*). This is because the power is independent of any manifestor.
Having become Śiva, one will shine forth by oneself like Śiva himself; in others, it remains merely as a fetter (*pāśa*).
Between the liberated and the unliberated, there is no obstruction for oneself; thus, by necessity, one's own mind arises as neither bowed nor elevated toward the thought of Śiva.
One whose office is practiced separately from Śiva, being equal to Śiva, [perceives] his own power as similar to his own power, and his own power as even more so.

Manifesting the power that illuminates others as distinct from himself, Śiva is experienced as both self-illuminating and illuminating others, just like Śiva himself. Since his own consciousness does not expand outwardly as something separate, he is experienced as being without pride toward the consciousness of Śiva; and because it is his own consciousness, he is experienced as not being the creator of the world.

Furthermore, it has been stated that the teacher, through the refinement of his own mind and by means of the instructions of previous scriptures, awakens the power of consciousness in others according to their own capacity and in accordance with their nature, while being dependent upon his own inherent power; thus, the light of both self and other is experienced. Now, one might object:
Since it is observed that the illumination of another is subject to destruction, how can it be the very nature of the Self?

Not so; for just as self-illumination is eternal, so too is the illumination of another, because an eternal quality is a property of an entity that exists at all times. This is the intended meaning: cognition is manifold.

And it is of the nature of ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*). Among these, that which was mentioned first—the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—is "knowledge" (*jñāna*) in the sense that "by this, something is known. Being of the nature of illumination, it is not the manifestation of ascertainment; rather, it is the well-expounded light of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is indeed impermanent. For, in relation to that [intellect]:

The cognition of a cloth is distinct from the cognition of a jar, and so forth; yet that [cognition], having become the object of the meaning determined by its own manifestation, remains subsequently as a form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) directed toward another, adhering to the synthesizer who remembers it— even when that mental [cognition] has vanished.

Even when the light of a lamp has been extinguished, like the residual radiance directed toward the eyes, it remains unextinguished and shines forth once again upon the proximity of its auxiliary conditions. [Objection: But is it not the case that the state of being a knower, though superimposed, appears as if it were one's own true nature due to delusion? [Reply: He says "no" to this:
This quality of being a knower cannot be produced by superimposition;
for it is accepted that the superimposition of attributes observed in one thing occurs upon another.
Since the status of being a knower cannot be established for anything other than the Self, superimposition is not accepted here.

This quality of being a knower—which is self-luminous—cannot be produced by superimposition (*adhyāsa*) nor can it be something superposed (*āropita*). For [the qualities] observed in one thing, such as a snake, do not [transfer] to another, such as old age.

The superimposition (*adhyāsa*), that is, the attribution (*āropa*), of [objects such as] a cow and so forth upon something else, such as a rope, is accepted. To this it may be asked: "What follows from that?"—but this need not be stated.
By supplying the word "anywhere" (*kvāpi*), the meaning becomes easily understood; this very point is experienced through one's own direct experience (*svānubhūti*).
For there is no delusion (*bhrānti*) with respect to one's own self. As it has been said in the *Sarvamālambane*: [textual citation].

How could it not be an error within its own self? If that [consciousness] were indeed an error, then even according to your own view, Brahman—which is established by one's own experience—would result in being unreal; thus, everything would become like the horn of a hare. But surely, one's own experience arises from an unreal limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)...

If, after the accomplishment of Brahman, it were to dissolve and become non-existent, this would be illogical; for in that case, Brahman too, having dissolved, would become non-existent. Why? Because it would lack any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, when the accomplishment of Brahman is postulated, then again—(p. 386)—that...
Experience arises as an accomplishment. If this is so, then Brahman too would arise;

thus, in the state of Brahman, one does not see an end to the submergence and emergence of self and other. Therefore, that which is characterized by being known as "other than itself" is the state of being a knower, and the state of being a knower characterized as "other than itself" is its inherent nature.
Since [the nature of reality] is established by one's own experience arising from self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), Śiva and the Self are not mere consciousness (*jñaptimātra*). [Objection:

But surely Śiva’s status as a knower is dependent upon an object of knowledge; therefore, arising from the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the object of knowledge, it is not innate. [Response: That is incorrect, because Brahman is mere consciousness.
Even you, while reciting [the scriptures], if asked by someone "What is cognition (*jñapti*)?", what would you say?

We, however, say it is knowledge (*jñāna*). Then, if he were to ask again, "In that case, what is its object (*artha*)?", what would you say? And if he were to ask further, "Is there no such thing as knowledge without an object?"—what then? It is a different category (*arthāntara*).

Furthermore, what is experienced? Having honored the Śruti which states that "the Self is the illuminator of its own nature," you should provide an answer as to whether it is [illuminating] itself or something other than itself.
Otherwise, fearing that [the argument] might be established otherwise, he refutes it:
Now, if the body were sustained by the intellect through the reflection of consciousness (cit),
then the intellect and so forth would also become consciousness itself through that reflection of consciousness.
For it is not the intellect that is sentient, since the nature of consciousness is reflected within it.

Now, if this were not so, the intellect would not possess innate subjectivity; rather, as in the case of the moon in water, the body is sustained by the intellect through the reflection of consciousness within the intellect, along with the experiences of pleasure and pain.

[It] would [be so]. For indeed, in that case, even the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth would become conscious (*cit*) by means of the reflection of consciousness (*cit-pratibimba*), because a reflection is observed only in that which possesses similar properties (*samānadharmī*). Alternatively, the self (*ātman*), being of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), would be sentient; for it is reflected in the intellect, which is devoid of the nature of consciousness. Therefore...

If one were to postulate another self [behind] the [notion] "there is no self," there would be an infinite regress. To this, he says: "And this reflection is not considered to be of the nature of consciousness, the Self. (p. 388)
The transition of the insentient into the insentient is logical for that which is subject to transformation.
Even a reflection of consciousness and so forth would not exist in the self, because it is impossible;
this doctrine of mutual superimposition is merely imagined by those of false views.

The meaning is as follows: because consciousness has reached a state of transformation [into the intellect], it does not pervade the insentient; for consciousness is not in the insentient, nor is the insentient in consciousness, nor is there a reflection of the insentient within consciousness.
This mutual... discourse is as follows:

through the reflection of consciousness in the intellect (*matau*), the superimposition of consciousness occurs; and by means of the reflection of that [intellect] in consciousness, the nature of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is produced.

The statement of mutual superimposition is constructed by those of false views; it is fashioned by treatises composed by those who are not omniscient. Other categories of objects are likewise [imagined]. Now, while there is a transfer of contact—as in the case of musk-scent and so forth being transferred to a cloth—why is it that a reflection is not like that? (p. 389) What is the point here?
It is true that it is expressed by the word "transference" (*saṃkrānti*). Even though there is no actual transference,

because the transformation is pervaded by the non-conscious [matter] which possesses similarity [to consciousness], the reflection is designated by the word "transference" (*saṃkrānti*), or the transference is designated by the word "reflection" (*pratibimba*), for the purpose of avoiding the faulty expression [that would otherwise result].
"Is fully explained" means it is thoroughly understood. And regarding the verses on experience (*bhogakārikāsu*):

in the passage, "Just as the reflection of the moon in water is the bestower of enjoyment upon the object of enjoyment," this refers to the sense of reflection; and in the passage, "Experience is the coloring of the modification of the intellect," this refers to the sense of transference. As for the mention at the beginning:

In the *Buddhiprakāśa*, the teachers maintain that the first illustration merely demonstrates the manifestation of the specific nature [of the Self] by virtue of its relation to the objects of enjoyment and the enjoyer; the second statement, however, serves to convey the mere fact of making that [nature] an object of cognition. The Self...

Just as a magnet moves its own body without physical contact, Śiva likewise impels the entire universe through the mere proximity characterized by a connection with His power, which is distinguished by the activity of His own volitional action; this has been stated previously and will be explained further as the occasion arises.

We state this clearly: thus, the mention of conjunction with impurities (*mala*) and so forth in various places is established by reasoning as being intended merely to indicate a relationship. Furthermore, Śiva, reflected in the intellect which stands in the place of a mirror, is here well-recognized as the *puruṣa*.
Thus, those who are permeated by the views of the Sāṃkhya with a Lord (Seśvara-sāṃkhya) are also refuted. [Objection:

But surely, since scripture states that "the perfected state (siddhi) is the complete awakening regarding the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower," how could the Person (puruṣa) not be illumined by the light of cognition? [Reply: True; it is not as an object of illumination, but rather in relation to the manifest and the unmanifest.

For the Puruṣa shines forth by itself as utterly undifferentiated from the intellect (buddhi) due to its being the illuminator of that [intellect] for the sake of cognition; this is because the possessor of eternal qualities has qualities whose nature is non-different from those [qualities]. He states that this [cognizing capacity] is eternal: "The state of being a knower is eternal for it."

O Lords of Sages, that nature of being a knower is also eternal, because it is a property (*dharma*) of an eternal entity; for there can be no subject possessing non-eternal properties, namely, an eternal self.

The meaning is quite clear: [the Lord] exists not as one who occupies only a single location. He says: "And that [consciousness], because it is a quality of the omnipresent [Self], is not desired by anyone to be otherwise; therefore, the Self is established as eternal, the seer and agent of all objects."

Moreover, that quality of being a knower is not admitted to be occasional or partial, because it is an attribute of the omnipresent [Self]. It follows that its eternality, too, cannot belong to an occasional entity.
Therefore, the Self remains the perceiver and agent of all objects, whether in the state of liberation or non-liberation, respectively.

Established as the manifest, the unmanifest, and endowed with the state of Śiva—thus demonstrating that otherwise there would be contradiction, and indicating that the argument of those who claim object-dependence is merely adventitious is to be treated with derision—it exists by its own innate nature even in states such as deep sleep and so forth. (p. 392)
And he states its dependence on objects and so forth:
"If its status as a knower were merely occasional, how could there be omnipresence?
For as far as the substrate extends, so far must its attribute abide."
Just as whiteness residing in a cloth exists pervading the entire cloth,
so too does the state of being a knower always exist pervading the self.
Furthermore, cognition is not devoid of an object and does not depend on another by its very nature.

If even the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*)—though it is a property (*dharma*) existing only occasionally—belongs to this self (*ātman*), which is the substratum (*dharmin*) characterized by that property and possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then from where could its omnipresence (*vibhutā*) arise? This is the logical connection (*anvaya*).
Knowledge is not devoid of its own nature as the characteristic of a dharma; nor is it devoid of its object by virtue of its own form when free from adventitious conditions (*anupādhi*).

Knowledge, which is the characteristic of the substratum (*dharmin*), appears as if dependent on itself, yet it is dependent on another—namely, the object—and that very [dependence] is its power (*śakti*). Furthermore, that same [knowledge], being dependent on itself, is the possessor of that power (*śaktimat*).
We shall clarify this in the *Pramāṇapaṭala*. A "clear" [object] is one other than that [unclear] category of things. (p.

393) Thus, when the views of certain modern Śaivas who have cast their own shadows into the womb [of our argument], as well as the views of the Vedāntins, have been refuted, we shall incidentally address the matter of the *Digambara*s.
From the perspective of the Pāñcarātra, the sages raise this objection:
"If the atom's omnipresence were established, then its pervasion of [all] attributes would follow.
But how can there be omnipresence for that which is not perceived elsewhere than within the body?"

The phrase "other than the body" (*dehād anyatra*) is to be supplied. The meaning of the verse is quite clear. [The author] demonstrates the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reason—namely, "because it is not perceived other than the body"—which was employed to prove that the Lord (*īśvara*) is not all-pervading (*avibhutva*), by means of the very reason that establishes his all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*).
It is not tenable that atoms possess the same dimensions as the body;
therefore, because they perceive objects situated elsewhere than the body, [the self must be distinct from them].
Thinking, "I know this for certain," because he knows the object situated therein, he employs another reason: furthermore,
wherever there is a manifestor, such as the body, the sense organs, and so forth...
In all those cases, because its effect is observed everywhere, it possesses the nature of a pervader.
Furthermore, just as in those places where the palate, lips, and their conjunction serve as the manifestors of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
there exists the pervasiveness of space— since its own effect, consisting of gross sound,
is observed— likewise, in those places where the body, senses, and so forth serve as the manifestors, that effect exists everywhere.

Because it is observed that the manifestation of consciousness is characterized by causal efficiency (arthakriyā) which is identical with its own nature; thus, the pervasiveness of the mind is established. Furthermore, he rescues [this argument] by means of another reasoning:
"This [mind] is pervasive because it is formless, just like space."
And that knowledge which constitutes its nature is all-pervasive and directed toward objects.

The meaning of "space" (*vyoma*) is clear; likewise, having supplied the application (*upanaya*) "and this [subject] is so," there follows the connection in the form of the conclusion (*nigamana*): "therefore it is so. Furthermore, by the principle of "the lamp in the middle" (*madhyamadīpakatā*), from that [reason], because of its incorporeality (*amūrtatva*), it is just like the Self (*ātman*), being of the same nature as its properties.

The distinction is that cognition directed toward objects is pervasive (*vyāpaka*). [Objection: But surely, the pervasiveness of space is limited by its own effects. [Response: True. Here too, its effect is simply the cognition of the object to be known; therefore, that [pervasiveness] is established as being limited by that [cognition]. Now, [what follows]?

"It is not seen because it is obstructed by impurity," as he will state immediately below; thus, there is nothing inconsistent. Alternatively, by the word "space" (vyoma), either the *bindu* or Śiva is intended.
Or, its omnipresence is established by the statement, "Because its nature is consciousness, it is like the Lord. [Objection: But if it is pervaded by one [entity]...

In this world, the existence of anything other than that [the body] is not tenable; furthermore, there would be the persistence of karmic impressions (*saṃskāra*). That is incorrect, because [the argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to cold, smoke, light, and so forth.
Just as there is no confusion of karma among those who possess desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), distinction, and volition, even though they are formless (*amūrta*).
Likewise, there is no contradiction in the fact that [the Self] arises in a state that is untouchable.
Having thus refuted the Digambaras as a digression, he concludes the refutation of the Vedāntins:
"That consciousness which is eternal in nature is also devoid of an object."
This [objection] has been refuted by the presiding officer of the position (pakṣādhyakṣa), on account of its being the apprehender of both itself and others.
Since the atom is established by direct perception, inference cannot subvert that perception;
nor does the intellect possess the status of a grasper here, because its insentience has already been proven.

That consciousness which is eternal in nature—that by which an object is specifically known as "consciousness"—is said to be devoid of an object, like a barren woman's son; this position is accepted by the Vedāntins. [This is so] because the atomic self possesses the capacity to grasp both itself and others.

Because it is established within each individual through direct perception characterized by self-experience— which, by its very nature, is devoid of the characteristics of perceiving objects, the characteristics of self-awareness, and the characteristics of being either the primary subject or anything other than that— as it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "That [is] the knower of self and other."

Regarding the term "bhāvataḥ" (in reality): this is the meaning here. Since it has been stated in the *Parākhya* that the nature of the Self is of the form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), characterized by the qualities of perception (*dṛk*) and action (*kriyā*), [the subject] is mere consciousness-form in its self-awareness (*svavedana*).
In self-cognition, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the state of being the grasper of itself; in the cognition of another, it is the innate [power] belonging to the consciousness-form.
The state of being the knower is the result (*pramātṛtva*), and the state of being the knower of another is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);

this [distinction] is refuted by direct perception, rejected by immediate experience, and liberated from the snare. This very thing pertains to the fruit of human effort (*pauruṣika-phala*) in the fourth state (*turya*), wherein the power has been paralyzed by the force of the manifestation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) established by the beginningless snare of the intellect.
He is to be worshipped as pure consciousness (*jñaptimātra*). Therefore, those who know the Śiva scriptures [regard Him] as Śiva.

As it is said in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*: "When the mind of one's own consciousness has transcended the body, the senses, and the objects, there arises the state beyond [these], which is the emergence of Śiva-hood. Also, in the *Svacchanda*:

Having abandoned the contemplation of the fetters (*pāśa*), that which is indeed the concealment of one's own true nature (*svarūpālopa*) constitutes this pervasion by the Self (*ātmavyāpti*); otherwise, it is the pervasion by Śiva (*śivavyāpti*).
When one meditates upon the all-pervasive [deities] for the sake of qualities such as omniscience,
this pervasion by Śiva occurs within consciousness, having the nature of the cause.
[Objection: Is it not the case that omniscience and so forth are qualified (sopādhika) because they are produced by the state of the Lord?

[Reply: That is incorrect, for it is not manifested there, nor is it manifested there. Why? Because it is accepted that while the gross, conceptual manifestation is manifest in every respect, it must be sublated by another manifestation. [Objection: But...
It is argued that there is no inference to establish the self as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). That is incorrect;

for an inference does not subvert perception. An inference cannot be a subverter of perception, since the existence of one's own experience is established by perception through its nature as the cognizer of another [object]. How could an inference [subvert] that?
There is no contradiction whatsoever. As they have said:
"The final establishment of the means of valid cognition occurs in their own experience; since that very [experience] is self-cognized, what need is there for other means of valid cognition? (p. 399)

The meaning of the passage beginning with "not here" (*neha*) and so forth is easily understood. Now, one might object: "Since [the self] is solitary (*vivikta*), characterized by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-lakṣaṇa*), and distinct from another cognizer (*parasaṃveditr*), it cannot be well-cognized as another's awareness. To this he says:
"Furthermore, this state of being a grasper of this [object] does not exist for selves due to their difference."
But their own essential nature [is established] by virtue of their existing as the apprehending subjects.

Furthermore, what indeed is the characteristic of liberation for the self? Is this state of being a grasper (grāhakatva) of the perceivers something distinct from the perception of another, established through difference; or rather, is their essential nature such that, by virtue of being a grasper or a perceiver, it is not established as separate [from the object], but is instead oriented toward the other?
The intention is that it is experienced in such a manner because consciousness does not abide in parts.
He concludes with the aforementioned example:
"Indeed, an analysis of objects into parts is never appropriate anywhere."
Nowhere does the thought arise as to what [the world] would be like without the power of fire.
Therefore, the object is always established as having both a self-grasping and an other-grasping nature;

this is clearly evident. This is the intended meaning: for just as there can be no reflection or deliberation as to what fire would be like without its power characterized by burning and illuminating, so it is here.
Likewise, without the power characterized by vision and action, what kind of self could there be? For it cannot be said "it is such" or "it is not such.
Indeed, that very supreme consciousness, which is of the nature of power—like the light of a lamp that illuminates both itself and others—is itself the self-consciousness;
being existent, it is established as self-consciousness. Thus is the nature of the possessor of power and the power itself.
Because they are established as distinct entities included within the category of *paśu*, he introduces the following [verse] to examine that which has been declared to be stainless:
"In that same way, those who are omniscient by their very nature possess limited knowledge due to a cause. (p. 401)
By which [ignorance], all-knowing wisdom is obstructed and described as being defiled.
Just as Śiva is omniscient, so too is the Self; by its very nature, it is the agent that sublates all objects of worship.
Being effortless in essence, it is omniscient regarding the object of everything. Because it is not limited by time, it exists as pure being alone.
It is self-cognizable and inherent within supreme consciousness; thus, for us, it is our own realized experience.

The perceivers of their own self-awareness possess the characteristic of functional activity. As it is stated in the *Ratnatraya*: "When there is no bondage for the power whose nature is supreme consciousness, the supreme alone shines forth; therein, the liberated souls are incessantly [established]."
Therefore, all-knowing ones are liberated, but they do not perceive mere consciousness alone;
for whatever state exists—whether past or future—it exists at that very time.
"The immutable consciousness, being self-perceived, grasps the state of things as they truly are. (p.
402) If that is so, how is it that limited knowledge is now observed as an object of experience?
True; however, limited knowledge at this time consists in the pervasion of the objects of knowledge as delimited by the state of being knowable.

However, experience [of pleasure or pain] arises from a cause due to its being an object of enjoyment for one who is deprived [of sovereignty]; it is inferred that its power is augmented by the *kalā* and that it does not arise spontaneously, but rather from another entity opposed to itself. The meaning of "obstructed" (*niruddha*) and so forth is clear; it defiles knowledge (*jñāna*).

"Mala" (impurity) is so called because it conceals action; "sārvajñam" means this omniscience, that is, the state of being all-knowing, belonging to the All-Knowing One. However, the knowers of Vedānta maintain that impurity is a quality that stands in opposition to the knowledge of Brahman as it truly is; he refutes them [as follows]:
That substance from which action is turned away is like a cataract or similar [obstruction];
moreover, the impurity is a substance possessing manifold powers, just like fire.

And because that substance— the object well-known as "impurity"— is removable by ritual action (*karman*), it is dispelled by the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*); for this reason, it is not like a cataract (*paṭala*) and the like, which,
though removable through the medical treatment of an ophthalmologist and so forth, does not [function in the same way].

Substantiality (*dravyatva*) is subject to deviation. Now, if it is argued that the reason—"being removable by mere similar cognition" (*samānākārājñānamātranivartyatva*)—is unestablished (*asiddha*), then there would also be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*): namely, that action (*karman*) is removable because it possesses substantiality while being an obstacle, and a substance is [defined] by being removable by action. This is true; therefore...

Thus, he employs another reason (*hetvantara*) for the purpose of refuting that [previous] lack of proof: Furthermore, for this reason as well, *mala* is a substance (*dravya*), because it possesses manifold powers; otherwise, its obscuration of the infinite conscious powers (*cicchakti*) of the individual souls (*puruṣa*) would be inexplicable. Moreover, because there is liberation for one, there must be liberation for all.

Because of the observation that [the soul] has departed from its own office, even though impurity (*mala*) is manifold and insentient, it is established that it is impermanent due to its multiplicity, and so forth. If one were to seek a cause for that impurity, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, however, it is without a cause...
Furthermore, it obstructs even those who have been liberated. As it is stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
"That [obstruction] is either beginningless or posterior; its cause is that [obstruction], or otherwise.
If it were to obstruct only those already liberated, then the effort for liberation would be in vain."

This very point is established by the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*): namely, that the infinite [Lord] possesses the power of internal differentiation (*svabheda-śaktitva*) directed toward the removal of the limits of His own office. Just as Nala is the power of fire (*analasya*), so too, within the infinite objects to be known, dried, burned, and illuminated, He possesses powers differentiated by internal distinctions, which constitute the effects of those powers.

It is removed by the door. And that non-audible substance (*sonala-dravya*) exists for the sake of favoring those powers of impurity (*mala-śakti*), because it follows the attribute characterized by obstruction for the purpose of their transformation. The power of Śiva (*śiva-śakti*) also exists for the sake of favoring consciousness (*cit*).
Although it is engaged in bestowing grace upon the conscious subject (*acid-anugraha-pravṛttā*), it is metaphorically designated as a "bond" (*pāśa*) because it is concealing.
When that very [power], by means of another power— the *samuddheśa* (the act of summoning)— of this *mantra-liṅga*,
turns those whose impurities have reached their fruition toward liberation (*kaivalya*), then it is the bestower of grace upon the conscious subject.

Having come into being, it remains. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "The power of Maheśvara, which is auspicious (*śivā*) and bestows grace upon all, is metaphorically designated as 'bond' (*pāśa*) solely because it conforms to [the nature of] *dharma*."
When those [energies], having been transformed up to the limit of the obstruction (rodha), manifest as the unfolding of some poison,
then, O Infallible One, You are the bestower of grace.
Having thus accepted [the opponent's position] and formulated it as an alternative, he refutes it:
"In this case, if ignorance is merely the absence of knowledge, how can there be a state of being ignorant?
Or is it an appearance otherwise? No other possibility exists."

The meaning is that what is designated by the word "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is none other than these two: the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*) and erroneous knowledge (*viparītajñāna*). The meaning of the words is clear. To the question, "What follows from this? he says: (p. 406) "The absence of knowledge is not ignorance, because it [the absence] is incapable of producing any effect."
For the non-existence of a jar never fetches water here anywhere.

If it were the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge, then the arising of knowledge would necessarily follow. In that case, ignorance would be characterized by the destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) of knowledge, which is the absence of knowledge. Furthermore, the meaning of the passage beginning with "And it does not obstruct omniscience" and ending with "in some cases" is clear. Moreover, as for that which is here...

The non-manifestation of knowledge—which is a quality conditioned by the cessation of purposeful activity (arthakriyā) characterized by destruction—is its persistence in the form of potentiality (*śaktyātmanā*). This very state is considered the impurity (*mala*), whose fruit is the cessation of purposeful activity; it exists for the sake of the fruit of purposeful activity.

Furthermore, there would be the fault of non-difference between [the agent] and the action. If there were a difference from that [action], then because it would be insubstantial, there would again be the undesirable consequence that knowledge and so forth which remove it would be fruitless.
If it is the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge that is denoted by the word "ignorance" (*ajñāna*), then it is simply the absence of knowledge.

If that very characteristic which [defines a thing] were to exclude omniscience, then [the following would apply]: prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and the persistence of the capacity for action at the final limit; for these have been examined in the "Examination of Space" (*ākāśaparīkṣā*) because they are not causes of cognition.

Therefore, it follows that cognition would arise [without an object]. Since absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) are not applicable here, they are disregarded; now, he refutes the second position:
"Nor is this [cognition] otherwise, because cognition does not arise by itself without an object."
The cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell would not occur without a film [on the eye].

Otherwise, this would not even be ignorance (*ajñāna*), characterized as the conceit of "I" and so forth regarding what is not the self; for even in one who has transcended omniscience, there remains, due to the non-distinction of the intellect,
a form of perversion such as "I am happy," "I am suffering," and so on.

Because it does not arise by itself, it is obscured internally by another power; just as a cataract covering the eye is distinct from ignorance— which is removed by perfect knowledge through the mere presence of its corresponding condition— and is removable by perfect knowledge alone.

The cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl would not occur. As it is said in the *Ratnatraya*: "But that consciousness, when unperceived, evolves as various objects for a person whose power of vision is obstructed by impurity, just as the moon [is obscured] by the bonds of Rāhu."
Therefore, that which is the cause for the arising of ignorance must be removable by the knowledge of reality;

because it obscures the self and its instruments, like cataracts, it is established as a substance (dravya) since it is removable by action. Knowledge and the like, being the means, lead to immediate liberation with its seed.

It has been indicated [in the *Purāṇa*] that this [practice] is to be performed as an ancillary (*aṅga*) only for one who has just been initiated (*dīkṣita*), and thus it does not apply to everyone. Furthermore, having raised an alternative view, he refutes it:
"Moreover, is this knowledge adventitious (*āgantuka*), or is it otherwise?"
If it were adventitious, then its power would never be obstructive.

Furthermore, regarding this [supreme knowledge] which sets aside omniscience: is it adventitious, established from the beginning, or something else? If it is eternally established, what is its cause? If it is adventitious, then it is the power of consciousness (*vicchakti*), which overcomes the bonds and is established as the power called vision and action for those who have attained perfection, and so forth.

In the face of contradiction with scripture, it can never again serve as a sublater [of that scripture], for it repeatedly departs; thus even its liberation is like an elephant’s bath. "The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is not a sublater"—this reading is also easily intelligible. If it were established from beginningless time, then it would be a host of defects.
He said:
"If it were not adventitious, then that cognition would not be otherwise;
O twice-born ones, that object of knowledge would be impermanent, just like the cognition of silver."
The clear meaning of the verse is that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that wherever there is falsity, there is impermanence.
He states that even if the effect of concealment were absent, [falsity] would not follow:
"Furthermore, this cognition otherwise is not a sublater of right knowledge."
The cognition of mother-of-pearl is not seen to be sublated by the cognition of silver.

Immediately after the erroneous cognition "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl, there must arise the cognition "this is not silver, it is mother-of-pearl. Since right knowledge does not arise again until its own attainment, that [subsequent cognition] is not a sublater of the cognition of silver;
thus, in the reading "bādhaka," the *bahuvrīhi* compound is clear.
As for the meaning of the term: it should not be said that [the cognition] is a sublater because it is established as beginningless;

for it has been stated that error is pervaded by non-eternality, and thus even if something is established as beginningless, if it persists through a continuous stream over beginningless time—like the darkness of a lamp—it does not [sublate].
[Objection: But [the object] is sublated by a contrary cognition. To this he says:

"If, however, it is said that the relationship between those two is eternally established, even so, this [relationship] does not constitute a sublation of the cognition here, because its nature is otherwise."
Even that which is eternal would be subject to sublation by present cognition if it were otherwise;
for a lamp that has remained for a long time dispels darkness for a long time.
Now, even if—just as in the expression "one might split even a mountain with one's head"—the literal meaning is easily accomplished, it is used here in the sense of possibility. He concludes:
"Therefore, by whatever powerful object the knowledge of the self is always [overpowered]..."
It should be accepted that when they are contradictory, that which is called "impurity" (tanmala) would not be sublated at all.
This is clear. Therefore, he employs a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) reason to sever the doubt attached to that [proposition]:
"The Self is veiled by impurity, because there is limited knowledge despite its being all-knowing."
But he who knows nothing at all is not even covered by impurity.
Just as Śiva is, so too is this [Self], for it is not at all enveloped by impurity (mala).

The words "when the nature of the reason exists" and "is seen" are to be supplied as ellipses. Even in the case of a purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) inference, there is no such [separate] statement as "and this is not so," because the cognition of the positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) is already finalized through the medium of the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*). Therefore, the application (*upanaya*) begins with "and so is this," and so forth; that is, "and so is this, provided it possesses omniscience."
Since it pertains to one who possesses only limited knowledge, the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) must be supplied as an ellipsis.
The rest is clear. Furthermore, he employs another reason of that same nature:
"Moreover, if this [person] were not defiled, how could there be attachment to worldly enjoyment?"
If that [impurity] were present even in the stainless, it would also exist in liberated souls.

"Stained" means established in impurity. "Attachment" is the desire for enjoyment (*bhoga*) and the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*); the rest is easy to understand. Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*) in this case: the Self is veiled by impurity because it possesses attachment to enjoyments;
for whatever is not thus [veiled] is not thus [attached], as is the case with Śiva. According to the intention of the Sāṃkhyas, however, it is otherwise.
Anticipating this objection, he refutes it:
"If it is argued that passion is the cause of attachment, what then is the use of [the doctrine of] impurity?
It is true that passion exists as its cause; however, it can do nothing toward that which is already pure."
If it were possible for even Amala to be attached to power, then there would be no distinction between him and one who is liberated;
for neither the liberated soul nor Śiva is ever attached to worldly enjoyment.

If it is argued that the passion (rāga) under discussion is that which will be described as causing attachment to each respective object, and not the passion belonging to Māyā—which, even if it were inherent, has neither been extracted [from the Śiva-nature] nor established by another means of knowledge—then the intention [of the objection] is: "Why is it not so in the case of the Impure State (mala)? [The response is: In the Pure State (amala), passion does nothing at all; for in that state, there is no self-interest whatsoever.

Action is the ordainer. As it is stated in the *Svāyaṃbhuva*: "The purification of karma and the states of Śiva—these three purposes for all the world exist for the sake of enjoyment and liberation. (p. 414)

Here, by the term "śivatva" (the state of being Śiva), the power of Śiva (śiva-śakti) is expressed; by the term "mukti" (liberation), the two-fold manifestation of the state of being Śiva through the release from bonds (pāśa-vimocana) is expressed. The rest is easy to understand.
Whether he possesses the power of independent passion (rāga-śakti) or not, that [passion] is indeed a stain (mala).
He explains how it suppresses power in some way: "Furthermore,
since this passion and so forth is said to be of the nature of cognition (buddhi),
and since cognition is established as being derived from primordial matter (prakṛti), therefore this [passion] is perishable."
How could there be a sublater of this power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is eternally established?

It is not stated here that passion (*rāga*) is the cause of attachment; for [passion] consists of cognition and is present in the form of cognition when it has reached the state of being an object of experience. Therefore, it is mental (*bauddha*).

Furthermore, since the intellect (*buddhi*) is established as having arisen from *prakṛti*, this passion (*rāga*), being a quality (*guṇa*) thereof, is perishable. However, how could it possibly obstruct the eternally established power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), even at the time when that [intellect] is withdrawn, for that [consciousness] is never subject to concealment? It cannot obstruct it in any way whatsoever.
The Jainas (Kṣapaṇakas) argue: "Even during deep sleep, karma alone exists; therefore, why postulate a 'mala' (impurity) as a separate obscuring factor? He says that this is incorrect:
"O twice-born ones, it is not possible for knowledge to be obstructed by karma."
Because the object of action is that which is to be accomplished, while the person exists as its accomplisher.

The meaning of the verse is quite clear. This is the intended sense: immediately after the conjunction with *kalā* and the other categories, which causes the manifestation of consciousness (*cit*) by means of the removal of obstructions, there arises the relationship between the object to be accomplished and the agent of accomplishment (*sādhya-sādhaka-sambandha*) between *karman* (action/obscuration) and the *puruṣa* (the self). For this reason as well, he says "not indeed" (*na hi*).
Furthermore, since that [ignorance] is the sole cause of experience, how could it be an obstacle to experience?
For experience consists of cognition; therefore, there is no obscuration of that [cognition] by it.

Furthermore, that [karma] is the sole cause for the experience of action (*karmabhoga*), because it transforms directly into the form of pleasure and pain; thus, the "portions" (*bhāga*) are the second cause. How could there not be, in some way or another, an obstructer or subverter of that experience? Now, it might be argued: "We do not [deny] the subversion of the experience of karma."

It is said: however, it is the veiling of the power of consciousness (cicchakti). True. This [veiling] exists for that purpose, because experience consists of knowledge, characterized by the perception of pleasure and pain born of karma, and is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa).
Therefore, by that karma, there is its obscuration; that is, the concealment of the knowledge of what is to be done by the power of consciousness. For it is not...
It is stated; furthermore, he elaborates the reasoning therein:
"Action consists of merit and demerit, and those two are established as being mental (bauddha).
Since they lack all-pervadingness (vyāpti), how could they be binders everywhere above [the head]?"

This is easy to understand. This is stated in order to fully comprehend the intention of others: because even beyond the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the subtle body remains well-established within the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, and because at the time of dissolution, it enters into *māyā* in the form of power (*śakti*) along with karma characterized by its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Regarding his own view concerning the subject of the *vijñānakevala*, the intention is as follows: Furthermore, when there is an inclination toward experience (*bhoga*), how do those two [the *puruṣa* and *prakṛti*] function while remaining veiled? Even though they are engaged elsewhere, they may still serve as the cause here as well.
The conjunction of multiple principles is obstructed by the diversity of effects;
therefore, no established factor can contradict the power of consciousness and karma.

Furthermore, since those two—dharma and adharma—are engaged in producing experience (*bhoga*), and because even *adharma* is the cause of the sensations of pain and delusion, they fulfill their functional purpose by having as their fruit the experience characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion; thus, he explains their restriction. When they cease, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is no longer obscured.

They exert themselves; they become active even in other effects characterized by enjoyment and so forth, as well as in this [present case] regarding the obscuration of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), such as karma and the like. Although it is said that "one cause alone is sufficient for everything," the agency [of the self] is manifested through the distinction of effects, such as the act of manifesting.
The complication of multiple principles (tattva) resulting from the differentiation of duties—the conceptualization of many principles such as *kalā* and so forth—is obstructed;
that is, it is rendered defective and impaired. Therefore, and so forth, is easy to understand.

[An action] that brings about the manifestation of consciousness (*cit*) is incompatible with its own causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), whereas that which does not bring about the manifestation of consciousness is [compatible].

"No," [it is said], because it has been examined in the investigation of *māyā* that *māyā* does not perform impure causal efficiency (*malārthakriyā*), and thus it is not *māyā*. He concludes very well:
"Furthermore, how could an activity that is a manifestor be a sublater of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*)?"
It was stated in the examination of that [illusion] that even illusion would not be subversive.
Thus has *mala* been described as that which obstructs the omniscience of persons;
the meaning of the words is clear. If it is argued that *māyā* acts as an obstruction by way of its effects, [we reply:
in the states of dissolution (*pralaya*) and isolation (*kaivalya*), since that [obstruction] is absent, there would be no distinction between bondage and liberation for all beings.
Omniscience may be approached through the door of its effects;

now, it has been well-discussed that [the opponent's position] is not illuminating by way of its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), even though it is illuminating in its manifestation (*jñatva-prakāśikā*). Likewise, it is examined in some respect and in some manner. If it were subverting by way of its own nature, then [it would follow that] the end of oneness [is reached] through initiation (*dīkṣā*).

If liberation were the cessation of only one [individual], it would follow that all are liberated simultaneously. If, on the other hand, there were a plurality of such cessations, then since they are insentient, their plurality would entail impermanence; thus, it is self-evident that in the state of dissolution or isolation (*kaivalya*), there would be no distinction between the bound and the liberated, as there would be the consequence of their simultaneous arising.

[Objection: "But surely, as you have postulated for *mala*, let there be powers (*śakti*) belonging to that [impurity] which produce their respective effects for each individual soul (*pratipuruṣam*). [Response: That is incorrect. Since a power cannot possess another power, the causal state is simply the state of power (*śaktyavasthā*), while the effect is simply the state of manifestation (*vyaktyavasthā*). Thus ends the section on the effect.

Because its nature consists of power (*śakti*). It is only the powers for producing effects that are metaphorically designated as "its powers," but there is no power in it produced by an effect; this has been explained in detail in the context of the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), so enough with further elaboration. Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) alone is characterized by *tamas*, and thus it is not the five [elements] that possess all natures.

Those who are permeated by the Sāṃkhya view maintain that "impurity" (mala) is associated with the opposite [of the soul's nature]; these proponents of the impurity of *prakṛti* have now been refuted along with the followers of the Pāśupata and other schools who assert the impurity of *māyā*, as they have already been rejected by the refutation of Samanīti. Therefore, that state of dependence (*pāratantrya*) is bondage within that eternal [soul].

Like consciousness (*cid*) and so forth; the collection of means for liberation is useless, as it is sufficient to know [the truth]—so says the *Mṛgendra-śruti*. Since lack of independence (*asvātantrya*) and other such qualities are not inherent, it is established that they are due to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of impurity (*mala*);
thus, from this too, the existence of impurity is proven. For instance, souls are bound by some form of bondage...
They are bound because their lack of autonomy is observed, like sheep and other sacrificial animals. Regarding the term *mala*, he states that there are seven things to be expressed by it:
"Impurity (*mala*) is also to be known as sevenfold: delusion (*moha*), intoxication (*mada*), and likewise..."
Passion, another called despondency, heat, and emaciation as the seventh.
That which is considered inconceivable by all is proclaimed as "malina" (the defiled).

Its meaning is to be fully understood through the exposition of its characteristics and its examination. Now, one might ask: why is that which is designated as "saharṣaṇa" in the Mataṅga-tantra not mentioned here, while that which is designated as "satāpa" is mentioned again?

Why is "impurity" (*mala*) not mentioned there? There is no contradiction, as it is included within "despair" (*viṣāda*) and included within the "diversity of the path" (*travaicitrya*). Establishing the definition and examination [of the paths], [it is said]: "In this world, the impurity of delusion (*moha*) is innate to men, beginningless."
O best of the twice-born, because pride and the other [faults] are predominant among those seated in the womb (yoni).
When there is delusion regarding women and the like even for one who possesses knowledge,
he is renowned as "one possessed of delusion" (samoha) due to his failure to distinguish between what is to be avoided and what is not.
O best of the twice-born, among these seven, the beginningless innate delusion (*moha*) of men is characterized by a relationship between the unobscured and the obscuring;
because it is primary, it is the source of the six [defilements], beginning with pride (*mada*), which effect the refinement of the intellect (*buddhi-saṃskṛti*).

Due to the inclusion of the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), [the impurity] acts as a cooperative cause for the agent at the time of its arising. For in its absence, even though the bond of *māyā* exists for those who have been initiated and whose impurities have been transformed—such as those within the sphere of *māyā* or the products of the Egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)—intoxication and the like do not occur. Therefore, they indeed [do not arise] in their own production.

Because they act as co-operating factors for innate impurity (*sahaja-mala*). Although, when the intellect (*buddhi*) is withdrawn, they exist in the form of causes, yet while remaining as mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) within the intellect, they constitute the material cause (*upādāna-dharma*) for the karma that takes the form of the mental impression of the intellect— characterized by *sattva* and so forth— as an inherent property of the intellect itself, such as knowledge (*jñāna*) and the like.

The specific forms designated by the term "sahaja" (inborn), which consist of the states of experience— namely pleasure, pain, and delusion— and take the form of cognitions such as success (*siddhi*) and so forth, as will be described later,

serve as the instrumental cause for the emergence of *kalā* and the other categories; thus, they are classified as a quality of impurity (*mala-guṇa*) because they are equivalent to impurity in their function.

It is illustrated as follows: just as when there is darkness—denoted by the word "delusion" (moha)—which consists of the obstruction of vision, a lamp, although characterized by illumination, becomes a "perverse illuminator" of blue lotuses and the like, appearing instead as red lotuses and so forth, being itself denoted by the word "delusion"; likewise, when [ignorance] exists, even for the Self which is cognizant, the *kalās* and so forth [appear erroneously].

Even for one who possesses manifest consciousness and understands that "this is to be avoided" and "this is not to be avoided," there persists a delusion born of *māyā* regarding women and other objects— a delusion characterized by the manifestation of what is to be sublated upon the ground of the individual's manifest cognition, [arising] from the distinction between the avoidable and the non-avoidable, even though [these objects] are in reality eternally pure, blissful, and non-self.

They become manifestors of that which is contrary to it. As it has been said: "The power of Māyā is all-pervading and eternal, the deluder of embodied beings; delusion, however, is attachment to sense objects, just as auspiciousness is withdrawn."

The nature of the impurity known as *moha* (delusion) consists of the cessation of knowledge and agency; it is clearly established that even the *māyīya-moha* (delusion pertaining to *māyā*) is of the nature of impurity and is dependent upon the cause of delusion. He now states the essential nature of *mada* (pride) and the other [impurities]:
Even when he has obtained a woman, he praises her limbs as being supreme;
thus, intoxicated with passion, he proclaims, "She alone is a celestial nymph."
In its absence, there arises despondency and tearful eyes;
for that which is called the impurity of dejection is the giver of extreme suffering to living beings.
Thereafter, an internal heat arises, consisting of excessive lamentation;
that is known as "heat" (*tāpa*), and from that, the impurity of "withering" (*śoṣa*) occurs.
