But when one is stiffened in soul, because of which impurity becomes exceedingly difficult to overcome, [one thinks]:
"This is my kinsman, this is my wife, and this is my wealth and land, all of which are delicious."
Or rather, who is it that has accomplished his purpose by protecting me and my great family? Such is the thought that arises in men.
This [impurity] consists of various mental states and is designated as "diversity";
these seven are declared to be the innate impurities of men who possess stainlessness.
In the absence of that [the male], when a woman is present, one whose self is stiffened by a parched body [is described].
"Mṛṣṭam" means thoroughly cleansed or purified; because the term "mṛṣṭam" is general in nature, it should be applied everywhere.
"Eṣa" and so forth refers to the characteristic of variety (*vaicitrya*). As for the statement regarding the characteristic of passion (*rāga*), it is due to a scribal error.

For such a fallen state, since it is not stated that "the human [nature] is merely a part," the Veda must be reflected upon. The meaning of the other words is clear. Now, one might object: let delusion (*moha*), which consists of the nature of impurity (*mala*) characterized by the obstruction of the power of vision, possess both innate-ness (*sahajatva*) and the quality of being an attribute of impurity (*malaguṇatva*).

Anticipating the objection that "how can *mada* (intoxication/arrogance) and the rest not exist within the illusionary delusion (*māyīya-moha*), since they are properties of the intellect (*buddhi*)?", he says:
"Just as a connection is maintained for *kalā* and the others when [the soul] is stained by impurity (*mala*)."
In the same way, even while these exist, the *kalās* and other factors bind [the soul].
These seven properties of men possessed of impurity have been declared together.

Just as it is accepted that when impurity (mala), which consists of the obstruction of vision, exists, there is a connection between the puruṣa and the principles beginning with *kalā* for the sake of experience (*bhoga*), so too in these [seven] cases, there is a connection with the delusion pertaining to *māyā*.

Even in states such as intoxication, when the intellect (*buddhi*) has dissolved, that [state] exists in the form of its cause, because it consists of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that intellect.

These very [factors], beginning with *kalā*, bind the person (*puruṣa*). Therefore, for persons possessed of impurity (*mala*), these [factors] exist together with the delusion (*moha*) whose nature consists of the qualities of primordial matter (*prakṛta-moha-mala-dharma*) internalized within themselves.

The seven factors beginning with "intoxication" (mada) are said to be innate (sahaja), having arisen simultaneously as impure by nature. Having accepted the category of "impurity," the sages— being attached to their duties and possessed of doubt— entertain these suspicions:
The obscuration of that which has a non-inert nature by that which is inert is not logical;
nor is its veiling possible, because of its all-pervasive nature.

The obscuration—namely concealment—of the conscious nature of the Self by that which is insentient and called "impurity" is not tenable. Even if such an obscuration were to exist, it is because the essential nature of the Self is all-pervading; for the reason that must be employed is its pervasiveness, and thus there can be no obscuration.
It is logical. Regarding the Lord, he provides the rebuttal for the first position: (p.
428) "The eternal power, though non-inert, remains concealed within the atom—which is permeated by that which is called impurity—accumulated since beginningless time, as if it were inert."

It is said that this arrangement is constructed from adventitious [factors]; however, it arises from the cause known as impurity (*mala*), which is not adventitious, but has been firmly rooted since beginningless time, and which—due to its nature as a relationship between the concealer and the concealed—is perfumed by latent impressions (*vāsanā*). By the phrase "known as impurity," [this is indicated].

Since its substantiality is established, it does not exist as a quality within the self by virtue of some latent impression (vāsanā) produced therein; for if that were the case, the consequence would be that the self undergoes modification. Thus, it has been indicated by you that the eternal power of the atomic self, though non-inert, is obscured by the impurity of an inert nature.
This is a mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) here, which cannot be touched [by valid cognition]. He provides the reason for this:
"Furthermore, that which is non-inert is never sublated by what is inert, nor by what is non-inert, because of the cause of belonging to the same class, just as atoms [are not sublated] by God."

Just as the scent of the *nimba* bark and sandalwood is overcome [by one another], so too is that which is non-inert (*ajaḍa*)—consciousness (*cit*)—afflicted and obscured by that which is inert (*jaḍa*).

There is no obscuration by that which is not inert, nor by anything other than consciousness; for even the power of impurity (*mala-śakti*), which has the capacity for obscuration, is itself [manifested] by consciousness.
Because it has been stated [in the sūtra], "At the door. This very proposition [is established] from the reason of being of the same genus (*sajātīyatva*);

that is, from the reason of having consciousness as their sole common genus. Just as Īśvara is of the same genus as atoms and selves, yet He is not an independent destroyer; just as [a scent] whose fragrance is overcome by something of a different genus, such as water.
The neem bark does not once again conceal the fragrance of the camphor that has become latent;
rather, by removing its adventitious lack of fragrance, it manifests its inherent fragrance.
For there is indeed no third entity existing apart from the conscious (cit) and the unconscious (acit).

Therefore, it has been established that consciousness (*citi*) does not undergo concealment. Furthermore, since the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is non-inert (*ajaḍa*), by what could it possibly be concealed? Thus he insists [on this point]. Moreover, if the non-inert were to be sublated by the inert, then by what would that [inert] be sublated?
It is certain that the two entities are either non-inert or inert.
This is easy to understand. The power of consciousness is not obscured by another power of consciousness;
thus, having reinforced this point, he concludes:
"The self is to be sublated by that which is other than the self, because it has the nature of being subject to destruction by the sublater."
Without the destruction of that [ignorance], liberation from the obstacles would not belong to the conscious self (cidātman).
Therefore, one must accept that what is insentient is not [itself] non-insentient; [rather, it is] that which is to be sublated.

This is easy to understand. [The meaning is as follows: The power of impurity (*mala-śakti*) possesses a nature characterized by obscuration; its cessation consists in a transformation into another state of being characterized by the alteration of that very nature. This [cessation] takes the form of a transformation into another state of being characterized by obscuration.
As it has been stated: "There is no liberation without destruction consisting of concealment" (p.

431). The intended meaning is that there can never be liberation for those whose nature is to be concealed, as long as there is no destruction inseparable from the insentience inherent in the form of the concealing power of the Self. Now, [one might object]:

The destruction of one's own power as a concealer does not occur through a change into another form; rather, it is characterized by the concealment of its own form through a transformation into another form. However, this is incorrect, because that other power which acts as the concealer— [...is also... Please note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a philosophical argument (likely from a commentary on *Pratyabhijñā* or similar Śaiva Siddhānta literature) concerning the nature of concealment (*tirobhūti*) and the relationship between powers (*śakti*). The ellipsis indicates that the final portion of the sentence was either omitted or illegible in the source. I have translated the available portion while maintaining the technical terminology.

If it is argued that "so be it," then an infinite regress (anavasthā) becomes difficult to avoid because the meaning [of the relationship] is thereby censured. The sages, however, uphold the second position: "Even if the relationship between the soul and impurity is said to be beginningless..."
What is done there by the impurity, or is it merely the veiling of power?

Alternatively, its nature might be non-luminous; however, the first case is not tenable, because since that [nature] would be non-different from itself, it would follow that the self is likewise non-luminous.

Although that relationship between the impurity (*mala*) and the self (*ātman*), characterized as the veiled and the veiler, is said to be beginningless, what is actually done to the self by that impurity? The intention is that it has not broken anything there whatsoever. Or rather, the "veiling of power" (*śakti-āvaraṇa*) means simply its non-manifestation.

Among these, the first [position] is not tenable; for since that power is non-different in form from it, it would follow as a consequence that the omnipresent Self would also occupy limited objects. Nor is the second [position] valid, as he says:
Nor is there non-manifestation, because that would entail the consequence of destruction;
for even the non-manifestation of manifestation does not remain after its destruction.
O Īśāna, tell us all of that; O Lord, we have a doubt.
For there would be the undesirable consequence of destruction if there were no manifestation. Why?
Because even the manifestation of moonlight and the like is [effected] by the rays of the sun and so forth. (p. 433)

Nothing remains after destruction. According to the view that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*), the very concealment of one's own nature by another form of its own essence is accepted as "destruction"; thus, the intention is that even the concealment of one's own nature by another, as held by opponents, is metaphorically designated as "that" (destruction) because it is equivalent to it.
The meaning of the verse beginning with "tat" is clear. The Lord refutes this by restating their position:
"Nor is obscuration (āvṛtti) by impurity (mala) intended [as the nature of bondage], because the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is all-pervasive;
nor is it the non-manifestation [of objects], but rather the non-engagement in its effects."

The non-activation of the effect: having somehow brought under control that power of consciousness which was previously obscured, there is the non-activation of that power of consciousness with respect to its effects—namely, the two consisting of the activity of knowledge characterized by self-referential efficacy and the activity of action;
this non-activation constitutes a lack of mastery, characterized by non-knowingness and non-agency.
The phrase "the cause produces an effect contrary to itself" is to be supplied from the following verse.
The meaning of the other words is clear. He illustrates this:
"The power residing in fire is produced [as smoke], its own power being obscured by the power of the mantra."
It does not cause an immediate burst, even when the fire blazes up instantly.
Although its nature is not obscured, it is indeed concealed from its own powers by impurity; thus, it does not engage in its effects.
Just as when fire, which possesses a single power characterized by burning and illuminating, is blazing,
that power inherent in the fire remains unobstructed even though it is eclipsed by the power of a mantra—
because the nature of the mantra’s power is not different from its own— and is subsequently brought under control by that very power; so too [is the case here].
Just as that which possesses the effect characterized by its own burning does not immediately— that is, without exceeding that very time—
cause a blister, so too the individual soul (*aṇu*), though possessing the single power characterized by knowledge and action and having its nature unobscured—
that is, its power remaining unrepressed— is [rendered ineffective] by impurity (*mala*) alone through its own powers.

By means of [the powers] that are present merely by their own proximity and yet do not touch [the soul], its true nature is concealed; thus, with its power subdued, it does not engage in its functions such as cognition and the like. This is an illustration: its power is indeed concealed, subdued, and rendered subject to itself.

In the investigation of power (*śakti*), it is established that [the Self], whose nature consists of its own vision and action, does not engage in those effects such as the cognition of objects; rather, being opposed to that [state of freedom], it produces an effect characterized by ignorance and non-agency. However, an effect does not arise in the absence of a cause. Thus concludes the examination of power.

Because it will be explained later, the effect is set aside by means of the mastery over power characterized by the non-alteration of its own nature; that is to say, the sages have said that there is no power apart from the effect.
O Supreme Lord, Śakti has been described as having the nature of vision and action;
and these two should never be understood as being devoid of the capacity for knowing and acting.
For there is no effect beyond this, insofar as it consists of the nature of knowing and acting.

O Supreme Lord! It has been stated and defined that primordial power (*śakti*) consists of vision and action (*dṛk-kriyā*), and does not possess any other defining characteristic. And those two—vision and action—which are of the nature of the definition of power, are to be understood as the object of knowledge and the object of action.

When there is separation (*virahe*), because the causes for the perception of the nature of power as purposeful action are obscured, they never manifest at any time; therefore, from where [could they arise]? For, by virtue of their essential characteristics consisting of knowledge and agency—that is, being defined by cognition and action—[these two] do not [exist apart] from power.
Since there is no other effect to be desired beyond the purposeful activity characterized by the act of perceiving,
they say:
"How can the concealment of the capacity for action by impurity be explained?"
O Śaṅkara, power is not a separate entity from that which possesses it, just as the effect is not separate from its cause.
(p. 437) How can it be said that there is no removal of Śaṅkara’s [objection]?

Because it has been stated that power (*śakti*) is indeed the effect, as its very definition; for this reason, power is not a separate entity from the effect. However, if the reading is "the effect is [defined] by the aforementioned causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of power," [then the objection remains].

The explanation that "the effect is not a different entity" is easy to provide; therefore, for that reason, having brought the power (*śakti*) under control by means of its non-alteration from its own nature, tell me—explain how—how it is said that there is concealment (*tirodhāna*) of the impurity (*mala*) within the effect, which is purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). The Lord replies:
Power alone is not to be made [an object], because it consists of the vision and action of power;
when there is a statement of division regarding that which is undivided, that division arises from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Even with respect to each object, there is a connection; that is its function. But that which consists solely in the cognition of the other [the universal] is designated as "potency" (śakti).
This is the designation for that which is innate; it is obstructed by its own impurity.
When that is obstructed, its effect—consisting of objective sensation—is likewise ceased.
Therefore, the concealment of the effect, which resides within the impurity (*mala*), does not arise; for,

according to the principle to be explained in the passage beginning with "since it is a category of reality" (*padārtha*), power itself is neither an action to be performed nor an objective causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) consisting of the forms of knowledge and action, because power is the very definition of vision and action (*dṛk-kriyā*).

When there is no division—that is, no difference—between power (*śakti*) and its purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), yet a statement of experience (*bhoga*) or a statement of distinction (*bhida*) occurs, then that division and that difference [of the one] arise from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). This conceptualization arises from the limiting adjuncts consisting of the knower and the object of action. For this reason, a relation is established toward each respective object, object by object.
That very realization is the ultimate effect, and it is also that other purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*).

Apart from the direct perception of its capacity, there are the activities of knowledge and action whose essence is the capacity for purposeful activity—these are the innate purposeful activities. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:
"In the examination of Śiva and Śakti, because there is no distinction from that One object, the non-distinction of difference proceeds.
Since it is non-different from that, agency likewise exists through metaphorical attribution.
This is because [Śiva] consists solely of consciousness for the sake of others, while other entities such as Śiva and so forth are distinct from Him.

The mere existence of the categories delimited by "you" (tvam) is consciousness alone, designated as the power of infinity (*ananta-śakti*), impelled by that power. And this has been stated previously, in the *Śivaśaktiparīkṣā*:
"The cause of these two cognitions is said to be the power of consciousness, whose nature is non-dual. Of that [consciousness], which is characterized by its own self-awareness...

That which is designated as *sahaja-śakti* (innate power) and known by the other name of *śivatva* (the state of Śiva), belonging to that whose nature is supreme consciousness (*para-saṃvitti*), should be understood as characterized by the performance of its own causal function (*svārthakriyā*), which consists in making manifest everything other than itself. Action (*kriyā*), being of the nature of differentiation, is a causal function consisting of cognition; it is not the power (*śakti*) itself.

It has been stated that it must be produced. Just as the capacity of fire for burning and so forth is its innate specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), yet it is not itself the object of definition (*lakṣya*)— for the characteristic is non-different from it—
so too the transformation (*pariṇati*) [of consciousness] is like the capacity of a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) and the like to perform the purposeful action of granting desires.

Being free from the process of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), it possesses a proven non-differentiation; this is that very *arthakriyā* (causal efficiency), as stated in the *Ratnatraya*, in the *Śivaśaktiparīkṣā*:
"The immutable Consciousness (*cid*), though itself devoid of desire, performs the work of desire while acting through its will."
Just as knowledge is of the nature of ignorance, so too is action [of the nature of] non-action.
That object of knowledge, characterized as innate and by its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), is obstructed by impurity;

for it is well-known through inference that there is no conjunction between the formless and the embodied self. Therefore, without touching [the object], and by its mere proximity—without any alteration of its own nature—it somehow [exerts] its power.

Having brought it under control, it is made subject to one's own will. When that [object] is restrained, and when its innate power (*sahaja-śakti*)—the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) of that innate power—is concealed, then that effect and that power become the innate causal efficacy for each respective object; [it is] the object, whose nature is sensation.

For every object, the instrument is established as distinct and consists of cognition; it does not manifest [as independent] nor is it autonomous. Therefore, even when the power of the mantra exists alongside the power of fire—which is characterized by non-destruction—there is, as it were, the suppression of its own specific characteristics and effects, such as burning.

From impurity (*mala*), by means of its own power—the power of consciousness (*cid-śakti*)—the concealment of the effect, namely the obstruction of the aforementioned purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), remains established. Having accepted this, the sages (*ṛṣis*) raise an objection once more:
"That power which was previously directed toward objects [is now obstructed] due to the suppression by impurity."
O Lord, tell me how its stability remains when it is directed toward sense objects.

That power of the Lord, directed toward objects, is said to be the agent of its own causal efficiency (*svārthakriyā*), characterized by the activity of the knowable and the objects to be accomplished; however, due to the obstruction of impurity (*mala*),
and because it is brought under the sway of impurity, it is directed toward objects while its innate nature remains unimpaired, yet it is not independent.

If, due to the power of impurity (*mala*), its capacity for causal efficiency is obscured such that it does not perform that function, then tell me, if you can say so: how does this power remain established? Īśvara:
Just as the eye, despite possessing the nature of light, does not clearly perceive form due to the obstruction of darkness;
And it remains firmly established, even when directed toward sense objects.
And thus, although this power of will is defiled by the power of impurity,
it remains established as performing its own function of cognizing objects.

Just as the eye— by virtue of being a defining characteristic— is directed toward the object within the scope of its power to apprehend the eye, and thus binds itself to the intended causal efficiency (*svārthakriyā*) consisting in the grasping of that object; so too, even though it is clearly of the nature of existence (*satvarūpa*), its own causal efficiency, characterized by its own presence (*sadbhāvalakṣaṇa*), is likewise [bound].

Or, even though its nature is luminosity, it remains established in its own state with its own causal efficiency (*svārthakriyā*) unmastered [by anything else]. It is just like that. This power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), too, being defiled by the power of impurity (*malaśakti*), has its own causal efficiency—characterized by knowledge and action—which is established in itself, rendered subject to limitation (*saṃkoca*).

Expansion and so forth are possessed by that which is like a conscious being; it possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) governed by existence and non-existence, and it is the agent that performs the effect of object-cognition. Because it is the cause of inert, vibratory activity, it is also designated by the word "activity" (*kriyā*);
yet, even while performing the causal efficiency characterized by object-cognition, it is opposed to its own [inert] nature.
Having known [this], she remains established as the agent who performs the effects consisting of agency. He concludes:
"Thus has *mala* been described as that which obstructs the omniscience of persons;
for by this very [obstruction], he is joined with the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*)."

(p. 444) Thus, having been awakened to the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*) through the instruction on counting and so forth, it is understood that *mala* alone is the obstructer of omniscience for persons. Indeed, ignorance and the like do not exist [independently], because they are never dissociated from, nor separated from, this *mala*; without it, the term "bound soul" (*paśu*), which is designated by the word "bound," would not exist here.

Because of its connection with the [other] categories, this category—along with the impurity (*mala*) that constitutes the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*)—is enumerated as "the bound soul" (*paśu*).

Thus, the singular number for the six categories, the statement of their enumeration and definitions based on verbal testimony, and their prior examination have been enjoined and investigated. In this manner, the bound soul has been awakened and examined.
The fourth chapter in the commentary on the venerable *Pauṣkarajñānapāda*, composed by the teacher Jñānaprakāśācārya, a resident of Śrīśārlivāṭipura.
Hariḥ Om.
The Chapter on the Pāśas:
Now, O best of sages, let the pāśas previously mentioned be heard:
kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, and niyati.

O best of the twice-born, these five principles are illusory (*māyeya*). Now, following the examination of the category of the *paśu* (the bound soul), and because the term *paśu* is applied to one who is bound by fetters (*pāśa*), the fetters—which were previously mentioned and indicated by the word *paśu* at the end of the preceding chapter—are here examined. O [sages], listen!

The phrase "the bulls among sages" (*muni-puṃgavāḥ*) is a statement for examination. The connection is that "you should hear those [teachings] which are like jars being brought forth," according to the *Vātulīya*. However, that which consists of words has the nature of the category of *pāśa* (bondage), while that which consists of sentences is of many kinds, such as *kalādyavanipaścima*, *nitya*, and so forth.

The meaning of the statement "beginning with *kalā* and ending with *dīkṣiti*" is that within the aggregate of the *māyīya*, *prākṛta*, and *tāttvika* [categories], the five starting with *sakala*—whether directly or through a lineage—are produced from *māyā*; this is the intended sense.
The rest is easy to understand. In that regard, he demonstrates the causal function (*arthakriyā*) of *kalā*:
Having slightly pierced through all impurities by means of the expansion of consciousness,
[she] indeed manifests consciousness here by removing the stains of the *kalās*.

Among those five, *kalā* is radiant like a lamp; it is the manifestor of the power of disease, and like a child who possesses the latent power of internal and external imbalances such as wind (*vāta*) and other humors, it is said to be the liberator of the consciousness-power (*cicchakti*) of Śiva’s energy when it is directly present within itself.
As the internalizer of *kalā*, it is declared to be the beloved of Śiva’s energy, possessing infinite powers.

Because consciousness has not yet expanded, and because the *kalās* and other principles have been withdrawn during the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the individual soul—whose own powers have not manifested and who is subject to matured karma—becomes fit for that manifestation once again.

This statement regarding "birth" is made with reference to a specific class of individuals: those who, though isolated (*kevalin*) during the dissolution, possess residual impurities (*mala*) and karma, and are thus qualified for the pure state.

The scriptural statement that "those who remain outside of *prakṛti*, having abandoned the group (*bṛnda*), are the *pralayākalas*," is true in some respects. However, this scripture is figurative (*upasṛṣṭimatī*), for even those *sakalas* who are impure, performers of ritual action (*karmiṇaḥ*), and joined with *kalā*, are utterly deluded by *māyā*, as if they were situated within the cognition of the *natas*. This is because all impurities are one within the Impurity (*mala*). Thus, they belong to it.

The powers are said to be distinct for each individual. As it is stated in the *Mṛgendra*: "But because those powers are seen to be manifold and not simultaneous. Having slightly set aside their state of being entirely non-distinct, [this is done] because they are characterized by manifestation (*āvṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*). Likewise, having altered the characteristics of their functioning, [one treats] the impurity (*mala*).
Because it turns [the soul] back; because it causes one to fall, characterized by the cessation of the power of that impurity (*mala*). It manifests consciousness and empowers the intellect;
for he says, "This indeed is consciousness": "The power of the Self consists of the nature of consciousness, knowledge, and agency."
That [nature] is indeed manifested by a portion [of it], for it is that very same [nature] which was previously obscured.
And that consciousness of the Self consists of power, knowledge, and action; it is characterized by being the knower and the agent, which is the power of agency. As it is stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
"The power of agency is eternal in the soul, like the power of the Lord."
Because it is obscured by darkness, the object does not appear as something devoid of assistance.

That [power], consisting of knowledge and agency—their innate characteristics and essential nature—is previously expanded through its own functions characterized by cognition and action. That, however, is manifested by means of *kalā*. A certain portion of its own work is brought under its control; for it is precisely that [power] whose function remains veiled—this is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Or else:

Indeed, in the *Śrī Mṛgendra* and other scriptures, it is heard that *kalā* is the manifestor of the power of agency (*kartṛ-śakti*), while *vidyā* is the manifestor of the power of knowledge (*dṛk-śakti*). This is true. However, because the powers are essentially one with their respective functions, their manifestation cannot occur through a partial division; rather, it is the object of knowledge (*vaidya*)— *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument as presented in the source.)*

By means of its functional activity (*vṛtti*), the power of the single eye— whose sole duty is illumination— is uprooted from the door of the film (*paṭala*) and strengthened; and just as by the application of collyrium, so too by the activity of the arts (*kalā-vṛtti*),
the power of the impurity (*mala*) is uprooted from its door, and the one whose sole characteristic is knowledge and action, whose sole duty is knowing and acting, is strengthened.

Furthermore, the capacity of the agent that produces the definition must be thoroughly examined; when the object is clearly demonstrated by knowledge, the cognition attains its own causal efficiency (*svārthakriyā*) characterized by non-duality, and thus there is nothing inconsistent. He states that power is manifested through partial engagement with the constituent parts (*kalā*): [He says: "And power is manifested through partial engagement with the constituent parts."
This consciousness does not manifest within the individual soul in its entirety or in its constituent parts;
rather, it manifests according to one's karma, through a partial function of those parts.
Regarding the Sugata’s sequence of activity, he says that this is the initial stage for men: "And therefore, this bond of *kalā* remains as the first state for men;
for without *kalā*, their manifestation of form cannot be accomplished."
Therefore, this "bonding with *kalā*" (*kalābandha*) is the primary state of persons (*puṃs*).

Why? Because without *kalā*, even for those persons who are connected to the sequence of creation, as well as to bestowal, time, and necessity, there would be no self-consciousness characterized by its own unique definition—namely, the characteristic of being both knower and agent—which serves as their own mark.

But the nature of being a single agent is not established. Now, one might object: "Granted that the nature of having multiple agents is not established—due to the obscuration of its own function by impurity (mala)—since it possesses the form of a single cause consisting of the single specific characteristic of the action of cognition; however, what is the harm in this? To this, he says:
Consequently, that [object] would be a mere void without the expansion of consciousness;
for it is established as an object of apprehension, and there can be no apprehension of it without [consciousness].
Since it is the agent of the act of cognition— which is its own duty to perform through its cause— characterized by the perception of itself and other things as the subject (grāhaka),

it [the Self] exists in the form characterized by self-perception (svasaṃvillakṣaṇa) denoted by the word "possessor of power" (śaktimat). This form is inherent, composed of its own natural qualities, and established by the powers renowned as "self-perception" and "perception of others," which constitute its own instruments.

Because it is established as having the nature of a male agent; for without its apprehension, without the instrument characterized by the power of self-other cognition, and without its manifestation, that which has the form of an agent does not exist as if real.
Therefore, for that reason, without the *kalā* which serves as the manifestor, and without the expansion of consciousness (*caitanya*), [it does not exist].

If its own other-cognition were not manifest, then that [cognition], being of the nature of an agent distinct from the person [who cognizes it] and devoid of its own causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), would be as if non-existent; it would be non-real, or rather, it would be similar to what was previously stated: "other-cognition exists because self-cognition exists, and self-cognition is established. Therefore, by this [it is shown that]: "the capacity does not depend on another."
Those who have asserted that "the object exists as a reality," while remaining ignorant of the existence of objects such as the *bindu* and so forth, are refuted; [the author] concludes:
"Due to the non-existence of the apprehended object, the subject remains like a void."
To prevent that [defect], however, first, from Māyā, Kalā is born.

Because there is an absence of the apprehension of that agent; because the instrument, characterized as power (*śakti*), is unmanifested through the non-manifestation of its function, which is the cognition of its own effect; he is the grasper. Although the agent himself is not concealed, he remains as if empty; or rather, he exists with an unmanifested essential nature. For the sake of removing that [state], [the following is said].
By means of the dismantling of the assembly of the instruments that had been established, there occurs the dissolution of their existence as agents; this instrumental cause, however,

arises first at the commencement of creation from Māyā, through the agitation of infinite powers presided over by Śiva and Śakti, due to the relationship between the two Puruṣas as enjoyer and enjoyed caused by karma.

It arises. Then, because actions and the like have fulfilled their purpose merely by producing results such as pleasure, the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) aimed at dismantling the semblance of the agent's state of being is no longer possible. Thus, first, in due order and gradually, so that [the self] becomes undifferentiated from its own true nature, all other activities of the factors of action (*kāraka*) cease.

Because it serves as the cause: when the innate power of agency (*kartṛ-śakti*)—which is the characteristic of consciousness—is manifested by *kalā*, it becomes associated with the instrumentality of agency through that [manifestation] and possesses the activity (*kṛti*) whose form is agency. Thus, based on its etymological derivation, *kalā* is established as that which "measures" (*kalayati*) or "casts off" (*kṣipati*) impurity (*mala*). *Kalā* is called the agentive factor (*kartṛ-kāraka*) because it is the *puruṣa* embraced by its own impurity.
As it has been said in the *Mṛgendra*:
"O Brahmin, these two, existing together as if they were non-different from one another,
perform the agency and the action of the individual soul (*jantu*) in the process of experiencing [the fruits of karma]."

For it does not act as an instrument or an agent like knowledge (*vidyā*) and the rest; rather, it demonstrates its purposeful activity through knowledge. Thus, for the sake of the self's experience, knowledge arose from the principle of *kalā*; and for the one who has become an agent by means of *kalā*, there arises the object characterized by the intellect (*buddhi*).
In the teaching of Śiva, that which is the instrument for perception is *vidyā*.

Therefore, immediately after the birth of the *kalā-tattva*, from the *kalā-tattva* agitated by *vidyā-ananta*, there arose for the sake of the self’s experience (*bhoga*) the cause of the threefold sensation consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion; this was for the purpose of *vidyā*.
Having analyzed [the process], he demonstrates the action with the words "by means of *kalā*," and so forth. By means of *kalā* in the manner described, for the knower who has become the agent—

[that is,] for the action of knowledge characterized by agency, which has become the agent— and for the object characterized by the intellect (*buddhi*), the cause is the coloring by external objects such as women and the like.

In the perception of the form of pleasure and so forth that has arisen, there exists that [power] by which—being inseparable from the instrument and acting as the instrumental agent (*karaṇakāraka*)—the power that effects the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) of knowledge, characterized by experience, is brought to fulfillment; this power is manifested through its own function while remaining undifferentiated from its own function. Thus it is established.

Knowledge (*vidyā*) is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), which arises because the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—which consists in the communication of linguistic proficiency—is otherwise inexplicable.

In this way, we shall explain that in the causal efficiency of an action denoted by words such as "potter" or "pot," the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) which is the locus of the creative arts (*kalā*). [Objection: But is it not the intellect (*buddhi*)?

[The opponent claims: "The manifestation of the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*) is the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) that manifests the consciousness of the intellect (*buddhivijñāna*); this is the various purposeful activity fashioned by knowledge (*vidyā*). This is incorrect. If that were the case, then even for the followers of Kapila (*Kāpila*), if the fashioning of the mind (*manas*) as the manifestor [of cognition] does not involve the fashioning of the intellect (*buddhi*) in such a manner, then what kind of fashioning would it be? Now, [the opponent asks]: "But..."

The assumption of a manifestor beyond the assumption of a manifestor is not purposeless; rather, the assumption of an instrument beyond the assumption of an instrument is faulty. That is incorrect, because for both of us, the definition of an instrument is established as having the sense organs (*indriya*) as its characteristic, since an instrument requires that which possesses the characteristic of being an organ. [Objection: But surely experience (*bhoga*) is defined as the singular means for the perception of pleasure, pain, and delusion, as it is well-known.

The fabrication of consciousness for the sake of objective causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is useless; that is incorrect. Just as one travels by means of a horse, a road, and a lamp, so too, regarding the single causal efficiency of consciousness which is the means of experience, the Śruti states: "The purpose [of all things] lies in experience. Thus, it is not contradicted from our perspective. Furthermore, even from your perspective, the argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of the fabrication of the sense organs. Now, if...

Even though there is equality in the purposeful activity of being the means for enjoyment (*bhoga-sādhana-artha-kriyā*), there is a postulation of various sense organs because they possess diverse purposeful activities as the means for knowledge (*jñāna-sādhana*) regarding diverse forms and so forth. If this is so, then even though there is equality in the purposeful activity of being the means for enjoyment for both *vidyā* and *buddhi*, there exists a difference in their purposeful activities characterized by distinct natures.
He states that because of the existence of the status of instrument and object in the sequence of internal and external to the intellect (*buddhi*):
"For the intellect, being graspable as an object by the Self, is like a jar or a wall;
it is observed that whatever is an object of perception is dependent upon an instrument, just like color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth."
For the intellect (*buddhi*)— being devoid of the illumination of memory, intuition (*pratibhā*), and so forth regarding external objects beyond the scope of action—

is the determination of external objects such as sandalwood, women, and the like, accompanied by pleasure and other sensations; and through the threefold gateways of cognition, namely memory, intuition, and so on, it possesses its own qualities produced by rites such as the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice within its own self.
Because it arises in the form of conditions (*pratyaya*)— characterized by the appropriation of karma which has the nature of *saṃskāra*, and characterized by sentient beings (*sattva*) and so forth—

and because it is to be grasped as an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) due to its state of being experienced as pleasure, pain, and delusion through the transformation of the nature of sentient beings and the like.

Because it is an object of cognition (*vedyatvāt*). This has been stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "In brief, consciousness (*buddhi*)—which takes the form of objects and consists of pleasure and so forth—is the object of experience; experience (*bhoga*) occurs within the object of experience; and for the experiencer, experience is the manifestation of consciousness as the object appears.
In this regard, that which is grasped is like a cloth, a pot, or a wall [inert matter]; furthermore, consciousness does not depend on a mere agent produced by the kalpas.

However, being an auxiliary to the instrument (*karaṇopakārī*), it must also be dependent upon an instrument characterized by the power of consciousness (*cid-śakti*) designated as the "instrument of knowledge" (*vidyā*). Because it is an object (*karman*), that which is to be grasped is seen to be dependent upon an instrument;
for example, that which is an auxiliary to the instrument is assisted by the instruments designated as the eyes and other sense organs.

That which is form and so forth, dependent upon the instrument characterized by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), is the instrument for the act of the awakening of the intellect; this is the accomplishment of *vidyā*. He states the result:
"Therefore, when the object has been determined in due order by that [power] and by the eyes and other [senses]," (p. 459).
By means of that knowledge, a person perceives it through those who have awakened to and ascertained its true meaning.

Immediately following the reflection of the object, and according to the method that will be explained right after this, when the object has been determined in succession by the eyes and other senses acting as instruments, those [senses], together with the objects thus determined,
possess the nature of being the self consisting of qualities arising from the cognition produced by the state of being reflected as objects— that is, by virtue of their being objects of enjoyment.
The Person perceives the intellect, which possesses transformations such as pleasure and so forth, through *vidyā*—the power of consciousness aided by *vidyā*.

As it is stated in the *Tattvaprakāśikā*: "When this intellect, in the form of pleasure and so forth, becomes the object of experience for him, then this *vidyā* is the instrument (*karaṇa*); but in the apprehension of objects, it is the intellect (*buddhi*) that serves as the instrument."
He states that the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is not an instrument merely by its own strength:
"In this world, the power of consciousness alone is not the instrument, whether through the intellect or the eye;
rather, it is conjoined with *vidyā*, and therefore *vidyā* itself is the instrument. (p. 460)
If the power of consciousness (cicchakti) alone were to perceive the intellect (buddhi) here,
then there would never be any experience in the form of enjoyment.
Since that [consciousness] consists of discernment, how could non-discernment be of such a nature?
Therefore, in the perception of experience, the instrument for the self is knowledge (vidyā).

Regarding the term *bhoga* (enjoyment), by way of its etymological derivation as "that which is to be enjoyed" (*bhogya*), it refers to pleasure and so forth. Even in the case of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is a manifestation of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*), the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) designated as enjoyment—namely, the act of feeling—is currently observed. However, it is not heard [in scripture] that such [efficiency] exists in liberation (*mukti*). Thus, the summarized meaning—that this [efficiency] is not without a cause—is clear from the literal sense of the words.
And the manner in which the power of consciousness experiences itself in the form of non-discrimination is described in the *Ratnatraya*: "Therein,
due to the non-discrimination between the reality of the intellect and its own inherent connection with consciousness,
the immutable [Self], having superimposed upon itself the fluctuations and modifications belonging to that [intellect], [remains as if affected]."
"Indeed, [the Lord] manifests to the individual soul (aṇu) His own self-bliss through birth and so forth—through [the states of] 'born,' 'perished,' 'various,' 'happy,' and 'suffering.
From this also, he states that knowledge is perfected: [He says: "From this too, knowledge is perfected."

Furthermore, that non-conceptual cognition which arises from the conjunction of the sense organ and its object is to be known as consisting of pure knowledge (*vidyā*), because the intellect (*buddhi*) does not operate therein.

Furthermore, even without a cognition distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*), there arises from the contact of the sense organs with their objects—specifically from the contact of the senses presided over by the mind with their objects—a manifest, non-conceptual awareness within the power of consciousness (*śakti*).
That non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) should be understood as being of the nature of *vidyā*; and that is non-conceptual knowledge.

How can that which is to be accomplished by the manifest power of consciousness (*vidyā-vyakta-cic-chakti*)—namely, the object of knowledge (*jñeya*)—be known [by the intellect], since the intellect does not function with respect to it? He reasons, introducing a refutation:
"Even if that [consciousness] were the cause for that [intellection], it too would be of the nature of certainty."
This awakening, which consists of the determination of that [object], has the nature of discernment.

Even though that cognition serves as the cause for the perception of the sense-object therein, it is of the nature of a preliminary determination (*viniścaya*), characterized by an absence of reflective judgment (*parāmarśa*) regarding its object; it is a cognition consisting of mere observation (*ālocanātmaka*). This [cognition], which is merely of the form of looking upon, becomes a cognition of the nature of reflective judgment (*parāmarśarūpa*) when it is subsequently cultivated into a state of ascertainment (*niścayātmaka*).

The intellect (*buddhi*), when augmented by knowledge (*vidyā*), does not deviate from the cognition of the objects of the senses; nor do the senses deviate from the cognition of the objects of the intellect when it is augmented by knowledge. For that [intellect], being of the nature of consciousness (*cicchakti*), manifests its own function—which is conjoined with *rāga* and established by the principles to be explained—unseparated from its own function and conditioned by its own function.

Having extracted the *puruṣa*— which possesses the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) as its own function, is empowered by the *kalās*, and consists of the will characterized by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which is the one-pointedness of volition directed toward the purposeful activity of perception and action (*dṛk-kriyā-artha-kriyā*)— and having impelled it through the path of the senses, [the Lord] joins that sense organ with its corresponding object.
This has been stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The light [of consciousness], joined with the mind, becomes united with the senses;
thereafter, the senses always proceed toward their respective objects."
And in the case of Mataṅga,
by means of a resolute intention free from passion, with throbbing vigor and speed,
having extracted that sense-faculty through the path of the senses and having impelled it [toward its object].
"Having conjoined with the object, it turns back from that which possesses passion.

Thereafter, the organ of knowledge (jñānendriya), having manifested its own function, brings about for the Puruṣa— through its own function which is informed by Vidyā and characterized by the purposeful activity of indeterminate perception (nirvikalpālocana) consisting of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti)— an experience that is presented by its own function and not yet distinguished from that function.

He perceives the object. Thereafter, indeed, the power of will—characterized by the power of action, which is manifested by its own function, endowed with its own function, and inseparable from its own function—arises through the purposeful activity of vision and action;
it is called "desire" by its own function, immediately following the mental function that will be described later, according to my [teaching].

By means of the function of pride (*kārikāgarva*), what does this object cause [the subject] to perceive? It becomes fit for reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Likewise, it draws forth the cognition that co-exists with the non-conceptual person (*nirvikalpapuruṣa*). As it is said in the *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra*:
"Empowered by *kalā*, consciousness perceives through *vidyā*; thus, the field of experience is revealed."
"And this [Self] is colored by passion through the instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth.
Following that, indeed: "The mind is impelled again by the Puruṣa with the desire to perform a determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) regarding an object of non-conceptual awareness;
for the mind is a wanderer, moving externally and internally," as will be stated hereafter.
By means of that [mind], even the movement of fear is [perceived] through its external movement; and by that [external movement], it is not joined with many [objects].

Furthermore, having properly governed that sense-faculty by means of its own function called "conceptualization" (*saṃkalpa*), the mind—by means of its own function called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) which will be described in the examination of the mind—discriminates one [object] from among the many perceived objects.

Having taken an object as its domain, [the mind], through its own function called *saṃkalpa* (volition), in accordance with prior experience, conceives of that very person possessing such-and-such qualities—and not another, such as a beast—as being "this one"; thus, while being brought to completion, it conceives of, causes one to remember, and fixes the attention of the person upon him. Furthermore...

By means of its internal activity known as *saṃkalpa* (volition), it brings about a state of focus upon that single object, characterized by the grasping subject (*grāhaka*) who thinks, "I shall determine what this object of cognition is.
Thereafter, indeed, the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), manifested through its own function, conditioned by its own function, and non-differentiated from its own function—(p. 466)

Through the purposeful activity of the power of knowledge directed downward, the group consisting of the conceit of the subject’s determination, the reflective awareness of the subject, and pride—namely, the sense of "I"—impels the person by its own function, thinking: "What is this object? I shall determine it. Following that, the mind (*manas*) again turns inward.

By means of its activity— namely, its own function called conceptualization— it produces a cognitive grasp (*grāhya-parāmarśa*) that is free from doubt and focused exclusively on that [object], namely, "this is indeed a woman. Following that, the intellect (*buddhi*), manifesting its own function,
possesses a power of cognition directed toward an object that is conditioned by its own function and non-differentiated from its own function.

Through the activity for the sake of self-knowledge consisting of an exertion established in itself, there arises a determination of the object, a reflective awareness of the object, and a certainty; by means of this multitude of instruments, through its own function— which consists of the conceit regarding objects attained within the sphere of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and is delineated by words— it grasps the form previously perceived.
By means of a cognition that is more intense, which is prompted by the purposeful activity of desire for one's own object and longing for the opposing object,

and which relies upon a non-conceptual awareness of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)— characterized by the recollection of the genus (*jāti*) defined by the similarity of various parts and various qualities, as well as the sense-faculty directed toward it— a man [perceives] "this is a woman" without doubt.
He will explain this in the *Adhyavasāya* [section] and likewise in the *Manasparīkṣā*:

"The cognition of an object occurs only in a sequence: first it consists of mere observation (*ālocana*), then it takes the form of doubt, and after that, it consists of determinate judgment (*abhimāna*)."

Subsequently, the nature of determination (*vyavasāyātmikā*) is established in this very sequence. For thereafter—namely, from the determination arising from any one of these, such as seeing or touching sandalwood, a woman, and so forth; or rather, from seeing after seeing, touching after seeing, touching after touching, or seeing after touching...

[The object is] either the continuity of determination arising from the continuity of perception and so forth, or [it is] when the intellect (*mati*) comes to possess the form of the reflected object. At that time, according to the principle that "that which transforms without being mixed [with the subject] is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)," it is established that the internal [organ], being the generator and the sustainer, is the object of experience (*bhogya*). Thus is the definition of action (*karma*) in the *Mṛgendra*.
And according to scripture, [pleasure and so forth] are of the same nature as that which experiences while depending on a Lord and other factors, because they have an objective basis.

They arise from an impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of mental states (*bauddha*) produced by prior qualities (*paurvaguṇa-bhūta*) conditioned by karma accumulated in previous lives; they arise from a mental cognition (*pratyaya*) consisting of prior qualities produced by that [impression]; and they arise from a present mental state (*adhunika-viṣayitā*) consisting of pleasure and the like.

When the activity of the *ahaṃkāra* and *manas* has previously perceived an object, the subject perceives it; this consists of the manifestation of an experience characterized by pleasure and so forth, which is the determination of one's own *sattva* nature and is self-luminous. This experience, characterized by enjoyment, constitutes the specific causal function (*svārthakriyā*) for the Person (*puruṣa*), who possesses power and whose own activity is indicated by his own self-awareness, leading to supreme consciousness.

The *liṅginī* is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). Although it does not come into contact with pleasure and the like (p. 469), when it is endowed with *vidyā* and its own inherent activity arises, it experiences itself as "with pleasure" or "with pain. It also possesses a distinct experience such as, "this is to be done by the mind," "this is to be performed by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*)," and "this is to be accomplished by the intellect (*buddhi*)."
Having stated that [the ego] transcends what is produced by *vidyā*,
he says: "That which is the feeling of pride (*abhimāna*), volition (*saṃkalpa*), determination (*niścaya*), and sensation (*vedana*)—
that too is [transcended] by *vidyā* through the effects of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), mind (*manas*), and intellect (*buddhi*)."
It is easily understood because it is permeated by the Buddhist view; it is the cause for the awakening of the intellect.

Why should one imagine some other consciousness (*cidantara*) and then postulate that "vidyā" is the manifester of that consciousness-awakening? One should not say that this is merely an expression of my own words intended to reveal the burden of such a conceptual construction (*kalpanā-gaurava*). Thus he says:
Intellect and the other faculties, being insentient, are not the causes of consciousness;
therefore, it is the power of consciousness (cicchakti) that, when obscured by ignorance (vidyā), brings about the awakening of the Self.
It is easily understood. Furthermore, this is clarified as follows:
"However, cognition and the like are illuminators of other things, like the sun;
yet, with respect to the illumination that is the nature of consciousness itself, they possess no causality whatsoever."

However, there is the state of being produced (*janyatva*). Although [the faculties] beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with the senses are illuminators like the sun compared to other things such as pillars and jars—illuminating both themselves and others—even so, if their illumination consisting of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), which is the nature of awakening, exists as the illumination of both self and other; even if that were the case...

Because it functions as a manifestor and because its fruit is the performance of its own innate, specific causal efficiency (*svalakṣaṇa-svārthakriyā*), it does not possess the status of a cause. The intention [of the author] is that consciousness exists as a manifestation of the ground of consciousness (*cidvyakti-bhūmi-bhūta-cit*), even when appearing in the form of an insentient object through metaphorical designation. Now, one might object:
since the intellect, like a lamp or the sun, illuminates both itself and others, it must perform the function of cognizing its own object.
Let it be an instrument; what [is required] is that the knowledge (*vidyā*) be established, as has been stated.
Just as the eye is augmented by the light of a lamp, so too is the accomplishment of knowledge augmented by the light of the intellect (*buddhi*).
This was already demonstrated previously in the *Bhogakārikās*, where the objection and its resolution were set forth.
Like a lamp, his cognition illuminates both itself and other objects;
since knowledge is the instrument for the person, what will [further] knowledge do?

"The lamp is the instrument for men in the perception of objects such as pillars; and just as it is [the instrument] in the perception of the lamp itself, let it be accepted as such even in the case of cognition. He concludes: "Therefore, in the appropriation of experience, *vidyā* is the instrument of consciousness (*saṃvit*)."
Without the function of time, there would be no confusion of effects between these two.
Kalā and Vidya are the two bonds of the self;
those called Kalā and Vidya are the bonds that serve the purpose of the agent alone.

The term *bhūtyata* is derived through a verbal analysis (*karmavyutpatti*) as "enjoyment," such as pleasure and so forth. Regarding the "appropriation of enjoyment"—that is, the perception of the object of cognition characterized by pleasure and so on—the remainder of the sentence is that this is the "obscuration" (*āvṛtti*) of this consciousness, which is the self characterized by self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*). The obscuration of the *kalā* [power] pertains to the agent, while the obscuration of the instrument pertains to the means of action.
The intention is that there is no confusion regarding the specific effects characterized by their respective functions, as expressed by the term "the functioning of knowledge" (*vidyāvṛtti*).
It should be understood that the nature of assistance—whether direct or indirect—is what is intended. The meaning of the other terms is clear.
He now reveals the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) of passion (*rāga*):
Attachment arises even for one already engaged in activity for the sake of further involvement;
yet it does not arise for one who is unattached, even while experiencing impure enjoyments due to the absence of such indulgence.
Therefore, for one who is unsatiated with enjoyments (*bhoga*), the agency itself is what provides benefit;

for one engaged in the act of enjoyment, the two principles [the subject and the object] have been established today as capable [of providing it], because there is an absence of enjoyment due to the impossibility of objects of enjoyment— such as wine, sandalwood, or women— or due to the impossibility of their proximity.

For one who is unattached and has no desire, [the world] proceeds toward attachment and the cause of longing for the sake of enjoyments— those "malīmasān" (stained) objects which are crowded with great blemishes and thus productive of detachment from the earth; and because there is no satisfaction in that enjoyment, passion (*rāga*) also proceeds, established by its instrumental derivation (*karaṇavyutpatti*) as that which colors (*rañjayati*), arising from the expansion of *kalā* for its own sake.
It performs the purposeful activity of attachment (*rañjana*). As it is said in the *Mṛgendratantra*:
"Even one who has seen the object, whose power of vision has been manifested by that [object], remains unattached;
therefore, the Lord creates that very passion which generates it."
One who is delighted by a hundred [pleasures] desires impure enjoyments;
one who, having taken up [the path], eats but four [mouthfuls] attains dispassion.

In that very context, having raised the objection that hatred (*dveṣa*) should likewise be a distinct reality (*tatvāntara*), it is refuted in detail—on page 474—that this is not so because its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not different from that of passion (*rāga*); this should be understood from there. Therefore, for this reason, it is established—as the remainder of the argument implies—that the assistance rendered by that passion is for the sake of the enjoyment of the agent, the person (*puruṣa*) himself. This concludes the examination.
It will come to pass. [The text] demonstrates the operation of Time (kāla) and Destiny (niyati):
"Time impels the atom already set in motion by means of its own functions;
and Destiny likewise regulates the atom with respect to the fruit of its karma."
Therefore, both destiny (*niyati*) and time (*kāla*) remain as auxiliaries to the agent.

Time is that which possesses infinite power presided over by the power of Śiva— described as the internal impeller that constitutes a limb of the subtle body— and whose etymological derivation is established as "that which measures" (*kalayati*) and "that which impels" (*prerayati*).

*Niyati*— whose etymological derivation is established as "she who impels (*kalayati*), draws forth (*ākṣipati*), and restricts (*niyamati*)"— by means of her own powers (*ātmaśaktibhiḥ*), such as the divisions of time consisting of *truṭi*, *lava*, *nimeṣa*, *muhūrta*, and so forth, which have emerged externally through the various parts of her activity, necessarily fashions (*kalayati*) the individual soul (*aṇu*) until its dissolution, [endowing it] with the experience of enjoyment produced by the three sheaths beginning with passion (*rāga*). Just as this is not [the case for others].

In that way, the mixture [of qualities] restricts the atom with respect to the fruit of its action; it determines it when there is the acceptance of error. Therefore, and so forth, is easy to understand. Now, an objection: experience and its means belong to the enjoyer, for they are the portions of his karma; since the variety of experience would otherwise be inexplicable without dependence upon that [karma], it must belong to him alone.

As for the claim that [everything] is determined by an unproven necessity (*niyati*), it has been said accordingly: "Because of what, by what means, in what manner, when, what, to what extent, and where—whether good or bad—the self's karma exists; therefore, by that, in that way, at that time, that which is, to that extent, and there, it comes to pass under the power of the Ordainer. This is incorrect, for it contradicts the purpose of human effort.

If [it were argued that everything] is dependent on karma alone, it would follow as a consequence that even the body, the senses, and so forth are useless. (p. 476) Now, if it is said that karma accomplishes the goals of man only when dependent on the body and so forth, then let it be dependent on *niyati* (destiny) in this case as well; thus he says: "The utility of karma also [is established] by way of preventing inconsistency among these [factors]."
In the same way, time also [is subordinate], since it is that by which the Self experiences its portions.

By preventing these inconsistencies, as in the case of the expression "the four Vedas" (*cāturvedya*), [the text]—through the removal of the misconception regarding the fruits of actions belonging to one's own class even when ignorant of their true purpose; through the removal of the notion that the fruit of an action belongs to another agent while denying that the agent possesses it;

and through the removal of the notion that the agent of the action possesses the fruit while denying that the agent is liberated from the action—[establishes] the agent who is liberated from the action.
Reciprocity: It is established that assistance is rendered in dependence upon destiny (*niyati*), and not by means of *karma*; for otherwise, there would be an inconsistency with destiny.
Thus it should be explained that "destiny" refers to the causal agency of destiny itself. Here, "destiny" (*niyati*) is a term used for *karma* as the controller;
it denotes the regulation characterized by the arrangement of subsequent powers impelled by the power of Śiva’s energy (*śiva-śakti*).

Because it arises from embracing [the body], when the King of Beasts (Śiva) has thus provided this objection and its resolution: "If that [body] is also bound by karma for the sake of experiencing all the principles (*tattva*s), then let karma alone be the body and so forth; therefore, everything else is useless."
"Then, that [agency] which accomplishes the goals of man is dependent upon the mountain of the body;
thereafter, it is dependent upon *niyati* (the principle of necessity) as the regulator of action.
This very [principle] is the solution for the projection of karma, by virtue of being the basis for the real functioning of all the *kalās* and other categories.

Just as the agency that effects the acceptance of one's own portions of experience, such as pleasure and so forth, exists as a causal agent through the state of [identifying with] another, in that same way, Niyati is a causal agent; and likewise, Kāla is a causal agent. To examine the principle of Rāga, he raises it once again:
(p. 478) Now, when the atom has been indeed affected by both knowledge and a creative impulse (*kalā*), passion (*rāga*) arises from that impulse for the immediate engagement of men.
For even one who eats without desiring it is seen to be minute in some respect;
because of being attached to enjoyments through passion, he is therefore fit to experience what is to be enjoyed.
The meaning of the words is clear. The sages asked: "But that passion residing in the intellect—is it desired to exist elsewhere as well?
If one [passion] is sufficient, what need is there for two? O Lord, tell us this."

For whom there is attachment to its own object—that passion residing in the intellect which is designated by the word "attachment"—is that person also considered "attached" even when there is another duty to be performed that is distinct from such attachment? Furthermore, the word [used here] is not uttered with the intention of including it; rather, it extracts a statement of negation. In this regard:
If it is maintained that [the soul] is attached, then one [of the two] is not sufficient for both; what, O Lord, would you say? The Lord:

This passion residing in the intellect (*buddhi*), which has been described as being of the nature of a cognitive state (*pratyaya*), exists in one who is colored by it, never in one who is not colored.

It has been stated that even impurity (*mala*) is its beginning; thus, in that investigation: if this passion residing in the intellect (*buddhi*), when it has not yet reached the state of a manifest cognition (*pratyaya*), were to produce an effect, then—because it would lack a final form even in the state of latent impression (*vāsanā*)—the person (*puruṣa*) would be joined with infinite impressions due to the intellect’s connection with endless impressions.
Because it would otherwise entail the absurd consequence of simultaneous and infinite contradictory cognitions, that which is of the nature of cognition is proclaimed [as the Self].

Having entered the state of being an object of experience and becoming an agent of action, it is designated by the word "cognition" (pratyaya) because it manifests the cognition of the person (puṃ-pratyaya). Its own nature is distinct from these cognitions; yet, when combined with this passion (rāga) produced by time (kalā), [it becomes conditioned].

It would be effective—that is, it would bring about the result—only for one who is impassioned (*rakta*) and desirous; never for one who is not impassioned, because [desire] resides in the intellect (*buddhi*), and since it is a specific object of enjoyment, it would follow by the logic to be stated later that there could be no one free from passion. Now, what will detachment accomplish for one who is already liberated? For even impurity does not belong to him.
Since the person is attached and since attachment is defined by that [object], it has been stated that the instrument is primary in the examination of that impurity;
thus, the instrument has been examined. Therefore, there is no contradiction in saying that one who is already impure becomes attached. He states the conclusion:
"Therefore, by this passion (rāga), [the intellect] is made turbid by ignorance (vidyā)."
That very power, being of the nature of will itself, [acts] through that which resides in the intellect.
In conjunction with passion, it moves toward each respective object;
distinct from that which has a specific form, it is another [faculty] characterized by a general form.
In that regard, this attachment, which culminates in the subject, is considered by the Buddhists to be distinct [from the self].

Therefore, for the aforementioned reason, through the manifestation of *kalā*, the power (*śakti*) of the agent—characterized as the knower and the doer—is rendered turbid by *vidyā*; yet, being empowered, it becomes capable of the causal efficiency of knowledge and action, and its objects are distinguished.
The capacity for knowledge regarding an object capable of being perceived, which is effective for purposeful action, is designated as "knowledge-power" (*jñāna-śakti*).

When this [power] is suddenly joined with passion (*rāga*), it becomes subject to its mere presence; though the desired object is non-existent, it takes the form of desire itself. This is manifested as the "limited power" (*kalā*) when one intends only the performance of purposeful action. That very same [power], colored by passion, is the "action-power" (*kriyā-śakti*).

At that time, being characterized by the purposeful activity of its own functions—namely, the manifestation of vision and action conditioned by limiting adjuncts—it possesses the purposeful activity of will. This very power known as the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), when in proximity with the mind, becomes endowed with the purposeful activity of volition characterized by vision and action; this indeed is the purposeful activity of will.
And when, through the passion residing in the intellect, it becomes once again thoroughly mixed with that very state of upliftment, it takes the form of desire;

differentiated toward each respective object as "this is a woman," "this is a forest," or "this is to be obtained," and being possessed of its own purposeful activity directed toward each particular object, it would possess a specific form.

The desire characterized by the performance of its own purposeful action (*svārthakriyā*)—such as "I desire meat," "I desire sandalwood," or "I desire a woman"—is one [type]. Another is this illusion (*māyā*), produced by the passion residing in the grasper (*grāhaka*); it possesses the performance of purposeful action consisting merely in the desire for a common object, and being of a general nature, it is distinct from the former.

"In that case, purposeful action would have the characteristic of being according to one's own will," and so forth; having thus clarified the meaning, he anticipates the opponent's intention and refutes it:
"Because its nature consists of the three *guṇas*, manifestation (*bhāvanā*) is held to be of the nature of pleasure."
If the thought occurs: "Since [the world] has already proceeded from that very [cause], what is the use of this?"
Therefore, because these [elements] specifically color all beings among all living creatures,
it follows that there would be an absence of those free from passion (*vītarāga*).

The existence of external objects such as women and the like arises from that very passion characterized by pleasure; the meaning of "other than that" is clear. The sages [ask]: "If passion resides in the subject, then, like the *kalās* and so forth, it would exist at all times."
And for one who has already experienced enjoyment, passion toward that object occurs only once at that time.
How can a human being who has already experienced enjoyment become dispassionate later?

If [the mind] were always established in the subject, like a digit of the moon and so forth, which is characterized by passion, then for one who has experienced enjoyment—even for one who has repeatedly enjoyed women and the like—that object, namely women and so forth, would continue to be within the range of his perception; this is the implied meaning.

But how is that man—who has already experienced enjoyments and has already enjoyed women and the like—subsequently, immediately after such enjoyment, become dispassionate and endowed with detachment? Īśvara says:
Passion is also twofold: consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and consisting of manifest cognitions (*pratyaya*).
In that regard, passion, which consists of the nature of sensation, is established upon sense objects.
And through the renunciation of sense objects, a person may become dispassionate toward that sacrifice,
either due to the absence of passion for worldly gain or because of the eternal nature of the Self.

Attachment (*rāga*) is also of two kinds: therein, one is essentially *māyā* produced through the door of *kalā*, being extremely subtle; the other consists of mental representations (*pratyaya*), being gross and intellectual (*bauddha*). Between these two, the former is metaphorically designated as "feeling" (*vedanā*) because it is the ground for the manifestation of feeling and is characterized by feeling. The latter is the object (*viṣaya*).
Established [in this state], when one is situated toward a particular object such as a woman or the like, at that time and in that regard,
through the quality of dispassion manifested by the contrary action and through detachment from other objects, there occurs a withdrawal from that object—
such as a woman— and its abandonment. And in that abandonment, by means of the relinquishing of the object, [there is the cessation] regarding that object.

And when passion (*rāga*) is not manifested, the person becomes dispassionate (*virakta*), meaning he is devoid of attachment toward its objects. This is because there is an absence even of passion in its form as a latent impression (*vāsanā*) within *māyā*. If that [person] is dispassionate, and that passion does not persist, why is it not the cause of attachment? To this, he says:
According to the Buddhist, when this passion exists, the self would be the instigator;
yet, in the absence of an object to be grasped, it would be as ineffective as an eye that exists [in darkness].

In this state characterized by dissolution, when the Buddhist [type of] passion (*rāga*) is absent, there exists the passion consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which is of the nature of *māyā*. Just as the eye, though present, becomes ineffective when there is no object to be grasped—that is, in the absence of the proximity of its own appropriate form—it does not become an agent of the act of perceiving itself; likewise, although it exists, the [Buddhist passion] is not an instigator, nor is it an agent of the act of being impassioned, provided that [the other conditions] are absent.

Having thus cited the example of illusion even among Buddhists— having established that illusion is old age (*jarāga*) with respect to the reality of the excellent substratum (*supādhakatattva*)— the Māyeyī Rāgā further causes [the opponent] to accept the supreme [truth]:
"In this way, even a Buddhist would be a promoter of the unreal (*asatya*) regarding this passion (*rāga*)."
Even the object of knowledge is not apprehended by the mind when the eye is absent.
Therefore, this passion, consisting of latent impressions, resides within the nature of the grasper;
if that too were absent, there would be detachment from sense objects for the individual soul.
Otherwise, he would never become attached to another object;
for this being consists of latent impressions (vāsanā), it remains fixed upon that [object] where it is colored.

The meaning of the words is clear, and this is also logical. That which exists externally as woman and so forth is the "enjoyed" (bhogya); the "enjoyer" (bhojaka) here is the passion (rāga) of the intellect (bauddha), impelled by the passion that has already passed. When the objects of enjoyment—woman and so forth—are colored within the nature of cognition (pratyayātman), there arises the desire for the mere object and its purposeful activity. This passion residing in the enjoyer is born of Māyā, directed toward the enjoyer.
