Nor should it be argued that karma alone is the coloring agent; for that [karma], when independent, has been refuted in the examination of *niyati* (fate). To put it another way, the sages raise an objection again:
"If Maheśvara is thus a stable passion consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),"
Tell me, how does a man immediately become free from passion?

If passion (*rāga*) consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then, even if detachment regarding one object has arisen, its stability— remaining until the end of dissolution— is established by the fact that attachment to other objects would otherwise be inexplicable. In that case, a person who has just obtained a highly desired woman or the like would immediately become free from passion.
"How does passion become manifest and arise? Tell me, Maheśvara. Īśvara:
"O Īśvara, through devotion to the Lord, or by means of initiation that has exhausted [the bonds], passion is removed from the person, either entirely or in part."

O Lords of Sages, there is no absence [of Śiva-consciousness] even for one who is free from passion (vītarāga); for this very reason, the word "or" (*vā*) here has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Indeed, it does not fall [into error], because the power of consciousness remains unstained when conjoined with devotion to Śiva, according to the scripture: "One conjoined with love for Śiva [is not stained]. This is because the functional efficacy (*arthakriyā*) of devotion to Śiva is observed even prior to initiation (*dīkṣā*).

O Lord, through the gradual descent of power (*śaktipāta*), initiation (*dīkṣā*), constant devotion to the Lord (*īśvara-praṇidhāna*), and uninterrupted meditation on Śiva, when the non-manifestation [of consciousness] has been exhausted, attachment (*rāga*) of the person ceases entirely. Like something non-existent, it no longer performs any purposeful action whatsoever, nor does it cease partially from objects or regions as previously described. Nor indeed...

In some cases, while not performing a causal function with respect to an object that is non-existent, it performs its own functional power with respect to another object. However, in the case of weak digestion (*mandapāka*), it must be explained as occurring either entirely or in part. Therefore, precisely because of the cause for the cessation of passion residing in the subject (*grāhaka*), there is no existence of one who is free from passion; thus, there is no absence of those free from passion.

The meaning is that the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) does not apply here. That one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) could not be made to feel attachment by anyone, anywhere. To show that he would indeed be subject to attachment, [the author] says: "Because of the relationship of invariable concomitance with the cessation of that [passion], his sphere of activity is pure."
Does passion not immediately unite even the smallest atom with that which is most excellent? This is no wonder.

Due to the relationship of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the cessation of that [impurity], and because of the rule of constant association (*sāhacarya-niyama*) with the cessation of the coloring of the *raktika* [the individual soul], the passion residing in the supreme body— which has pure Śiva and other such categories as its object, which performs its own causal function (*svārthakriyā*),

and which belongs to Great Māyā— is immediately [effective] toward auspiciousness, because it is conducive to the highest good (*śreyas*). Toward the auspicious redness of Śiva, it is [immediately effective].
Immediately after [attaining] self-luminosity (*svaprakāśa*), he initiates the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) upon the individual souls (*aṇu*s) and,
in accordance with that self-luminosity, joins them— through a sequence of stages brought about by the removal of their own respective attachments—
and establishes a connection; this is not surprising, nor is it a wonder, for seeking out a teacher and so forth for the sake of Śiva is not extraordinary.

Because of [this] vision: it must be stated that when the body is purified by the vehicle (*vahya*), that pure passion (*śuddharāga*) does not become a manifestor among those who are related [to it]. Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), being the differentiator between the state of a bound soul (*paśutva*) and the state of Śiva, and being the differentiator between the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*) and the Person (*puruṣa*), and being the awakener of Śiva-consciousness, bestows grace upon those who have been well-initiated (*sudīkṣita*).

It is understood that impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*) becomes an illuminator when augmented by power (*śakti*), because this is well-established in the *Mataṅga* Tantra’s *Paṭala*. It is further understood that pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) itself, which resides within the city via the gateway of sound (*nāda*), does not manifest in Śiva through the two attributes of attachment (*rāga*) and duality (*dvitva*), which are the characteristics of one's own [impure] knowledge. For this has indeed been shown here.

And [this is stated] in the *Mantraparīk�ṣā*. Nor should it be said that "the mayic passion does not cease by becoming the auspicious passion (*śivarāga*)," because this is consistent with the well-known saying beginning with "simultaneously with its cessation," and so forth. Furthermore, in the *Mataṅga*, a well-known statement is heard which demonstrates that the mayic [passion] is distinct from this [auspicious passion].
Furthermore, even another's subtle passion is distinguished from that which consists of it [the self],
by virtue of which the inclination of men toward the supreme good arises.
And it is observed that men who have become dispassionate diligently seek out a teacher with devotion, directed toward Śiva, in order to transcend the sphere of bondage.
"One proceeds with a joyful soul, colored by passion for Śiva;
therefore, passion is the supreme cause for the removal of the net of Māyā.
And since "the desire to know arises," this very Mātaṅgī is liberation itself, having as its object passion for Śiva.

It is stated in the *Mataṅga* and other scriptures that the arts (*kalā*), knowledge (*vidyā*), passion (*rāga*), and so forth—along with Mahāmāyā—exist within the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*) as the agents for the discernment of the Person (*puruṣa-viveka*) and the awakening to the reality of Śiva (*śivavastv-avabodhana*), as well as for coloring [the soul] and other functions;
this is intended here in the *Avirāgaparīkṣā* of the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*. (p. 492) [This applies to] Śiva and the others.

Because it produces attachment toward pure objects, having concluded by stating that it is designated as "attachment to Śiva," he introduces [the following] to examine time in terms of being an agent or a non-agent:
"This which is called attachment to Śiva brings about even the destruction of impurity."
Thus, the time of passion has been described in brief.
It brings about the destruction of even impurity; by means of the medicinal herb that is the desire for the discernment of impurity, it effects its destruction.
By the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that it also serves to dispel the net of *māyā*. He clearly rescues the other matter that was introduced:
Now, Time (Kāla) is described briefly as it arrives in due order:
it proceeds from the three principles beginning with Kalā, and from that, it reaches Puruṣa.
Time measures itself through its own functions, such as the lava, truṭi, and so forth;
and since those functions exist solely for the sake of the body of the Bhuvana, they are therefore indeed actions.

(p. 493) Now, following the examination of attachment (*rāga*), and according to the sequence of the successive order of activity, the manifestation of the process of engagement proceeds; although these [manifestations] consist of causal efficiency (*svārthakriyā*) and temporal durations such as the *kalā* and so forth, they proceed as an activity not separate from the agent. The body born of the world (*bhauvana-deha*) is indeed for the sake of the purpose of the world-born (*bhuvanaja*). It is manifested as the physical form.

They conceive of the Person as consisting solely of the process of cognition. Therefore, at those various times, that conceptualization manifests as the impurities of action, such as birth, maintenance, death, and experience. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:
"Thus, by means of the instruments of activity, which have ascended to their effects and belong to the world of beings..."
"One who conforms to time does not enjoy pleasures in the lands of enjoyment. The meaning of the other words here is clear. Furthermore:
"That which is the cause of the past, present, and future functions..."
It should be understood as "possessing time," for it is the producer of objects of enjoyment for human beings.
That which is the cause of the effects— namely, the arising, abiding, and destruction of external objects of enjoyment such as flowers, which possess the characteristics of past, present, and future—
that cause is declared by the Self through its effects for the sake of men.
It should be understood that time is external to and distinct from the limbs of the subtle body (sūkṣmadeha) which produces objects of experience.
He elaborates upon this very point:
"No one is born at an improper time, nor is anything created at an improper time."
Just as with a wheel and other tools in the production of a jar, time is therefore the activator.

This is clear. He clarifies it further with reasoning: "This jar, while being produced, was not born anywhere prior to this, even though the clay, staff, wheel, and so forth were present, and even though the potter existed."

Prior to this [time], it had never been born, nor had it ever arisen. In that regard, the cause for its own delayed production is that which impels the manifestation of entities; one should not suspect that time is the impeller rather than karma.
For he says that [the production] is dependent upon that time, yet independent [of other factors].
If time existed, all things would arise at all times;
in that case, karma would not be the cause, for it is time that acts as the impeller.
The sages, easily accessible, raise an objection from the perspective of logicians:
"Time is accepted by some as one, all-pervading, and eternal;
why is it not likewise accepted here as the Lord? You should explain this."
The meaning of the syllables is clear. The Lord provides the resolution:
"If time were perceived as a single entity, it would not be distinct from action;
for action, by its very nature, does not possess the form of past and so forth."
If that very [time] were to be perceived, then it would follow that time itself is the cause;

for if time alone were perceived, then the manifestation, activity, and restriction of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest— which are characterized by the rise and fall of activity, and which consist of creation, maintenance, and dissolution— would have to be governed by action (*kriyā*).

Time does not exceed nor is it divided from its own causal basis; therefore, since it is action itself that is characterized by pastness and so forth, while time merely possesses a conceptual construction produced by those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), this is— according to the perspective of the Śiva-śāstra which dispels the ignorance of wicked logicians— the view that action is inherently devoid of such adjuncts.

On the contrary, its nature as past and so forth is produced by the limiting adjuncts of time; such is the intention [of the author], which sprouts the tree of refuting arguments—a fortress of destructive reasoning—to strike down the opponent's position. Regarding the phrase "of that" and so on:

if the nature of past and so forth were observed to belong to that very action itself by its own nature, then what need would there be for an internal conceptual construction? That very action itself would be time.

It follows [that this is so]. It is logical that time, which performs its function at a specific time, is designated by the word "time" (*kāla*). He concludes: (p. 497) "Therefore, O Lords of Munis, the determination of things such as the present occurs through times that are distinct, characterized by the forms of 'present' and so forth."
And therefore, this time is not one, but rather consists of infinite modalities of the Self.

The "infinite modalities of the Self" refers clearly to the categories previously mentioned, beginning with the *tattvas* (principles) and so forth; the other categories are likewise evident. The sages, indicating their own composition, either acknowledge this or manifest it without formal acceptance.
O Maheśvara, the two times that are perceived— the future and the past—
are not accepted as existing in the middle [present] moment, because such existence is impossible.

The present moment is the present time; this is easy to understand. Regarding the Lord [Īśvara]: he says that even for as long a duration as the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of a jar or other object is observed, that much is indeed the present time—"In past time, the jar also existed in the form of a lump of clay."
Then, for those seeking functional efficacy, the jar will come into being from its shards.
Let it be accepted that [the pot] is brought [into existence] while existing between those two;

the phrase "it will come to be" (eṣyati) is connected here with the meaning "it exists as the essence of the portions of time" (kāleśakalātmā). At that time—namely, when the past and future states of the jar consist of the sequence of the lump of clay and the collection of shards—[the jar exists].

"Abiding in its own nature" means that at that time, by those seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) who are intent on accomplishing actions such as fetching water for themselves, it is neither "determined" nor "taken up" for that purpose; "between those two" refers clearly to the interval between the past and future times—that is, the other category of object. He clarifies this very point:
Through these two aspects, that which consists of the veiling of entities exists;
the third, distinct portion is that through which entities are manifested.

That which is other than the two aforementioned parts— the past and the future— which are delimited by the prior and posterior limits, and which consists of the *varaṇa* (obstructive) nature of the entities of existence (*bhāvanā*),
is so described because its own function has "varaṇa"— that is, grasping (*ādāna*)— as its metaphorically designated essence (*svarūpa*). It is that whose own effect is such.
The first part [of time] manifests existence; the second part manifests the performance of the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) of objects. The third part is common to all and arises from time;
this indeed is the present time. Now, regarding the proof that time is manifold and non-eternal, what follows?
It follows that its eternity, while being insentient, consists in the persistence of its manifold nature.

By means of a negative inference (*vyatirekin*), he establishes that impermanence is proven through the inference itself, and he demonstrates that the reason of "pervasiveness" (*vibhutva*) adduced by the opponent is unestablished (*asiddhi*) when it serves as his own probans—
stating: "Because it is manifold while being insentient (*jaḍatve sati*), this [space] is non-eternal, just like a jar."
The omnipresence of that which is itself impermanent is refuted.
The object [of cognition] is easily obtained; anticipating the objection that nothing arises at an improper time by following the aforementioned statement, he offers a rebuttal:
"Now, if it is argued that this time is produced either by itself or by another time?"
The arising [of things] does not depend upon time, for time itself is not established [as a cause].
However, the origination of entities is postulated through their connection with time.

Yet, regarding the origination of the principles (*tattvas*), it is the power of Śiva (*śiva-śakti*) that is the regulator, not time; for since time itself is a principle, its own origination cannot be established in dependence upon another time. Rather, the origination of those entities which are [constituted by] the principles— [...is what is meant].

It is conceptualized and regulated through connection with time (*kālayoga*). The rest is easy to understand. Time is the cause because the power of Śiva’s will, whether separated by time or not separated, never fails to produce its effect.
Regarding the statement previously made that "the cause is that which does not fail to produce its essential nature," he says [the following] to show that there is no such failure:
Unconditioned by time and Śiva, [the Lord], through His own power arising from Māyā,
brings forth the universe from His volition according to the sequence of emanation.
The "universe" refers to time and so forth. The meaning beyond this is clear: the sages, having cast down such [an opponent] as if he were a mere straw, expose his flaws:
"Time has been declared to be non-eternal; how then can there be eternity for the selves?"
O Lord, eternity consists in the state of persisting through all time;

for it has been established by the reasons set forth in the preceding sūtra that time is indeed eternal, designated as such, and manifested as such. Furthermore, eternity is the state of being devoid of origination and destruction, which is the persistence through eternal time. Origination—

[Opponent: Since it is not delimited by time—which is itself devoid of destruction—therefore, because it is impossible for it to be delimited by that [time] through the medium of its existence, how can you speak of the eternity of the Self, O Lord? [The Lord: Eternity is the state of being devoid of delimitation by time;
it is eternality that transcends time.
For time cannot possess eternity, because the entity that is time does not persist.

Because the selves (ātman) are devoid of both prior and posterior limits, they are free from temporal restriction; thus, their eternity is beyond time. It transcends time. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "That [Self] is eternal because it is not delimited by time; because it is non-dual, it is without spatial extension. Now, one might object: "Let such eternity of time exist, but that is incorrect," to which he replies: "For indeed..."

Since it has been stated that the eternity of time consists in its being devoid of temporal limitation, another time must be established; and if eternity were admitted for that [time] as well, then that [time] would likewise be unconditioned by time. Thus, there is an infinite regress regarding the substance of time. Now, if it is argued that impermanence consists in being conditioned by time, that too leads to an infinite regress. Furthermore, time itself cannot be impermanent.

Therefore, it is incorrect for us to claim that the state of being delimited by Śiva and Śakti—which we have described as both dependent and independent of time—is easily understood through the aforementioned ancient statements; for it is stated even here in the *Ṛṣivindu* chapter that "the faces of Time and so forth exist here as well. Those who forget this may harbor doubts.
Since this Time (Kāla) has been established as being below the principle of Māyā,
how can there be the regulation of creation, dissolution, maintenance, and so forth within the pure path (śuddhādhvan)?
Īśvara says: It has been stated previously that in the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan), time is indeed pure;
therefore, those situated therein are not conceived as being subject to time, due to the power of Śiva.
The meaning, beginning with the objection and ending with the resolution, is clear. The sages, however, ask: "How can Time ever deviate from its own restrictive function? They reply:
"Because it is of the nature of *māyā*, the perishability of Time is established."
How, O Great One, does the rule for the withdrawal of the great purpose occur in terms of time?

Regarding Time (*kāla*), whose nature is both pure and impure, its perishability is established by virtue of being an object of *māyā* and by virtue of having arisen from the *māyā* that is both pure and impure. This is intended for the purpose of the Great Dissolution (*mahāsaṃhāra*) in the *Pralayapaṭala* of the *Mataṅga*.
Just as there is a regulation of emanation and maintenance from Śrīkaṇṭha-Kāla according to the manner previously described, [so too is this dissolution].

Furthermore, for the sake of a great creation, there is the rule of the withdrawal of the Great Purpose (*mahārthasaṃhāraniyama*), because one's own state (*svāvasthā*) is also indicative [of this]. That great withdrawal is a conceptualization of sleep, since even time is withdrawn at that point; how, then, could it occur through time? The Lord says:
That is incorrect; for this dissolution is not restricted by time, but rather Maheśvara [brings it about] for the sake of providing rest to those who are weary of worldly enjoyments.
He establishes a rule regarding withdrawal by his own will alone;
therefore, dependence on time for the withdrawal of ritual action is not accepted.

As for what was asked—how there can be a fixed order (*niyati*) at the time of dissolution—that is incorrect. For although [the power] is obstructed by the interval of time, it is called the "obstructing" (*kalayitrī*) power because it is established as being endowed with the capacity to perform its own function; it possesses that very capacity. For example:
the regulation of this great dissolution is not due to time, but rather [is determined] by those who are weary of worldly enjoyments.
For the sake of providing rest to those who have not yet attained it, Maheśvara— the ordainer of destiny—
acts with immediate or delayed timing according to His own will. By His own power, which fashions and withdraws all that is intended to be willed,
He establishes the regulation of time limits for as long as it takes for the dissolution, the great dissolution, sleep, creation, and maintenance.

It performs—that is, it brings about—conceptualization (*kalpana*). Therefore, for the reason stated above, the power (*śakti*) characterized by the desire to perform its own duty, which possesses activity, is not accepted when there is dependence on time during withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*). For this very reason, he says that even during the sleep of Śiva, the fivefold subtle activity exists:
Even during dissolution, the Blessed One bestows grace, creates, protects, and withdraws [the world],
always without depending upon time.
The Blessed One, whose own inherent power of action consists in the concealment of his own duties such as the creation of the gross universe,

even during dissolution and even during his sleep, directly creates the power of *māyā* through his Mother and ordains it so that it is fit to manifest the future. He protects [the world] immediately after its manifestation, in whatever manner it occurs.

He perceives that object as being fit for persistence and remains as such; He destroys the karmas while ripening them, and once the karma is ripe, immediately after the cessation of the giving of its future fruit, He renders that object fit for withdrawal and conceals it. Indeed, O bound soul, He does not cause you to fall away from future enjoyments.
He unites [the soul with his own nature]; he bestows grace by means of his power of grace upon those whose impurities have become exceedingly attenuated.

Having performed the act of casting down, characterized by the cessation of the impurity's power through its transformation from being an obscuring force, he manifests their state of Śiva-hood. And this has been stated in the *Mṛgendra*:

"Even during [Śiva’s] sleep," and so forth—this is the distinction regarding grace (*anugraha*): those who are graced during the period of sleep at the root of the Great Creation (*mahāsṛṣṭi*) which concludes with the Great Dissolution (*mahāsaṃhāra*), attain supreme liberation characterized by equality with Śiva, possessing the immediate manifestation of the state of Śiva-hood. Those who are graced during the first or middle Great Dissolutions...
Due to the difference in the ripening of their impurities (*malapāka*), some attain immediate supreme liberation.

Others, however, being favored by grace while still possessing their respective offices (*adhikāravat*), exist as *rudrāṇavas*; they will become office-holders when creation is about to occur, having been graced at the time of emission and becoming equal to Śiva immediately upon that.

They become partakers of liberation. Having been favored by the grace corresponding to their respective offices—which is based on the ripening and attenuation of impurities—they become enjoyers and inhabitants of the worlds, presiding over the duties of the intermediate Vidyās and Vidyēśvaras. This occurs at the time of [cosmic] sleep and dissolution.
At the juncture—the juncture between dissolution and creation—they are immediately favored by Śiva and become liberated.

During the period of cosmic maintenance (*sthitikāla*), some individuals, through the grace of Śiva bestowed without cause based on the ripening of their extremely intense impurity (*mala*), become partakers of supreme liberation. Others, however, [attain it] due to the variety in the ripening of their impurity.

According to their superior, middling, or inferior devotion and other qualities, those initiated by the prescribed common initiation (*sādhāraṇadīkṣā*) attain the status of the levels beginning with Śiva and ending with Śuddhavidyā; they also attain the status of the Lords of Mantra (*mantreśvara*) beyond Māyā, as well as the status of the fifty-eight Rudras. Now, [the following occurs].

There is falling away from two of the three liberations; for it is said that in the case of one who possesses worldly qualities (*lokadharmiṇī*), as long as there remains a portion of birth, she is appointed by the Lord of the World to her own state through purification. However, due to the exhaustion of karma, there is the descent of the Lord (*nāthāgati*) when the ripening of extremely intense impurity occurs, according to the scripture: "In every world, there are Gurus."

Furthermore, those who are initiated by the teachers of Svabhuvana become Śivas immediately. Even in that case, depending on the specific ripening of their impurities (*mala*), there is liberation characterized by the attainment of the level above them through the falling away from their own station, just as those initiated into *pākanda* [attain it]. They undergo a falling away from their respective lower stations, and even in that state— (Note: The final sentence fragment appears to be an incomplete thought regarding the process of descent.)

In the case of purification through mere rite for one subject to worldly dharmas, as is appropriate, there is the descent of the head (mūrdhāpāta); likewise, there may be re-initiation (punardīkṣā), fitness for [higher] yoga, or abiding in one's own state (svasthiti). Beyond abiding in one's own state, there are two paths until the end. When some ripening of impurity (malapāka) has dawned, those who have been initiated undergo both the initiation of the rule (samayadīkṣā) and the special initiation (viśeṣadīkṣā).

In the *raudra* [state], on the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*), by means of words appropriate to its own level; in the *aiśvara* [state], for the sake of one's own stability, through the arising of karma, there may be a fall from one's own station for the sake of becoming fit for initiation,
or there may be a fall from that [station] preceded by [the state of] stability, or [the presence of] impurity (*mala*) in the world.

When the ripening of karma (*pāka*) is intense, those initiated by the teachers of their own respective worlds become Śivas immediately. In the case of a different type of ripening (*vailakṣiṇya*), when there is the ripening of impurity (*mala-pāka*), [the soul] first undergoes a fall from its own state by the teachers of the worlds situated above its own world, or by the teachers of the worlds below it; or else, preceded by the destruction of its own respective karma, [it attains stability] as follows.

Each [deity] is joined, in due order, with its respective higher station; or, by a single application, they may all be joined simultaneously on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). Having fallen from their former stations, they eventually become equal to Śiva. Those situated behind the *śānti* and *śāntyatīta* kalās are to be united with Śiva, possessing the very form of Śiva.

The Śāntinilayas, who possess proximity to Śiva (śivasāmīpya), are the Jñānakevalins; the Vidyānilayas, who possess the same world as Śiva (śivasālokya), are the Yogakevalins; the Pratiṣṭhānilayas, who possess the presence of Śiva (śivasānnidhya), are the Śaktikevalins; and those residing in the two worlds of Nivṛtti and Sadāśiva are the Kāmyas, the Mūrtikevalins, who possess the two principles of Īśvara and Vidyā.

The Rudras are the inhabitants of the worlds (*bhuvana-nilaya*). According to the scripture, "He places the one who follows worldly dharma (*loka-dharmin*) as the sustainer of the worlds (*bhuvana-bhartṛ*)," those such as Kapālīśa and others, who are manifestations of *māyā*, have been joined to the initiation of the "one who follows worldly dharma" and so forth among those ranging from Kālāgni up to the sustainers of the worlds within their own respective systems. Until the end of their bodily existence, they possess prowess equal to that of the sustainers of the worlds in their own systems.

Of one's own self, which is present [here]. Upon the fall of the body, those whose prowess is equal to that of the Lord of the World according to their own doctrine shall attain union (*sāyujya*) with that Lord of the World according to their own doctrine. As it is said in the *Niśvāsa*:
"One attains union with Viṣṇu, with prowess equal to Viṣṇu. [The term] *svamatabhuvana*...

Through the excellence of meditation upon the form of their own chosen deity (*svamatabhuvana-bhartṛ*), those yogins possess a world that shares the same nature as the world of their own chosen deity; they are intent on the practice of propitiating their own chosen deity; they are in the proximity of their own chosen deity; and they engage in conduct characterized by the observance of the vows dedicated to their own chosen deity—that is, their own chosen deity.

Since they remain as *sālokya* (in the same world) even during dissolution according to the stated method, performing the five-fold functions at all times, and because it has been declared that Śiva’s power characterized by being merged with Śiva exists at all times—even during the period defined by the characteristic of being absorbed in Śiva—His power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) performs [these functions] through Māyā and the object, depending on Time.
Recalling our previous statement, the sages raise an objection once again: "It is our settled rule that Śiva performs these actions in dependence upon Māyā, the object, and Time."
The times such as the present and so forth, which were previously explained,
are not logically tenable, because [the distinctions] exist only when a pot is present.
The jar would also possess its own pastness, which is nothing other than its prior non-existence;
therefore, how can this [jar] be determined within a single moment?

The times such as the present and so forth, which were previously explained in detail for each specific term starting with "But by means of the forms of the present and so forth," are therefore logically established; for this reason,
when a single jar exists, its own jar-form— unobscured by its own clay-form— is real.

The jar would also possess its past state; it would have its own form obscured by the form of the potsherds. Furthermore, this very same [jar] would possess its prior non-existence; it would exist with its own jar-form obscured by the form of its clay. How can there be such things as the present and other times for this jar, which is manifested at a single moment and at a single time? In this regard, how can these times be questioned?
"Let it be examined; let it be scrutinized. The intention is that [this] is impossible. Īśvara: (p.
514) "The arising of all things occurs in the present moment, and the destruction of all things occurs only in the past time."
Thus, there would be no such fixed rule; for this very reason, there is fear:
that at the very moment one thing perishes, another arises.
But another exists in the form of potentiality, having a future nature;
therefore, in every moment, the present and the rest exist within all things.

In the present moment, when a single entity is performing an action, all things arise during that present time; that is, all entities delimited by the property of being produced arise. At that time, there is no destruction of them. Only in the past time is there the destruction of all things, even those delimited by the property of being effects; at that time, there is no arising of them.

If such a restriction were maintained, there could never be a conceptual construction capable of encompassing the three times for each individual object simultaneously. For, at one moment (*ekadeva*), while the destruction of one jar pertains to the past time,
the arising of another jar occurs at that very same moment.

To the question, "How can both expressions be used—'the production constituted by the present time exists'?"—he says: "But another jar, at that very same time, exists and remains in its own cause in the form of clay as a potentiality (*śakti*), having the nature of the future and being constituted by future time; therefore, for every individual object, there is the application of the three times simultaneously."

Because there is no room [for them to coexist]. Since at a single moment, at one time, contradictory individual causal efficiencies (*arthakriyā*) cannot be established across all things, and because it is impossible for multiple things to exist simultaneously in one place, the times—such as the present and so forth—exist by becoming one by one in each respective location. He clarifies this very point:
Objects are differentiated by actions alone according to their own respective natures;
therefore, [temporal distinctions] such as "present" and so forth do not apply to each individual object.

Objects always differ from one another according to their own nature, through their own appropriate sequence, and by means of such activities as the manifestation of their own causes in the present, past, and future times; the application of causal efficiency for their own sake; the cessation thereof; the production of connection therewith;
and their characteristics of stability and so forth. Therefore, for each individual object...

Because time is that which is characterized, for each individual object the three times—present and so forth—are not perceived as such; rather, they are seen as being designated by a single time through the worldly usage of action. Thus he says:
"And the usage in the world is likewise: 'The jar exists right now.'"
O bulls among sages, the oil in the sesame seeds perishes even while it exists.

The remainder [of the sentence] is: "In the world, usage and conventional practice are seen to be thus. For example: "How is it that at this present moment the jar exists? [It is said to exist] because it is engaged in its own activity of fetching water; "the cloth perishes" because it is divested of its own activity of covering; "there is oil in the sesame seeds" because of their own heat and extraction.

From that point on, the action becomes capable of arising. Having thoroughly examined the time and brought it to conclusion, he—having determined the fixed order—elevates his own understanding regarding the movement [of the breath], saying:
"Thus, time has been explained to you in brief."
Now, O bulls among sages, hear the summary of Niyati.

In brief, for the sake of ease of understanding, he begins the examination—concise yet providing great meaning on the subject—of *niyati* (the principle of necessity), which is easier to grasp than its opposite:
"Experience belongs to one who has entered [into manifestation] through the functions of *kalā*, *vidyā*, and the rest. (p. 518)
When there is the bringing forth of the fruit of accumulated karmas, however...

When the destruction of that [kalā] has commenced, there is the principle of *niyati* (destiny) in the Śiva-scripture; for the activity of *kāla* (time), which consists of the function of *kalana* (differentiation), is preceded by the activity of *niyati*. As it is stated in the *Mṛgendra*: "Determining [the object] through *niyati*, [it acts] invariably until the emergence [of the next stage]. [The text continues: "By means of the functions of *kalā*, *vidyā*, and so forth—[namely] *kalā*, *vidyā*, and the rest."

[The soul], whose nature consists of the manifestation of the divine, which is its own function, which is manifested through its own function, which is distinguished by its own [nature], which is metaphorically designated as "its own" [body], and which is characterized by the purposeful activity of the power of consciousness— consisting of action, knowledge, and desire—
having turned toward enjoyment for the sake of experiencing the fruits of its own accumulated [karmas], possesses a movement directed toward objects of enjoyment.

The fruit of karma consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, characterized as that which is to be experienced; its "appropriation" (*upaharaṇa*) is the seizing [of it] by another. When that appropriation of the fruit occurs, and upon the destruction of that [fruit], there arises the cause for the removal and obstruction of what belongs to another—this much is *niyati* (destiny), which has proceeded forth, having emerged from *māyā*.
In the teaching of Śiva, it is proclaimed that [the power of action] is the destroyer of the removal of fruits; having said this, he states for a person who possesses discernment therein:
"Restriction (niyati) makes [the soul] well-restrained, yet not so by restriction alone regarding the impurities known as *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman*."
But it has indeed proceeded, O twice-born ones, only for the person endowed with that [nature].

O twice-born ones! Such is the rule for those possessing that [nature]; such is the rule regarding that. Not merely by dirt and the like, nor even by one of those [impurities], do they proceed toward the self-restraint of a purified soul.
Nor is there a rule regarding them through action known as *mala* or *māyā*, because, being insentient, they cannot steal away the fruits of another.

Because there is no agency in the act of tasting one's own fruit; rather, it is the person associated with the fruit of their own karma who is bound by it. This is because the principle of *niyati* (destiny) operates according to the specific determination of every individual, as taught in the Puruṣa-śāstra. Alternatively, just like that [agency], *niyati* does not operate in the restriction of actions known as *mala* and *māyā* for each individual, since they possess the fruits of their respective karma.

Even in the absence of destiny (*niyati*), because a restriction is observed among those [principles] by their own nature, and because it is well known that for *kalā* and the others, their respective causal powers alone are the restrictors, [destiny] does not operate even in regard to that restriction. He explains its restriction at length, along with an illustration:
She forcibly compels him to engage in enjoyments even when he has no desire for them;
yet she does so only with those acquired by himself, never with those obtained from others.
If that [right] did not exist, others would consume what was earned by another;
for, as if by the king's command acting as an obstacle, bandits consume what belongs to others.
In the same way, those [actions] accumulated are destroyers of the inconsistency of Yama;

by this [knowledge], that body, senses, and so forth are certainly destroyers of inconsistency—that is, they are the destroyers of the reversal of results. Like bandits and thieves, they do not bring about happiness and the like.

By this necessity, there is merely the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); however, that which consists of the body, sense organs, and so forth— such as the body of a human or a god which is distinct from others, the eye of a snake which has the causal efficacy of perceiving sound, the eye of a cat which has the causal efficacy across day and night, and the upturned tongue of an elephant— is the fruit of the karma of those specific characteristics.

It is certain that by the word "body" (śarīra), the gross body is intended. By the word "senses" (indriya), the fruit of karma—characterized by the completeness or deficiency of the sense organs and the completeness or deficiency of the functional capacity of the senses—is expressed.
The remainder is easy to understand. For this very reason, destiny (niyati) does not even exercise its own regulation over what...

It should not be suspected that [the Lord] acts [directly]. For, following the statement regarding the passage of time (*kālaparīta*), it is easily understood that the power of Śiva (*śivaśakti*)—which is the regulator (*niyantrī*)—exercises its restrictive control (*niyati-niyama*) over each individual person through the mediation of karma. If this is so, let the regulation be by the power of Śiva directly; what is the use of an internal conceptualization?
Anticipating this objection, he refutes it:
"Now, if you argue that the power belonging to Śaṅkara is itself the regulator, that is not so;
for it does not act by its own nature, but rather through the mediation of *niyati*."
If that very destiny (niyati) were to release them from that connection,

it would be like wind and other [elements] which, through the intervention of unwholesome factors, become capable of producing a contrary disease; likewise, the power of Śaṅkara, through the intervention of destiny, produces a contrary realization by means of restriction.

By the words beginning with "tat," it is stated that if she is omniscient (*sarvajñatā*) and so forth, she is the manifestor (*vyañjikā*). The meaning of the other terms is clear; however, regarding the objection and resolution concerning *kalā* and the rest, it should be understood as follows: he employs an inferential statement (*anumānavākya*) to the effect that "action (*karman*) is not self-regulating" (p. 523):
Karma cannot connect men with their own fruits, because it is an action, like agriculture; therefore, karma is not the regulator here.

The meaning is that, just as agricultural labor and other such activities performed on a field are ineffective without the king’s command, so too [the individual soul] cannot be connected with its own fruit—characterized by pleasure and so forth—without *niyati* (the principle of necessity), which is impelled by the power (*śakti*) directed by the Controller, Śiva. This was previously stated in the passage: "even action is an auxiliary [to the Lord]."

Having observed that [the matter] has been thoroughly examined by the words of the Lord of Beasts (Mṛgendra), one should proceed. Recalling [this], the sages raise a doubt regarding a discrepancy in the illustration:
"Even though agricultural work and other such actions are performed by others, it is they who obtain the fruit."
O Lord, it is seen that in some places that [world] is not pervaded by the agent of action.
Even though the example of the king is dissimilar to that [of God],
for although agriculture and other such actions are performed by oneself and not by the king— even though he is the sovereign—
yet their fruit is seen in some cases to be pervaded by others, and not pervaded by the agent of the action; therefore, it is an [inappropriate] example.
Viṣama: "The lords are the employers and enjoyers of the fruit born of agriculture; the farmers perform the labor only when commanded. Īśvara:
"And those employers enjoy the fruit born of agriculture; the farmers perform their work only as directed."
Just as a sacrifice performed by the *adhvaryu* priest brings fruit for the sacrificer, so too are they the performers here; therefore, the aforementioned objection does not apply.

It is true that the instigating agents (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) enjoy the fruit belonging to another. This is because those very people, being commanded by them, perform the labor of cultivation as the employed agents (*prayojya-kartṛ*). Therefore, it is demonstrated that the fruit belongs to the instigators and not to the others; this is clear from the statement beginning with "as has been said" (*yathoktyādinā*). [This concerns] the state of being an instigator (*prayojakatva*).

Although it may appear that the royal command is sometimes thwarted by those who are hostile, thieves, or those more powerful than those engaged in dharma, [the author] again raises the objection of inequality and resolves it:
"Wherever the royal command exists, free from partiality..."
In that case, the fruit produced by that cultivation must necessarily be pervaded by its agent.
The meaning of the syllables is easy to understand. Or, as he says:
"Furthermore, there exists karma consisting of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) which is exceedingly powerful;
those lords of sages experience its fruit in accordance with that."
Therefore, destiny (*niyati*) is the principle that regulates the objects of experience for men.

Furthermore, O lords of sages, there exists a force even more powerful than that: *karma*, which consists of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), and which remains beyond the range of one's own perception; those men [are subject to it].

The fruit of dharma consists of happiness characterized by heaven and so forth; the fruit of adharma consists of suffering and delusion characterized by hell and so forth. "In accordance with that" means following that [karma];
they experience [the results] by means of that following. They do not experience them by knowing [them] for themselves and taking [them] away.

Therefore, the principle of Niyati (Restriction), impelled by the Śiva-power as declared by the Controller and augmented by the power of Ananta, is that which regulates the objects of experience for individual souls. It is not for others [such as the insentient] that this restriction of experience—characterized by pleasure and so forth arising from karma—is established. Furthermore, according to the principle that "the postulation of an unseen causal efficiency (*adṛṣṭa-kṛti*) is weaker than the force of what is directly perceived (*dṛṣṭa-phala-bala*)," [Niyati is required].

Just as the production of jars and the like by a potter is seen, so too the mutual acquisition of the fruit of agriculture is established; yet there exists a further, more powerful unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) which is karma.
O lords of sages! They enjoy the fruit in accordance with that. Therefore, this meaning must be supported.
The examination of the five principles beginning with *kalā* is completed.

The Chapter on Masculinity (Puṃstattva). Listen now, O bulls among sages, to the nature of masculinity as it truly is: conjoined with the five coverings (kañcukas), it is intent upon enjoying primordial nature (prakṛti).

The person (*puruṣa*) is proclaimed as being joined with ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other [categories]. Now, it has been stated that these five principles (*tattvas*) belong to Māyā; thus, immediately following the examination of the five principles, the principle of the person (*puṃstattva*), which possesses its own specific characteristics distinct from those [five], remains as the category of the fetter (*pāśapadārtha*). Its true nature and its differentiation from others are as follows.

Following the discourse on abandonment and appropriation, the subsequent chapter is examined separately within another chapter that possesses its own distinct nature. O bulls among sages, listen now to this examination:

among the three kinds of bound souls (*paśu*), that which is conjoined with the five coverings (*kañcuka*) is metaphorically designated as a "covering" (*kañcukatva*) due to the establishment of its own inherent capacity.
Endowed with the *kalās* and beginning with *avidyā*, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cognition of the natural as contrary [to reality] through the medium of the intellect (*buddhi*).

As the venerable Patañjali said: "Ignorance is the cognition of the impermanent, the impure, the painful, and the non-self as permanent, pure, pleasant, and self. Regarding that which is designated by the terms "impurity of manhood" (*puṃstvamala*) and "sound" (*śabda*), [it is removed] by initiation (*dīkṣā*).
It will be pure, as stated in the subsequent three verses. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), smiling and so forth are included.

The *puruṣa* (Spirit), who is intent upon experiencing *prakṛti* (Nature) through the gateways of the intellect (*buddhi*) characterized by pleasure and the like, is proclaimed as "the bound soul" (*paśu*). Having been thoroughly examined as "the *puruṣa*," he is not [bound] because he is devoid of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest, as well as the *kalās* and the rest.
The two [principles], Consciousness (vijñāna) and Dissolution (pralaya), receive the designation "Puruṣa" (Spirit). Māyā is the presiding authority over the womb;
it is the cause for those headed by Śrīkaṇṭha who are subject to the Kalās and other categories, and for those defiled by Vidya and the rest.
Because of the existence of that which is called Puruṣa, caused by Kalā, Vidya, and so forth, the other [category] is the Sakala (the embodied one) who is subject to that; this too is logical.
He says that [the soul] would obtain [this state]: (p.

529) "Therefore, it does not obtain the stage of pure consciousness (*vijñānakala*), nor the isolated dissolution (*pralaya-kevala*); for it does not obtain what is called the state of the *puruṣa*, as long as it is not devoid of ignorance and the rest."
Therefore, the entire atom (aṇu) alone receives the name "puruṣa.

The meaning of the verse is easy to understand. He states that the combination of *kalā* and so forth, as well as *avidyā* and so forth, is not the cause: "If the fivefold group beginning with *kalā* were the cause for the state of being a *puṃs*..."
Then, Prakṛti would not possess the state of being an enjoyer, just as in the case of one who is devoid of knowledge.

If the five principles beginning with *kalā* were the sole cause for masculinity— that is, for the state of being a person and for the status of being an enjoyer, which consists in being the agent of the experience of pleasure and so forth— without the assistance of *avidyā* and the rest, then, just as at the time of pure knowledge (*vijñāna-kevala*), there would be no enjoyment of *prakṛti* due to the impossibility of *avidyā* and the rest, so too it would be in this case of the *sakala* (the bound soul).

The nature of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) consists in the activity of enjoyment characterized by sensations that are the opposite of the sensations [experienced by] *prakṛti*, namely pleasure and pain; it would not belong to *prakṛti* itself. Now, one might ask: even though Śrīkaṇṭha and others lack such contrary perceptions, how can they possess this state of being an enjoyer? That is incorrect, for this [state] belongs to them just as it does to those who abide in the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*).

Because it is free from pleasure, pain, and delusion, and because it experiences happiness by following its own will, it is said: "Even in the conjunction with *kalā*, [the soul] is not subject to the *kalās* like the multitude of bound souls (*paśu*). [This applies] even to *vidyā* and the others independently of *kalā* and so forth.
Thus he says:
Likewise, ignorance and the rest alone are not the cause of [the soul's] being a person (puṃstva);
for in the absence of the limited powers (kalā) and so forth, there would be an absence of agency—how then could one be an enjoyer?

Just as, by means of the example of the *jñānākala* and by the reason characterized by the impossibility of *avidyā* and the rest, the *kalās* and so forth do not constitute the instrumental cause [of the soul's state]; likewise, by means of the example of the *jñānākala* and by the reason characterized by the impossibility of the *kalās* and so forth, even *avidyā* and the rest do not constitute the instrumental cause of the state of being a person (*puṃstva*). Therefore...
How could that [agency] be impossible? Because in the absence of the *kalās* and other factors, there is an absence of agency;
for the self-activity (*svārthakriyā*) characterized by the activity of consciousness—namely, knowledge, action, and will—is not manifested.
Since the activity of sensation does not exist, the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) is the manifestation in the determination of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

How could that which possesses its own power, instruments, cognition, and purposeful activity become an agent? It could not be so in any way, for both of these are mutually dependent causes; thus he concludes:
"That which is primordial—ignorance and the rest—is traditionally held to be the impurity of manhood (puṃstva) in men."
Pervaded by that [Prakṛti], the Puruṣa, enriched by the Kalās and other [categories], is thus designated.

In its state of masculinity (*puṃstva*), that is, in its state of being an enjoyer, the Intellect (*cicchakti*)—due to its own defilement—becomes the cause for the activity of enjoyment whose nature is the perception of the contrary; it thus stains [the Self] and produces "masculinity," which consists of the manifestation (*vivarta*) of pleasure and so forth. This is established through etymological derivation: "masculinity" (*puṃstva*) is "impurity" (*mala*). It belongs to this very principle called the Puruṣa-tattva.
The scriptural statement regarding its arising from *māyā* is not appropriate for that which is conscious by nature; this is the clear meaning of the words. The sages raise an objection:

since the Person (*puruṣa*) is partless and consciousness, he cannot possibly be the support of the worlds; why then, in the *Kriyāpāda*, is the initiation of the three worlds mentioned as something to be purified?
Indeed, it was previously stated that the worlds reside within the person during initiation;
how then do they abide here? Cut through the darkness of doubt regarding this.
"That body is born"—cut through, that is, perform the cutting away of the ignorance that is the seed of doubt. The rest is easy to understand.
The Lord says: "Wherever the stability of the worlds is described by means of metaphorical function (*lakṣaṇā-vṛtti*)."
Therefore, let it be postulated within the very primordial nature that exists at the limit of that.
Just as when it is said "the village on the Gaṅgā," its bank is understood [as the locus], so too,

since the state of being occupied by the world of persons is subordinate and situated near that which is occupied by the aesthetic power (kalā), let the state of being occupied by the world of persons be understood as residing in the principle of passion (rāga), because it is conceived as being below that.

As it is stated in the *Mṛgendratantra*: "The wise have declared that indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs in the substratum, the cause, the effect, the proximate, the benefactor, and in accordance with qualities (*dharma*) and so forth."
The other [view], however, is easy to understand. Now, one might object: since primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is also subtle, it surely cannot be the support of the worlds. True.

But in that case, by the exclusion of its defining characteristics, the sense is that it has the qualities of its effects as its summit; for the seers [use] the word "principle" (*tattva*) because it is common to both [the cause and the effect]. What kind of purity belongs to the person (*pums*) through differentiation? (p. 534)
They further object:
"The purification of the five principles beginning with *kalā* has been taught as distinct;
yet here, it is held that even *prakṛti* is [purified] through its connection with the *puruṣa*."

What kind of purification could there be for that [individual soul] through differentiation? From that arises doubt. The purification of the five principles beginning with *kalā*, as well as of *prakṛti*, is taught here in this Śiva-scripture as being brought about by differentiation—by differentiation from this and that, whether through connection with *kalā* and so forth, or through connection with *vidyā* and so forth which are born of *prakṛti*. This is established by the author of the *Klipti*. By means of yoga—that is, by means of the connection with *kalā* and so forth, or by means of the connection with *vidyā* and so forth born of *prakṛti*—[purification occurs]. Thus it is said in this Śiva-scripture.
"The animal nourishes nature"—thus is the person (puruṣa) considered and accepted as one whose realization is established.
What kind of purity belongs to that person through distinction? From this, we have a doubt; therefore, speak so that it may be logical—this is the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). [The Lord says: The Lord—
O twice-born ones, the purification of the principle of the Person (puruṣatattva) has not been described here separately;
rather, it follows from the principle of Nature (prakṛtitattva), which consists of the world of Śrīkaṇṭha.

When one extracts the *pudgala* and applies it for the discernment of reality (*tattva-vicchi-ti*) within a particular reality-level (*tattva*), the soul’s (*aṇu*) nature as a person (*puṃstva*) is severed from that [reality], and it assumes the form of the true principle of the person (*puṃstattva-rūpatā*). Now, in the case of the *bhauvana-dīkṣā*, purification pertains to that which consists of the world-spheres (*bhuvana-ātman*). Furthermore, in this Śiva-scripture...

In the initiation of the worlds (*bhuvanadīkṣā*), the purification of the *puruṣatattva* is not described separately by way of the purification of the worlds of *prakṛti*; for that reason, from the *prakṛtitattva*,
the world of Śrīkaṇṭha is situated at the top of the qualities (*guṇa*), because it arises immediately after *prakṛti*.

Having extracted the individual soul (*pudgala*) from that which consists of the world of Śrīkaṇṭha, one should apply it to that principle called *Puruṣa*, which is pervaded by *kalā*, for the sake of severing the connection with *prakṛti* through the cutting away of the bonds of the principles.
In that *puṃstvatattva*, the state of being the *puṃstvatattva* belongs to the individual soul (*aṇu*) once the *puṃstva-mala* has been severed. It is not [otherwise].

The state of the *puruṣa-tattva* being occupied by *pradhāna* [is purified] through the cessation of the *prakṛti-tattva*. Because the gross state of *puruṣatva* consists of the removal of impurities, through the initiation (*dīkṣā*) into the *tattvas*,

there occurs the purification of the *puruṣa-tattva* occupied by *prakṛti* via the purification of the *prakṛti-tattva*, and the purification of the *puruṣa-tattva* occupied by *kalā* via the *rāga-tattva*.

Purity (*śuddhi*) is understood as consisting of the removal of the impurities (*mala*) from the subtle state of manhood (*sūkṣmapuṃstva*). Now, regarding initiation into the worlds (*bhauvanadīkṣā*): that [initiation] pertains to the one whose nature is the world (*bhuvanātman*), specifically to Śrīkaṇṭha whose nature is the world of primordial matter (*prākṛta*). Alternatively, it pertains to the principle of the individual soul (*puṃstattva*) belonging to Śrīkaṇṭha, who resides within the principle of passion (*rāgatatva*).

The purification of the world consists of two types of Puruṣas as examined in the investigation of the intellect (*buddhi*): the gross Puruṣa, who is joined with *vidyā* and the other [tattvas] and is overcome by *pradhāna*; and the subtle Puruṣa, who has transcended *prakṛti*, is joined with the five coverings beginning with *kalā* (*kalā-ādi-pañca-kañcuka*), and is overcome by *kalā*. (p. 537)

This is the meaning, as it will be explained later: Śrīkaṇṭha, however, during the intermediate dissolution (madhyama-pralaya), resides in the world together with Viṣṇu, the abode of the *guṇas*. Presiding over the collection of souls who possess only subtle bodies dissolved in *prakṛti*, he receives the designation "Puruṣa. He [is] the master of all the senses...
And he receives the name Sarvatanu.
Having descended from Pradhāna, the all-pervading Śrīkaṇṭha, who dwells there, divided his own potency into two for the sake of the stability of the Rudras. Thus [it is said].

From scripture: In the creation of the middle [world], he is perceived as residing in the world of unmanifest *prakṛti* and as residing in the world of manifest qualities, designated as both manifest and unmanifest. Therein, through the purification of the world of *prakṛti*, there is the impelling of the *puruṣa* who is presided over by *pradhāna*, and of the Rudra named *Puruṣa* who is its presider. (p.)

538) Furthermore, there is the impelling power (*prerakatā*) characterized by a specific distinction (*vicchitti-śuddhi*). Then, following the sequence of the intermediate dissolution (*madhyama-pralaya*), because even the world-spheres of the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its progeny have been withdrawn, at that very moment [the Lord], having divided His own potency (*svavīrya*), is perceived as residing within the world-sphere of the individual soul (*puruṣa*) in the realm of passion (*rāga-tattva*), along with the worlds of passion and so forth; thus it is stated in the scripture (*śruti*).
As it has been said in that very [text]:
"In that [state], the Puruṣa is to be known as the protector of the grasp of Pradhāna.
Through the purification of the world of attachment to that [Pradhāna], for the Puruṣa who is pervaded by Kalā and its presiding deity, the one called Puruṣa—

Furthermore, the relationship between Rudra and the impelled [puruṣa] is characterized by a distinction consisting of the state of being the impeller and the impelled; this is their purity. Nor does the *puruṣa*-tattva abide in its own place like one *tattva* abides within another *tattva*. Rather, the *puruṣa*-tattva transmigrates through every world (*bhuvana*) according to its own karma. If this is so, since it is seen in the worlds below *prakṛti*, how can it be considered "prākṛta" (belonging to *prakṛti*)?

The sages raise this doubt: that the purification of the impurity of *puṃstva* (the state of being a limited subject) follows only the measure of the extraction of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the worlds;
for this impurity of *puṃstva*, which was previously considered to consist of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, [is thought to be removed by such means].
And it exists in all the locations, beginning with Kalāgni.
In the world of Kalāgni, this impurity is not severed; why?

[This is] easy to understand. Just as purification occurs through the extraction of the worlds situated below Īśvara, so too is it purified. By the extraction of the world of Prakṛti alone, the gross impurity of the individual soul (puṃstva) belonging to Prakṛti is removed without remainder.
A severance is effected; it is not by extracting [the quality] from another. Having stated this along with its reason, he concludes:
"In that case as well, the impurity of masculinity is severed everywhere;
it is severed completely within primordial nature (prakṛti) alone, and nowhere else."
For this very reason, the calculation of the *puruṣa* follows after that of *prakṛti*.
Thus has the *puruṣa* been described as being eternally embraced by *prakṛti*.

In this context, "embracing" refers to the relationship between the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer. The meaning of the words is clear. He now begins the examination of *prakṛti*: "Now, the principle of *prakṛti* is defined in its proper sequence."
And that [universe] arises from Māyā, because it has attained grossness through the principle of Kalā.

Now, even though [the Puruṣa] possesses sovereignty, because his masculinity was brought about by *prakṛti*, following the investigation of the *puruṣatattva*— for which the conceptual framework has been established— the *prakṛtitattva* is next examined and defined as it follows in due order. That *prakṛtitattva* is that from which, in terms of time, there is the direct arising of *māyā*, which is eternally agitated and possessed of *vidyā*, *rāga*, and so forth.

Immediately upon its birth, it attained grossness and assumed the nature of a manifest individual. Therefore, during dissolution, having remained in the form of the power (*śakti*) that is the cause—the form of *māyā* which is its own cause—and in the form of the power that is the form of *kalā*, which is its own cause;
[it exists] during creation as the essence of the *kalā*-power, as the essence of *kalā*, and through its own power as that which arises from *māyā*.
He establishes that as well by means of the reason characterized as an effect:
"That collection of principles, beginning with the qualities (guṇas) and ending with the earth, from which [the world] arises—
that is declared to be the Unmanifest (avyakta), which is to be agitated by the strides of Śrīkaṇṭha."

By the strides of Śrīkaṇṭha—[the Lord] who abides in the midst of the qualities (guṇas), who stands at the head of the qualities, who dwells below passion (rāga), and whose nature consists of the qualities, primordial matter (prakṛti), and passion, and who is the abode of the three worlds through his powers—the Unmanifest (avyakta), which is common [to all], is agitated and proceeds toward its own appropriate effects. For the Unmanifest is not uncommon; thus it is said by Ananteśa.

We shall explain that when the *śakti* is agitated, it proceeds toward its own appropriate effect. The Sāṃkhyas maintain that *prakṛti*, characterized by manifest and equal qualities (*guṇas*), is the cause, while the effect is characterized by manifest and unequal qualities, such as bondage and so forth. The sages refute this from the perspective of the Sāṃkhya system:

The qualities (guṇas) themselves, when they have reached a state of equilibrium, are called primordial nature (prakṛti). How then can that [equilibrium] be established as the material cause (upādāna) of that [nature]?

This is easy to understand. That [position] is incorrect; for when consciousness exists, because there is multiplicity, it is impermanent, and thus its own cause is impelled by the characteristics of the qualities (*guṇas*). He says that they make *prakṛti* known: "The Lord (*īśvara*)—"
O best of sages, in the teaching of Śiva, the equilibrium of the guṇas is not the primordial nature (prakṛti),
because the guṇas are insentient and manifold.
It is accepted that [the world] has a cause, and that cause is designated as *prakṛti*.

This is easily established. The sages urge [this point], saying: "Indeed, because it possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) similar to that of the objects [of perception], it is by virtue of its qualities (*guṇa*) that *prakṛti*—or alternatively, something else such as *māyā*—is manifested. Thus they challenge [the opponent].
Activity is said to have the nature of being grounded in manifestation, and its qualities are described as passion (*rajas*) and the rest;
because primordial matter (*prakṛti*) also possesses that same nature, it is not distinct from these qualities.
And because they possess that same nature as Māyā and the others, their status as being composed of the *guṇas* is established.

"Light" (*prakāśa*) consists in being the manifestor of effects such as the intellect (*buddhi*), and so forth; it is the manifestation of the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*) by means of its own effects, such as the intellect. "Action" (*kriyā*) consists in being endowed with purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), such as the supporting of its own effects, and so forth.

Through its own effects such as egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, it brings about the manifestation of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*); and through cessation, it brings about the withdrawal of its own effects. Furthermore, through the intellect (*buddhi*), it generates contrary cognitions. These, in sequence, are the functions of *sattva* and the other qualities. That whose own characteristic effect is this nature of action— [The remainder of the sentence appears to be a definition of a specific entity.]
Based on the etymology "the self of action" (*kriyātman*), the word *ātman* should be applied to each [element]. Because it is archaic (*chāndasa*), [the form] *rajāditi* is used.

Due to its identity with that [nature], it does not differ from its own nature—characterized by luminosity and so forth—which consists in manifesting its own appropriate effects. It is not distinct; its being of the nature of the qualities (*guṇātmakatva*) means its non-difference from the qualities.

The other [case] is easy. For those learned in the scriptures declare that the qualities of an effect conform to the qualities of its cause. Furthermore, since the nature of the effect does not pervade the nature of the cause, Māyā and the rest do not consist of the *guṇas*; thus, luminosity and so forth are not their essential nature by virtue of consisting of the *guṇas*, but rather are established by themselves (*svataḥsiddha*).

The Lord refutes [the objection] with a statement containing the previously cited reasoning— that because the *guṇas* are, according to the stated method, of the nature of *māyā* and so forth, their being of the nature of light (*prakāśa*) and so on is not established by themselves:
"Because they consist of the *guṇas*, their nature as light and so forth is not established."
But that [cognition] is established by its own nature, because it is an effect, even in the case of the qualities.
"O twice-born ones, the nature of light and so forth is established as not being composed of the *guṇas*;

O sages, it is clear that the production of effects by *prakṛti* does not depend on an agent, but rather occurs spontaneously. Thus, from the standpoint of the Sāṃkhya, they raise an objection once again. (p. 545)
The production of an effect arises from *sattva*, activity is established through *rajas*, and cessation is accomplished by *tamas*; so how could there be any dependence on Śrīkaṇṭha?
According to your view, characterized by the doctrine of the effect being pre-existent (*satkāryavāda*), the manifestation or appearance of the effect— even from qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth—

is its birth from its own cause, which according to our view, characterized by the Sāṃkhya system, is *prakṛti* (primordial nature) designated as having both unmanifest and manifest qualities, [and which gives rise] to delusion (*moha*) and the rest.

It is established that creation (*sṛṣṭi*) arises from the quality of goodness (*sattva-guṇa*), which exists within its own cause. Activity (*pravṛtti*), which is purposeful action, is established and determined to arise from the quality of passion (*rajas-guṇa*), which exists within its own cause. Cessation (*nivṛtti*), which is finality or withdrawal into one's own [cause], arises from the quality of darkness (*tamas-guṇa*), which exists within its own cause.
[The opponent says: It is established [that Prakṛti acts]. For the sake of producing that [world], why—from what cause—does Prakṛti depend upon Śrīkaṇṭha?
For it has been proven even in the *Śrīkaṇṭhāpekṣāpaṭala* that there is no spontaneous activity (*svataḥ pravṛtti*) for that which is insentient; therefore, she [Prakṛti] depends on him.
The intention [of the opponent] is that [the argument] would fail. The Lord (Īśvara) refutes this:
"Since they are insentient and manifold, the qualities (guṇas) are cited as the cause of the effect;
but what need is there for other qualities as causes for their own production and so forth?"
Nor does an infinite regress arise here regarding the nature of the mother and so forth;
therefore, the mother and others remain entirely dependent upon an agent.

Let it be that, according to the Sāṃkhya view, the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest possess the designation "prakṛti" because they produce [their effects], while according to the Śiva-siddhānta view, they bear the designation "guṇa. For you have stated that the guṇas are designated as "prakṛti" because they possess the characteristics of being manifest and consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa).
Because the reason—being non-conscious and manifold—is one whose pervasion is established, the "effect" (kārya) is cited as an example;

the neuter expression is used in view of the predicate "characterized as an effect. Consequently, [the existence of] mothers and so forth, who are pervasive of that [effect], is established. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), one's own birth and so forth, as well as activity and cessation, are also included.

Are [the qualities] caused by other qualities, or are they caused by something other than qualities? In that regard, if they were caused by other qualities, then those other qualities produced by them would themselves require further causes; thus, if such a postulation is made here, an infinite regress (anavasthā) occurs. Why? Because those other qualities produced by them are essentially characterized by production and so forth. He states the conclusion: "Therefore" (tataḥ).
Since qualities such as birth and so forth are distinct from other qualities due to the absence of any other cause possessing those same qualities,

it is impossible to postulate their spontaneous occurrence; therefore, the production and other states of effects characterized by causal features remain necessarily dependent upon an agent, specifically dependent upon a creator ranging from Śiva down to Brahmā.

Because Māyā is of the nature of power (*śakti*), and because even though it is manifest in the form of *prakṛti*, it remains subtle; the worlds situated there, along with the lords of those worlds, are recited therein. However, having stated that it stands at the summit of *prakṛti*, he concludes:
But Prakṛti, Kṛta, and the others abide within Māyā;
the station of those belonging to Māyā is in the principle of Guṇa, while that of the Kalās is in the principle of Kalā.
Thus, the principle of Prakṛti has been briefly described.

Within Prakṛti reside Akṛta and the others, while the lords of the worlds, beginning with A-kṛta-pramukha, are situated within Māyā—just as Gahaneśa and the others are situated there. The station of those beginning with Akṛta is in the Guṇatattva, whereas that of the Māyeyas is in Māyā.
Above Kalā are the twelve [lords] beginning with Kapālīśa and Ananta; in Gahana are the twelve [lords] beginning with Śānta;

and in Vigraha are the eight [lords] beginning with Vigeśāna. Thus, there are twenty lords of the worlds here, residing in locations equal to the worlds of Time (*kāla*), because they are to be grasped by the undivided Niyati within the principle whose nature is Kalā. At the end [of this sequence].
[This is] the state of persistence (*sthiti*). As it is stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
"Even within Māyā, the presiding lords such as Gahaneśa and others are recited;

and the purification of the principles (*tattva-śuddhi*) during initiation—everything that [is taught] in the *Kṛtimastaka* [is applicable here]. The passage beginning with "In this way" (*evam*) and so forth is easy to understand.
He begins the examination of the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva):
Now, from the principle of primordial nature (prakṛtitattva), the principle of the qualities was born;
sattva and the others, having reached a state of equilibrium, constitute the principle whose essence is the qualities.

The qualities such as manifest, distinct, conjoined, and balanced existence are the qualities; the meaning "the reality expressed through qualities" is the explicit sense. At the time of the commencement of creation, [He] is without support, favored by Śiva, residing within the final quality of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) below the sphere of passion (*rāga*), and is the foremost leader of all Rudras. (p. 550)

Śrīkaṇṭha, for the sake of manifesting the worlds, the self, the qualities, and the principles, is the agitator of primordial nature (prakṛti), which is characterized as the common principle; thus he says:
"The agitator here is the one of great splendor, Śrīkaṇṭha, of infinite prowess."
O Supreme Lord, he becomes awakened solely through contact with Śakti.

Having awakened everywhere to the unmanifest power of consciousness (*avyakta-cic-chakti*), he possesses infinite prowess (*ananta-vikrama*). He is so described because his prowess—meaning his capacity for purposeful action (*vikramārtha-kriyā*) or effective activity—is itself infinite and devoid of end; everything other than that is easily accomplished.
Indeed, the functions of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are seen by living beings only through the medium of the intellect (*buddhi*), not directly.

Anticipating the objection that it is sufficient for things to exist by their very nature without any intermediate fabrication (*antaraklipti*), he states that the reality of the *guṇas* is established because the effects characterized as the intellect (*buddhi*) would otherwise be inexplicable:
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are the *guṇas* born of *prakṛti*. (p. 551)
Because intellect and the rest consist of the three qualities (guṇas), whereas the unmanifest (avyakta) does not consist of qualities.

Let it be accepted here that [the manifest] possesses the nature of the *guṇas* by virtue of its arising from the impossible; for everything from the intellect (*buddhi*) down to the earth consists of the three *guṇas*. Since the manifest is characterized by visible, heterogeneous *guṇas*, it cannot possibly arise from the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is the Primordial Nature (*prakṛti*) and is characterized by unmanifested *guṇa*-potencies and lacks the nature of *guṇas*.

That whose arising (*udaya*)—that is, manifestation—is non-existent is "one whose arising is impossible" (*asaṃbhavodaya*). By the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*), let it be accepted here that the nature of intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest consists of the *guṇas*, meaning they have as their essence that which is produced from the *guṇas*. If that is so, it has been stated that because intellect and the rest consist of the *guṇas*, they do not arise from *prakṛti*. Likewise:

Then, because it possesses those characteristics and because it pervades the principles of the *guṇas*, if there is an origination from *prakṛti* itself, they suspect that this might also apply to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the others by means of the principle of universal application (*samanaya*). (p. 552) The Sages say:
"If the origination of the principles of the *guṇas* from *prakṛti* is accepted here in this manner," [then...]
In this way, [the existence of] the principles beginning with intellect is not accepted; how much less so that of primordial matter?
In this Śiva-śāstra, the word "cause" (kāraṇa) is to be supplied [as the subject]. The meaning of the verse is easy to understand. Īśvara says:
