For this very reason, the state of being composed of the qualities (guṇātmatva) is not admitted for the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva).
Even if a quality were itself of the nature of a quality, an infinite regress would result.

For this very reason, because it is of the nature of the *guṇas*, like the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, and because production from *prakṛti* is impossible, the state of being composed of *guṇas*— that is, having the *guṇas* as its essential nature— is not admitted for the *guṇatattva*, which is the cause of effects such as the intellect that are themselves composed of *guṇas*. Rather, it is simply the *guṇas* themselves, existing in a state of equilibrium, whether separated or combined, just as they exist in isolation.
Regarding the term "clay": it is not accepted that the effect, such as a jar, which has clay as its essence, possesses the nature of clay [merely] because its cause is clay.

Even if a quality were to possess the nature of a quality, just as one clay would have the nature of another clay through the imposition of a further clay, so too would there be the consequence of an infinite regress through the imposition of further qualities. This is stated on the grounds that there is an essential difference between primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and its qualities (*guṇa*).
He summarizes:
"The reality of the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti) is differentiated, yet not in substance;
that very same activity is divided by the high-souled Śrīkaṇṭha."
Therefore, the principles such as the intellect (*buddhi*) have indeed arisen from the *guṇas*.

Since the intellect and the rest are of the nature of the *guṇas*, they are established as the reality of the *guṇas* by virtue of being their effects, their dependence upon an agent, and their non-difference from primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
This is the implicit meaning made clear by the word-meanings, provided this is so according to the perspective of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
"The cause itself is divided into the form of the effect; thus, with respect to the cause, there is no real difference for anything.

This is true. However, since there is indeed a difference between the states of potentiality (*śakti*) and manifestation (*vyakta*), the intention [of the author] is that even though cognition and so forth are likewise [composed of these], there is no absolute difference here.
With this thought in mind, he states the difference:
The equilibrium of the unmanifest qualities is taught as the Pradhāna;
however, the equilibrium of the differentiated qualities is here declared to be the Guṇatattva.
O twice-born ones, the implied meaning is that reality—consisting of intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest—is a single essence characterized by a differentiation of divided qualities;

it appears as distinct only through the difference in its functional activities (*arthakriyā*) according to its various states. As it is said in the *Mataṅga*: "Just as a clay pot and other such objects exist for the sake of worldly convention..."
"And even though the substance is non-different, [the cognitions arise] separately due to the difference in individual manifestations.
The meaning of the words is clear. He demonstrates the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) of the quality *sattva*:
"Steadfastness, fortitude, as well as dexterity, gentleness, and lightness."
Contentment, straightforwardness, purity, perseverance, patience, and mindfulness.
Passion, extreme longing, self-restraint, tranquility, and supreme compassion—these are said to be the functions of *sattva*. Now, those of *rajas* are being described.

Steadfastness (*sthairya*) is the readiness to fulfill one's own duties as promised and so forth. Fortitude (*dhairya*) is the state of not being easily disturbed. Dexterity (*dākṣya*) is the quality of acting with speed. Gentleness (*mārdava*) is softness. Lightness (*laghutā*) is the capability for swift rising, moving, and so on. Contentment (*santoṣa*) is joy; it is expressed in the neuter gender because of its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*). Straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is the absence of crookedness.
Purity; purification by means of earth and water; resolve, which is determination;

forbearance, which is the endurance of the actions of others that are adverse to oneself; memory, which is the very rapid recollection of a forgotten object; contentment, which is the state of being well-satisfied; supreme eagerness; attachment to excellent objects; and self-restraint, which pertains to the external senses.

Restraint; tranquility is the restraint of the internal senses; the supreme is compassion, which is the highest concern for the welfare of others. These are declared to be the functions of *sattva*. Now, the function of *rajas*—the quality of passion—is described.
How so? It is said:
Valor, cruelty, great energy, pride, deceitfulness,
firmness, ruthlessness, indulgence, and hypocrisy are the qualities of rajas.
Valor is not turning one's back in battle; cruelty is the performance of inconceivable harm to others;
great energy is great exertion accompanied by pride and all forms of arrogance; it possesses guile, enmity, and firmness;
and it is mercilessness in wielding one’s own bow and other weapons, as well as in bearing the weight of the maces and other arms of the enemy.

The thought of subjugating others. Here, "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) is derived from the instrumental sense (*karaṇavyutpatti*), meaning that by means of it one enjoys; thus, it refers to the activity of producing the consciousness characterized as enjoyment.
Deceit (*ḍambha*) consists of seizing the objects of others and so forth by speaking of greatness that does not exist within oneself. These [are the qualities of] *rajas*.
The phrase "the qualities have been declared" connects back to what was previously stated. Now, he demonstrates the purposeful activities (*arthakriyā*) of that [ignorance]:
"Discontent, dullness, wretchedness, malice, heaviness, as well as excessive sleep, intoxication, laziness, suppression, and whatever constitutes delusion."
The functions of *tamas* are said to be diverse among all living beings.
Thus, O Brahmins, the true nature of the *guṇas* has been briefly explained.

*Arati* is lack of pleasure. *Mandatā* is slowness. *Śanakair-svakṛti-kartṛtva* is acting slowly or with hesitation. *Dainya* is dejection. *Odana* is the manifestation of one's state before a donor by means of low-toned speech for the sake of obtaining food, gifts, and so forth. *Paiśunya* is the act of informing a person who intends to punish of the misdeeds and such committed by others that have been witnessed. *Gurutā* is the capacity for the actions of rising and moving [from a seat] due to the influence of a blessing (*śīghra-utthāna-gati-kriyā-sāmarthya*).

Excessive sleep; the intensification of sleep. (p. 558) Intoxication and sloth. Regarding their treatment as a single unit: intoxication (*mada*) is the remainder of a morbid transformation that impels one toward improper actions; sloth (*ālasya*) is the lack of exertion toward proper duties. Likewise, there are also the functions of *sattva* and *rajas*. Thus, the meaning is easy to grasp from the concluding summary beginning with "in this way" (*evam*). Now...

He begins the examination of the state of awakening: "O best of sages, the intellect of others arises from the principle of the qualities (guṇa-tattva); their mental modifications are dominated by sattva, with rajas and tamas rendered subordinate."
That intellect which has arisen in the Tantra as the determiner of objects—

whose function is purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), which is produced by the elements other than *rajas* and *tamas*, and which, being intensified by *sattva*, performs the functions of the predominant elements— that [intellect] is described in the Śiva-darśana Tantra as "determinative" (*adhyavasāyinī*).
The intellect (*buddhi*), which possesses its own function consisting of the discernment of objects, has arisen; it is that which is designated by the word "intellect" (*buddhi*).

The meaning of the first half-verse is clear. Now, it was stated that the function of the intellect is the manifestation of knowledge, which is the function of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). To the question, "What then is this determination? he says:

In this context, cognition (bodha) is of two kinds: that which consists of ascertainment (vyavasāyātmaka) and likewise that which does not consist of ascertainment (anadhyavasāyātmaka). Of these, the first is that which does not consist of ascertainment, while the other is that which consists of ascertainment.
That cognition is the nature of the other selves within the self of the grasper.

Awareness is twofold: it is both an entity (*bhāva*) and of a determinative nature (*vyavasāyātmaka*). Among these, the first is non-determinative in nature, appearing as non-conceptual and not delineated by words. Furthermore, that which is of a determinative nature [appears] externally.

The determination (*adhyavasāya*), characterized by the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of pleasure and so forth, arises when one perceives the blade, sandalwood, a woman, and the like. This [determination] is distinct from the self-awareness (*ātmabodha*) that consists of the ground of its own manifestation, its own adventitious attributes (*aupādhika*), and its own conceptual construction (*svaviklipti*). By "intellect" (*buddhi*), one means the modification of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*) through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The other, however, is of the nature of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) and belongs to the subject-self (*grāhakātman*).

The word *svabhāva* (nature) denotes power (*śakti*) as the very essence of the Self (*ātman*). Even in that context, by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it refers to the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is the knowledge of what is to be accomplished. For this very reason, even when the light of the lamp has vanished, it shines forth eternally as unvanquished—just like the ocular luster that persists even when the lamp’s flame is extinguished—even when the illumination of the intellect (*buddhi*) has ceased, it shines forth eternally as unvanquished.

This is the awakening of the Self. And so he will state later on: "Because it is the ground for the manifestation of awakening, even the illumination of the intellect (buddhi) is metaphorically designated as 'awakening'. Furthermore, this was previously elaborated upon in the *Paśuparīkṣā*, where the intellect was established through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) by means of inference, based on its being the substratum for the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) born of external action. Previously, that...
He defines the nature of cultural construction (*saṃskṛti*):
Furthermore, works such as water-booths and tanks are constructed by those seeking results;
yet they do not yield their fruits immediately here [in this world].

Because they pertain to the future life, those actions, even though destroyed immediately after occurring, persist until the time of the fruit; therefore, there exists a latent impression (saṃskāra) designated as the "unseen force" (apūrva).
It is postulated that [the soul] is not neuter because of its quality of being subject to modification;
furthermore, the purification of agriculture and other such acts is observed to pertain to the neuter.

Furthermore, even without the causal reason of "determination" (*adhyavasāya*), how could the existence of the intellect (*buddhi*) be established? For agents who desire the fruit characterized by their own effects—those seeking results—perform actions such as building water-stations, rest-houses, and tanks by means of the body, speech, and mind, which serve as the instruments; thus, the [existence of the intellect] is established through its functional manifestation.

Those gross actions, which grant their fruits, possess the characteristic of being auxiliaries to Śiva and are defined by external exclusion; these activities and those actions do not yield their fruits in this world immediately after they have been performed— that is, in the very next moment— but rather, because they pertain to the hereafter, they remain even though they have perished once performed.

Even though [the causes] perish in a single moment, they bestow fruits such as heaven—which are distinct from the fruits of this world and are visible in a higher realm or at another time—subsequently. Therefore, one should not ask "what [follows] from that?
because the causes persist until the time of the fruit, and because the producers necessarily continue to exist without interruption until the time the produced effect arises. Indeed, it is not so.

The *daṇḍa* (the staff-like instrument), though itself perishing, produces the jar produced by itself at the time of the jar's generation; therefore, because it is produced by that action and thus "is being made," it is established as having its etymology [in this sense] and is designated by the term *sūkṣmakarman* (subtle action).
As it has been said in the *Mṛgendra*:

Because it is produced by the operation of karma, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is subtle; thus, it is postulated as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) designated as *apūrva*, which conforms to the time of the fruit. This is inferred through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) characterized as inference by those who know the scriptures. This is the view of others, such as the Naiyāyikas.

If it is argued that there is no birth or persistence for one who is devoid of the false construction (*kuklipti*), [we reply: "No. By whom was this state established? This state is the result of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Since the nature of destruction is established by its own concomitance with transformation, and since transformation is established by its own concomitance, if there were any refinement (*saṃskṛti*) in the person (*pums*), then there would also be transformation therein; if not, then neither exists.

That persistence is [established] by the reason of its being subject to modification, which serves as a subverting argument (*bādhaka-tarka*). Therefore, indeed, no impression (*saṃskāra*) from agriculture and the like is observed in the person (*puruṣa*), nor is it inferred through its own effects.
But if that is so, what then is the soil-like element that possesses the refinement demonstrated by the example of the field? To this he says:
Wherever they perform a refinement (*saṃskāra*), that action is an eightfold cognition; O best of sages, in this same way, the refinement of knowledge and so forth should also be inferred.

Actions such as wells, tanks, and so forth have been described; therein, they produce or generate a refinement known as "prior" (pūrva), which is a latent impression (vāsanā). This is the eightfold intellect (mati). From that action characterized by refinement, through its own specific ripening (pāka), that which is to be described hereafter arises.

The intellect possesses eight qualities, beginning with virtue (*dharma*). Now, it might be argued that the intellect is not distinct from the soul because its qualities are identical to those of the soul. [We reply: This is not so, because the fruits of actions performed by a southerner who has migrated to Kāśī or Kaśmīra would lack connection with him, since the results to be experienced have arisen in a different location. Furthermore, there is no relationship between the agent and those fruits produced elsewhere.

How do they produce [them]? This is the speech of a fool, because a connection is easily established through the medium of *māyā*, which is the substratum for the activity pervading all one's own functions. In this manner, the cultivation of knowledge and so forth should also be inferred; let it be considered that those who have produced the cultivation resulting from the experience of objects such as women and the like are also [regarded as] Buddhas. (p.)
565) Indeed, by the power of that [intellect] alone, the manifestation of objects is observed even in dreams, memory, intuition, and so forth, despite the absence of external objects.
Since it was stated that "the intellect possesses eight qualities," in response to the inquiry as to what those qualities are, he sets out to define and examine them along with their characteristics:
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty are the functions of the intellect;
among these three, those headed by dharma are proclaimed to be sattvic.
Attachment is of the nature of *rajas*; the remaining [qualities] are proclaimed to be of the nature of *tamas*.

From the word [“and”], dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and power [are also included]. Adharma, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of power are the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛttayaḥ*). [These arise] along with the group of conditions consisting of their own material causes.

They are accompanied by the perception of form. Of what nature are they? Among these eight, three are primary dharmas and are proclaimed to be *sāttvika*, having arisen from actions characterized by *saṃskāras* composed of the quality of *sattva*.
Attachment (*rāga*), as well as non-detachment (*avairāgya*), is *rājasa*; it is characterized by *saṃskāras* composed of the quality of *rajas*.

The remaining four—known as *adharma*, *jñāna*, *aiśvarya*, and *anaiśvarya*—are proclaimed to arise from *karma*. These are characterized by *tamas* and are defined as having the nature of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the quality of *tamas*. Now, one might object: "In the *Mṛgendra-tantra* and other texts, sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is said to consist of *sattva*."

It has been stated: "True; because it produces delusion and attachment. Here, it is understood that there is a description of the nature of both. Therefore, it is said that one would produce *sattva*. Furthermore, he will state that "Buddhist sovereignty" arises through the intoxication and delusion of sovereignty. These [states] are born from the appropriation of karma in the manner described. For instance, those which...

Dharma and adharma—such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and the killing of a Brahmin—are established by sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). Having been previously performed, they consist of momentary vibrations inherent in the body, speech, and mind; like impressions deposited within one's own intellect, they exist as qualities (*guṇa*) that maintain their own persistence through that [intellect].
However, until they have reached full maturation, the [elements] transform in a mixed manner; but once they have become fully matured through mutual assistance,
they remain during the period of stability and present themselves for experience in the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion,
as qualities arising through the gateway of conditions in the form of their specific results (*vipāka*).

That which takes the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion is said to be directly experienced through the doors of pleasure, pain, and delusion, along with the cognitions arising from itself. As it is stated in the *Bhogakārikā*:
"That which is called *rūpa* (form) consists of the forms of delusion, pain, and pleasure; it is twofold."
The Buddha is awakening; and because it exists for that purpose, the objects of enjoyment, such as Māyā and so forth, are also [the Buddha].
"The triad beginning with dharma is passion (rāga), and the tetrad beginning with dharma consists of the qualities of tamas, rajas, and sattva; that form is considered born of karma in the intellect.
Thus, the statement regarding the nature of dharma and the others as being denoted by the word "bhāva" is now revealed:
Since these eight—beginning with *dharma*—are cultivated, they are designated as the "cultivated signs" (*bhāva-liṅga*); they shall now be described in their proper order.

Because these factors, beginning with dharma, when practiced, cultivate the signs or marks of the self and so forth for their own practitioner; and because, through their respective innate predispositions, they infuse the intellect with the characteristics of their own qualities, they are therefore designated as "bhāvas" (states of being). As it has been said: "They cause [the self] to be perceived."

Since the categories (bhāvas) are proclaimed by means of that *liṅga*, those *bhāvas* are now described in their proper order. In order to demonstrate that virtues (*dharma*) and the rest, when practiced, possess the nature of *bhāvas*, [the author] first analyzes virtue (*dharma*) itself in order to establish its various modes of practice, distinguishing it from ignorance (*ajñāna*) and the other [negative states].
He defines its essential nature:
"In that regard, dharma is twofold, namely *yama* and *niyama*. The restraint (*saṃyama*) of the mind therein is what is traditionally taught as *yama*. (p. 569)
Through the abandonment of unscriptural action, even regarding scriptural duties,
that which is taught as a rule in the scripture is this very restraint of the senses.

In that regard, among the eight categories of existence (*bhāva*), *dharma* is twofold: *yama* and *niyama*. Between *yama* and *niyama*, that which is the restraint and stabilization of the mind and the internal organ (*manas*) is recited as *saṃyama*. This results from the abandonment of actions not prescribed by the scriptures and the avoidance of actions such as anger that are prohibited by the scriptures.
This restraint of the senses, which is to be described in relation to scriptural rites as well as anger and other passions,

is taught in the scriptures— beginning with those of Śiva— as *niyama*, the sustained application for the sake of practice. Therefore, for one who is filled with the reality of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that constitute these means, and for whom darkness (*tamas*) has consequently ceased, [this discipline is required].
A slight inclination toward the Great Principle (mahattattva) arises; endowed with that, the Lord impels the person. Furthermore, he distinguishes between restraint (yama) and observance (niyama):
"Restraint is indeed fivefold: non-violence, truthfulness, and non-stealing."
Celibacy and freedom from deceit—thus, self-restraint (yama) is fivefold.
Freedom from anger, service to the teacher, purity, contentment,
and straightforwardness— these are proclaimed as the fivefold observances (niyama).
Restraint (*yama*) consists of the five [virtues] beginning with non-violence, and observance (*niyama*) consists of the five beginning with freedom from anger. The meaning of the words is clear.

In this context, "service to the guru" is an illustration for other duties such as the worship of the deities, as well as regular (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites; likewise, the mention of these will be elaborated upon later in due order.

He indicates: here, it refers only to the hidden meaning because of its lack of clarity. "Non-injury" (ahiṃsā) is that which does not produce suffering in others even by means of hundreds of acts of malice;
for that injury which is enjoined by the scriptures is to be understood as non-injury.

That which is enjoined by the scriptures and prescribed by the scriptures—namely, the slaughter of sacrificial animals—is indeed to be understood as "non-violence" (*ahiṃsā*). As for the characteristic of truth:
even if one speaks the truth out of fear during times of distress, it is not called "truth."
O divine teacher, even that which is untrue becomes true when it serves a purpose.
Truth that is not factual is not called truth. "Teacher and deity" is an elliptical expression for cows, Brahmins, and so forth.
The definition of non-stealing is:
the taking of what is not given—whether it be cattle, wealth, or anything else acquired unjustly—is not truth.
Having treated what was heard and clearly perceived as if it were mere straw, he committed theft.
The characteristic of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is this:
through action, mind, or speech, and even by hearing or seeing,
one should always regard a woman— even when she solicits one— as one would one's own mother.

That alone would be true celibacy (*brahmacarya*); the rest are mere hypocrites in their observance. (p. 572) For a householder, celibacy consists in following the path of the Vedas according to the prescribed rules; the others are merely those who feign the observance of celibacy through a display of external conduct, while remaining inwardly unmasked—this is the meaning. The defining characteristic of being free from guile (*akalkatā*) is as follows:
Transparency, equanimity, and love such that even through hundreds of injuries one does not stir toward turbidity or enmity— this is what is called being free from guile.

Thus have the five restraints (*yama*) been declared for ascetics whose nature is that of the auspicious Śiva (*suśivātman*). Considering that "impurity" (*kāluṣya*) is an ill-famed state and that "awakening" (*bodhana*) is the opposite of enmity (*vaira*), they are thus described.
For ascetics—meaning yogis—whose nature is that of the auspicious Śiva and who possess manifest pure power (*śuddha-śakti*) revealed by pure intellect, this constitutes their discipline (*niyama*).
The characteristic of one who serves their teacher without anger is as follows:
one whose impurity is eternally destroyed does not become angry even when struck,
whether by the gods, by those endowed with the power of Śiva, or even by one's parents or teacher.
One should constantly observe the commands regarding optional rites, obligatory duties,
acts of giving, fasting, pilgrimages, as well as the hearing and study of the scriptures.

The performance of service by men with faith is proclaimed as *śuśrūṣā*. Even when one is suffering, the absence of anger until the very end is to be known as the characteristic of *akrodha*. The two characteristics of purity (*śauca*) and contentment (*santoṣa*) are as follows: washing the body with earth and water is declared to be purity.
In the Tantra, contentment and joy consist in equanimity toward gain and loss.
Having stated the characteristic of straightforwardness (*ārjava*), he concludes:
"O best of Brahmins, even though he knows, he acts like one dull-witted and likewise like one mute;
he abstains from harming others, being full of faith and purified in his being."
That is declared to be his straightforwardness (*ārjava*); thus, O best of Brahmins, the observance (*niyama*) is fivefold.

Even though he knows that this [person] is subject to the power of a *niyāta-lakṣa* who inflicts pain, and even though he understands and hears it clearly, he remains as if dull-witted, as if not understanding, and likewise as if mute, like one who is truly mute.

Even deafness is established by his attainment; for he has been permeated by such a disposition that, as if not hearing, he remains among the eightfold group [of sense objects], having desisted from harming others and being devoted to helping others—that is his nature, which is called "straightforwardness" (*ārjava*). Thus, the rule is fivefold. When, through the practice of dharma, nothing whatsoever remains [unfulfilled]—
When the *sattva* is free from passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*) has been destroyed, it becomes thus within the intellect (*buddhi*).
Then, the Blessed One, without overstepping the proper sequence, enjoins the person endowed with such a transformed intellect to the practice of knowledge.
Thereafter, proclaiming the distinction [between the self and the intellect], he states the reason for that state being designated by the term "perfection" (*siddhi*):
That fivefold knowledge which has as its objects the qualities, the unmanifest, and the person—from that comes the perfect attainment of liberation; thus it is called "attainment."

That knowledge which has the unmanifested qualities (*guṇa*) as its object, which pertains to human beings, and which has the *prakṛti*, the *guṇas*, and the *puruṣa* as its domain— that knowledge, because the *guṇa* possesses a threefold characteristic, falls into three types therein. Having taken the form of the discrimination between the *prakṛti*, the three *guṇas*, and the *puruṣa*, it consists of five [aspects] and has five bases.

It consists of five members; therefore, for the Sāṃkhyas, liberation (kaivalya) is established through the knowledge of the qualities (guṇa), the unmanifest (avyakta), and the knower (jña). However, according to the perspective of the final tenet (siddhānta), even they do not attain isolation (kevalatā) by themselves;
rather, because they do not relinquish their state of being "possessors" (sakala), they fall into the condition of being objects of enjoyment for others due to their Sāṃkhya knowledge and so forth.

The perfection of one's own material cause (*svopādāna*), which consists of the state of its own excellence and is filled with the sovereignty of detachment from phenomena stained by the passion for characteristics (*lakṣaṇarāga*), is established as *siddhi*. Because it is the cause of such establishment, that knowledge is called *siddhi*. That which is designated by the word *siddhi* is this aforementioned *siddhi*, which is characterized by knowledge in each of its distinct aspects.

(p. 576) Since perfuming (*adhivāsanā*) arises from both existence and non-existence as its characteristic, and is established by means of the two truths, he says: "And that [perfuming] is proclaimed in brief by way of the number eighty."
The gross elements, the subtle elements, the sense organs, the mind, the ego, and the intellect.
The Guṇas, the Unmanifest, and the Puruṣas, having reached the abodes of the Vāsins,
attain their perfections there through the very intellect of the Tarātman;
for indeed, they are called Vāsins because they have no dwelling other than the principle of the Puruṣa, which arises from the absence of the characteristics of knowledge.

For those who reside therein, there are places to be attained as liberation, beginning with the principle of the Person (*puruṣatattva*) and ending with the elements. Therefore, within each of those [levels], such as the elements and so forth, the various accomplishments (*siddhi*) are reached and known through the very notion of self— that is, through the conviction of one's own self— due to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of knowledge that serve as their own causes.

Demonstrating the diversity of the establishment of the self through the habitual tendencies of existence (*bhāvādhivāsanā*), he now explains and analyzes in sequence that which was previously mentioned as the locus of its establishment: "Since the Cārvākas, who maintain that the body is the self, are established [as such] by means of the elements (*bhūta*)."
In the same way, those who know the science of astrology [know] that from which the city of stars (tārāpura) is to be reached.

However, because it is subject to destruction due to the doctrine of the self being identical with the body, the view that the body is the self is materialistic; this has been demonstrated in the *Paśupaṭala*. But for those who know the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), the connection between the person (*puruṣa*) and his instruments of action is indeed beginningless. Since that which is beginningless cannot be destroyed, liberation consists in the attainment of the most excellent [state].

Some say that liberation consists in residing in the city of the stars, which are the instruments of action. Others declare that liberation is the attainment of equality with Agni and the other deities through the Āgneya, Saura, and Vāruṇa initiations. The proponents of Karma-mīmāṃsā, asserting that "this world was never otherwise," recite that the attainment of heaven alone is the human goal, achieved through one's own performed good deeds. As for the Kaulas:

According to the logic of the jar and the sparrow, there are theories asserting that the self (*ātman*) consists of atoms within the body; for they maintain that the elements (*bhūta*) produced from atoms—such as the body, stars, cities, and so forth—are the very nature of the self. These and other proponents of the five [elements] also accept the annihilation of the self upon liberation, because they regard the self as a property of the body, like the extinguishing of a lamp.

And those disputants who, being cultivated by the nature of the true self of the elements and perfected through the elements, declare that they are liberated in those elements alone— the followers of the Smṛtis say that Brahman is the cause of the cosmic egg (bhūtāṇḍa), and therefore they [hold such a view].
The objects of knowledge are established as being merely those [elements]; the eyes and other sense organs are [merely] beyond them.
Some among the sages, considering consciousness to be that [the cause], are established in their view;

they are followers of the Smṛti who hold that the Supreme Brahman is the cause of the cosmic egg of beings, and that nothing else is to be attained through knowledge because of its impossibility. Thus he says that it is the cause of beings in relation to the subtle elements (tanmātra).
Those who maintain that [the self] is constructed through logical arguments should be known as proponents of "mere-ness" (*tanmātra*) among the supreme sages.

Furthermore, certain sub-sects of the Cārvākas, who hold that consciousness resides in the senses, assert that there is no substantial entity of a self distinct from the objects characterized by the senses;
they consider the sense-faculties, such as the eye and so forth, to be the conscious self, and are thus permeated by that very notion.

The Siddhas are those who have attained perfection through the senses. Regarding those who have attained perfection through the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), he speaks of the Buddhists (*bauddha*): "But the Buddhists are established by means of the intellect (*buddhi*); they are proponents of a self consisting of the activity of knowledge (*jñānavṛttyātmavādin*).
Likewise, the Naiyāyikas are proponents of a self whose nature consists of the qualities of the activity of the intellect (*buddhivṛttidharmātmavādin*)."

And this is an illustrative indication: among those whose consciousness resides in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the mental consciousnesses (*manaś-caitanyika*) are again the cause for the activity of the senses; they say that because it is directed toward Brahman, the entire universe proceeds from that.
By means of that knowledge, they become perfected in mind (*manassiddha*), for they possess mastery over the senses; by whomsoever [this] is attained therein—
They say that the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya), which is devoid of any [external] designation, arises solely from the knowledge of Brahman as that which is to be attained.

Those Buddhists who are permeated by that knowledge and established in the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), however, maintain that the self consists of the activity of cognition (jñānavṛtti); furthermore, they hold that [the self] is differentiated by determinations (adhyavasāya) and so forth within a continuum (santati).

Knowledge itself, when conjoined with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*), arises as the cause of *saṃsāra*; there exists no other entity such as a "self" (*ātman*) distinct from that [knowledge]. Therefore, for those who maintain the conceptual construction of a self-nature, since that [self] is well-cultivated by means of this knowledge of the self—which is actually a function of knowledge—it is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*).
Even those logicians who are experts in reasoning and who maintain that the self consists of the functions of the intellect—

constructing a contemptible hypothesis regarding the nature of the self as a substance possessing qualities, where the nine established functions of the intellect (buddhi) consist of cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression.

Those who do not understand the distinction between quality (*guṇa*) and the possessor of quality (*guṇin*), and who— due to their ignorance regarding the absolute non-existence of the nine qualities within that [Self] which is characterized as being of the nature of that [Self]— propound false doctrines such as insentience like a wall or a miserable liberation, are themselves established in their own intellect through the well-cultivated speech of those who speak for their welfare; they are called "proponents of the establishment of qualities" (*guṇasiddhāḥ*).
The proponents of the "perhaps" (syādvādin), however, worship the self as being non-absolute (anekānta);
for since the qualities (guṇas) have a fluctuating mode of existence, they are established as being composed of those very qualities.

The proponents of *syādvāda*, however— being proponents of both existence and non-existence through the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) such as "in some respect it exists" and "in some respect it does not exist"—

worship their own self, which is of a non-absolutist nature (*anekānta*) consisting of the modes of existence, non-existence, and change. They contemplate this because, as stated by Patañjali, "the functioning of the qualities (*guṇas*) is ever-moving, and the functioning of the qualities is both moving and unmoving."

According to that system, only the *guṇas* are cultivated; therefore, by virtue of that state, those Jainas (*kṣapaṇakas*) and the proponents of the enjoyment of sentient beings (*sattvasambhogavādins*) have their *guṇas* perfected. Let them be distinguished from the devotees of the Buddha. Thus, in some places, there is the definition of the two principles (*tattva*) of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. (p. 582)
He speaks of those who have attained their own liberation:
the Prākṛtas and the Pāñcarātras consider Prakṛti to be Hari;
those known as Vedāntins are proclaimed to be Siddhas who have transcended Pradhāna.
Those who follow the Sāṃkhya system, being well-established in the doctrine of the Puruṣa, believe that the Puruṣa is all-pervading; yet he is also traditionally held to be pervaded by the Kalās.
Those who consider Prakṛti to be Hari say:
"The Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is the supreme Prakṛti beyond the qualities (guṇas);
they call him the unmanifest and eternal; there is nothing higher than him."

Those Pāñcarātras, who are established by nature and perfected through their own nature, maintain that all things—consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious—are subject to transformation because they are modifications of themselves; thus, they consider even the Puruṣa to be designated as "Brahman. These Vedāntins are proponents of the transformation (pariṇāma) of Brahman, [asserting that] it is pervaded by Pradhāna.

Like a clod of earth established by a man (puṃsiddhāloṣṭavat), because its nature is the dissolution of primordial matter (prakṛti), the Sāṃkhyas hold that knowledge and the rest are born of primordial matter; they maintain that the perfected beings (siddhas) in the world of the Puruṣa are well-established at the limit of primordial matter, untainted by the impurity of the Puruṣa.
Likewise, the Pātañjalas [hold] that the Puruṣa is established through primordial matter. And that Puruṣa is not, however, the dissolution of primordial matter.

[The soul] is defiled by the impurity of natural gross masculinity according to the Sāṃkhyas, because for them there is a distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. However, [in our view], it is overcome by *kalā*, because it has been stated in the *Pumparīkṣā* that even *kalā* and the rest serve as the cause for the state of being *puruṣa*. Furthermore, through the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), [it is affected by] the qualities of *prakṛti*, such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth.

There is also pervasion even above *prakṛti*. One who is defiled by the subtle state of manhood (*sūkṣmapuṃstva*), whose lower portion is stained by passion (*rāga*) and who has attained perfection in the world of men arising from passion, is known as *sakala* (the embodied). The *vijñānakevala* (the isolated one through knowledge) is of two kinds: one who has attained perfection through the knowledge of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, and one who has attained perfection through the knowledge of *māyā* and *puruṣa*. Among these:
For the first type of Sāṃkhya-vijñānasiddha, once thus examined, everything becomes clear.
But the second type— the Śaiva-vijñānasiddha—

is a *vijñānakevalin* who, due to being either still bound by *māyā* or having transcended it, is sometimes and in some way initiated into the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*) through the ripening of his own impurities.

One who is pure in every respect becomes liberated from that [bondage] due to its extreme intensity. Even those who profess Māyā—having set aside the state of Brahman and being permeated by the realization of their own essential nature as the fourth state (turya-pada), namely "I am Brahman"—are to be known as perfected beings who have transcended the limited individual (kalā-krānta-puruṣa). As it has been said: "And those who know the Vedānta..."

And the Sāṃkhyas and Yogins are established in the Puruṣa. Now, it may be objected: "The Sāṃkhyas have indeed declared eight perfections (*siddhis*); yet they have also described perfections established by their own specific doctrines—such as Vedānta—which are distinct from those [eight] perfections, and satisfactions (*tuṣṭis*) which are distinct from the satisfactions previously mentioned, being established by doctrines to be described hereafter. This is true.

In that case, with respect to the primary power culminating in the thirty principles, even the *siddhis* of the Sāṃkhyas would be included within the [eight] contentments (*tuṣṭi*); thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. He concludes:
"Thus, ten *siddhis* have been declared according to the distinctions of other systems."
This is liberation, the ultimate pinnacle; this is the final stage of life.
Having thus resolved, they were satisfied; for them, those supreme siddhis have been proclaimed in this tantra, as well as the non-supreme ones, up to the reality known as dissolution (laya).

Due to the differences between philosophical systems (*darśana*) and the distinctions between various scriptures (*śāstra*), ten types of accomplishments (*siddhi*) have been described, consisting of the contemplation of one's own self as distinct [from the following]: the elements (*bhūta*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs (*indriya*), the mind (*manas*), the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the intellect (*buddhi*), the qualities (*guṇa*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the primary cause (*pradhāna*), the person overcome by *kalā* (*kalākrāntapuruṣa*), and the person overcome by *svarūpa* (*svarūpākrāntapuruṣa*). These ten are the objects [of such contemplation].

Possessing their respective accomplishments, these disputants— having determined that this is liberation, the supreme, subtle, and unsurpassed pinnacle of this stage of life (*āśrama*), which is the ground of liberation fashioned by various disputants,
and that this stage of life is the final and most exalted ground of liberation— are satisfied with it.

Those are the supreme accomplishments (*siddhi*s). He says that they are superior and not so for us with the words beginning "In this... In this Tantra, which originates from the mouth of Śiva and is divided into the *Kāmika* and other sections, there are indeed not only these [accomplishments] up to the state called *laya*; rather, there are also those consisting of the attainment of the two paths—the pure and the mixed.
Those designated as "lower" (apara) consist of the attainments of the impure path (aśuddhādhvan), such as those beginning with the Paurāṇika mentioned below;
those designated as "higher" (para) consist of all the attainments (siddhis) based on systems such as Sāṃkhya mentioned above.
Because they possess characteristics similar to Śiva and serve as the foundation for all [attainments], they are declared to be "lower" in relation to liberation (mukti).

And it was stated in the *Pratipadārthaparīkṣā* regarding those who have applied themselves to the reality of the *ālaya*: "They are liberated here and elsewhere. He says that by dividing each of the ten into eight ways, they become eighty in number:
"And these are further divided eightfold according to the distinction of their limiting conditions (*upādhi*)."
Due to the power of prior mental impressions, cognition does not arise with respect to form through modification.
Since the accomplishment of that which is undertaken would be subject to the threefold suffering,
there are three accomplishments corresponding to the three knowledges, which serve as the counteragents to those three obstacles.
And that [realization] is held to be achieved through the instruction of friends,
or by oneself reflecting upon the scriptures, or indeed through study under a teacher.

The two types of knowledge that belong to a person are held to be the two kinds of perfection (*siddhi*). That which is to be cultivated through actions such as giving and so forth is called the single perfection.
The ten siddhis are divided by means of the eight abhissiddhis;
when combined, those siddhis are reckoned as eighty in number in brief.

These ten, by being appropriated through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) within the nature of the self which consists of the state of cognition characterized by knowledge, are further divided eightfold according to the distinction of the causes for their own arising. How so? By virtue of prior latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), [they arise] through the ripening of the latent impressions deposited by specific dharmas prescribed in previous births.

Based on the instruction, there arises from that [instruction] a cognition in the form of an inference; from that, through mental impression (*saṃskāra*), there proceeds a cognition consisting of spontaneous reasoning (*ūha*) characterized by latent disposition (*adhivāsanā*). It is established as correct.
At the stage of its own excellence, for practitioners, there shall be accomplishment (*siddhi*). This threefold statement is made with respect to the person to be instructed (*vidheya*).

That [cognition] is the sign of the ripening of past formative forces (*saṃskāra*); it belongs to a practitioner who, though incapable of such deliberation (*ūha*), is struck down and tormented by the threefold suffering—consisting of the internal, the celestial, and the elemental—in its physical form. The remedy for that [suffering] is the cessation thereof; that which consists of deliberation (*ūhātmaka*) is the means for the cessation of those three sufferings. (p. 589)
The three types of knowledge that have arisen for him, established in their excellence, constitute the three forms of accomplishment (*siddhi*).

That knowledge which arises through the instruction of friends—that is, through the instruction of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*)—is held to be one accomplishment. This is the state characterized by knowledge.

The phrase "is to be cultivated through actions such as giving" is to be supplied [to the previous statement]. The meaning of the other words is clear. In response to the inquiry as to why the perfected beings (siddhas) beginning with Kalā and ending with Rāga are not counted here, he says:
"Beyond this, those who take pride in the ultimate limit of Kalā and the rest..."
Nor are those [other established entities] counted as "established," because the discussion begins from the standpoint of what is established by the intellect.

Those who, from the beginning of the Kalas, possess the conceit of being "Supreme" (parā), thinking that there is nothing higher than this and maintaining the conceit of having attained a subtle and unsurpassed liberation; those who belong to the tradition of the vision imparted by the Lord who presides over the womb of Māyā (Māyāgarbhādhikārīśvara) and those who follow it— even though they are Siddhas, they are included here because the discussion begins with the attainment of intellectual perfection (buddhisiddhi).

Because they have begun the examination of the *buddhisiddhi* (p. 590), they are not counted; for they follow the Śaiva [tradition] through the *dīkṣā* of the Śaiva Paurāṇikas, which possesses the arrangement composed by Vyāsa. They are the *rāgasiddhas*, the followers of the *somasiddhānta*, the *vidyāsiddhas*, those arisen from *kalā* (*kalottha*), those situated at the limit of *kalā* (*kalāprāntastha*), and those situated in the world of *māyā* (*māyābhuvanastha*).

The Kāpālas are those initiated by means of an initiation fashioned according to the Kāpāla-śāstra composed by Rudra; they are perfected in their respective arts (kalāsiddhas). Likewise, the Pāśupatas are those born [into that state] who have been initiated by means of an initiation fashioned according to other scriptures such as the Pāśupata, composed by Rudra, which reside within the world of Māyā situated at the limit of the arts arising from Kalā. They are thus produced.

The Siddhas of Māyā— both the Samyavadins and the Aveśa-samyavadins— are initiated by a consecration (dīkṣā) fashioned according to the scriptures promulgated by Rudra, which reside in the world-levels arising from Śuddhavidyā;
they are the Mahāvratas, the Siddhas of Śuddhavidyā, who reside in the world-levels arising from Īśvara.

Those initiated by the initiation (*dīkṣā*) fashioned according to the treatises composed by Rudra are: the proponents of agency directed by Śiva (*śivaprayojyakartṛtvavādinaḥ*), who are the followers of the doctrine of the Lord of the Stream (*pravāheśvaravādinaḥ*); those who have realized the Lord (*īśvarasiddhāḥ*), who are the proponents of [the identity with] Śiva (*śivasamavādinaḥ*), who have realized Sadāśiva (*sadāśivasiddhāḥ*), and who reside in the worlds (*bhuvana*) described by Śakti; and those who are pure, having been made so by one of the Śivas other than those already liberated (*aparamuktānyatamaśivakṛtaśuddha*).

Those initiated by initiation consisting of the ritual arrangements of the Śākta scriptures are the Śaktisiddhas; those initiated by initiation consisting of the ritual arrangements of the Gārūḍa, Dakṣiṇa, Vāma, and Bhūta Tantras— performed by any one of the four Śivas presiding over the eight kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, and presiding over the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta— are [the Bhūtasiddhas].

The perfected beings (*siddhas*) of the four levels beginning with *nivṛtti* are those directly arisen from the five faces of Śiva-Īśāna; they are initiated therein by means of an initiation that possesses a specific arrangement (*kliptimatī*). Due to the variety of desires produced by the diversity in the ripening of their impurities (*mala*), they are the perfected beings starting from the level of *śāntyatīta-kalā* down to the end of *kālāgni*. Furthermore, there are those who have transcended even that, the supremely liberated ones (*paramuktas*).

Having undergone initiation, through the sequential performance of the rites to be performed thereafter, there shall arise the attainment of union (*sāyujya*) characterized by the essence of what is appropriate [to that state], along with those perfected ones whose success is characterized by the illumination of the intellect.

Due to the perfection of the intellect, which is the cause for being counted among them, there is no longer any temporal limitation or other such constraints regarding the manifestation of the pure consciousness.
Why is this so? He says:
"O twice-born ones, for it is not possible for knowledge to perceive Kalā and the other [categories], since that reality which exists above Puruṣa is the exclusive domain of the Śiva-tantras."
The soul’s dependence on Him would not exist without the favor of His specific grace;
therefore, through that sequence, the power descended and awakens the individual souls (aṇus).

O twice-born ones! Regarding the manifestation of the principles beginning with *vidyā* and *kalā*: those whose initial [principles] are pure, such as *Śuddhalakṣaṇeśvara* and others, and whose final [principles] are both pure and impure, such as *Īśvara* and others—[this refers to] the manifestation of those principles beginning with *vidyā* and *kalā*. In the intellect (*buddhi*), this is according to the Sāṃkhya and other systems.
Knowledge arising from the study of [other] scriptures cannot have that reality as its object; for what reason?
Because that reality which transcends the individual soul (puruṣa) has Śivatantra alone as its domain.
It is the object of knowledge produced solely by the Śiva-scriptures, and it was proclaimed by Īśvara, who presides over the womb of Māyā.

According to the Tantras, even in the absence of a discrimination between the impure person (*malapuruṣa*) [and Śiva], a discrimination between the *kalā*s and other [categories] and the Person (*puruṣa*) is possible; therefore, they too are designated by the word "Śiva. If that were so, since the Śiva-scriptures also serve to purify the intellect (*buddhi*), the intellect purified by them would have as its object the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) arising from it. That is incorrect, because [the scriptures act] without [requiring] a specific favor toward individual persons.

O disciple, as declared in the Śiva-śāstra, without the initiation of Śiva (śivadīkṣā), there can be no devotion to that [Śiva], nor any qualification for the study of that Śiva-śāstra. For that reason, there exists a variety of applications and instructions regarding the ritual of initiation (dīkṣākriyā), which corresponds to the fitness for attaining each respective stage in due order.

Power belonging to Śiva descends in accordance with the recipient's capacity. Through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other means, it awakens the individual souls (*aṇu*) and makes them cognizant of the categories of reality, such as *vidyā*, *kalā*, and so forth. Therefore, initiation is that which possesses the power to manifest the consciousness of the soul, characterized by a purified refinement arising from the previously studied scriptures of Śiva.
To the doubt that "intellect is the awakener," he says that this is incorrect:
"The stainless, all-encompassing knowledge, arisen from initiation by Śiva and so forth,
which has manifested as Śiva-hood, shall consist of the very nature of Śiva’s power."
In the Śaiva system, it is the [Śiva-]śāstra that reveals the highest good (*śreyas*), and not the intellect (*buddhi*).
Even the Śiva-scripture, because its own fruit consists in the non-determination of the Buddhists,
does not directly reveal that knowledge characterized by the qualities of the person (*pums*) which has as its essential nature the non-determination [of objects].

Regarding the statement "the fruit of the Śiva-scripture" (p. 595): if it were merely a refinement (*saṃskāra*) distinct from the refinement characterized by the manifestation of Śiva-nature, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the person being subject to rebirth. Therefore, [the scripture] is that which refines through a lineage (*paraṃparayā*) the refinement characterized by the manifestation of Śiva-nature; however, that scripture does not do so directly.
It is a refinement of the person (*puruṣa*); however, when accompanied by reasoning, it is a direct refinement of the intellect (*buddhi*). As it is said in the *Mataṅga*:
"By the rays of the outpouring of knowledge issuing from the lotus-like mouth of that [teacher]..."
By those pure lamps of the world who approach him through his grace.
"O Brahmin, it is seen [only] when empowered by the Buddhas, and never otherwise.

Here, "is seen" refers to the *māyās*. Therefore, through initiation (*dīkṣā*), by means of the removal of the bondage that is produced by itself, there occurs the manifestation of one's own true nature as Śiva, characterized by the state of being easily attained.

In the case of a person possessing a refinement (*saṃskṛti*) arising from [the study of] Śiva’s scriptures that have been well-practiced, it is the power of Śiva (*śivaśakti*)— resplendent within the intellect (*buddhi*) that has arisen from that refinement— that is the awakener (*bodhikā*), and not the intellect itself. For instance, even though the mind and intellect do not directly reach Śiva, and even though they act as indicators of the jewel, it is like the light of the jewel [which reveals it].

Even the radiance of the mind and intellect, though fashioned with form, falls entirely upon the auspicious *lakṣa*; and in the intellect, the power of Śiva’s vision, possessing the nature of grace and supported by *śuddhavidyā*, shines forth directly in that supportless place which is the station of the emergence of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) and the rest. As for that which is therein:

To the extent that it is not augmented by anything else, it is an illuminator; thus, being with an object, it becomes an illuminator and a cognizer of the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) of the power of the Person (*puṃśakti*) everywhere, in such a way that it is distinguished from the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
This has been stated in the *Mataṅga*:
"But when the power of knowledge shines forth in the intellect of a person,
then [the soul] proceeds, endowed with the rays of its own potency.
Thus, in one initiated into Śaivism, that [power] has arisen and become fully manifest through the initiation of Śiva and other such rites, according to the manner described.

It is declared to consist of Śiva and Śakti; it is characterized by the relationship between the manifestor and the manifested, wherein the manifestation of Śiva-ness reaches its culmination. For this very reason it is stainless, and for this very reason it is all-pervasive.

Because it is free from the duality of the impeller and the impelled arising from limiting adjuncts, and because it is the dawn of the discernment that destroys the notion of being a limited self, it is Śiva.

It is similar to the characteristic of Śiva (Śiva-nature), yet distinct from the characteristic of bondage (Paśu-nature) which consists of impurity as its limiting adjunct; it is its own specific characteristic, consisting of the discernment of one's own Śiva-nature; and it is both similar to and distinct from all categories such as Śiva and impurity, being essentially the nature of one's own discernment. As it has been stated in the *Mokṣakārikās*:
Through the light of consciousness empowered by the radiance of Śakti,
one perceives Śiva together with Śakti and the other [principles], as the veil residing within the self has fallen away.

Therefore, it is manifested as Śiva-hood. By means of one's own *kriyā-śakti* (power of action), which is presided over by the power of Śiva and preceded by ritual acts consisting of the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*)— characterized by retention (*kumbhaka*) pregnant with meditation and recitation (*japa*)—
one pierces the knots of the principles (*tattva-granthi*) with the syllables *huṃ*, *guṃ*, and *phaṭ*.

In the heart— wherein the palace is interwoven with the weapons of the remembered dagger-mantra, adorned with the digit of the syllable *auṃ*, wherein the Supreme is present in the waking state, and which is the very nature of the characteristics of reality (*tattva*)—
there exists, in whatever manner appropriate, the distinctness of consciousness and non-consciousness from one another, just as their respective natures are established.

Just as one's own [limited] activity, through the examination of its respective specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), immediately upon the vision of the reality of its own nature, does not dissolve directly because it possesses the essential nature of characteristics such as insentience (*jaḍatva*), so too is the abandonment of the conceit of self (*svātmābhimāna*) regarding one's own self within that which is other than oneself. Just as a knot is severed by one's own knife.
Through the dissolution of its own causes, by means of that which is designated by the term "purity of reality" characterized by contemplation—

arising from the power of the impressions (saṃskāra) sprouted in the intellect through the study of the Śiva-scriptures— one [perceives] the distinct [elements] beginning with earth, which are no longer governed by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the state of being male (puṃstva) as overcome by primordial nature (prakṛti), but rather governed by the limiting adjunct of the state of being male as permeated by the limited power (kalā).

Having become the cause for the attainment of *rāga* (attachment) through the self (*svātman*) by means of the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, and then again, while abiding in those *kalās* adorned with the *kalā* of the *sūkara* (the boar), in that state of supreme dream where *ramā* (consort) is present— having become the cause for the attainment of *vidyā* and the rest through the self (*svātman*) consisting of the discrimination between *puruṣa* and attachment (*rāga*) etc., which proceeds sequentially in the throat, and then again...
At the tip of the throat and in the palate which is about to be described, the single and double-kramika-kalās— having become the cause for the attainment of *pralayakaivalya*, *karma-kaivalya*,
and *vijñānakaivalya* through the discrimination between Māyā and Puruṣa by means of one's own self—
[reside] again within those kalās; specifically, in the palate where Rudra is present, in the state of supreme deep sleep (*paramasuṣupti*) adorned with the *makāra*-kalā.

The nature of the Self, which is characterized by knowledge and agency when obscured by impurity (mala), and whose true form is revealed through the act of transcending that impurity, is set forth here. Just so, the individual soul (paśu), characterized by knowledge and agency when affected by impurity, is likewise [described] as being further conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) once it has manifested the means for transcending that impurity.

The state of Śiva-ness consists of the characteristics of consciousness (*jñatva*) and agency (*kartṛtva*). Because these two characteristics of the Self are mutually distinct, when one examines each respective characteristic as it is being performed, immediately upon the realization of the true nature of the Self, [one perceives] within oneself—distinct from the other—the impurity consisting of the characteristics of a bound soul (*paśu*): "I am ignorant; I am a non-agent; once again, by Māyā..."

"I am a knower of only a little; I am a doer of only a little"—this is the nature of the consciousness of the bound soul (*paśu*). By abandoning this conceit of self (*svātmābhimāna*) through that which is termed "purity of self" (*ātmaśuddhi*), which consists of one's own essential nature, one should arise from the supreme fourth state (*turyāvasthā*)—which is the cause of one's own [awakening]—in such a way that one's own nature, though conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is realized as "I am Śiva."
Through the discernment of the impurity from the Self— strengthened by the awakening of Śiva which has some slight manifestation—
there is liberation from impurity; [this leads to] the principle of the Vidyeśvara, strengthened by the gross *nāda*, arising from that,
characterized by sovereignty yet possessed of the state of bondage (*paśutva*) sprouted by the impurity of gross authority, [and occurring] immediately upon its own unfolding.

Having become the cause for the establishment of the manifestation of one's own nature as conditioned by gross Śiva-hood, there then arises within those *kalās*— in the Supreme Fourth State (*turya*) adorned with the *bindu-kalā*, where the Lord is present at the center of the brows, and where the stainless waking state has dawned—
the limited perception of the bound soul (*paśubodha*) thinking "I am dependent," and the perception of Śiva (*śivabodha*) thinking "I am Śiva."
By means of one’s own self— which has been augmented by a slight elevation and possesses a discernment whose nature is the *vidyeśvara-tattva* along with its entire range of functions—

one’s gross state of Śiva-hood, together with its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is instantly dissolved. Thereupon, the subtle authority arising from that [state]— consisting of the *sadāśiva-śakti-śiva-tattvas* augmented by the suddenly arisen subtle *nāda*— is attained.

Having become the cause for the accomplishment of the manifestation of one's own nature—which is characterized by sovereignty, yet conditioned by the state of bondage (paśutva), and which arises immediately upon the unfolding of that [sovereignty] while being conditioned by subtle Śivatva—[one attains the state] known as Sadāśiva, extending from Īśāna up to Tattvaśānta, according to the Mṛgendra-śruti: "That which transcends Īśāna and extends to the end of Tattvaśānta is remembered as Sadāśiva. Furthermore, in those [states]:

In the *kalās*, from one's own limit to one's own self, there is that which is adorned with the four *kalās* beginning with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*). Furthermore, above that, extending downward from the *dvādaśānta*, is the *mahāmāyā-śakti* situated below its own arrangement;
[within it are] the four *kalās* beginning with *vyoma-rūpa*, separated by *samanā* and *vyāpinī*. These are the *śakti* and so forth, up to *mahāmāyā*.
O you who have become one with me, O you whose end is the mind, adorned with the four *kalās*, O you who abide in the supreme state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*),

O you in whom the totality ending with Śakti is present, O you who possess the individuality ending with Īśāna, O you who consist of the five elements, having once again transcended the subtlest *nāda* characterized by the adjuncts of your own world; [I bow to you].

Following the crest-lock (*śikhā*), having pervaded its own [level], the *samanā* and *kalā*; becoming one with *mahāmāyā*, the *unmanā* state; the *kalā*, *kṛmikā*, and *anāhata* becoming Śiva, then becoming Paraśiva, and finally becoming the absolute (*kevala*)—[this occurs] within Sadāśiva, who consists of the form of Īśāna, at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), where the arising of a stainless dream takes place. He [is] the collection of his own activities, the power of Sadāśiva.

Through the discernment of the Self as the essence of the Śiva-tattva, one’s own subtle state of Śiva—which consists of qualities such as omniscience and the capacity for all conceptualization—along with its own limiting adjuncts (upādhis), instantly dissolves; likewise, the consciousness of the bound soul (paśu-bodha), characterized by lack of autonomy, dissolves along with the consciousness of Śiva. Thereupon, having merged into the Power (śakti) whose nature is Mahāmāyā, one becomes absorbed in the mantra whose nature is Mahāmāyā.

And when that [state] exists as the pervasive Śivamantrin throughout the entire white and black paths, it suddenly arises from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of the power of obstruction (*rodha-śakti*) out of the stainless state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Having become self-dependent and having transcended all its own limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it becomes the unstruck (*anāhata*) Brahman of Śiva, adorned with the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*).

Having fully observed and embraced Mahāmāyā, who is designated by the word "sound" preceded by the three [syllables], O you whose form transcends peace (*śāntyatīta-kalā*), whose own form is the nature of Śiva-tattva, whose own form is...
whose own form is the unstruck (*anāhata*) supreme Śiva, whose own form is both with form and without form— by way of being that very own form.
Then, having perceived his own nature as freshly purified of all adjuncts (*upādhi*),

the Guru— being devoted to his own form, devoted to the Guru, and upholding his own bliss— meditated upon the Lord Īśāna, who is white with the dance, who possesses three forms, whose own form is his very embodiment, and who is present as a manifest form.

"Below the end of the twelve-finger space, in the plane where the stainless deep sleep arises, the wise man should proceed to the middle region together with the slender-limbed woman. Without reaching the middle region, he should abandon that fickle woman. Thus it is said.

Based on the *Sarvajñānottara* scripture: having drawn up [the breath] from the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*) while the woman, whose nature is Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), is facing downward, he shakes off [all things] through the skill of discerning reflection and action by means of the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*), which consists of the state of stainless deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and his own mental construction; then, having cast it upward, he absorbs it into himself.

Furthermore, O Śivamantriṇī, Mahāmāyā, whose essence is mantra, pervades [the soul]; and when she abides there as the mere power of grace from Śiva for the sake of assistance, then— at the end of the twelve fingers— there arises the Turya (the Fourth State), which possesses the stainless dawn of Turya that is another name for the pervasion of the Self as proclaimed by the Śruti, namely "one's own consciousness-intellect," yet it remains conditioned by the *āṇava* impurity.

In the Supreme Self, which is all-pervading, self-luminous, and the manifestation of the supreme state of Śiva— arising between the dissolution of the state of the bound soul (paśubhāva) brought about by the removal of the impurity of Māyā, and the purity of the Self preceded by that dissolution, which conforms to the nature of Paraśiva— there occurs the manifestation of the supreme Śiva.

O you whose nature is the characteristic of Śiva, O you who are the very form of Śiva! Just as the individual self (*ātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), as well as Śiva and the supreme self, are mutually distinct according to their established designations and their respective characteristics as they are being examined, so too, immediately following the vision of Śiva— *Note: The provided text fragment appears to be an introductory or transitional passage for a philosophical discussion concerning the distinction between the individual soul and the supreme reality within the Śaiva tradition.*

Indeed, when one abandons the observation of fetters (pāśa) and observes one's own true nature (svarūpa), this constitutes the pervasion of the Self (ātmavyāpti); otherwise, it is the pervasion of Śiva (śivavyāpti). When one thus contemplates the pervasive [deity] as possessing qualities such as omniscience, [that is the latter].
This pervasion of Śiva exists as the causal form within consciousness;
the supreme pervasion (paravyāpti) between those two consists of qualities such as omnipresence and so forth,
according to the *Svacchanda-śruti* on the division of the *Lalita*.
"Having meditated upon Śiva himself, one becomes Śiva oneself;
through the yoga of attaining the state of *samarasībhāva* (taste-union), that is here called *samādhi*.

This is because of the scriptural authority of the *Skandakālottara*, which speaks of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), identity (*tādrūpya*), abandonment (*tyāga*), and [attainment of] Śiva by means of the Self and the Supreme Self.

By means of that which is delineated as pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is a manifestation of one's own omniscience and other qualities characterized by identity with Śiva— this being the state of innate liberation (*anādimukti*) intended as direct purity; it possesses a form equal to Śiva’s own omniscience and other qualities, which are manifested in the state of innate liberation intended as direct purity, though separated [from it] by the [conceptual] desire for purity.

By means of that state which is characterized by a lineage and attributes equal to Śiva, arising from the relationship with the two Śivas (Śiva and Śakti), and which—being focused solely on pure non-duality (*śuddhādvaita*), qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*), and absolute unity—is free from conceptual construction, free from objective support, free from the need for meditative reflection (*nididhyāsana*), and unwavering;
and which is celebrated by the three names Śiva-samādhi, Śiva-yoga, and Śiva-vyāpti; [one attains] the staff-bearing state, as distinct from all others.
Just as one might say "I am Devadatta" after assuming the state of a staff, so too, having assumed for the state of being an animal (paśu) the condition of the impurity belonging to others,
one realizes "I am Śiva"— characterized by recognition— as the nature of Śiva through one's own self,
which is difficult to perceive except through the mouth of a Guru.
That syllable is the letter *śi*, and the word ending in *vā* becomes the word;
the word *asi* and the letter *ya* constitute the nature of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*).

When the five-syllabled mantra "Śivāya" has been recited and purified according to the scripture— even through that means by which the mind culminates in the realization "I am Śiva," following the sequence of the three syllables and three feet—
one should abandon it, just as someone with a torch in hand might discard the object once it has been clearly perceived.
"Having illuminated the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should subsequently relinquish that knowledge."

According to the scripture, it is the goal to be attained; according to the scripture, it is the emergence of the state of Śiva, which has transcended [the levels]. It is the stainless emergence of its own specific characteristic beyond the fourth (turyātīta).

Being directly nothing but purity, independent of anything else, it is such a Śiva, resembling the state of Śiva-ness, the supreme form that illuminates the mere existence of categories such as Śiva and the rest.

The supreme state of Śiva—consisting of the three qualities such as sovereignty (*svatantratā*) and the differentiation of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), which manifests through distinct functions performed separately from Śivā; which is free from the three qualities (*triguṇa-varjanīya*); which is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) and devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*) due to the differentiation of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) characterized by the consciousness of others (*parasaṃvitti-lakṣaṇa*)—has been unveiled. [This is] the gross and subtle [state] accompanied by limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*).

O Śiva, you who possess all forms and are imperishable; you whose manifestation is distinct from all forms and imperishable; you who possess cessation and the bliss of Śiva; you who are the enjoyment of Śiva and the supreme self-sufficient happiness; you who are the state beyond all states, recited as the first of all states, the state of unsurpassed... Furthermore, you consist of the supreme manifestation, independent of Śiva and Śakti.

The manifest, which is of the nature of non-dual consciousness and consists of the activity of its own essential form, is in every way directly realized through its flashing forth in one's own experience. At that very moment, although Śiva is ungraspable within the array of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he becomes clearly discernible by the method of analytical investigation, such that there occurs a vivid manifestation resembling the graspable object.

Likewise, by means of the connection with its own similarity—whose sole nature is the state of Śiva characterized as the perceiver that has somehow flashed forth—it becomes once again the directly realized Śiva. This is the twofold Śiva-nature;
it is the knowledge manifested as Śiva-nature, which serves as the means for the manifestation of that [Śiva-nature], for the sake of one's own power of consciousness.

It has become action; it reveals the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) according to the stated sequence for one who pursues the goal beyond attachment and the like. Therefore, even the perfection of equal vision (*samarśana-siddhi*) should not be said to be a property of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*). For the intellect is not the revealer of the highest good.
[The passage] beginning with "unveiled by the state of Śiva" and so forth—this much is extremely secret; having analyzed its internal nature...

Furthermore, let it not be written by reciters or translated into other languages; let it not be given again to one who is unworthy. When a man’s intellect is endowed with *sattva*, the Lord permits detachment (*vairāgya*) through the purification of *rajas* and *tamas*; thereafter, immediately upon that engagement, [the distinction arises] due to the difference in causes.
It is like the various types of spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). Therefore, detachment (*vairāgya*) arises from one or another form of knowledge.

According to the *Śrīmat Parākhya Śruti*, because there are differences in the causes of detachment arising from the causes of knowledge belonging to any one of the Lokāyata schools and so forth, [the result] is associated with the fourfold set beginning with *dharma* (merit/virtue), or produced from the triad beginning with *dharma*.
The varieties of contentment are now described. Furthermore, the varieties of detachment (vairāgya) are also briefly stated here:
it is the state of dispassion even toward one's own body in one who is afflicted by disease and other such sufferings.
Being content in all undertakings, one who is free from desire recoils from suffering—
whether internal or otherwise— and detachment will certainly arise.
For one who considers the acquisition, preservation,
and protection of wealth to be suffering, detachment arises suddenly.
When one who is affectionate is separated from a loved one, he is tormented by grief;
realizing that affection is the cause of suffering, he becomes dispassionate.
But a lustful man, upon seeing even a slight cause for detachment in a woman,
immediately attains detachment, which is the cause for attaining the highest good.
The body cannot be sustained without truth, nor can it be otherwise maintained by water and such;
for even the loss of truth for a single day brings exhaustion upon it instantly.
For this reason, it is difficult to satisfy; thus, dispassion arises.
In some cases, one attains dispassion through [the realization of the faults of] receiving gifts and so forth.
Someone may become detached all of a sudden through the power of merit;
thus, contentment is said to be tenfold in the teaching of Śiva.
O best of the twice-born, all other forms of contentment (tuṣṭi) are likewise withdrawn right here;

that which exists with reference to oneself— such as the serenity of the mind resulting from favorable conditions that serve as causes for internal happiness, or agitation caused by their opposites— arises from the sight of living beings afflicted by disease and the like.

Because of its power (*prabhavatvāt*). It exists with reference to the deity (*adhideva*), meaning that it exists as the cause of the happiness of beings (*bhūtasukha*)—such as favorable wind, rain, and sunshine—and because it has power over what is adverse to them, such as fierce winds, excessive rain, and extreme heat. It exists with reference to beings (*adhibhūta*).

Regarding the external world (*adhibhūta*): it consists of the enjoyment of women and other objects that are causes of happiness for living beings and are favorable to them, as well as the overcoming of adverse things such as lions and tigers.
