Because these arise from [the subjugation of] those [adverse forces], there are internal (*ādhyātmika*), divine (*ādhidevika*), and elemental (*ādhibhautika*) sufferings;
from those internal, divine, and elemental sufferings, [there arises the need for] the acquisition of wealth and so forth, [as well as] affection...

[Disgust arises] from separation, from weeping born of grief, from sexual intercourse, from impurity, from accepting gifts, from [the realization that] past-earned merit is not the cause [of lasting happiness], and from natural detachment. Thus, from these ten causes of detachment, there arise in sequence:
disgust toward the internal (ādhyātmikī), the divine (ādhidaivikī), the elemental (ādhibhautikī), the self-reproachful (svāparādhikā), the mocking (viḍambākṣepikā), and so forth.

The meaning is that the ten contentments (*tuṣṭi*), namely *vaikhānasā* and *kāmodbhavā*, become distinct due to the different means of attaining dispassion (*vairāgya*). Furthermore, contentment is a specific form of knowledge. As it is stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
"In this context, the intellect whose objects are the Person (*puṃs*), Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*), and so forth, is what constitutes perfection (*siddhi*)."
"Contentment is the thought of one who has not achieved his goal that 'I have achieved my goal.
Therefore, since that [contentment] also has the self as its object, it indeed becomes a cause for liberation through a traditional succession. As they say:
"But he who should delight only in the self, and be satisfied with the self, O Mānava..."

"Having risen above all evils, he goes to the eternal Brahman. This satisfaction, moreover, is said— according to the various systems of philosophy— to be like a spiritual attainment (*siddhi*) for each of those beginning with the Cārvākas and ending with the Sāṃkhyas, who possess a sequential knowledge of the principles starting from the elements (*bhūta*) up to primordial nature (*prakṛti*), as well as the Puruṣa distinguished from them.
He states that the tenfold [set], by way of bringing about the principles beginning with *puṃstattva* and *prakṛti*, becomes a hundred in number: "(p.
615) And these, by virtue of bringing about the elements, the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the other principles..."
When combined, there are one hundred forms of contentment in the teaching of Śiva.

This is clear. Now, when [the Lord] brings about the state of identity with Rajas and Tamas, He likewise employs the intellect (buddhi) in its own duty, which is the production of sovereignty. This too is examined in brief through its own distinctions; thus he says:
Now, the various divisions of sovereignty are also briefly indicated;
the eightfold sovereignty exists through the differentiation of the conscious self.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "by means of the distinction from the quality of intellect (buddhi) which is one's own self. To the question "Of whom is this? he says:

"In the case of the wise man who is established in knowledge, possesses the desire for dispassion, and is a knower of the Self, [the yogin] may, by his will, produce the sattva of the intellect belonging to that atom for the sake of its sovereignty."

The subject (*dharmin*) has been described as one who practices violence and so forth, or one established in knowledge; one endowed with any one of the [five] types of knowledge regarding the elements and so forth; one desiring dispassion (*virāga*), or one endowed with any one of the aforementioned forms of dispassion or attachment; and for that very reason, the wise practitioner (*sādhaka*), the subtle self (*aṇu-ātman*), [acts] according to his will upon the senses and so forth.
Through the creative ideation (*saṃkalpa*) of Śiva, who is the indifferent cause, or through the creative ideation of the practitioner, *sattva*—
which has attained identity with *rajas* and *tamas*— should produce the powers of sovereignty such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and the rest. He defines them by distinguishing them individually.
Aṇimā is a state of existence subtler even than an atom;
laghimā is the possession of swift velocity and the non-sinking even in mud and the like.
And having attained the state of *mahimā*, [he exists] with a vast body, sense organs, and so forth.
By the word "sense organs" (*indriya*), the locations of the sense organs are intended. Now, he explains where the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) are employed here:
The triad consisting of the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth is established through their effects;
the five qualities beginning with *prāpti* belong to the yogin and are born from the instruments (*karaṇa*).

The triad refers to the triad beginning with *aṇimā* (the power of atomization) as effects. Through a traditional lineage, it is established that sovereignty (*aiśvarya*)—which is the effect of a common intellect arising from external worlds and bodies—has entered into a state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyadaśā*), resting upon various other states such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, according to its specific form. Thus, the body and the rest are maintained as the very essence of power (*śakti*).
Having become its power, the subordinate qualities (guṇas) manifest as the five yogis;

they are born from the instruments (karaṇa) of the practitioner. Having become the powers of the internal organs—intellect, ego, and so forth—and the external organs, both directly and indirectly, they manifest for the sake of the individual soul.
He defines the five [perfections] beginning with attainment (*prāpti*):

Attainment is the accomplishment of one's desired object through the mind; the abode of qualities is called *nāma*; the creation of thousands of women is *krīḍā-prākāmya*; and swift movement is *āśuyā*.
The execution of commands regarding Brahmā and the others, as well as their worship, is considered mastery (*īśitā*).
Mastery (*vaśitva*) consists of subjugation and indeed the creation of the world.
For one who enjoys [this state], there is non-obstruction by karma and the like; this is called mastery (*vaśitā*).
Depending on the excellence or deficiency of one's qualification (*adhikāra*), there is likewise excellence or deficiency [in the enjoyment].
Each of these individual sovereignties (*aiśvarya*) being eightfold, they become sixty-four in number.
He says that it exists as follows:
"The eight qualities, such as the power of the jewel (maṇi) and so forth, which have been specified for the Piśācas,
should be known as twofold for the Rakṣasas and threefold for the Yakṣas."
The Gāndharva soma possesses four qualities, while that of Indra possesses five;
that of the Somas is sixfold, and that of Prajāpati is sevenfold.
The sovereignty of a Buddha is recorded as being sixty-four times that of Brahmā;
therefore, the sovereignty [of the Tathāgata] is considered to be sixty-four times greater than that.
And these deities, beginning with the Piśācas and ending with Pitāmaha (Brahmā), as perceived in the Sāṃkhya and other systems,

reside within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and not within the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*). This is to be understood as being sixty-four-fold, including the lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśvaras*) who dwell above each of those respective levels in their own worlds.

For the presiding deities of Māyā, such as Śrīkaṇṭha and others, it is not the Buddhist [view]; rather, it is said that they are presiding authorities over non-dharma by means of a distinction in their causal conditions, consisting essentially of the powers of knowledge and action.
Consequently, through the delusion of their sovereignty, they become intensely attached to sense objects.
Those whose karma is exhausted move about in the houses of the pure and the prosperous.
Consequently, they become joined with unrighteousness, agitated by the intoxication of wealth and sleep.

Then, immediately after attaining that sovereignty, being freed from the delusion of power characterized by ignorance— thinking "there is no one else superior"— they are thoroughly identified with unrighteousness toward sense objects such as women and the like.

Then, being deeply attached, their karma is exhausted and their virtuous deeds are thwarted— like Nahuṣa, Yayāti, and others who fell from the sovereignty of the gods. O Brahmin, they waver from their appropriate power and undergo a fall, for it is stated in such scriptural passages as, "This is the land of action," and thus it cannot be said that there is no acquisition of karma there.

The scripture [speaks of Indra and others] departing for the sake of the abundance of the fruits of their merit; yet, since there is scriptural testimony that Indra and the others perform both good and evil deeds, those who possess limited sovereignty and the like, when they reach that particular point in time—their constituent parts having been exhausted and their karma spent—depart from that station. Even they do not experience the fruit of unrighteousness, as did Nahuṣa and others.

They eat [the remnants] because unrighteousness was practiced there; however, solely by the residue of their auspicious karma, they obtain enjoyments among people in the homes of the pure and the prosperous. This is what has been stated: "In the home of the pure and the prosperous, he attains that which is purified by yoga."

Immediately thereafter, those who are intoxicated by wealth and sleep, agitated by pride, think: "There is nothing more intoxicated than I, nor anything beyond me. Their minds are fragmented from knowledge regarding the objects of enjoyment, with injunctions and prohibitions shattered; their goodness (*sattva*) is destroyed, their intellect is increased by the growth of predominant darkness (*tamas*), and they are driven by a slight degree of rectitude.

One becomes joined with unrighteousness (*adharma*) arising from that. That righteousness (*dharma*), as previously mentioned, is divided into ten types by way of being the opposite of the nature of unrighteousness consisting of violence and so forth; thus he says:
"Whether in violence, or in theft, or even in false speech..."
In approaching the wife of one's guru, and in retaliating for an injury received.
Those of blind vision constantly engage in anger, or in the neglect of daily rites, or in impurity, or in dissatisfaction, or indeed in constant dishonesty.
Those who follow unrighteous conduct (*adharmavṛtti*) have been stated to number ten, as before.
According to the rule *upasargasya ghan amanuṣye bahulam*, there is a lengthening of the vowel of the prefix;
thus they are called *andhadṛṣṭayaḥ*—those whose vision is blinded, whose knowledge is defiled by darkness (*tamas*). Now, regarding the beast engaged in unrighteousness:

The Blessed One says that he unites [the individual soul] with the knowledge of the specific characteristics of error, which arises from a state of excellence produced by the three factors beginning with dharma— these being anointed by the fourfold set beginning with dharma— which itself arises from a buddhi that has become pure darkness (tamas) alone, having destroyed sattva and rajas through its five-fold nature.
Then Maheśāna impels that slight unrighteousness which has arisen within the continuum of ignorance,
so that the deluded one does not perceive it.
The remainder is "beneficial and harmful. He indicates that it possesses five joints: "Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and andhatāmisra—these five are considered the functions of ignorance (ajñāna)."
Andha, Pūrvakānta, Miśra, and Andhatāmisra—he defines them in sequence: "The notion of self in that which is not-self is proclaimed as *Andha*;
it is distinguished according to the various views of reality (*tattva*), beginning from the elements (*bhūta*) and ending with the unmanifest (*avyakta*). (p. 623)
Darkness (tamas) is declared to be tenfold, while delusion (moha) is considered to be eightfold;
this is because, even when powers such as atomization (aṇimā) have been attained, there is still the realization of "otherness" [regarding those powers].
That determination of superiority regarding all ten objects, beginning with sound, through the distinction between the divine and the non-divine, is proclaimed as great delusion (mahāmoha).
Or, due to the distinction between divine and non-divine regarding the ten [objects] beginning with sound,
or because of the deficiency in the accomplishment of even the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇimā*.
The torment arising from the destruction of food that has been obtained is proclaimed as *tāmisra*;
likewise, when the powers such as *aṇimā* or sounds and so forth are being enjoyed by another.
In bringing about that happiness, there is first the *tāmisra* and then the *andha*;
thereafter, the various types of ignorance (*ajñāna*) are considered to be of sixty-four kinds.

The notion of selfhood (*ātmabhāva*) regarding what is not the self—such as the body and so forth—is the cognition characterized by a misconception (*viparyaya*) concerning the self, namely the thought that "when this body is discarded, I myself no longer exist. This is called darkness (*tamas*). Furthermore, this darkness is said to consist of the views of the Cārvākas and others, distinguished by their failure to perceive the reality of the principles (*tattva*) ranging from the elements (*bhūta*) up to the unmanifest (*avyakta*).

Because it is an effect of *tamas*, [the state of non-accomplishment] is characterized by the distinctions of the attainment of self-realization through the excellence of the knowledge of reality— ranging from the elements (*bhūta*) up to primordial nature (*prakṛti*)— and by the non-attainments designated as the incapacity of the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists in the absence of accomplishment due to the incapacity of that intellectual power.

That which is indicated by those characterized by *tamas* is "otherness" (*aparatva*) through its apprehension; that is, from the knowledge characterized by error, [one thinks] "there is no happiness beyond this. The divine is unseen by people such as ourselves; it is what is heard (scriptural), pertaining to the next world, and consists of the fivefold objects beginning with sound. The seen is worldly, pertaining to this life, and consists of the same fivefold objects beginning with sound. By means of that...

The determination of superiority—based on the distinction between the divine and the non-divine, and the distinction between what is seen and what is heard—is a misconception regarding superiority, because there is a deficiency in the factors such as the *dharma* used as a means of proof. This is due to the failure of [the means] being complete, fruitful, and reaching completion. Alternatively, it is due to the destruction of what has been attained through the incompleteness of the means of proof, as in the case of Nahuṣa and others.
When another powerful yogin, by the power of yoga, extracts that pleasure— namely, the withdrawal of the pleasure arising from the eighteen signs beginning with sound—
the [states] are tenfold: *pūrvanta*, *ātmakānta*, *miśra*, *andhapūrvaka*, and *andhatāmisra*.

Through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of supernatural powers (*siddhi*), darkness (*tamas*) is tenfold; through the limiting adjunct of the eight powers beginning with atomization (*aṇimā*), delusion (*moha*) is eightfold;
and through the limiting adjuncts of sound and the rest, great delusion (*mahāmoha*) is tenfold, as are the states of *tāmisra* and *andhatāmisra*.

Sound and the rest are ten, while the eight beginning with atomization are [eight]; and through the limiting adjunct of the yogi’s seizing of strength—such as the loss of what has been gained or the loss of power—it is likewise.

Since each [type] is eighteenfold, there are sixty-four varieties of ignorance. Now, by way of contentment (*tuṣṭi*) as its own effect, he describes the varieties of detachment (*vairāgya*): "And non-detachment is of a hundred kinds, due to the reversal of the contentments. (p. 626)
At that time, there was no loathing or such feelings toward any objects for those people.

The reversal of contentments—which arise from the cause of dispassion—is their non-existence; this is the state of abiding in the self as unmanifest power. That whose nature (ātman) is such an effect characterized by contentment is thus described as "having the nature of reversal" (*vyatyayātmatas*). Non-dispassion is attachment (*rāga*); it is said to be slightly straightened, a cognition characterized by the perception of darkness (*tamas*).

When that which has arisen [from the intellect] is divided into a hundredfold—this is the remainder of the sentence—then, regarding all objects, the contentments (*tuṣṭi*) such as non-disgust (*ajugupsā*) and so forth are indeed of the nature of their own absence; thus, if disgust and so forth were not mentioned... the ten types of contentments would not exist. Furthermore, when the *rajas* and *tamas* in the mind have arisen from an unevolved *sattva*...
He states that from those causes, a lack of sovereignty arises through their respective divisions:
"The eightfold lack of sovereignty is the opposite of sovereignty;
and that [lack of sovereignty] arises from incapacity, which consists of one hundred and seventy-six [divisions]."

The remainder [of the statement] is that sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), which consists of the self, becomes eightfold non-sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*)— characterized by the non-manifestation of *aṇimā* and the other [powers], and having as its nature the absence of one's own form— and thus comes to be. Furthermore, since that non-sovereignty is described as being of the nature of incapacity (*aśakti*) regarding the body and so forth, which are the very essence of the powers such as *aṇimā*, it arises as incapacity.

The non-manifestation of powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth, which consists in abiding in one's own nature, constitutes an eightfold absence of [limited] form through its own effects. And that power, when stained by passion (*rāga*), arises from the triad beginning with merit (*dharma*) and consists of one hundred and seventy-six [powers]. Now, are all these [powers] indeed of such a number?
To the question "What is the designation of these powers? he says:
Because they consist of ignorance and contentment, there are one hundred and sixty-four;
however, the power of the intellect (buddhi-śakti) belongs to the defiled instrument (karaṇa) and is twelvefold in number.
Thus, in brief, incapacity (*aśakti*) consists of one hundred and six varieties.
Because it takes the form of ignorance (*ajñāna*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and knowledge (*jñāna*), there are sixty-four divisions based on ignorance;

the hundred divisions based on knowledge are due to the cause of dispassion (*vairāgya*); and because it takes the form of perfection (*siddhi*) and contentment, the incapacity of the intellect (*budhyaśakti*) consists of one hundred and sixty-four [varieties].

Therefore, according to the method described, the power of intellect (*buddhi-śakti*) consists in the specific states of the culmination of ignorance and dispassion; it does not, however, consist in the specific state of the culmination of non-sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*), as is held by the Sāṃkhyas. This is because that non-sovereignty is not admitted to be of the nature of the incapacity of the body, senses, mind, or ego.

Then, the power consisting of lack of sovereignty belonging to the perceived instrument—comprising the senses, mind, ego, and the self—is twelvefold by way of the number twelve. This incapacity is indeed distinct from the capacity of the body; thus, according to the aforementioned sequence, the total sum is six hundred and sixty-six.

One hundred. Then, by way of the twenty-threefold lack of sovereignty (*anaīśvarya*)—consisting of the threefold incapacity of the body, the tenfold incapacity of the sense organs, and the tenfold incapacity of the mind and ego (*ahaṃkāra*) as conditioned by their respective adjuncts (*upādhi*)—it becomes twenty-three in number. Thus, for every individual entity, there is that [lack of sovereignty] through the differentiation of its respective conditions (*pratyaya*).
Having stated the enumeration, he concludes:
"Thus, entities such as dharma and the rest exist in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā);
they are said to be, in sequence, of the nature of cognitions due to the differentiation of their functions."
They cause the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) to have conviction; therefore, they are called "convictions" (*pratyaya*).

The word "in the intellect" (*buddhau*) is to be supplied [as the locus]. "Due to the difference in its modifications" (*tadvṛttibhedataḥ*) means due to the difference in the operations of its attributes and so forth.

For, at the commencement of the examination of non-existence (*abhāva*), they bring about the nature of the self and so on; thus, they are "cultivations" (*bhāvanā*) by virtue of being the self of cultivation.

Since entities have been described as having activity (*vyāpṛti*), [the author] now says "pretya" and so forth, because there is a distinction in the activity of the application of the word *pratyaya* here. That by which those factors such as *dharma* and so on perform the activity of conveying [their objects] through the nature of intense cultivation— that is the sense-faculty characterized as the mind (*manas*), together with its connection to the object within its own domain.
Through the determination arising from their origin, they cause the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) to understand;
they constantly produce cognitions whose object is the Person (puruṣa). Therefore, they are known as "cognitions" (pratyaya), and are thus metaphorically designated.
This has been stated in the Mṛgendra-tantra as well:
Thus, this manifestation of the intellect, characterized by abstract notions (*bhāvapratyaya*),
is called "awakening" (*bodha*) for the bound soul (*paśu*), because it serves as the ground for the manifestation of consciousness.

Having stated how many in number the collection of categories of existence (bhāvapratyaya) is when combined, he concludes by saying: Dharma is of ten kinds, knowledge is one hundred and eighty, detachment is sixty-four, sovereignty is sixty-four, and adharma is considered to be of ten kinds.
Ignorance consists of sixty-four [types], non-detachment would be one hundred;
lack of sovereignty is eightfold, and [the remaining afflictions] are three hundred and thirty-six.

(p. 631) Intending to express only the nature of the absence of the [powers] such as *aṇimā*, and considering that sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is eightfold, the collection of conditions—including dharma, adharma, and the rest—is counted;
thus, it amounts to thirty-six hundred and forty [conditions]. Furthermore, previously...
Having stated that when combined with the previously examined incapacities (aśaktis), the total would be six hundred and twelve, he concludes:
"The incapacity is considered to be one hundred and seventy-six in number;
when their functions are combined within the intellects (buddhis), they amount to six hundred and twelve."

Thus, the intellect (*buddhi*), consisting of eight states, has been briefly described. Now, the power of awakening (*budhya-śakti*)— which consists of the elevation of knowledge— is said to be [the same as] that which was recited immediately following [the intellect], characterized by the notion of self within the non-self through the distinction of accomplishment (*siddhi*).

Furthermore, since contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is of the nature of the non-arising of dispassion (*avairāgya*), how is it that the non-arising of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*)—like the [eight] powers (*śakti*)—is not considered a distinct category? Thus, there would be one hundred and six plus six [additional] categories. True.

However, insofar as incapacity (*aśakti*) results in the non-attainment of success (*asiddhi*) and so forth, there is indeed a distinction in its form as non-arising; therefore, these are not included among the aforementioned lords of the categories (*gaṇanātha*).

When one state, such as dharma and so forth, undergoes decline, another state arises in that very same manner; thus, this sequence of men’s states, characterized by the sinking and rising [of fortune], is difficult to cross and causes suffering.
To this he says: "In this great wheel of eight spokes, they wander again and again."
Those are persons, yet those persons do not perceive their end.
They wander there, moving about through occasional manifestations; they do not perceive the internal distinctions between those states. Now, beginning the examination of the *ahaṃkāra*:
henceforth, the principle of *ahaṃkāra* will be described in brief.
And that [consciousness], which is restricted to each individual, is established as having "I" as its essence.
Since the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*) arises immediately prior [to the senses], the examination of the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*) is described here until its conclusion;

this is very clear. "That which has the mind as its predecessor" means that for the ear and so forth, the mind is the first, i.e., the immediate antecedent; thus it is so called. Its material cause (*upādāna*) is from which [the mind] arises. Therefore, the examination of the principle of intellect is explained up to the end.

Then the reality of "I-ness" (*ahantattva*) arises. That is the reality called "the maker of 'I'" (*tadahaṃkṛt*). And why is that [reality] restricted to the nature of a cognition like intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth? Because it consists of the "I" (*ahamātmaka*). Although it is itself insentient, it is characterized by the activity of the power of stable knowledge directed toward the Self and others; and through being nourished by the supreme, it brings about its own manifestation.

The nature of its own appearance and disappearance consists of the reflective awareness of the object as "this is this," characterized by stability; like the intellect (*buddhi*), it possesses the state of being "I" and "mine" even though it is insentient (*acid*). It is defined by the function of the power of stable knowledge directed toward itself, and through being nourished by its own self-experience, its own manifestation consists of the nature of its own appearance and disappearance.
Just as the self-referential determination (*pratyātmaniyati*)— characterized by the cognitive grasp (*parāmarśapratyaya*) of "I, I" through stability—

is well-known as having its own direct perceptual function (*pratyakṣasvavṛttika*) designated as *garva*, which is delimited by itself and leads to its own inference; so too, through the medium of that function, it is correctly inferred.

And this is an illustration; it also possesses its own function, augmented by the power of action consisting of effort—which is designated as "impulse" (*saṃrambha*) and is the driver of life-force (*jīvana*), the maintenance of the body, and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "The five bodily winds move due to the impulse of which. And the movement of *prāṇa* and the others [is likewise].
The leading upward of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) is taught in the *Mṛgendra* and other scriptures; that is well understood. The sages raise an objection:

"Since it has been stated that [the subtle body] consists of egoity (*ahaṃkārika*), how can it be shown to be distinct from the effects of the intellect (*buddhi*)? How then can it be said to be something else? Thus they suspect.
Since I am here as the self whose nature is determination, O Lord, let that [determination] belong to the intellect alone; what need is there for this [other principle]? Tell me.

"Now, you have just said that I am the self (*ātman*), but that [self] is devoid of cognition; rather, it is of the nature of determination (*vyavasāyātmaka*), because such a quality belongs only to the function of the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, let there be only the intellect constantly present. What purpose, O Lord, do you see in this so-called ego (*ahaṃkāra*)? The Lord said: There is a distinction between them; thus he says:"
Whatever determination of an object exists with respect to each particular thing,
having the nature of "this," all of it is reckoned by the term "intellect" (buddhi).
That determination of an object which is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of what is grasped is established through differentiation with respect to each object;
it is firmly ascertained through the distinctness of each object, such as a jar or a cloth, which are mutually different.
Furthermore, that which consists of the form "this is all" and has the aspect of "this" is designated by the term *buddhi*.

It is reckoned as such; that word "intellect" (buddhi) is established by the term "effect" (kārya) and is thus remembered. Therefore, what has been accomplished by defining the distinction of the effects of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra)? To this he says: "But the self (ātman), being of a single form as 'I', is always firmly established."
How could this [cognition] consist of the determination of a grasper?

This [cognition] is intended by us as being of the nature of the *ahaṃkāra* (the ego-maker). Since it is distinct from that which is intended as the "I-self" (*aham-ātman*) when considered from the perspective of the intellect (*bauddha*), this form "I am" is further characterized by a distinctness consisting in the certainty of difference produced by the difference of objects, such as "I know the jar" and "I know the cloth."

Being of a single nature as "I myself," and possessing identical characteristics, this [cognition] nevertheless consists of a determination of the subject (*grāhaka*) which, by virtue of its difference from the determination of the object (*grāhya*), takes the form of a determination of the subject. How could this be the effect of a single cognition? It could not be so in any way, because the establishment of a difference in effects would entail a plurality [of causes].
Because it would follow that if there were conceptualization (*kalpanā*), there would be no [single] conceptualization of multiple principles (*anekatattva*), the cause is not a unity; thus he says:
"The intellect (*buddhi*) is directed toward the object; I am the grasping of the object."
O Brahmins, how can the oneness of those two, who are utterly distinct, be explained?

The intellect (*buddhi*), according to the manner described, is directed toward objects; by its orientation, it is proficient in grasping objects characterized as the graspable (*grāhya*). The ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), however, is the "I" which encompasses objects. By way of being oriented toward those same objects characterized as graspable, yet facing away from them [as the subject], it exists as an object characterized as the grasper (*grāhaka*) in the form of "I."

"Saṃgraha" means that which possesses the grasping of objects; thus it is so described. Therefore, O Brahmins, how could there be any identity between those two, which are absolutely distinct and possess entirely different effects? Not in any way whatsoever. The Sages [ask]: "Having set aside the statement that the effect is now of a single form, [explain] the previously accepted causes restricted to each individual self..."
Enduring their critical remarks, they retort:
"I alone must be accepted as the creator of all things, for I am the self of everyone;
since [the notion of] 'self' arises as a cognition, why should it be restricted to each individual?"

Let it be granted that the proof of the non-duality of the Self arises from the emergence of the notion "I" without distinction among all people; nevertheless, since that [notion] must be accepted as being one and the same for each individual, if it were so, then even the plurality of selves would not exist. Why should this not be the case? To this, the Lord replies:
In every case, the cognition "this" indeed arises;
yet on that account alone, its identity [with the object] cannot be asserted, because it is contradicted by perception.
Furthermore, in all jars, the cognition "jar" alone arises;
nor is the identity of all jars perceived through that cognition.

By means of the instruments of cognition determined for each individual self, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is thus established; the word "first" (*tāvat*) has the sense of "initially. For all people, regarding all objects, there first arises a cognition (*dhī*) characterized as "this," which is the manifestation of that which is to be cognized. To this extent, it is said that "this" arises; such is the unity of that cognition.
That unity does not exist because it is devoid of individual determination; why? Because it is contradicted by perception.
For when one person thinks, "This is a blue lotus," and another thinks, "This is a red lotus," there is an individual determination of the cognition toward its own substratum;
this individual determination of the cognizer’s mental state constitutes a contradiction of [the opponent's] position by perception. Furthermore, regarding cognition...
There is no identity of manifestation for all [objects], yet there is a cognition consisting of mental determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding all jars;

specifically, the notion "jar" arises without distinction in respect to every jar. Even though the identity of the jar and the identity of its manifestation are not perceived as one, it is thus established that cognition is restricted to each individual self (*pratyātmaniyata*).
He establishes this by means of inference based on an illustration:
"The thought 'I, who am restricted to each individual self, go' occurs;
at that time, one perceives another's [thoughts], such as 'I see,' and so forth, through cognition and the like. (p. 640)
Otherwise, the ego-sense "I am of one nature" would apply to both [the self and the body];
let it be understood that the ego-sense is distinct for every individual.

The notion "I," though functioning similarly [in all], is the ego-maker (*ahaṃkṛt*) restricted to each individual self (*pratyātmaniyata*). When, in one person, the cognition "I am going" occurs, then that very cognition—by means of its own manifestation—demonstrates to its own substratum the restriction to another self as established by the impossibility of it being otherwise; and thus the cognition "I see" also occurs. That which is so...

Thus, although the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties function similarly in the sense that "this is such-and-such," their specific determinations for each individual self are established by the fact that otherwise the distinct cognitions— "this is a blue lotus" for one person and "this is a red lotus" for another— would be inexplicable. Otherwise,
if the determination for each individual self did not exist, there would be no sense of "I"— such as "I see," "I [hear]," and so forth.
The self-evident cognition "I see" would be of one and the same nature for both [the self and the body]; however, it is not observed as such.

Therefore, let it be understood that the *ahaṃkāra* (I-notion) is distinct from all people and is the very essence of all people. Having again rendered [the opponent's position] untenable by means of destructive reasoning (*bādhaka-tarka*), he causes them to accept [his own view]:
If "I" were non-different from the whole, then the cognition "I" would arise even with respect to Devadatta;
it would arise for others as well, and thus the oneness of the self is not established.

If the "I" were immediately and entirely distinct [from the body], then the notion of "I" would arise even with respect to Devadatta; yet it never arises with respect to another. Since this is not observed, it is therefore certain that there is no identity between the ego (ahaṃkāra) and the Self;
that is, it is established that the ego is not of the nature of the one Self—hence, "non-identity of the Self" (nātmaikatvam). Furthermore:

Furthermore, although the cognition "pot, pot" arises repeatedly, the identity of the object characterized as a pot with its substrate—the cognition—is not established. Just so, although the cognition "I, I" arises repeatedly, there is no unity of the self among the various selves that are the objects of the cognitions denoted by the word "I. The self is the object of those cognitions denoted by the word "I."
The oneness of beings—their non-duality and the state of the oneness of the Self—is not established or ascertained;
and that egoism (ahaṃkāra) is inferred through its own effects by way of the three qualities (triguṇa) acting as three groups (triskandha). Thus he says:
"And that is declared to be threefold; among them, the first is the Taijasa."
The Vaikārika is the second [evolvent], and likewise, the Bhūtādi is the other.
This is clear. However, if [the cause] consisted solely of *sattva* and the other qualities (*rajas* and *tamas*), it would not transform in an unmixed manner;
thus, by sound reasoning, its own effects would be impossible to produce. Anticipating this objection in his own mind, the Lord provides the following resolution:
"That which possesses a preponderance of *sattva* is here called *tejas*."
The Vaikṛta [ego] is predominant in rajas; the Bhūtādi [ego] has an excess of tamas.
It is easy [to understand]. And thus it has been stated by the Lord of Beasts (*mṛgendra*):
"The individual hearing of these [senses] is the cause of the increase of delight.
First, the luminous [element], having produced the organs of knowledge—the internal faculties (*samanāṃsi*)—from the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), is to be examined hereafter.

It manifests the functions of volition (*saṃkalpa*) and cognition (*jñāna*). Having produced the organs of action (*karmendriya*), it manifests activity as the *vaikṛta* [ego]. Indicating that the *bhūtādi* [ego] produces the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and, through them, the gross elements (*bhūta*) which serve as the supports for the senses, and thereby effects the movement of the senses, he describes their sequential origination:

From the taijasa ego, the five sense organs arise; from the vaikṛta ego, however, the five organs of action emerge. From the taijasa ego, the mind and the organs of perception [arise]. From the vaikṛta ego, the five organs of action shall come into being.
From the ego (ahaṃkāra), however, arises the aggregate of the subtle elements (tanmātra) from the source of the elements (bhūtādi).
This is clear. Therein, he begins the examination of the mind (manas):
"That internal cognition of men, which consists of volition and conceptualization..."
On account of the difference in their functions, he said: "I am neither a maker nor a Buddhist."
In this ocean of liberation, that [cognition] is intended to be purely mental;

its nature (*ātman*) is that whose essence (*svarūpa*) consists of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)— namely, the aforementioned recollection (*anusmṛti*) which determines, "this dharma belongs to the jar, not to anything else"— and which, among many perceived objects, takes on a single one as its object.

The internal cognition (*pratyaya*), whose nature consists of conceptualization and discursive thought (*saṃkalpa-vikalpa*), is the agent of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). It is the essence of seeing and acting, the impeller of the external and internal organs, and—briefly stated—the state of focused attention (*avadhāna*) and one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*). It is neither of the nature of ego (*ahaṃkārika*) nor of the intellect (*bauddha*); why? Because there is a difference in function; for the intellect (*buddhi*) and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) consist of the reflective awareness of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka-parāmarśa*).

Because it consists of the function of knowledge (*jñānavṛttika*), it is distinct from that [ordinary mind] due to the differentiation of purposeful action characterized by the ascertainment of the nature of vision and agency (*dṛkkriyā*). However, because it demonstrates one's own doctrine—which is the liberation of all doctrines—within this tantra, which is an ocean of liberation, the mental is indeed intended as the manifestation of the mind (*manovyakta*); the mind is the ascertainment that has become its own function.

The meaning is that [the mind] is inferred through this door. He states that the mind is established because the activity of the external organs and the internal organ would otherwise be inexplicable without attention:
"For when an object has been perceived by the eye, that object [is grasped] within the range of the intellect..."
O Brahmins, that which the mind ordains here is what is recited as such.

Otherwise, there would be a determination regarding a jar that has been perceived. It is clearly stated [in the text] from "by the eye functioning through its own attention" up to "it is perceived," and so forth. In that context, regarding the word "performs" (*vidadhāti*), it means being solely established in the function of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) through one's own attention.

The phrase "according to the prescribed rule" (*vidhāna-pūrvam*) must be supplied [as an ellipsis], for without a reference to the subject (*grāhaka*), a reference to the object (*grāhya*) is untenable; the meaning here is "among these principles" (*tattveṣu*). Otherwise, if the subject and object—the entities consisting of the grasping and the grasped—were not attended to by the mind, no such references would arise.

It might be argued that its arising could somehow occur even without that [perception], such that even when a jar has been perceived once, there would be a simultaneous determination regarding a cloth even without the determination of the observed sequence; however, this is not so, for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is established as being like a mental image (*kalpa*) due to the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the determination of the object of speech (*vācyādhyavasāya*), must indeed exist.

He says that the [universal] is inferred as being of the nature of a conceptual construction (vikalpa) whose intention is established through the otherwise inexplicable nature of the speaker’s determination:
"Furthermore, having experienced the word 'cow' in a physical body possessing dewlaps and so forth..."
Furthermore, when something similar to that is perceived, it is caused by the utterance of the word "cow."

In the Tantra, that mind is said to consist of conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa-pratyaya*). Furthermore, there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*): having experienced the word "cow" (*go-śabda*) with respect to a physical body possessing a dewlap and so forth, by means of the intellect’s presiding [over it], because [the cognition] is caused by the utterance of the word "cow. Otherwise, if it were impossible [to connect them], the mind would not be focused there upon the cow.
The utterance of the name does not arise [from the mind]. If it were to occur somehow, it might even be the case that "horse" (*aśva*) would appear there as well.
In this context, the word *vikalpa* should be supplied as *saṃkalpa*. Having raised the most extreme objection, he refutes it:
"Some maintain that the mind is atomic, because objects appear to it sequentially."
If, on the other hand, there were always a movement toward all objects simultaneously;
Therefore, due to the power of past actions, the arising of knowledge occurs for human beings gradually,
depending upon the completeness of causal conditions and even through the influence of darkness and rebirth.

Certain Naiyāyikas and others maintain that the mind (*manas*) exists; why? Because objects appear sequentially. If "appearing" means "cognition," then cognition would not occur sequentially, but rather there would be simultaneous cognition of all objects at all times. This [objection] is incorrect, because [sequentiality] is due to the power of karma; it is dependent upon karma.

The cognition of succession is not based on [the soul's] atomicity, because it is established otherwise; furthermore, the collection of means that manifest those respective cognitions, which depends upon the causal totality (*sāmagrī*), is the basis, as it is established otherwise;
and because it occurs even in the presence of darkness.

The statement that the mind (*manas*) is of the nature of *sattva* is based on the predominance of its particular function, since it has been stated that [the internal organ] transforms without being mixed [with other qualities]; for the nature of *tamas* is also established [in the mind].

Furthermore, this is otherwise accounted for by the fact that when the mind is sometimes overwhelmed by *tamas*, yet at other times remains unoverwhelmed even by its own *sattva*, the yogi perceives objects situated at a distance through that mind. Thus, the claim of the mind’s purely *sāttvika* nature is not proven.
He employs an inference that sublates the opposing view: "If the mind were atomic, it would always be a perceiver of atomic substances;
for as far as the pervasion of the perceiver extends, so far is the perceived object grasped."

Just as perception occurs by means of a lamp and not so by the rays of the sun, if the mind were an atom, it would always be the perceiver of atomic substances; yet it would not be the perceiver of mountains and the like, which are neither pervaded nor non-pervaded by its own [atomic] extent, because it is a perceiver [only of what is within its range]. To whatever extent it is a perceiver...

The pervasion of that [object] exists; that which is pervaded is grasped by the grasper. From the word "and" (*ca*), it follows that the grasper is grasped by its own pervader alone. It is not [grasped] by that which is not pervaded by its own pervasion. Just as, for example, the sun's rays are perceived by the sun’s light, but the sun’s light is not [perceived] by a lamp.

"In the case of an object that is pervaded [by light], there is no non-perception due to the pervasion by the lamp; likewise, because it is pervaded by the mind, the perceiver would not fail to perceive. Having raised and refuted this objection concerning the intention of another, he concludes:
"If the thought is that the mind is small because it perceives only a small object..."
Therefore, the perception of even a large object as small is observed.

O Mahādeva, that which is the reality of the mind (*manastattva*) and is restricted to each individual self—by this much, because it grasps great objects (*mahadartha*), the mind is said to be "great" (*mahat*). This is established by equal reasoning.
If you think that the mind is "small" (*alpa*) because it grasps small objects, that is incorrect for those who possess wisdom, since [the mind] has been made so.

It is observed that even from a large source, such as the sun's rays or a net, there is the perception of small objects, such as motes of dust; and in both cases, the pervasiveness belongs to the large object, not to the [perceived] small one. If it is argued that the mind is a reality like the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, and because it is restricted to each individual self (*pratyātmaniyata*), therefore it must be large—otherwise, [the aforementioned phenomena would be inexplicable].
The sages raise an objection again:
"The mind, ego, and intellect—these three, because they determine objects through their collective functioning—are said by some to act in succession; which of these views have you accepted?"

He is the Lord. Some say that the three—mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*)—together with the senses, constitute a "composite purpose" (*saṃhatārtha*), meaning a combined utility; and that "ascertainment of purpose" (*arthaniścaya*) is that very composite purpose. Therefore, they state that [the Lord] is the cause for whose sake the operations [of these faculties] are not established separately (*apṛthaksiddha*). (p. 651)

Some say [the process occurs] gradually; therefore, between those two, which method has been accepted by you? Which position have you adopted? Īśvara says: "In the operations of the four—beginning with the sense organs—which are established as distinct perceptions occurring sequentially, [the mind] is endowed with dharma. Thus he speaks.
The cognition of an object occurs sequentially: first, it consists of mere sensory observation;
then, it takes the form of doubt; and thereafter, it consists of ascertainment.
The determinative [cognition] is subsequently established in this very sequence.

Because the mental resolve (*manasaṃkalpa*) consists of doubt and because the ascertainment of the apprehender (*grāhaka-niścaya*) consists of self-conceit (*abhimāna*), it is said to be "of that nature. The [first stage], consisting of mere observation, has the form of non-conceptual knowledge of the object alone.

The nature of resolve (*vyavasāyātmikā*) consists of the initial determination of its specific object; it is established as being well-ascertained. As for the "gradual comprehension of the meaning" (*kramārthasaṃvitti*) previously demonstrated during the examination of knowledge (*vidyāparīkṣā*), the Venerable One will explain it further below. Therefore, no detailed exposition is provided here.
Anticipating a further objection regarding the nature of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), he refutes it:
"If it is argued that because cognition persists everywhere, the internal organ is all-pervading—that is incorrect;
for that cognition is declared to be insentient, being the consciousness of another."

Is it not the case that in all instances, purposeful activity arises from the sense organs— such as the eyes and so forth— because of the persistence of cognition, that is, because of its conformity with knowledge? Or rather, even when one has gone to Kāśī or Kashmir, because of the persistence of cognition there and there, such as the knowledge "this is the Gaṅgā" and so forth, it follows that the intellect (buddhi) exists here [in the sense organs], and it does not fail to exist.

For it would not be seen [therein], yet the persistence of cognition is indeed observed. If it is argued that, therefore, the intellect (*buddhi*), being non-existent and conforming to cognition, is all-pervading and omnipresent—that is incorrect. In the *Paśupata* school, that [intellect] is said to be pervasive as it conforms to consciousness within one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), which is endowed with power (*śaktimat*) and inherent; for it is taught that the awareness of another and the awareness of oneself are both powers.

In that regard, cognition (*buddhi*) is not said to be insentient (*jaḍa*), for it is not merely a follower of the [external] object; rather, being conformable to the cognition, it is the manifester (*vyañjikā*) of everything. Since the object to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*) is all-pervading, the manifestation is connected to the cognition.

It has been shown previously that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and so forth, residing in the manifestor, are experienced as non-different from that [object]. For the Blessed One will state later:

And he will say: having concluded the examination of "simultaneity" along with the examination of the knowledge of sequential order as an incidental discussion, he begins the examination of the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) according to their enumeration and definition in their sequential order:
"Therefore, in due order, once the eyes and the other [organs] have determined the absence of [objects] being simultaneously complete..."
When the triad of internal organs has been thus established, now—
The sense organs are said to be five: the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose; these are well known.
Since they are established as objects of direct perception, no further arguments are stated;
these [elements] have arisen from the sāttvika aspect of the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra).
How can a perceptible object be well-established without the statement of an inference? True;

for those sense organs, the perceptible is their verbal object. These [objects] have perception as their domain; "perceptibility" (pratyakṣaviṣayatva) is that state of being an object of perception, by means of which they function as the instruments of apprehension.

Cognitions such as those of sound and so forth must be understood by some instruments as having the nature of grasping objects of perception, because they are actions, like the action of consciousness (*citi*). Here, "action" means the operation of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*); this is the meaning. And the Blessed One [stated] in the *Pramāṇapaṭala*: "The probandum belongs to its own locus."
He will state that "activity is desired as the fruit"; since this is established beyond doubt by this single inference, [these] are the arguments.
Other inferences are now being stated. (p. 655) How could the seers [accept] the fact that the sense organs are the effects of the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*) rather than the effects of the elements?
They raise a doubt by employing the following inference: "Because it is praised by the Naiyāyikas and others;
for that which manifests something must indeed be of the same genus as it, just as the bark of the *nimba* tree and sandalwood manifest their respective odors which have been suppressed."
That which manifests sound is the auditory organ, which is of the nature of space alone;
in the same way, the other organs such as the skin should be inferred [to be elemental], so how can it be said that they are derived from the ego-principle (ahaṃkārika)?

The ear has the nature of space because it manifests the qualities of space; having supplied the word "that which" (*yat*), the three members of the syllogism ending with "that" (*tat*) are to be analyzed. [It is like] the inner bark of the *niba* tree, which manifests the fragrance of sandalwood whose scent was previously suppressed by water or other obstructing substances.
And [the tree] is of the same genus as other trees. The Lord refutes this:
"Because they are composed of the elements, the sense organs possess form, like jars and other such objects;
furthermore, they are perceivable by other senses and do not abide anywhere [as a single substratum]."

Let it be granted, for the sake of argument, that they are composed of material elements (*bhautikatva*). Where there is the state of being composed of material elements, there is corporeality (*mūrtatva*), as in the case of a jar and so forth;

thus, by means of the reason "being composed of material elements," whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established, the corporeality of the sense organs is proven to be like that of a jar and so forth. Nor is this a desired conclusion, for wherever there is corporeality caused by being composed of material elements, there is the property of being perceivable by the senses.
By means of the reason "possessing such corporeality," whose pervasion is established by the example of a jar and so forth,

it is proven that the sense organs are objects of apprehension by other sense organs. Nor can one accept this as a desired conclusion (iṣṭāpatti), because by the same sound reasoning, those sense organs which apprehend the [original] sense organ would likewise be objects of apprehension by yet other sense organs.

Because [the argument] "it is established" leads to an infinite regress, there is no establishment anywhere; thus, by showing that the opponent's position is non-material, he causes them to accept his own desired view once again:
furthermore, there is no movement of material things through the obstruction of other material things.
But the eye would not perceive an object situated inside a crystal.
Furthermore, because it penetrates even into water, the eye is not composed of light (taijasa).

Moreover, for corporeal objects, there is no movement through the interior of another corporeal object by way of obstructing that object; indeed, there is no penetration into its interior. Nor is that object [the eye] [perceived] from within it. Therefore, [it is not taijasa].

It should be stated that [the term] *kākṣati* refers to the apprehension of what has not been previously established (*aprāptagrahaṇa*). Since the existence of solidity (*sattva*) is established for both parties, [the text] negates its being a crystal and so forth by means of its materiality (*mūrtatva*). By [the example] "water" and so forth, it negates its being fire (*tejas*) because of the entry of water. [The phrase] "it would be extinguished" negates its being fire. Thus, they apprehend what is not [otherwise] obtained through the approach of the Lokāyata and other such disputants.
The sages raise this doubt:
(p. 658) "If this were so, then even an object placed behind a wall would be perceived, provided it is formless, because [consciousness] does not arise from the ego."

Therefore, let there be the [proponent's] claim: "By the reason of being formless (*amūrta*), which is established, if it is thus established that [the eye] is included within the category of the formed (*mūrta*), then wherever there is formlessness, there is inclusion within the formed.
This is because of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) [that applies even] to an object placed behind a wall for one who perceives it.

Grasping would be the instrument. Having set aside this [objection], he states that what was said—that the determination of objects is dependent on the material nature [of the sense organs]—is also incorrect:
"Its non-existence is due to its unreality, because it is obstructed by being inside a wall."
As for that which has been stated regarding the similarity of kind between the signified and the signifier:
Furthermore, that which is an action arising from the nature of its object is not tenable;
for it does not have form as its sole object, and thus its luminous character is lost.
If that were the case, even the apprehension of the desired object would not be possible.

As for what was said—that [the cognition] "it might be"—that is incorrect; for when darkness has been dispelled by the power of accomplished collyrium (*siddhāñjana*), even the capacity to perceive what lies behind a wall is seen, because that capacity to grasp what is hidden within it is also visible. For where there is an undifferentiated object...

In that context, the immateriality of power (*śakti*) is *sāttvika*, while being material is included within the category of substance alone. Because of this limitation, there is no pervasion [of the sense organ] through walls and the like, since these are *tāmasa*. Consequently, due to the obstruction of the wall by the eye, there would be no perception of the object contained within it. Otherwise, there would be apprehension without reaching [the object].

The author will state that even for those who maintain this view, it results in the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of denying [intrinsic] capacity (śakti). As for the claim that there is a similarity of genus (sājātīyatva) between the manifestor (vyañjaka) and the manifested (vyaṅgya), that too is not tenable; because the two—action (karman) and genus (jāti)—are merely indicative (upalakṣaṇa) of the elements (bhūta), and because the qualities (guṇa) and forms (rūpa) of other elements are objects of perception.

That eye has form as its sole object; it is not composed of fire (*taijasa*), nor does it have form alone as its object. Therefore, because there is an absence of the restriction [of the sense organ] to perceiving the quality of a single element, its being composed of fire is lost. Even if that were the case, its [status as a] reality would not be lost. If the eye were composed of fire, then the perception of desired objects would be that very eye acting upon the desired object.

It is not tenable that there is a grasping of the qualities of elements belonging to different classes [of existence]. Nor should it be argued that, despite their lack of distinction in being derived from *ahaṃkāra*, there is a restriction of their objects due to a difference in their fixed natures; for such a distinction among the transformations (*vikāra*) will arise from differences in their origin, just as in the case of molasses, sugar-candy, and sugar. Therefore, the sense-organ is simply the physical orb (*golaka*) and so forth.
He refutes those who prattle that "the illuminator grasps its object without reaching it": "No grasping of anything is observed through an obstruction;
rather, every sense organ grasps only what it has reached, just like the sense of touch."
Since it serves as an intermediate illustration, let the meaning of the verse beginning with "tathātve" (p.

661) be explained once more: if the sense organs were merely physical parts of the body, such as the eyeballs, then the apprehension of objects by the eye and other senses through direct contact would be impossible; thus, the apprehension of desired objects [would not occur].

The apprehension of an object that is not in contact with us is not tenable. It cannot be said that its object is reached [by the sense organ], because every sense organ, such as the auditory organ and the rest, being external, perceives only an object with which it is in contact; this is observed in the case of the tactile organ, and it applies to the other organs as well.
Whatever is obstructed is not perceived; thus, the apprehension of what is not in contact is not observed. Furthermore, he refutes the opponent's position:
moreover, if [the sense organ] were a part of the body, the non-arising [of cognition] in cases such as a mute person would follow as a logical consequence.
One who possesses the sense organs, such as the nose, is observed to be mute and so forth.
Furthermore, it would follow that upon entering another body, the state of being mute and so forth could not arise; for why?

Because [according to your view], the nose and other organs, when endowed with their respective parts, are accepted by you as sense-faculties (*indriya*). Yet, a person who is mute or otherwise deficient is observed to possess those very parts of the nose and so on, which you maintain to be flawless sense-faculties. And yet, such a person is not seen to possess [functioning] sense-faculties.
He states the concluded meaning: "Therefore, the eye alone is held to be pervasive in the perception of distant objects;
the ear and the others are mentioned in sequence, as are their five respective objects."

Since the sense organs are established as manifestors once they have emerged separately from the body, it is therefore accepted that the eye extends as far as its vision reaches distant objects. At the commencement of the investigation, the ears and other organs were mentioned in their sequence, and accordingly, their respective objects—
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell— are presented in that same order.
To the question "How is there a fivefold sequence?", he says:
"The auditory faculty (*śruti*) is the perceiver of sounds in relation to the five elements;
thereafter, among the remaining elements, touch is held to be perceivable by the tactile faculty."
In this same way, it should be understood for the others; those five objects of apprehension [arise] in sequence.
Thus, the sequential arising of the ear, skin, eyes, and so forth has been described.

"Śruti" means hearing. Now, it may be argued that the Vaiśeṣikas and others proclaim that sound is a unique quality of space (*ākāśa*) because it is perceived elsewhere than its substratum. That is incorrect. For the reason that "here [is] the drum," sound is heard in the very substratum itself; thus, because this contradicts both perception and scripture, the argument is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed). Now, [it may be asked]: [The opponent continues: "But..."

Sometimes, the cognition of sound occurs even at the root of the ear. It is not established that space alone is the substratum of this quality merely on this account, because there is a deviation: the cognition of odor occurs at the root of the nose as well. [Objection:
But surely the odor, accompanied by its own subtle constituent parts, will travel to the root of the nose; if that were so, the same would apply to sound.

"Does such a movement not abandon its own nature? Why do you not say so? He will reply: "The sound of the drum itself reaches the ear through a continuous series. Therefore, from among the remaining elements [after sound has departed], touch remains as a quality perceivable by the sense of touch. In this same way, from among those remaining elements, the remaining element... [remains].

Considering that [the sense organs] are what remain after [the elements], it should be understood that the eyes and so forth are to be grasped sequentially among the other [objects] such as form and so on, by way of those respective qualities. Having thus applied [this logic] again and again, the conclusion—that the five [objects] are to be grasped and known in sequence starting with sound for the ear and so forth—is established here through reasoning. Furthermore, the sages [state]:
They argue as follows:
"Indeed, some maintain that the eye is merely the physical orb (golaka),
supported by reasons such as the perception of objects at a distance and the simultaneous perception of the branches of a tree and the moon."

And why is it not likewise accepted by certain Lokāyatikas and others that [the eye] grasps gross objects? For surely the eye is a manifestor without reaching [its object]; if its nature is such, what is the reason for desiring the eyeball itself to be the cause? To this he says: "Without an interval" (*antareṇa vyavadhānena*).
Because it exists together [with the object], there is an interval; because of the apprehension of an object situated within a crystal, and because of the apprehension of that which has an interval;

because the branch and the moon exist simultaneously; and because they are perceived at the same time. Furthermore, why is it not accepted that a gross object is apprehended in this way? This is the intention: [the sense organ] reaches...

Regarding its nature as an illuminator, there would be no illumination of objects such as letters that are obstructed by intervening media like crystal; furthermore, because the moon and a branch are situated at a great distance from one another, it is impossible for them to illuminate each other by reaching one another, even in the case of a gross object.

Since mountains and the like consist of many parts, there would otherwise be no simultaneous perception of them as they appear; however, it has been established that for an immaterial sense-object, there is an entry into another clear, material substance, and that it does not illuminate without reaching its object. Therefore, the perception of objects at a distance (*sāntaragrahaṇa*) is accounted for in another way.
The Lord (Īśvara) refutes [this objection]:
"It is held that perception with an interval [from the object] occurs because the sense organ is distinct from the physical ball [of the eye].
For it is considered that the perceiver, like a lamp, must grasp [its object] as something pervaded [by its own light]."

At that time, the visual nature of the eyeball is completely excluded by [the theory of] pervasion. By you, however, the eyeball and so forth are considered to be sense organs because they apprehend objects at a distance;
for the apprehender is held to be like a lamp. Therefore, since it moves toward the object, the object would have to be apprehended as already pervaded by the apprehender itself.

Because of its [the atom's] production, and because it does not reach objects that have intervals due to a lack of pervasion, its capacity to grasp up to the limit of the visual field is effectively ruled out. Furthermore, he states that the apprehension of gross objects is established otherwise:
"That which is the apprehension of gross objects is compatible with [the atom's] being pervasive."
If there were not the apprehension of an entity as large as a ball.

If not— that is, if there is no perception of the pervader— then there would be the apprehension of a thing (*bhāva*, *padārtha*) that possesses a transformation similar to the eyeball (*golaka*) itself. Having stated the refutation of the second objection by accepting simultaneous apprehension, [the author] sets forth his own view.
And he reveals the [logical] movement:
"The simultaneous apprehension of both branches occurs because of pervasiveness;
however, in terms of the actual state of things, the apprehension of both branches does not arise at one and the same time."

There is no conceit regarding its non-simultaneity, just as in the case of piercing a thousand petals; for by the nature of things, according to their actual state, it is like saying, "I have simultaneously pierced a thousand lotus petals with a needle. Furthermore, its pervasiveness is conceivable except in the specific location of the physical organ (the eyeball).

However, the sages raise this doubt: since vision is all-pervasive, it cannot be that it perceives distant objects through a physical connection; for [otherwise] there would be no such thing as "distant.
But surely the eyeball itself is accepted as the locus of the eye?
For wherever the locus exists, there the located object is established.
Existence that is all-pervasive is considered to be ineffective;
just as the soul, though all-pervasive, is not made known by the space of the ether.
But how, then, does the eye perceive an object situated at a great distance?

Indeed, there is a point of doubt here. However, according to the reasoning already stated, it is not the physical eyeball (*golaka*) alone that is intended as the locus of the visual organ; rather, it is that specific location where the presence of the locus and its blackness (the sclera) are established.

In that location, the butter and so forth to be placed are situated. Now, it might be argued: "We intended to express its existence there by way of pervasiveness; that is incorrect. That which is connected [to the location] by way of pervasiveness is incapable of performing any function. Since it does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*), let it not be called 'possessing efficacy' (*samartha*). It is like the *jīva*."

The possessor of a body, situated in the space of the void (*vyomadeśa*), which serves as his own support and constitutes the ground of his own manifestation, is the illuminator by means of a portion of *māyā* in the form of power (*śakti*) at the place where the body of the individual self (*vyaktyātmaśarīra*) is not yet reached. He is not, however, the agent of the action characterized by his own cognition. Furthermore, how, and in what manner, is the eye [the illuminator]?
It grasps the most distant object, such as a desired thing or a fixed object like the pole star, even though it is far away; this would not be possible in any other way. The Lord explains:
"That [grasping] occurs because the eyeball, being composed of light (*taijasa*), extends outward."
Just as a lamp, that which is produced by it—the locus—perceives the eye; this is not surprising.

The claim that "existence (sattā) is ineffective because of its pervasiveness," as stated by means of the analogy of a living being, is like an eye aided by a lamp perceiving a collection of objects in the darkness;

it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because [pervasiveness] is observed in the case of grasping pervasion while residing within its own substratum, such as in lamps. Therefore, that [argument] is invalid, whether [the self] is considered luminous (*taijasa*) or composed of the *sattva* quality (*sāttvika*).

Assisted by its own light, like an eye or a lamp, [the sense-organ] moves outside the physical globe (*golaka*). Furthermore, having been brought back to its place—that is, returned to its own substrate within the darkness—it is like an eye assisted by a lamp that perceives and grasps a collection of objects even when they are situated at a distance; this is not surprising. He concludes:
Consequently, the over-extension [of the argument] regarding odor and so forth, as previously mentioned, is effectively precluded;
for the eyeball, which serves as the substratum for the visual faculty, has not been brought forward [as a subject].

Since it has been stated that the eye’s grasping is for the purpose of reaching and apprehending external objects by virtue of its luminous nature (*taijasatva*), the objection— that such [external reaching] would be impossible if the eye were material (*bhautika*) due to its corporeality (*mūrtatva*)— has already been refuted at length in the preceding argument beginning with "just as [the nose does not grasp] a scent that is overwhelmed by another scent," which aims to establish its non-materiality. Furthermore, regarding the substratum of the eye and so forth...

Because that which has come into being does not function [externally], there is no outward extension. Now, as for the objection beginning with "the eyeball" (*golaka*), which aims to prove that the eye is merely a physical orb—that has already been refuted at length. The seers (*ṛṣayaḥ*) consider this by way of demonstrating a logical contradiction (*bādhā*).

(671) But surely, even when the eyes are closed, an object would be perceived by the visual rays that have already issued forth; for those rays do not perish immediately after the closing of the eyes.

"Like the light of that lamp within a jar due to its covering"—this is indeed a further objection (*parāśaṅkā*). [The opponent argues: "When the eyes are opened, by the visual rays (*nāyana-tejas*) which emerge immediately upon the opening of the eyes, having issued forth from the eyeballs (*golaka*) and traveled toward objects such as jars, [the object is perceived]; whereas when the eyes are closed, [it is not]. Even though the eyes are closed... [the object is not perceived].

It would be perceived. Why is it not perceived? The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is not so, because of its being covered. Just as the light of a lamp situated inside a jar [is not seen] after the jar is closed, immediately after the eyes are covered, one's own view [is that perception does not occur] due to the rapid destruction of the ocular luminosity (*cakṣustejas*).
Having established [his own position] by way of avoiding the refutation of others, he now rejects the opponent's view:
(p. 672) "If the eyes were merely the eyeballs, then there would be apprehension of objects without contact;
and if they could apprehend what is not in contact, then there would be [apprehension] even through an obstruction."

Therefore, the eye must be admitted to be all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*) in order to perceive distant objects. By supplying the word "hi" (for) and connecting it with the phrase "because of not extending outward," [the argument is as follows]: if it were to perceive what is unattained, then it would perceive even what is obstructed by a wall or the like at that time. Thus, [it is concluded].
Because it would lead to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). Fearing the consequence that the other categories (*padārtha*) would be easily established as one's own [view], he refutes it:
"If that were so, there would be the apprehension of the meaning of 'going' (*gati*) from the word *gā* and so forth.
If this is argued, it is not so; for [the word] has as its domain the presiding deities of the elements (*bhūtādhiṣṭhāna*), such as wind (*vāyu*) and the rest.
If it is argued that these [senses] do not go out to grasp the object, but rather bring about the attainment of the object already reached— this being so,

when the eye has gone to the location where the object resides and grasps the object, the same would apply to the sense of touch and the others, such that they too would grasp the object after having gone there— if this is your thought, it is not correct.

But as for these [senses], such as the tongue and so forth: their domain is the presiding deities of the elements, beginning with air. Having gone to—that is, having reached—their respective objects, such as touch and the rest, which have the four elements beginning with air as their substratum, they do not grasp the object by means of reaching it;
rather, they themselves go and bring about the apprehension of the object already reached. [This applies] to their own manifestation.

The power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*), when its own functions are not yet distinguished from their specific manifestations, perceives objects that have come into its immediate proximity; regarding this, the seers (*ṛṣis*) say that there is no contradiction here: "If the sense of hearing, like the eye, did not go out [to the object], it would not perceive sound."
How can a sound that is conditioned by direction and location be apprehended here?

[The opponent claims: "It is conditioned by direction and place; this [sound] is heard in the southern direction, and again this [sound] is in the northern direction—thus it possesses the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of direction and place. The Lord refutes this with clear words:
"That sound, having moved with velocity, reaches the ear through a continuous series (saṃtati)."
Like the flight of an arrow or similar objects, it would immediately cause one to infer the direction and location.
Likewise, the inference of a drum or similar object based solely on prior perception,

as well as the scent of a *ketakī* flower situated at a distance, should be understood to have arrived by means of a continuous series— according to the principle of waves and ripples— mounted upon subtle particles of air that have been driven forth. The word "yā" (which) refers to that [inference].

The word "it happens" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied [as the verb]. Having attained the state of being a manifestor and having withdrawn [the senses], he states that there is no plurality of the sense organs:
"The sense organs grasp only the object that has been reached; therefore, this is the established position."
A single sense-faculty alone is not accepted, because it cannot perceive both the eye and visible form.
Therefore, according to the manner stated, the established conclusion is that in the expression "cakṣurūpa" (eye-form), it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

The meaning is: "because of the perception of any one among form and the other [objects]. This same principle applies to the sense organs other than the eye. Furthermore, there is a disparity in the functions of the external and internal instruments (*bahirantaḥ-karaṇa*) due to their difference in nature. And [there is a disparity] among the internal instruments themselves...
He states that there is a slight difference between them:
"The three instruments [of speech] consist of conceit, mental continuity, and determination, directed toward objects existing in the past, future, and present times."

External [objects] have the three times as their domain, yet they have the present alone as their immediate range. Regarding entities arising in the past, future, and present times— through [mental] impressions (*bhāvitaiḥ*), that is, through those made manifest by self-conceit (*abhimāna*), mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*), and determination (*niścaya*).
