By means of the three effects as logical marks—namely, the determination of the subject (*grāhaka-adhyavasāya*), the attention directed toward the subject and the object (*grāhakagrāhyāvadhāna*), and the determination of the object (*grāhya-adhyavasāya*)—the triad of instruments characterized by ego (*ahaṃkāra*), mind (*manas*), and intellect (*buddhi*) is inferred. These have as their domain objects situated in space and time, whether distant or near, and belonging to the three periods of time; for it is thus that the intellect [functions].
That which is past is remembered as such through the medium of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by previous experience;
that which is present is indicated as "this" by the power of renewed experience;
and that which is future is [inferred] from the perception of an invariably concomitant sign (*liṅga*), such as rising clouds. (p. 676)
They demonstrate rain and so forth as the ground for the manifestation of their own power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*).

This [consciousness] is perceived as having the three times as its object: "I have seen," "it is being seen by me," and "it is to be seen by me"—thus, the nature of the Self is characterized by the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*) which is oriented toward grasping the three times, even within the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).

That which is recited as the state of the self consisting of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is experienced as being in the very act of manifesting the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*) directed toward itself. The mind (*manas*), however, is the locus for the manifestation of the powers of vision and action (*dṛk-kriyā*) of consciousness; it effects the attention toward objects of the three times, producing [cognitions] in accordance with the manifestation of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Thus, it pertains to the three times.

The object [of the senses] is being discussed. To the question, "Is it thus that they are excluded? he says: "An external instrument has only the present as its domain. For even when the internal faculty such as the intellect exists, there is no cognition of external form and so forth for the blind and others.
In this regard, he states that the internal instrument is dependent upon the external instrument: (p. 677) ...he says—
The internal [cognition] is dependent upon the external when perceiving external objects;
for if the internal [faculty], such as the intellect (*buddhi*), exists, there is no manifestation of form and other [sensory qualities].
It is clear that when the object is unknown, purposeful action cannot be averted; therefore, he says that the organs of action depend upon the organs of cognition, which are independent of them:
"If the organs of action possess their objects and are assisted by the organs of cognition..."
Since an instrument cannot function with respect to what is unknown, the sense organs are not [the instruments] in this way.
The objects of the sense organs have been explained; now the examination of the action organs (*karmendriya*) is undertaken, including their enumeration, definition, and investigation.
The action organs are speech, feet, hands, the private organ, and the anus.
Because the sense organs are the cause of knowing and because they are connected with their respective functions.

For that purpose, the five organs of action must be accepted here. This is because they are the cause of the state of being a knower, because they manifest the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*), and because of their connection with action (*kṛtya-yoga*). Due to the application of activity and the perception [of objects], they serve as the instrumental cause for action; the rest is easy to understand. What is "action" (*karman*) in this context? It is the vibration of the insentient.
He states that [the action] is not [inherent]: "For here, action is incapable of inhering in a person (pudgala).
That which manifests it is known as the organ of action (karmendriya)."
The power of action (kriyā-śakti) is that which is attached to action. Otherwise, having raised the objection regarding what is already established, he refutes it:
"In this case, the sense organs of cognition (buddhīndriyas) alone are not its manifestors;
rather, due to the distinction between contradictory things manifested [by them], they are as numerous as the sense organs of cognition."

Indeed, the differentiation of the principles (*tattva*) is a conceptual construction (*saṃklipti*) based on the differentiation of their functions (*kāryabheda*). From that [differentiation of function], there arises a differentiation of the manifest forms (*vyaṅgya*) characterized by the operation of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*)—which consists of the intellect (*buddhi*), the senses (*indriya*), and the objects of action (*kartavya*)—and the operation of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*)—characterized by the visible object (*dṛśya*) and its objects of action (*kartavya*). This occurs through the mutual distinction of these manifest forms, such as the cognition of color and so forth, which are differentiated from one another.

It is like the plurality of the sense-faculties (*buddhīndriya*). Just as there is a distinct manifestation of the sense-faculties—such as "this is the eye," "this is the ear," and "this is the skin"—there is likewise a distinct manifestation among the sense-faculties such that one says, "this is a sense-faculty of cognition" (*buddhīndriya*) and "this is a faculty of action" (*karmendriya*).
Regarding this "distinct manifestation," it is not the case that among the sense-faculties, the sense-faculties of cognition are not the manifestors of that [plurality].

These [senses] are the manifestors of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). Now, one might object: since the Sāṃkhyas and others do not admit that the individual self (*puruṣa*) possesses a power of action—otherwise known as agency—belonging to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consisting of the *mahat* and so forth, how can the existence of other senses be established by their being the manifestors of such a power? Anticipating this doubt, he offers a rebuttal:
If it is not accepted that the soul’s own capacity performs actions such as going and so forth,
then by what can the agency [of the soul] in a dead body be prevented?

Agency also belongs only to the atom, which is non-inert, just as in the case of a jar. We do not accept agency through the penetration of action; rather, it is that which is the cause of such action—namely, that which performs actions such as moving—which serves as the cause for inert movements like locomotion.

Indeed, there is no agency that is inherently of the nature of motion; for how could bodily agency exist [without it], unless the capacity of the Self is accepted? If so, then agency would also follow in a dead body, which performs actions such as its own movement and vibration—by whom can this be prevented? [Objection: But that [body] is separated from it because of the separation from the vital breath (*prāṇa*), wind, and so forth.

In that regard, it is not observed [therein]. That is incorrect. Agency also belongs only to the atomic self (*ātman*) and not to the insentient (*jaḍa*), because there is an exclusion of non-connection with the word [“agency”] only for that which is not associated with consciousness (*cit*). Wherever agency does not exist, there consciousness does not manifest, as in the case of a jar. Since enjoyment (*bhoga*) is also a type of action, that enjoyment is an agent.

If [the self] were non-existent [in that context], then even the self’s conceit of being an enjoyer would again be rendered meaningless. Anticipating another possible objection regarding its establishment, he refutes it once more:
"The insentient object does not possess agency merely by the proximity of consciousness."
And because of its constant proximity, the pot and other such things would possess agency without distinction.

Because it is all-pervasive (*cit*). The implication is that, since there is no distinction in its proximity to the body as well as to objects such as jars, its agency would exist at all times. Thus, the Self alone possesses the power whose single nature is characterized by knowledge and action. Likewise, although that power is eternal, it remains as if non-existent due to adventitious limitations (*aupādhika*); this is the characteristic of the two-fold nature of the senses.
He says that it is characterized by the instruments (karaṇa):
"That power whose nature is knowledge and action, which is dependent upon the *pudgala*,
that very power is perceived through the nature of the cognitive and active organs (*buddhi-karmendriya*)."
This is easy to understand. He states that this alone is the fruit of the senses:

"O twice-born ones, through discernment, they who know the truth make that which has been obstructed for many ages and has long resided within the infinite Self [manifest]; this is the fruit of the senses."
"Anekakāla" means that whose time is manifold and immeasurable; that is to say, beginningless.

By that impurity which has been obstructing and subjugating his power for such a manifold duration of time—thus [referring to] him who is obstructed by that manifold-time [impurity]. For this very reason, in that state, his vision and action are conditioned by the limiting adjunct of that impurity.

O twice-born ones! That which consists of the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) characterized by the nature of agency (*kartṛtva*), which was permeated—that is, rendered latent—by ignorance; which, through discernment (*viveka*), tears asunder the impurity of its own portion and makes itself manifest; and which, through the arising of knowledge, makes one a knower of reality by generating true knowledge—that is not the fruit of the senses.
Or else, [the production of the existent] would follow the Naiyāyikas and others, because it would entail the consequence of being subject to modification and so forth.

This is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) regarding both the arising of action and the agent; for since intellect and the rest have already been described as manifestors of knowledge and agency, there arises the doubt: "What, then, is the fruit of a composite [entity]? To this, [it was said] previously...
Because it has been examined in detail by the passage beginning with "in due order" (*krameṇaiva*), he states that [the process] is not simultaneous:
"The person, joined with mental attention and assisted by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*),
perceives external objects through the instruments such as the eyes."
Then, prior knowledge free from conceptual construction arises;
for when the object has been thus perceived, conceptualization follows immediately thereafter.
When many [objects] have been perceived, the act of making one object the focus is taught as the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of that which was previously perceived by the mind.
If that were not the case, by whom could the simultaneous arising of cognitions be prevented?
For the mere act of perception is simply the operation of the eyes and the other senses.
In this purely imagined object, there arises a mental construction through the mind;
and that [construction] is a determination of its nature (dharma) due to its conformity with previous experience.
The recollection that "these phenomena belong only to the jar and not to anything else" is the connection with the apprehender of an object already accepted by the mind.
Egoity (ahaṃkāra) has been defined; it is considered to consist of self-conceit (abhimāna).
If it were not existent, it would not be a grasper, nor would it be the self, because it would be indistinguishable from other [non-existent] things.
The ego-principle (ahaṃkāra), whose purpose is internal enjoyment, is the initiator of activity everywhere;
only afterwards does the intellect (buddhi) proceed, determining its objects.
Due to its adherence to the singular focus of what is intended by the mind,
that which is of the nature of determination and ascertainment is indeed nothing other than the intellect (buddhi) alone.
Like the eye of a crow, the mind roams both externally and internally;
it is only when an object has been made an object of the mind that the movement of the intellect and the ego proceeds toward it.
The determination of objects by means of instruments such as observation (*ālocana*) and so forth [is preceded] by the mind (*manas*);

therefore, before [the mention of] "accompanied by passion" (*rāgasahabhāva*), [the phrase] "preceded by consciousness-power" (*cicchakti*) should be supplied, and before [the mention of] "consciousness-power," the phrase "knowledge (*vidyā*) which is defiled" (*vidyā kaluṣitā*) should be supplied.

In the phrase "the eye, the sun," and so forth, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) intends to refer to the external sense organs (*bahiḥkaraṇa*) in general. [Objection: But conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is indeed a modification of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*). [Response: True. For this very reason, he demonstrates the distinction of the mental conceptualization (*manovikalpa*) by means of the passage beginning with "among many. In the reading "that which has been made an object" (*viṣayīkṛtam*), the suffix *-kta* denotes the action (*bhāve*). In the case of "of that which has been perceived" (*ālocitasya*), the suffix *-kta* likewise denotes the action.

When the mind has apprehended an object and the senses are presided over by it, there arises the activity of the non-conceptualizing power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*), which is the origin of knowledge; here, "conceptualization by the mind" is the implied connection. Otherwise, if it were not so, it would be conceptual (*savikalpa*) as it measures such an object. This refers to cognitions characterized by the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of objects such as forms that arise subsequently. Now, [one might ask]: *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "nanu" (now/if one asks), indicating the beginning of a new objection or inquiry.*
Let this conceptualization apply to the eye and the other [senses]. Why not to the mind? To this he says:

by the term "mere observation" (*ālocanamātra*), the meaning is that [the sense] is exhausted by mere observation alone; since it is conceived as being solitary, let it be connected with what precedes—namely, when many things have been observed by the mind through its own conceptualization. And that is that.

And [the term] *kalpa* means determination (*niścaya*). He says "no" to the question of whether it is like the cognition (*buddhi*) itself, by means of the passage beginning with "these" (*amī*), which refers to recollection (*anusaṃsmṛti*).

That [recollection] is the taking as an object through one-pointedness amidst doubt; it is the conjunction with the grasper (*grāhaka-saṃgati*), that is, the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) by the grasper. It is for the sake of enjoyment (*bhoga-artha*), meaning it is the cause of enjoyment, by others who are endowed with non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpa-bodha*).

The thought "I" regarding that which is mentally conceived belongs to the mind endowed with doubt, following the inclination of the mind; it proceeds according to the mental construction of the attentive perceiver. By contrast, the ego-function (*ahaṃkāra-vṛtti*) which takes as its object the thought "I" without doubt—being fixed upon a single point—is [the perception] of that which is mentally conceived as "this," belonging to the mind endowed with doubt.

Due to conformity, these properties belong to the jar alone and not to anything else; this is to be understood through the application of the mind following a focused intention. By being made the object of a mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) as residing in a single substrate and being grasped by the cognition "this," the intellect determines the object to be grasped. This very process, consisting solely of ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*), is what constitutes knowledge (*vidyā*).
Since this has been analyzed and explained in great detail in the *Parīkṣā*, one should discern the meaning here by consulting that work;

thus, for those who fear excessive prolixity or who find it difficult to follow every step, this concise commentary (*vivṛtti*) has been composed. By the verse beginning with "the crow" (*kāka*), he states that the mind (*manas*) operates in both ways because it impels both the external and internal faculties; this is not [merely] accepted [without proof].

Regarding the object intended by the mind, characterized as the grasped and the grasper, this is what is meant: the mind, consisting of intention (*saṃkalpa*) and conceptualization (*vikalpa*), possessing its own activity and operating in both ways, has a twofold function. That mind, through its external operation, impels the external sense organ; having apprehended a single external object such as a woman, it intends it. Internally...
Through its activity, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), characterized by egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) and intellect (*buddhi*), further impels [the consciousness] toward its respective objects.
By means of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding external objects such as women and the like, it conceives of the objects of mental pleasure and so forth arising within;
thus, it mingles the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) with ignorance (*avidyā*), which is combined with volition (*saṃkalpa*), intellect (*buddhi*), and determination (*adhyavasāya*).

It reports [the object] through the mediation of the impulsion of the *ahaṃkāra* of cognition (*budhyahaṃkāra*). Furthermore, it becomes an object that is both pure and impure, augmented by attachment to the auspicious (*śiva*) and the inauspicious (*aśiva*). As it is said in the *Mataṅga*: "The mind has two peaks" (*dvekoṭi-manasaḥ siddhaḥ*).
By the word "perception" (*ālocana*), the eyes and other [senses] are denoted according to the etymology of being instruments (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*); [it refers to] the determination of the object.

The meaning is that it occurs according to the sequence previously stated. For the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth does not belong to the Self, but rather to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) itself.
With this premise, the sages refute the erroneous fabrication of those false logicians, foremost among whom are the proponents of Māyā (*māyāvādins*).
Whatever knowledge there may be, none of it arises from the power of consciousness;
all that must be accepted as being of the intellect (*bauddha*), by reason of its perishable nature.

Because it is impossible for knowledge arising from that [consciousness] to perish if consciousness-power (*cicchakti*) were unchanging, whatever knowledge there may be, all of it originates from consciousness-power. However, this knowledge is mental (*bauddha*), because while being knowledge, it is perishable; for that which is not mental is not perishable while being knowledge, as, for example, [the Self].

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: "Brahman-knowledge" must be understood as being exclusively of the nature of *buddhi* (intellection), because its cause is perishability; for otherwise, [the definition] would be established in a different way. Furthermore, the explicit statement that "it is not the fruit of the sense organs," and so forth, is accompanied by reasoning.
Īśvara:
Since that cognition is insentient, how could it produce knowledge?
It is claimed [to do so] only occasionally through its connection with a manifesting agent.
Even that which is eternal is experienced as momentary;
for as long as a lamp remains, it continues to illuminate objects.

What was stated—that it belongs to the Buddha—is not correct. Since the intellect (*buddhi*) is insentient (*jaḍa*), its sattvic manifestation is known as that which manifests knowledge; thus, it is rightly said that [the term] "knowledge" (*jñāna*) possesses an instrumental derivation meaning "that by which something is known. How then could it be known that [the intellect] has the capacity to produce knowledge? (p. 690)

Regarding the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*): it is not the case that its established existence arises from some occasional cause of production; rather, it belongs to the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) alone. [Objection: But if this is of the nature of power (*śākta*), how is it that it is experienced as eternal in this way? [Response: True. It is due to its connection with a manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*). [The manifestor...]

Due to its connection with the Buddhist illumination renowned for impermanence— characterized by momentariness consisting of various arisings and vanishings— the consciousness of the Śākta cognition (citi-śāktajñapti) exists at times as a jar and at times as a cloth; thus, through that non-distinct manifestation, it becomes at once both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karma*), even though it is eternally prior.

Immediately following the conjunction of the two flames of the lamp, momentariness and permanence—characterized by momentariness—are experienced as if they were real. To illustrate: for as long as the lamp remains, for that long the objects, such as the jar and so forth, [remain].

Or [it is] the illuminator or manifester of the perceiving eyes. Just as when there is the destruction of a lamp, there is the non-manifestation of the jar or other objects manifested by it—despite their existing in their own nature and being present in the darkness—this is expressed by a statement of non-existence; so too here, for as long as the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) [persists].

For that duration, she remains as the manifestor of the powers of consciousness (*śāktajñāna*). When there is a cessation of the fluctuations of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*), then, because of that [cessation], the power of consciousness—which exists by its own nature—is not manifested due to the presence of that which is called "impurity" (*mala*), which is essentially darkness; hence, it is described as being non-existent.

Because the attainment of the manifesting capacity by a specific non-perception—which is established as the absence of a manifestor of something otherwise existing—is immediately followed by deviation [from the probandum]. For that non-perception is not the cause for proving the absence of the object in question. Now, according to the stated method, this is a jar...

Regarding the non-momentary nature of the pot, as expressed in the cognition "this is a pot," there is no experience of momentariness. However, the repeated arising of the conceptual cognitions "this is a pot, this is a pot" makes the experience of their momentariness appear extremely vivid and non-figurative.
To show that this is incorrect, he says:
Furthermore, even a continuous stream of cognition is experienced as momentary,
because its manifesting causes proceed only in a succession.
For this very reason, the painful hope of those who assert that consciousness is momentary because all entities are momentary has been dispelled.
Because manifesting causes— which serve as the instrumental conditions for the manifestation of cognition—

proceed solely through a continuous stream (*santati*) or a flow-like operation (*dhārāvāha-vṛtti*), the eternal cognition (*nityabuddhi*), though characterized by its own lack of conceptual determination (*anadhyavasāya-lakṣaṇa*), is nevertheless indicated by the momentary [states] arising from a stream of conceptualization (*savikalpika-santati*).

Because it flows in a continuous stream (*dhārā*) by means of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) conditioned by its own functional activity (*vṛtti*) and limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is called "streaming" (*dhārāvāhikā*).
That [cognition] is both a cognition (*dhī*) and such [a streaming one]; thus, that streaming cognition is also experienced as momentary.
Therefore, it appears as momentary. It is for this reason that the Buddhists, who are devoid of such discrimination, are refuted; hence he says:

"From this" means: because of appearing as if momentary due to their rapid destruction, the objects that serve as the manifestors of entities are characterized by impermanence; for consciousness, which is the cognition in the form of the grasper, is momentary. And regarding those who assert the momentariness of consciousness, there is this statement in the *Mṛgendra*:
Because the karma and other factors that manifest consciousness are momentary, it is manifested again and again;
thus, it is held by others that [consciousness] is indeed momentary as it arises.

The affliction of hope and the mental agitation arising from the cause of hope have been warded off. However, on the grounds that the statement regarding the momentariness of cognitions (*saṃvid*) serves as a basis for [the doctrine of] entities, the sages raise an objection from the perspective of the Buddhist position: "Why is it that cognitions themselves do not possess momentariness?"

O Lord, why is it not accepted that entities are momentary by virtue of their existence? For existence is defined as the capacity for causal efficiency, and this [capacity] is absent in non-momentary things.

He is the Lord. "Whatever exists is momentary, just like a mass of clouds"—by means of this reason of existence (*sattva*), whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established, why and for what reason are entities (*bhāva*), which are things known through their existence, not accepted as being momentary?
Or rather, why is no investigation made into existence itself? For existence is the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*), and that...
The meaning is that among momentary things such as consciousness and the like, that which performs a purposeful action is necessarily momentary; this is the conclusion.
Now, one might ask: "From what [source] is this restriction clear? To this they reply:
"Because [purposeful action] is incompatible with permanent things, due to the distinction between succession and simultaneity."
Because a cause for delay is impossible, and likewise because of the loss of stability.
For that which is inherently capable, even hundreds of auxiliary causes are superfluous;
therefore, its momentariness is established by its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

In the case of stable, non-momentary entities, there is no connection with causal efficiency (arthakriyā) through either succession or simultaneity—that is, through the division of sequential and simultaneous action. This is because causal efficiency is logically untenable [in such cases]. For instance, if consciousness or the like were stable, it would either be inactive toward any object or else, being inherently capable by its own nature, it would possess the innate, singular character of cognizing objects and so forth; yet, in that case, it could have no need for auxiliary causes.

"Enough with even hundreds [of reasons]" means that there is no cause for delay, because there is no ground for postponement. Why then would an entity such as consciousness not perform at that very moment the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) that is to be accomplished at a later time?
If it is argued that this is because its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are difficult to assemble, then it must be admitted that it performs something [at least].

Because they possess an excess of intensity, their nature undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*), whereby their stability is destroyed; thus, there is no successive causal efficiency (*kramikārthakriyā*). Nor can there be simultaneous causal efficiency for a non-momentary entity, because if that [efficiency] were to exist, it would have to come into being after not having existed previously; and if such simultaneous causal efficiency occurred, then in the case of cognition and so forth, there would be a distinction between each respective object.

If, moreover, that which is eternal were to possess simultaneous causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) arising from various inherent natures (*svabhāva*) produced at once, then it would never cease; for if it were to cease, it would follow that it possesses an impermanent nature and is subject to destruction, because of its association with a different inherent nature consisting of that cessation. Such is its stability.

Since even for that which is non-momentary there would be no simultaneous performance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), momentariness is established—and indeed ascertained—for consciousness and so forth by virtue of their performing causal efficiency, which otherwise would be impossible. This is the meaning: the preceding [entity], having performed its causal efficiency, perishes, while another [entity] is indeed a novel object.

He proceeded to dispel this delusion arising from the fabrication of the extremely false view of a Creator—the notion that "an agent arises together with the action," for such [simultaneity] is indeed impossible for a momentary entity.
[The opponent argues: "If all things are momentary, the relationship of cause and effect would be destroyed."
The effect exists in the form of the cause; it attains the state of being the cause.
A lump of clay, existing as such, attains the state of a jar;
therefore, a cause must endure for two moments in order to produce its effect.

To that extent, existence and so forth constitute a reason [for momentariness] because it is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) that the nature of both self and other is momentary. [If one objects that] even a jar or the like is perceived to be non-momentary, then [the reason] would be "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
Furthermore, this [reason] is contradictory (*viruddha*) because it is pervaded by non-momentariness; and it is unestablished (*asiddha*) because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has not been grasped.
Because there is no means of valid cognition [to establish it]. Now, one might argue that there exists a proof to refute its non-establishment and so forth:
"The universe under dispute is momentary, because if it were not momentary, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) would be impossible.
This is incorrect, because you yourselves do not admit that anything whatsoever is non-momentary.
Furthermore, this [argument] is unestablished with respect to its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). Let us grant that things are non-momentary;

however, if things were momentary—meaning they perish at the very moment of their own arising—the causal relationship between a cause and its effect would be destroyed, because the cause and its immediately subsequent momentary effect would not coexist. For instance, according to the view that the effect is pre-existent (*satkāryavāda*), the effect is already established.

That which is designated as a "jar," though existing as a past moment and lacking manifestation, exists in the form of its cause; having been fashioned from a past momentary lump of clay, it attains the state of being clay through its causal nature. The lump of clay, possessing the arrangement of causes—though not itself a [present] momentary entity—becomes manifest once again while existing in the present.

Existing as a momentary effect in the form of a jar (*ghaṭatva*) at the present moment, it would attain the state of a pot (*kumbhatā*), that is, the state of being an effect. Therefore, because the effect exists at the time of the cause and the cause exists at the time of the effect, the cause is not momentary in the production of the effect; rather, it persists for two moments. But [one might object]: *Note: The text provided contains a page number marker (p. 699) and a partial sentence ending with "nanu" (but/if one objects), which has been translated according to the context of the preceding argument.*

What is the purpose of postulating the existence of the cause as having that very nature at the moment of the effect? Let the producer and the produced be related by existing for only one and the same moment. To show that this is incorrect, he says:
"But if they are distinct entities, then the cause [is defined] by its production of that [effect]."
Otherwise, why would an entity that exists at the same time [as the effect] not be its cause?

How can there be a difference in time between those two, given that they are distinct entities? Regarding those two—the cause and the effect—at the moment of its arising, the fact that the cause, which consists of the power to produce, is manifested simultaneously with the moment of the effect is something that cannot be avoided even by proponents of the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*); it is established by the principle of equality (*samanaya*).
Or rather, it must be stated that there is an interval [between cause and effect]. For in that case, it cannot be said that "one of them exists as a distinct entity" [in the other].
This is because a cause cannot be the cause of an effect if it is not delimited by the capacity for that effect;
for a cause does not exist as a distinct entity from the effect such that one could say, "this cause has arisen from that."

Because it is not within the range of cognition (*buddhi-gocaratvāt*), and because that which is non-existent cannot serve as a material cause (*anupādānatvāt*). Rather, by way of its functional efficacy (*arthena*), the cause is characterized by its existence in the past moment as a non-manifested effect-nature, while the effect is characterized by its existence in the present moment as a manifested cause-nature; thus, through their own actual presence, there is a distinction between them based on their respective specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-viveka*) such as priority and posteriority.

The cause exists either as the same entity or as a different entity. Otherwise, if it were through immediate contiguity (*nairantarya*), then since the effect existing at the time of the cause would be of the nature of a manifestation, the manifesting object—such as a jar—would exist simultaneously [with its cause];
why then would it not be the cause of itself? [In the case of] contiguity, there is non-difference; otherwise, there is difference.

The sense is that because [the cause] persists, the effect is not established [as distinct]; rather, by virtue of being an effect, the unity and permanence of that which is intended as such are established.

He states the conclusion: when the two—the cause and the effect—are shown to be different entities according to the aforementioned method, and their duration across two moments is established, there arises a temporal distinction between them: the causal moment is past, while [the effect] is present.
The meaning is: how could the characteristic known as the "moment of effect" not be easily obtained?

Regarding the statement that "the performance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is impossible for a momentary entity," he begins to offer a resolution: "From where does the excellence of the cause arise through its association with auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*)?"
Or why, O twice-born one, would the production of a jar not arise from threads?
Therefore, the relationship of cause and effect is established only among stable entities.
The distinction between the cause—such as the cognition of clay—and its auxiliary conditions—such as the staff or the sense organs—is as follows:
if the prior nature [of the cause] were destroyed, from what source could any superior excellence arise? (p. 702)

What is the cause of existence? If it is argued that it is for the sake of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), meaning the capacity to accomplish its own purpose through an arising that sublates previous specificities,
then since it is produced immediately by auxiliary causes as something possessing specificities, what is the "distinctness" (*viśiṣṭatva*) of the clay particles?

Why then would the production of a jar not occur from threads? Therefore, the assistance rendered by auxiliaries consists merely in their cooperation, not in the imparting of a different nature to one another; thus, because they do not produce any additional capacity (*atiśaya*), the relationship of cause and effect is established only among stable entities. If momentariness is intended, then causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) [is impossible].
To the question "How can there be delay?", he says:
"The capacity for causal efficiency belongs to enduring things only through successive stages;
moreover, there is no rule that what is capable must always produce its effect."
Furthermore, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) resides in permanent, non-momentary entities through successive stages.
For that which is capable and whose excellence cannot be imparted by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), there is no necessity of always producing its effect;
rather, it produces its effect either successively or simultaneously upon the presence of auxiliaries, due to its innate, singular nature of performing that action.
Because it is accepted that [the cause] possesses a specific nature (*viśiṣṭasvabhāva*). He demonstrates this very point:
"Even though fire is capable of burning, it requires a finger for the blister;
through the alternatives of succession and simultaneity, there arises the cognition of distant extension and non-momentariness."

Fire, although capable of burning and possessing the innate, single nature of both burning and illuminating, requires for its own cessation— the purposeful action characterized as burning— a combustible object such as a finger, and for its illumination, objects to be illuminated such as a jar; yet there is no contradiction in these purposeful actions occurring simultaneously.

Since it is observed that a lamp— which possesses a single power consisting of burning and illumination— simultaneously accomplishes its purposeful activities, such as the consumption of the wick and oil and the cognition of all objects grasped by a single act of perception, and yet it is also seen to sequentially consume portions of the wick and oil and to cognize other distinct objects;

When the auxiliary conditions for the purposeful activity of making known and so forth are present, consciousness—whose nature is established as consisting of a single, innate, and specific act of cognition not produced by those [auxiliaries]—is capable of accomplishing its own purposeful activity in the form of a cognitive act directed toward multiple objects of knowledge simultaneously, such as an insect or a single pair. For it is thus: he indeed...

Devadatta perceives the actions of a pillar, a jar, and so forth, both successively and simultaneously; however, one whose purposeful activity is not distinct from cognition perceives successive acts such as bathing,
worshiping, cutting grass, cooking, using utensils, eating, and washing, as well as the simultaneous bearing of a heavy load.
It performs such actions as walking, touching grass, moving its limbs, eating, and speaking.

Therefore, the notion of momentariness based on the conceptual alternatives of "succession" or "simultaneity" is a vain hope, unfit to be desired even by one in distress; furthermore, he states that if [the self] were indeed momentary, this [notion] would also be undermined:
Furthermore, this cognition that arises is one that was previously experienced;
for if all things were momentary, how could recognition of it ever occur?

The cognition that "I am such-and-such a father now, as I was in childhood," which was previously experienced when [the self] was situated within its object and manifested in one's own consciousness— that very same cognition arises at the time of unification (sārdhikye) as this recognition: "I am such-and-such a father then, and I am such-and-such a young man now."
Regarding that [memory], the cognition previously experienced would be without a cause if it were momentary;
furthermore, why would Devadatta not remember what was experienced by his son? For recognition indeed arises [only from such a connection].
But surely, those who maintain the doctrine of a stable self also accept a distinction between experience and memory. True.
The acceptance of that [distinction] is based on the perspective of the manifestation of cognition through a manifesting agent;

however, in reality, for the experiencer, memory and experiences characterized by innate activity—supported by the intellect (*buddhi*) and the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) which constitute its very form—are not distinct. They should be known as non-different.
We speak even while accepting momentariness; thus he says: "Or let there be momentariness of entities that are insentient in nature, wherein only three causes are postulated for all effects."
Even those entities such as *bindu* (the drop) and others undergo a uniform transformation;

or rather, let there be momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) for insentient objects—yet even that kind of momentariness does not undermine the relationship of cause and effect as you intend it. Rather, it is that specific kind of momentariness [which we maintain]...
In order to remedy the faults mentioned regarding the causal relationship in all effects, it is stated in the venerable *Matanga* and other scriptures:
"The Lord is indeed the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), while the powers (*śakti*) are the material cause (*upādāna*).
Likewise, Māyā is the inherent cause (*samavāyin*); this world is thus real."

In the manner described, the characteristic of Īśa and the others is the *nimitta* (efficient cause). That which is designated by the term *upādāna*—meaning "that by which [the effect] is taken up in this"—is the inherent cause (*samavāyin*) characterized by Māyā and the rest. Furthermore, that which is designated by the term *anupādāna*—meaning "that by which [the effect] is not taken up"—is characterized by Śakti and the rest; it consists of service to Maheśvara within the *maṇḍala* of authority pertaining to the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*).

The characteristics of karma and so forth—namely, the impurity of *āṇavamala* and the objects of cognition (*meyādi*) within the impure path—and karma and so forth as auxiliary causes, being delimited by such a nature, constitute and establish merely the three causes. It has been stated that there exists momentariness in that; thus, it concludes that impermanence conforms to its own specific form.

For this very reason, even the momentariness existing in lightning and such is postulated as a cause; for lightning also produces its own effect, beginning with the manifestation of the perception of form. But surely, you do not postulate a separate non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) in that way, as is postulated by the Naiyāyikas?
Why is it postulated? True. For us, even the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is not a substance;

however, because it will be stated that it is its power (*śakti*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is merely a specific modification of the inherent cause. What is the purpose of this postulation—whether for the sake of explaining its necessity or establishing its proof? [Objection: But is it not insentient (*jaḍa*)?

Regarding the objection that there is no eternal entity arising from common discourse, he provides this rebuttal: those entities or things which are eternal—namely the *bindu*, *mala*, and *māyā*—are indeed characterized by a common transformation;
they transform equally, universally, and in their entirety, not merely in part.

The transforming [factors] (*pariṇāmin*), which are of the nature of causes, remain as effects while undergoing change; however, impurity (*mala*) transforms by way of its own power through the cessation characterized by the removal of the state of being an obstacle and the alteration of its own nature (*svarūpa-sattva-anyathātva*). Thus, insentient entities undergo transformation into other modes corresponding to their respective natures.
Having stated that momentariness exists as something constructed— that is, that the momentariness of cognition is conditioned by those [external] adjuncts and not intrinsic— he concludes:
"Cognition alone is stable and eternal, the illuminator of the mass of insentient things."
Its momentariness is to be understood from the momentariness of all things.
While the sages among the Sugatas clearly proclaim selflessness,
the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādins) further object:
"If external entities truly exist, then stability of mind might indeed be possible."
In the case of non-existent things, the momentariness of cognitions follows from themselves by virtue of the non-difference of their substrates.

When external objects exist, there would be stability even for the intellect—that is, for cognition—according to the manner described. Because of the non-difference between knowledge and its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the intellect perceives objects through the designations of those things that serve as its own limiting adjuncts; thus, [it perceives] objects even when they are non-existent. Indeed, momentariness is not adventitious (*aupādhika*), but rather intrinsic (*svataḥ*) by virtue of being natural.
[The opponent asks: "How is it divided? To this they reply:
"For it is cognition itself that appears in the form of external objects;
because no division is perceived, since [cognition and its object] appear simultaneously."
And objectivity is not possible for something other than cognition;
if it were a different entity, how could that cognition belong to it here?

For it is indeed cognition (*buddhi*), or consciousness (*saṃvid*) itself, that appears in the form of external objects. But surely, consciousness does not appear in the form of objects such as blue; rather, it is something distinct from that—the blue and so forth—that appears in the form of cognition. As it has been said: "Because they appear simultaneously, and because there is no perception of difference."

Because blue and so forth arise within consciousness through cognition, there is no object that exists as a distinct entity separate from the thing [itself] by virtue of being isolated; such being the case, that other entity—blue and so forth—does not possess the status of an object.
In short, the very cognition of blue is itself the blue. As it has been said: "The difference between blue and its simultaneous apprehension is [unreal]."

For that distinction between the two—the cognition and [the object]—is seen by erroneous cognitions as being non-dual. Among the cognitions of blue and so forth, if that object such as blue were a different entity (*arthāntara*) from the consciousness, or if it were situated elsewhere than in the consciousness, then that cognition of blue and so forth would be a different entity from the blue and so forth; and that [blue and so forth] too would be something other than the consciousness.
It might be asked: "How could that [nature] exist within this consciousness? To this he replies with the words "Not so" (na hi):
"For how could the essential nature of one thing possibly belong to another?
Indeed, the form residing in a jar cannot be the form of a cloth."
This is clear. He concludes:
"Therefore, whatever form exists in consciousness, that is the very nature of consciousness itself.
There is no difference between the nature of consciousness and its forms; tell me, how could there be such a distinction between the object and the cognition thereof?"

Therefore, according to the manner described, that form which appears as having arisen within consciousness—consisting of the duality of object and subject, yet appearing as non-dual—is none other than the very nature of consciousness itself. As it has been said: "If blue were other than consciousness, it would not appear within consciousness. Thus, because no distinction in form is perceived between the object and the cognition, [they are one].
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is: "If you say there is no difference between consciousness (*saṃvit*) and its form (*rūpa*), then explain [how they differ]. The Lord (*Īśvara*):
That is incorrect. Consciousness is differentiated by the object (*artha*), but the object is not differentiated by it.
If the object is not that which differentiates it, how could there be a differentiation of consciousness?

As for what was said—that there is no difference—that is incorrect. Consciousness, by conforming to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of various flowers, is differentiated by objects through their conformity to various limiting adjuncts such as blue and so forth; it is metaphorically treated as if it were differentiated. That object, by conforming to the limiting adjuncts of various flowers, [is like] a thread [colored] by the object... (p. 713) ...through various [colors].

It appears differentiated by following after limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as blue and so forth; it is metaphorically treated as if it were differentiated. That object, being consciousness itself, possesses the state of having various forms such as blue and so on; thus, due to the delusion of the intellect that it possesses various differences not distinct from that [consciousness], one might think it is differentiated.
However, because this would uproot direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and because it must be followed [as the true nature], it is not differentiated from that consciousness.

The passage beginning with "That" (*tad*) and so forth is clear. Now, one might object: "Let it be that [the cognition] persists; however, let there be an internal differentiation within itself. To this he says: "Indeed, there can be no inherent differentiation within a single cognition of a jar."
Due to the consequence of an infinite number of distinctions, the object is considered to be the differentiator of cognition.

There can be no difference [in the cognition] by its own nature; whence then could this clear restriction arise? For a single cognition of a jar—which exists in the form of a single, momentary jar characterized as "this is a jar"—its existence at that very moment remains unimpeded even with respect to other things characterized as jars, cloths, or carts, provided one does not consider where else it might reside.

Because of the consequence of an infinite regress of distinctions, the cognition of the object is considered the differentiator. However, knowledge, while being the establisher, does not establish itself by itself, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon its own self.
Since it is established as something distinct, the object is proven to be perceived; by means of that [cognition] acting as an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*), these [objects] are differentiated.
He clarifies this very point by means of an illustration:
furthermore, a single entity assumes various forms due to the proximity of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as is the case with consciousness and a crystal.
This is clear. He concludes:
"Therefore, because objects are momentary, consciousness is not momentary.
By way of a secondary consequence following from the primary argument, the Buddhist doctrine has also been described.

This is clear. Following the examination of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) as the subject at hand, he establishes them by way of their effects: "The subtle elements, which have now arrived in due order, are also described."
Because it is a quality perceivable by the external senses, it is withdrawn along with the primary elements.
O Brahmins, that which is the cause for our direct perception of things as being preceded by causes is indeed the withdrawal of the subtle elements (tanmātras).

The proposition that the dissolution of the elements is preceded by a cause is established; this reason is to be understood as applying to the external world being perceptible to people like us. For this reason also, he states the proof of those [subtle] elements:
"Because sound and the rest possess specific qualities, and these are preceded by universals."
And one should meditate upon that which is common even there as being merely that.
Because sound and the other qualities, which are the attributes of the elements such as space, possess particularity; because they are manifest;

and because those sounds and so forth are preceded by universals and have unmanifest qualities as their cause. Furthermore, regarding the establishment of their particularity therein, that universal which is unmanifest is merely that much.

"Merely sound and so forth" means, alternatively, merely that much—the mere form of the primary elements (*bhūtaprakṛti*). One should contemplate "merely that" (*tanmātra*) with complete proficiency. He sets forth the sequence of "merely that": the dissolution of the *tanmātras* consists of one, two, three, four, and five qualities (*guṇa*).
For this very reason, the intention of the elements [is determined] by the qualities in their successive order.
In this context, the distinction between the gross elements (*bhūta*) and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) is based on their coarseness and subtlety.

The subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*) is that in which the quality of sound is unmanifest. The subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*) is that in which the qualities of sound and touch are unmanifest. The subtle element of form... [is that in which] the qualities of sound, touch, and form are unmanifest.

The subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*) consists solely of the qualities of sound, touch, and form. The subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*) consists solely of the unmanifest qualities of sound, touch, and form. The subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*) consists solely of the unmanifest qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. For this very reason, it is the cause.

"Following the qualities" (*guṇānuvidhāyinaḥ*). According to the principle that "the qualities [of the effect] follow those of the cause," for those things established by logic—beginning with space (*ākāśa*) and proceeding in order—the intended meaning is that they are manifested by their respective qualities, such as sound and so forth. There is an alternative reading, *guṇābhiyogaḥ*, which means "application by means of the qualities.
Even if there were equality of qualities, the meaning is easily understood by supplying the word "grossness" (*sthaulya*) based on the context.
This has been stated in the *Mataṅga*: "The subtle elements (*tanmātra*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), intellect (*mahat*), and the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the 'lepa' (the coating).

The point is that their subtlety is inferred through their effects. Because they are not perceptible to people like us—just like the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and other such entities—the effect of this aggregate of subtle elements and gross elements is what is designated by the term "sound" (*śabda*).
The performance of its own purpose is known as the eyes and other organs maintaining their instruments.

Regarding the relationship between quality and the possessor of quality as that of container and contained, the sages raise an objection by means of the stages of Māyā and so forth, which act as the agent.
It has been stated that "mere sound" and so forth refer to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which are without a substratum;
since sound and the rest are qualities (*guṇa*), how could they be the cause of a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*)?

This is clear. [Regarding] Īśvara: being the substratum of qualities (*guṇāśrayatva*) does not mean being a possessor of qualities (*guṇitva*), but rather, as for us Buddhists, having the nature of integrated qualities (*saṃgataguṇātmatva*). He refutes [the objection] that even in that case [the Lord] would possess them, stating:
"There is no insentient entity whatsoever that is a possessor of qualities and a substratum of qualities."
Only the qualities are experienced, and the designations "possessor of qualities" are merely conventional associations.
When they are united, they become known as "possessors of qualities" (guṇins); this is the remainder [of the meaning]. He clarifies that there is no object whatsoever other than the qualities:
"Because the universe consists of the qualities, being of the nature of the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded."
Likewise, by the reason that it has the purpose of illuminating the restriction of activity.
Delusion is not a separate entity from that [state], because it consists of the nature of both suffering and pleasure.

For this reason, the universe is peaceful when consisting of *sattva*; it is terrible when consisting of *rajas*; and it is deluded by nature when consisting of *tamas*. Therefore, it proceeds in such a manner through the aforementioned process, for the purpose of regulating activity and providing illumination.

By the reason that Rajasic effort, Tamasic restraint, and Sattvic knowledge are the causes [of the states], it is likewise characterized as having the nature of Sattva and so forth; furthermore, because its nature consists of delusion, suffering, and pleasure, it is composed of the Guṇas and is not something other than them. It is like the six-fingered [boy] who is sweet-tasting, fragrant, and harsh-sounding.
"Even when she is asleep, she possesses the soft rustling sound of touch; for what quality other than a quality can be perceived by the possessor of qualities?
Yet, O sages, how could that [perception] not occur if they were distinct? Furthermore, they cite the statement: 'Indeed, it is a single object that is apprehended by both sight and touch.'"
How could that not be a category (padārtha), such that there would be some possessor of qualities (guṇin) distinct from it?
And this is an illustration [that applies] clearly to the ear and the other senses as well. [The opponent says: "The Lord [is perceived]. [The author] refutes this:
That perception of form and so forth by the eye and the other senses is established as being unreal. How, then, is the apprehension of an object other than those [senses] by means of them possible?

The meaning of the first half [of the verse] is clear. Therefore, by means of those [faculties] such as the eye, and from that—namely, from the quality (*guṇa*) consisting of the two forms of matter (*rūpa*), namely color (*varṇa*) which is graspable by the eye, and shape (*saṃsthāna*) which is graspable by the eye and the tactile faculty (*tvagindriya*)—how could the apprehension (*graha*) or grasping of another distinct entity, the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), be tenable? Now, how then [is it possible]?

"It possesses a sweet taste" and "it has six fingers"—this is true. Just as in the expression "a forest with pleasant banks," there is a designation based on a specific part of the whole; thus, nothing is inconsistent. Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that many things are perceived? To this he says:
"If the cognition here were of two qualities, then the sense organ would be the perceiver of the substance."
Because it is exclusively devoted to the form of that [object], the sense organ of sight is composed of fire (taijasa).
If one were to argue as follows: "The eye is indeed internal;
for, by virtue of being the locus and that which is located therein, the sense organ is the grasper of both substance and quality"—if such is your thought, it is not so. For this has been stated:
"The visual faculty consists of light because it is restricted to form alone; because it grasps only the quality of form," and so forth.
By speaking thus, through the employment of a probans (hetu) characterized by pervasion (vyāpti), you— who occupy the position of a Naiyāyika—

accept the desired nature of the eye by means of its exclusion from non-pervasive things. For, internally, the self as the subject of experience is indeed "I," which is not possible without being endowed with the qualities of form and so forth that constitute the objects of another name, namely, the presiding deity (sadadhibhūta).

For it would follow that [the self] is connected with the qualities of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) which has become an object; yet, even while granting this, he states that a return [to the original position] is made:
"Or rather, let that substance be the producer of action, such as illumination and so forth."
If it were other than its qualities, or if it were not other than them, what kind of entity would that thing be?
Because of the diversity of transformation, the qualities themselves are the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*).

Alternatively, let that substance other than the qualities be distinct from the qualities; does it perform the purposeful actions of illumination, activity, and restraint, or not? In that regard, if it were to perform such actions as illumination and so forth...
If it were not distinct from the qualities (*guṇa*), then what kind of entity would that be which performs the threefold action of illumination and so forth?

It would be without proof, equal to a hare’s horn; the meaning is that it would be insubstantial (*tuccha*). Therefore, the quality such as *sattva* and the rest is itself the "possessor of qualities" (*guṇin*) due to the diversity of its own measure (*parimāṇa*); it is the quality in the form of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) and the like. That is the possessor of qualities.

The sages have declared that [the Self] exists in the form of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, having conjoined with its own transformations and qualities suitable for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Furthermore, let it be said that "quality" (*guṇa*) is indeed the "possessor of quality" (*guṇin*). As for the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), their respective lordship is established by the number one, two, three, and so on; thus they are said to possess qualities. How can there be self-ownership if [the Self] is non-different from the qualities?
They raise the objection that [the elements] possess ownership (*svāmitva*).
For it has been stated here that the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) possess qualities such as sound and so forth.
Tell me: are these qualities, such as sound, distinct from their own substrates, or not?
This is clear. However, the Lord, intending to speak of only a specific portion [of the self], metaphorically attributes to it the status of being its own master; thus he says:
"Those qualities, through their sequential division, become the five subtle elements (tanmātras).
That which is the non-division of sound and the others is called the subtle element of smell."

The non-differentiation of one taste from another is one thing, while the non-differentiation of another form is held to be different; likewise for touch and so forth, the non-differentiation of one is distinct, whereas for sound and the rest, it is merely sound itself.

The manifestation that is non-differentiated is existent and not distinct [from the essence]; it is designated by the term "sound" (*śabda*), beginning with the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*) and so forth.

Beginning with sound and proceeding sequentially through smell, taste, form, and touch—starting from the subtle elements of smell and the rest—the sounds such as "intense" (*tīvra*) and so on are proclaimed. These are to be understood according to the sequence of the words. Now, [one might ask]: *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)*

There are no qualities superior to sound; therefore, how could there be a connection with the One? True. For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras stated "from the word *tīvra* and so forth. Thus, [the Lord] consists of both the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) and the qualities (*guṇa*). He says that [the Lord] is indeed not distinct from that:
"In this manner, the connection with the qualities has been proclaimed."
Therefore, there is no relationship of substratum and superstratum between those two qualities alone.

The sages, through the framework of logic, clearly establish the non-erroneous proof for the purpose of establishing those subtle elements (tanmātra) as follows: "The aggregate of the subtle elements is declared to be the cause of earth and the other gross elements."
If there is an intention to express a specific magnitude, why would it not be called an atom (paramāṇu)?

The meaning is: since the intention is to express a specific magnitude and because of their equal status as observers, let the atom itself—established by both disputants—be the cause of the world; what is the use of establishing a connection with those subtle elements (*tanmātra*)? To this, Īśvara replies:

An atom cannot be the cause of the world because it is non-omnipresent, like a jar and other such objects; for just as a clay jar is distinct from its material cause, clay, even while existing within it.

That which is known as the atom (*paramāṇu*) should therefore be accepted as being composed of the primary elements (*bhautika*). The atom is not the cause of the world, because it lacks omnipresence (*avibhutva*) and possesses form (*mūrtatva*), like a jar or similar objects. Furthermore, its status as a cause of the elements has not been stated; on the contrary, it is said that it is an effect of the elements. That which you maintain to be the cause of earth—[is thus refuted].

One asserts that an atom is composed of earth because it possesses the quality of being most minute (*yavīyastva*). Whatever possesses the quality of being most minute is composed of earth, as for example, a jar—this is the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*).
And the atom is most minute—this is the application (*upanaya*). Therefore, let it be accepted that "composed of earth" means "material" (*bhautika*).

Is this not a conclusion? Indeed, this reason (*hetu*) is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because it is adduced after having passed beyond the time for the application of a reason. For one who takes atoms established by our own scripture (*asmadāgama*) as the subject (*pakṣadharmin*), there is a delay in the establishment of those atoms which are established by the scriptures of others.

It is necessarily established by our own scripture that the acceptance of [the soul's] being of the nature of *mātrā* (atomic measure), eternality, and so forth, constitutes your probandum— namely, its non-earthiness, non-eternality, and so on; yet this is incorrect,
because the existence of atoms (*paramāṇu*) is well-established in our scripture through the authoritative testimony of the Vedas regarding the three times (*adhvan*).
This is established through the acceptance of your own scriptures; as it is stated in the venerable *Svatantra*:
"When there is a conjunction of eight atoms, that is called a *trisareṇu*; that is said to be a lotus-dust particle (*padmarajas*)."

Thus, regarding atoms: since the subjects (*dharmin*) are established by our respective scriptures (*āgama*), when we two are proving both impermanence and permanence, neither our own scripture nor yours can establish that either our reason or yours is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). This is even more so in the case where [the subject] is established by scripture.

That fault remains precisely in the subject (*dharmin*). Nor is it the case that atoms are established by scripture, because you yourselves have proven them through this [argument] when proving properties such as being composed of water-atoms and so forth. When there is a plurality of "otherness" (*aparatva*) and so on, the application of the reason is: "that which establishes the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) as the probandum (*sādhya*) establishes the state of being a cause (*kāraṇatva*)."
Having established that, he employs another reason for its proof:
"Those things which are corporeal and those which are distinct from a corporeal object, such as a jar,
are seen to be merely effects, just like the parts consisting of the neck and so forth."

Atoms are effects because they possess form (*mūrtatva*) and because they are distinct from that which possesses form. Those things which possess form and those which are distinct from that which possesses form are seen to be mere effects when their substrate has perished and they have become loosened; just as, for example, when a formed object such as a jar is destroyed, its parts—the neck and so forth—are likewise [seen].

Even atoms, when the fuel has been consumed by fire and the material [world] has been rendered completely dense by means of the earthly atoms and so forth, subsequently arise again in the form of *trisareṇu* (three-atom clusters) and in their own specific forms. Therefore, the conclusion should be understood by supplying the final word "tathā" (so it is).

Now, one might object that even if atoms possess form and are distinct, they cannot produce effects because they lack parts; anticipating this, [the author] establishes their possession of parts in order to prove their status as effects.
Furthermore, atoms have parts, because we observe their persistence [in composite objects].
For the stability of a property is never observed when its substratum is unperceived.
Therefore, it is never logical for the two atoms to be mere parts [of one another].
Furthermore, for this reason as well, their status as effects is established:
because atoms are seen by others to exist in the midst of other entities distinct from themselves... [wherever such a state is observed].

Since it has already been refuted that partless entities can possess the nature of being perceived—and since the relationship of locus and located, as well as the existence of those specific qualities, has been denied—the establishment of a property upon a subject whose very perception is unestablished is merely a partial view for others; it is not the case that there is an established state of partlessness. Indeed, such things have not been seen to be equal to that.

"Since it possesses parts by virtue of its stable nature, therefore here again... [the word] 'dhṛti' (support) is to be supplied; thus, the claim made by those learned in logic—that the existence of an atom as a mere part, being joined with other partless atoms, constitutes its state as a cause for dyads and so forth—is indeed not tenable. Rather, to this he says:"
If the stability of atoms were due to their connection with subtle parts,
then such [atoms] would have to be established as effects, just like a jar.
The state of atoms, characterized by their subtlety and possession of parts, would establish their status as effects— just like a jar— since such things are inherently established as having parts.
However, the seers declare through inference that [the argument] is subject to the fallacy of *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed).
When atoms are measured by the standard of the discernment of their own nature, they are indeed devoid of parts;
how then can it be stated otherwise?

The atoms (*paramāṇu*) are the subject (*dharmin*). By means of the inference that establishes the atoms—the subject characterized by the property to be proven (namely, being partless)—as you intend them, [we argue]: "The dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is not composed of a substance that is partless, because, while being devoid of intermediate magnitude, it is an effect. This is our [position].

How can you, who possess [logical] application, state otherwise—that which is devoid of parts (avayava) and is free from what you yourself accept as having parts—is a property of the very subject (*dharmin*) to be proven? [This is impossible. God (*Īśvara*).
That is not so, because of the distinction of location due to conjunction with the eastern and other directional parts.
By what means can the consequence that atoms possess parts be averted?

That is not so. As for what you have stated— that our formulated and being-formulated inferences are dependent [upon them], and consequently [our reasons] are "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) because of the time of the application of the means of cognizing your own subject (*dharmin*), or that [your reason] is "inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇa*) due to our inference regarding passion (*rāga*)— [we reply as follows].

Since it has been stated that the atom exists as the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) [of the inference], it follows that at that very moment, due to its conjunction with spatial divisions such as the eastern direction— which are themselves conditioned by their own constituent parts— there arises a distinction of location for the atoms. Consequently, how can the fact of having parts (*sāṃśatva*), resulting from this natural division of its own constituent parts, be prevented?
Refuting the opponent's position, he criticizes it: "If the conjunction occurs at one and the same location at each respective time,
then there can be no inherent distinction among the directions themselves without a distinguishing limiting condition (*upādhi*)."

If, for the sake of establishing partlessness, atoms were to possess conjunction with spatial divisions within a single location, then, because the spatial directions themselves inherently possess distinct locations,
there would necessarily be a distinction among them; for even according to you, spatial directions do not exist without a distinguishing adjunct (*upādhi*).

He says: "Even while accepting partlessness (*niraṃśatva*), we state that the division of the directions— arising from the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of the spatial points of atoms— is established as being like the division of the directions arising from the limiting conditions of the various types of world-regions."
Furthermore, how could the production of an effect be logical if [the cause] were partless,
since there would be no spatial location for them that exceeds their conjoined location?

Furthermore, let it be granted that [the atom] is partless; for what purpose has this been postulated? If it is for the sake of establishing its status as the ultimate cause, that very point is useless according to your own view. If it were partless, the production of an effect would not be possible, following the logic of a corpulent man’s sexual union. Why? Because, first of all, regarding the effect which is a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), two...

When two atoms become conjoined among composite things, there can be no spatial region belonging to them that is greater than the region of their conjunction—just as with water and salt of equal measure. If such a [distinct] own-region did exist, it would follow that the atom has parts; this is established even without explicitly stating it. If the atom were not to have parts, [the formation of] a dyad from two atoms would be impossible.

The sages raise this doubt: "There is no distinction whatsoever between the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and its cause or effect; since earth and the other elements possess form (*mūrtitva*), their characteristic is material form, whereas the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), being of a different nature from that, cannot be the cause, because [the gross elements] conform to them; therefore, the atom (*aṇu*) alone [is the cause]."
But surely, the subtle elements (tanmātras) are indeed formless; how then can they be the cause of that which possesses form?
Therefore, earth and the other gross elements must have a formal cause that corresponds to their own nature.
In the phrase "it causes [them] to be inferred," those atoms which are the causes are corporeal;
this is clear. The Lord says: Therefore, that effect which possesses form is non-existent [in itself], such as a jar, a cloth, or the like.
And these, by virtue of possessing form, are established on the side of being effects.
If these [atoms] were formless (*amūrta*), this dispute would be made regarding names alone.

As it has been said: "Because that which is formed (*mūrta*) must have a cause corresponding to its own nature, the atom is formed. That is incorrect, because there is no such stability; for the implication is: "Whatever is possessed of form is an effect," and yet these atoms [are claimed to be eternal].

[The author] distinguishes: Since the state of being an effect is thus established, if each respective cause is likewise analyzed in that same manner, an infinite regress (anavasthiti) is proven. To avoid this fault, if atoms (paramāṇavaḥ) are held to be corporeal (mūrta), then there is merely a dispute over names—between you and others they are called "atoms" (paramāṇu), while for us they are called "subtle elements" (tanmātra). Thus, the dispute is rendered trivial.

[It] may be so. [Objection: But surely even those [subtle elements], while being formless in relation to the gross elements, are indeed possessed of form in relation to primordial matter (prakṛti) and the rest. [Reply: True. For this very reason, the status of being the ultimate cause is not attributed to them. If so, where [is it attributed]? To this he says:
Māyā, however, is supreme, formless, eternal, and the cause of the non-eternal;
it is rich in the divisions of the one and the many, having the nature of an entity, and is of the essence of inauspiciousness.

This Māyā, rich in manifold divisions and inlaid with the power for immeasurable effects, has been thoroughly examined within its own domain. Furthermore, by the force of the observation of pervasion— that "Māyā is material because it is the material cause, like a thread"— the sages raise this doubt:
But how can that [space], being formless, be the cause of something with form?
For it is observed that only that which possesses form is the cause of what possesses form.
This is clear. [As for] God: that is not so, because the causality of atoms has been demonstrated; in that position, by whom can the fact that atoms possess parts be prevented?

That is not so; that is incorrect. Let it be granted that corporeality (*mūrtatva*) has been adduced as an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭa*); we do not deny it. However, in your position—that of those who hold atoms to be corporeal—by whom among you is the causality of parts demonstrated? For [corporeality] is pervaded by being a material cause (*upādānatva*).

"Atoms have parts because they are material causes (*upādāna*), like a thread"—this argument seeks to refute the established partlessness (*niravayavatva*) of atoms. [Objection: Even though they are material causes, since atoms are intended to be the ultimate cause (*paramakāraṇa*), they certainly do not possess parts. [Response: If that is so, then because they are intended to be the ultimate cause...

"Indeed, even for illusion (*māyā*) there is no corporeality; thus the resolution is indeed equal. [Objection: In that case, would it not follow that two ultimate causes are established? [Reply: That is incorrect, because we do not observe a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between being an effect and being incorporeal, whereas we do observe a pervasion with respect to corporeality. From corporeality...

Because atoms do not persist due to their impermanence, their status as the ultimate cause is unestablished. Now, [the opponent might argue]: "Being composed of parts (*sabhāgatva*) is pervaded by being an effect (*kāryatva*); therefore, it is incorrect to say that they are formless (*amūrta*). To this he says: (p.
734) "If being composed of parts is not the cause [of being an effect], then being possessed of form (*mūrtatva*) is likewise accepted [as not being the cause]."
If it is argued that the state of being a constituent part (bhāgavatva) of objects is pervaded by the nature of being an effect;

And since corporeality (*mūrtatva*) is likewise pervasively distributed, there is no excess [of the reason] in either case.
