In atoms, which we do not accept [as having parts], it is precisely the state of having parts (*sabhāgatva*) that is the probans for establishing their being effects; if corporeality were not the probans, then the state of having parts would likewise be accepted [as the probans]. Or rather, [it is the state of having parts] in the production of an effect...

If it is argued that "having parts" (*sabhāgatva*) is accepted by you as being without a cause and without a reason (*ahetu-akāraṇa*), then we may likewise assert that "corporeality" (*mūrtatva*) is also accepted by us as being without a cause; such is the logical connection (*vānvaya*). It should not be said that there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) for the establishment of the effect-status of either one of these two; this is clearly stated in the passage beginning with "having parts," etc. Or else, [the meaning is] "having parts."
One might say that the [single] cause does not exist in atoms; to this he replies: (p.
738) "The partlessness of an atom is not found, for it is not corporeal.
Thus, atoms of such a kind are not accepted in the world by those who know reality."

The meaning is that those who know reality have stated that corporeality is pervaded by having parts. Since this is clearly evident in objects other than [consciousness] through their movement and so forth, and since it resides in atoms, the reason characterized by multiplicity—and the reason characterized by having parts—would establish impermanence, which is invariably concomitant with being an effect, provided consciousness exists. Thus he says:
Furthermore, one might argue that these [atoms] possess multiplicity and homogeneity;
however, whatever entity is manifold and insentient is a non-entity, like a jar or similar objects.

In the first half [of the verse], however, the word "impermanent" (*anityam*) must be supplied. The meaning is that the nature of existence and non-existence—whether it be a real entity (*vastu*) or a non-entity (*avastu*)—is impermanence; the literal meaning of the other words is easy to understand. [Objection: But then there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to universals (*jāti*).
[Reply: That is incorrect. For us, a universal is similarity (*sādṛśya*); it is not something distinct from the individual (*vyakti*). Therefore... (p. 739) its [meaning].

Because the position that universals arise simultaneously with individuals is included within the [critique of the] "womb" (pakṣakukṣi), he concludes by distinguishing cause and effect through the description of the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*):
"Therefore, that which is formless and unitary is the cause of the manifold."
That which is impermanent, dependent, composed of parts, manifold, and an effect is so asserted.
Therefore, it is stated in the Śiva-darśana that [the opposite] is the cause;
hence, the causality of atoms is not considered logical by means of reasoning.

Therefore, that which is eternal, formless, pervasive, and one is accepted as the supreme cause of the many; whereas that which is non-eternal, dependent, material, composed of parts, and manifold is accepted as the effect of the one. This is stated in the Śivadarśana. Thus, it is said that the cause is the opposite—that is, distinct in character—from the effect.

"Causality" (*hetutva*) means being the supreme cause (*paramakāraṇatva*). The passage beginning with "from that" (*tataḥ*) and so forth is clear. Now, [it may be argued]: "An immaterial thing does not move because it is inactive, like the self (*ātman*). How can an immaterial, non-moving cause produce an effect? True; it is not by itself, but rather because the cause consists in the withdrawal of the causal capacity (*kārya-śakti*), [and thus] the causal capacity...

It is resolved that [the subtle elements] move by way of their individual manifestations. He states that from the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), beginning with the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) and so forth in sequence, the gross elements (*mahābhūta*) arise, headed by space:
"The great elements are born in sequence from the five subtle elements."
Space, wind, fire, water, and earth—by these names.
This is easy. Therein, the examination of space (*ākāśa*) along with its characteristics is undertaken:
"O bulls among sages, let that which serves as the cause for the activities of men—such as going and coming—to occur, be accepted as space."

O bulls among sages, that space in which there occurs for humans activity such as coming and going— and by the word "etcetera," [activity] such as contraction and expansion— is characterized by being a cause. That which serves as the cause provides room for another in its own location, just like the self (*ātman*) and other [entities].

That which is formless is precisely what should be accepted as space (*ākāśa*). He establishes this by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "If that [space] called 'vacant room' did not exist, where could living beings move about?
For when no other substance such as earth is perceived, there can be no coming and going for sentient beings."
Therefore, space must be accepted as the cause of room;

for just as there can be no movement within the earth without the support provided by the earth itself, so too, external movement to and fro would not be possible without the common space belonging to the outside world— this is the meaning.

This is an illustration; that subtle hand is unique, whereas that which resides in the gross body—the space within all the channels—is both common and unique, as it provides room for the vital breaths and so forth. The other [the gross] is easily understood.

Now, one might object: "Since this provision of space exists equally for the self (*ātman*) and other things as well, how can space be established as distinct by means of its specific purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*)? Anticipating this doubt, he establishes it through that specific purposeful activity: "Furthermore, sounds such as 'intense' and so forth depend upon a substratum (*guṇin*), because they are qualities (*guṇatva*)."
And it has been stated that space possesses qualities, yet it is beyond the senses of human beings.
The qualities such as intensity (*tīvra*) and so forth are the defining characteristics of an echo; by the inclusion of "and so forth," dullness (*manda*) and other qualities are meant.
Just as the word "pot" and the like have earth and other elements as their basis, the echo has space as its basis for the purpose of producing sound.
Otherwise, through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is established that space—and nothing else—is the cause.

Since [the existence of] the self and so forth is established through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for other causal functions, such as their being apprehenders of themselves or others, how could one not incur the fault of postulating numerous entities?
The meaning of the term is clear. [This refers to that which is] beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
Unable to accept the statement that [space] is to be inferred as the substratum of sound, the followers of Jaimini challenge it from their own standpoint:
"But surely space is perceptible, because we observe the upward flight [of birds] within it."
If it were not perceived by the eye, then the flight of birds in the sky would not be seen.

Is it not the case that, because of the perception of conjunction when a bird flying from a distant location in space away from a tree or similar object is seen to be in conjunction [with another point], and because the perception of conjunction presupposes the perception of its two relata, the perception [of the bird] is nothing other than the perception of the nature of space?
"Space" (*ākāśa*). The passage beginning with "not" (*na*) and so forth is clear. As Maṇḍana said:
"How could it be understood that the falling of milk is restricted to another location, if its arrival at the location of space were excluded by the ox? Thus [he says].
Īśvara: If that is so, then space would be material due to its connection with qualities such as touch;
by such qualities, earth would excel in its possession of attributes.
When the nature of one thing is determined through the effect of another,
their conjunction is indeed perceived upon contact with light.

If it were thus— that is, if, through the conjunction with the effect of one thing (in the form of contact), there were a determination of the essential nature of another thing characterized as an effect, and if, upon the discernment of properties such as perceptibility, one were to impute the quality of touch belonging to earth and so forth— which is non-existent therein— to space on account of its connection with the quality of touch; [then this would be a fallacy].

For one who asserts that "space is corporeal, like earth and so forth," the earth shines forth as space by virtue of their common properties (*dharmya*). If it is argued that [the example] is stated because [space] is other than space through its effect, then whose effect is this? It is the conjunction of the bird with light; for the entire world is pervaded by light when there is conjunction with the bird.

The conjunction of these two is seen; it is directly perceived. Now, one might ask: "How can there be a perceptual cognition in the world that 'the sky is blue,' given that such [a cognition] is unreal? To this he says:
"The notion that 'the sky is blue' is false, because it is based on factors such as distance."
Space is a mere collection of atoms because of its extreme distance, just like [the other] subtle elements.

The cognition that "the sky is blue" arises because the light of the eye has been dispersed due to causes such as distance; it takes on the form of a blue appearance through the superimposition of the nature of space upon the darkness perceived by the eye. Thus, for a wise person, that [cognition] has a false and contrary object. The reason for its being beyond the senses is as follows:
He applies [the following]: "The void," and so forth. "Void" (*vyoma*) means space (*ākāśa*), which is without sense organs (*anakṣa*), that is, beyond the reach of the senses.

Because it is most distant, it attains subtlety due to its remoteness, just like the collection of subtle elements (*tanmātra*). If this is so, let there be no [need for] the conjunction of birds; let space itself be the non-substantial (*avastu*) element, with the intention that the element of space exists as such.
The sages, through the perspective of the Jainas and others, further object: "No entity called 'space' exists, because there is no such thing as empty space;
and that which is called space is merely the absence of earth and other material things."

Thus others have said; let a solution be provided for this: that entity called "space" (vyoman), designated as "ether" (ākāśa), which has been posited, does not exist as a distinct nature. Why? Because it is nothing other than space (avakāśa); since we maintain that space itself is ether.
Now, if there is no absence [of space], what indeed exists from which that space arises?

Since space is of the very nature of the absence of earth and so forth, it follows clearly that space is nothing but the absence of corporeal substances. As for God (Īśvara), He who is called the "ether" (vyoman) is not in any way an absence, but rather space itself.
With the intention that the meaning of the term *padārtha* consists in being established (*klipti*), maintained (*dhṛti*), and an agent of action (*kṛtimat*), he reveals the explanation of its sense:
"Non-existence possesses the properties of existence, and likewise existence resides within non-existence;
for if non-existence did not possess those properties, the absence of a jar would belong to a cloth."

Non-existence (*abhāva*) is the state of non-being (*nāstitā*). An existent property (*bhāvadharma*) is a property belonging to its own respective counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), which is defined as a category of entity (*padārtha*). Likewise, existence (*bhāva*) is also the state of being (*astitā*). If that [non-existence] does not belong to that [existent], meaning if it is not a property of the entity characterized as its own counter-correlate, then [the following applies]: the non-existence of a jar [cannot belong] to a cloth that is possessed of existence.
If it were so, there would be no confusion [of categories] and no loss [of logical consistency]. Having restated the opponent's intention, he refutes it:
"If this non-existence were a property (dharma) of the object, then like a rabbit's horn, it would never be perceived";
but this objection is not valid.

(p. 748) [Objection: "If this non-existence (*abhāva*) is a property (*dharma*) of the entity according to your view, then because it is non-existent at all times throughout the three periods, like the horn of a hare, the entity possessing it would not be perceived; indeed, it could never be an object of perception. This is the challenge you have raised here. [Response: Why is there no refutation of this? For what reason is the rule not clear?
To this he replies, "It is not so":
"For that non-existence is indeed non-apprehension, and it is dependent upon an effect;
being the effect of its cause, it exists through the predominance of tamas."

Non-existence (*abhāva*) is not, as some claim, a mere absence like a rabbit’s horn in our perception, which would imply the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the thing and thus entail the aforementioned fault. Rather, this non-existence is indeed non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), just as in the expression "ghee is longevity. By the term "non-apprehension of that," it refers to the cessation of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) which is the cause of that [thing], characterized by the non-occurrence of its own effects once they have ceased.

The characteristics of an object consist in its power (*śakti*), its form (*ākṛti*), and its state (*sthiti*), or else they consist in its state as something remote from the nature of an individual (*vyakti*). Furthermore, stability (*sthirībhūti*) is mentioned; this is the non-perception of others, which is the absence of cognition (*jñānābhāva*), and since that is a property of cognition, it is certainly not said to be the absence of an entity distinct from cognition.

If it is asked what non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is, and one replies "it is non-apprehension," there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, that [non-apprehension] consists of power (*śakti*), action (*kṛti*), and persistence (*sthiti*), characterized by prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), and is dependent upon the effect.

When the effect—consisting of power, action, and persistence—is present, its cause is the collection of causal factors whose nature is the power of the effect, due to the predominance of the *tamas* quality.
Due to a preponderance of connection with the quality of *tamas*, she exists as the established form of the power of action (*kārya-śakti*), which is the effect; she abides as the state of being.
As it is said in the *Mataṅga*:
"Sattva is slightly unfolded, while the activity of rajas is well-known."
"Since the occurrence of *tamas* is withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), therefore [withdrawal] does not exist apart from it.
Here too, it is stated that "cessation is *tamas*... He states the final conclusion:
(p. 750) "Non-existence is the state of power (*śakti-avasthā*); existence is persistence in the form of an effect."
Neither existence nor non-existence is accepted by you as coexisting in a single entity.

Therefore, for this reason, the state of power (*śaktyavasthā*) of an entity that possesses the form of its manifested effect is the persistence of the form of power (*śaktyākṛtisthiti*), characterized by the non-manifestation of the form of the effect due to its being obscured by power. Consequently, non-existence (*abhāva*) is said to be existence (*bhāva*) insofar as it persists as the essence of that power, rather than as the essence of the manifestation of the effect.

The existence and non-existence of entities—that is, of things—cannot both be accepted in one and the same place, nor anywhere else, nor even in the thing itself at the same time. To address the question, "Let that be so; what follows for the present case? he says:
"Even the absence of a material object, because it is an absence, is established only within material objects."
Therefore, how could this absence of it not be space here?
Whatever property belongs to something, its existence is necessarily connected to that substratum;
moreover, this [property of] space is seen to be pervasive everywhere.

It has been established that an entity characterized by prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is a property (*dharma*) of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); for a property does not pervade without transcending its substratum (*dharmin*). You have stated that "space is the absence of corporeal substances," yet [if space were merely the absence of corporeality], it would not exist as something pervasive by transcending corporeal things; therefore, space is not the mere absence of corporeality.
This is the meaning. The meaning of the words is clear. Even so, he says that no formal definition (nirukti) is provided for it there: "Let this ether be defined as the absence of material form;
yet it cannot be the antecedent negation (prāgabhāva), because it exists even after the arising of entities."
Where could there be the persistence of an entity through the destruction of that space [in which it resides]?
For the persistence of entities is never observed anywhere without space.
Let this space be defined according to the position that it is the absence of corporeal matter; let its etymological derivation be established.

There are four kinds of non-existence (*abhāva*); among these, since the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of corporeal substance is not applicable here, this space cannot, in sequence, be the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the corporeal, because... [of that].

Space, which consists of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), would not exist immediately after the arising of an entity, because material objects arise without delay. Since there is no space due to destruction, the persistence of an entity is the persistence of a material object. For where and how could there be destruction? Thus, it is clear that there is no other absence (*itarābhāva*).
He says that both [cases] are not so:
"Nor is it mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), because that would entail [the non-existence] of even that which has form;
nor is this [non-existence] called 'destruction' (*pradhvaṃsa*), because it is incompatible with prior existence."

The destruction of entities existing somewhere is also logically possible. This [space] is not mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), because its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are both corporeal and incorporeal.

Furthermore, even for that which is incorporeal, there is mutual non-existence, as in the case of "this is space" and "that again is space"—this is because it would contradict our established tenet (*siddhānta*).
By way of a consequence: this is the opportunity [for the objection]. Nor is destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) a non-entity (*abhāva*), because it has arisen;

prior to its arising, there was no room [for it]. Since it is impossible for corporeal things to remain anywhere, the destruction of entities that are corporeal things while they persist is indeed possible. For it is not the case that...

It must be stated that prior to the existence [of the world], there was the destruction of some things therein, while others existed within that very self which is designated as "space" because it provides room; for such is seen to be the case before its existence. Having thus refuted the opponent's view, he concludes:
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, space (ākāśa) is indeed established even prior [to the other elements];
it should be known as having sound as its quality, due to the inherence of qualities in its own effects.

Having supplied the words "not so" (*na*) in the sense of "because it is the cause of space," one should connect the word "previously" (*prāk*). This is because its own effect, space, possesses qualities (*guṇa*). Since sound conforms to the qualities of space, the meaning of the other syllables is easily understood.
The sages suspect that sound is not a quality because of the perception of contradictory characteristics (*viruddha-lakṣaṇa-upalambha*).
Because it is endowed with qualities such as intensity (*tīvra*), why should sound not be a substance?
For it does not persist as long as the substance lasts, and its manifestation occurs elsewhere than in its [material] substratum.
Among these three reasons, the intention [of the opponent] is that in the first case, a quality is not perceived because of another quality.

In the second case, when a drum or similar object is treated with water or fire, even though that [object] remains present, there do not subsequently arise sounds that are progressively more intense or more intense still, nor sounds that are progressively weaker or weaker still; furthermore, when it is excessively treated with water, even the two [types of sound] do not exist.

The intention is that, like the heat and other qualities of fire, there is no destruction of the substratum prior [to the destruction of the quality]. Regarding the third [reason], "from the substratum": the point is that since sound is manifested and perceived by a listener in a location other than the drum or its source, if it were a quality, it could not move away from its substratum.
By these arguments, would sound not be a substance? The meaning is: it certainly would be.
The Lord refutes this: "That reason is not inconclusive, because of the same nature of odor and so forth;
for even though odor and the like are observed to be intense and so on, they are nevertheless recorded as qualities."

As for what was stated—that it is a substance (*dravya*) because of the threefold reasoning—that is incorrect. For even odor (*gandha*) and so forth, which are of the nature of qualities (*guṇa*), are likewise [perceived] through the correspondence [of the senses]. Because the threefold reasoning lacks pervasion (*vyāpti*), the threefold logical reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Since this is so, he demonstrates the inconclusiveness of the first reason with the words beginning "odor," etc.; for even odor and the rest...

"Seen as intense, etc. means it is so called because it is seen together with qualities such as intensity. Furthermore, even if it is not a substance but is recorded as a quality—if [you argue that] intensity and so forth exist apart from the possessor of the quality (guṇin) in the case of odor and the like, then that is the same in both cases. He demonstrates this for the second [case]:
Even in the case of other qualities, there would be equality [with the substance], because they do not persist as long as the substance exists;
for instance, no color whatsoever is perceived in water or fire.
The rebuttal—that it is clear because it exists there in an unmanifest state—is equally applicable in that case as well.

As for the third [reason], its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) due to the manifestation of odor from a location other than the house is already well-established and has been shown; therefore, it is disregarded here. Now, [one might object]: "But odor exists together with a subtle substance (*sūkṣmadravya*)."

It is postulated that [the sound] reaches the location of the nose. If this were so, one might ask why the same is not said of sound as well—that it exists in an unmanifest state—and thus its non-existence as long as the substance [lasts] would be impossible; to this he says: "Either through connection with a manifestor, or at some time..."
And the manifestation [of the sound] occurs elsewhere through the continuity of the sound that has already passed away.

Because the manifesting agents—the palate, the lips, and so forth—are intermittent, this [sound], though existent, is manifested intermittently due to its conjunction with those manifesting agents. Alternatively, the third [reason]—that of the *hotṛ* priest—is unestablished (*asiddha*) in this way: immediately after the manifestation of that which is already manifested...

Furthermore, regarding the past, unmanifest sound: its manifestation elsewhere than at the location of the ear and other sense organs is explained by means of manifesting factors such as air, through a continuous series, according to the principles of waves, ripples, and the opening of a cluster of buds. Having thus dispelled the objection that has arisen, [the author proceeds].
He further summarizes:
"Therefore, only a quality is accepted for that which is called the space of qualities;
the collection of qualities is substance, while their separation is designated as 'quality'."
The distinction of the directions does not arise from space (*avakāśa*), for it is likewise [established] through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).
[The author] recalls what was stated previously with the words "of the qualities" (*guṇānām*) and so forth. "Separation" (*viśleṣa*) means a specific location (*viśiṣṭaikadeśa*).
To the question, "How is it designated (*saṃjñita*) as such? he replies with the words "not" (*na*) and so forth. Just as space [is designated] by its capacity for accommodation (*avakāśa*).

Regarding the directions such as east and so forth, which are designated as "one part of the effect" (*kāryaikadiś*), there is a distinction based on conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) because they are presented as specific parts conditioned by the substratum of corporeal substance (*mūrtidravyopādhika*). However, in reality, no such distinction exists. Similarly, regarding the word "sound" (*śabda*), the sages—upon hearing this common expression—suspect a difference in meaning when they perceive a distinction in the referents.
Surely, O Lord, sound is said to be a quality of space; how then was it previously stated to be purely of the nature of *bindu*, through the distinctions of *vaiśvarya* and the rest?

Previously, in the *Bindupatala*, the meaning of the words was made clear. The Lord [Śiva], having accepted the non-difference between the signifier and the signified, employs the word "truth" (*satya*) and offers this rebuttal:
"It is true that there is a certain sound whose nature is resonance (*dhvani*), and it is considered to consist of phonemes (*varṇa*)."
Arising from space, this [sound] exists solely in the form of resonance.
But there is no grasping of phonemes (*varṇa*); rather, the bindu is the cause of the absence of phonemes.

Even in that case, it has been stated that "it is sound" (*śabda*). This is true. In that context as well as here, although the signifier (*vācaka*) is common [to all], there exists a certain resonance (*dhvani*) which is distinct from the signified (*vācya*), and this is what is meant by the word "sound" (*śabda*); it is essentially of the nature of resonance (*dhvanyātmaka*).

Although its nature is beyond syllables (*anakṣara-ātman*) and it bestows knowledge of the non-objective (*anartha-jñāna*), it nevertheless appears in a clear form through the medium of *dhvani* (resonance). Because it is extremely distinct, this first sound mentioned previously—which consists of phonemes (*varṇa-ātman*)—is produced from space (*ākāśa*) alone; such is the meaning of the word "sound" (*śabda*). It is solitary.
The meaning of the word is that there is no acquisition of phonemes (*varṇa*) in the form of sound (*dhvani*), but rather it is the "Bindu-sound" (*baindava-śabda*).
It is designated as *nāda*. Regarding the reason why the ethereal sound (*vyomadhvani*) is not the cause of the nine phonemes, he says:
"Because they transcend space, the phonemes do not arise from the ethereal sound."
Whatever is distinct from something else does not have that as its cause, just as [the example].
Therefore, by the aforementioned consequence, the elements such as earth and the sense organs [are transcended];
for those phonemes are beyond the ether (vyomātīta), established in the pure path (śuddhādhvan) and so forth.

The ether (*vyoma*) is the manifestor of that [sound], while the phonemes (*varṇa*) are the manifested; they are established as such by means of their own respective sounds. It should be understood that the phonemes—which are distinct from and transcend the [ether]—pervade the three paths of white, black, and grey. The sound of the ether does not [so pervade them], because it has a more restricted occurrence than that of earth.

Just as it is with the sense organs and so forth, there is no grasping (upādāna); rather, the clear meaning established is that sound (*dhvani*) manifests the phonemes (*varṇa*) without being their material cause.
As it has been said: "Sound, originating from space and air, emerging from the body, proceeds toward speech."

"When divided into other locations, it attains the state of phonemes (varṇa); that is sound. Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Bindupatala* that "the manifestor is not the manifested," and in the *Pramāṇapatala*, we shall explain as follows: "Space, however, is the cause of phonemes in their material aspect (*ādhibhautika*). This is relevant to the context.
In this context, he cites a verse containing its definition in order to elucidate the examination of *nāda* (the primordial sound):
"That which is the undivided state of the phonemes (*varṇa*) is *nāda*, the signifier of meaning;
however, the phonemes consist of exactly fifty, beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'."
By those very [phonemes], the sentence is inlaid and characterized as being in the form of words.

There is no division of phonemes; rather, it is a collection of powers consisting of non-manifestation that is the signifier (*vācaka*) of the signified meaning (*vācya*), producing cognition. Whether one follows the view of the Naiyāyikas and others, let there be phonemes, or let there be words and sentences.

[The opponent might argue: "Let them [the two conditions] exist. What is the point of this [definition], since it is already established? To refute that and for the sake of brevity, he stated the three characteristics beginning with "akāra" and ending with "lakṣitam. [The opponent asks: "Even so, what is the objection? To this he says:
"But the meaning of a sentence is not [conveyed] by the letters alone, nor even from that which is called a 'sentence' [as a single entity]."
Their existence is indeed successive, because the cognition of objects occurs successively.

However, the meaning of a sentence is not established by the phonemes themselves as they sequentially attain the status of words and sentences. Why is this so? To explain this point, the passage beginning with "krameṇa" and ending with "vedanāt" implies that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of each individual phoneme, existing in a sequential state, cognizing a single sequential meaning. And it is not the case that...

Since that which is non-existent apart from the phonemes (varṇa) cannot be designated by the name "sentence" or even the name "word," the intention [of the author] is this: the phonemes themselves—possessing sequential articulation and differentiated by the application of conventional designations—are what constitute words and sentences when they are uttered as such. He clarifies this very point by stating a subverting argument (*bādhakatarka*):
If there were hearing of words or sentences apart from the nine phonemes,
it would be perceived as something external to the letter *ka* and the rest.
In the phrase "What are you?", the word "here" (atra) is to be supplied; the meaning of the words is clear. He further reinforces this point:

"Dissolved immediately after being uttered, and existing according to the sequence of priority and posteriority, those phonemes, not being perceived even in relation to one another, do not express the meaning."
Since they are not distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), neither the word nor the sentence exists;
thus, being unperceived, they cannot be beneficial [to cognition], and the meaning of the other letters is easily established. This is the intended meaning:
in the word "gauh," the *visarjanīya* is perceived, whereas the letter *a* and the letter *au* are not perceived; therefore, as for these...

Because they do not exist simultaneously, the *visarjanīya* is not perceived as a single entity. If the manifestation of consciousness (*cidvyakti*) were to arise from the characteristics of the "hoof" (*khura*) and the "blanket" (*kambala*), then it would also occur in cases such as "horse" (*aśva*) and "man" (*puruṣa*). Consequently, the phonemes (*varṇa*) would not be the signifiers, because [the word] is not distinct from them; and thus, neither the word (*pada*) nor the sentence (*vākya*) would be intended as the signifier. This is the intention expressed in the *Bindupaṭala*.

It has been established that even the cognition and determination [of meaning] does not denote the object independently. Furthermore, he will establish in the "Chapter on Origination" (*Utpatti-paṭala*) of the Tantra that the *sphoṭa* also does not denote the object. By process of elimination, he states: "Therefore, the sound (*nāda*), manifested by the phonemes (*varṇa*), is the denoter of the object."
The sound that constitutes the word arises from the phonemes alone, because the word exists within them.

The sentence, which is of the nature of speech, arises from its constituent parts, the words. Consequently, through the principle of *anyathānupapatti* (presumption of the otherwise impossible), it is manifested by the phonemes (*varṇa*) uttered by the speaker—which are produced by the vocal resonance (*nāda*) residing in the speaker and perceived by the listener—as that resonance residing in the listener serves as the signifier of the meaning for the listener. Thus, the resonance belonging to the speaker is the expressive agent of the meaning.

In this way, through the striking together of the phonemes uttered by the speaker within the gateway of the sense of hearing, an internal resonance (*nāda*) blazes forth within the listener. Having become the nature of the *madhyamā* speech, which consists of phonemes that are not objects of the auditory faculty but are closely associated with the intellect, it arises as the nature of the word (*pada*), since the status of a word is established solely through phonemes.

But for the speaker, according to the principle to be explained, the *nāda* itself, becoming fully radiant, arises as *vaikharī*, consisting of words and sentences. The phrase "consisting of sentences," etc., is clear. Now, one might object: why should the cognition of the meaning not arise from the visarga alone in the word *gauḥ*, when it is accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the previously arisen *ga* and *au*?

[The opponent] might think: "Even though the phonemes perish in a moment, let there be the cognition of the meaning; for that [cognition] does not result from the destruction of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), since we observe recollection at a later time. Anticipating this intention of the followers of Gautama, [the author] refutes it: "But the final phoneme, refined by the impressions arising from the preceding phonemes..."
If it is argued that [the word] must be the denoter of objects, that is not tenable.
This is clear. To the question "Why does it not shine? he says:
"Just as the phonemes were previously known in their specific sequence, so too do the latent impressions (saṃskāras) bring them forth; thus they become the indicators of memory."

The meaning is that the phonemes, having been experienced in a certain way, produce mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) in the intellect accordingly; subsequently, those [phonemes] are remembered in that same way by means of those impressions, but not the object itself. As they say:

"Indeed, when the forms of objects have been clearly manifested as mental impressions, they become the causes of cognition regarding them; therefore, no cognition of an external object is postulated. Now, let it be granted that this is so.

The cognition of the meaning arises from the *visarjanīya* [the sound 'ḥ'] accompanied by its linguistic refinement (*saṃskāra*). However, that [cognition] must arise from the word consisting of the *visarjanīya* which is currently being experienced, as it is recollected through a memory produced by the cause of that refinement, and as it is preceded by the experience of the phonemes *ga* and *au*.
[This is like] the cognition of the meaning characterized by the dewlap and hump [of a cow]. That is incorrect, because [the word] is being recollected...
Because lamps and the like lack the capacity to illuminate objects, they merely remove their own obscurations and remain as they are.
Furthermore, because they lack the capacity to impart a specific quality and because experience [of such qualities] does not occur,
no cognition of an object arises from them, since simultaneous existence is impossible.

Then, through gross phonemes (*varṇa*), the manifest sound (*nāda*) becomes the signifier. This is because the phonemes possess the capacity to deposit a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) through the experience of them, owing to their connection with the capacity for imparting a specific quality. From the latent impression deposited by that [experience], the cognition of the phonemes does not arise otherwise; [they are perceived] simultaneously.

And because of the impossibility of [the sound] persisting, there would never be a cognition of the object from those phonemes; this is the remainder [of the argument]. The passage beginning with "therefore" (*tataḥ*) and so forth is clear. If it were thus that the cognizer’s internal apprehension of the object (*pratipattuḥ antar-artha-pratipatti*) occurred through the sound manifested by the phonemes uttered by the speaker, then how could the speaker have the internal apprehension of the object (*vaktur antar-artha-pratipatti*) without which that speaker [could not exist]?

Anticipating the objection that the inability to convey understanding does not apply with respect to the person who understands, [the author] states— revealing the variability of letters precisely by stating the refutation of that objection and indicating that they do not possess the capacity to denote meaning:
"Furthermore, letters are observed to convey meaning only in certain instances."
In some cases, the resonance vibrating within you is not always a means of awakening for you.

Sound (*nāda*) is not the denoter of meaning because it is not an object of the sense of hearing. Furthermore, we do not say that sound, even when manifested as phonemes (*varṇa*), is the denoter; rather, it is the phonemes, once uttered by the speaker, which, having come together, manifest within the listener—the respondent—without any intervening cause.
They are the indicators for the sake of that door [of speech]. In some cases, when there is a speaker or an instructor,

without the striking of the phonemes uttered from another mouth resonating within the throat, one’s own internal monologue— blazing in the form of *paśyantī*— having fashioned the internal signifier (*antarvācaka*) in the form of *madhyamā*, which is closely associated with the intellect (*buddhi*), [proceeds].
For the sake of the listener’s comprehension, it exists in the form of *vaikharī* consisting of phonemes for the purpose of its own articulation;
likewise, for one who merely desires to know its own meaning, it exists in the form of *madhyamā* as the indicator of its own meaning or the meaning [of the object].
This has been stated in the *Nādakārikās*: "That expressive power of speech (*vākśakti*), which is distinct for every individual, stands as the signifier. From that [arises]:

"Or rather, [the opponent argues] that because they are produced one by one without interval, [the letters cannot express meaning]. This refers to the case of a speaker, an instructor, or a person seeking only their own benefit;
for such a person, there is no dependence on hearing the phonemes uttered by another speaker for the sake of manifesting their own internal sound (*nāda*).

Thus, those phonemes are never expressive of meaning [in this context]. However, in the case of a listener or a recipient of instruction, it is for the sake of the comprehension of meaning... [that they are uttered].

Because they depend upon audition, the phonemes (*varṇa*) uttered by a speaker for the purpose of manifesting their own sounds are not expressive of meaning as sounds residing in the speaker, since they are not within the range of the hearer. Rather, having become phonemic in nature, they reach the external hearer and [become expressive] toward that hearer.

Having manifested the sound (*nāda*), it expresses the meaning through that medium; thus, even the sound heard by the listener, if it is not manifested independently of the phonemes (*varṇa*), does not express the meaning while shining forth by itself. Therefore, sound is never the direct expresser of meaning. Unable to tolerate this statement, the sages challenge it:
Is it not the case that the *nāda* (sound-monad) is manifested by the phonemes either successively or simultaneously?
If it is successive, let the object itself be [manifested] by the phonemes; what is the use of a postulated intermediate entity?

It has been stated that in some cases, because the *nāda* (the sound-manifestation) possesses manifestation through the successive striking (*saṃtāḍana*) of phonemes (*varṇa*), it is the expressive agent of meaning; for that purpose, is it then manifested by the phonemes in succession, or rather without succession? If it is manifested by them without succession, is it by many [phonemes] combined, or by one taken individually? In this regard, the first [alternative] is not tenable.

Since you yourself have stated that because phonemes perish in a single moment, their aggregation cannot constitute a word, even if that were the case, it would still denote a different object due to its sequential nature. Nor can the second [position] hold;
for in the case of the word "cow" (*go*), there would follow the absurd consequence of perceiving endless contradictory objects such as a cow, a buffalo, or the sky.

Even you, when refuting the Grammarian who asserts that the *sphoṭa*—manifested by the phonemes—is the signifier of meaning, have effectively performed a rejection while simultaneously offering an acceptance. Now, if it is argued that the meaning is understood through multiple phonemes in succession, why resort to an imagined intermediate entity? Let the meaning itself be directly presented to the intellect by the phonemes known as *nāda*. Īśvara: [Objection: ... [text fragment] ... [Response: No, because there is no difference in the cognition. Just as the cognition of a single letter-sound (*varṇa*) does not differ whether it is produced by one person or many, so too the cognition of a word-sound (*pada*) does not differ whether it is produced by one person or many. Furthermore, since the phonemes are perceived in a sequence, how could they produce a simultaneous cognition of the word? Therefore, the *sphoṭa* must be admitted. [Reply: This is not so; for we see that even without a *sphoṭa*, the cognition of the meaning arises from the phonemes themselves, provided they are grasped in their proper order and are free from defects such as being uttered too quickly or too slowly. Thus, the postulation of a *sphoṭa* is redundant. Moreover, if the *sphoṭa* were the signifier, it would be either eternal or non-eternal. If it were eternal, it would be perceived at all times, which is contrary to experience. If it were non-eternal, its production would require causes other than the phonemes, which is unproven. Therefore, the phonemes alone, manifested by the effort of articulation (*prayatna*), are the signifiers of meaning. As the saying goes: "The phonemes themselves, when manifested by the effort of articulation and perceived in their proper order, convey the meaning. Thus, the theory of the *sphoṭa* is rejected.
Therefore, the phonemes (varṇas) never express meaning directly, nor do they ever manifest [it];
rather, it is the sound (nāda) that is manifested by the phonemes—how then could there be an equal refutation?

Just as the manifestors, such as the phonemes *ka* and so forth, are not the performers of the fetching of water— since that fetching of water is the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) belonging to some [entity] manifested by them— so too, sound (*nāda*) is manifested sequentially by many phonemes; therefore, we have determined that its existence is fragmented even for you.
How could there be merely an equal refutation for us regarding some point of dispute?
As they say:
"Where the fault is equal for both sides, and the rebuttal is likewise equal..."
"One should not interrogate [the opponent] alone regarding such an investigation of meaning.
Having thus severed the bond of one's own conceptual constructions and having extracted equanimity, he brings it forth:
"The wheel and other factors operate in the production of a jar, and they do so sequentially."
Thus, the phonemes (varṇas), situated in their sequence, are considered to be the manifestors of the sound-principle (nāda).
And this objection applies equally to the individual pot (*ghaṭavyakti*), so it is not a refutation [of our position].

The wheels and other tools are active with respect to the individual pot; the dilemma as to whether they act successively or otherwise is easy to understand. The sages (*ṛṣis*), however, explain the analysis differently.
He establishes this: "Now, is this word a denoter of an object when it is known, or even when it is unknown?
If it were [denotative] while unknown, then every [word], being equally unknown, would be a denoter of every object."
If it were known by him, then because the relationship has not been grasped, it would be as before.

But surely, that which expresses an object is not known by all people who know the object; or rather, is it unknown? If it is unknown there, then even an object such as a sense organ is capable [of its function] by its very power, even while unknown.

Because it is a producer [of cognition]. For [the producer] performs its own causal function (*svārthakriyā*). The denoter (*vācaka*), however, does not perform its own causal function because it is a communicator (*jñāpaka*)—that is, it makes known [an object] to one who has already grasped its own power [of denotation]. Thus, unlike the sense organs and so forth, it is difficult to perceive; for since there is no fixed rule that "this is the denoter of this [object]," every word would be a denoter of everything.
If it is argued that there is no inconsistency because [the word] denotes all objects, [we reply:

since the relationship between the word and its object would not be grasped by that means, the capacity of the signified and the signifier—characterized by the relation of the known and the knower—is not apprehended through another's convention, because [such apprehension] does not arise without prior discrimination. This very [point is as follows]:
Regarding "the relationship," he will explain it in the *Tantra*’s Chapter on Origination:
"The object resides in the ground, while the word resides in the mouth; their inherence (*samavāya*) does not exist.
Rather, the relationship known as 'the cognizable' and 'the cognition' follows upon the former. It would be as before; indeed, even in its entirety.

Because [the sphoṭa] expresses all meanings without exception, the Lord (Īśvara) refutes that: "That is incorrect, because the phonemes possess the status of being causes through the intervention of the *nāda*;
rather, it is the *nāda* that is postulated as that by which the cognition of meaning arises in its proper sequence."

What has been stated by thus conceptualizing is incorrect. That sound (*nāda*) by which the cognition of the object arises is not said to be "directly heard, known, or grasped" as having a [perceived] relationship; rather, it is so called because of its causal status and its nature as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the phonemes (*varṇa*) that are directly heard and known, even though they are separated by those [phonemes].
Since it is established that [the word] is conceptualized—that is, inferred—by means of the door [of the phonemes], and because the signifier has been grasped, he says:
"But the apprehension of the relationship and so forth is established by the phonemes alone;
thus, even if unperceived, it may be the signifier, as it is logically justified by its being the cause thereof."

Because sound (*nāda*) is an object of perception arising directly from auditory hearing, there is no direct apprehension of it as being the [denoter] "nāda. However, the grasping of the relationship [between word and meaning], such as the connection [to the denoted object], occurs through the recollection of the convention established by the Lord within the city of the body regarding the denoted meaning. Furthermore, the determination of the expressive power (*vācaka-śakti*) belonging to that meaning, which coexists with the convention, is accomplished by the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves; for even when sound is heard, it is through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the preceding phonemes [that cognition arises].

The *nāda* (sound-manifestation), though arising from the ear and being directly within the range of auditory perception, is difficult to apprehend because its relationship [to the word] is established through the experience of the final phonemes produced by memory; yet, it is the cause of that [word],
for its relationship is one with that which is apprehended as the object of the cognition directly arising from hearing.

Because it has phonemes as its material cause, and because its relationship [with meaning] has been perceived, that which is radiant is rightly the signifier (*vācaka*). This is precisely because, in its aspect as *paśyantī*, it gives rise to non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Therein, there is no genus (*jāti*) as an opposing factor; for the power resides in the individual (*vyakti*). However, in the form of *madhyamā*, [it consists of] the dewlap, tail, and so forth, according to the Śaiva tradition.

Regarding the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), since the universal (*jāti*) is indeed nothing but similarity, and because it gives rise to determinate cognition (*savikalpajñāna*) that apprehends the universal as non-distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), the capacity (*śakti*) of that word resides in the individual as non-distinct from the universal. Thus, according to the views of the followers of Gautama and Jaimini, does the expressive power (*vācaka-śakti*) reside in the individual or in the universal?

Furthermore, since [the universal] is established as residing in the individual form (*ākṛti*), there is no room for doubt; yet, suspecting in his mind how this [universal] can be perceived while remaining therein, he says:
"And even in the case of effects, it is logical that causality belongs to the cause itself."
The causal capacity (*śakti*) is held to be the cause of all entities whatsoever.

Just as it is appropriate for a cause— whether it be a sequence of flames perishing moment by moment or a persisting fire— to possess a sequential cooking power grasped within effects that arise and perish moment by moment, so too is it appropriate for the causality of phonemes, which likewise arise and perish moment by moment, to possess a sequential [power] grasped within their effects.

The expressive power (*vācaka-śakti*) of a cause—which is stable and characterized by sound (*nāda*)—is logically consistent with its reaching the limit of the object of cognition; for how else could it be fully understood? Since the cause of all entities, that is, all effects, is certainly not distinct from them, yet power (*śakti*), which is synonymous with capacity (*sāmarthya*), is concomitant with the infinity of those effects.
[Sound] is held to be the cause. Now, if it is thus concluded that *nāda* is merely the power (*śakti*) of the phonemes (*varṇa*),

then— considering in one's mind how the power of speech can belong to this *nāda*, which is itself of the nature of power given that power lacks [independent] power— one offers the following rebuttal:
That which is the root cause, however, is crowded with a multitude of potencies;
from each individual potency within it, the fruit of many effects arises.
The statement "itself is not the supreme cause" means that the supreme cause, which consists of its own power and is characterized by power (*śakti*),
exists as Mahāmāyā— remaining unmanifest both as the essence of individual manifestation (*vyakti*) and as the essence of the power of phonemes (*varṇa-śakti*).
Thus, the *nāda* is not merely of the nature of power, but rather the primordial cause (*mūla-kāraṇa*) consisting of both the power and its individual manifestation.

That supreme cause, however, is called Mahāmāyā or simply Māyā; it is filled with a multitude of powers (*śakti*) whose authority for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is distinct for each respective object. Furthermore, those powers which are manifested through the cessation of that [causal process] are the unmanifested causal powers.

"Pervaded by a multitude" means, in effect, that [the cause] consists solely of unmanifest causal potencies (*kārya-śakti*). Thus, because the cause is crowded with a host of distinct causal potencies,

each individual effect possesses its own result through a specific potency— the manifestation of its own appropriate causal power— resulting in the performance of its respective appropriate purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*).
This must be accepted; for even by those such as the logicians who do not desire it, this indeed cannot be ignored. Thus he says:
"Otherwise, the *pārijāta* tree might arise from a nimba seed."
And that [cognition] is indeed distinct for each object; yet no difference in its effects is perceived.

Otherwise, if the cause were not crowded with a multitude of causal powers (*śakti*) [capable of producing] the effect, but rather distinct from it, then—because of its prior non-existence—it would follow that the effect arises as something non-existent. Having supplied the word "then" (*tadā*) and connected it with the word "nimba," the meaning of the verse can be easily established. Now, however:

The prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of an effect is of a positive nature (*sadrūpa*), because it is impossible for that which is non-existent to function as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). Rather, it is a certain specific aspect of the cause itself, characterized by its being the delimiting factor for each respective effect among those various effects.
If this is so, then the prior non-existence of the effects in the cause is their persistence in the form of potentiality (*śakti*).

Since it has been concluded that "the concealment of the specific characteristics" (lakṣaṇatirobhūti) is the final point, even the statement that "there is a distinction in our own system for the sake of avoiding the destruction of the necessity of effects" ultimately results in [admitting] power; therefore, the sages, being of the Nyāya school and finding this unacceptable, raise an objection:

But surely, power (śakti) is not perceived apart from the object (artha). Indeed, it has been stated that the effect is the category of the thing (padārtha), and that the essence of the cause consists in its own power, which is of the nature of manifestation. Even when manifested, power is not perceived as distinct from the possessor of power (śaktimat). [This applies to] the Lord (īśvara).

Employing the word "truth" (*satya*), he refutes [the objection] by accepting the following meaning: the power residing in the final and initial objects—such as burning, illumination, and so forth—is established as a separate causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in the form of a universal; thus, it is not perceived through a distinct [individual] perception. He resolves this as follows:
The capacity to grasp the truth is indeed postulated as being effective;
for instance, the fire that produces a flash of light appears suddenly when the fingers are first joined together.
Thus, since he does not accept the production of a *sphoṭa* through the power of mantras,
this *sphoṭa*, when refuted, leads one to postulate another cause.
As for the reason why power (*śakti*) is perceived there even in the absence of fire:
it is true that you have stated that power is not perceived as distinct from the possessor of power;
however, [power] is perceived through its own causal activity (*arthakriyā*), which is characterized by a relationship with its own object that is non-separately established (*apṛthaksiddha*).

In the *Paśuparīkṣā*, because [the power] is not established as separate from its fresh form (*pratyagrūpa*), an investigation of categories (*padārtha*) by way of parts is not appropriate; for it has been stated that nowhere does the thought "what would it be like without the power of fire? ever arise. Furthermore, because of non-duality (*advaitatva*), in reality, there is no possessor of power (*śaktimat*) apart from the prior apprehension of the power itself.
Even apprehension is impossible; for power— whether being directly perceived through its own distinct causal efficiency,
or being perceived in some way as not distinct [from the possessor of power] because it is not separately established from it,
or because the causal efficiency of the power is not separately established from the possessor of power— is [in all cases] impossible.

Let it be accepted through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), [it is known] through inference characterized by the presumption that some purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) would otherwise be inexplicable.
Although, in reality, this power (*śakti*) is inseparable from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) and thus possesses no distinction.
[The power] is that which is inseparably established from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*). It is "conceived" or "understood" as being separately established.
He reveals that very *arthāpatti* (presumption) by means of the passage beginning with "first," and so forth. "First" means prior to the employment of the mantra;
immediately after the sudden contact of the fingers, [the effect] consisting of a blister (*sphoṭa*) is produced.
Fire is observed to be a burner; yet that very same fire, even while blazing, [does not burn] when a mantra is applied.
This occurs through the efficacy of the mantra, caused by the power of the mantra. Consequently, the production of a *sphoṭa*... as it has been said:
"By whomsoever this *sphoṭa* is intended to be warded off, this mantra previously directly perceived [the obstacle] and rendered it ineffective."

The definition of burning (*dāha*)—as the causal factor for its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*)—is that which leads one to imagine another cause; namely, the non-manifestation of itself due to the delay of some cause other than fire. Thus, it is clear that [the inference] "that which is there" and so forth leads to the understanding of a cause other than fire. Anticipating and refuting the objection that this might be established otherwise, he says:
If fire qualified by the absence of mantras were the cause for the act of bursting,
then even the application of a mantra for every individual finger would never occur according to Aṅguli.
If the effect of the *sphoṭa* arises even when the first mantra is present,
then let the existence of the second mantra also be a cause.

In the act of bursting, that is, the process of burning, if fire— characterized by the absence of mantra— is the cause [of the effect] either prior to the application of the mantra for the sake of suppressing the bursting, or subsequently upon the withdrawal of that [mantra],
then even when a counter-mantra is employed to suppress the action of the mantra that suppressed the manifestation characterized as bursting, the deity [remains the same].

Regarding the characteristic [of the sphoṭa], it is not the case that it perishes immediately upon being uttered; for if there were non-existence at the first mantra, the sphoṭa would certainly not arise from the finger-snap. On the contrary, even when the first mantra exists, the effect of the sphoṭa arises repeatedly, overcoming and displacing any deviation or obstruction. Even if fire is indeed deviant...

Just as the postulation of causes such as grass and the like occurs in the case of a specific effect characterized by a particular mark (*lakṣaṇa*), so too, when a pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established in some instance, that postulation is valid. However, since a pervasion is observed in some instances even for fire qualified by a second mantra, what would specifically be the restrictive factor for grasping one or the other? Thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of universal application (*ananugama*).

Even if it is stated that "the cause is the absence of the first mantra, which is qualified by the presence of both the fear that has arisen and the stimulator," there remains the insistence on the question, "What is the absence of the absence of the stimulator as a qualifier?
Consequently, it is ultimately established that the second mantra is the definition of the stimulator. Thus, regarding the second mantra:
Let the existence [of the second mantra] be the cause. But surely, there is no deficiency for us in postulating that the existence of the second mantra is its causality. To this it is replied:
"But when the first mantra exists, the second does not exist even in the slightest degree now."
How is the binding of the first mantra performed?
Whether it be the destruction of that effect, or the establishment of its prior non-existence,
or the assistance rendered by its own power— it is thus conceived and deliberated upon.

How can the obstruction now be effected by a second subtle mantra (*aṇu-mantra*) employed for the sake of producing a *sphoṭa*, against that first mantra which was intended to suppress the *sphoṭa*? For that effect—
the suppression of the *sphoṭa* which was to be produced by that first mantra— would either be destroyed or rendered invisible.
Alternatively, there may be a positive prescription of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), or a state of existence consisting of a power characterized by the exclusion of that causal efficiency,

or the concealment of its own nature; in other words, with respect to fire, some kind of assistance is rendered through its own power by the counter-agent to the counter-obstructer of fire, either as a cooperative factor (*sahakāra*) or otherwise.

Having reflected thus, it is immediately examined. To the question "How so?", he says: First of all, even the restriction [of the mantra] is not established as a positive entity prior to its non-existence, because the mantra remains established in its own essential nature.
The connection... the prescription of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is established. Why? Because the object is thus [established];

for the deity is not merely the word, since the nature of the object of the first mantra—which is characterized by its denotation—is fixed in its own form. He says that even the final position (*pakṣa*) is not so:
Nor can it be said that [the cause] assists by means of its own existence, because no such assistance is demonstrated;
rather, whatever is included within the causal complex (sāmagrī) assists by performing some specific action.
Therefore, causality is observed; however, that which performs no action has no such status.
The various causal factors of the assemblage (*sāmagrī*), such as the potter’s wheel and so forth, are included therein;
they are "cooperators" (*sahakāraka*) because they provide assistance by performing a function. The meaning is clear: it refers to that which does not perform even the slightest action.
Furthermore, he says "in some way or other":
"However, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, there must always be a state of abiding;
how could there be a second [state] prior to that? The mantra itself is thus intended."
Or from where is it accepted that the subsequent [mantra] exists when the preceding mantra is absent?

Furthermore, even if the second mantra were to assist sentient beings, it would not remain as something that assists them at all times; for it is not observed to be so. If indeed it were so, from where would that subsequent second mantra [arise] from the preceding mantras?

If assistance is indeed admitted [to exist], why is it not accepted? Or rather, since there is no prior mantra, one must accept that the efficacy of the second mantra—which is dependent on that [first]—is established through destruction;
thus he says, "it is as stated in the first position."
Therefore, the effect of the first [cause] must be contradictory by virtue of its pervasion; and this contradictoriness of the effect consists in its being an obstruction, and nothing else.

Therefore, since the second and third positions are untenable, the second mantra (*p. 788*)... being manifested, because of the absence of pervasion in the first mantra, it is the adversary of the effect; it is to be understood as the agent that effects the concealment of the effect, characterized by the suppression of the effect of the *sphoṭa*. It demonstrates the absence of pervasion regarding the effect. Of the effect...
Opposition and the concealment of the effect constitute the obstruction of the instrument; the concealment of the cause [is likewise].
Nothing else—that is, nothing other than this—is [the obstruction]. Why? To this he says:
"But the effect is not produced without the deficiency of the cause."
For there is no deficiency in the other finger; rather, that [finger] alone possesses the deficient power.
The existence of that which lacks a subverting mantra is never subject to sublation;
for if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of its being capable of sublation even at a later time.

Without a deficiency or an obstruction of the cause, the final effect does not arise, nor does it disappear from the first mantra during the process of the *sphoṭa* (manifestation). This is because, in the case of the two causes [the fingers], there is neither deficiency nor disappearance, as they are perceived; this is due to the second mantra. Furthermore, for the purpose of stimulating the *sphoṭa*:
The sublation or negation of the existence and manifest presence of one mantra is not logical; why?

Because even at another time, or even at the moment immediately following the withdrawal of a second mantra, that which is seen as residing in manifestation would entail the consequence of being a sublater [of the first]. However, that which is the effect of the *sphoṭa* beyond its disappearance—

*Tirobhūtiḥ* (concealment) is that which has become the cause; even though it is incomplete (*vikalā*), it has reached a state of being hidden (*tirohitā*). That whose nature is oriented toward the effects such as burning in the case of fire, a finger, and so forth, is thus called *śakti* (power) itself. Now, this [power], whose nature is oriented toward the object, is not distinct from its own self—the fire—whose nature is a face well-situated within itself.

[The Lord is] the essential nature [of Śakti]. True. That very [nature] is His power; thus everything is consistent. ... Furthermore, regarding concealment (*tirodhāna*) and [emergence] through power (p.

790): is it non-existence (*aprati*) or non-manifestation (*aprakāśa*)? If the first [option] is accepted, then because it is non-different from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), it follows that [concealment] would be the very essence of that [possessor]. If the second [option] is accepted, then according to the view that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*)...

"Even though it is eternally luminous, it does not differ from that which is subject to destruction; thus, its perishability is established"—let such false conceptualizations be made. For this has already been refuted in the *Cicchaktiparīkṣā*, where it was stated that for a power (*śakti*), non-activity—characterized by mastery over its own effect without any alteration of its own nature—is what constitutes concealment (*tirodhāna*). [The author] concludes the result... [Note: The text appears to be a commentary on a philosophical argument concerning the nature of consciousness (*cicchakti*) and its apparent concealment or transformation. The ellipsis at the end suggests the conclusion of a section.]
"Therefore, let the potency (śakti) that resides in all objects be understood.
In this context of the sphoṭa of words, the sphoṭa of meanings has also been described.
It bursts forth, makes known, and causes the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the effect (*kārya*) to arise;

thus, *sphoṭa* is power (*śakti*), sound (*śabda*), *sphoṭa*, the power of speech (*vākśakti*), and the *bhāvasphoṭa*. The remainder—the power of all other categories of meaning—is easy to understand. In this way, [it pervades] space (*ākāśa*) and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
Having promised to examine the four elements beginning with earth— which were reached through the sequence of investigation—
he sets forth [the topic]:
"The origination of air and the others is described precisely in their proper order."
Wind, fire, water, and earth—these constitute the fourfold [elements].
It is stated that air (*vāyu*) is clearly established there through its own functional effects, such as its own composition; thus he says:
"From the subtle element (*tanmātra*) of the touch of air, that which consists of upward movement arose;
it is beneficial by being the cause of activities such as throwing upwards."

Arrangement (*vyūhana*) is the joining of parts; even the joining of the parts of a jar and so forth is established by the pervasive wind (*vāyu*) within the body of the potter and others. This is also an illustration. As they say: "Wind is characterized by touch, sound, support, and motion. By this, upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), rising (*utthāna*), moving forward (*agrahāt*), and going (*gamana*) are included.
Furthermore, he states that [the breath] is divided by its tenfold manifestation according to its functions:
"Existing in ten ways within the bodies of all living beings,
it is known by the designations of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, udāna, and so forth."
The activity of the aggregate of egoism is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which has cast off its [gross] state; it is the subtle body, possessing its own function of leading downward.

For the intellect (*mati*) of persons, mounted upon the vital breath, wanders like a blind person while seeking the "I," even though it possesses its own function consisting of reflection. And the downward-moving breath (*apāna*)... [is] the semen.

The *apāna* has the function of downward removal; the *samāna* has the function of equal distribution of food and drink; the *vyāna* has the function of pervasion. Now, the *udāna* has the function of upward movement. It is associated with the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), serves as an assistant to the organ of speech through its exertion, and is the basis for the functions of speech and the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The gross articulation of sound, manifested by the resonance in the space [of the mouth] during separation [from the source], possesses its own function alone. As it has been said:

"Sound, originating from space and air, emerges from the body as a resonance (*nāda*) when articulated; being divided among various places of articulation, that which attains the state of phonemes (*varṇa*) is called 'speech' (*śabda*). (p. 793)

We shall explain how the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, which are parts of the external body or constitute the subtle body, maintain their causal state through their own functions. Now, it is said that fire is established by the effect of digestion:
"From the wind, the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*) is born, characterized by cooking."
And it exists in the world in three ways, under the designations of Gārhapatya and so forth.
Therefore, the Śaiva fire is indeed distinct from that; it resides within the interior of the Bindu, and whatever this world eats is digested by this very fire alone.
Because he is the ultimate benefactor of living beings, transcending all [other fires],

the Śiva-fire— born from the letter *ma*, distinct from the divine digestive fire (*audarya*) and the sacrificial fires such as the *dakṣiṇa-āhavanīya* and *gārhapatya* which arise from the subtle elements (*tanmātra*)— is to be worshipped by those initiated; it is, in other words, exceedingly pure compared to those.

"In the interior of the *bindu*"—the word "arisen" (*samudbhūta*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. That which is named Vāgīśa and Vāgīśvarī, having *mahāmāyā* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), is the occasional (*naimittika*) [cause] consisting of Śiva and Śakti; that is to say, it has the *bindu* as its material cause (*upādāna*).

He states the accomplishment of the two principles (*tattva*) characterized by the two functions of support (*avaṣṭambha*) and maintenance (*dhṛti*): [The text continues: "...endurance, the characteristic of action, and the two principles... etc. It is said: "The accomplishment of the two principles."
From the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra) arose water, whose function is cohesion;
upon water alone is the foundation of this world and its entities established.
By its own nature as consisting of dust, the earth was made firm by this [tanmātra];
from the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra), the earth arose through the activity of supporting.

This has been clearly stated by certain partial Vedāntins: "The qualities of the effect are indeed the qualities of the cause; possessing activity, they merely come into manifestation. From the perspective of those who know this principle, [the opponent's view] is untenable because it contradicts that. For [the qualities] intended by them do not exist anywhere even in the causes, such as ether (*ākāśa*).
Because of the observation of an excellence of qualities (*guṇātiśaya*). Having stated that this is incorrect, he concludes:
"Wind is not born from space, nor is fire produced from wind;
water is not from fire, nor earth from that [water], because of the observation of an excellence of qualities."
The transfer of qualities from the cause to the effects is logical, but not by itself;
otherwise, space would possess five qualities, and such would be the order of creation.

From the five *tanmātras* arises the pentad beginning with Soma; the meaning of the syllables here is clear. This aforementioned group of ten—the five *tanmātras* and the [five] elements—having entered the instruments (*karaṇas*), performs the activity characterized by the movement from womb to womb and the act of sustaining [the body], which is designated by the term "effect" (*kārya*).

It is called "the support of the instruments" (*karaṇadhāra*), for the activity of the instruments is difficult to achieve without the maintenance of that [body] as their effect; thus it is further designated by the term "support of the instruments. As it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (p. 796):
"This body, having entered into ten ways by means of the instruments, is made to perform activity."
"But because they lack pervasiveness, the instruments (karaṇas) exert themselves by presiding over their respective effects.

Thus [it is said]. Māyā is common [to all]; being the deluder through its own effects, it is the mother of Kalā and the others. Because it fulfills its own effects, Kalā and the others, it pervades the entire subtle body. Since its nature is that of Śakti, it is not formless.
The [world] beginning with Nabho and ending with Vanā is called Veśavatī; it is not manifest directly, but rather through its own *kalā*.

It consists of the aggregate of worlds (*bhuvana-skandha*) such as Gahaneśa and others, which are its own effects. Being differentiated for each individual (*puruṣa*), it resides in the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) as something unique; such is the nature of *vidyā*, *rāga*, and *prakṛti*.

The function that manifests the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which consists of the aggregates (*skandha*) and is of the nature of ignorance and action, is itself composed of the aggregates. Furthermore, when it is common to all, it is the progenitor and sustainer of the worlds, being the source-nature (*prakṛti*) of such [entities] as knowledge, passion, and primordial matter, as well as the body and so forth, which possess both forms. It is the progenitor and sustainer of the worlds.

And it would consist of the aggregates (*skandha*). Since knowledge and passion exist in each individual with differentiation, they reside in the subtle body; yet, being common in nature, they manifest as the powers of cognition, will, and action, thus consisting of the aggregates. Furthermore, being common in nature, they constitute the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) of their own dual form, such as the body and so forth.
The two [principles], Time (Kāla) and Necessity (Niyati), which consist of the aggregates of origination and support for the elements and the worlds,
exist as specific (asādhāraṇa) natures residing within the subtle body (sūkṣmadeha) with differentiation for each individual (pratipuruṣam), consisting of the aggregates of activity and regulation.
Furthermore, existing as common (sādhāraṇa) natures, they constitute the bodies and so forth of both [the individual and the collective] through their own dual forms.
The two [principles], consisting of the aggregates (*skandha*), would be the progenitor and the sustainer of the world in its primordial state (*prakṛtibhūta*).

Puruṣa, on the other hand, is characterized as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) who is overcome by *kalā* and the rest, beginning with *avidyā*. Furthermore, he is joined with passion (*rāga*) and possesses the arrangement of his own world, which is born before *prakṛti*. *Prakṛti* [acts] for each individual *puruṣa* through non-discrimination (*abhedya*).
Abiding in the subtle body, being of an uncommon nature, she is the support and fulfiller of the aggregate that generates such a triad of qualities;

yet, becoming again of a common nature through those qualities, she is the support and fulfiller of the world— the source of both her own forms, such as the body, and the head— which exists by way of those qualities.

And it would consist of the aggregates (*skandha*). The reality of the qualities (*guṇatattva*), existing with differentiation for each individual soul, resides in the subtle body; being of an uncommon nature, consisting of *sattva* and the other [qualities], and being of such an insubstantial character, it is composed of the qualities and consists of the three aggregates—the support, the fulfiller, and the impeller—which produce the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. It is characterized by illumination and the rest.
