The function (vṛtti) consists of three groups (triskandha), having the nature of these aggregates. Furthermore, being common [to all], it consists of such a triad of discordant qualities (triguṇa); it takes the form of both the intellect (buddhi) and the self (sva), and serves as the support and fulfiller for the body and other things produced by primordial nature (prakṛti), as well as for the worlds; thus, it consists of the three groups of aggregates. The intellect (buddhi) exists individually with respect to each person.

Abiding in the subtle body, she is unique, composed of the three unequal guṇas, the support and generator of such ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra), and consists of the aggregate of the vital breaths; she [is manifested] through the various functions of consciousness— distinguished by external objects such as women and others, by pleasure and the like, and by the states of determination, memory, intuition, and latent impressions.

Furthermore, that which is recited among the intermediate states of rebirth (*punarbhava*)— namely, dispassion (*vairāgya*), passion (*rāga*), and desire (*icchā*)— is, according to each respective term, characterized by the manifestation of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), consisting of the aggregates (*skandha*) that produce the suffixes of existence (*bhāva-pratyaya*). Moreover, when it is common [to all], it consists of the unequal three qualities (*viṣama-triguṇa*).

In me, let there be such an ego (ahaṃkāra) which consists of both the self and the body, etc., and which serves as the support for the maintenance and fulfillment of the worlds that constitute primordial nature (prakṛti). This ego, by effecting the differentiation between nature and spirit (puruṣa), resides within the subtle body and the physical body; being common to all, it is composed of the three unequal qualities (guṇas).

Such a [state] consists of three aggregates (*skandha*) that serve as the support and fulfiller for the group consisting of the mental aggregate (*manas-skandha*), the intellect (*buddhi*), the sense organs (*indriya*), the action organs (*karmendriya*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). It consists of the three aggregates that manifest the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which are directed toward oneself through the functions of self-conceit (*svagarva*) and exertion (*saṃrambha*).

Furthermore, being common [to all], it consists of the three qualities in a state of imbalance; it is of the nature of both the sixteen principles beginning with the mind (*manas*) which are internalized within itself, as well as the body and so forth; it is the source, the support, the fulfiller, and the aggregate of the world-born *prakṛti*;
and it comprises the mind, the organs of knowledge, and the organs of action.

The uncommon [elements] residing in the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) exist; they consist of the aggregates (*skandha*) that manifest the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
The subtle elements (*tanmātra*) residing in the subtle body are likewise uncommon; such [elements] correspond to their own respective [causes].

The elements (*bhūta*) consist of the generative, the supporting, the filling, and those whose nature is the aggregates (*skandha*); likewise, the instruments (*karaṇa*), their sustenance, and their functions (*vṛtti*) consist of the aggregates. Furthermore, from the mind (*manas*) down to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), these are common [to all];
in some cases they exist separately as subtle entities, and thus do not inherently possess the nature of worlds (*bhuvana*), while in other cases they are non-separate from the ego (*ahaṃkāra*).
In the *Garbha* [Upaniṣad], they are described as consisting of the aggregates (*skandha*) of the worlds. As it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:

"The worlds, which are the support for the continuity of the mental stream, consist of fragrance. Furthermore, the subtle bodies (*sūkṣmadeha*) beginning with the elements (*bhūta*) exist as unique to each individual, consisting of the aggregates of the functions of the instruments (*karaṇavṛtti*).

Furthermore, there exist common [elements] possessing functions such as support (dhṛti) and so forth; they exist both within and outside the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) in gross and subtle forms; they consist of the nature of bodies and the like which possess common and uncommon functions of accumulation; and they are of the nature of the aggregates (skandha) that generate and sustain the worlds.

In that regard, although the uncommon principles from *kalā* down to *kṣiti* are all-pervasive, they are not perceived by our senses— just as [the presence of] *piśācas* and the like is not perceived— and they pervade their own respective worlds and so forth in the form of subtle bodies for each individual soul; these consist of the principles from *kṣiti* up to *kalā*, which are common to all.

The worlds, beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Kapālīśa, pervade the body born of those worlds through their persistence. The purification by initiation (*dīkṣā*) of the subtle bodies— which arise from the future enjoyment [of karma], which have as their causes the impurity (*mala*), the power [of *mala*] (*śakti*), and accumulated karma, and which emerge from the creation produced therefrom— is such that the effects already begun [by karma] do not recur.

In initiation (*dīkṣā*), which grants immediate liberation by obstructing the experience of karma, the purification of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that have not yet been exhausted and those currently manifesting must be performed daily; for the sake of worship, the purification of the currently manifest subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) must also be performed. However, the gross body and so forth do not constitute the subtle body.

The material causes [of the body] begin with *kalā*. However, together with those [causes] such as *pūraka* and so forth, which pertain to the gross body, there are the material causes for the transformations of the cosmic egg (*bhauvana*), beginning from the common elements such as the gross elements and ending with *kalā*. At the end of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the uncommon principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā* and ending with earth, as well as the universal principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with earth, [are dissolved].

The worlds, the bodies of the Bhauvanas, and so forth, have as their creator one who is not subject to death. It is understood that the bodies of the Bhauvanas arise either directly from *prakṛti* or through the medium of Brahmā. At the end of the intermediate dissolution (*madhyama-pralaya*), the worlds of *prakṛti* situated below the head [of the cosmic egg]—the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with the *guṇas* and ending with the earth—are common to all.

These are the real [entities]. Those created by Śrīkaṇṭha consist of the primordial nature (prakṛti), the worlds from the subterranean regions down to the fire of time (kālāgni), and the bodies of the Bhuvanas; those created by the two Brahmās consist of the abode up to the Egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa), which is the locus of the qualities (guṇas);
furthermore, there are the uncommon [powers] such as Kalā, and those beginning with the primordial nature, the individual soul (puruṣa), and the internal and external bodies of the Bhuvanas.

The specific results of the maturation of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the intellect (*buddhi*) and karma residing within the body, as well as the primary principles beginning with *dharma*, the bodies born of the worlds, and the individual souls (*kalā*) and other ancient [principles] characterized by their own causes—all these constitute the reality, nature, beings, and worlds arising from the abode of Śiva, as described in that incomparable scripture. (p. 804)

Sound and the other [objects] would be those [results]. The collection of principles (tattva) beginning with kalā, which constitutes the subtle body, although consisting of different classes, has a single fruit—just like the various parts of a lamp’s wick. As it is heard in the *Mṛgendra-śruti*: "Furthermore, karma brings about experience as its sole fruit. And regarding the diversity of experience, it is heard in the *Ratnatraya*: "There is variety, such as sandalwood and so forth."

In the case of an effect, there is a dependence on a portion of the action (*karman*) and so forth; for action is the cause of the diversity of *kalā* and the rest, while *kalā* and the rest are the cause of the diversity of experience (*bhoga*). Since the diversity of experience would otherwise be inexplicable, it is determined for each individual soul (*puruṣa*) and is unique, being caused by an action that possesses its own internal diversity. As for impurity (*mala*), however—

It is common insofar as it exists by its own nature through its own power, yet it is uncommon because it is restricted to each individual soul (*puruṣa*). Its characteristic of Śiva-hood (*śivatva*) is common to the eternally liberated (*anādimukta*), the recently liberated (*mukta*), and the Supreme Śiva (*aparamukta-śiva*). It distinguishes [the soul] from other categories of entities, namely the bound souls (*paśu*) and the fetters (*pāśa*). This [Śiva-hood] belongs to the eternally liberated and the others up to the Śivas.

Any one of the uncommon, beginningless characteristics belonging to the various types of bound souls (*paśu*)—such as *vijñāna-kala*, *pralayākala*, or *sakala*—distinguishes that particular soul from both its own kind and from other classes of bound souls. This is because the common characteristic of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) distinguishes it from the other two categories: the *pati* (the Lord) and the *pāśa* (the bonds).
It distinguishes [the subject] from two types of entities: first, it distinguishes any one of the uncommon factors such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) and *kalā* from other entities of its own class;
and second, it distinguishes it from other entities belonging to the category of bonds (*pāśa*) and the Lord (*pati*).

The fetters of impurity (*mala*), action (*karman*), and illusion (*māyā*) distinguish their nature as common fetters from the categories of the Lord (*pati*) and the bound soul (*paśu*). Any one of these— impurity and so forth— is the uncommon [fetter],
characterized by any one of the defining marks such as "impurity-ness" (*malatva*), which distinguishes it from other entities of its own class (*svajātīya*).
And it distinguishes [the Self] from both the individual soul (*paśu*) and objective categories (*padārtha*). Its belonging [to the Lord] is to be discerned in this manner.
This concludes the fifth chapter in the *Śrīmatpauṣkarajñānapādavṛtti* composed by the teacher Jñānaprakāśācārya, a resident of Śrīśālivāṭipura.
May there be auspiciousness! Written by Kṛṣṇa with his own hand, together with the assistance of Śrī Śālivāṭīśvara Svāmī and the illustrious Śrīkāntimatī Ambā. Hariḥ Om.
Hariḥ Om.
The Chapter on the Means of Valid Cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, it has been stated that the establishment of all objects of cognition (*prameya*) is dependent upon the means of valid cognition; therefore, this [chapter on] the means of valid cognition [is commenced].
First, it must be understood what these six categories (ṣaṭpadārtha) are like;
thus he begins an incidental chapter consisting of an examination of their prior and subsequent limits. Then, the sages spoke together regarding the intended connection for each one:
O Blessed One, Lord of Gods, you who are intent upon bestowing grace upon your devotees,
have out of compassion explained the six categories (padārthas) through manifold logical arguments.
Now we wish to hear about the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), O storehouse of compassion,
without knowing whose nature even an object of cognition (prameya) is postulated.
Therefore, O Īśāna, you ought to explain this to us here.

[Objection: But was it not stated that there are six categories (*padārtha*), and why has the meaning of the word "six" not been examined? [Reply: True; it was not by means of statements in other chapters, but because it was separated by the *Paśu-paṭala*. As in the case of those whose form is grace (*anugraha*).

Since the realization of Śiva-nature—which is the exhaustion of all [limitations] of those who argue—is established by the impossibility of its being otherwise, no further investigation is required; for according to the maxim, "When the desired object has been attained, what wise person would perform another [action]?
To the question, "For what purpose is this prayer? it is for that very purpose that the words beginning with "That whose nature... and so forth are stated. Because, first of all...

It should be understood that the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is such that, once it has been cognized— its own form and its definition— the object of cognition (*prameya*) becomes "devoid of purpose" (*vigatārtha*), meaning its purpose, which was the manifestation and clarification of knowledge regarding its own object, has ceased. This is said because otherwise, even the means of valid cognition would be a category of existence (*padārtha*), and thus the object of cognition would possess its purpose.

Therefore, it must necessarily be understood that [these topics] are to be known through enumeration (*uddeśa*), definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and critical examination (*parīkṣā*); the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) is to be supplied as a connective. The rest is easy to understand. Thus entreated, Īśvara, having begun to dispel the non-authoritative knowledge of the sages, first divides and enumerates the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Listen, O twice-born ones, if you have the curiosity to hear them: those four means of knowledge (*māna*) are perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the others.
Perception, inference, verbal testimony, and presumptive testimony—these indeed are the means of knowledge.
However, there is no fixed sequence for hearing them immediately one after another. Nevertheless, if you have curiosity and a desire for pleasure, listen; the remainder is easy to understand.

The intention is that other means of knowledge, such as analogy (*upamāna*) and so forth, are included here within the category of "arrogance" (*andarpa*). Now, having thus indicated [the topic], he defines the characteristic of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) as established in the Śiva-śāstra, which is not established in the [Vedic] scriptures on animal sacrifice (*paśu-śāstra*):
"The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), entirely free from doubt and the like, is called the means of valid cognition."
Doubtful cognition has two objects because it perceives two similar forms.
Error is cognition otherwise, not established in the form of that [object].

Here, memory is said to be a cognition whose object is a previously experienced thing. It is the power of consciousness, when devoid of these [two], that is accepted as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

That power of consciousness which, being entirely free from doubt and the like, and existing within the very transformation of doubt, is characterized by memory that is liberated from sequential succession and endowed with an intellectual illumination that manifests accordingly; which, while sometimes possessing an intellectual illumination associated with determination and sometimes devoid of it, reflects— she is the one described in the Śiva-śāstra.

Therefore, "māna" (the means of knowledge) is said to be none other than the cognitive power (*cicchakti*) itself, which possesses purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*)—a synonym for the non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) to be described later. It is not, however, the instrument for achieving that [knowledge], such as the sense organs and so forth, which are synonyms for the resulting cognition (*pramiti*). Thus, there are four [categories].

It is true that the statement defining power as having a single characteristic—namely, that it is "somehow directed after being differentiated"—is correct. This is because the powers of Śiva, the Liberated (mukta), and Śivas, which shine forth with purity due to their stainlessness, do not depend upon the senses and other such instruments; for those [powers] do not exist in a fourfold manner. As it has been stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
"The stainless knowledge of Śaṅkara shines at all times regarding all objects, neither as perception, nor as inferential, nor even as verbal. Thus,
even that power is included within the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) by means of a single statement of its general definition.

For he will state that even these [other means of knowledge] are included within the limit of the [four] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that regard, it is said: "The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is independent of the senses and has completely abandoned all bonds," and so forth.
Therefore, the single power of the Self (*ātman*), though one, exists as fourfold when it abides through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the senses and other factors.

He will say: "In that regard, having analyzed the manifestation and the action... He defines [the object] by means of the words beginning with "dvi" (two), etc., for the purpose of making known the liberation of the consciousness-power (*cicchakti*) from that which is associated with the Buddhist illumination of doubt and so forth, and from other things that appear clearly.
Because of the perception of a common form, when a thing characterized as a post or the like is seen, it is common to both possibilities: "Is it a post? or...

The cognition whose objects are "Is it a person? and so forth is doubt (*saṃśaya*). By way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*), the illumination of cognition is doubt. This arises from the perception of common characteristics. Because of the direct perception of qualities such as smoothness and coldness, [the mind] is not established in that which is not of that nature; "that which is not of that nature" (*atadrūpa*) refers to forms such as those of mother-of-pearl, which are not [actually] of that nature.

The form of silver and so forth, appearing by the power of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by a previous experience, is established as being that [silver] though it is not of that nature; thus it is said to be "fallen" [into error]. Otherwise, cognition that is not in accordance with reality (*ayathārtha*), which is the manifestation of a mental state, is a misconception (*viparyaya*). It has as its object an experienced thing—an experienced thing...
Because it arises from the perception of similarity and other causes within the intellect,

and because it is produced by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) generated by a previous experience of that object, it is transformed into the form of that object; for this very reason, even when the object is absent, there occurs in those who are sleeping or waking a cognition— whether through speech or the eyes— that takes the form of direct perception (*sākṣātkāratayā*), such as "that" or "this" in its proper place.
When [cognition] arises from mental formations (*saṃskāra*) and is delineated by objects such as women and so forth, it flashes forth; that is the manifestation of the intellect (*bauddhī mati*).

That which is "with its limbs" (*sāṅgaṅgā*) and so forth—the manifestation according to reality—is here in the Śiva-scripture called "recollection" (*smṛti*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Paśu-paṭala*: "Knowledge is never, anywhere, without an object."

The speech arising from the mouth of Śiva constitutes a refutation of those Vedāntins, Cārvākas, and certain followers of Buddhism who maintain that cognition is devoid of an object; for they define consciousness (*cicchakti*) as being free from doubt and other such states,
and devoid of the relationship between a manifestor and the manifested, yet accept it as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

He refutes the objection— "What is meant by the term 'conscious power' (cicchakti), which is defined and accepted according to the characteristics of the means of valid cognition?"— by stating: "And conscious power is nothing other than awareness that is independent of anything else."
His knowledge is not directed toward that [object], nor is it turned outward toward another, for it is free from the notions of "me" and "mine."
The supreme object of cognition (*prameya*) consists of existence and so forth; its operation (*vyāpāra*) is held to be the fruit.
And the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which depends on the Supreme, has as its sole face that which is well-established as the object other than itself.
Awareness (*bodha*) is nothing other than the Supreme; there is no other awareness, nor is it one whose face is well-fixed upon its own subject (*mātṛ*).

Self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is either cognition (*buddhi*) or illumination (*prakāśa*). Since the illumination of cognition is not an object for Śiva and others, and since its being "aware by itself" will be refuted later on the grounds that there is no distinction in its nature as awareness, if one intends to maintain that self-awareness possesses validity (*mānatva*) as qualified by awareness, there is a threefold contradiction regarding its own self and the non-establishment of the means of knowledge (*mātuḥ-asiddhi*).

He says "it might be so," beginning with "no" (na), and so forth. Of that cognition—which arises from its own state (*svapadasamutthita*), which is established as "to be known by itself" (*svasaṃvedya*) here, and which is what is meant by "the cognition of another" (*parasaṃvitti*)—there is the cognition directed toward [itself]. This is what is established by the word *saṃvit* in the phrase "self-cognition" (*svasaṃvit*), and it is what is established by the word *vedya* in the phrase "to be known by itself" (*svasaṃvedya*).

"This is established by its own word" means that it is self-evident (*svasaṃvit*), namely, "I am," which is the supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvit*). It is not an object of measurement, for even the subject who measures it is established without being explicitly stated. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:
"In the Vedāntas, there is only one Self, characterized by the manifestations of both the conscious and the unconscious."
This is merely a thesis; on what basis is there certainty?
"Then, where the self becomes the object of knowledge (*prameya*), there the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is also present; wherever these two exist, all four are established.

Here too, the "fourfold" refers to the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, the knower (*pramātṛ*), and the act of knowledge (*pramiti*); for the act of knowledge is indeed cognition (*vedana*).

Furthermore, these are called, in order, the instrument, the object, the agent, and the action. Therefore, supreme consciousness directed toward the external is said to be the means of knowledge (*māna*). As it is stated in the *Ratnatraya*:
"The perception of the two forms of every single object."

Now, if it is thus established that having parts (*sāṃśatva*) is invariably concomitant with being an effect, then that is incorrect. For there are not two cognitions; rather, that very power which is the nature of supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvitti*) is itself self-consciousness (*svasaṃvitti*).

Since self-consciousness is established as the very form of the possessor of power—whether that be Śiva or the Self—it is not a separate entity, because they are non-differentiated (*apṛthaksiddhatvāt*).

It was stated [in verse 815] that [the subject] is "turned toward the other" (*paronmukha*). One might ask: "What is this 'other' (*para*) which is entirely above and below, beginning with Śiva? He dispels this doubt with the words beginning with "the other" (*para*). Here, the word *para* does not signify "superior," but rather signifies "that which is distinct from oneself. Thus, the "object of knowledge" (*prameya*) distinct from the supreme means of knowledge (*paramāna*) is the entire collection of categories (*padārtha*) beginning with the Lord (*pati*).
As he will say:

"That which is the object of measurement is not itself the means of measurement, because it is measured by a means of measurement. Now, if this is so, then since the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is not an object of measurement, it lies beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, regarding that [power] again...

Because it is denotable, it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); wherever there is denotability, there is cognizability (*prameyatva*), as in the case of a jar. Thus, by virtue of this pervasion (*vyāpti*), the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) does not deviate from cognizability. Furthermore, if it were not within the scope of another means of valid cognition, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would ensue; therefore, there is no means of valid cognition for the establishment of the power of consciousness. And that...

Power would then be devoid of any basis in valid cognition (*apramāṇikī*). From that, what undesirable consequence (*akṣati*) follows? [The opponent replies: "O Great Lord, the existence of power would be without a basis in valid cognition; it would be both existent and non-existent, like the horn of a hare. [The proponent replies: "In that case, this very power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), being both existent and non-existent, would likewise be like the horn of a hare. [The opponent says: "True."

The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is self-awareness; it is not cognizable by another awareness, for that would lead to an infinite regress. Furthermore, because there is no infinite regress, it declares itself to be the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and being inexpressible by anything else, it is called "self-awareness" (*svasaṃvit*). Although the Śiva-scriptures also read it as "self-cognition" (*svasaṃvedya*), [it is so called] with reference to that very [power].
Upon careful reflection, an action directed toward itself cannot be self-cognized due to the contradiction of acting upon oneself;

rather, when such a state exists, what is observed is both self-cognition and the cognition of something other than itself. These two apprehensions are not established as separate entities, because—as previously stated according to the aforementioned reasoning—there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, there is no knowledge that is directed toward itself.
According to the method thus declared— "the measure of the mother [consciousness] is directed toward itself"— the supreme consciousness, the power of Cit, by its own nature,
through its own revolving, becomes oriented toward itself; having become the self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*) for the sake of its own experience,
it is well-established within that subject (*pramātṛ*), who is its own immediate form and possesses that power, with its face turned inward.

818) Self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), possessing the function of self-experience, while shining intensely within itself as something not to be illuminated by anything else, appears— within the existence of other entities such as Śiva— as its own bliss characterized by non-dual establishment, which is defined by its own manifestation.

The concise statement is that [the object] appears as having a fresh (pratyagra) form. Because it has fallen into the power of supreme manifestation (*paraprakāśa-śakti*), it is established as mere power (*śaktimātra*) through its manifestation as a fresh form—that is, as power. Thus, the subject (*mātṛ*) and the means of knowledge (*māna*) are non-existent [as separate entities], because it is impossible to deny what is established by experience. As they say:
The final establishment of the means of valid cognition occurs in experience;
since that very [experience] is self-cognized, what need is there for other means of cognition therein?

But surely, if the self (*ātman*) is not manifest to itself or to others, how was it stated in the *Ahaṃkāra-parīkṣā* that it is manifest to the "I-notion" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*) consisting of the *ahaṃkāra*? True; it is not manifest to that "I-notion," but rather, when that "I-notion" consisting of the *ahaṃkāra* is manifest, [the self is manifest] through that "I-notion" consisting of the *ahaṃkāra*.

The cognition (*pratyaya*), having become the power that illuminates its own self, shines forth while blazing within the self-luminous possessor of that power (*śaktimat*). Now, although the self-awareness of Śiva and other conscious beings, whose nature is to illuminate others, is established in this manner, [one might ask]: since they exist in the form of the knower (*mātṛ*) and the means of knowledge (*māna*), and thus differ from the object of knowledge (*meya*), how then [is this possible]?

Mutual cognition. True. First of all, in the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) which is the cause of its own manifestation, there is no appearance of another cognizer as being itself in the form of another's cognition; nor does the cognition of that other cognizer appear [therein], because it is "other," like a jar or similar objects. If that were the case...

Furthermore, because of the consequence of non-metaphorical non-duality, [your] duality would be defeated; for selves, being mere self-cognitions, do not intermingle with one another. Otherwise, there would be the consequence of universal omniscience for all, along with the consequence of a single self. Rather, just as one's own self is directly perceived...

In one's own self-awareness, which appears as its own experience, the supreme cognizer (parānumātṛ) manifests in some way as that which is designated by the term "means of knowledge" (māna), being clearly distinguished from the object of cognition; likewise, in another's body,
the supreme Self manifests through signs such as walking, moving about, and other activities, being clearly distinguished from the object of cognition.
The subject (māna), denoted by the word "measure," is inferred through the deliberation of another's consciousness by one who infers for others.

However, for the omniscient ones such as Śiva and others, the state of being an object (meyatā) resides within subjects; thus, it is the reverse. Consequently, that [consciousness] is both visible and invisible:
it is visible insofar as it manifests in some way through the door of the manifestation of the visible, and it is invisible because its own consciousness has manifested in some way.

By means of the relationship with the single genus of Śiva-nature—which consists of similarity to that which is other than itself—the various individual cognitions and powers of vision of the Supreme Self are directly realized. Enough with this excessively subtle investigation and prolixity; let us return to the subject at hand. "Bhāva" (being) is "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature) with respect to the object of knowledge, in relation to everything other than itself.

Alternatively, because the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is a quality and is unchanging, it does not undergo conjunction or similar relations with objects; thus, it is "fallen" upon the power of consciousness that has become the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This refers to non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) related to Śiva and others, which is the "beginning" of that [process] which is mixed with the illumination of the intellect (*bauddha-prakāśa*).
For all cognition associated with the subject, whether it be conceptual knowledge or the knowledge of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, its very existence is its activity;
that is, its activity consists in the presence or absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
The innate fruit of the cognitive power (*cicchakti*), which constitutes the means of valid knowledge (*māna*), is intended as the result called "ascertainment" (*pramiti*).
A definition has three ornaments; since those do not exist elsewhere, he says:
"In this case, there is never the possibility of defects such as under-extension (*avyāpti*) and so forth.
In the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), under-extension is a defect [due to lack of] pervasion (*vyāpti*)."
There is no over-extension [of the definition] with respect to objects of cognition, because it does not apply to multiple non-existent things;
nor is there any lack of pervasion, provided that such is the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The statement of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been correctly illustrated by him up to this point. Here, however, in the definition of the means of valid cognition for establishing the doctrine (*siddhānta*) just stated, [the term] "non-pervasion" (*avyāpti*) is to be supplied as a grammatical ellipsis. Why?

Because [the definition] does not pervade [all] the means of valid cognition, such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and so forth, nor [does it apply to] the sense-organ (*akṣa*), smoke (*dhūma*), and so on.

The definition, characterized as the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) augmented by the concomitant implication of the meaning of the term *liṅga*, exists entirely within each individual object. It does not suffer from the fault of being too narrow (*avyāpti*), because it does not fail to apply to various objects of knowledge that are distinct from the means of knowledge, since it is present even in the very limits of those categories. Nor is it [too broad], for it is the very thing to be defined.

Furthermore, over-extension (*ativyāpti*) consists in being applicable even to that which is not the object of definition (*alakṣya*). If such a characteristic of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) were the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be no under-extension (*avyāpti*); otherwise, pervasion (*vyāpti*) would be different. Pervasion is the complete presence [of the definition] within the object of definition, whereas partial presence in only one part of the object of definition is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*). Non-pervasion is the total absence of occurrence anywhere within the object of definition.

This means that it is not impossible. He concludes with the words "pretya" and so forth: since those three are free from defects, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is distinguished from the object of cognition (*prameya*) and stated;

by this, the statement of the means of valid cognition—that is, the definition of the means of valid cognition, or the correct exposition of the means of valid cognition—is well-illustrated. [The unseen (*adṛṣṭa*)...]

To speak: even though [the truth] is established by itself (*svatas-siddha*), as long as opposing views have not been refuted, one's own position remains unestablished; thus, observing this maxim of those skilled in policy, we shall first effect the subversion of the desired positions of the logicians (*tārkika*) by means of objections.
Surely, that which is the means for producing valid cognition would not be a means of knowledge;
for otherwise, it would follow that lamps, eyes, and so forth would also possess the status of being instruments of valid cognition.

[Objection: Surely, why should that which is a means of valid cognition (*pramiti-sādhana*), i.e., an instrument of knowledge (*pramā-karaṇa*), not be a measure (*māna*)? [Response: That is incorrect; the word "lamp" (*dīpa*) is to be supplied as a consequence. [Objection: Surely, it would be like the accepted principle regarding lamps, eyes, and so forth being considered instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [Response: This does not constitute a refutation of our position. He says that this is incorrect: *...bhūmikānānneṣṭavighātaḥ tadayuktamityāha -* (p. 824) [The intended conclusion is not undermined by the examples of the stages; he says that this is incorrect.]

That which is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not itself an object of cognition (*meyam*); however, the state of being an object of cognition remains established there, because it is inferred by the cognizer through its status as an object such as sound and so forth.
That by which something is measured is not itself a means of measurement;
for in the world, it is well known that "I see" occurs through the eye due to its utility.

That which is characterized as being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be that which is characterized as the object of cognition (*meyatva*); or, if the object of cognition were somehow [identical] to it, then there would be an absence of the means of valid cognition. Furthermore, if the object of cognition were also the means of valid cognition, then the absence of the object of cognition would be established. Nor can it be said, for the sake of pacifying this fault, that the ear and so forth are the objects of cognition.
In that regard, because the ears and other [senses] have sound and so forth as their objects, and because they provide assistance through the arising of cognitions of objects such as sound,

those ears and others are also considered by you to be the means for the apprehension of sound and so forth. Through the process of inclusion and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*), it is inferred by the intellect that these are accomplished by an instrument (*karaṇa*), because they are actions, like the action of cutting wood.

Since it is inferred by the mind in this manner, therefore there would be a confusion [of categories] such that "that which is to be reached" (yanneya) would be the instrument of knowledge (pramāṇa), the object of knowledge (prameya), and the knower (pramātṛ). Thus, it is not a valid means of knowledge (māna). [Objection: But surely, the eye and so forth must be accepted as instruments of knowledge based on worldly consensus. [Reply: That is incorrect, because they are established otherwise; for thus it is seen in the world: [The text continues with the verse: *na cakṣurādinā mānaṃ kintu jñānena gamyate | jñānaṃ tu kevalaṃ mānaṃ nendriyādi kadācana ||* "The instrument of knowledge is not the eye and so forth, but rather it is known through cognition; cognition alone is the instrument of knowledge, never the sense organs. [The commentary continues: For in the world, it is observed that when one says, "I see a pot by means of the eye," the word "by means of" (*yena*) denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*). And since the pot is perceived through the cognition "this is a pot," it is understood that cognition alone is the instrument. Furthermore, the eye and so forth are not the instruments, because they are themselves objects of perception. For instance, when one says, "I see the eye with the mind," the eye is clearly an object (*karman*), not an instrument. Therefore, cognition alone is the instrument of knowledge. The well-known status [of the statement] "I see" as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is by way of illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). For example: "The smoke-sign (*dhūma-liṅga*) is the single means of valid cognition that makes known the possessor of the sign (*liṅgin*)," or "Is this statement true, having been spoken by the Lord (*īśvara*)? and so forth. Even such renown arises from utility (*upakāra*), characterized by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

Because it manifests the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The seed for this metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is that the power of Śiva (*śiva-śakti*) also manifests the means of valid cognition characterized by consciousness (*cic-chakti*) for the practitioner (*sādhaka*), who perceives the categories beginning with Śiva until the attainment of supreme liberation.
Thus, the power of Śiva brings about the self-established Śiva even for the practitioner.

The basis for the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is stated in relation to each means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, this will be analyzed and distinguished later in the investigation [of that very point].
For he says: "Even without intending to express the status of the eye and so forth as objects of cognition (*meyatva*), there is no such thing as a means of valid cognition (*mānatā*).
Indeed, there is no means of valid cognition that occurs without some object (*padārtha*).
Therefore, that alone should be accepted as the means of valid cognition; the eye and so forth are not such.

That whose manifestation results in the valid cognition (*pramiti*) of every object of knowledge, such as sound and so forth, and without which—due to its non-manifestation—there is no valid cognition of any object whatsoever; that alone must be accepted as the means of knowledge (*māna*), not the eye and other [senses], for they are not of such a nature. To explain:
The eye is not for the cognition of sound, nor is the ear for the perception of form;
rather, it is that cognition which grasps everything that is considered the means of knowledge.
That by whose establishment this [cognition] is established, and by whose non-establishment nothing at all is established:

the eye is not [the cause] in the cognition of sound, nor is the ear in the cognition of sound; [likewise], the ear is not in the perception of form, because it is merely an indicator for the valid cognition of form. Neither is the nose or other [senses] in the cognition of taste and so forth, nor is smoke [an indicator] in the cognition of fire.

Even a mark such as smoke [would not serve] for the inference of water and the like; nor would a word such as "the moon does not shine" serve for the cognition of the sun and the like; nor would the state of being non-Vedic (*avijātva*) serve as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the cognition of the "state of being a bound soul" (*paśutva*) which is to be described later. Therefore, that upon whose establishment this [other thing] is established is the means of valid knowledge.
The establishment of the means of knowledge (*pramiti*) occurs through the act of cognizing "this"; for if that were not established, nothing at all would be established.

That very consciousness (*saṃvit*), which is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), is the apprehender of sound and other objects throughout all cases—even when they are mutually inconsistent with respect to the eyes and other senses—provided it performs the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) characterized by its own appropriate means of knowledge (*pramiti*). This is considered the valid means of knowledge (*māna*). Now:
Having restated the Buddhist position, he refutes it:
"Why is cognition not accepted as the means of knowledge, since it is the final [cognition] of all?
For there is no distinction between the eye and other [senses], as they are equally natural."

The validity of cognition does not consist in its being non-conscious in nature; for the proof of "this" [the object] is established by that [cognition], and so forth—this [argument] applies here as well. That cognition consists in non-contradictory awareness (*avisaṃvāda-vijñāna*). Because it is the final of all [cognitions] and because it is the singular means of cognizing all objects of knowledge (*prameya*), [it is valid].

Why is it not accepted as non-erroneous? True; it is said: because, by the words "pretya" and so forth, it lacks the nature of self-awareness (*asaṃvidātmakatva*), lacks the nature of non-discrepant cognition (*anavisaṃvādajñānātmakatva*), and lacks the state of being self-reflexive (*svasaṃvittitva*);

and furthermore, because it is inferable by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) augmented by its own effect, namely the determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding the eyes and other [senses].

The literal meaning [of the passage] is as follows: even the lack of self-awareness (*asvavedyatva*) which conforms to the doctrine of the Sugatas is [defined as] being endowed with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) regarding objects such as rain that fall within its own domain; furthermore, the cognition [of such efficiency] deviates from the valid cognition of past and future objects, and likewise, non-conceptual valid cognition produced by the sense-faculties alone is not a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is because it is inseparable from all forms of valid cognition.

Even though cognition consists of pleasure and so forth, it deviates from its own apprehension as having the nature of form; thus, in order to establish the validity [of knowledge], he recalls the various arguments set forth at length:
"Furthermore, cognition is perceived as having the nature of pleasure, pain, and so forth."
Therefore, even the absolute validity of cognition is not accepted by him.

The absolute certainty of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is its non-deviation from the object of cognition (*pramiti*). The rest is easy to understand. However, the sages raise an objection regarding the status of the eyes and other [senses] as "means": "Indeed, why is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) not accepted as the means for the establishment of the object of cognition?"
Because the ascertainment of a jar occurs only when the cognizer and all other factors up to the jar itself are present.
Now, if [the senses] possess individualized forms (*vyaṣṭimat*), then the eyes and other [senses] would deviate from the external cognition of sound and so forth;

and they would likewise deviate from the internal cognition—ranging up to the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)—of pleasure and so forth, which is augmented by the internal mental determination (*svādhyavasāya*).
Even while possessing individualized forms, the mind (*mati*) [would deviate] in the cognition of the forms of pleasure and so forth as determined within.
As for the statement that external factors such as the eye and so forth deviate in the determination of the object, let that be true;

however, when the subject and the rest—beginning with the self, the senses, and the internal organ—are present, the ascertainment of the jar occurs because the cognition of the object arises. Therefore, the totality (*sāmagrī*) of those means of cognition is what constitutes the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Why is this desired? The Lord says:
Because that would result in the destruction of the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) consisting of the knower, the object of knowledge, and so forth;
for the existence of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge is already contained within That.
Furthermore, apart from those [individual factors], no causal complex (sāmagrī) is perceived;
for that which is not distinct from something else cannot be different from it by way of its own nature.

If it is claimed that the cognitive power (*cicchakti*), being free from doubt and the like, is intended as the means of valid cognition (*māna*), that is incorrect. Why? Because it would result in the abolition of the conventional distinctions between the knower (*pramātṛ*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and so forth;

for the distinct designations of the knower and the rest, which arise from their differentiation, would be shattered by the confusion (*sāṃkarya*) of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

Even if the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) were the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would not be so; for if you were to maintain that the separate mention of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and so forth is redundant, then this "economy" (*klipti*) of yours would be as audacious as the saying, "The mother herself devours her own son. Why? Because the cognizer, the means of cognition, and the object of cognition are established as being included within that [totality] itself. Since they reside within the belly of the causal totality...

Because it has been set aside. Now, one might object: "Let there be a real difference between the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), etc., just as there is between a quality (*guṇa*) and its possessor (*guṇin*).

That is incorrect. Having rejected the logicians (*tārkika*) who maintain that difference exists in reality, and having made the Buddhists our own fellow practitioners of the system, [we hold that] the possessor of qualities is merely the collection of qualities itself, existing as an inseparable establishment (*apṛthaksiddha*) of their nature; that is all.
Because it has been established through examination that the whole (*avayavin*) is merely the collection of its parts;

for apart from them, no separate existence is perceived, nor is a composite whole (*sāmagrī*) seen as distinct. If there is no separate existence, how can there be any difference? Indeed, that which exists as a reality (*bhāvika*)—such as a wall—is not distinct from its constituent elements, yet it is established separately [from them].

Furthermore, those who establish dualism by taking experience as their authority—claiming that [the self] is distinct from its own nature in reality—fall into the error of conflating the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with the resulting cognition (*pramiti*). This is because experience would then possess the functional efficacy (*arthakriyā*) characteristic of a valid cognition. Moreover, this definition would over-extend to erroneous cognition (*bhrama*); for if it were to apply to that which possesses cognition other than error, then the term "valid cognition" would become meaningless.
And they refute [the following view]: The Bhāṭṭas, however, maintain that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which apprehends an object not yet reached [by another cognition].

They argue that all Śaiva cognitions are valid because they have as their objects either (1) objects already apprehended by perception and so forth, augmented by scripture (*āgama*), or (2) objects already apprehended by themselves, unaided by scripture. Thus, [the opponent's view] is refuted.

Thus, demonstrating indifference, he concludes with the words beginning "saṃśaya" and so forth, which is easy to understand. Furthermore, the sages—even while speaking from the standpoint of the Naiyāyikas—seemingly accept [the view] that "bahiśca...
[and so on], as if it were something that could contribute even slightly to establishing their own position, serving merely to refute the positions of others.
They set forth this cavil:
"The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is not capable of engaging with objects through the path of the senses;
for the power of consciousness itself does not indeed turn toward objects."

How can there be a relationship with an object without that [object] being an instrument through the path of the senses? It is through the reinforcement of the senses; it is the conjunction of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) with the object, characterized as the relationship between the signified and the signifier, and not as a physical contact, because [consciousness] is formless.

Because that [direct perception] is impossible as a quality (*guṇa*). To indicate this very point, he will say: "How can there be a relation in the case of a word-meaning? It is not direct. By means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), for the sake of connecting with the object, it is called "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) because it is augmented by the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of its own consciousness, which is the result of cognition; thus, the sense-organ (*akṣa*) operates upon the object, and therefore it is "direct" (*pratyakṣa*).

This is also an illustration. Because it is augmented by the conceptual construction (*kalpti*) of the meaning of words such as "smoke" which serve as logical marks (*liṅga*), inferential cognition (*laiṅga*) and verbal cognition (*śābda*)—which consist of the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) characterized by the knowledge of an object arising from the connection between its own [internal] object and that [external] object—are likewise considered to be of this nature, just like perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). Thus, their power of consciousness (*cid-śakti*) is identical to that of perception.

"May he obtain worldly activity. But not by himself; "from where? from himself"—this is the connection [of the words]. The rest is easy to understand. Regarding the Lord: the orientation of objects toward him, as well as their subsequent dependence on instruments for obtaining that orientation, is not inherent to the powers of Śiva established in the Śiva-tantras.
Because that [power] is not heard of as being cast into the womb of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but rather it is conditioned by impurity (*mala*);
therefore, he says that its dependence on instruments for the sake of accomplishing all powers is real: "True; because it is veiled by impurity, it remains established solely within itself."
But when consciousness is joined with objects through the manifestation of the instruments, such as the kalās and so forth, [then it perceives].
Then it is said that "pratyakṣa" [is so called] because the sense-faculty (*akṣa*) operates upon the object (*artha*). (p.
835) The meaning of the words is clear. Having raised up and exposed the hidden intention of the opponent, he refutes it:
Perception is not held to arise from the mere conjunction of the sense-faculties and their objects,
because those [objects] devoid of conjunction with consciousness are incapable of producing any effect.

The characteristic of the cognition of an object consists in its being an effective action (*arthakriyā*). [This occurs] through a relationship characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), or the like. Those [senses] devoid of that [relationship] are likewise [ineffective]. Thus, those senses which are deprived of conjunction, or rather, those which are destitute of the relationship between the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) and the manifested (*vyaṅgya*)—consciousness—possess no efficacy; they result in the non-cognition of an object.

The performance of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) belongs to them; however, those [characteristics and actions] are performed by the conscious power (*cicchakti*) as their agent, through its conjunction with the conscious purposeful action. Alternatively, the conscious power—the conscious purposeful action—being related to that which is manifested (*vyaṅgya*) by the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), may perform some slight action. And this has been stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Manifested [consciousness], when conjoined with the mind, is joined with the sense-faculties;

thereafter, the sense-faculties always proceed toward their respective objects. The word "since" (*yataḥ*) is to be supplied [at the beginning]. The remainder is easy to understand. The Buddhists [assert] non-conceptual [perception].

They maintain that perception, as defined by the characteristics of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), has as its object the excellent characteristics of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and is thus non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), because it does not have as its object mental constructs such as names and so forth. Having considered this, the Blessed One accepted [perception] from you, having set aside the inferential [cognitions], because verbal cognitions and [other types of] valid cognitions are conceptual.
He states that even such perception is not to be denied:
"Due to its association with conceptualization (*vikalpa*), that very power is held to be twofold;
the apprehension of the mere intrinsic nature of the object is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*)."

That which is associated with the connection of name, genus, and so forth is conceptual (*savikalpaka*). That [other] power, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), is the innate, non-conceptual, and natural single power; it is that which is called "efficacy" (*arthakriyā*) because it is to be cognized as a single [entity]. Knowledge, due to its association with conceptualization, functions through the process of determination (*adhyavasāya*).

The phrase "is of two kinds" is to be supplied because it is a qualifier (*vyañjana*). Having supplied the word "this" (*idam*), [the two types are] "the thing" (*vastu*)—as in "this is Devadatta," "this is a Brahmin," "this is dark-complexioned"—and "the name" (*nāman*); let this also be supplied. As they say:
"That which is determined by the intellect is also accepted as being of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."

[Objection: But surely, when power (*śakti*) performs the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) of cognition accompanied by conceptualization (*savikalpaka-pramiti*), it appears as "this is pleasure" or "this is pain.

Because of the contradiction of an action upon itself, it is clearly perceived as an object of knowledge (*meyatayā*). [Response: True. Being inseparable from the intellect (*buddhi*) whose nature is that which is to be enjoyed (*bhogya*), it manifests through the manifestation of that [intellect], appearing as if it were not self-luminous despite being self-luminous.
Even if it is clearly perceived by that [intellect], there is no fault; as it is said in the *Ratnatraya*:

"In that regard, because of the failure to distinguish the reality of the intellect from its own inherent connection, the immutable Self, through superimposition, appears to possess the modifications that are actually functions of that [intellect]."

"...born, destroyed, manifold, possessing two kinds of happiness, or possessing suffering— it shows its own self as 'the atom' (aṇoḥ). Thus, he says that this threefold activity of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), consisting of both conceptualization and non-conceptualization,
comes into being:"
This [perception] is held to be of three kinds: dependent on the sense organs, independent of them, and likewise dependent on the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
This is easy to understand. While defining the threefold valid cognition (*pramiti*), he defines independent valid cognition (*nirapekṣapramiti*):

"In that regard, being independent of the senses and having completely abandoned all bondage, because of its infinite union with the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), yoga is naturally the supreme."
Among those three, it is independent of the senses because it serves as their defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). It is also independent of the internal and external organs;

for even in all ways and in its entirety, there is a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of consciousness by Ananta and the others, who possess a portion of the impurity of office (*adhikāra-mala*). This is the *baindavakalā*.

Since there is dependence on the *kalās*, even the portion of the *adhikāra-mala* (the impurity of office) is completely abandoned; thus, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is endowed with a remainderless abandonment of bonds. This non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpa-pramiti*), which is the self-fulfilling activity of the subject, belongs to the liberated Śiva and is connected to Śiva due to its infinite nature. Therefore, it is so because of the infinity of its objects.

According to the scripture, "it attains infinity through differentiation," the infinity of objects is known as yoga-mana (the mental state of yoga) because it possesses the relationship characterized by the knower and the known, which is manifested by its own nature. Self-awareness is its defining characteristic; its own cognition is preceded by a cognition that is free from conceptualization regarding all objects. Furthermore, this union is natural and is considered self-established.
As it has been stated in this very *Paśupata-paṭala*:
"In that same way, although they are omniscient by their own nature, their state of knowing only a little arises from a cause;
because [that omniscience] is obstructed, he is recited as being 'with impurity' (*samala*)."
Thus, the reading is *sarvadā* ("always"). In some places, the construction is *tadādāne sarvadāyogaḥ* ("in the case of taking that, there is always a connection").

This means "never, for anyone, at any time. This [is the view] of certain partial Śaivas who, being steeped in the scriptures established by other deities, seek to obstruct the contradiction with the scriptures established by Śiva; [this is] the meaning of this verse.

This has already been correctly established immediately above in the passage beginning with "the knowledge that is directed toward Him" (*tasyābhimukhi jñānam*), and the meaning of the verse from the *Paṭala* placed within one's own belly has also been correctly established by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha in the *Mokṣakārikā*: "Śiva is realized through the light of the power of Śiva’s sun, by means of the vision of consciousness."

Having brought the meaning of the verse beginning with "The Self perceives together with Śakti and the others" and "the function has departed" into its own domain and thereby rendered it trivial, [the opponent argues that] in the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra),

because the power of consciousness (cicchakti) possesses two parts— being both defiled and undefiled by ignorance (avidyā), attachment (rāga), and so forth— it exists indeed in a gradual sequence; thus, there is the subject (pramātṛ).

Form (*rūpa*) is of the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, when it is mixed with the activity of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*), it takes the form of the result of knowledge (*pramiti*). However, in the state of power (*makti*), because it is not defiled by ignorance, passion, and so forth, it is purely the nature of the knower (*pramātṛ*). Thus, for both the perfected one (*siddha*) and the seeker (*sādhaka*), when they shake off all instruments of cognition or when beholding Śiva and the like, [this is established].

Furthermore, since there is a deviation characterized by the defilement of *vidyā*, *rāga*, and so forth—which were fashioned by one's own conceptualization—within that which was fashioned as the very form of the authority of Śiva’s power, this conceptualization has been established by one who brings about its own subversion. Alas! How can this be conceived as useless? For it is not the case that even the slightest thing ought to be done by those who know the principles (*nīti*).
It tolerates this differentiation, for indeed:

by us, the Śaiva authority characterized by its own intrinsic valid means has been correctly understood as being directed toward Śiva alone; whereas by you, who have attained [knowledge] through the direct perception of the liberated Śiva, the power of Śiva (Śiva-śakti) is characterized by its own intrinsic valid means as being directed toward the liberated Śiva.

[The power] is defiled by ignorance, passion, and so forth; or else, is it undefiled? In that regard, if it were defiled, then its status as Śiva would be lost; thus, [the opponent’s argument that] the power of the bound soul (*paśu-śakti*) alone is the means of knowledge for both the liberated Śiva and the seeker is a mockery. If, on the other hand, it were undefiled, then because it would not fall within the range of the definitions of the means of knowledge as stated by you, [it could not establish] you.

In that case, its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be undermined. For where could the postulation of Śiva’s power as a means of valid cognition apply—to the liberated Śiva? To the practitioner (*sādhaka*)? Or to Śiva who is not the subject of dispute? Because [the power] lacks the attainment of its own self-nature, when there is the perception of the liberated Śiva and others by Śiva himself, it is simply the power of another Śiva.

Otherwise, an instability of the *kliṣṭa* (the afflicted mind) would result. Now, one might object: even though the power of Śiva (*śivaśakti*) is free from being defiled by *vidyā*, *rāga*, and so forth, it nevertheless manifests sequentially as the three forms known as the subject (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of knowledge (*pramiti*)—in terms of its own nature, its dependence on another, and its intended causal efficiency (*svārthakriyā*). If this is so, what wrong has the liberated one done?

In the *Paśupaṭala*, it is stated that consciousness— being common to both Śiva and the practitioner (*sādhaka*) as well as to their powers (*śakti*) due to their shared nature— is established by itself and is eternal, possessing a threefold unity consisting of the powers of the subject, the means of knowledge, and the result of knowledge, as well as the power of the object and its causal efficiency, occurring in successive order.
Furthermore, the Self is experienced as self-luminous by its very nature;
for it possesses the quality of eternally illuminating others, being eternal itself.

By such statements as these, it is established that [the teaching] is endowed with thorough examination. Regarding the phrase "it was spoken," and the statement "there is no knowledge directed toward that," it has been well-examined. Enough, then, with those teachers who, through despair, agitate the minds of ascetics and cause their intellects to become disordered. Indeed, [this concerns] the supreme life of the two-footed beings.

In the state where the fruit has been augmented by the recitation of the stages of liberation augmented by individual [practices], when the Siddha and the Śivasādhaka perceive objects such as Śiva through their power (*śakti*), they remain dependent upon both Śiva and Śakti;
thus we say that it is not Śiva-śakti alone that is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). True. [This concerns] the practitioner (*sādhaka*) who has commenced...

Because the bondage consisting of impurity (*mala*) and the rest has not been entirely destroyed—due to the persistence of residual karma, actions, and enjoyments—absolute cessation has not been achieved. Therefore, for the manifestation of one's own innate Śiva-nature every day, [one should practice] either through the empowerment by a mantra (*mantrādhiṣṭhāna*) or through the conquest of the bonds (*pāśajaya*), such that, preceded by the vision of one's own Śiva, there is non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*) as follows: at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*),...

In that way, for the sake of the fruit which is the manifestation of the state of Supreme Śiva (paraśivatva) through supreme contemplation (parabhāvanā), or for the sake of directly knowing the three categories beginning with Śiva, Śiva’s power— characterized as the power of consciousness (cicchakti)— manifests itself as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) by presiding over the Śiva-āgama; thus, it is the unqualified (nirupacarita) [means] with respect to Śiva, and likewise with respect to the practitioner (sādhaka).

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is said to be the seed of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), just like the eye and other sense organs. Now, one might object: "But surely *śivajñāna* (the knowledge of Śiva) is the [means of valid cognition]," because of the scriptural benediction of the Guru. Regarding this, some have maintained that when the practitioner perceives Śiva, the *śivajñāna* inherent in Śiva alone is the means of valid cognition. This is the talk of children; for in the case of the expression "the knowledge of a jar" (*ghaṭajñāna*)... [p. ...]

845) [The claim that] "the cognition of a jar is inherent in the jar" is laughable. Now, if it is argued that the cognition of a jar is inherent in the one who perceives the jar, then why is it not said that the cognition of Śiva is inherent in the one who perceives Śiva? Why this partiality? Therefore, it is called a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it manifests the means of valid knowledge.
A refined statement: Now, do not say that even for the liberated Śiva there is no dependence upon the power of Śiva; that is incorrect.

Because the bonds have been absolutely removed, and because the manifestation of Śiva-hood—which is produced in every respect and accompanied by the conscious power (cicchakti) constituting the relationship between the self and its Lord—is established, it is not possible for Śiva to be the presiding controller over the liberated Śiva.
Śiva-śakti is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being the manifestor of consciousness. Now, an objection might be raised:

just as a jar or similar object is not manifested when unattended by a manifesting lamp or other such factors, so too, if Śiva-śakti were not attended by a [higher] Śiva-śakti, there would be the consequence of the total disappearance of the manifestation of Śiva-śakti. This is incorrect; for, unlike a lamp, there is no absolute obscuration [of consciousness].

Furthermore, while effecting cessation (*nivṛtti*), it directly intends to express mere perfection (*siddhatva*) alone; and while expanding an unmanifested state similar to its own manifestation, it is established by the scripture (*śruti*) itself. As it has been said in the *Mokṣakārikās*:
The manifestation of the suggested meaning occurs only as long as the suggester is present;
it is argued that once the capacity is established, there is no further requirement for its repeated production.

The Śaiva power is that which effects manifestation; it is the state of being in proximity to Him. Because she has attained that [proximity], even the Siddha-power does not perish. Otherwise, if the Siddha-power—which possesses a manifestation equal to the manifestation of Śiva’s power—were dependent upon Śiva’s power, then for Śiva’s power as well, there would be another Śiva.
How could [Śiva] not be dependent upon Śakti? If he were, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, if the established Śiva is defiled by impurity (*mala*), then because of that dependence, he would be like one possessing all powers (*sakala-śakti*); thus, the return of the liberated soul to a state of transmigratory existence accompanied by impurity is well-established. [This applies] to the state of being dependent on the object of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-viṣayitve*).
Alternatively, if its object were only a portion of the categories beginning with Śiva, it would follow that it possesses impure contact and thus its perfect realization would be impossible;
consequently, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) would be contradicted. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:
"Those [categories] which perceive the manifestor are enveloped by impure powers."
It may be argued that those [universals] would remain unobstructed even while conforming to their manifesters.

Then, the supreme consciousness—which consists of the manifestation of the state of Śiva—is the established power of Śiva (śivaśakti). Just like Śiva and Śakti, even when there is ignorance of one's own nature, bondage exists;

thus, according to the manner previously described, having become one's own consciousness and being independent of any other internal Śakti, it indeed always perceives the mere existence of all objects such as Śiva and others as being essentially non-enjoyable. As it has been said:
"This consciousness is luminous by nature; the stains are adventitious. When these [stains] are removed, there is the indestructible manifestation of all objects. And in the *Ratnatraya*:
"Bondage belongs to the deluded self; liberation is the release from that bondage."
Whether bound in every way or liberated from the atomic impurity (aṇavamala), you are capable [of this].
This most exalted power, liberated from all veils, unfolds like the power of Śiva that illuminates all objects.
Having encompassed a very small portion of the objective field, one should clearly demonstrate it,
for the power whose nature is supreme consciousness is difficult to bind.
Only pure consciousness (paramātra) would shine incessantly for liberated souls;
consequently, they would be omniscient, but not knowers of mere consciousness (cinmātra).
"When the external exists, there would be knowledge of that object; however, because it is obscured by darkness (tamas), they do not become liberated. Thus it is said in the *Mṛgendra* as well.
"The power of agency in the individual soul is eternal, like the power of fire or that of the Lord. (p.

849) Now, an objection: knowledge that produces an effect does not exist independently of a substratum such as a body, because we observe a pervasion based on such dependence. Likewise, how could Śiva or a liberated soul (muktaśiva) possess [knowledge] without a substratum?

The statement that "the knowledge of the effect is [the definition] of the instrument" is refuted because it is inconclusive due to air (*vāyu*). Air, while having the body as its substratum, performs its own functions such as breathing through the nature of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth; yet, without a substratum, it also performs the function of shaking a tree.
Now, he defines [the instrument] as being dependent on the sense organs:
Furthermore, for the cessation of concealment, there must be dependence on the sense organs;
through the power of dependence on the sense organs, there occurs the perception of objects by means of them.

For the sake of removing [the notion of] concealment, with respect to the sense-faculties presided over by the mind (*manas*) which co-exists with knowledge and passion, it is self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) by virtue of its capacity; thus, it is first non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*). Furthermore, with respect to the sense-faculties assisted by the intellect (*buddhi*), it is conceptual (*savikalpa*), being mixed with the mental modification of egoism (*ahaṃkāra-vṛtti*) such as "I am."

Self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*). As previously stated, just as it occurs as conceptual (*savikalpa*), so too, through that [self-awareness], the observation of objects such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest is a valid cognition (*apramiti*) entirely connected to the subject (*mātṛ*).
Likewise, through the gateway of the pure senses, it is connected to the Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*) who is beginningless and infinite; this is independent of what was mentioned before.
And [perception] would otherwise depend on the external sense organs. Now, he defines that which depends on the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*):
"The connection of the power of consciousness with the object of thought depends on the internal organ, yet it occurs through the conquest of the external senses."

This occurs for the yogi due to the greatness of the qualities of attainment. Furthermore, through mastery over the external senses, having withdrawn the objects of the external senses as they arise— those that are present and desired— and having restrained them so as not to cause the external senses to rise up, he brings about volition (*saṃkalpa*), self-identification (*abhimāna*), and determination (*adhyavasāya*) in such a way that they are dependent upon the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The union of the power of consciousness, whose nature is meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), with the object of meditation (*dhyeya*)— consisting of the direct apprehension (*pramiti*) of things such as the fragrance of the *pārijāta* flowers, though situated at a great distance— is dependent upon the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). As it is said in the *Mataṅga*:
Whatever the lord of yogis desires with his mind, all that he attains at that very moment without a doubt, or wherever it pleases him.

Thus ends [the section on] that which is called perception (*pratyakṣa*). He states that perception arises from the contact of the sense-organ alone with its object: "The sixfold connection with the sense-organ alone is designated as perception;
the cognition of substances such as jars arises merely from the conjunction with the eye."
The cognition of a quality and its universal [arises] from inherence in that which is conjoined;
the cognition of "quality-ness" [arises] from inherence in an object that is inherent in what is conjoined.

Just as each [individual] possesses its own specific class-character (*jāti*), which consists of a totality of qualities (*guṇasamaṣṭi*) that are distinct from those of other classes and co-existent with those of its own class; and which, arising from a totality of various parts, is characterized by similarity; so too, in some manner, there is a simultaneous manifestation of this [universal] together with the possessor of the universal (*jātimat*).
Immediately following non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is the cognizer of the object and consists of a collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of qualities not delineated by words,

there arises the Abhidharma belonging only to a Brahmin and no one else; this refers to the individual and collective aspects of the genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*) characterized by similarity, which arise from the collective totality of the defining characteristics of the qualifier and the qualified.

[The cognition] is of the nature of a conceptual knowledge (savikalpajñāna) produced immediately after a mental construction involving doubt arising from poison; it consists of the grasping of the denotative power (*vācakaśakti*) regarding a substance that is a collection of qualities such as "darkness" (*śyāma*),
preceded by the grasping of the specific individual (*vyaṣṭi*) within a genus (*jāti*) characterized by similarity, as in "this is Devadatta," or "this is a Brāhmaṇa."

Prior to the apprehension of the individual instances of the quality, there is the cognition "this is dark"; prior to the apprehension of the individual instances of the genus characterized by similarity to that quality, there is the cognition "it is dark.

Through the three relations—conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), and inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*)—the substance possesses the substance, the genus, the quality, and the genus of the quality.
It may be so. Regarding the capacity of the fourth and fifth types of contact:
the apprehension of sound resides in the auditory organ by way of inherence (*samavāya*);
the universal "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) is perceived through the inherence of that which is inherent [in the substratum].

Because the sound of a lute or other instruments, whether consisting of phonemes or not, inheres in the auditory organ; the apprehension of sound occurs in the form "this is the sound of a lute," "this is the letter *ya*," and so forth. Valid cognition would thus be established through the inherence of the object inherent [in the sense organ]. This is because the word-sound inherent in the hearer’s [organ] possesses the inherence of "soundness" (*śabdatva*), which is the sound of the resonance (*dhvani*).

This genus [of sound] is "this is a sub-genus of the sound of a lute," or "this is a co-genus of the word-sound of a letter," or "this is a sub-genus of the word-sound of a specific form and letter"; thus, through the nature of similarity and connection with such sub-classes of the sound of resonance, the sound of letters, and the sound of words, there exists the universal property of "soundness" (*śabdatva*).

It is perceived.
