Now, one might object: since sound, whose nature is resonance (*dhvani*), travels to the location of the hearer along with its subtle substrate such as space (*ākāśa*) and its own qualities, how can there be a conjunction (*samavāya*)—due to proximity or similarity with the *sāttvika* [element]—between it and the innate auditory organ (*śrotra*), which consists of the *tanmātra*s such as the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) that serves as its own substratum? For this [conjunction] exists for my sake.

It is said that because it appears as if inseparable from that [the object], even though the designation "quality" cannot strictly apply to another quality, this serves as the basis for metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). How can sound, which consists of the bindu-syllable, be real?
Even for that, it is somehow metaphorically applied due to extreme proximity; this is stated according to the view of the Naiyāyikas.
Or, whether this is a figurative description or a literal one, there is no fault whatsoever. He defines the sixth [category]:
"For it exists as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or as a qualificand (*viśe�śya*) with respect to an object;
abiding in inherence (*samavāya*), it clearly manifests the object."

The cognition "inherence" is manifested by remaining upon its clear object. And that cognition may be either as a qualifier—such as "these threads [are inherent] in the cloth"—with respect to an object conjoined with the eye, ending with the inherence of the cloth;
or as the qualified—such as "here, in these threads, there is the inherence of the cloth"; or it may be the cognition of absence, such as "it is not here."

He states [the following] by way of restating "inherence": "Alternatively, through its inherence as qualified by antecedent non-existence, or by way of being a qualifier, non-existence is inherent; such is the established position."
Or rather, the established position is that non-existence is the qualificand (viśeṣya) and inherence (samavāya) [is the qualifier].

The concealment of the self consists in the state of a thing being restricted to itself, characterized by its own attributes and powers. And since it has been stated that non-existence is the concealment of the self consisting in a remote state, [it is understood] through the specific type of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva).

The established position is that "these threads possess the absence of a cloth" means "the ground possesses the absence of a jar," or rather, that the threads possess the inherence of the cloth by way of inherence; thus, the absence is [established] through its specific relation as inherence. This is expressed in the cases: "there is no cloth here in these threads" and "there is no jar here on this ground. Here, in the case of "there is no cloth in these threads," [it refers to] the relation [of inherence]. (p.)

Furthermore, if one were to postulate another relation [to connect inherence], there would be an infinite regress. Thus, whether it is expressed as "the inherence in the pot" (where the pot is the substantive) or "the inherence of absence," such is the established position. In this way, since it has been stated that even the sixfold relation of categories is perceived by the sense organ alone, it cannot indeed belong to the power of consciousness.
Having thoroughly examined the relationship characterized by the signified and the signifier with respect to external objects, [the following is considered]:
indeed, some describe an beginningless conjunction of the selves with impurity (*mala*), and furthermore, a beginningless and endless conjunction with Śiva;
others describe an inherence (*samavāya*) with those two; and still others describe them as being unconnected.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used here as a descriptive term. Therefore, the doubt arising from this [text] is indeed justified.

For, since the two related entities are inactive, formless, and in some cases conscious, the relationship between part and whole, quality and qualified, and genus and individual consists in being one of those [categories] that are inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddhi*) with their respective possessors of action.
Because [the relation] exists in some cases due to being sentient or insentient— given that these two reasons establish its non-existence—

it is, in every respect, too closely proximate; thus, even if it is in some way metaphorically designated as "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) or "inherence" (*samavāya*) in certain instances, there is no such thing as a non-metaphorical conjunction or inherence for the words "conjunction" and so forth heard here and there.

Since [the relationship] merely indicates a connection, the relationship characterized as the veiled and the veiler between the impurity (*mala*) and the Self (*ātman*) is also untenable because [the Self] is all-pervasive; therefore, by means of the expression "the host of bound souls" (*paśupaṭala*), it results in a relationship characterized as the controlled and the controller, due to the contradiction [otherwise]. Thus, it was stated by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha:

This has been described in the Mataṅgavṛtti, the Kiraṇavṛtti, and other works: although there is a dissimilarity (visādṛśya) characterized by the relationship between the one to be graced and the gracer during the state of bondage— which is caused by the limiting adjunct of impurity (mala)— there nevertheless exists an intrinsic similarity (sādṛśya) of the same class (sajātīya), known by another name [i.e., *vimarśa*], between Śiva and the self.

[He explains] the relationship. As the author of the *Vṛtti* said: "And because Śiva is of the same genus as the Self, [the relationship] is not one of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth. And the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha stated: "For that which is singular and self-cognizing, where could there be a connection? Even by means of *māyā* or by the *prakṛti* arising from it, the relationship characterized by seer and seen [is impossible]."

Even though it is innate, in the state of bondage there exists its own relation characterized by the status of being an enjoyer of objects of experience caused by karma, mediated through its own effects. It is not [a relation] such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), as established in the *Mṛgendravṛtti*:
"Conjunction, for its part, between the Spirit (*puṃs*) and Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) is defined solely by the relationship between the seer and the seen; it is not a mutual physical contact."
And in the *Matangavṛtti* it is stated: "Since both are indeed formless (*amūrta*), there is no impossibility of such a [relationship];

for the relationship between the formless conscious and the formless unconscious is distinct [from them]. And here it is said: "The transfer of the insentient into the sentient is logical, provided it is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*). Now, he defines inference (*anumāna*), which follows in the sequence:
Inference is that which makes known an imperceptible object through a firm pervasion;
and that [inference] here consists of five members: the proposition, the reason, and so forth.
These two are the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the fifth.

Through firm pervasion (*vyāpti*), the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), mixed with the modifications of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*), becomes the ground for the manifestation of the object to be proven (*sādhya*)— which is well-ascertained by the memory of its own duty— by means of the necessity of the concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyati*) between the means of proof (*sādhana*), such as smoke, and that which is to be proven.

Inference is that which makes known an object beyond the senses; it is defined as the cognition of the world-creator and so forth, which does not fall within the range of the senses. And that, being twofold—namely *svārtha* (for one's own sake) and *parārtha* (for the sake of others)—by virtue of being the cause for the realization of oneself and others, is further [discussed] here in this Śaiva scripture through smoke and other signs.

Strengthened by its own innate power (*svacicchakti*), in order to awaken another through its own intelligence, the inference— characterized as the cognitive power of the other person— consists of five members (*pañcāvayava*) when it takes the form of speech uttered from one's own mouth;
it does not, however, consist of five members in the manner of the Buddhist, Mīmāṃsaka, and other systems.

In this context, there may be either two members or three members. The description of the five members—such as the proponent, the opponent, and the cognition of the proof—is easy to understand. Having enumerated the five members in sequence, he defines them:
"The statement of the desired object is the *pratijñā* (thesis); the *hetu* (reason) is the statement of that which possesses its pervasion (*vyāpti*)."
The example is of two kinds; likewise, the reason is examined in the same manner.

In the examination of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there should be the expansion of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the application (*upanaya*). Furthermore, the restriction of the proposition (*pratijñā*) constitutes the conclusion (*nigamana*), which is accompanied by its reason (*hetu*). In this context, the proposition is the statement of the intended object as it resides within the subject (*pakṣa*), such as "this mountain possesses fire" and so forth; the reason, however, is the statement of that [subject] as possessing the pervasion, such as "because it possesses smoke" and so forth.

The statement of smoke and so forth, which is present in the subject (*pakṣa*) and possesses the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the desired object, is the reason (*hetu*). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*), however, is that which is endowed with the same properties as that [reason], such as the smoke and so forth in a kitchen, characterized by having its base clearly visible. The reason, such as the smoke on the mountain, proceeds according to the same mode [of being] as that [example], namely, the nature of the smoke in the kitchen. As for that which is stated... the nature of the smoke in the kitchen... [is the basis].
"Having smoke, it possesses fire, just as in a kitchen"—this is examined. The remainder [of the definition] is that this is the statement of examination (*parīkṣokti*).

The expansion of pervasion (*vyāpti-prastāra*) occurs through the examination of the example; thus, the statement of the ascent of pervasion, "and so too is this," is the application (*upanaya*). In the term *prastāropanaya*, the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) is due to its being Vedic (*chāndasatvāt*). Therefore...

"So be it"; furthermore, this [inference] is based on a reason (*sahetuka*). The restriction is the proposition (*pratijñā*). The statement of the proposition is for the sake of the conclusion (*nigamana*).
He says that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is as follows:
"The concomitance (*anvaya*) of the means of proof (*sādhana*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) by its own nature is called pervasion."
And that pervasion (vyāpti) should be known as twofold, consisting of negative (vyatireka) and positive (anvaya) concomitance.

From [the perspective of] Śrīmataṅgapāda himself: "In some cases, the property-possessor (*dharmin*) is established by means of its property (*dharma*); in some cases, the cause is established by means of the effect (*kārya*); and in some cases, the self is [established] through perception. According to this scriptural statement, the ground for the manifestation of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which serves as the direct means of realization for the practitioner (*sādhaka*) by way of being the property and so forth, is [the self].

The causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which constitutes the ground for the cognition of real entities (*bhūta*) through signs such as smoke, is the concomitance (*anvaya*) of fire and so forth; this relationship, characterized by the rule of association, is called pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Furthermore, that pervasion is to be understood as twofold, consisting of negative (*vyatireka*) and positive (*anvaya*) concomitance. This very point is made explicit [in the following].
Pervasion that is accompanied by positive concomitance (anvaya) is said to be known through the aspect of presence;
the other pervasion between the probandum and the probans is known through the aspect of absence (abhāva).

In that regard, that which is by way of the general [positive] aspect—wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen—is known as being preceded by similarity (*sādharmya*). That positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans is so called.
Furthermore, that which is by way of the negative aspect—where fire is absent, there smoke is also absent, as in a great lake—is [the pervasion of dissimilarity].

Because the property-bearer (the subject) precedes [the property], that other [type of] concomitance is known as negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Stating that inference is of two kinds based on such concomitance, he says:
"That means of proof is twofold: the perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and the generally perceived (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*)."
Among these, the first is the inferential indicator for an object that is not subject to decay.

That which makes known an object not perceived even through its own nature is "perceived generally" (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*). It is distinguished from the three types of reasons to be described by being common to both specific and general cases. That means of proof, characterized by the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*), is inference (*anumāna*).

It is of two kinds: that which is seen as distinguished and that which is seen as undistinguished. Of these, the first is inference from what has been seen; for instance, the causal efficiency of an object toward the senses serves as the ground for inferring that which is not capable of being perceived by the senses, such as the fire on a mountain, which is established therein by its own occurrence.

The effect of fire, such as smoke and the like— which consists of one's own experience and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and serves as the ground for the manifestation of the power of consciousness— is not seen elsewhere in a general sense; nor is it seen even from itself, nor by its own nature, nor as something immediately arisen, nor as being without conditions, nor in any other way, regarding that which has passed beyond the senses, lacks causal efficiency, and is [alleged to be] the creator of the world and so forth.

Furthermore, that which has arisen immediately, which is not yet obscured, and which is conditioned by its own existence and other limiting adjuncts—such as the blue lotus and so forth—is the inferential indicator (*anumāpaka*) in that case.

Therein, the property of being an effect of the world and so forth—which serves as the ground for the manifestation of the power of intentionality and purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) within one's own inference—is established through another reason (*hetu*). That [reason] consists of the creator’s attributes, powers, and so forth, which belong to the world.

And that includes the specific qualities of the blue lotus and so forth, such as its fragrance. Thus, having explained inference characterized by what is seen specifically and what is seen generally, he further states that it is of three kinds:
"Anvaya-vyatireka," "Kevala-anvayi," and "Kevala-vyatireki."
It is observed to manifest sequentially in the form of pure positive concomitance alone.
It is characterized as "purely positive" (kevalānvayin) by virtue of its purely positive form. The remainder is easy to understand. To the question of how it is said to be "perceived," he says:
"It is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma), present in the similar instances (sapakṣa), and absent from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa)."
It is unassailable, free from counter-arguments, and consists of both negative and positive concomitance.

In that regard, [the reason] consists of both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). The reason that possesses both positive and negative concomitance has five characteristics (*pañcarūpa*):

it is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), meaning it possesses the characteristic of being a property of the subject; it is present in the similar class (*sapakṣasatva*), meaning it possesses the characteristic of existing in the similar instances; it is excluded from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*), meaning it possesses the characteristic of being absent from the dissimilar instances; and it is uncontradicted (*abādha*).

Furthermore, [the reason] possesses the characteristic of having its object uncontradicted (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), and it possesses the characteristic of having no counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*). Regarding where the presence [of the reason] as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth is stated, he says:
"The *pakṣa* is that which is endowed with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); the *sapakṣa* is that which is endowed with a property similar to that."
Therefore, that which is contrary to the Dharma would be its opposite, namely, the arising of another cognition.
The two types of probanda possess the three characteristics; the presence of the similar class (sapakṣa) constitutes the dissimilar class (vipakṣa).
A reason that possesses positive concomitance (anvayin) has no dissimilar class, while the other [reason] has no similar class.

In that context, it has been stated that the fourth characteristic [of the subject] consists of being endowed with the property of the thesis (*pakṣa-sādhyadharma-yukta*), possessing the property to be proven which is still in doubt (*sandigdha-sādhyadharmavān*), being unsublated (*abādhita*), and having the state of being easily provable (*susādhyatva*). This is the sublation (*bādha*) of a valid reason (*saddhetu*) arising from another cognition, as in: "Fire is not hot, because it is an entity, like water. Here, against the valid reason [of the opponent], there is the sublation: "Fire is hot."

It has been stated that the fifth [condition] is "the absence of a counter-argument" (*asatpratipakṣatva*), which arises from other means of valid cognition such as perception by the sense of touch (*tvagindriya-pratyakṣa*). A "counter-argued" (*satpratipakṣa*) reason is one where there is no [valid] reason; for example, regarding two [conflicting] things to be proven (*sādhya*), there might be two [reasons]: "Sound is eternal because it lacks the properties of the eternal," and "Sound is non-eternal because it lacks the properties of the non-eternal. These are the two [types of] things to be proven.

Of those two probanda (*sādhya*), even though one [of the two] may exist in reality, the three-fold character (*trirūpatva*)— consisting of the property of being present in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth— is established without doubt as a mental construction (*svamanassaṃklipta*) by the proponent and the opponent. For this very reason, [the reason lacks the third characteristic] with respect to the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), such as space (*ākāśa*) and the like, which has been made a similar instance by the proponent alone.

When the opponent first employs a reason (*hetu*) against [the proponent's thesis], that [subject]—such as a jar which has been made the subject (*pakṣa*) by the proponent—is a "counter-example" (*vipakṣa*) with respect to the reason employed by the proponent. Such being the case, it constitutes "having a counter-thesis" (*satpratipakṣatva*); this is the remainder [of the sense]. "Without a counter-example" (*nirvipakṣaḥ*) means devoid of the form of exclusion from counter-examples.

And the positive concomitant reason (*anvayīhetu*) possesses three characteristics; that is to say, it lacks a dissimilar instance (*niḥsapakṣaḥ*), meaning it is devoid of the property of being absent from similar instances (*sapakṣe sattva-rūpa-vihīnaḥ*), and thus it possesses the three characteristics. Another is the negative concomitant reason (*vyatirekīhetu*). He cites examples of these two according to the tradition: "A mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke, just as a kitchen does."
The universe, as an effect, must exist as a real entity because it is presided over by someone.

Just as clay is dependent upon a potter, this positive concomitance (anvaya) further shows that an effect is produced only from what already exists; for an effect being produced does not arise from a non-cause.
A portion of the subject (*dharmin*) that is previously non-existent is like the horn of a hare.

Another place under dispute, such as a mountain and so forth, possesses fire because it possesses smoke, just like a kitchen; furthermore, for the sake of the negative pervasion (*vyatireka-vyāpti*), [it is] just like a kitchen.
The example "a pond full of water" should also be cited. A reason characterized in this way is both positive and negative (anvaya-vyatirekin):

the universe, which is the subject of dispute and consists of both conscious and unconscious entities, must be presided over—that is, governed—by someone endowed with specific knowledge and action, so that it may be an effect, performing its respective causal functions as a real entity.

In terms of its nature: it is inherently devoid of spontaneous activity because that is its very essence. For example, clay is dependent on a potter and is presided over by a potter. Furthermore, this reason is "concomitant" (*anvayin*), specifically a "purely concomitant" (*kevalānvayin*) reason. Whatever effect is not presided over by something [else] is not, by its own nature, devoid of spontaneous activity. For example, [clay].

"Such-and-such" [is the opponent's position]. Since no example is observed within the range of the opponent, the effect, being non-manifest prior to its manifestation, arises as something already existent by virtue of its nature as potency (*śakti*), its nature as persistence (*sthiti*), and its nature as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

By means of the causal factors (*kāraka*), it becomes manifest through the manifestation of its own potency, due to the reason of its being "that which is being produced" (*kriyamāṇatva*), which is the defining characteristic of being an effect (*kāryatva*).

That which previously lacked the parts, portions, or divisions of the properties (*dharmāṃśa*)—that is, the effect-entity (*kāryapadārtha*)—is not produced even by causal factors (*kāraka*) possessing unimpeded power, because it is non-existent, like the horn of a hare. This is a purely negative-only (*kevalavyatirekī*) reason for proving non-existence. Now, he defines the five fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*):
In this Śiva-āgama, five refutations of reasons (hetu) are stated:
the first is the non-establishment (asiddhi) of the reason when its presence in the subject (pakṣavṛtti) is not certain.

In this Śivāgama, five types of fallacies (*dūṣaṇa*) are stated, characterized by the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the counter-balanced (*prakaraṇasama*), and the mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), as well as non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*). Among these,

[the first four] arise respectively from the absence of the basis for the indication of the reason (*hetu*), the absence of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and the absence of its qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).

When there is uncertainty regarding the presence of the reason in the subject—either because the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) does not exist, or because the qualified (*viśeṣya*) does not exist, or because the subsistence in the subject (*pakṣavṛtti*) is not ascertained, such that the status of being a subject-attribute (*pakṣadharmatva*) is unestablished—this constitutes the first type of unestablished reason (*asiddhi*). This includes: unestablishedness of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), unestablishedness of the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*), unestablishedness of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), unestablishedness of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*), and unestablishedness of the qualified (*viśeṣyāsiddhi*).

Because the non-establishment of the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) is directly included within the definition of a reason, and because through that [non-establishment] the perception of all things as distinct would be possible, he illustrates the non-establishment of the essential nature:
"The atoms are the cause because they are eternal"— this is non-establishment by way of essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*).
Because the qualifier, the qualified, and so forth are unestablished, it consists of those very things.

"Atoms" refers to the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*). Regarding the reason (*hetu*) employed by the Naiyāyikas and others—namely, "because they are the cause of the world and because they are eternal"—it has been stated that the establishment of their non-eternality through reasons such as "being multiple while lacking consciousness" is well-established. Therefore, there is no establishment [of atoms] either by way of the definition of eternality or by way of their own nature (*svarūpa*). (p. 871) [The non-establishment of] their own nature...

This refers to "accomplishment" (*siddhi*). The atoms (*aṇu*) are eternal because they possess consciousness and are partless. Regarding the [syllogism] "because they are partless and possess consciousness," since the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and so forth are unestablished, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes such fallacies as: "The sky-lotus is fragrant, because it is a lotus, like a lake-lotus"; or "Whatever exists is momentary, like a mass of clouds."

In the case of the argument "sound and so forth are possessed of consciousness," because the pervasion of the locus (*āśraya-vyāpti*) is unestablished, there arise the fallacies of the unestablished qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*), the unestablished qualified (*viśeṣyāsiddhi*), the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), and the unestablished pervasion (*vyāptyasiddhi*); such is the distinction. He now defines the logical reason (*hetu*) that is vitiated by the fault of contradiction (*virodha*).
A present [reason] would be contradictory with respect to both the subject (pakṣa) and the counter-subject (vipakṣa).
It may be either pervasive or non-pervasive, depending on whether it is spatially delimited by its cause.

A reason that exists in both the similar class (*pakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), thus possessing presence in both the similar and dissimilar classes, and which lacks the required form [of being present only in the similar class], would be a contradictory (*viruddha*) reason. To illustrate: "The self (*ātman*) is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), because it is not limited by space (*deśānavacchinnatva*);
for example, like a jar. Here, the reason—on account of its non-limitation—is present in the similar class.

In a jar, which possesses the state of being pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya-vyāpakatva*), existence does not exist; furthermore, that [existence], being pervaded by the state of being pervaded by what is contradictory to its own probandum (*svasādhya-viruddha-vyāpakatva*) in the case of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) such as a *śiva* [or other non-existent things], is excluded from it. He now defines the logical reason (*hetu*) that is vitiated by the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anekānta*).
O twice-born ones, that which exists in all three states of the [three] propositions is the inconclusive (anaikāntika) reason;
"the self is eternal because it is knowable" is the example cited here.

That which lacks exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is called the "inconclusive due to being over-common" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*); this refers to the case where the reason "because it is an object of cognition" (*prameyatvāt*), when employed, exists in the subject characterized as the Self (*ātman*), in the similar example (*sapakṣa*) characterized as a jar, and also in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) characterized as Śiva. Now, it may be objected: "But was it not stated that 'being an object of cognition' does not exist in either Śiva or the Self? True; however, in that context...

Since it has been stated that the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is distinct from both the visible and the invisible, whose characteristic is that of the seer, and whose sole nature is the state of Śiva, proceeds as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by effecting a cognition of similarity through another mode,
there is no fault whatsoever— whether one considers this [similarity] to be metaphorical according to the Nyāya view, or non-metaphorical.
It should be understood that [the argument] "earth is eternal because it lacks smell," and so forth, constitutes an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) due to its being common (*sādhāraṇa*).
He defines the reason as being vitiated by the fault of non-ascertainment (*anadhyavasāya*): "The reason is not effective for the probandum when the subject is not ascertained."
"The universe exists as a continuum because it possesses substantial reality"—thus it has been stated.

A reason that exists in the subject (*pakṣa*)—characterized as the universe and so forth—in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—characterized by jars and so forth—and in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*)—characterized by Śiva and so forth—is not a prover of the probandum (*sādhya-aprayojaka*), yet it is cited as a determiner of the probandum (*sādhya-paricchettā*). How so? [Because] the universe is continuous and without gaps.

"It exists because it is a real entity, due to its undergoing both decline and rise, and because of its total dissolution. Now, one might object: "Is this not simply a case of *prakaraṇasama* (the 'equal to the point at issue'), which should therefore be defined and cited again? True; since that which is undetermined (*anadhyavasita*) is included within the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), it need not be treated separately.
However, that which has a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) must indeed be cited as such. Nevertheless, this very [point] concerns the counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*).

In order to indicate that [the fallacy] somehow falls within [the category of] *asiddha* (unestablished), it was [previously] set aside with indifference; now, [the author] defines the reason (*hetu*) as being vitiated by the defect characterized as "mistimed" (*kālātīta*), which is defined as follows: "The mistimed, however, is [that reason] where there is a contradiction between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*)."
The entire universe is without a material cause, because it is adventitious.

Because there is a contradiction with the means of knowledge regarding the probandum in the subject (*pakṣe*), due to sublation by valid cognitions such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the reason is "past" (*atīta*)—that is, it has been transgressed—at the time of its application; thus it is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) called "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). He illustrates this with the words beginning with "nirūpa," which serves to demonstrate the non-existence of the universe.

The Buddhists [Saugatas] maintain that an effect which possesses origination must not depend upon a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), because it is adventitious (*āgantuka*)—that is, it comes into being after having previously not existed. However, this thesis is sublated by the inference: "The universe possesses a material cause and has an origination, because it is something that has originated, like a jar and other such things," since we observe that jars and the like do indeed possess a material cause.

That which is "kālātīta" (overlooked by time) is that which is sublated by perception, such as: "Fire is not hot, because it is a substance, like water"—this is *kālātīta*. That which is sublated by scripture (*āgama*) is: "A human skull is pure, because it is a part of a living being, like a conch shell"—this is *kālātīta*. The distinctions such as "unestablished due to non-existence" (*asiddhi*) and so forth are not discussed here, as they are incidental.
Regarding the statement "it is expanded," the specific extent of its expansion is easily understood from other treatises.
Having thus stated the specific definition, he states the general definition of the modes of proof (*bhāsā*): "The correct cognition of pervasion is the means for the establishment of the probandum."
It is sufficient for any reason whatsoever to prove that which is non-existent.

The first recognized defect of inference is the failure of pervasion (*vyāpti-bhaṅga*). That inference which possesses a correctly uncontradicted cognition of pervasion— that is, whose means of proof (*sādhana*) is a correct cognition— is sufficient for the accomplishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) and for the inferential knowledge that necessarily descends upon the object to be inferred.

This concludes [the discussion]. Furthermore, since the reason (*hetu*) is non-existent, there is a breakdown of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of any path whatsoever—such as the failure to determine the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth.
It is considered that the first refutation applies to an inference that has been formulated after determining it to be existent. Pervasion...
To the question "What is refutation? he says:
"The proposition 'fire is not hot' and so forth is stated along with its reason.
Regarding the five members of an inference, however, [the refutation applies] to the first two.
The contrariety has been pointed out; now the illustration is being stated.
"Fire is not hot," and so forth—by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed), the counter-thesis (*pratijñetara*), and the thesis itself are included.
"With reason" (*sahetukam*) means accompanied by a reason, such as "because it is an entity" (*padārthatvāt*). These constitute the thesis (*pratijñā*) of inference.

Among the five members [of a syllogism], the reversal of the first two—the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*)—is designated by the term "violation of pervasion" (*vyāptibhaṅga*). Next, regarding the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is stated that its nature is "fallaciousness" (*ābhāsatva*); as to how this is so, he says:
When it is asserted that "the eternal self is all-pervasive like space," the example would be deficient in the property to be proven (sādhyavikala), and the same would apply to the proof itself.

The example, space (*ākāśa*), is devoid of the probandum because it has been examined as being produced from that alone [the atoms], and thus lacks the probandum characterized by the nature of being a grain of rice (*nīhya*). This means, in short, that it is a fallacious example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*). Furthermore, with respect to the proof—the reason characterized by omnipresence (*vibhutva*)—it would likewise appear so through that [example]. The meaning of the first half-verse, however, is clear.

Since various fallacies of the thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*), fallacies of the example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), and fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*)—when examined—are ultimately subsumed under the nature of fallacious reasons, their detailed description has been omitted; this should be understood. Now, he defines the means of valid cognition that is scripture (*āgamapramāṇa*).
Scripture is the word of a reliable person, and it is also the sole means of establishing objects that are beyond the reach of the senses;
provided, however, that the object has been well-ascertained through either perception or inference.
He who knows [this] is an authoritative person (*āpta*); therefore, he is the foremost among you.

By the term "authoritative" (*āpta*), there is the establishment of non-contradiction, fulfillment of expectation, semantic competency, and proximity; thus, an authoritative statement (*āptavākya*) is defined as a collection of words possessing these qualities. Tradition (*āgama*) is so called because things are understood (*āgamyante*) from it completely and without remainder.
That by which objects are known is the means of valid cognition termed "scripture" (*āgama*).
This scripture, being distinct from other forms of inference, is a means for establishing supersensible objects through its own inherent capacity as a proof;

it functions by manifesting the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) as its defining characteristic. It is a singular means for [establishing] objects that have not been apprehended through inference.
A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is not common [to others] is that which apprehends an object not previously cognized by the senses.

Even in the case of an object already apprehended by perception or inference, that [cognition] would be a valid means of knowledge if it were uncommon. For this very reason, its superiority exists. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "The superiority of that which has an immeasurable object over that which has a measured object."

Regarding the term "the wise" (*sūrayaḥ*): since [one might ask] who is an authoritative person (*āpta*), he says "pretya" and so forth. By means of this statement—whether in the form of the science of astrology (*jyotiṣa-śāstra*) or the like, or by means of a mantra-pāda or a treatise on spells (*mantra-śāstra*) stating that "through this conjunction, there will be an eclipse of the sun or moon, rain, and so forth"—the spell-mantra, when its own form is being uttered, immediately seizes its object.

When that [Rāhu] has become a part of the eclipse, it is well-ascertained that the sun is now eclipsed by Rāhu through direct perception; that rain and so forth have occurred in another region beyond one's own range of vision through inference based on the flow of river water and the like; and that poison has arrived through the cause of the body’s lack of well-being.
Furthermore, he who first speaks of a matter that has been well-analyzed because of his excellent discernment is an authoritative person (*āpta*).

As it is said: "He is accepted as authoritative because of the observed absence of poison and the like, because of the power of mantras, because of his voice, and because of [his knowledge of] the *rasopaniṣad*. Therefore, Śiva is authoritative, and by him [this teaching] was made manifest.

One who functions correctly with respect to all categories of objects is "more authoritative" (*āptatara*), which is to say, one who has attained the supreme [knowledge]. Now, if that is so, since even the Vedas and other scriptures possess authority precisely because they were composed by an omniscient being, it would follow as a consequence that all scriptures (*sarvāgama*) are authoritative.
To this, it is replied:
With a group of sense-faculties perfectly serene, omniscient, and having all things as his domain,
he is forever free from partiality and perceives things exactly as they are.
The immutable, the perfectly complete, the independent Lord of the fettered and their bonds— He alone is the authority, His word is the truth, and He is the eternal treasury of the highest good.

True. We do not raise the objection that there would be a lack of authority for the Vedas and other scriptures whose authors were Hiraṇyagarbha and others, for we indeed accept that they too are authoritative. Nevertheless, they were not composed by an omniscient being. But surely their authors were omniscient; as it has been said:
Because they are mutually contradictory. As they say:
"If the Sugata is omniscient, what proof is there for Kapila?
Or if both are omniscient, how can there be a difference of opinion between them?"
Even those who are not omniscient [are accepted] because, despite a contradiction in their manner of expression, they bring about the intended goal, just like the words of a friend or others;

this he will state later: "Their own words are authoritative. Of what nature is this Śiva, whose word is said to be "without a second"? (p. 882) He is one whose collection of sense-faculties is perfectly serene, free from the impurities of passion and the like; *indra* refers to the sense-faculties (*indriya*).

Because it is stated in the *Patipaṭala* that the form of Sadāśiva has its senses fashioned by the powers (*śakti*), he is one whose [senses] are thus constituted by a collection of powers. For this very reason, he is omniscient (*sarvajña*); indeed, because his own group of senses is tranquil, those who are the agents of [creation] and so forth are omniscient through their own [powers]. Śiva too is himself...

The claim that Śiva is not omniscient because he knows nothing beyond his own limit (*svāvadh*) is true; however, since for Śiva there exists no object beyond his own limit—being as non-existent as a hare’s horn—his lack of knowledge regarding such a thing is indeed an ornament, as described in the *Patipaṭala*. Thus, there is nothing inconsistent here. Hiraṇya...

Just as from conception onwards, until one’s own limit of human existence, there exists a non-realization of passion and so forth that obstructs the highest good (*śreyas*), how could this [non-realization] not also be an ornament? Thus, there is no room for doubt.
For this very reason, it is the object of all; it is the non-existence of everything other than itself above its own level, and it is the "all-above" (*sarvordhva*).

Its object is Śiva, beginning with the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha) and others who are beyond the range [of ordinary perception] yet within the range of its own perfected existence, down to the earth; for this very reason, it is free from partiality. Between the two—partiality toward that which is not one's own self and partiality toward that which is one's own self, characterized respectively by having conditions (sopādhi) and lacking conditions (anupādhi), and between the two consisting of the purposeful activity of one's own conscious power—there is a falling toward the side of that which is not one's own self, being oriented toward it.

[This refers to] partiality. At some time and in some place, the intellect (*buddhi*) belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha and others possesses the notion of the causal efficiency of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) conditioned by its own [limitations]. One who is not liberated from that is described as such. For this very reason, he is always a perceiver of reality. Starting from the beginningless [past], the notion of the causal efficiency of his own power ceases within his self; for this very reason, [he is so called].

The expenditure (*vyaya*) is distinct from Hiraṇyagarbha because its manifestation of power is not obscured internally; thus, it is characterized by a manifestation of power that is unobscured. For this very reason, it is "perfectly full" (*paripūrṇa*), being different from other [beings] such as Hiraṇyagarbha who possess limited powers, and it possesses the manifestation of supreme power. For this very reason, it is independent (*svatantra*), unlike Hiraṇyagarbha and the rest.

He is the awakener of consciousness and matter; for this very reason, he is the destroyer of the bonds of the bound (paśu). When the impurity (*mala*) is matured, he is the ordainer of the manifestation of Śiva-nature, which is characterized by the severing of the bonds of the bound—beginning with Hiraṇyagarbha and others—and the attainment thereof. For this very reason, his word is the scripture (*āgama*) arising from the mouth of that Śiva; it is true, uncontradicted, and possesses the power of conveying its own meaning.

The term *śreyonidhiḥ* (treasure of the highest good) uses the masculine gender because it culminates in the word *āgama* (scripture). It is the locus for the manifestation of Śiva’s power, which is the primary cause for the manifestation of the *śreyaḥ* (highest good) that is distinct from the mere manifestation of Śiva-hood. "The Buddhists are established in the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*), while the Ārhats are established in the *guṇas* alone"—such statements refer to those who have mastered and those who study these respective systems.

Because it first demonstrates the goal to be attained and then, by way of its nature as that which leads to the ultimate state of Śiva, [removes] attachment to objects not yet realized and so forth; it is the one, non-dual means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as stated in the *Vāyavīya-saṃhitā*:
Whatever is stated in other scriptures is found in the Śiva-āgama;
whatever is not seen in the knowledge of Śiva is not found elsewhere.

Thus, having defined the Self as that which is to be accepted by the wise because it is the supreme teaching of the Lord, the sequence of its manifestation from Śiva is declared: immediately after creation, the Lord [engages] the individual souls (aṇus) whose domain is the pure path (śuddhādhvan).
Having made [the senses] intense through the functions of seeing and acting by the mere touch of their own rays.
Even the Lord Sadāśiva has entered into the form of sound;
that knowledge consisting of the six categories is indeed manifold in its metrical forms.
To the east, he [bestowed] the ten-fold division of Śiva, as well as another;
or rather, from them, the treasure-house of compassion [bestowed] the eighteen-fold Raudra division according to the directions.

The Lord, in His state of authority, immediately after the creation by Śiva— and specifically immediately after the creation of the pure principles from Śiva down to Vidyā— selects from among the Vijñānākala souls those bound souls (*paśus*) whose impurities (*mala*) have matured to the point where they are fit to abide on the impure path, though they are otherwise objects of the pure path; He [selects] these as His own portions.

Merely by contact, there is no lack of actual union; thus, through the manifestation of their own innate power of action characterized by free will, may these [beings] be freed from their state as bound souls (*paśu*) and become possessed of the manifestation of their Śiva-nature.
Through the predominance of vision and action, they come to possess the manifestation of their own appropriate Śiva-hood.
Furthermore, having joined them with the Bindu-deity, the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva, the ocean of compassion and the merciful one, reflected:

"These men are seekers of the highest good; nevertheless, the means taught in the scriptures for bound souls (paśu-śāstra) are not sufficient to manifest their state as both Paraśiva and Aparaśiva. Therefore, I shall indeed create one great scripture for them. Thus he spoke.

I directly set [the Veda] into motion, and furthermore, having considered that other systems such as the Vedas grant progressively higher degrees of enjoyment and ultimate beatitude, I have proceeded by employing Brahmā and others who are fit to be their authors,
setting them in motion through my mediation; thus, at the time of dissolution, [the world] consists of objects impelled by Śiva.
In whatever manner, the power (*kalā-śakti*) consisting of sound, characterized by the syllable *u* and established as such,

having withdrawn its own causal power and manifested its own potency, remains having withdrawn the power of the *nivṛtti-kalā* characterized by the syllable *a*, which was possessed of its own causal power and manifested its own potency. Following that is the syllable *ma*.

The power of the *kalā* characterized by *vidyā*, having withdrawn the power of the *kalā* of *pratiṣṭhā*, remains as that which possesses its own causal power and possesses the manifestation of that power. Subsequently, the power of the *kalā* characterized by the *bindu*,
having withdrawn the power of the *kalā* of *vidyā* which was [previously] withdrawn into the *praṇava*, remains as that which possesses its own causal power.

Having manifested her own power (*śakti*), she remains as the possessor of power (*śaktimatī*), consisting of the aggregate of the four powers denoted by the term "the fourfold *bindu* of non-elevation. Thereafter, having caused the power that is the essence of *nāda* to dissolve into herself, she possesses the two names "the digit of *nāda*" (*nādakalā*)— characterized by the crest of sparks of her own poison— and "beyond peace" (*śāntyatītā*).

Making his own elevated state of mind the fifth digit of the *praṇava*, he remains manifest through his own power (*svaśakti*) after having ascended the power that has become identical with himself; for although he is connected to the power of the digit beyond peace (*śāntyatīta-kalā*) by means of his own resonance (*nāda*), he is nonetheless mounted upon the power of the digit of peace (*śānti-kalā*).

The power of the *śāntikalā* is thus described. Thereafter, the power of the *śāntyatītakalā*, characterized by *mahāmāyā*, having withdrawn the *nāda* consisting of the five parts of the subtle *praṇava*—due to the absence of its own manifestation and stability—remains possessing the power of its own effect, which is characterized solely as *nāda*. (p. 889) Then...

The fourth [state] is characterized by the four powers, because even *nāda* possesses the power of *śāntikalā*. Having agitated Mahāmāyā, who consists of form, at the commencement of the creation of sound, [the Absolute] proceeded from that agitated cause in the form of *nāda*. It emerged as the unstruck (*anāhata*) supreme resonance (*paradhvani*). Six.

Having made known the category of the object (*padārtha*) through the relationship characterized by the signifier and the signified, one should— by means of the sequence of vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *m*, starting from the *anuṣṭubh* meter— formulate the knowledge pertaining to the divine (*ādhidaivika*), which pervades the categories such as the Lord (*pati*) and so forth,
consisting of manifold meters. Now, in the venerable *Mataṅga*, regarding Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*)...

It has been heard that [the scriptures] are the source (*yonitva*) of mantra and tantra. This is true. The reason "source" is used as a metaphorical designation is that [the sound], having arrived there through the sequence beginning with *nāda*, attains the state of being the *mātraka* (the source-syllable). That very [source] is, first of all, the ten-fold division of Śiva, and likewise the eighteen-fold supreme Raudra [division], according to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the listeners.

Having performed [the rites] beginning with *tobhya*, this is the intended meaning: previously, he taught the twenty-eight tantras of the Lords of Mantras, such as Ananta and others, according to the sequence of the Great Current (*mahaugha*); following that, [he taught] the *kāmuka* and other [tantras] of the ten Śivas, such as Praṇava and others, who reside in the principle of Sadāśiva.

It should be understood from the *Kāmika* that he taught the *Vijaya* and other [Tantras] to the eighteen Rudras beginning with Anādi, who reside below the level of Sadāśivatattva; thus, their individual names are described separately. Among the *pralayakevalins*, having thus prepared those eligible for the office of *māyāgarbha-adhikārin*, [he empowered them] through the gateway of Ananta, pertaining to *māyā*.

It is also observed that, having endowed them with distinguished bodies, he taught the tantras according to the sequence of the great currents; now, the sequence of their descent from those [tantras] is declared:
from Meru, through the sequence of those respective regions, [the teaching reached] the ocean via the lineage of the masters.
In this regard, this Pauṣkara Tantra [is established] by omitting the explanatory passages (arthavāda) and so forth.
Having extracted [this] and explained it extensively with many arguments for the sake of the long-lived Brahmins,
establish this upon the earth along the worthy paths of the gurus.

By means of Ananta and other incarnators, as well as Praṇava and other incarnators, through their respective disciples, [the teaching] came from Meru and descended upon Meru in due order to various regions; thus, by changing the grammatical case, it is called the *Tantrasāgara*.
This ocean of the Tantras, characterized by the profundity of the meaning of the Tantras and so forth, was [received] within this ocean by Ananta, the incarnator of Śiva.

It was brought down by Mahāṅgha in the number of ten million; then it was brought down in the sequence of the *saṃhitā* by Śrī Devī in the number of one hundred and twenty thousand. Furthermore, it was brought down upon me by Anantāvatāraka in the number of one hundred thousand. And by Śrī Devī, through her descent, [it was transmitted] to her own disciple who was worthy of it.

It was brought down among the disciples. Having extracted the essential meaning from the *Pārameśvara-nāma-gīta-tantra* by omitting its explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and so forth, and having composed it in the form of aphorisms (*sūtra*), he made it the *Pauṣkara-tantra* and taught it; the remainder is easy to understand. By this, [it is shown that] the aphorism (*sūtra*) was indeed composed by Śiva himself, though he provided some introductory context as his own statement.

It has been shown that [the teaching] was well-composed and compiled. Now, it may be observed that it was indeed set forth by the sages (ṛṣis) in the form of questions. True; however, having perceived this, some scholars of the scriptures—because they see such a pattern even among contemporary authors of treatises—maintain that this scripture was set in motion by the Blessed One himself in the form of questions and answers.

They say that these questions were composed by the sages out of favor [toward humanity]; thus, it is faultless that they have been established on the path beginning with the Vedas upon this earth. Nor should it be said, "What is the use of them?"—this is indicated in the phrase "one means of valid cognition," which he now clarifies:
Furthermore, other paths such as the Vedas and so forth, which reveal the meaning of the fettered souls (paśu) and their bonds (pāśa),
are pervaded by the injunctions regarding the principles (tattva) taught by [Śiva] himself, and have Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others as their agents.

[The path] stands apart from the path of liberation through the enjoyment of heaven and other [worlds]. (p. 893) Furthermore, it is called *mārga* because by means of it, objects (*padārtha*) are sought after and examined. The Veda and so forth, whether established in oneself, established in another, or established in Śiva—that primordial [state], beginningless Śiva-nature—is what is studied.
And it does not demonstrate the establishment of individuality; rather, this is because [the Self] is conditioned by impurity residing in a different substratum.

Even if it demonstrates that Brahman is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), it does not recognize its own "state of being a bound animal" (*paśutva*)—which consists of agency and resides inherently in itself—as something actually residing in itself, but rather perceives it as if it were inherently residing in itself, though it is actually rooted in impurity and in objects.

"He shows" means he is the "revealer of the meaning of the individual soul (paśu) and its bonds (pāśa). Even so, he is not the "revealer of all sins," because he did not speak above [the level of] Puruṣa; thus, his own stated limit of reality is pervasive. For this very reason, he is not Śiva as the direct agent; rather, through the presiding presence of Śiva, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others act as the agents. Therefore...

The spiritual (*ādhyātmika*) [scripture] stands apart from the mundane enjoyments of heaven and so forth—enjoyments that are distinct from the supreme [liberation]—as it is directly composed by Śiva for the sake of the path to liberation. For indeed, scriptures are fivefold: those with visible results in this world (*laukika*), such as medicine (*āyurveda*) and the like; and those concerning the self (*ādhyātmika*).

The Veda consists of that which pertains to the seen and the unseen fruits... [the portion] consisting of the examination of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and categories (*padārtha*), such as Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika;
and the first part, consisting of the Upaniṣads, is the scripture of established tenets (*siddhānta-śāstra*). These are the [scriptures] of Śiva for the sages.

They raise a pointed objection as to how the teaching of the scriptures can belong to one who is devoid of a mouth and other such organs: "It has been stated that the path of knowledge proceeds from the partless [reality] in the form of sound; this would be illogical because of the absence of the organ of speech."

This is clear. Even for people such as ourselves, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) alone belongs to Īśvara, though it is veiled by impurity (*mala*). He refutes [the objection] that speech requires the organ of speech (*vāg-indriya*) by stating that he utters sound through the function of his own volition (*sva-saṃkalpa-vṛtti*); thus, there is no need for the organ of speech.
(p. 895) "The power of one who is independent of the organ of speech is released everywhere."
What wonder is there in its revolving by means of that [wisdom], which is absolutely pure?

The state of being a speaker consists in the power of one's own consciousness; from that [consciousness] proceeds the resonance (nāda) which is conducive to its activity, from which the emergence of the bindu occurs, and from that, the manifestation of words.
Words, however, indirectly indicate the knowledge of Śiva through their respective portions of authority;
for Śiva— who is utterly stainless and independent of the organ of speech— his power has issued forth everywhere toward all objects of knowledge and all effects.

The activity of cognition, characterized by the performance of its own purposeful action, has fallen away from that [state]. Because it possesses the power of cognition designated as the "power of will"— characterized by the volitional intention arising from itself— and because it lacks any other power of action, yet possesses the nature of protecting through speech,
it is called "upward-facing" (*ūrdhvavaktra*) when referring to those who are nourished by peace and are full.
What is this wonderful commentary on the Siddhānta scripture? What kind of speech of Śiva is being described?

Speech is the mouth of Nāda; it is the manifestation and emergence through its own volition from Mahāmāyā—who consists of the principle of Power (śaktitatva), whose nature is the power of Nāda, and who has cast her own womb within [Nāda]. But surely—
"According to the scripture, 'All scriptures have issued forth in the form of sound,' the Vedas and other treatises likewise emerged from them;
so what is the distinction of the Śiva-scripture [from them]? True. It is presided over by the power of Śiva.

It is distinct because it issues from the will of the power of a Person who is Śiva himself—not from that beginningless *guṇa* which is the source of the subtle elements (*ātmika-varṇa*) and other [material] qualities.

Even the direct word of Śiva is not intended here; rather, this *nāda* is the generator of the divine phonemes corresponding solely to one's own power of consciousness (*svacit-śakti*), characterized by the will that "let it be again composed of sound," [and] consisting of the syllables of the Veda... and so forth.
The emission (*nisṛti*) and manifestation (*samabhivyakti*) of that which conforms to one's own volition and is characterized by the Śiva-scriptures—

namely, the prior emission and manifestation of both the *bindu* and of sounds, having as their sole cause the character of the Śiva-scriptures— is the direct word of Śiva. This was stated by Sadāśiva in the Mataṅga[tantra]:

The *Nibandha* was spoken by the Lord in ten million verses (*koṭisaṃkhyayā*), and from that, the wise Ananta [abridged it] to a mere hundred thousand (*lakṣamātreṇa*). Indeed, this *Śiva-śāstra*, though consisting of words, is not like the Veda and similar texts which are obscured by the intervention of the powers of Brahmā and others, and thus rendered difficult to access; for it is directly manifested by Śiva himself. Regarding creation...

For a woman, [the creation] begins with the *nāda* and so forth. As it is stated in the *Siddhāntadīpikā*: "The creation of the *praṇava* pertaining to the divine (*adhidevika*) proceeds in the order of *nāda* and so forth;
its creation pertaining to the self (*ādhyātmika*) is considered to proceed in the order of the letter *a* and so forth."
This script was composed in due order by the supreme-minded God of Gods from his own form, for the purpose of imitating [the divine] speech... by him who is the end of all.
And thus, it has been proven that the whiteness of these lines and letters is material (*bhautika*).

The internal [reality] consists of the subtle *nāda*, *bindu*, and *praṇava*—namely the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*—which possess prior gross forms and so forth; that is the Śiva-śāstra. Because it arises from the understanding of the Śiva-śāstra, those such as Śivasamkalpa and Ananta perceive it. This is what is meant.

The Śiva-scripture, which is of the nature of Sound (nāda), emerged from Śiva through the Bindu and the Face; it was then again [rendered] by Śiva himself as the gross form consisting of phonemes (varṇa) and endowed with meters (chandas). Likewise, the Vedas and other [texts], though having emerged in the form of Sound, were again recited by the Paśu as the gross form consisting of phonemes and endowed with meters.

The *paśuśāstra* is that which is manifested by Brahmā and others through their own illusory effects and instruments (*kāryakaraṇa*), and is characterized by the powers of action (*kriyāśakti*) whose nature conforms to their own [limited] earth-element (*mṛcchakti*). It is thus figuratively designated as such within the *Śivaśāstra*.

Furthermore, it possesses the characteristics of the Tantras known therein as the Left (*vāma*), Right (*dakṣiṇa*), and Central (*gārūḍha*), and it serves as a source for other streams of revelation (*śrotontara*) as well. (p. 899)

Even though [these scriptures] were composed by Śiva, some maintain that the Siddhāntas—such as the Kāmika and others—which originate from the mouth of Īśāna, are the most excellent because they primarily bestow spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). Furthermore, they hold that these [Siddhāntas] are taught by an internal self designated as Śiva, who is presided over by specific forms such as Tatpuruṣa and the rest. On the other hand, the Gārūḍa and other [Tantras] are [presided over by different forms]. Because they have Īśāna as their primary face, they are superior. Thus, the Siddhānta originating from the mouth of Īśāna is the most exalted. As for the Gārūḍa and so forth, however, they are taught by another self known as Śiva, who is specifically presided over by the forms of Tatpuruṣa and the others. Some say this.
The teachers [object]: "But it is not heard anywhere that the *Kāmika* and other scriptures originate from the mouths of Sadyojāta and the others. True.
However, there is no fault, because even for the form of Īśāna, there are five faces beginning with Sadyojāta, and he possesses fifteen eyes.
[The opponent objects: "But in the *Kāmika* and other texts, it is heard that the Vedas and horses again emerge in sequence from the mouths of Sadyojāta and the others."

True. It arises from the four faces of Brahman—designated by those names and presided over by the forms beginning with Sadyojāta—and superintended by them; for although there is a pleasant scriptural passage stating that it arises from the face of Īśāna, even that [face] is described as having five faces and three eyes. (p. 900)
And there is nothing inconsistent in the statement that "it must be explained. Thus it is said in the Svacchanda Tantra:
"One should not revile Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, or the Veda, because they all originate from Śiva and bestow the fruit of liberation."

But surely, the *Kāmikā* and other scriptures, arising from their own power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) along with their essential principles (*sāraka*), are further constructed by means of the sense of speech (*vāg-indriya*) once they have been brought forth? True. This is so regarding the phonemes (*varṇa*) that are internal (*ādhyātmika*) and constructed by the practitioner.
In those places corresponding to charcoal, the fires corresponding to Śiva— the divine manifestations—

become manifest through the power of Śiva; together with Śiva’s energy (śakti), they manifest and empower the respective consciousness-powers (cicchakti) of the practitioners, demonstrating all categories beginning with Śiva for the sake of manifesting their own state of Śiva-hood.

Everything is incorrect. In whatever way it may be, having been studied through various means, we have perceived the words characterized by the Śiva scriptures among the sounds uttered by us; however, these could not have been [perceived] by those who are not omniscient due to their lack of power.

And because they are neither sequential nor non-sequential, but rather through a lineage of teachers (*guru-santati*) in reverse order (*pratiloma*), these words—well-considered and well-practiced—are characterized by omniscience and fashioned by the power of the Creator. Because they have all objects as their domain, they serve as the basis for a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatireki-anumāna*) that indicates the knowledge of Śiva; thus, they are the power of Śiva.
The commentators then state the following objection:
"Alternatively, [if it were so], the virtuous would not have attained that which is beyond the scope of Śiva through faith;
yet other good people have indeed reached the spheres of primordial nature (prakṛti) and the like."
Therefore, the understanding of the words of Śiva arises from his speech and not otherwise;

or rather, that which pertains to Śiva—namely, the knowledge of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth concerning the domain of Śiva—which has not been attained or known by the virtuous who will speak of it [on page 902], [is what they seek]. Thus, they have come to the virtuous.

Words composed by ṛṣis and others that are dissimilar to those [scriptures] naturally have worldly objects as their domain; they are distinct from the words designated as the Siddhānta and Āgama produced by Śiva, which are rich in yoga and characterized by the status of being the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) and the absence of a prior position (*pūrvapakṣa*). As it is said in the Kāmika:
The knowledge that reveals Śiva is remembered as the supreme Śivajñāna;
it is the higher realization beyond the Vedas and other sciences, which reveals the true nature of both the bound soul (paśu) and its fetters (pāśa).
Just as the eye is distinct in its capacity regarding objects at night and during the day, so too is knowledge distinct; thus is this [reality] both supreme and non-supreme.
For those [objections] were indeed stated by Śambhu as the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) for the sake of determining,
in accordance with ultimate reality, what among the garments is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.
"Having set all that aside, one should take refuge in the Śiva-siddhānta.
Thus it is said in the *Ratnatraya*:
"The Siddhānta alone is the Siddhānta; all others are merely prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣas*)."
"But the Self alone is Śiva; all else is considered non-Śiva.

Thus, from that [statement], there arises the understanding (*bodha*)—the knowledge of the meaning of one's own sentence—of the words of Śiva, the sounds originating from the mouth of Śiva. However, this understanding is "non-understanding" (*abodha*) by virtue of the speech that will be spoken hereafter; it is a "misunderstanding" (*vibodha*), meaning an understanding that has departed or been sublated.
Why is it not sublated? He says: because of its superiority—"Neither is the word of the Ṛṣis [sublated] by human speech, nor is the divine [word] likewise;
nor is the word of Brahmā [sublated] by the gods, nor is the Vaiṣṇava [word] by birth."
Likewise, the Raudra [tattva] is not sublated by Hari, nor is that which has Śiva as its essence sublated by Rudra;
for due to the increasing excellence at each higher level, what is below is sublated by what is above.

This is clear. Nevertheless, he states that it is not invalid: "All scripture is established in accordance with the Śiva-āgamas, and not in contradiction with other scriptures, because it is in harmony with them—or rather, because it is their purpose. (p. 904)
The Śiva-śāstra is to be established as the all-pervading [principle], since it pervades that which is pervaded.

When the confusion regarding contradictions, parts, and portions has been dispelled by the Śiva-śāstra, everything composed by Rudra and others— such as the Kapāla and other systems— is in harmony with the Śiva-āgamas through non-contradiction with the Śiva-śāstra.

Because its scope is limited to minor matters, it is established as authoritative—just like perception and other means of knowledge—but the Śiva-śāstra is not [established] by way of non-contradiction with other scriptures. Alternatively, it is to be established and made authoritative by way of being in agreement with them, through statements that bring about harmony with other scriptures. Why? Because:
That Śiva-śāstra is authoritative because it makes known meanings that have been either previously understood or not yet understood by other scriptures.

It is the counteragent to one's own status as being outside the Veda (*vedabāhya*), as a heretic (*pāṣaṇḍin*), or as a fabrication of evil intent. One should first establish oneself in the Vedic [tradition] and only afterwards take refuge in the Śaiva [tradition]. The Buddhists are situated in the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*).

"The Arhats are established in the qualities alone," and so forth; by such statements which favor the Vedas and other scriptures... [regarding] "other perspectives" (*dṛgantara*)... he says that even those other perspectives do not abandon their own validity within their respective domains:
"For whatever scripture has whatever extent of scope that is intended..."
O Brahmins, the authority of each one of those [scriptures] shall be exactly as much as that [of the Veda].
That [limit] is easily understood and has been demonstrated in the *Buddhiparīkṣā*; therefore, it is not written here. Now, one might object:

"If this is so, then even the Śiva-āgama would lack authority beyond its own temporal limit, because the necessary pervasion (*vyāpti*) is impossible, just as in the case of the Vedas and other scriptures. True. Regarding the Śiva-āgamas, beyond their own temporal limit—

Since an object not seen in any other scripture is as insubstantial as a hare’s horn, the lack of authority of [other scriptures] in that regard is indeed an ornament [to the Śiva-āgama]. Nor should it be argued that because the object of the Śiva-āgama is insubstantial after the limit of the Vedas and so forth, the authority of the Vedas and others in that regard is an ornament; for [the Śiva-āgama] is established by means of the *sadbindu* and other [authoritative sources]. (p.)
906) Now, having indicated presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he examines verbal testimony (*śabda*):
"When the scripture has thus been described, the remainder is stated;
and that is the demonstration of the reality of liberation established by other treatises."
Therefore, if anything whatsoever is contradicted by the Śiva-tantra, it undoubtedly leads to the conclusion that [the contradicting work] was composed by one who is not omniscient.

The means of valid cognition known as presumption (*arthāpatti*) is described in another way. When the traditional authority (*āgama*) has been stated in this manner, the remaining means of valid cognition called presumption is now being discussed. How is it illustrated? By demonstrating the reality of liberation as established in other treatises.
Since [the teachings] beginning with the Vedas other than the Śivaśāstra are connected to Brahman and so forth,
their characteristic is the exposition of liberation as having the nature of [Brahman]; therefore, because they speak of non-duality (*advaita*) and so on,
if some scripture were to be directed toward cessation (*uparama*) once again, it would be exactly as it is.

The doubt regarding the Vedas and other scriptures is sublated by the Śiva-mantra— which cannot be refuted by any other means of knowledge— and by the teachings of the Śiva-scriptures, which are adorned with the exposition of the reality of liberation; thus, for the sake of bestowing grace, the delusion concerning the doctrines of non-duality and so forth is dispelled, and one's own non-duality and such are established.

Through the presumption (*arthāpatti*)—also known as postulation (*kalpanā*)—arising from the fact that the impossibility of the scriptures being otherwise (i.e., being composed by someone other than an omniscient being) must be explained, one should infer, or postulate, that the causal efficacy of the power of consciousness establishes that these [scriptures] were composed by an omniscient being who knows everything up to the limit of what is knowable by a limited knower; thus, it should produce a cognition reinforced by that [postulation]. Otherwise, and...

It is concluded. Furthermore, presumption (*arthāpatti*) is illustrated by another method. To the question "How so?", he says: "That which is observed—non-omniscience—would necessitate its own substratum, namely 'animalhood' (*paśutva*), provided that omniscience is established by scripture."
And that [cognition] is distinct from inference because their objects differ;

it is established by scripture through the characteristic of sublation. By means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arising from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the causal efficiency that constitutes its own sublation, [the existence of] an omniscient author is established, in whom resides the state of Śiva characterized by omniscience.
While the name "Śiva" remains established, [the opponent's position] is rendered false. Alternatively, disregarding the presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on scripture,

when there is a tradition arising from his own mouth regarding Śiva— who is known through that [tradition]— and if the reading were instead *siddhavat punaḥ sārvajñaḥ* (as if he were already established as omniscient),
then at that time, that which consists of consciousness, light, and action exists eternally within the Self, and from all sides.

Since it is heard from the scriptures of the Lord of Beasts (*mṛgendra*) and others that the Self is established as being eternally situated in omniscience— characterized by the state of Śiva— and is further elevated by means of the scriptures consisting of the various Vedas and so forth,
which have the nature of sublation, because its own sublation would otherwise be impossible.

The establishment [of the probandum] through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arising from the fact that non-omniscience and limited knowledge— observed in living beings characterized as having their own agents, or otherwise— are otherwise inexplicable,
serves to establish its own cause by means of a conscious power (*cicchakti*) which assists in its own causal activity and brings about its own production.
One should conceive of that which is designated as "animality" (paśutva) by the name "impurity" (mala). One should cause that [impurity], when reinforced, to produce valid cognition;

and that is the means of knowledge called presumption (arthāpatti), which is distinct from inference. For it cannot be intended by the Naiyāyikas as a purely negative inference (kevalavyatireki-anumāna), because of the difference between those two: inference and presumption.

Because the distinction of the object leads to a distinction of its own result, the fruit of inference (*anumāna*) is the inferential cognition produced by the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*). Because that [recollection] would be delayed if there were no opportunity for the recollection of pervasion,
the fruit of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is the postulation of an object as the cause of another object, based on the fact that the perceived object would otherwise be inexplicable.
Because one's own cognition is distinct [from the object], there is no opportunity for the recollection of a pervasion due to the delay of the consciousness of existence;

thus, the mention in the Āgamas of the inclusion of comparison within inference is merely according to some manner of speaking. Now, it may be objected that the Naiyāyikas have described comparison as a separate means of knowledge. True; however, this is not so in our established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

The state of being the same is *sāmānya* (commonality); indeed, similarity itself is the universal (*jāti*). For instance, a certain city-dweller, having heard from a forest-dweller that "a gavaya is like a cow," and having previously experienced the universal of cowness (*gotva*), recognizes it again through that commonality as "this is that very same cow," and thus having made the recognition perceptual, [he perceives] the similarity once more.
Because there is some dissimilarity [between them], a specific type of cow is inferred to be like a specific type of human, such as a Kṣatriya; therefore, it is not described separately.

Having thus examined the category of *pāśa* (the fetter) along with its manifold details according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), the order of its withdrawal (*upasaṃhārakrama*) is now stated:
In this way, for objects established by valid means of knowledge, the withdrawal and emanation must be understood through the relationship of cause and effect, even when they appear to be reversed.

"In reverse order" means by way of inversion. Now, one might ask: for what purpose is the withdrawal of the causal subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth—prior to their effects such as the gross elements—considered necessary? [The author] replies: "Because the cause is pervaded by its own effect. (p. 911)
It is not logical that the withdrawal of the cause occurs first through the withdrawal of the effect;
rather, the withdrawal proceeds from the final effect, such as the earth.
But how is it that [the intellect] reflects the effects? To this he says:
"The gross elements are in the subtle elements alone; the subtle elements and the senses are in the ego;
and the mind is in both, as well as in the qualities."
Those qualities, along with the pentad beginning with passion and ending with the final state, undergo dissolution into Prakṛti; but she (Prakṛti) is eternally established within Māyā.

It should be understood that she governs [the soul] sequentially, with the intellect (*buddhi*) being her instrument; *prakṛti* consists of the triad of *rajas*, *tamas*, and *vidyā*. Through the medium of *kalā*, [this occurs] within *māyā*, not directly. ...

[The passage beginning with] "not knowing" and so forth should be understood as the dissolution of the *puruṣa-tattva* itself, characterized by its separation from the fivefold covering of *kalā*. [This concludes the] *Vindupaṭala*.
The path of purification dissolves into the *bindu* above *māyā*;
