the *bindu*, whose nature consists of the powers beginning with *kalā*, has its form presided over by Śiva.
It remains eternally before this Śiva as the very essence of his objective field;
then the universe proceeds again, beginning from the *bindu*.

The pure path consists of the principles (*tattva*) known as dissolution (*laya*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and agency (*adhikāra*). It is characterized by the principles of Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā.
Here too, let the relationship of cause and effect be understood to apply. [The principle] beginning with *kalā* is of the nature of *śakti*;
[the principle] beginning with *śānti* is the power (*śakti*) whose form is the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of *kalā* and the others.

By the phrase "by way of having the object as its nature" (*viṣayātmatayā*), he clarifies in the *Paśupaṭala* that, unlike the Vedāntins or certain followers of the Buddhists, cognition does not lack an object (*nirviṣayatva*). The rest is easy to understand. An extensive treatment of dissolution (*pralaya*) and the sequence of worlds (*bhuvanapaṅkti*) is found in the *Śrīmataṅga*; [specifically] in the *Pralayapaṭala*, the *Māyāpaṭala*, and so forth.

Therefore, having grasped what has been revealed by the commentary composed by the illustrious Rāmakaṇṭha, I shall expand upon it here out of fear of prolixity. Now begins the chapter on the descent of the Tantra (Tantrāvatārapaṭala).

Now, in order to clearly understand the origin of the Tantra— which was previously indicated by the statement that the diverse world proceeds again from the *bindu*, giving rise to the recollection of the Mantras within— the disciple asks the Guru: "How did the Tantra originate, along with the Mantras and their Śaktis?"
How many are its divisions therein, as well as their means of accomplishment and their establishment?
"O Supreme Lord, tell us all of this in brief.
Because it is incidental, no separate connection is intended [to be stated].
However, due to the abundance of repetitions, this is not a chapter from the Pauṣkara; rather, it is according to the Kāmika."
The masters say that some have interpolated this very chapter on the introduction to the *tantra* here;

they further state that because the statement in the response is somehow a different kind of expression possessing a melodic quality (*gītimat*), it cannot be considered a mere repetition. Others, however, say that for that reason, the commentary does not in any way attempt to abbreviate it.

The *sādhana-mantra* is that which brings about subjugation by means of the powers (*śakti*) such as Ambhikā and others; its fruit is *siddhi*. The rest is easy to understand. The Lord says: "In the beginning, the supreme Brahman, being pure, attained the state of the primordial syllable."
O you seven twice-born ones, listen to that which has attained the state of Tantra and Mantra.

Because it is Brahman, because it is the state of being Brahman, Mahāmāyā, which is designated by the word "Brahman," first attained the form of the *vidyut* (lightning-like) resonance; thereafter, it assumed the nature of the primordial phoneme (*ādivarṇa*), reaching the state of mere form and the state of having form. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:
The *ṇāda* (vowel) of the power (*śakti*) becomes the *bhindu*, which consists of a single syllable; this is the distinction. The rest is easy to understand.
Now, as to how this occurs, he says:
"When the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is present, the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is the cause."
By his very nature, he is supremely intent on bestowing grace upon all living beings.
True. To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"Then, in the face of Time, through union with Śiva’s power, by the will of Śiva alone, I am the immediate cause for the arising of all."
The entire universe was then agitated by the causal *yogamāyā*.

At the break of day, when the time for creation had arrived, [she]—acting as the power of Śiva (*śivaśakti*) while performing the act of preservation—was to be protected through union with the cause of the universe, characterized by the Great Māyā (*māhāmāyā*). This is due to their connection.

When Śiva’s power (*śivaśakti*), performing purposeful action characterized by conceptualization (*saṃkalpa-lakṣaṇa-artha-kriyā*), gradually [attains] the state of authority (*adhikārāvasthā*)... then, through the emergence of a connection with the agitation (*kṣobha*) of that which is to be agitated (*kṣobhya*), it becomes so; thus it is stated in the *Yogamataṅga*. So it has been said.

Because she brings about the power of Śiva’s action (*kriyāśakti*), she is called *māyā*—that which "measures" (*mayati*) or "effects" (*karoti*) the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*). Thus, it is said that through her, the creative intent (*saṃkalpa*) and purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) arise; in that *yogamāyā*, the cause of the universe, characterized as the *bindu* and possessing the quality of agitation (*kṣobhitva*), came into being.
To the question "What [happened] after that?", he says:
From the agitation of that [state], the Śāstra arose in the form of sound;
and from that, slightly below, Śiva appeared in the form of a flame.
And that [point] is known as the *bindu*, an arrow with a radiance like the moon; this is easy to understand.

That *bindu*, having first become the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), then becomes the three lines characterized by the vowels beginning with *ā* and the goddesses beginning with Lakṣmī; thus he says it exists in the form of various lines:
He is declared to be the fourth, the supreme treasury of the luminaries;
the Bindu is agitated by the will of Śiva, and below that is the energy Ambikā.
Then, from that, there arose the three powers (Śaktis) possessing the form of the full moon with its crescent:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise Raudrī, resembling a sleeping lord of serpents.
Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Śṛṅgā abide as your left staff;
she is Māyā in her other form, celebrated as Jayā (or Tyā).
Jayā, Vijayā, and also Jitā and Aparājitā;
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Sthiti.
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, and the supreme Mocikā;
likewise Vyomarūpā, Anantā, Anāthā, and Anāśritā.
All this, from Śiva down to the realm of the earth, is pervaded by these;
from them have arisen all the thirty-two letters.

The meaning is that, having become composed of speech in the manner to be described hereafter, they attain [their state]. He states that when the *kalās* such as Ambikā and the others are joined together, the phonemes beginning with *a*, *ā*, and so forth—which are the forms of the *kalās* of the *praṇava*—emerge:
"Raudrī is situated in her head; Vāmā is proclaimed to be her mouth."
Ambika has her arms clinging [to him], while Jyestha stands like a staff.
This letter *a* is well-known; now hear, O twice-born ones, about the letter *ā*. This very same second vowel is distinguished by a staff (*daṇḍa*) placed at its top.

Out of fear of prolixity, I have not described the characteristics of the remaining [energies]. Among these— Ambikā and the others, who consist of vowels, bindus, and kalās— the energy Raudrī resides upon the head of whichever letter by means of her own head-form, while Vāmā is proclaimed to be its mouth by means of her body-form.

Vāmā is situated [to the left]. Ambikā is situated with her arms joined to the outside; she is the outer self. Jyeṣṭhā indeed stands like a staff; because of her own length, Jyeṣṭhā stands like a staff. This is the phoneme; Jyeṣṭhā is situated, and this phoneme is renowned as the letter Ā. This very [phoneme] is the letter A, by virtue of its own non-grasping.

By means of the staff (*daṇḍa*) and the elder [vowel] (*jyeṣṭhā*), the second [consonant] is joined with the vowel *ū* and the letter *ā*; thus it is renowned as the first among the *śleṣas*, beginning with the vowel *ī*. The rest is easy to understand. Now, indeed...
the power (*śakti*) that has arisen from the subsequent syllable... is divided into Ambikā and others, appearing in the form of the fifty letters.
He says that she is the benefactress of all:
"Her power is known to be non-different [from Him], fivefold and yet divided ten ways;
she should be understood as the benefactress of all, embodying the form of every word and its meaning."
Without them, however, there would be no word, nor would there be the comprehension of the injunction through its meaning;
therefore, they are proclaimed to be the abode of all accomplishments.

The rest is easy to understand. The phonemes, consisting of both tantra and mantra, arise directly from the cause that is Śiva... [arising] from that... their single, non-dual source is that light which is the Supreme Lord.
The Lord is their efficient cause (nimitta), and that Bindu is the sovereign material cause (upādāna).
Because it arises through the cooperation of its own karma, the effect is therefore possessed of a cause.

The supreme splendor of the Lord, Śiva’s power, having become the presiding subject over Mahāmāyā, is the producer of *nāda*; and having become the presiding subject over *nāda*, it is the producer of the syllables and *bindu*.
Having become the presiding deity of the *bindu*, she is the producer of the *kalā* of the *bindu*, such as Ambikā and others;

furthermore, having become the presiding deity of the *kalās* and bearing their names, she is the womb (*yoni*)—that is, the agent and the auxiliary cause (*sahakāriṇī*)—and the instrument (*karaṇakāraka*) for those letters beginning with *A*. The rest is easy to understand. [This applies] in the case of insentience (*acaitanye*).
Because they are multiple; because they are effects; and because they possess causes—therefore he says:
"The *bindu* is the material cause (*upādāna*), for the phonemes (*varṇa*) do not know that.
The phonemes exist in many ways, being produced and dependent upon consciousness."
Letters, through their conjunction with vowels, constitute words; and words, together with their endings, are held to form a sentence.
From that, the comprehension of meaning arises, which serves as the basis for worldly transaction.
The consonants, beginning with *ka*, [attain their specific forms] through conjunction with vowels—that is, through connection with *ā* and the other vowels. The rest is easy to understand.
He says "it is said" regarding that which consists merely of the collection of letters beginning with *ā*:
"The Mother of All-Knowing Wisdom is to be known; she stands like a mother to the world."
And just as that Goddess exists through the differentiation of her power of will (*śiva-śakti*), so too does the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) exist through its own differentiation.
The supreme deity is situated in the group beginning with *a*, while the Goddess is established in the groups beginning with *ka*.
Furthermore, the Lord Vināyaka is divided by the eight groups [of consonants].
Brahmā and the others are well-established in groups of seven within the vargas beginning with *ka*;
they are to be known as Īśvaras who bestow grace upon all.

Likewise, the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) should be understood as Mātṛkā, the Mother of the World. She withdraws the phonemes beginning with the letter *a*. She stands like a mother to the world, the expansion of sound. Because she manifests the knowledge of all objects, Mātṛkā is to be known as omniscient; she is the Mother of the World.

The Mātṛkā is the differentiation of one's own power (śakti). Through the Veda, which consists of the two deities Śiva and Śakti as the self-sustainers, it exists in the form of the letters beginning with 'a'. Just as it is, so too—because it manifests the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti)—it is known as the object of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti-jñeya*). Even for that which is extremely remote, there is no connection otherwise than through the ninefold [arrangement] within the letters beginning with 'a'.

Having understood that the vision of the deities, such as Śiva and Śakti, is established [within her], and that she bestows grace through [the words] beginning with "avetya" and ending with "anugrahakāriṇā," he states that the origin of the scripture occurs within Mātṛkā alone:
"Within her, however, everything consisting of speech, including the mobile and immobile, is born."
But having made that the basis [of his argument], the Deva says many things.

The Tantras, beginning with the Kāmika and so forth, are established in that number. This is easy to understand. Hereafter, something has been stated in some manner in the *Pramāṇapaṭala* (Chapter on the Means of Knowledge) during the introduction to the means of knowledge; in the chapter on the introduction to the body of the five mantras; and in the *Pāśapaṭala* (Chapter on Bonds) during the introduction to the examination of the power of *nāda*.
It should be understood that [the scripture] will be endowed with excellence. The sages said:
"Śiva, who was previously described as formless and devoid of the organ of speech, is not capable of composing the scriptures; therefore, he is [only] partial in that respect."

It is said that even Śiva is "vikala" (deficient) by implication, due to the characteristic of being the author of the scriptures; whereas [the other] is "sakala" (complete). By means of bestowing instruction through the composition of the scriptures, he indeed performs the functions of *kalā* and the other [categories], which constitute the state of having a body.

...because it is seen that [the power] of the gurus likewise exists in the state of being threefold; however, that [power] does not consist of unstable constituent parts (kalā). Even for the formless God, by virtue of the application of His own will and sovereign power...
All arrangement of letters and so forth would there be as if it were an actual effect.
However, that Lord is indeed entirely capable of being a giver of instruction;
and how he is so, in his entirety, I shall now explain.
Every undertaking is for the sake of man, because the Lord’s own body is incomplete;
that [body] becomes complete through the five [faces], beginning with Vāma, Aghora, and Nara.
That body of Parameṣṭhin is accompanied by mantras associated with Īśāna:
Īśāna is the head, Puruṣa is the face, Ghora is the heart, and Vāmadeva is the private parts.
This deity is recited as being possessed of all parts (sakala) even while manifesting in an immediate form;
yet his "possessing all parts" is not to be conceived as literal, just as it is not for the Self.

Since his worship cannot be otherwise [than through the body], and because there is the discarding of skin, bone, and so forth, he does not possess the status of being the author of the scriptures; therefore, he remains entirely [in this state].
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "In whatever manner Śiva possesses totality, in that same manner he is the giver of instruction.

Just as the self possesses totality from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), so too does that Śiva; however, this totality is not [inherent] in an ultimate sense, but must be conceptualized (*kalpanīya*). Otherwise, if even such a conceptualized totality were absent...

[It] does not exist. In that case, because this Śiva is formless (*anākāra*), there can be no worship of him; consequently, the discarding of skin, bones, and so forth [as a means of purification] is also untenable. Furthermore, his authorship of the scriptures, his status as a teacher, and his being an object of veneration are not logically possible. Therefore, he exists as *sakala* (with parts/attributes). He is firmly established as *sakala*, possessing the imagined skin, bones, and so forth, along with pride and the mountain [of ego]. The rest is easy to understand.

To the question of how many works have been composed by Śiva as a means for attaining the status of a Lord and so forth, he says: "By him, the means for achieving one's purpose was composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter in many crores— namely, in the form of Śaṅkhas, Padmas, Kharvas, and Nikharvas."

The number of [mantras] such as *parārtha* and so forth for the *Kāmika* and other [Tantras] should be understood according to their respective order within those texts; it is not written here by one fearing prolixity. The sages, from the standpoint of the Grammarians (*vaiyyākaraṇa*), raise this doubt: "Because phonemes (*varṇa*) perish in a moment, it is the *sphoṭa* that conveys meaning."
It is said that the all-pervading and eternal sphoṭa, manifested by the phonemes, reveals the meaning.
It bursts forth; that is, it manifests. The Lord [Śaṅkara] refutes this:
"There is no existence of a *sphoṭa* as a separate entity apart from the phonemes (*varṇa*).
And whether it is different or non-different from them, being neither different from them, it does not exist as a distinct object."
If there were no difference [between the word and its meaning] other than the phonemes themselves, then the cause for that [distinction] would not exist.

And that *sphoṭa*—which stands as if it were distinct from those [phonemes] and possessed of a different meaning—is not established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*). Now, if this is so, when the sound (*nāda*) manifested by the phonemes and denoting the object is conceptualized as being either different or non-different [from the phonemes], then of the different...

Because it is authoritative. How could that be established? True. *Nāda* is the power (*śakti*) whose nature is the subtle state of the phoneme (*varṇa*). Thus, it is established separately: "Having become the phoneme *ha*, I am named *svarṇa*; having become the phoneme *sa*, I am named *svarṇa*. Since this is established through experience by not differentiating the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*) as "haṃsa, haṃsa," there is no contradiction whatsoever. [Regarding] the phoneme...

And its being suggested (*vyaṅgyatva*) is like that of the sound residing in the respondent, not like that of the [original] sound. That has been stated by you as being produced from the *samu...* [conjunction]. In the examination of the power of sound (*nāda-śakti*), the sages, adopting the perspective of the Naiyāyikas, raise an objection once again:
The phonemes perish in each moment, yet the linguistic impression (*saṃskāra*) remains through them;
the final phoneme, conjoined with the impressions produced by the preceding phonemes, is the signifier.
Īśvara:
The phonemes do not enter into a composite whole by which that memory could occur.
If there is memory of that [whole], why do you abandon the object?

Therefore, there would be activity toward the object because the determination of the object arises from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*). True. Although the phonemes do not enter into a combination, nevertheless... [there arises] the recollection of the denoted object. Even if that were not a recollection, it would be a recollection if [it were based on] the phoneme as a whole.

The memory of that phoneme has the object as its referent; that is, it is the memory of the phoneme. How does it abandon [the phoneme]? It relies upon the gateway of that phoneme. Therefore, from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the determination of the object—although the recollection of the object might proceed by way of the memory of the phoneme—how is it that activity proceeds from that? To this [it is said]:
He said:
"The phoneme is a conditioned entity (saṃskāra) that possesses the capacity to accomplish a single object;
and by means of those phonemes endowed with such capacity, linguistic usage occurs through their expression of meaning."

The cognition of the perceiver is produced by the phonemes of the speaker's uttered sequence; this is the linguistic refinement (*saṃskāra*). When multiple meanings are present, it is that which expresses a single meaning. It is capable within a power (*śakti*) that possesses the capacity for comprehension and is designated by the term "relation. It is the experience of the final phoneme, arising from itself and producing its own [result].

It is capable [of denotation] by way of being the apprehender through the recollection of the phonemes (*varṇa*). By means of those phonemes—endowed with power, having grasped the denotable object, and combined—the linguistic usage characterized by "Let the cow be brought" and so forth occurs, through the phonemes which, as their own cause, give rise to the internal, blazing sounds that denote the object via the hearing of themselves. This [usage] is preceded by the cognition of "cow."

The ellipsis is "the activity of seeing and so forth is observed. [Objection: But if its connection is characterized by perception (*dṛk*), that is impossible; it would be like a hare's horn. To address this, he says: "Because it is easily apprehended, how could the connection between a word and its object not be certain? (p. 930)
For a word does not denote its own meaning unless it is divested of its connection [to that meaning].
[The previous section] is easy to understand. If one asks, "In that case, what is its definition? he says:
"There is no connection between cause and effect, because that [sound] arises from the cause of articulation;
sound is not established as an inherence residing in the mouth or revolving within the earth."
The relation between the probandum and the probans does not exist as something fixed by way of bondage;
rather, the relation known as that between the cognized and the means of cognition is preceded by an internal [mental] factor.

The relation of cause and effect is not the intended meaning here; therefore, the causal relationship is not a *yoga*. There is no connection here, because that object (*artha*) is not born from phonemes (*varṇa*), but rather is born from the cause of phonemes—that is, produced by space, air, and so forth, which are the instrumental causes of the phonemes. A relation of inherence (*samavāya*) between the phoneme and the object is not established, because...
On the ground that the object resides in the meaning and the word resides in the mouth, it must be supplied [in the argument] that even the relationship of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is not established.
"The means of proof and the object to be proven do not exist as a bond... established," just like the two relationships mentioned previously;
[therefore, it is] well-established. As it has been said:

In some cases, the property-bearer (*dharmin*) is established by means of the property (*dharma*), and in other cases, the cause is established by means of the effect; and in yet other cases, the effect is established by means of the cause. If this is so, what then is called the "concluded relation" (*paryavasita-sambandha*)? It is that which is preceded by internal [reflection], preceded by the discernment of conventions and the like, and which consists of the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*jñāpya-jñāpaka*).

The connection has already been indicated previously. "O best of the twice-born, that by which the six categories, beginning with Pati, are known—that is called the Jñānapāda. Thus, it does not establish a connection based on the literal sound of the words, but rather expresses the meaning according to the definition provided. Therefore, the person [attains] his own activity... having attained the object through the connection...
Where a connector is remembered, the word is employed by the intellect as if impelled by him;
in that case, the word would not be the connector, but the person would be the connector.

The ascetic [continues]: "In that regard, the convention (*saṃketa*) of mantras was established by Śiva. Whatever phoneme is known by someone for a particular meaning, that [phoneme] is the designator (*vācaka*) of that meaning;
however, one who is devoid of the convention of others does not grasp that much of a meaning."
The secret signs and mantras have not been fully proclaimed;
they are indeed established along with their substances in the Kāmika and other scriptures.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the commentary on the venerable *Pauṣkarajñānapāda* composed by the teacher Jñānaprakāśācārya, a resident of Śrīśālivāṭipura.

Hariḥ Om! Salutations to the venerable Gurus who illuminate the wisdom of the illustrious Devaka. May there be auspiciousness! [This concerns] those who, though bound by the specific fetters of initiation, are radiant with the qualities of a self that is directly equal to Śiva.
For those distressed by the burden of carrying the body and so forth, the supreme state— which is the cause of ultimate welfare— is attained through the falling away of the body.

Having meditated upon Sadāśiva, one should receive [the water] with the hands joined in añjali while reciting the root mantra. Having first performed three rounds of the Śivagāyatrī with the hands joined in añjali, [the ritual] should be carried out.
Afterwards, having offered the arghya with the Śiva-mantra ending in svāhā, one should mutter the root mantra and the Brahmāṅgas once.

The propitiation of the mantra-deities and others. In the year Saumya, [in the month of] Paṅkuni... during an auspicious conjunction, for the sake of service to Śālivāṭīśvara, the resident of the city of Śrī-Śālivāṭipura, [this is] the Taittapauṣkara.
